articles.title: Forget GPU heists: police say someone used a bomb hidden in an Xbox 360 to sabotage a rival
articles.text:
A hot potato: The most noteworthy crimes involving electronics vendors usually involve GPU and server equipment theft, scams involving swapped GPU and RAM components, or cyberattacks. Many of these also tend to involve the AI boom these days, but a recent case in Brazil centers on something much more direct and low-tech – hiding a bomb inside an Xbox to eliminate the competition.
Police in Santo André, near São Paulo, have arrested a local businessman on suspicion of attempting to assassinate a potential competitor by rigging an Xbox 360 to explode inside the rival's shop on the day of its grand opening. No one was killed in the blast, which was caught on camera, but the store was left heavily damaged.
According to Brazilian media (via Dexerto), police suspect Everton Yoshizumi Lima, 39, of arranging for a rigged Xbox 360 to be delivered to the targeted store under the pretext that it needed modifications to play games.
Security footage captures the moment two people, including the store's owner, notice something is wrong and try to flee the building seconds before it explodes. Despite being caught in the blast, which damaged furniture and equipment and tore into the ceiling, both escaped with seemingly minor injuries.
Earlier footage shows a delivery driver dropping off the sabotaged console, which the owner placed in a drawer. The bomb hidden inside went off about 40 minutes later, and police believe the driver had no idea what he was transporting.
 – g1 (@g1) November 16, 2026
Forensic analysis found two pressurized flammable liquid cylinders and a timer, allegedly meant to kill the shop owner, but only one of the two charges detonated.
Police suspect Lima was trying to eliminate incoming competition. He owns three electronics stores, two of them on the street where the bombing occurred. The previous owner of that property also reported being sabotaged, but didn't link the incident to Lima.
Interestingly, Lima was arrested while being investigated in connection with a much more minor matter – a possibly stolen motorcycle. After police encountered him at his business, a check of his records turned up an outstanding arrest warrant tied to the bombing. He is now being investigated for attempted aggravated murder with an explosive device.

articles.title: Intesa Sanpaolo Cuts ATM Costs With Quantum-Inspired Algorithms- EE Times
articles.text:
An ATM running out of cash is a problem customers notice immediately. Keeping too much money inside it creates a quieter problem for the bank: Funds sit idle, while replenishment visits add costs. Across hundreds of machines, deciding how much cash to deliver, where, and when becomes a substantial optimization challenge.
Intesa Sanpaolo claimed double-digit cost reductions from a new approach, without compromising service levels. The work emerged from the Italian banking group’s quantum computing research. The calculations, however, run entirely on classical GPUs.
That apparent contradiction gets to the heart of quantum-inspired computing. Researchers can borrow ideas from quantum algorithms and find useful ways to apply them on existing hardware. Whether a quantum processor will eventually improve on those results is a separate question.
According to Davide Corbelletto, quantum specialist and team leader of Intesa Sanpaolo’s Quantum Competence Center, what changed was the approach. “It’s a shift in the way you model the problem you’re trying to solve,” he told EE Times.
A new way of looking at the problem
Intesa selected ATM cash replenishment as a proving ground because it combined business relevance with technical suitability. Its broader outsourced network exceeds 1,000 ATMs. The bank validated the optimization system using a real network comprising hundreds of machines.
Using historical data, the team compared its approach against operational strategies and traditional optimization methods previously employed. Measures included costs, service levels, and the risk of machines running out of cash.
The team expressed the problem as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization, or QUBO, model. Decisions become binary variables, with their costs and interactions combined into an objective for a solver to optimize.
Corbelletto described quantum-inspired computing as starting with an approach conceived for quantum hardware, then reformulating it for classical execution. The adaptation may not deliver all the advantages anticipated from a future quantum implementation. It can nevertheless offer something useful today.
“But if this limited version of the solution is better than the classical one you were using, you still have a kind of advantage,” he said. “And that’s precisely what we demonstrated with the ATM cash flow optimization.”
The bank uses GPU-accelerated classical solvers. Corbelletto also identified FPGAs and specialized ASICs as possible platforms for quantum-inspired methods, depending on the application.
The reported savings establish improvement over Intesa’s previous approach. However, they don’t demonstrate quantum computational advantage or establish that a future quantum implementation will outperform the strongest classical alternatives.
Inspiration without quantum hardware
Banking is not the only area where quantum-inspired algorithms are being developed. A similar path appears in engineering research at TU Delft, although the mathematics differs.
In an interview with EE Times, Matthias Möller, a professor and applied mathematician, described composite material design as a problem involving discrete choices: Successive laminate layers can be oriented at different angles, creating a combinatorial optimization challenge.
The team he’s part of began work with a quantum algorithm and developed it into a quantum-inspired implementation using matrix product states, or MPS. He said Airbus is supporting further research to scale the initially academic work toward practical applications.
The terminology can suggest something exotic happening inside the computer. Möller offered a simpler description: “There’s no quantum magic in it. It just takes inspiration from how a quantum computer would work.”
MPS and the broader family of tensor-network techniques predate the current interest in quantum computing. Möller sees quantum research bringing renewed attention to them, including in computational fluid dynamics. Those methods can run on graphics cards or other classical hardware, although he cautioned that the CFD approaches he discussed are not production-ready.
Their usefulness must ultimately be judged against the application’s requirements. In discussing quantum algorithms, Möller argued that the benefit must be provable. That could mean faster computation or, in optimization, a guaranteed better solution.
Quantum-inspired methods offer a way to explore useful approaches on classical hardware today. Establishing where quantum computers themselves will excel remains an open research challenge, with progress needed in the algorithms as well as the machines.
“It’s not only hardware that has to evolve,” Möller said. “It’s also the algorithm or application side. There are some really hard nuts to be cracked there too.”
The whole workflow counts
For Intesa, the test begins with the ATM system. Quantum-inspired methods have already improved its cash replenishment calculations on GPUs, giving the bank a working solution against which to assess future quantum hardware. Introducing a quantum processor would require evidence of further gains across the banking process.
“Quantum hardware must demonstrate a clear end-to-end advantage in concrete optimization tasks, taking into account problem size, execution times, reliability, and integration with existing classical workflows,” Corbelletto said. For the bank, the relevant measure is whether the complete process improves.
“Preparing the data, encoding it, interfacing with classical systems, and extracting usable results may ultimately cost more than the quantum computation itself,” Corbelletto said. “Quantum computing will become commercially relevant only when the advantage survives the entire workflow and not just a benchmarked kernel of the algorithm.”
The challenge therefore extends beyond reproducing the ATM calculation on different hardware. A quantum implementation must earn its place against the available alternatives, including continuing improvements in classical optimization.
Even clearing that performance hurdle would leave another obstacle. A bank cannot build an operational dependency around a calculation that works only when experimental equipment happens to be available. Corbelletto argued that technical advances must be accompanied by sufficient capacity and dependable access.
“From an industrial perspective, the challenge lies not only in building a better quantum computer but in deploying enough of them to both guarantee high service levels for customers and comply with regulatory requirements regarding business continuity,” he said.
Classical hardware gives Intesa a route to service arrangements appropriate to its operations. Future quantum offerings must satisfy those operational requirements alongside the computational ones.
Preparing for the customer’s test
Intesa continues investigating applications spanning credit risk, fraud detection, derivatives pricing, and portfolio optimization. Corbelletto identified portfolio optimization as a candidate for nearer-term production because the team has developed a promising quantum-inspired prototype.
The bank also experiments across hardware platforms rather than selecting a presumed winning architecture. “Our starting point is always the business need rather than the hardware platform,” Corbelletto said.
Its ATM work provides a practical reason to continue. Investigating quantum methods can produce benefits before suitable quantum hardware arrives. But those benefits also establish a benchmark for the machines that follow.
“The key milestone will not be a laboratory record but a real-world banking use case where the quantum advantage survives the entire workflow, from data preparation to business outcome, and can be reproduced reliably,” Corbelletto said.
“That would be a much stronger signal than any individual hardware announcement.”

Tuesday, November 17th 2026
Geometric Future Introduces the Eskimo Ultra 42 AIO and Squama Ultimate 3003-14 Fans
Geometric Future, an innovative PC components and peripherals brand, expands its cooling lineup with the launch of high-performance Eskimo Ultra 42 AIO and Squama Ultimate 3003-14 fans. The Eskimo Ultra 42 features a 420 mm radiator, a 2600 RPM pump (1.5 L/min), and a 55.8 x 55.8 mm copper coldplate. Its CNC-machined aluminium housing has a mirror top with ARGB lighting. It includes three interlocking 30 mm-thick Squama Ultimate 3003-14 fans. Also sold separately, these fans deliver up to 106.27 CFM airflow and 4.72 mmH2O pressure using a patented daisy-chaining system. They feature Fluid Dynamic Bearings, a 3-phase 6-pole motor, 800-2400 RPM PWM control, ARGB lighting, and standard or reverse airflow options for high performance and clean cable management.
The Eskimo Ultra 42 is a performance-focused 420 mm liquid cooler designed for both cooling capacity and refined presentation. Its 27 mm aluminium radiator is paired with three 140 mm Squama Ultimate fans, and the pump block features a large, pure-copper contact surface that efficiently transfers heat from the CPU. The CNC-machined, anodized aluminium housing gives the cooler a premium finish, complemented by a mirror-like top surface and a narrow, diffused ARGB accent that adds lighting without overwhelming the overall design.Squama Ultimate 3003-14
The Squama Ultimate 3003-14 is a 140 mm performance fan with a 30 mm thick frame and a 9-blade design, producing up to 106.27 CFM of airflow and 4.72 mmH2O static pressure. It features a patented interconnect system for daisy-chaining multiple fans, Fluid Dynamic Bearings, a three-phase, six-pole motor, and PWM control. Geometric Future's ARGB lighting surrounds the frame, providing a soft glow that enhances the design without overpowering the build. Compatible motherboard software supports synchronization. Available in black and white, with standard and reverse airflow options.

articles.title: Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference
Serving large language models (LLMs) efficiently requires sufficient GPU memory and careful coordination of prompt processing and token generation. GLM-5.3’s FP8 weights, for example, exceed the 640 GB of GPU memory on a single ml.p5.48xlarge instance, before accounting for KV cache and runtime overhead. Long prompts can also slow token generation when both share the same GPUs.
Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference now supports NVIDIA Dynamo, combining Dynamo’s distributed inference capabilities with the infrastructure management of HyperPod to address these challenges. Dynamo is an open source distributed inference framework that supports multi-node deployment, disaggregated prefill and decode, and KV-aware routing with engines such as vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM. HyperPod supports these deployments with high-performance Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking, coordinated GPU scheduling, and node health monitoring and recovery. In this post, we illustrate multi-node and disaggregated serving through a deployment example, share benchmark results, and outline best practices for optimizing inference on HyperPod.
How the integration works
The HyperPod Inference add-on installs the Dynamo custom resource definitions and these serving and scheduling components:
- HyperPod Inference Operator manages endpoint deployment through an InferenceEndpointConfig (IEC) custom resource. Its dynamoSpec section supplies the Dynamo configuration.
- Dynamo operator manages resources defined in a DynamoGraphDeployment (DGD), including the frontend, model workers, replica counts, and resource requirements.
- Grove coordinates related groups of pods, including multi-node workers, and their scaling relationships.
- Kubernetes AI (KAI) Scheduler places pods on GPU resources, using gang scheduling to schedule the pods required for a multi-node worker together.
AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) provide the Dynamo runtime, while the add-on manages integrated component versions. To adopt a supported Dynamo release, update the add-on.
Deployment architecture
The following diagram shows the deployment paths, serving components, and infrastructure management for disaggregated inference on SageMaker HyperPod. The Dynamo frontend routes requests to prefill workers, which process prompts, and decode workers, which generate tokens. These separate pools allow independent scaling and tuning. Both pools load the full model weights, and KV cache transfers between them over EFA.
Dynamo also supports aggregated serving, where prefill and decode run in the same worker. In either topology, workers can run on one instance or span multiple instances using tensor and pipeline parallelism. Dynamo’s KV-aware router considers reusable prefix KV cache and active worker load in both topologies. Prefix reuse can reduce prompt recomputation and improve time to first token, while load awareness helps avoid overloading workers. For more details on the Dynamo architecture, see the Dynamo Knowledge Base overview.
HyperPod provides node, GPU, and EFA health monitoring and manages node replacement, while the orchestration components recreate affected workers. Deployments configured through InferenceEndpointConfig with dynamoSpec support invocation through SageMaker endpoints.
Two ways to configure your deployment
Whether you are new to HyperPod, new to Dynamo, or both, the add-on offers two deployment paths to fit your workflow:
Bring-your-own DynamoGraphDeployment (DGD) lets existing Dynamo users continue using upstream documentation, recipes, and manifests, with the Dynamo operator managing the deployment. To bring an existing DGD to HyperPod, use a supported container image and configure storage, networking, and pod placement for your cluster.
InferenceEndpointConfig with dynamoSpec lets existing HyperPod Inference users deploy a new Dynamo endpoint using the same configuration format and OpenAI-compatible interface they already know. For the inference engine, you can choose vLLM, SGLang, or TensorRT-LLM, with vLLM used by default. The operator also supplies defaults for KV-aware routing and replica counts.
Both paths support single-instance and multi-node deployments. In either case, HyperPod manages node health and replacement. The table summarizes the responsibilities for each path.
|  | Bring-your-own DGD | InferenceEndpointConfig with dynamoSpec | 
| You write | Complete DGD manifest | IEC containing dynamoSpec | 
| Best for | Teams wanting direct control of the serving graph or reuse of existing DGDs | Teams wanting managed endpoint setup through IEC | 
| Model weights | You configure downloading or mounting the weights | The operator stages weights from Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon FSx | 
| Endpoint, TLS, registration | You configure and manage these resources | Managed through the HyperPod Inference Operator | 
| Autoscaling | You configure and manage scaling | Kubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling (KEDA) through autoScalingSpec for aggregated and disaggregated deployments | 
Deployment example: GLM-5.3
The following excerpts use the InferenceEndpointConfig (IEC) deployment path with vLLM on ml.p5.48xlarge instances. Dynamo-specific settings belong under spec.dynamoSpec. Model source and endpoint settings are included in the complete manifest.
Multi-node aggregated serving
This configuration runs one model-worker replica across two instances (16 GPUs), with two frontend replicas for request handling. Setting dynamoSpec.frontend.routingMode to kv-aware turns on KV-aware routing.
Here, spec.replicas controls the number of model-worker replicas, while frontend.replicas controls the number of frontend replicas.
Multi-node disaggregated serving
Replace aggregation under spec.dynamoSpec with the following disaggregation block, keeping the preceding frontend configuration. Replica counts are set separately for prefill and decode. This example runs one prefill replica and two decode replicas, each spanning two instances, for a total of six instances.
Apply the deployment
Apply the complete manifest with kubectl apply. The HyperPod Inference Operator makes the configured model weights available to the workers and generates the DGD. Grove and KAI Scheduler coordinate placement so that the pods required for each multi-node worker are scheduled together.
After the SageMaker endpoint is ready and configured for chat completions, clients can send an OpenAI-compatible request payload through the SageMaker Runtime API:
Benchmarks
We benchmarked Dynamo on SageMaker HyperPod across two models to compare serving configurations.
Disaggregated prefill and decode for Qwen3-235B
We used AIPerf to compare aggregated and disaggregated serving for Qwen3-235B-A22B-FP8 using Dynamo with TensorRT-LLM on two p5en.48xlarge instances (16 H200 GPUs). Requests contained 4,000 input tokens and 200 output tokens. We retained measured points that met two targets: P90 time to first token below one second, and median generation speed of at least 50 tokens per second per user. Among these points, disaggregated serving achieved 2.05× the highest aggregated throughput: 207 versus 101 output tokens per second per GPU, at concurrency 80 and 32, respectively.
Multi-node aggregated serving for Qwen3.5-397B
Dynamo supports multi-node serving in both aggregated and disaggregated modes for models that exceed a single instance’s GPU memory. To evaluate a worker spanning nodes, we used AIPerf to benchmark multi-node aggregated serving for Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8 with Dynamo and vLLM, using TP4 × PP2 and eight active H200 GPUs. This model fits on one instance, so in practice you would not split it. It serves here as a controlled baseline. We compared eight GPUs on one p5en.48xlarge against four GPUs on each of two instances, using the same model, parallelism, and workload configuration. With an agentic workload featuring high prefix reuse at concurrency 32, the two-node configuration delivered 126.4 output tokens per second per GPU, retaining 99.1 percent of single-node throughput. This shows that Dynamo on SageMaker HyperPod can serve a model that needs more than one instance across nodes. The node boundary itself does not become a significant throughput penalty.
Best practices for optimized inference
NVIDIA Dynamo provides recipes and tools to help you select a serving configuration, benchmark performance, and tune your deployment on SageMaker HyperPod.
- Start with a matching recipe – Choose a Dynamo recipe for your model, inference engine, and GPU type. Account for model weights, KV cache, and runtime memory when sizing workers. For supported configurations, AISimulate can help compare aggregated and disaggregated serving, choose parallelism, and size prefill and decode worker pools before testing on GPUs.
- Verify communication before benchmarking – For deployments spanning instances, confirm that communication uses the intended EFA transport, including KV-cache transfers between prefill and decode workers. See the Dynamo EFA guide.
- Benchmark representative traffic – Replay your traffic with AIPerf, or use a generated agentic trace with representative prompt lengths, output lengths, and prefix reuse. Sweep concurrency for each configuration, retain points meeting your SLAs, and choose based on cost and latency priorities.
- Tune from measured bottlenecks – Adjust topology and worker allocation before engine settings, changing one variable at a time. Follow the performance tuning guide, or use Dynamo optimization agent skills to assist with benchmarking and tuning. Validate each candidate on your target HyperPod deployment.
Conclusion
NVIDIA Dynamo on SageMaker HyperPod Inference simplifies deploying and operating large models with multi-node serving, disaggregated prefill and decode, and KV-aware routing. The managed add-on installs the serving components, and configuration defaults simplify endpoint setup. HyperPod manages model weights, auto-scales clusters based on GPU and inference metrics, monitors node health, and replaces failed nodes. Together, these capabilities reduce undifferentiated infrastructure work so teams can focus on their models and applications. Get started with the setup instructions and complete deployment examples in the linked repository.

articles.title: San Diego dumps both Flock cameras and smart streetlights
articles.text:
On Monday evening, San Diego’s city council voted to end its contracts with two surveillance equipment vendors, Flock and Ubicquia. San Diego is one of the largest cities to end its relationship with Flock, the startup with an estimated valuation of $8.3 billion.
“We fucking won!” said Lilly Irani of the Transparent and Responsible Use of Surveillance Technology (TRUST) SD Coalition, speaking in her personal capacity.
She and her colleagues have been among the loudest critics in recent years.
“The national energy creating left and right and center coalitions was the major cause [of the political victory],” she said, noting that it was only last month that one of the councilmembers revoked his support, creating an opening for a political majority to halt the surveillance.
That council member, Stephen Whitburn, said in an October press conference that he wanted his fellow citizens to “feel safe.”
“If Flock cameras are causing many San Diegans to feel unsafe, then they have lost effectiveness as a public safety tool,” he said at the time.
After the Monday vote, San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria said in a social media post that he “respect[ed] the Council’s decision” and would not veto the move to stop operation of the cameras across the city.
Andrew Smith, a spokesperson for Flock, told Ars in an email on Tuesday that the company also “respect[s] the city’s decision.” But Flock isn’t happy about it. “When a tool that is actively helping solve violent crimes is removed, public safety moves backward,” Smith wrote. “That has real consequences: cases will take longer to solve, organized retail theft crews will operate with fewer obstacles, a missing child may not be returned home, and victims may wait longer, or indefinitely, for justice.”

articles.title: Nvidia’s startup stakes ballooned to $65B, but Huang’s exit puts future deals in doubt | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Nvidia’s equity in private companies continues to grow: it revealed its stakes are now worth $65.5 billion on Tuesday, up from the $22 billion reported in January. The increase includes both new investments and significant markups of existing portfolio companies.
The company invested $16 billion into equities in the past quarter alone, it said, and $58 billion in the past nine months of its fiscal year. This amount includes buying shares in public and private companies, yet it shows how the chipmaker made massive bets over the course of the year, especially compared to last year; in November 2025, the company reported spending $5 billion buying equity in the first nine months of that fiscal year.
But it’s unclear if this growth will continue under the interim CEO and Jensen Huang’s successor.
Nvidia stated in late 2023 that the goal of its corporate investing is to expand the AI ecosystem by backing startups it considers to be “game changers and market makers.” Over the nearly three years that followed, the chipmaker has invested in nearly 350 startups, according to PitchBook. The companies Nvidia backed include Anthropic, OpenAI; neolabs like Thinking Machines and Reflection; neoclouds, like Lambda, Nscale, and Crusoe; as well as other companies developing AI infrastructure, robotics startups, and applications.
It’s also become a big financier of the data center build out, reporting $118 billion in guarantees with $105 billion of that the backstop it supplied for OpenAI’s $500 billion data center in Ohio.
The company made those commitments by allocating a meaningful portion of its excess cash flows. In Tuesday’s earning call, Kress said Nvidia would continue providing financing assistance to strong customers and that “as the market matures and additional sources of capital become available,” the company would be “rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees.”
But the question for the VC ecosystem is whether the company will continue to back startups at anywhere near the same level without Huang at the helm.
Huang’s rampant dealmaking has reportedly been a source of concern for Kress. Investors have told TechCrunch that they anticipate that she will take a more conservative approach to startup investing, becoming more selective with new investments and writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio companies.
“We intend to return all excess free cash flow net of strategic uses to shareholders during this last quarter and going forward,” Kress said on the earnings call on Tuesday. Just how strategic startups will be under her leadership, and under the future permanent CEO, remains to be seen. But for now, VCs are bracing for a meaningful pullback in capital.

articles.title: Autonomous orchestration helps Kubernetes keep up with AI agents - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Idle, then spiking: Why AI agents are breaking Kubernetes resource planning
AI agents are changing the economics of cloud infrastructure, and autonomous orchestration is becoming the way platform teams keep up. Agentic workloads sit idle and then spike without warning. That pattern leaves static resource settings either wasteful or likely to fail.
Container orchestration for AI is fast becoming the backbone of production AI, and agents are adding a new layer of strain. Compute costs are climbing and reliability problems are harder to contain because everything an agent does ultimately runs on CPU and memory, according to Yodar Shafrir (pictured), founder and chief executive officer of ScaleOps Inc.
“Agents and all the agent workloads pretty much made everything way more complex when managing infrastructure,” Shafrir said. “Eventually, all the complexity that existed before just got much worse. Today, the compute cost has grown dramatically. Everything that agents execute eventually runs on compute.”
Shafrir spoke with theCUBE Research’s Paul Nashawaty and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how autonomous orchestration lets ScaleOps adjust resources in real time as AI agents spike, cutting both costs and crashes. (* Disclosure below.)
Why autonomous orchestration fits the agentic era
Agents behave differently from traditional microservices. An agent waits for a human or another agent, checks with a large language model and then runs its task in a burst. Teams must provision for the highest spike while the agent holds its memory the whole time, Shafrir explained. When resources fall short, a crashed step has to rerun and burns tokens all over again.
“We actually see that agents crash due to not having enough resources 80% more often compared with traditional microservices,” Shafrir said. “The reliability is much harder to manage.”
For ScaleOps, the answer is to make resource decisions in real time. It adjusts allocations, replicas and node placement for every application, agent and Model Context Protocol server, which the company says cuts cloud costs by 70% to 80%. Customers such as Adobe Inc. and Salesforce Inc. build trust by first running the platform in read-only mode on their hardest environments, according to Shafrir.
“We understand for every application: What is it connected to? What does it communicate with? What is the business state of every application?” Shafrir said. “We learn from historical patterns.”
ScaleOps has also added a capability that lets other workloads use an agent’s resources while it sits idle. It also uses memory swap so an agent gets memory only when it needs it. The company says this makes running agents 90% more cost-efficient without moving off Kubernetes. Given the cost of always-on agents, Shafrir sees autonomous orchestration as the only workable model.
“We are now in a phase where humans and all the traditional scaling capabilities that existed in the past are pretty much irrelevant for today’s world because they’re too static and they require a human to go and configure them,” Shafrir said. “When things are so dynamic, it no longer works the same way.”

articles.title: J'ai pris des photos avec le Xiaomi 18 Pro Max : ça claque, mais j'ai quelques réserves
articles.text:
En amont de la présentation officielle du nouveau fleuron de Xiaomi, 01net a été invité essayer le 18 Pro Max et son fameux écran arrière. Le test complet du smartphone devrait suivre dans les jours qui viennent avec les habituelles mesures du 01lab, et nos commentaires, bien entendu, mais voici déjà un premier avis sur la partie photo du smartphone premium.
https://www.youtube.com/shorts/3VX7iJIqPmc
Commençons dans l’ordre en évoquant la configuration photo :
- Module grand-angle de 200 Mpx, 23 mm, ouverture f/1,67 ;
- Module ultra-grand-angle de 50 Mpx, 17 mm, ouverture f/2,4 ;
- Module téléobjectif de 200 Mpx, 75 mm, équivalent x3,4, ouverture f/2,4.
Nous avons donc une fiche technique digne d’un smartphone haut de gamme avec son double 200 Mpx. Seul le module ultra grand angle est légèrement en retrait sur le papier. La présence d’un téléobjectif avec capteur de 200 Mpx offre la possibilité de zoomer numériquement sans perte jusqu’à X12,8. Une belle polyvalence et donc un beau joujou pour la street photographie.
Comme vous pouvez le voir, on retrouve la pâte Leica avec ses ombres marquées, son tein légèrement jaune assumé et son excellent piqué. Le tout ne manque pas de caractère.
J’ai particulièrement apprécié le jeu sur la dynamique et sur les ombres, qui permet de poser une ambiance très facilement sur un cliché. La présence d’un bon zoom permet aussi d’attraper des moments de vie comme un vélo passant devant une bouche métro.
Un peu trop de personnalisation ?
En revanche, la firme chinoise va peut être un peu loin dans la personnalisation à mon avis. Il y a trois modes colorimétriques. Deux sont siglés Leica, Leica Vibrant et Leica Authentic et un est appelé Style Original. Celui-ci est le petit dernier fraichement arrivé. Il a pour mission de proposer une expérience photographique qui s’éloigne un peu de la pâte Leica, pour celles et ceux qui y seraient allergiques.
Voici à quoi ressemble les trois modes sur une même scène avec dans l’ordre le mode Original, puis le mode Vibrant et Authentic.
De façon tout à fait personnel, j’ai une petite préférence pour le mode Leica Authentic, qui conserve le petit style Leica, mais de façon un peu moins agressive.
Le mode portrait du smartphone est plutôt efficace, mais là aussi, il offre beaucoup trop de possibilités, ce qui oblige à pas mal jouer avec avant de trouver quelque chose de satisfaisant. Vous pouvez, par exemple, ajuster le Bokeh, mais aussi modifier la forme de petites bulles de lumière à l’arrière, ou encore ajuster la colorimétrie. Lorsque l’on pousse l’ouverture jusqu’à f/2.0, soit une ouverture simulée très large, le détourage me semble trop agressif et peu naturel. C’est sans doute la raison pour laquelle le mode portrait propose par défaut de démarrer à f/4.0.
 👉🏻 Suivez l’actualité tech en temps réel : ajoutez 01net à vos sources sur Google, et abonnez-vous à notre canal WhatsApp.

articles.title: Fatehpuria Hygiene secures Rs 100 Cr in first equity fundraise
articles.text:
Fatehpuria Hygiene secures Rs 100 Cr in first equity fundraise
The company will use the funds to expand into more than 50 cities over the next 24 months and strengthen its warehousing, distribution and AI-enabled supply chain infrastructure.
Fatehpuria Hygiene, a trading, supply chain and fulfilment company, has raised Rs 100 crore in its first equity fundraise, led by investor Madhu Kela.
The company said it plans to use the capital to strengthen its nationwide presence and build a technology-driven supply chain ecosystem. It aims to expand into more than 50 major cities over the next 24 months and develop an AI-enabled, integrated supply chain network.
The expansion strategy will focus on strengthening warehousing infrastructure, enhancing technology capabilities, scaling distribution networks and developing end-to-end fulfilment solutions to meet the evolving requirements of brands and retail platforms.
Founded in 2017 by Gautam Fatehpuria, the company has established a warehousing, distribution and fulfilment network across 16 states. Its clientele includes Unilever, Wipro, Kimberly-Clark, Flipkart, Amazon, Myntra, Zepto, Swiggy Instamart, Blinkit, DMart, Meesho and FirstCry.
“Over the years, we have grown by focusing on strong execution, operational efficiency and long-term partnerships with leading brands and commerce platforms. This fundraise is an important validation of the business we have built and the opportunity ahead. We see significant potential in transforming India's supply chain ecosystem through deeper technology integration, stronger infrastructure and more efficient fulfilment capabilities,” said Gautam Fatehpuria, founder, Fatehpuria Hygiene.
“Fatehpuria Hygiene has built a strong business backed by execution capabilities, deep industry relationships and a scalable operating model. We believe the company is well-positioned to capitalise on India's growing demand for integrated, technology-led supply chain solutions,” said Madhu Kela.
As brands expand their geographical reach and adapt to changing consumer expectations, integrated warehousing, distribution and fulfilment networks are becoming increasingly important to their operations.

articles.title: Meta lanza Direct, una plataforma para hablar con amigos en Instagram sin tener la aplicación
articles.text:
Meta lanzó Direct, una aplicación independiente que reúne solo los mensajes directos de Instagram. Está disponible en Android y iOS, por ahora únicamente en Turquía y Tailandia, y se puede usar con o sin una cuenta de Instagram.
La empresa no dijo cuándo ni si llevará la app a otros países. TechCrunch la describe como una prueba (“testing”) y señala que el lanzamiento inicial se limita a esos dos mercados.
Meta presenta Direct como un espacio para conversar de a uno o en grupos con amigos y familiares. Los usuarios de Instagram pueden entrar con su nombre de usuario y contraseña, y sus conversaciones se sincronizan entre las dos aplicaciones.
Engadget describió que la disposición de la bandeja es casi idéntica a la de Instagram, con los chats existentes trasladados si el usuario entra con sus credenciales de esa red.
Quien no tiene Instagram puede registrarse con un correo electrónico o un número de teléfono. El medio 9to5Google señaló que, en ese caso, el usuario solo puede recibir mensajes: sus contactos deben iniciar la conversación y la edad mínima es de 13 años.
Los usuarios sin cuenta de Instagram deben agregar contactos de forma manual, mediante el nombre de usuario o un código QR, para poder empezar a conversar, un sistema similar que se parece al de los nombres de usuario de WhatsApp.
Qué ofrece la app y qué cambia respecto de Instagram
Direct incluye funciones habituales de mensajería, como reacciones, notas de voz y emojis. Además tiene “Draw”, que permite dibujar dentro de la conversación, y “Notes”, las actualizaciones breves que aparecen en la parte superior de la bandeja de mensajes de Instagram.
También permite crear stickers propios, añadir efectos de audio a las respuestas, como risas de multitud o sonidos bajo el agua, y cambiar el fondo del chat con temas visuales. Según 9to5Google, la app usa la misma estructura que los mensajes de Instagram, pero sale en una aplicación propia.
TechCrunch interpreta que Meta busca retener a quienes usan Instagram sobre todo para chatear. Ese medio añade que la nueva app le permite a la empresa contar a esas personas como usuarios activos aunque no abran Instagram. Meta no formuló esa explicación.
Controles para adolescentes y padres
Meta afirmó que solo los contactos o personas ya conectadas pueden iniciar una conversación o sumar a alguien a un grupo. Los usuarios pueden denunciar, bloquear, restringir o eliminar contactos en cualquier momento.
La empresa dijo que usará su tecnología de estimación de edad para detectar interacciones potencialmente inapropiadas con menores. Los padres tendrán herramientas para ver con quién chatea su hijo, ajustar la configuración de seguridad y fijar límites diarios de uso. Los adolescentes que entren con su cuenta de Instagram mantendrán las restricciones de mensajes de las Cuentas para Adolescentes.
No es el primer intento de Instagram con una app de mensajes aparte. Digital Trends recordó que, según informó Reuters en su momento, la red probó una aplicación Direct independiente en seis países en diciembre de 2017, entre ellos Turquía, y que Facebook la cerró en 2019 y devolvió los chats a Instagram.
Meta probó una app de predicciones donde se apuesta con puntos
Meta prueba entre empleados una aplicación de mercados de predicción llamada Takes, donde se apuesta con puntos (“cred”) y no con dinero real, según The Wall Street Journal.
A diferencia de Kalshi y Polymarket, que operan con dinero real, Takes solo usa puntos: acertar suma cred y errar lo resta. Entre las preguntas probadas figuró si Tim Cook sucederá a Jensen Huang en Nvidia.
El proyecto, conocido en junio como Arena, surgió por pedido de Mark Zuckerberg. Meta no descartaba entonces permitir apuestas reales más adelante.
Mientras tanto, Kalshi y Polymarket enfrentan demandas estatales que las acusan de juego ilegal. El presidente de la CFTC, Michael Selig, criticó esos cargos penales y pidió que el debate llegue a la Corte Suprema: “Eso no es algo que deba poner a nadie en riesgo de ir a la cárcel”.

articles.title: NVIDIA Establishes National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee
articles.text:
Tuesday, November 17th 2026
NVIDIA Establishes National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee
NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today announced that the Board of Directors has established the National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, a new standing committee responsible for board-level oversight of the company's national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management. NVIDIA's existing National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team will report directly to the Committee and to Interim CEO, Colette Kress, on day-to-day operations.
The Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and will also include directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members. It will meet at least quarterly, including with management and in executive session. The Committee will oversee the Company's ongoing efforts to enhance its internal National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team, and work closely with independent third-party experts in law, national security and global trade compliance."NVIDIA recognizes that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security. As the world's leading advanced computing company, NVIDIA has both a responsibility and an opportunity to lead the industry in addressing these challenges. We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation," said Harvey Jones, Chairman of NVIDIA's Board of Directors.
The decision to create this new committee reflects the Board's further commitment to enhance its engagement with relevant government stakeholders, and to demonstrate the highest standards of governance and oversight.

articles.title: Reducing token costs and latency in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore JSON workloads | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Reducing token costs and latency in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore JSON workloads
As enterprises build production agents with dozens of tools and large structured inputs, token consumption and latency become the primary blockers to a good user experience. When these agents process large JSON data, every additional tool invocation injects the full payload into the large language model (LLM) context window, causing token usage and response latency to spike. Over multi-turn conversations, this pressure compounds, driving up costs and degrading response quality. Effectively managing context-window pressure in agentic systems is key to reliability and responsiveness at scale. In this post, we share three composable strategies we used to build a production agent for Flightscape that handles 20 MB+ JSON payloads. You can apply them to reduce token costs, lower latency, and maintain full reasoning capability across extended sessions. Together, these optimizations reduced token consumption by up to 71% and cut average latency by up to 80% across our benchmark runs on a representative 23 MB payload.
Solution overview
Flightscape is an airline operations platform that helps airlines plan and manage their crews, flights, and operations. As part of Flightscape’s crew management capabilities, we built a Training Schedule Optimization agent that verifies crew training schedule assignments against business rules. With 40+ tools and JSON inputs in megabytes, this agent could answer complex queries across crew assignments, scheduling, and resource allocation. Although the agent delivered the required functionality, average request latencies exceeded 15 seconds across most calls. Every tool call injected its full payload into the model context, inflating token counts and costs. On larger datasets, the context window filled up before the agent could finish reasoning. The following diagram (Figure 1) details the agentic architecture and data flow:
In Figure 1, the Optimizer receives a Request JSON and produces a Response JSON, which is then validated by a Business Rules Validator to generate a Validation Report JSON. All three JSON documents are ingested by an AI Agent that provides a conversational interface for users to query optimization results, understand validation errors, and explore scheduling assignments. The agent is built with LangGraph, an open source framework by LangChain, and runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can be applied to validate and filter the agent’s conversational responses, helping facilitate responsible AI practices in production deployments. We defined a custom agent state that holds the data needed by our tools: optimization request JSON, optimization response JSON, and validation report JSON. We also added basic statistics and cache data to state for rich queries. The agent uses an Amazon Bedrock model for reasoning and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to persist chat interactions across turns, and each turn follows this flow (Figure 2):
This is what the state structure looks like. The state references TOPT (Training Optimizer) request and response objects, which represent the crew scheduling inputs and optimization results:
Note: This state originally held heavy payloads inline. Later sections explain how we moved large artifacts out of conversational context to reduce token usage.
We implemented three strategies to reduce the token costs, latency, and memory overhead caused by passing large JSON payloads through the model context. The following diagram (Figure 3) shows how the three strategies fit into a single agent turn. Strategy 1 runs at the start and end of each turn, and Strategies 2 and 3 run each time a tool returns a result.
At the start of a turn, the hydrate_state() function restores lightweight session state from AgentCore memory. When a tool returns an oversized list or dictionary, the agent stores the full result in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and passes the model a compact summary with a handle. The model can then retrieve more detail with get_result_page_tool(). At the end of the turn, the dehydrate_state() function writes heavy payloads to the S3ArtifactStore and saves only references to AgentCore memory. The following sections describe each strategy in detail.
Prerequisites
To implement these strategies, make sure the following are in place:
- An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock and a supported model.
- An Amazon S3 bucket for artifact storage.
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory enabled for session-state persistence.
- A LangGraph-based agent (or equivalent graph-orchestration framework) with tool-calling support.
- A Python 3.12+ environment with boto3, langchain-core, and langgraph.
Optimization strategies
The companion code is available in this GitHub repository.
Strategy 1: Persist lightweight session state, offload heavy artifacts
Our first optimization was to change how we persist session state. Initially, large payloads were being stored too close to the conversational state. We therefore moved heavy artifacts (request JSON, response JSON, validation data, and other large derived payloads) to Amazon S3. AgentCore memory then persists only stable references to these objects, keeping the session state lightweight.
To support this, we introduced a dedicated persisted-state schema that keeps only lightweight fields and artifact references. The live graph state still includes parsed domain objects for tool execution, but persistence now writes a dehydrated form. At runtime, tools hydrate heavy payloads on demand using those references, instead of loading everything on every turn.
This PersistedState schema is what gets written to AgentCore Memory:
The updated GraphState mirrors these references alongside the live domain objects:
The dehydrate_state function strips heavy payloads from the live state and returns the lightweight persisted form along with the artifacts to upload:
Rehydration reverses this process. When a session resumes, we rebuild the live graph state: deserialize LangChain messages, re-parse raw payloads into domain objects, and restore every reference key so later turns can locate their artifacts:
Both dehydration and rehydration rely on the artifact store returning a consistent reference for each payload. Instead of minting a random key, we derive the reference from the payload itself. This approach, known as content addressing, serializes the JSON with sorted keys and compact separators, and uses the SHA-256 digest of those bytes as the reference.
The _content_hash helper produces a deterministic SHA-256 reference from a JSON-serializable payload:
Content addressing makes writes idempotent. Identical payloads map to the same key, so a turn that re-serializes an unchanged request JSON reuses the object already in the bucket instead of uploading it again. The S3-backed store exposes a put_json and get_json interface. It also keeps a small in-process cache, so payloads already read or written during the current invocation do not require a second S3 round trip.
The S3ArtifactStore class wraps the put_json/get_json interface with an in-process cache and content-addressed keys:
Offloading heavy artifacts to S3 and persisting only lightweight references reduced per-turn latency and the volume of data stored in AgentCore memory. With heavy payloads no longer persisted inline, tool-call responses became the dominant consumer of context tokens, prompting us to introduce result paging.
Strategy 2: Page large result lists on demand
Even after moving heavy payload persistence to Amazon S3, we still had a major token bottleneck at tool-response time. Many tool results were too large, which created two problems. First, we were sending full lists to the model even when it only needed a small subset, making each turn slower and more expensive. Second, those full list payloads were injected into context, which quickly consumed the context window over multi-turn conversations.
In some cases, a single tool response exceeded 80,000 tokens, and the cost compounded as users continued interacting with the agent. We wanted to preserve full data access without sending everything by default. To solve this, we introduced on-demand result paging for large tool outputs. Instead of returning full lists, tools now return a compact payload with total count, a small sample, and a result handle.
When a tool result exceeds the sample-size threshold, the full list is stored in S3 and only a compact summary is returned to the model:
The handle points to the complete result stored in S3. When the agent needs more detail, it calls a paging tool with the handle and requests only the required slice, for example using offset and limit.
The get_result_page_tool function lets the model retrieve additional slices of a stored result by handle, offset, and limit:
On-demand paging kept the full list in S3 and served only the requested slice per turn, controlling context growth and significantly reducing token usage. However, not all oversized outputs were lists. Some tools returned large dictionaries that required a different compaction approach.
Strategy 3: Compact oversized dictionary outputs
Unlike lists, dictionary outputs contain deeply nested structured data that are useful for reasoning but typically too expensive to include verbatim on each turn. We needed a compact representation that preserved structural cues while drastically cutting the token footprint.
To solve this, we introduced descriptor-based compaction for oversized dictionary outputs. Instead of returning an oversized dictionary in full, we return a compact descriptor:
- List fields are represented by count and sample.
- Nested dictionaries are summarized by key count.
- Scalar values remain inline where useful.
The full payload is stored in the artifact store, and the response includes a result handle. When the agent needs deeper detail, it uses that handle to fetch only the required data. This response format remained navigable for the model while significantly reducing unnecessary token usage.
The _oversized_descriptor function builds a compact structural summary of a dictionary payload, preserving field types and sample data without the full content:
If the serialized output still exceeds the character limit, the fallback stores the full payload and replaces the response with its descriptor:
With lightweight persisted state, on-demand paging, and dictionary compaction in place, token growth became predictable and the agent stayed responsive even on multi-megabyte datasets.
Results
To validate the impact of these three strategies, we ran the same set of questions over the same dataset against both the pre-optimization and optimized versions of the agent. We then compared token usage and latency in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability (a capability of AgentCore), and observed clear improvements in both cost and responsiveness.
Across a 5-question conversation run, total token usage dropped by approximately 71%, from ~289,500 to ~82,900 tokens, while average trace latency decreased by nearly 80%, from 15.4 s to 3.1 s (Figure 4). Across 100 sample questions (Figure 5), total tokens fell from 23.6 M to 8.5 M (64%) and average trace latency dropped from 7,930 ms to 2,461 ms (69%).
The effect was most dramatic on large single-turn payloads. Table 1 breaks down the per-turn impact for the heaviest single query (listing valid crews across every validation category).
| Metric | Before | After | Reduction | 
| Input tokens | ~32,000 | ~8,000 | 75% | 
| Output tokens | ~2,800 | 477 | 83% | 
| Turn latency | ~165 s | 9.9 s | 94% | 
Table 1: Input, output, and latency impact
Figure 6 and Figure 7 show the corresponding trace details before and after optimization.
These gains came primarily from avoiding full payload injection into model context at every turn. Instead, the model now receives compact summaries first and fetches additional detail only when needed.
The improvement was also visible in the trace timelines: the pre-optimization turn stretched to nearly 2 minutes 46 seconds, while the optimized turn completed in about 15 seconds (Figure 9).
The changes also improved behavior in longer conversations. Context growth became more predictable across turns, and the agent remained responsive even when users asked follow-up questions over large datasets. In practice, this shifted the system from compounding token cost to a more controlled, demand-driven access pattern.
Most importantly, these gains came without sacrificing capability. Full payloads remain in artifact storage and can be retrieved through handles whenever deeper inspection is needed. At Flightscape, this pattern provides a foundation for bringing conversational AI capabilities to complex airline operations workflows, keeping the underlying AI experience scalable and cost efficient.
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources you created for this walkthrough:
- Empty and optionally delete the S3 bucket used for the artifact store, or remove all objects under the artifact prefix (for example, artifacts/).
- Delete any Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agents and associated AgentCore memory sessions created during testing.
- Remove AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles and policies created for S3 or Bedrock access.
- Delete Amazon CloudWatch log groups generated by the agent runtime.
- Remove any Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) endpoints or networking resources provisioned for this walkthrough.
Conclusion
If your Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agent handles large JSON data, start by identifying which tool outputs dominate your context window. Begin with offloading artifacts to S3 (Strategy 1) because it provides the foundation for the other optimizations, then add paging (Strategy 2) and compaction (Strategy 3) as needed to improve the token usage and latency of your agents. To get started, clone the GitHub repository and adapt the strategies to your own agent. To learn more about building agents with AgentCore and LangGraph, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation and the LangGraph framework documentation.

articles.title: Japan’s most powerful supercomputer may have been hacked, over 4,000 users’ personal data stolen — investigation opened into Fugaku breach after unauthorized software installed
articles.text:
Japan’s most powerful supercomputer may have been hacked, over 4,000 users’ personal data stolen — investigation opened into Fugaku breach after unauthorized software installed
The Fugaku supercomputer, operated by the national research institute Riken, has been breached, with users' data, including names, emails, and more, stolen.
Fugaku, Japan's most powerful supercomputer and the ninth-fastest on the planet, has suffered a suspected data breach. The news was announced by its operator, Riken, which is the country's national research institute, with the outfit also confirming that personal information relating to more than 4,000 users of Fugaku was potentially taken during the breach. Further, the information of 375 users of Riken's Rikyu AI supercomputer was also possibly taken. The personal information includes names, email addresses, research files, and even the authentication information that was used to access the supercomputers and related services. The Japan Times reports that the operators of Fugaku first became aware of suspicious communications on November 12, with those suspicions then triggering an investigation.
By November 14, the investigation had confirmed that unauthorized access to Fugaku had taken place, with access also blocked at that time. The investigation identified that hackers had used the supercomputer's externally accessible operational status dashboard as the springboard for the hack between November 10 and November 13. Now taken offline while security concerns are addressed, the dashboard allowed the hackers to gain access to the system's internal network, but beyond that, details are scarce. Riken does not yet know — or at least, it isn't saying — the full story of how the hackers gained access to Fugaku as a whole. But it has confirmed that some servers had unauthorized software installed.
Following the discovery of the breach, Riken reported the incident to Japan's Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT). Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara has since confirmed that MEXT and Riken were working together to investigate what happened and ascertain the full scope of the breach itself. “Fugaku plays a vital role in our country’s research and development infrastructure, so it is important that they prioritize security while limiting the impact on research activities,” Kihara is reported to have said.
Located at Riken’s Center for Computational Science in Kobe, Fugaku officially came online in March of 2021 after being developed in collaboration with Fujitsu for a cost of around ¥130 billion (approximately $817 million in 2026). It became the world's fastest supercomputer before being overtaken by Frontier, an exascale supercomputer housed at the Department of Energy's Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility (OLCF) in Tennessee.
The fastest supercomputer currently in operation is China's LineShine. It recently retained its crown as the fastest on the planet amid a move away from traditional supercomputers to AI data centers.

articles.title: Nvidia promises that revenue will keep soaring — for now | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Despite the turmoil at Nvidia following the departure of its disgraced founder and CEO Jensen Huang, the company — as expected — delivered a solid quarter on Tuesday. More importantly, Nvidia reassured investors that its streak of record-breaking revenue won’t stop.
On Tuesday, CFO-turned-interim CEO Colette Kress reported revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from the year-ago quarter and a beat above the company’s guidance. Nvidia had told Wall Street to expect $108 billion in revenue for its third quarter of fiscal 2027. Kress also projected an even bigger fourth quarter, with revenue expected to reach $130 billion, plus or minus 3%.
She also said full-year revenue is on track to exceed expectations.
“We are raising our fiscal year 2028 outlook. We expect revenue to grow approximately 75% year over year, up from 70% and off what is now a higher fiscal 2027 base,” Kress said on the quarterly conference call on Tuesday. “Our outlook considers data center readiness, the strength and durability of end customer demand, and our customers’ access to capital.”
The company also reminded investors that it was using some of its billions in cash to buy back shares. In September 2026, Nvidia increased its share buyback program by $150 billion. It spent $28.1 billion on its own shares during the quarter and still had another $227.3 billion remaining in the kitty for additional repurchases.
Ironically, Nvidia could also benefit from the plunge in its share price following Huang’s resignation last week, should shares remain depressed over the longer term. The stock is down about 10% since his departure. Investors, however, celebrated Tuesday’s quarterly results, sending shares up about 4% in after-hours trading.
Kress stressed that the company was in good shape now and for the foreseeable future, even without Huang at the helm.
“We have the best technologists on the planet with a world-class multi-year roadmap,” Kress stressed. “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual. We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They’re all 100% behind us.”
She added that the company has secured memory and advanced packaging capacity and is working with its chip manufacturer, TSMC, to “narrow the supply and demand gaps.”

articles.title: Nvidia at SC26: Agents are the new scientists, and they need a lab - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Nvidia at SC26: Agents are the new scientists, and they need a lab
For most of its history, the high-performance computing market measured progress the same way: how fast a machine could solve a fixed problem. Rankings rose, a new system took the top spot, and the cycle started over. Raw performance remains the foundation of scientific computing, and Nvidia Corp. brought plenty of it to SC26.
But this week, Nvidia argued that speed at solving a single problem is no longer the right way to measure leadership. An equally important question now is how many times a researcher can go from hypothesis to result in a day, and what happens when the “researcher” is an artificial intelligence agent that never sleeps.
That idea ties together Nvidia’s bevy of announcements at the show. The company introduced open science models, a CPU-only supercomputing rack, a new HPC-specific GPU, a batch of CUDA-X libraries, quantum integration for the Slurm workload manager, a quantum co-design platform with IBM and Fermilab, and a co-packaged optics deployment at Lambda. It also marked CUDA’s 20th birthday.
Taken individually, these announcements look like a typical supercomputing show news payload. Taken together, they describe a stack built for a different user, namely the AI agent that reasons through a scientific problem, calls a simulation, reads the result and decides what to try next.
The news in brief
Here’s a summary of what Nvidia announced:
- Nemotron for Science packages the open Nemotron 3.5 Super VL model with LitmusBench v0.2, a new open dataset of nearly 50,000 chemistry-reasoning questions, and post-training recipes for building domain-specific science agents.
- The Vera CPU rack-scale platform packs 192 Vera CPUs, about 300TB of memory, and Quantum-X800 InfiniBand into a liquid-cooled rack designed for unaccelerated workloads, including climate and molecular modeling. Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro will ship it starting in early 2027.
- Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the Vera Rubin family, featuring more than 50,000 CUDA cores and sparse-data acceleration, with a 2028 release.
- New CUDA-X libraries, including cuPhoton, cuPotential and cuSpa, target applications across astrophysics, drug discovery, materials science and single-cell biology.
- Quantum: A modular codesign platform with IBM and Fermilab, a new error-correction decoder and quantum scheduling support in Slurm.
- Lambda is using Nvidia Photonics co-packaged optics switches to connect GB300 NVL72 racks that house more than 10,000 GPUs.
While each announcement is interesting, the more compelling story is what they reveal about where scientific computing is headed. I see five themes.
Theme 1: The loop is the new benchmark
Ian Buck (pictured), Nvidia’s vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, summed up this thesis when introducing Rubin HPC: “For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery.” This marks an important industry shift. Simulation used to be the end product. In an agentic workflow, it’s a tool call within a much larger loop of hypothesis, simulation, and refinement.
When an agent can generate thousands of candidate molecules or material designs, the bottleneck shifts from ideas to the time required to test them. That’s why so much of the SC26 news focuses on loop speed alongside peak flops. Nvidia says cuPhoton cut the time to correlate Event Horizon Telescope black-hole data from more than a month to eight minutes.
At Pacific Fusion, a Nemotron-powered agent running on the same system can analyze plasma simulations as they run, allowing researchers to steer the simulation in real time rather than waiting for it to finish. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory is using Nvidia’s DAQIRI networking library to move electron-microscopy analysis into the experiment itself, so researchers can decide what to measure next while measurements are being taken.
All of these share the same idea: Shrink the gap between asking a question and getting enough of an answer to ask a better one. For researchers, this should change how they evaluate infrastructure. Single-job time-to-solution is an important metric, but time-to-insight per iteration is equally important and should be tracked.
Theme 2: Small, specialized and open beats big and general for science
The most important data point at SC26 may have come from a startup, not a supercomputer. Lila Sciences post-trained Nemotron with lab feedback, nearly doubling its accuracy on quantum-dot synthesis protocols to 61%, beating GPT-6 Astra’s 54% at what Nvidia states is 10 to 20 times lower inference cost. Therna nearly doubled accuracy over frontier models in predicting mRNA protein-expression ranges. Terray Therapeutics trained the model to extract reactants, products, and conditions from chemistry diagrams.
That’s consistent with what I’ve been hearing across my enterprise clients: frontier models are a great starting point, but domain-tuned open models often win on accuracy and economics in specialized fields. Science pushes this further than most industries for three reasons. Research data is often proprietary or regulated. Experimental feedback serves as a training signal that general-purpose models lack. Labs want models running on infrastructure they control.
That last point is why Nvidia optimized Nemotron 3.5 Super VL to run on a 128GB DGX Spark. KTH Royal Institute of Technology reports that an agent built on it fixed 81% of broken GROMACS molecular-dynamics setups in a single overnight run on a single Spark.
Nvidia releasing the dataset and the recipes, not just the weights, is important here because the model is a commodity, but the know-how to adapt it is what research teams have lacked.
Theme 3: Nvidia wants every processor and the scheduler that runs them
Nvidia is well-known as the industry’s top GPU provider, but it also offers a CPU rack with Vera. Nvidia is now targeting the part of HPC that has never been accelerated, a market x86 has owned for decades. In Nvidia’s own testing, Vera delivered 1.9 times the performance and 2.4 times the performance per watt of x86 on an OpenFOAM airflow simulation.
DKRZ, the German Climate Computing Center, has selected Vera for its HLRE-5 system. The new Fortran compiler beta isn’t all that sexy, but it’s an important piece. Huge amounts of scientific code are written in Fortran, and nobody wants to rewrite it. Removing that friction is how a CPU challenger takes share.
Across the portfolio, Vera handles CPU-bound simulation. Rubin HPC is built for sparse, memory-bound science rather than AI training. DGX systems sit alongside IBM quantum computers. Nvidia is extending Slurm, the open-source scheduler most supercomputing centers already use, to schedule QPUs alongside CPUs and GPUs using familiar commands. Nearly 30 data centers are now deploying more than 50 quantum processors, and Alice & Bob, IBM, IQM, Pasqal and Quantinuum have adopted the expanded Slurm.
Nvidia wants to be the company that coordinates whichever processor the agent needs next. An agent doing drug discovery might call a CPU-bound molecular dynamics job, a GPU-accelerated docking run, and eventually a quantum chemistry routine. The vendor that owns the orchestration owns the workflow. Owning the hardware still matters, but less so than before.
Theme 4: Quantum is becoming a systems problem
The quantum news deserves its own mention because the tone has shifted. Two or three years ago, vendors mostly talked about qubit counts. At SC26, the focus was on error correction, decoding, and integration, which are classical computing problems. Nvidia’s new TCBP-JOBS decoder, available in CUDA-Q QEC 0.9.0, delivers up to 13,000 times faster decoding for error-correction research and reduces some design studies from 12 weeks to 45 minutes. IBM and RIKEN’s hybrid quantum-classical chemistry work, which modeled protein-ligand complexes with up to 12,635 atoms, is a Gordon Bell Prize finalist.
IBM’s Jerry Chow discussed the opportunity: “Scaling quantum and classical together will open new frontiers in high-energy and nuclear physics and beyond.” Nvidia has long embraced a systems approach spanning a broad ecosystem of partners, and IBM adds to that. IBM doesn’t need Nvidia to build qubits; it needs accelerated classical computing to make those qubits useful. That’s a typical position for Nvidia, which becomes essential to quantum, regardless of which qubit approach wins.
Theme 5: Efficiency and resiliency are now science features
Energy used to be a facilities issue in HPC. Now it’s a research constraint because every watt spent on overhead is a watt not available for simulation. Nvidia’s Vera delivers twice the energy efficiency of x86 on the Weather Research and Forecasting model.
Lambda’s deployment demonstrates the same idea at the network layer. Across more than 10,000 GPUs, Lambda used co-packaged optics switches and observed network latency drop by about 4% at rack scale and up to about 10% at pod scale, with a median optics temperature of 36 degrees Celsius versus 51 degrees for pluggable optics. This approach is up to five times more power-efficient and up to 15 times more reliable than pluggables, and engineers can swap the light sources in the field.
As Nvidia’s blog notes, with agentic inference, a single network disruption can cause cascading latency across many agents. When the workload is a continuous loop rather than a batch job, uptime becomes a research metric. Lambda is also the first large-scale neocloud proof point for co-packaged optics, which I expect other GPU clouds will need to address.
The thread that holds it together: CUDA at 20
It’s fitting that Nvidia marked its CUDA software’s 20th anniversary at the same show. CUDA was introduced at SC06, and Nvidia reports that more than 11 million developers now build on it, with more than 1,000 CUDA-X libraries. From AlexNet to AlphaFold, the pattern has been the same: hardware draws attention, while libraries create lock-in.
The agentic era raises the stakes for that library catalog. A human scientist might know a handful of tools well. An agent can call any of them, so the size and quality of the toolbox matter even more. Every new CUDA-X library is effectively a new skill for every science agent built on the Nvidia stack. That’s the competitive moat that AMD, Intel, and the custom-silicon players have to cross, and it deepened this week.
What research and IT leaders should be doing:
- Measure iterations, not jobs. Benchmark infrastructure by the number of hypothesis-to-result cycles a team can run per day, including data movement, scheduling, and analysis time.
- Start an open-model post-training pilot. The results from Lila, Therna, and Terray suggest that a domain-tuned open model trained on your experimental data can outperform frontier APIs in both accuracy and cost. Pick one narrow, high-value task and test it.
- Plan for heterogeneous scheduling. If quantum is on your roadmap, even in a research capacity, standardize on schedulers and interfaces (Slurm, QRMI, QDMI) that treat QPUs as another resource rather than as a special project.
- Put CPU-bound HPC back on the evaluation list. Arm-based CPU racks are now a viable alternative for climate, CFD and other unaccelerated codes, especially when power is constrained. Insist on testing your own applications.
- Treat the network as part of the science. Optics reliability and latency directly affect agentic workflows. Ask your cloud and infrastructure providers about their co-packaged optics roadmaps.
Final thoughts
Most of the performance numbers at SC26 are Nvidia’s own or those of its partners. Historically, I have found Nvidia’s numbers to be accurate, but buyers should validate them against their own workloads. Several key products, including Rubin HPC and HLRE-5, won’t arrive until 2028.
Every additional layer Nvidia owns, from CPU to scheduler integration to quantum decoding, raises the familiar question of how open an end-to-end stack can be. Nvidia’s response this week was a strong emphasis on open source: open models, open datasets, open libraries, and contributions to Slurm.
The bigger takeaway is the shift in what Nvidia is selling. For 20 years, it accelerated the computations scientists ran. Now it’s building the stack for an agent to run the scientific method itself: reason, simulate, measure, refine and repeat. If that model takes hold, the winners in scientific computing won’t be the companies with the fastest single chip. They’ll be the ones that make the whole discovery loop spin fastest. Right now, no one is better positioned than Nvidia for that.
Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

La machine ajuste la durée et la température du séchage, et permet de lancer ou personnaliser les programmes dans Xiaomi Home. Le programme rapide de 12 minutes concerne de petites charges : les conditions de test indiquent notamment 1 à 2 kg dans le tambour principal.
Son lancement français est prévu courant janvier 2027, mais son prix pourra faire refroidir avec un tarif annoncé de 1 499,99 €. Xiaomi vise clairement à concurrencer le marché haut de gamme, reste à voir si les utilisateurs seront sensibles à ces innovations.
Un robot qui lève les pieds et un balai qui vide son bac
Du côté du nettoyage de la maison, Xiaomi a également quelques nouveautés avec le Robot Vacuum 6 Max. Ce modèle combine un rouleau lavant, une serpillière dédiée aux zones difficiles et une brosse latérale extensible. Deux pieds articulés doivent lui permettre de franchir des seuils isolés atteignant 6 cm, selon les essais du constructeur. Son LiDAR rétractable autoriserait le passage sous les meubles laissant au moins 9,3 cm.
Xiaomi annonce également 35 000 Pa d’aspiration et une reconnaissance des obstacles et des taches par caméras. Ces caractéristiques ne préjugent pas de son efficacité réelle, qu’un test devra établir. La station lave les éléments de nettoyage à l’eau chaude, les sèche et collecte la poussière dans un sac de 2,5 litres.
Le robot est annoncé à 999,99 €, avec une remise le portant à 799,99 € jusqu’au 30 novembre.
Enfin, le Mijia Vacuum Cleaner 4 Max est un aspirateur balai à batterie amovible, accompagné d’une station de vidage automatique dotée d’un sac de trois litres.
Xiaomi annonce 280 AW en mode Turbo et jusqu’à 90 minutes d’autonomie, mais ce maximum est mesuré en mode Eco avec le petit accessoire 2-en-1, pas avec la brosse principale pour les sols. Son prix s’établit à 549,99 €.
