articles.title: SheSparks 2027 set to spotlight the multiplier effect
articles.text:
The power of one, the progress of many: SheSparks 2027 set to spotlight the multiplier effect
YourStory’s flagship women-focused event returns to Delhi on February 19–20, with a focus on collective progress, entrepreneurship, and access to opportunities.
When one woman succeeds, the benefits can extend beyond her own career or business. The knowledge she shares, the connections she builds, and the opportunities she creates can help other women move forward.
This idea is at the heart of SheSparks 2027, YourStory’s flagship women-focused event, which returns to Delhi on February 19 and 20 at The Ashok Hotel.
With the theme ‘The Multiplier Effect’, the event will explore how women's individual achievements can drive collective progress through mentorship, shared knowledge, access to opportunities, and networks of support.
Since its inception in 2018, SheSparks has brought together women from business, arts, science, sports, public service, and other fields to exchange ideas, share experiences, and build connections. The 2027 edition will focus on how these relationships can help more women advance across business, technology, entrepreneurship, leadership, and society.
For the first time in its history, SheSparks will be held as a two-day programme. Across both days, the event will feature keynotes, panel discussions, fireside chats, and workshops covering ambition, identity, reinvention, the future of work, women in the AI age, financial independence, entrepreneurship, and leadership.
Conversations will also examine how mentorship, sponsorship, allyship, and professional networks can help address barriers to women's workforce participation and economic progress.
Beyond the discussions, SheSparks 2027 will offer several opportunities for women to connect with investors, employers, customers, and peers.
The Capital Room will connect women founders with investors based on investment fit, while the Returnship Fair will bring women looking to restart their careers in touch with employers and career guidance. The SheCommerce Bazaar will showcase women-led brands and businesses, helping them reach customers, markets, and potential partners.
A major highlight of the event will be SheSparks 100. Building on YourStory and HerStory’s Future Shapers: She Leads Change Awards, the initiative will recognise 100 women across entrepreneurship, business, technology, capital, policy, culture, and social impact. The focus will be on their achievements and the opportunities they have helped create for others.
Over the years, SheSparks has hosted leaders and changemakers, including Sudha Murty, Nivruti Rai, Soha Ali Khan, Vani Kola, Tessy Thomas, Chetna Gala Sinha, and Swati Bhargava.
The 2027 edition expects to bring together over 600 attendees, with an anticipated reach of more than five million women.
Through conversations, connections, and practical initiatives, SheSparks 2027 aims to demonstrate how individual achievements can create opportunities for others, helping more women participate and progress across industries.
Edited by Teja Lele

articles.title: Jensen Huang says he'd be "honored" to return as Nvidia CEO if the board wants him back
articles.text:
Crystal ball: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has released a public statement, saying he'd be "honored" to return as chief executive if the board wants to reinstate him in his previous role. Huang resigned last week following allegations that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including with at least two Nvidia employees. He had earlier admitted to an affair with a woman suspected to be a Chinese spy.
In a lengthy statement posted on X, Huang said he was willing to return as Nvidia CEO "if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America."
He added that he was "overwhelmed" by the support of friends, industry colleagues, and strangers, and thanked them for their good wishes. He also noted an "outpouring of calls" from employees, investors, business partners, and customers for him to return.
 – Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) November 17, 2026
Without referring to the salacious allegations, Huang admitted to making "serious mistakes" in his personal life, saying that he knows he did not live up to the standards expected at Nvidia. He added that he regretted creating problems for the board and reiterated that he was cooperating with the company's independent investigation.
Jensen Huang's statement comes less than a week after he resigned as Nvidia CEO, after news of his affairs became tabloid fodder and spawned a million memes and AI videos on social media. Following his resignation, Colette Kress, the Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, took over as the company's interim CEO.
Nvidia's stock fell nearly 20% since the crisis unfolded, wiping out almost a trillion dollars from the company's market cap. Faced with uncertainty without the popular and charismatic former CEO, more than 170,000 people, including thousands of Nvidia employees, signed a petition called 'Stand With Jensen' to bring him back despite the alleged HR violations.
The campaign to reinstate Huang also gained support from prominent business leaders, including Elon Musk, who said he signed the petition. President Trump, who has praised Huang's leadership, said he "would not mind" seeing him return, though he also floated Tim Cook as a replacement.
Supporters argue that Huang's management skills and pioneering vision are essential to Nvidia's success, and by extension, the growth of the American AI sector.
The Jensen Huang affair saga started in late October, when the New York Times reported that US intelligence officials believed Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman, was spying for Beijing. Huang admitted to the affair and apologized to his family, but was forced to resign less than a week later amid reports of two additional affairs with his co-workers.

articles.title: Yet another satellite company is jockeying for a rocket—but this one makes sense
articles.text:
Finnish satellite developer ICEYE announced Tuesday that it is seeking to buy Italian rocket-maker Avio for more than $2.2 billion in a transaction aimed at creating Europe’s first true vertically integrated end-to-end space company.
The announcement came as an all-cash voluntary tender offer from an Italian subsidiary of ICEYE to Avio’s shareholders, led by the Italian defense conglomerate Leonardo. Avio said its board of directors “has taken note of the notice” from ICEYE and is considering the purchase offer.
Avio builds the Vega C rocket, a solid-fueled launcher designed to carry up to 3.3 metric tons (7,300 pounds) of payload to low-Earth orbit. The Vega C has flown successfully seven times in eight attempts since 2022. It is a follow-on to an earlier version of the Vega rocket that amassed a 20-for-22 record since debuting in 2012.
ICEYE is, by far, the most successful space startup in Europe, where access to private capital, regulatory barriers, and fragmented markets often hinder startup growth, according to a recent report from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. ICEYE’s valuation stands at more than $12 billion after the company’s most recent fundraising round in June.
In pursuit of sovereignty
In a statement, ICEYE said it wants to join forces with Avio to meet Europe’s need for “sovereign space and defense capabilities.” ICEYE manufactures and operates its own satellites for radar surveillance and sells data to commercial customers and national governments, including Ukraine, which uses ICEYE imagery for targeting and tracking Russian troop movements.
“Governments need control of their critical space infrastructure, and Europe needs it most,” said Rafal Modrzewski, CEO and co-founder of ICEYE. “Avio has built the launch and propulsion capability Europe relies on. With ICEYE’s long-term capital behind it, we can integrate the supply chain, grow output and strengthen the European programs that already depend on it. Together we can build, launch and operate sovereign space systems end-to-end, made in Europe for governments across the world.”

articles.title: El Departamento de Justicia usó un detector de IA para acusar a abogados defensores de usar ChatGPT
articles.text:
Abogados del Departamento de Justicia de Estados Unidos presentaron ante un tribunal federal de Texas los resultados de Pangram, un servicio que detecta textos escritos con inteligencia artificial (IA), para sostener que la defensa de un acusado redactó sus escritos con ChatGPT, la plataforma de OpenAI.
“Este caso se convirtió en una defensa por ChatGPT”, escribieron los fiscales, según el 404 media. Agregaron que responder a los escritos de la defensa equivale a contestar documentos generados por “un robot que intenta ejercer la abogacía” y los calificaron de “basura de IA”.
El acusado es Khalwinder Bhengura, un indio que llegó a Estados Unidos con visa de inmigrante en 2022. Se registró para votar en Texas en 2024 tras presuntamente declarar falsamente que era ciudadano al tramitar su licencia de conducir. Fue arrestado en septiembre de 2026 y declarado culpable en octubre de dos de los tres cargos.
Los fiscales ejecutaron varios escritos de la defensa por Pangram y presentaron los resultados como anexo de uno de sus argumentos. Esos resultados fueron mixtos: no indicaron que los textos fueran totalmente de IA. Aun así, los fiscales sostuvieron que no debían responder de fondo a escritos parcialmente generados con esa tecnología.
Un juez que reprendió a la defensa
El juez Mark Pittman escribió que se siente “perturbado” por escritos que “doblan sutilmente la ley” con argumentos “claramente generados por inteligencia artificial”. Recordó que el acusado no se representa a sí mismo, sino que tiene tres abogados con décadas de ejercicio.
El Distrito Norte de Texas adoptó hace poco una norma que obliga a declarar el uso de IA generativa en los escritos. En algunos documentos, los defensores incluyeron la advertencia de que partes del texto se prepararon con una herramienta de ese tipo.
Los fiscales argumentaron que casi todo el texto que no era de IA correspondía a citas de pruebas, documentos del expediente o jurisprudencia. Concluyeron que “prácticamente nada de fondo” parecía redactado por una persona del equipo defensor.
La defensa niega haber violado alguna norma
Mario Herrera y Nicole Knox, dos de los abogados de Bhengura, dijeron a 404 Media que recurrieron a la IA por una emergencia médica y por los plazos ajustados antes de la elección. Según Herrera, Knox sufrió una emergencia médica mientras preparaban el caso con los fiscales, y él armó un juicio con jurado en cuatro días.
Herrera sostuvo que Pangram solo identifica patrones de estilo y no puede determinar quién escribió un documento ni si la ley aplicada es correcta. Afirmó que la Fiscalía no señaló citas falsas. Aseguró que las partes cuestionadas son de su autoría, con ayuda de IA y posterior revisión.
Knox dijo que la IA “nunca podría haber ideado” el argumento de la defensa. Según Herrera, la absolución en uno de los tres cargos muestra que el acusado recibió la representación que merecía. Bhengura, de 70 años, habla punjabi y tiene un inglés limitado, según sus abogados.
Pangram, usado sobre todo dentro de los estudios
Max Spero, director ejecutivo de Pangram, dijo a 404 Media que supo de manera informal que algunos estudios jurídicos empezaron a usar su programa. Según él, la mayoría lo emplea de forma interna para revisar si abogados junior y asistentes legales redactan escritos con IA.
Bhengura está detenido desde el veredicto y enfrenta su deportación, además de la pena que reciba por los delitos por los que fue condenado.
El 4 de noviembre de 2026, el juez Pittman rechazó una solicitud de Bhengura para recuperar la libertad antes de la sentencia. En su orden, sostuvo que el acusado no demostró que no fuera a fugarse, según el registro público del caso.

articles.title: Xiaomi dévoile les Xiaomi Clip, ses premiers écouteurs qui se clipsent sur l’oreille
articles.text:
En parallèle du lancement de la Watch S5 et du Smart Band 11, Xiaomi a dévoilé les Xiaomi Clip, des écouteurs ouverts à clip. Si les Xiaomi OpenWear Stereo se placent autour de l’oreille, les Xiaomi Clip se fixent quant à eux directement sur celle-ci. C’est la première fois que le constructeur chinois propose ce type d’appareil. Voici les caractéristiques et le prix des Xiaomi Clip.
Design et confort
Avec ses Xiaomi Clip, Xiaomi promet un confort d’écoute optimal, même lors de longues sessions d’écoute. Ainsi, chaque écouteur pèse 5,5 grammes. Ils intègrent par ailleurs un arceau flexible en alliage à mémoire de forme qui se clipse sans pénétrer dans le canal auditif, tandis que le boîtier incurvé de la batterie répartit uniformément la pression sur l’oreille. Par ailleurs, ce système de fixation par clip permet aux écouteurs de s’adapter à différentes morphologies d’oreilles. Au niveau du design, nous pouvons noter une petite zone semi-transparente qui laisse entrevoir certains composants internes de l’écouteur.
Rappelons au passage qu’il s’agit d’écouteurs à conception ouverte. L’intérêt de ce type d’appareil est de pouvoir écouter de la musique ou un podcast, tout en restant attentif à son environnement. Nous ne retrouvons donc pas de fonction de réduction de bruit active.
Conception audio, fonctionnalités et autonomie
Le principal défi des écouteurs à conception ouverte est de parvenir à restituer un son puissant, notamment des basses relativement profondes. Pour tenter d’y parvenir, les Xiaomi Clip s’appuient sur un haut-parleur dynamique de 11 mm doté d’un diaphragme à revêtement métallique microcristallin. Par ailleurs, selon Xiaomi, la conception acoustique directionnelle oriente le son vers le conduit auditif, tout en limitant les fuites sonores. De leur côté, les algorithmes DRC et d’amplification des basses ont pour objectif d’affiner le rendu des basses fréquences. Notons également que ces écouteurs prennent en charge l’Hi-Res Audio Wireless et le codec LHDC 5.0 sur les appareils compatibles.
Au niveau de la clarté des appels, Xiaomi a intégré à ces écouteurs un réseau de trois microphones associé à un microphone à conduction osseuse VPU et à une réduction de bruit par IA qui permet d’isoler la voix de l’utilisateur et d’atténuer les bruits ambiants. Notons également la présence d’une fonction de traduction instantanée avec un smartphone Xiaomi compatible. Côté connectivité, deux paires d’écouteurs Xiaomi Clip peuvent être connectées à un même smartphone ou à une même tablette Xiaomi, tandis que le basculement audio permet de passer instantanément d’un appareil Xiaomi compatible à un autre. Enfin, notons que Xiaomi annonce jusqu’à 9 heures d’écoute musicale sur une seule charge et jusqu’à 38 heures avec le boîtier de charge.
Les Xiaomi Clip sont disponibles dès maintenant via les canaux officiels de Xiaomi et auprès des revendeurs agréés. Quatre coloris sont proposés : or, blanc, noir et violet. Le prix de vente conseillé est de 149,99 €. Cependant, du 17 au 30 novembre 2026, dans le cadre d’une offre de lancement, les écouteurs sont proposés au tarif de 126,99 € (soit une réduction de 23 €).

articles.title: Cut generative AI costs: Code for rules, models for judgment | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Cut generative AI costs: Code for rules, models for judgment
The biggest cost lever in a generative AI system is whether you call a model at all. We often see teams route every task through a large language model (LLM), including input validation, formatting, and routing. Each call is cheap in isolation, but at production scale these small costs become one of the largest line items in the architecture. Wherever a deterministic rule can do the job, skipping the model saves money, cuts latency, and removes a source of non-determinism. In this post, you learn how to decide whether each step in a workflow needs a model at all. You can then map each option to AWS: deterministic code, a constrained decision call, or a right-sized model on Amazon Bedrock.
Why unneeded model calls add up
The pattern usually starts in a prototype. A model call works for one step, so it becomes the default for the next. Those steps include validating input, reformatting a request body, and picking a route. At prototype volume, nobody notices the cost.
At production volume, unneeded model calls cost you in three ways:
- Spend grows with request count, even for low-value steps.
- Latency stacks, because every model call in a chain adds hundreds of milliseconds.
- Output can vary, because the same input can return a different answer. That makes testing harder and audits slower.
Each new model launch then restarts the debate about which model to use. The earlier question, whether the step needs a model at all, goes unasked.
Cost guidance, including the AWS Well-Architected Generative AI Lens, often starts at model selection. This post starts one step earlier: Does the step need a model at all?
How to decide whether a step needs a model
Figure 1 shows the whole decision as a flowchart with three labeled lanes: Runs as code, Questions, and Runs on a model. Take each workflow step through three questions in order, and stop at the first option that meets the step’s requirements:
- Can a rule check success, such as a format, a schema, a keyword, or a range? If a rule settles only part of the step, a fast path runs the rule first.
- Can a model write the rule once, such as a regular expression or a JSON schema?
- Does the step pick one answer from a fixed list, such as a route, a class, or yes or no?
If the answer to all three is no, the step is open-ended and runs on a right-sized model.
Consider a customer support assistant. The following table shows how five of its steps go through the chart.
| # | Step | Path through the chart | Where it runs | 
| 1 | Check an order number’s format | A rule can check success. | Amazon API Gateway REST API request validation, or an AWS Lambda function | 
| 2 | Route a message by intent | A rule settles part of it. A keyword match on the fast path resolves messages such as “refund”, and the residual goes to the third question. | An AWS Step Functions Choice state that uses JSONata. The residual goes to a constrained decision call. | 
| 3 | Extract a tracking number from a carrier email | A model can write the rule once. It drafts a regular expression, and you review and commit it. | Code, as a committed pattern in AWS Lambda | 
| 4 | Pick one of four support queues for a ticket | The answer comes from a fixed list. | A constrained decision call. Unsure answers escalate to the right-sized model. | 
| 5 | Draft a reply to the customer | The task is open-ended. | The right-sized model, the smallest Amazon Bedrock model that meets the requirements | 
You can use a model when a task is open-ended, ambiguous, or generative: summarizing a document, drafting a reply, extracting meaning from prose. Use deterministic code when the task has a checkable rule: an email format, a schema, an exact keyword, a numeric range. The following table shows what you trade away when you send a rule-shaped task to a model.
| Property | Deterministic code | Model call | 
| Cost per invocation | Typically orders of magnitude lower | Per-token, non-trivial at scale | 
| Latency | Single-digit milliseconds or less | Hundreds of milliseconds | 
| Correctness on a well-specified rule | Exact for the rule as written | High, but with a non-zero error rate | 
| Auditability | The rule sits in source control | Harder to explain to an auditor | 
| Behavior over time | Stable until you change it | Changes when you move to a new model version, or when a version is retired | 
A model can also hallucinate and return different answers to the same input. A temperature of 0 makes varied answers less likely, but it doesn’t guarantee identical output. Amazon Bedrock model evaluation and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails help you measure and contain these risks. A rule has neither problem, which is one reason regulated workloads favor rules. A useful test: If you can write the acceptance test as a rule, you can usually write the step as a rule. For more information, refer to Orchestration models: From rule-based to AI-native in AWS Prescriptive Guidance.
Decide, don’t generate
Most routing and classification steps sit between a rule and open-ended generation. A rule can’t decide every case, but these steps don’t need generated text either. They need one answer from a fixed list of options that you define in advance, like the support queues in the preceding example. Use a component that limits its output to the allowed answers and gives you a signal for when to escalate. Confident answers proceed, and uncertain ones escalate. The AWS Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens describes this tiered, confidence-based escalation. On AWS, you can build it four ways:
- A small Amazon Bedrock model with structured outputs – The answer is limited to an enum of options, plus an ‘unsure’ option that triggers escalation. This is the model’s own judgment, not a calibrated score, so check it against labeled data before you use it to decide escalation.
- Embedding similarity – Embed the input with an Amazon Bedrock embeddings model and pick the nearest labeled example. Use the similarity score as an escalation signal, and set its threshold on labeled data.
- Strands Decider, an experimental open source decision model under the Apache License 2.0 – It picks from options or scores against a rubric, and it returns a calibrated confidence with each answer. Its README reports that answers at a confidence of 0.9 or more are right about 95 percent of the time on short classification tasks. Because the model is experimental, validate that result on your own data before you use it in production. You host it yourself, for example on an Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint, by following the deployment guides in its repository.
- A trained classifier on Amazon SageMaker AI – It returns class probabilities with low latency and cost once you have labeled training data.
The following JSON schema limits a structured-output answer to four queues plus ‘unsure’. Amazon Bedrock requires every object in the schema to set additionalProperties to false.
Whichever option you choose, check its escalation signal against your own labeled data, and set any threshold there. Keep your authorization decisions, such as a refund limit, in a rule.
The deterministic fast-path pattern
Many cost patterns focus on routing between models. The fast path goes one level earlier: Run the deterministic check first, and send only what the rule can’t settle to a model. Intent routing is one example. Many messages carry an unambiguous signal, such as “refund” or “reset my password”, which a keyword match resolves in single-digit milliseconds or less. If rules resolve 95 percent of requests, only 1 in 20 requests reaches a model, before any savings from model selection. (Illustrative arithmetic, not a benchmark.)
On AWS, you compose this from existing building blocks:
- AWS Step Functions Choice states branch before the workflow invokes any model.
- AWS Lambda hosts rules that need more than a Choice state, such as validation and schema checks.
- Amazon API Gateway (REST API) request validation rejects malformed input before any compute runs.
- A constrained decision call or an Amazon Bedrock model handles only the residual.
The following Choice state is a keyword fast path. It uses JSONata to send refund and password-reset messages straight to code, and it sends everything else to the constrained decision call.
You can also let a model write the rule once instead of running it every time. Have it draft a regular expression or a JSON schema, review it, and commit it. At runtime the rule runs at rule speed and cost. Review a model-written regular expression, and test it against known good and bad inputs. Avoid nested quantifiers such as (a+)+, which can make matching very slow on some inputs (regular expression denial of service, or ReDoS).
When you do generate, Amazon Bedrock structured outputs constrain a response to a JSON schema that you define. The response then matches the schema, so your code can parse it without custom parsing logic (check content for correctness). Keep range checks, such as numeric bounds and length limits, in code. For supported models and schema features, refer to Get validated JSON results from models.
If your rules live in configuration, allow only known primitives, such as regular expressions, schema checks, keyword lists, and range checks. Never run arbitrary code from a configuration file.
When you do need a model, right-size it
Choose the cheapest and fastest model that meets your quality floor. That is often not the newest or largest model. The Generative AI Lens covers this in its best practice on right-sizing model selection. Effective cost optimization strategies for Amazon Bedrock covers it in depth. Define the requirements before you compare models:
- Quality floor: The minimum acceptable output quality, measured on a golden evaluation set (labeled examples of the task with known-correct answers).
- Cost ceiling: The most you pay per request or per successful outcome.
- Latency target: The p95 or p99 response time the experience can tolerate.
- Compliance constraints: Requirements such as data residency that can rule out candidates.
Amazon Bedrock offers many model families and sizes behind one API, so you can right-size each task without changing your integration. Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing routes each request to a suitable model within a supported model family. Amazon Bedrock Model Distillation transfers knowledge from a larger model to a smaller, cheaper one for your use case. Model providers evaluate a new frontier model on broad benchmarks, but your workload is one task with one quality floor. A larger model can add cost and latency without improving that task. Before you switch, evaluate each launch against your requirements, such as quality on your golden evaluation set and your latency target.
Treat model choice as tested configuration
The Generative AI Lens recommends testing candidate models against your ground truth data and having a way to update the model quickly. Go further and treat the decision as a tested configuration:
- Keep a golden evaluation set per task, with labeled ground truth, and run it in continuous integration.
- Gate on your requirements. Treat a cheaper model that drops below the quality floor as a regression.
- Put the model behind a configuration flag so that you can reverse a swap.
- Verify with the right oracle. Check rules against ground truth. Reserve model-as-judge evaluation for open-ended outputs.
- Watch for drift. Sample some rule-resolved requests through a model in shadow mode, and reclassify a step when they disagree.
Putting it into practice
Spend model capacity where judgment is needed, and nowhere else. You can get there in four steps:
- Instrument – Tag every call as deterministic code, a constrained decision call, or a model call. Track cost per successful outcome.
- Move the rules to code – Run rule-checkable steps on AWS Lambda or AWS Step Functions. This is usually the largest and safest win.
- Add constrained decision calls – Route fixed-choice steps through a call that escalates when it is unsure.
- Test before you switch models – Run every new model through your golden evaluation set before it becomes the default.
Conclusion
In this post, you learned how to decide whether a workflow step needs a model at all. Rules belong in deterministic code, and fixed choices belong in a constrained decision call. Open-ended work goes to a right-sized Amazon Bedrock model. Aim to meet each requirement at the lowest cost and latency that your quality floor allows. Ask whether a step needs a model before you ask which one.
For more information, refer to these posts on the AWS Artificial Intelligence Blog:
- Use decision models with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations.
- Use Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing for cost and latency benefits.
- Structured outputs on Amazon Bedrock: Schema-compliant AI responses.
- Fix evaluation bias to unlock better models on Amazon Bedrock.
To try a constrained decision call, open the Amazon Bedrock console, or deploy Strands Decider from its GitHub repository.
Start with one high-volume workflow and measure how much of it never needed a model.

articles.title: GAMDIAS Unveils ATLAS P7 Mid-Tower PC Case
articles.text:
Tuesday, November 17th 2026
GAMDIAS Unveils ATLAS P7 Mid-Tower PC Case
GAMDIAS, a global provider of high-performance gaming hardware, proudly announces the latest addition to its ATLAS Series, the ATLAS P7. As a key expression of GAMDIAS's 2026 vision, "AUGMENTED IMMERSION," the ATLAS P7 reimagines the PC case as more than a functional component, transforming it into an expressive, immersive display. Combining striking aesthetics, innovative floating design, optimized airflow engineering, and user-focused features, the ATLAS P7 brings a new dimension to modern PC building.
"The ATLAS P7 represents the culmination of our vision for immersive PC design—where performance, creativity, and personal expression converge into one unified experience," said Stimson Wang, CEO of GAMDIAS. "This is more than a case; it is a platform that transforms every build into a dynamic showcase."IMMERSIVE PANORAMIC VIEW WITH FIGURE DISPLAY STAGE
The ATLAS P7 features four-sided tempered glass in a columnless panoramic design, delivering an unobstructed, multi-angle view of the system interior. A dedicated figure display platform paired with an omni-directional spotlight creates a dynamic showcase for collectibles and hardware. The tool-free side panel clasp allows easy access for effortless customization and figure swapping.DYNAMIC AIRFLOW - NATURAL CHIMNEY COOLING
The ATLAS P7 comes equipped with three pre-installed 120 mm NOTUS M1 PWM ARGB fans at the bottom, along with an 8-port PWM ARGB fan hub for synchronized control and efficient cooling management. The case utilizes a chimney-style airflow design, drawing cool air from the bottom and exhausting heat through the top for consistent, unobstructed performance.
ENHANCED CONNECTIVITY, COMPATIBILITY, AND CLEARANCE
The ATLAS P7 supports ATX, microATX, and Mini-ITX motherboards, CPU coolers up to 165 mm, GPUs up to 425 mm, and PSUs up to 200 mm, with radiator support up to 360 mm on the top and flexible fan configurations throughout the chassis. Storage options include up to 2 x 3.5-inch + 1 x 2.5-inch or 1 x 3.5-inch + 3 x 2.5-inch. The front I/O features a USB 3.2 Gen 2x2 Type-C port (20 Gbps), two USB 3.0 ports, LED control, a spotlight switch, and HD audio, while dust filters on the top, side, and bottom ensure long-term protection without compromising airflow.
KEY FEATURES FOR ATLAS P7
- Four-sided Tempered Glass Display
- 3 Built-in 120 mm NOTUS M1 ARGB Fans
- Pre-installed 8-port PWM ARGB Fan Hub
- Natural Chimney-Style Ventilation
- Floating Aesthetic Design
- Action Figure Display Stage
- Dual-Chamber Clean Cable Management
- Supports Mini-ITX, microATX, and ATX Motherboards
- Gen 2x2 Type-C Port Ready
- Supports GPUs up to 425 mm
- Magnetic Dust Filters
Scheduled for retail availability on Newegg in early December 2026.

articles.title: Sony releases new PS5 firmware as hackers set their sights on GTA VI
articles.text:
Grand Theft Hacking: Console makers have always played a dangerous game of cat and mouse with firmware hackers, and the stakes are even higher now that AI-assisted exploit development is becoming a reality. With the release of Grand Theft Auto VI fast approaching, Sony is working hard to patch every vulnerability it can find to keep hackers at bay.
Sony recently released a new system update for the PlayStation 5. Firmware version 26.07-14.23.00 includes only some vaguely described "security fixes" to the console's system. However, the timing of the release suggests that the new firmware could be intended to do more than simply patch a few unnamed vulnerabilities in the PS5's software.
The 26.07-14.23.00 update weighs in at more than 1GB and arrives just a couple of days before GTA VI is set to land on PS5 and Xbox consoles. The generation-defining crime adventure is expected to reinvigorate the entire gaming industry, but hackers could spoil the party by releasing a working pirated copy of the game in record time.
Fueled by the growing popularity of vibe coding and Sony's controversial stance toward physical gaming, crackers are now targeting the PS5 platform with unprecedented focus. The Relapse exploit provided a new avenue for jailbreaking PS5 consoles running firmware versions released before September 2026, while more recent firmware releases have proved somewhat harder to crack. Nevertheless, hackers are still finding ways to break through.
The new 26.07-14.23.00 firmware arrived just a day after the previous version, 14.22, following claims by a PS5 developer that they had dumped a game's binary using an undisclosed exploit on a console running that firmware. No conclusive evidence has emerged regarding the jailbreak status of version 14.22, but the PS5 piracy community continues to search for opportunities to breach Sony's DRM defenses.
We don't know whether GTA VI will require the latest firmware version to run on the PS5. The game's preload is now available, and Rockstar will likely continue updating its files until its November 19 launch. The 14.23 firmware could simply be Sony's attempt to block potential hacking attempts targeting one of the most important releases of the ninth console generation.
Either way, the industry is well aware that things are looking increasingly bleak for its traditional, closed-console business model.
Former Rockstar North technical director Obbe Vermeij said that creating a PC port of GTA VI through vibe coding would be difficult, but that people would try anyway. In a recent interview, Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick acknowledged that combating piracy across the GTA franchise is becoming increasingly challenging. However, he believes the publisher will ultimately be able to "manage" the threat and turn GTA VI into another money-printing machine.

articles.title: Stripe backer Atomico calls for Europe to own its success stories | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Europe is home to many of the world’s fastest growing companies of all time, veteran VC firm Atomico highlighted in its latest annual State of European Tech report.
The report, for instance, notes that the likes of Black Forest Labs and Microagi have reached $100 million in revenue in months, not years. “I think we can put to bed the idea that there’s a fundamental reason or constraint on the ability to scale a breakout company from here in Europe,” Atomico partner and head of intelligence Tom Wehmeier (pictured) told TechCrunch.
Yet, there’s still more that the VC firm founded by Skype’s Niklas Zennström would like to see — and its call this year is for Europe to “build it” and “scale it,” but also “own it.” That’s a way of wishing these companies will remain European longer. But there’s also a sense that this success hasn’t been acknowledged enough, perhaps obscured by louder calls for improvements.
Wehmeier, the report’s lead author, was quick to opine that “policy, procurement and capital are not moving at the same speed as our founders.” But he said the tech sector should advocate for itself in an inspiring way.
“When it comes to policy, I think the language needs to be, ‘Hey, this is not us complaining. This is us saying here is an opportunity to make the magnitude of impact even greater,’” Wehmeier said. “When we frame it as problems, that becomes harder.”
This reframing may also help European tech improve its image abroad, where complaints around overregulation may have overshadowed Europe’s potential to leverage its deep tech talent and growing pool of repeat entrepreneurs to have even more of success stories.
Plenty could be still done to fully unlock this potential, and Wehmeier said that “the next few weeks are going to be a really important test, with EU Inc.” Also known as the 28th regime, this initiative would create a unified European corporate regime akin to the Delaware C Corp.
If the last stretch of EU Inc’s grassroots campaign achieves it goal, it will become much easier to create and operate businesses across the EU. It would also show that the tech system got itself heard, which could open the door to the kind of endorsement Atomico is hoping to see more of.
Politicians have strong incentives to give the tech sector what it wants. If it is Europe’s second largest sector, biggest contributor to growth, and biggest job creator, “Do we not want more of that?” Wehmeier asked rhetorically. But it is unclear whether it will win them any votes.
To make the answer more straightforward, the tech sector will have to work on having public opinion on its side. For Wehmeier, one key is to “demonstrate that this is translating into value for citizens.”
The report is supporting this endeavor with a mix of high-level data and examples from its portfolio; for instance, it notes that ICEYE’s satellites monitor severe weather, flooding, and other hazards; and Daniel Ek’s Neko Health has now done more than 100,000 body scans, some of which helped identify severe or life-threatening health conditions.
One limit to this argument is that Neko Health’s scans will seem pricey to most Europeans, who largely rely on collective, public health insurance. But Atomico seems to hope that its report will give readers FOMO not just as potential customers, but also as potential shareholders.
There’s more to be done for this to happen. Beyond joining the sector’s push for an EU capital markets union, he hopes more of Europe’s institutional investors will invest in the region’s own tech companies. “We must get to the place where Europe and European beneficiaries are the biggest shareholders in the success that we create,” Wehmeier said.
Before that can happen, the industry must overcome anti-industry beliefs like fears of AI-induced job destruction. But Wehmeier is a believer in the power of proof. “I think that trust is going to be earned through showing results to the public — be that lower energy bills, better healthcare, more homes built for cheaper and faster, and having infrastructure that we can rely on.”

articles.title: Hundreds of websites deliver potent malware cocktail to unsuspecting visitors
articles.text:
Hundreds of websites using the Optimizely website personalization platform served unsuspecting visitors a potent malware cocktail that targeted cryptocurrency wallets, stole payment card data, cookies, and screenshots, and delivered exploit kits for infecting iPhones and iPads, researchers said Tuesday.
ReportURI said it identified 178 websites—including CNN, Zoom, the BBC, and Salesforce—that were affected. JavaScript digitally signed by Optimizely and then loaded into customer pages had been modified to include malicious components that attempted to infect visitor devices with multiple payloads. When wares were installed successfully, they swapped user cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attackers. Other components skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and, on iPhones and iPads, delivered iOS exploit kits known as Coruna and DarkSword.
Optimizely infrastructure delivers multipurpose malware
Optimizely serves JavaScript “snippets” that include both company code and code that is provided by each customer. The JavaScript, which can be served directly from Optimizely or from a customer endpoint, runs on every page the customer serves. Somehow, the attackers wrote their own code into a portion of each affected customer’s JavaScript and then delivered it from cdn.optimizely.com. A valid certificate for that domain signed the JavaScript.
ReportURI researcher Scott Helme said the delivery mechanism wasn’t a CDN cache poisoning attack, which uses HTTP to cause a CDN to cache harmful responses. Instead, the attack relied on Optimizely’s legitimate infrastructure, including its domains, to serve the tainted code. Optimizely’s own customer JavaScript for the www.optimizely.com and login.optimizely.com URLs were also affected.
“We don’t know how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated customer projects: a compromised Optimizely system, a compromised credential with cross-customer access, or something else,” ReportURI Helme wrote. “That’s for Optimizely to explain.”
Optimizely representatives didn’t respond to questions sent by email.

articles.title: Microsoft rolls out new first-party models and updates to agentic AI continuous improvement - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Microsoft rolls out new first-party models and updates to agentic AI continuous improvement
Microsoft Corp. today rolled out new generative artificial intelligence models and updates to Foundry, the company’s unified enterprise platform that helps developers and organizations ground, test and deploy AI applications and autonomous agents.
Updates to Foundry IQ, part of Microsoft IQ, now provide an enterprise knowledge graph out of the box, delivering a full estate of unstructured and application data to provide rich context for building applications and delivering on essential use cases.
Microsoft also said Foundry now uses existing transparency and observability capabilities to help customers create learning loops. Internal evaluations allow autonomous agents to establish baselines for quality, safety, latency and cost, enabling continuous behavioral improvements.
This includes human annotations, now in preview, that allow experts to rate and comment on agent traces based on business judgment. It feeds back into an improvement loop. It’s combined with optimization tests against evaluations and comparisons against real-world results. Foundry now also has new capabilities to adapt to supported models with organizational data to apply reinforcement learning while Foundry runs compute.
Each improvement becomes the next baseline and teams can continue measuring results and test changes, allowing them to improve quality.
Microsoft’s updated decision model and first-party AI models
Microsoft today announced Decision-1.1 is generally available. It’s a fast, cost-effective model designed to make reliable decisions in software at scale.
The generative AI model can make decisions dynamically at low cost, rather than relying on hard-coded rules, while offering superior decision-making capabilities compared with large language models. LLMs spend a lot of time making decisions in routing, classification, prioritization, verification and workflow control by “thinking it through,” which is unnecessary. Decision models are designed to reach answers quickly within constrained definitions and provide calibrated confidence scores, allowing applications to defer when uncertainty is high.
The new model builds on the previous generation, Microsoft-Decision-1, released in October. The new model delivers a significant improvement in intelligence and speed at a competitive price.
The company said it’s built on a new base, Google LLC’s Gemma 4 26B A4, adding multimodal support so it can analyze images in instructions.
Microsoft also extended its MAI, a Microsoft AI first-party family of models added to Foundry for enterprise trust.
These models include the new MAI-Code-2, which can handle demanding agentic coding work; MAI-Code-2-Flash supports high-volume, everyday coding, so developers can choose between performance and cost. Both are now generally available on GitHub, with Code-2-Flash in private preview in Foundry.
MAI-Image-2.7 and MAI-Image-2.7-Flash are now in preview and offer sharper editing and more consistent image generation. These will help brands maintain a consistent look across campaigns at a lower cost.
In cybersecurity, MAI-Cyber-2-Flash is a purpose-built model for cyber efforts and available in preview in Codename MDASH – the company’s agentic code security system in preview for eligible organizations.
Microsoft Foundry itself now has an expanded model pool featuring the top 50 models, supporting a model router and AI Gateway for intelligence model selection. The Foundry also offers more than 11,000 models from OpenAI Group PBC, Anthropic PBC, Meta Platforms Inc., Mistral AI SAS, the open-source community and others.
The company said supported models can be evaluated and deployed in Foundry as part of the same continuous improvement workflow used for agents.

articles.title: Free publie déjà une nouvelle mise à jour de sécurité pour les Freebox, la cinquième en onze jours
articles.text:
Free a déployé lundi une mise à jour du Freebox Server, sa cinquième en onze jours. Cette fois, elle ne porte que sur des correctifs de sécurité.
Une énième mise à jour du Freebox Server est disponible depuis le lundi 16 novembre à 14h30 très exactement, pour les Freebox Revolution, Pop, Delta et Ultra. Elle prolonge une série entamée le 5 novembre, qui a vu l'opérateur de Xavier Niel publier pas moins de cinq versions en onze jours. Comme la plupart des précédentes, elle se limite à des correctifs de sécurité que l’opérateur ne détaille pas.
Désormais cinq mises à jour Freebox en onze jours
Bon, à force, Free risque de nous donner le tournis. Rappelons que le jeudi 5 novembre, l'opérateur lançait la version 4.13.3 du logiciel qui équipe ses Freebox, avant d'enchaîner avec les 4.13.4 et 4.13.5, cette dernière à minuit pile d'ailleurs, soit trois versions en 38 heures à peine. La 4.13.6 a suivi dans la nuit du 10 au 11 novembre, et voici donc la 4.13.7. Toutes, comme la 4.13.2 du 22 octobre, renforcent la sécurité.
Seule la 4.13.6 sortait du lot, avec deux bugs nommés noir sur blanc et corrigés. Selon les abonnés, les enregistrements de chaînes comme TF1 et M6 sur le disque de la box échouaient depuis la 4.13.3, et la console des machines virtuelles ne répondait plus depuis la 4.13.5. La 4.13.7, elle, revient au service minimum, avec pour seule explication donc, le déploiement de « correctifs de sécurité ».
Comment installer la mise à jour 4.13.7 sur votre Freebox
Free cultive donc le mystère. Son application mobile éponyme parle toujours d'un « renforcement de la sécurité et de la protection du système », sans nommer la moindre faille. Une discrétion courante en matière de sécurité, puisqu'on le sait, détailler une faille tant que des box tournent encore sur l'ancienne version reviendrait à renseigner d'éventuels individus malveillants.
Quoi qu'il en soit, pour installer la version 4.13.7, il faut, choix numéro un, redémarrer le Freebox Server en naviguant, sur le boîtier, avec les touches directionnelles qui mènent au menu « Redémarrage », qu'il suffit de valider.
La solution la plus simple, c'est peut-être de passer par l'application Free. Dans la partie consacrée aux équipements Freebox, choisissez « Serveur internet », puis « Version logicielle » et « Mettre à jour », ou lancez directement « Redémarrer ». Pour vérifier que la 4.13.7 est bien en place, l'écran du boîtier affiche la version via « Informations avancées » puis « Version » sur Pop et Ultra, « Système » puis « Version » sur Freebox Revolution, et directement « Version » sur Delta.

Tasks in Gemini is not to be confused with Google Tasks.

articles.title: Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron form unlikely alliance to standardize robot charging as chipmakers push toward unmanned chip fabs — standard specs would allow manufacturer-agnostic charging equipment
articles.text:
Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron form unlikely alliance to standardize robot charging as chipmakers push toward unmanned chip fabs — standard specs would allow manufacturer-agnostic charging equipment
Semiconductor manufacturers are increasing automation to boost the productivity of existing fabs
Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, and Micron are reportedly working together to develop common charging standards for mobile robots used in semiconductor fabrication plants, according to a new report. Representatives from the three companies have reportedly formed an early-stage consultative body to lead standardization efforts, alongside major industry stakeholders such as the Semiconductor Equipment and Materials International (SEMI) industry association.
According to a report by Seoul Economic Daily, the initiative aims to establish common technical specifications that would allow robots from different manufacturers to share charging equipment, reducing the cost and complexity of deploying large robotic fleets across semiconductor manufacturing facilities. The broader goal is to accelerate factory automation, particularly in older fabs, while laying the groundwork for fully autonomous semiconductor manufacturing.
So why are three of the world's biggest memory manufacturers, who are also competitors, coming together to establish standards for the robotics industry? What exactly does the collaboration involve? And what are the implications of something as seemingly minor as robot charging for the broader semiconductor and robotics industries?
Why robot charging is becoming a problem for semiconductor fabs
Soaring demand for semiconductor memory chips used in AI infrastructure has driven manufacturers to automate as many production processes as possible to optimize manufacturing speed and capacity in existing facilities to increase output, while they build additional fabs. Modern semiconductor fabs already have extensive automation systems. However, even these facilities still require human workers for certain operations, such as moving materials between floors and unpacking products, that existing automation systems cannot perform. The issue is even more pronounced in older fabs, which generally have fewer automated material-handling systems and still rely on workers to move wafer containers using manual carts.
One potential solution is to hand these remaining manual operations over to mobile robots, allowing manufacturers to automate tasks without undertaking extensive renovations or installing complex fixed transport systems. These could include autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) that transport materials around the factory, mobile manipulators that combine robotic arms with moving platforms, and humanoid robots capable of performing more complicated handling tasks.
The problem, however, is that these robots come in different builds and configurations, often with their own batteries and accompanying charging infrastructure. A semiconductor fab deploying multiple robot models from different manufacturers could consequently end up requiring separate charging stations for each model. In addition to increasing equipment and maintenance costs, these installations consume valuable factory floor space.
The proposed initiative seeks to address this problem by establishing common charging specifications that different robot manufacturers can adopt. Standardized charging infrastructure would allow multiple types of robots to use compatible charging stations, reducing the need for separate installations and making it easier for semiconductor manufacturers to expand their robotic fleets without adding operational inefficiencies.
What the proposed standard covers and how it would work
The alliance is considering standards covering battery specifications for different mobile robots, charging-station equipment and communication protocols, charging connectors, and battery management systems (BMS). Together, these specifications would establish common requirements for the physical and electronic interfaces involved in charging robots inside semiconductor fabs.
The initial objective is to achieve charging compatibility across different robot models. In addition to letting a fab deploy robots from several manufacturers without having to install a separate charging system for every model, this would also give manufacturers greater flexibility when purchasing new robots, since their choice of supplier would no longer be as heavily influenced by the charging infrastructure already installed in the facility.
A subsequent step would involve integrating robot charging data with the fab's manufacturing execution system (MES), the software that coordinates and monitors manufacturing operations. With access to information such as battery charge levels, robot availability, and production schedules, the system could coordinate when individual robots operate and when they return for charging. For example, robots could be scheduled to recharge during periods of lower demand or while other robots handle critical material transfers, minimizing interruptions to production. This integration would become increasingly important as manufacturers deploy larger fleets of robots across the hundreds of individual processes involved in semiconductor fabrication.
Interestingly, the three chipmakers leading the standardization efforts are primarily customers of industrial robotics manufacturers, not manufacturers of the robots themselves, except for Samsung, which has an established robotics business. The objective is to develop specifications that robotics manufacturers and charging-equipment suppliers can incorporate into their products.
On the other hand, the three companies are not independently creating specifications and dictating them to suppliers. The initiative would likely follow an industry standardization process in which robotics manufacturers, equipment suppliers, and other stakeholders contribute to developing and validating the technical requirements. For now, the project remains in its early stages, with participants still determining which components and interfaces should be standardized and consulting robotics and smart-factory specialists.
Why the chipmaking rivals are joining forces now, and the broader implications
According to DigiTimes, semiconductor industry participants first explored establishing common robotics standards roughly a decade ago, but discussions made little progress until recently. The renewed momentum is largely attributed to the ongoing semiconductor boom, which has coincided with rapid advancements in industrial robotics.
Unprecedented demand for AI-related memory products, along with record financial performance, has given semiconductor manufacturers both the incentive and the financial resources to invest more aggressively in factory automation. While manufacturers are expanding production capacity to meet demand, new fabs take years to construct and bring online. As a result, they are simultaneously looking to squeeze out as much capacity as possible from existing facilities by increasing automation and improving productivity.
As for why Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron are collaborating despite their intense rivalry, the answer likely comes down to shared commercial interests. Incompatible robot charging infrastructure is an industry-wide problem, and all three companies stand to benefit from a common solution. The AI boom has already encouraged numerous partnerships across the semiconductor supply chain, including between companies that are considered fierce rivals, as manufacturers look for ways to overcome common production and infrastructure constraints.
The involvement of these particular companies also gives the initiative considerable weight. Together, Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron control almost the entire global DRAM market. They also operate extensive semiconductor manufacturing networks and represent a substantial potential market for fab-specific robotic equipment. A common set of specifications backed by all three would therefore provide robotics manufacturers with a strong commercial incentive to develop compatible products, potentially shortening development cycles and accelerating adoption.
Although the current collaboration focuses on a relatively small aspect of factory automation, it is a significant step for broader standardization across the semiconductor manufacturing and industrial robotics industries. Common charging infrastructure would make it easier to deploy and manage mixed robotic fleets, while future integration with production management systems could bring fabs closer to operating with minimal human intervention. This longer-term ambition of completely autonomous facilities is already taking shape. Both SK hynix and Samsung have outlined plans to develop an autonomous semiconductor fab by 2030.
Etiido Uko is a news contributor for Tom's Hardware covering the latest updates in big tech and the PC industry. He is a mechanical engineer and senior technical writer with over nine years of experience in documentation and reporting. He is deeply passionate about all things engineering and technology, and is an expert in gadgets, manufacturing, robotics, automotive, and aerospace.
