articles.title: Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing
Today, Amazon SageMaker AI introduces KV cache-aware routing (KV-aware routing), a new routing strategy for real-time endpoints. It uses the cache state that the model container reports. It sends each request to an instance that already holds a long cached match for its prompt and isn’t too busy. It’s for teams that serve large language models (LLMs) with multi-turn conversations, long shared prompts, or heavy load. You turn it on in two places: add one environment variable to your model so the container reports its cache contents, and set RoutingStrategy to KV_AWARE in the endpoint configuration. Your clients call the endpoint with the same APIs as before.
Here’s the problem it solves: LLM applications such as chat assistants, Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), and agents with long system prompts send many requests that start with the same text. A model keeps the work it did on a prompt in GPU memory, the KV cache, and skips that work when the same start reaches the same instance again. In part 1 of this series, we introduced prefix-aware routing for Amazon SageMaker AI, which sends requests that start the same way to the same instance. Prefix-aware routing infers where a prefix is cached from the request alone, so it can’t tell when an instance has evicted that cache.
Prefix-aware routing picks an instance from the request alone. It hashes the start of the request, up to the PrefixLength you configure (bytes of the InvokeEndpoint payload, or characters of the message text for the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API), and sends requests that start the same way to the same instance. It never sees what an instance actually has cached. This works well when every request starts with the same shared text, and less well in two cases:
The cache on an instance changes over time. An instance evicts older KV cache entries when its GPU memory fills up, but the router keeps sending matching requests there as if the cache were still warm.
A conversation starts out short. In a multi-turn chat, each turn adds to the history. While the request is still shorter than PrefixLength, every new turn changes the text the router hashes, so the next turn can land on a different instance than the one that cached the earlier turns. The turns of a conversation stay on one instance only after the request grows past PrefixLength.
In this post, we explain how KV-aware routing works, when to use it, and how to enable, invoke, and verify it on single model endpoints and inference component endpoints.
How KV-aware routing works
KV-aware routing has three parts: the model container reports what it has cached, SageMaker AI keeps a managed cache index of that state for the endpoint, and the endpoint uses the index to choose an instance for each request.
When you turn events on with SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG, the container publishes a KV cache event each time it stores or evicts cache entries, and SageMaker AI uses these events to keep the index current. The index holds only pointers: one-way, truncated hashes of cached content, each mapped to the instance or inference component copy that holds it. It never stores prompts, token IDs, request payloads, or KV tensors. When a request arrives, the endpoint tokenizes the prompt and looks up the tokens in the index. The index returns the instances or inference component copies that hold part of the prompt in their cache, and how much of it each one holds. For example, if instance A holds the cached start of a conversation, the next turn of that conversation goes to A. Because the index matches on tokens rather than a fixed number of bytes, a multi-turn history can match in full as it grows. A request that shares only part of its prompt still goes to the instance with the longest match.
The endpoint then picks among these candidates by weighing how much of the prompt each one has cached against how busy it is. A candidate that is too busy is skipped, so if the instance with the longest match is busy, the request goes to the next-best one that is available. If no candidate has a useful match or all of them are busy, the request falls back to load-aware routing, as described in Routing overhead and fallbacks. You don’t configure a concurrency threshold for this, as you do with prefix-aware routing. The index also follows the fleet. When you scale in, entries for removed instances are dropped. When you scale out or an update replaces instances, the new instances start with empty caches, so latency can be higher for a short time.
In Figure 1, the endpoint has three instances, A, B, and C. Each instance runs the same model in its own model container (the AWS vLLM Deep Learning Container listed in Requirements and limits) and has its own KV cache in GPU memory, so each instance holds different cached content: A holds turns 1 to 3 of conversation 1, B holds conversations 2 and 3, and C holds document 7. When turn 4 of conversation 1 arrives (step 1), the router tokenizes it and looks it up in the managed cache index (step 2). The index shows that A holds the first 6,000 of the request’s 6,200 tokens, so the router sends the request to A (step 3), and A only has to compute the remaining tokens. If A is busy, the router sends the request to the least busy instance instead (step 4). KV-aware routing needs a choice of destinations, so it is active only with at least two instances, or at least two copies of an inference component. With a single instance, every request goes to that instance and the setting has no effect.
Routing strategies on SageMaker AI
With this launch, SageMaker AI offers four routing strategies for real-time endpoints. You set the strategy per production variant in the RoutingConfig of your endpoint configuration.
| Strategy | How it routes | Recommended for | 
| RANDOM (default) | Sends each request to a randomly chosen instance. | General-purpose workloads, non-LLM models, and requests that are interchangeable. | 
| LEAST_OUTSTANDING_REQUESTS | Sends each request to the instance with the fewest in-flight requests. | Workloads where processing time varies and you want to keep all instances equally busy. | 
| PREFIX_AWARE | Sends requests that share the same prompt prefix, up to PrefixLength, to the same instance. Overflows to another instance at ConcurrencyThreshold. | LLM workloads with shared text at a fixed position at the start of the request, on any serving framework that supports prefix caching. | 
| KV_AWARE (new) | Sends each request to an instance that holds a matching cached prefix, based on cache state reported by the container, weighing match length against load. Falls back to load-aware routing. | LLM workloads on a supported container with multi-turn conversations, frequent cache eviction, or requests that share only part of their start. | 
Prefix-aware or KV-aware
Both strategies send requests to where their prefix is likely to be cached. They differ in how they know where that is, and in what they need from your container.
|  | Prefix-aware routing | KV-aware routing | 
| Source of cache location | Inferred from the request prefix | Cache state reported by the container | 
| Added latency per request | 1.3–1.9 milliseconds in part 1 | A few milliseconds for short prompts, more for long ones, mostly for tokenization | 
| Matching | First PrefixLength bytes (Invoke API) or characters (OpenAI-compatible API) | Tokens, longest cached match | 
| Parameters | PrefixLength, ConcurrencyThreshold | None needed | 
| Container | Any container with prefix caching on | A supported container, with prefix caching and KV cache events on (see Requirements and limits) | 
| Request payload | Any | OpenAI-compatible Completions or Chat Completions format | 
Performance
We measured KV-aware routing against random routing in two ways: a large-scale benchmark on production-sized instances, and a smaller, reproducible comparison you can follow in Verify that KV-aware routing is working.
Benchmark results
In our benchmarks with Llama 3.1 70B Instruct on seven ml.p5.48xlarge instances, we ran 30-minute tests with 20 or 100 simulated users holding multi-turn chats and document Q&A sessions, with prompts of up to about 64,000 tokens. Compared with random routing, and with long prompts under load, KV-aware routing reduced p50 time to first token (TTFT) by up to 97 percent and increased throughput by up to 234 percent. It raised the KV cache hit rate from 3–48 percent to 80–93 percent. Long prompts gained even at lower load. The gain was smallest with short prompts, where there is less prefill to save. Results depend on your workload. To measure them for your own traffic, use the checks in Verify that KV-aware routing is working.
Routing overhead and fallbacks
Before it routes a request, the endpoint tokenizes the prompt and looks it up in the managed cache index. The lookup takes a few milliseconds for short prompts and longer for long ones, mostly for tokenization, but it stays small next to the time a cache hit saves. For text-only requests that use standard options, the tokens it computes are passed to the model, so the prompt isn’t tokenized twice.
If the lookup is slow, finds no useful match, or all matching instances are busy, the endpoint routes the request with load-aware routing, the same behavior as the LEAST_OUTSTANDING_REQUESTS strategy. The request is still served, without the cache benefit. The same happens when the endpoint can’t tokenize a request, except in the two error cases described in Invoking the endpoint. These fallbacks aren’t reported in the SageMaker AI console or metrics at launch, so use the checks in Verify that KV-aware routing is working to confirm that routing is effective for your traffic.
With very short prompts there is less prefill to save, so prefix-aware routing can be all you need.
When to use KV-aware routing
Prefix-aware routing needs no changes to your container, but it can’t see what an instance actually holds. KV-aware routing asks the container what it holds, which makes it more precise. It pays off when there is a lot of cached context to reuse and that cache is under pressure: long prompts, high load, and instances that run short of GPU memory for the KV cache. When that happens, the container evicts the least recently used parts of the cache, including parts of shared prompts and conversation history.
For example, a support assistant runs on three instances, and each conversation begins with the same 6,000-token knowledge-base excerpt. Conversation 1 starts on instance A, which caches the excerpt. Traffic rises, A runs short of memory, and the container evicts most of that excerpt. Instance B recently served another conversation over the same excerpt and still holds its first 4,000 tokens. When the next turn of conversation 1 arrives, prefix-aware routing sends it to A again, and A recomputes the excerpt. With KV-aware routing, A’s container has already reported the eviction, so the index shows that B holds the longest match, and the request goes to B, which recomputes only the remaining tokens. At low load, A wouldn’t have evicted anything, and both strategies would have sent the request to A with the cache intact.
KV-aware routing helps most when requests reuse cached context in ways a fixed-length prefix can’t capture:
Multi-turn conversations: Each turn sends the full conversation history, so the cached prefix grows with every turn. KV-aware routing matches the whole cached history and keeps each conversation on the instance that holds it. This matters most for long conversations. After the managed cache index reflects an eviction, the router doesn’t keep sending the conversation to an instance that has already dropped its cache.
High-throughput inference with shared context: RAG applications prepend retrieved documents, and assistants send long system prompts with every request. KV-aware routing fits when these prompts are long and instances are under memory pressure. With a stable shared prefix and moderate load, prefix-aware routing also fits. Put the shared content first and in the same order: if the same documents appear in a different order, the prompts no longer share a start, so they don’t match.
Workloads where prefix length is hard to tune: With prefix-aware routing, you choose a PrefixLength that covers your shared text without scattering requests that should stay together. KV-aware routing has no prefix length to tune, because it matches on what is actually cached.
Prefix-aware routing is a good fit, with no container changes, if your requests share a stable system prompt or document at the start, your prompts are short, or load is moderate. In these cases, instances have enough GPU memory to keep the shared text cached, so both strategies find it. Prefix-aware routing is also the choice if your container isn’t supported by KV-aware routing, because it works with any container that has prefix caching turned on. If your requests are short and interchangeable, or your model isn’t an LLM, there is little cached context to reuse, so use RANDOM or LEAST_OUTSTANDING_REQUESTS.
If you aren’t sure which fits, start with prefix-aware routing, run your own traffic against a KV_AWARE endpoint, and compare time to first token, throughput, and hit rate as described in Verify that KV-aware routing is working.
Requirements and limits
Before you enable KV-aware routing, check that your container, endpoint, and requests meet these requirements:
Container: At launch, KV-aware routing supports the AWS vLLM Deep Learning Container for SageMaker AI: images with vLLM 0.33.0 or later, or the Amazon Linux build server-sagemaker-cuda-v2.8.0 or later. Prefix caching must be on, which is the default, and KV cache events must be turned on with the SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG environment variable, as shown in How to enable it. SageMaker AI doesn’t set it for you.
Endpoints and instances: Real-time single model endpoints and inference component endpoints, including dynamic Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters, on GPU instance types. You can also configure KV-aware routing with AWS CloudFormation. Routing is active only with at least two instances for a single model endpoint, or at least two copies of an inference component, which can be on the same instance. With fewer, you can still set KV_AWARE and the endpoint isn’t rejected, but every request goes to the single instance or copy.
Requests: OpenAI-compatible Completions or Chat Completions payloads, sent with InvokeEndpoint, InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream, or the SageMaker AI OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API. InvokeEndpointWithBidirectionalStream isn’t supported. If you set the model field, it must match the value of SM_VLLM_MODEL.
SDK versions: Detailed observability, which you use to track the KV cache hit rate, needs AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) version 2.35.6 or later, or Boto3 version 1.43.31 or later.
SageMaker AI checks these requirements before your endpoint serves traffic. If a check fails, the request or deployment fails with a message that describes what is missing. For the full list of settings, validation behavior, and quotas, see the SageMaker AI documentation.
How to enable it
You turn on KV-aware routing in two places: the model and the endpoint configuration. The example notebook runs every step end to end, for both a single model endpoint and an inference component endpoint.
1. Turn on KV cache events in the model – When you create the model, add SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG to the container environment. Without it, the endpoint has no cache state to route on. The ports in this setting are used only inside the instance, so you don’t open them to your network.
2. Choose KV-aware routing in the endpoint configuration – Set RoutingStrategy to KV_AWARE in the RoutingConfig of the production variant:
If your container image is built for CUDA 13, also set InferenceAmiVersion in the production variant to an AMI that supports it, such as al2023-ami-sagemaker-inference-gpu-4-1. Otherwise the container can fail to start. See Inference GPU drivers.
Check that your account has enough endpoint quota for the instance type and count you choose, and request an increase in Service Quotas if needed.
The same RoutingConfig setting works for inference component endpoints, including dynamic LoRA adapters. For adapters, KV-aware routing chooses among the instances that already have the adapter loaded.
Invoking the endpoint
Nothing changes in how you call the endpoint. Send a Chat Completions payload with InvokeEndpoint, or with InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream and "stream": true in the request body:
You can also call the endpoint with the OpenAI Python client through the SageMaker AI OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API. The Use the OpenAI-compatible API with SageMaker AI notebook on GitHub shows how, for both single model endpoints and inference components.
KV-aware routing doesn’t apply the multi-tenant prefix isolation from part 1: it ignores the prefix-aware ID header and the prompt_cache_key field. A request that sets a top-level cache_salt field to a non-null value is rejected with a 400 error.
KV-aware routing adds two error cases: a request whose model field names a model that the container doesn’t serve fails with a ModelError, and a request with a non-null cache_salt is rejected with a 400 error. Errors from inference itself are returned as before, and your model container’s own logs in Amazon CloudWatch can help you find the cause. The endpoint doesn’t deliver logs about its KV-aware routing decisions to your account, so use the checks in Verify that KV-aware routing is working, such as cached_tokens per request and the KV cache hit rate, to see how routing behaves.
Verify that KV-aware routing is working
KV-aware routing doesn’t add metrics of its own, so you check its effect on your model. There are three ways to do this.
Check cache hits per request – The container doesn’t report prompt token details by default, so set SM_VLLM_ENABLE_PROMPT_TOKENS_DETAILS to true in the model environment. Each response then includes usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens, the number of prompt tokens that were served from the KV cache. When you send a follow-up turn, or another request that starts the same way as an earlier one, a non-zero value shows that the request reached an instance that held its prefix.
Check model metrics in Amazon CloudWatch – Turn on detailed observability by adding --metrics-config '{"EnableDetailedObservability": true}' when you create the endpoint configuration, using the SDK versions in Requirements and limits. SageMaker AI then publishes the model container’s metrics, including the KV cache hit rate and TTFT. Query them as described in Detailed observability with PromQL.
Compare with the strategy you would otherwise use – For most LLM workloads the real choice is between KV_AWARE and PREFIX_AWARE, so compare those two, and add a RANDOM endpoint as a baseline. Use the same model, instance type, and instance count for each endpoint, and send the same prompts at the same concurrency for the same duration, so that the only difference is the routing strategy. Make sure your test reuses context the way your production traffic does, for example with multi-turn conversations or shared documents. If KV_AWARE and PREFIX_AWARE perform about the same for your traffic, prefix-aware routing is the simpler choice.
As an example of this comparison, we compared RANDOM and KV_AWARE on a small endpoint. We sent the same multi-turn workload to two endpoints that differ only in routing strategy. Each endpoint had two ml.g5.xlarge instances serving Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on a supported container. Each run sent 128 requests: 32 simulated users, each asking 4 questions about a document chosen from 12 documents of about 7,400 tokens. Each question resends the conversation so far, so every question after the first can reuse cached context. We ran two pairs of runs, with RANDOM first in pair 1 and KV_AWARE first in pair 2, and used new documents for each pair so that both endpoints started with empty caches. Table 1 shows the results as pair 1 / pair 2.
| Metric | RANDOM | KV_AWARE | 
| CloudWatch ModelLatency average (ms) | 4,124 / 5,100 | 1,235 / 1,314 | 
| CloudWatch ModelLatency p50 (ms) | 3,153 / 4,083 | 656 / 700 | 
| CloudWatch ModelLatency p90 (ms) | 8,334 / 10,746 | 3,213 / 3,535 | 
| CloudWatch ModelLatency p99 (ms) | 17,779 / 16,249 | 6,876 / 7,238 | 
| Time to first token p50, questions 2–4 (ms) | 1,284 / 1,632 | 237 / 245 | 
| Time to first token p90, questions 2–4 (ms) | 5,039 / 6,101 | 456 / 367 | 
| Time to first token p90, all requests (ms) | 5,003 / 5,683 | 1,465 / 1,759 | 
| Share of prompt tokens served from cache | 0.761 / 0.701 | 0.903 / 0.903 | 
| Run duration (s) | 31.1 / 36.9 | 17.9 / 18.0 | 
| CloudWatch OverheadLatency average (ms) | 13.1 / 8.1 | 27.1 / 27.5 | 
Table 1: RANDOM and KV_AWARE routing under the same workload. Each cell shows pair 1 / pair 2. ModelLatency and OverheadLatency are Amazon CloudWatch metrics for the endpoint. The client measured time to first token and run duration. The cache share is the sum of cached_tokens divided by the sum of prompt_tokens over a run
In both pairs, KV_AWARE had lower CloudWatch ModelLatency (average 1,235 and 1,314 ms against 4,124 and 5,100 ms) and lower time to first token for questions 2–4 (p50 237 and 245 ms against 1,284 and 1,632 ms). Its cache share was higher, at 90 percent in both pairs against 76 and 70 percent. OverheadLatency, the time SageMaker AI spends outside the model container, was 14 to 19 ms higher on average with KV_AWARE. This is one model, one instance type, and one workload with long shared documents, so measure your own traffic as described earlier in this section. Figure 3 shows the model latency charts that the SageMaker AI console displays for the two endpoints.
If neither does better than RANDOM, check that prefix caching and KV cache events are turned on in the container, as described in Requirements and limits.
Example notebook
The example notebook applies the steps in this post to Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on two ml.g5.xlarge instances, the minimum for a single model endpoint, and on an inference component endpoint with two copies. It calls the endpoint with both APIs, shows in the container logs that follow-up requests are served from the KV cache, and doesn’t compare routing strategies. Run its cleanup cells at the end to avoid ongoing charges.
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources you created. For an inference component endpoint, delete the inference components first (delete-inference-component), then the endpoint, endpoint configuration, and model (delete-endpoint, delete-endpoint-config, delete-model).
Practical guidance
These three practices help you keep KV-aware routing effective after you turn it on.
Monitor the KV cache hit rate – Keep detailed observability on after launch and watch the KV cache hit rate over time in the SageMaker AI Insights dashboard (Figure 2b), or query it with PromQL, as described in Verify that KV-aware routing is working.
Plan for cold starts – The first request with new context, such as a new document or the first turn of a conversation, has nothing cached on any instance. KV-aware routing speeds up the requests that follow, not the first one.
Plan for cache rebuilds during scaling and updates – As described in How KV-aware routing works, new instances start with empty caches. To soften the latency increase, use a rolling or blue/green update for single model endpoints, or a RollingUpdatePolicy for inference components.
Conclusion
KV-aware routing gives SageMaker AI real-time endpoints a second way to send requests to where their prompts are cached. It uses the cache state that your model container reports, so it follows the cache when instances evict it under memory pressure. Prefix-aware routing from part 1 of this series remains the simpler choice for stable shared prompts, short contexts, and moderate load. SageMaker AI handles routing inside the endpoint for both strategies, so you don’t build or run a routing layer yourself. You turn it on with one environment variable in the model and "RoutingStrategy": "KV_AWARE" in the endpoint configuration.
KV-aware routing is available today in all commercial AWS Regions that support SageMaker AI real-time inference, for endpoints that use a supported container. It is available at no additional charge. SageMaker AI runs and manages the cache index for you, and you pay only for the instances your endpoint uses. KV_AWARE is a new value for the existing RoutingStrategy field, so you don’t need a new configuration object, and older versions of the AWS CLI and Boto3 accept it. To get started, read the documentation, run the example notebook on a small endpoint, and then compare KV_AWARE with PREFIX_AWARE on a copy of your own traffic.

articles.title: Nvidia is abandoning China after Jensen Huang's ouster | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, acting CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country.
China’s access to leading AI accelerators was an important topic during the company’s first earnings call since CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down last week. The disclosure comes the same day Nvidia announced it was creating a board-level committee to oversee national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risks.
Nvidia’s deal to sell H200 chips in China was brokered by Huang and President Donald Trump. The arrangement required the chips to be shipped through the U.S., allowing the government to collect a 25% tariff.
The pathway angered China hawks who wanted to deny Chinese labs computing power and maintain the United States’ lead in AI, but Huang long argued that it was more important for the U.S. to compete in China. In April, he told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that “to concede that market for the United States technology industry is a disservice to our country.”
Huang’s ouster — in part over an affair with the CEO of a company under investigation for smuggling chips into China — has coincided with new rules, issued Monday, barring advanced U.S. chips from foreign data centers that serve Chinese customers remotely.
Investment bank Jefferies forecast that those rules might trim between $44 billion and $62 billion from Nvidia’s data center revenue next year. Referencing the new export controls, Kress said that the backlog of demand for advanced chips like Vera Rubin means the rules would have no impact on the company’s top-line revenue.
In the long term, the company may face the loss of potential customers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia. Critics of Nvidia’s dependence on China claim that as much as 20% of its revenue comes from demand linked to the country — annual revenue at its Singapore subsidiary hit $104 billion in 2025 before Nvidia stopped disclosing those figures — but that’s clearly going to change.
Even before Nvidia decided to stop shipping H200s, China had largely refused to accept their delivery. The government would prefer to generate demand for the country’s domestic chip industry, even if major AI compute users want the still-superior Nvidia equipment, according to Jacob Feldgoise, a researcher at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology.
Meanwhile, Chinese frontier labs are finding ways to access Nvidia chips elsewhere. All of China’s leading AI models show evidence of having been trained on Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips that are prohibited from being exported to China.
That training may have taken place at data centers outside of China, but sales to those facilities will be barred under the new rules. If large data centers suited for training AI models want to buy Nvidia chips, they will have to certify they aren’t serving any Chinese customers, export control attorney Dan Fisher-Owens told TechCrunch.
If they can’t provide that certification, the new rules may force them toward other chip options and further eat into Nvidia’s market share.

articles.title: Data intelligence lifts enterprise AI factory accuracy to 94% - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Dell puts a single gateway between enterprise AI agents and the data they crave
Data intelligence is becoming the deciding layer of the enterprise AI factory as companies learn that racks of graphics processing units deliver little value when agents lack trusted, governed context.
Neocloud providers built the first wave of large-scale AI systems, and core enterprise customers now want the same capabilities inside their own organizations. Dell Technologies Inc. recently extended its AI Data Platform with semantic and knowledge graph features aimed at that market shift. But both the challenge and the opportunity lie in pairing structured and unstructured data so agents get full context while maintaining guardrails and human oversight, according to Srinath Alapati (pictured, right), senior director of product marketing for AI Data Platform at Dell.
“The bottom line is if you feed the wrong data, you get the wrong outcomes,” Alapati said. “What we’ve found is in our own testing — by giving the right context — you can improve the accuracy from roughly 60% to like 94%.”
Alapati, Alison Biers (center), senior director of product marketing for compute, networking and global industries at Dell, and Adam Glick (left), senior director of AI solutions product marketing for compute at Dell, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Dell is tying data, infrastructure management and validated designs together to move enterprise AI factories into production. (* Disclosure below.)
How data intelligence feeds the AI factory
Enterprises can’t give agents unfettered access to their systems, which is where Dell’s newly announced Agentic Data Gateway fits. The gateway sits in the orchestration layer as a single point of control, backed by a Model Context Protocol server, Alapati explained. Storage intelligence tells customers what data they hold, who owns it and how large it is, while Dell’s new data intelligence capabilities track lineage and provenance. Hybrid workflows extend that model across the edge, the cloud and the data center, where companies can struggle to meet the data consolidation requirements of other data platform providers.
“They want you to bring all the data to wherever the platform is. That’s not always possible,” Alapati said. “Number one, it’s super expensive. Two is data is always being generated. It’s a never-ending game. You can’t always keep bringing in data, consolidating data. What we do is we only send metadata … That way your data stays where you want to be.”
On the infrastructure side, Dell OpenManage Rack Scale extends management beyond compute endpoints to the network fabric, power and cooling. That gives operators a single operational plane from day zero through day two, according to Biers. A rebuilt, intent-based Dell Fabric Manager replaces the company’s SmartFabric Manager, and Dell’s PowerRack systems treat the full rack as the unit of deployment.
“It is literally six hours from the time it hits your loading dock to full production,” Biers said. “Something that used to take maybe months and months [is] now cut in half, maybe even less.”
More than 6,500 customers now use the Dell AI Factory, and a growing share are core enterprises asking for help putting AI to work, Glick noted. Validated designs built with Nvidia Corp. and other partners cover both the hardware and the full software stack, and Dell is expanding its labs to keep pace with independent software companies joining the ecosystem. Compute still draws most of the attention, but that is only one part of a larger system.
“If you’ve got a factory, compute is your assembly line. It’s the important part,” Glick said. “It’s what you think of when you think of ‘factory’, but that assembly line doesn’t run if you don’t have a warehouse that’s feeding it the raw materials — that’s the data that goes into it.”

articles.title: México tiene 71 centros de datos y Brasil 225: la falta de electricidad frena la inversión en IA
articles.text:
México tiene 71 de los más de 500 centros de datos de América Latina, frente a los 225 de Brasil, y la falta de electricidad y los trámites lentos frenan la llegada de nuevas inversiones en inteligencia artificial, según un reportaje de Bloomberg.
Chile, un país mucho más pequeño, cuenta con 66, de acuerdo con el directorio Data Center Map. Cerca del 70% de las instalaciones mexicanas está en Querétaro, en el centro del país, una zona donde la red eléctrica ya muestra señales de saturación.
Juan Carlos Mondragón, de la Asociación Mexicana de Data Centers (MEXDC), dijo a Bloomberg que el área de Querétaro está “muy saturada” y que México no es competitivo en suministro eléctrico.
La cercanía con Estados Unidos juega a favor: los datos viajan hacia ese mercado casi a la misma velocidad que desde su propio territorio. Expertos agregan que el rechazo a estas instalaciones en Estados Unidos podría empujar proyectos hacia México.
Hasta tres años para conectarse a la red eléctrica
CloudHQ, una desarrolladora de centros de datos, anunció el año pasado una inversión de USD 4.800 millones para seis instalaciones en Querétaro. Su máximo responsable en México, Luis Lugo, describió a Bloomberg los obstáculos del proyecto.
“En circunstancias normales, se tarda al menos ocho meses en obtener un contrato de conexión eléctrica”, afirmó Lugo. Con consultas y revisiones, el proceso puede llegar a tres años. Además, dijo, tuvo que tramitar unos 111 permisos sin contar los de energía.
Mondragón señaló que los clientes necesitan proyectos terminados en 12 o 14 meses, mientras que la Comisión Federal de Electricidad (CFE) suele tardar bastante más en construir las líneas de transmisión. Según Bloomberg, la empresa estatal se negó a comentar cómo agilizaría permisos u obras para estos centros.
El plan del Gobierno depende de la CFE
La presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum prometió sumar 32 gigavatios de generación antes de que termine su mandato en 2030, más de un tercio de los 91 GW actuales de la red nacional. Por ley, la CFE debe producir la mayor parte, lo que limita a los generadores privados, según Bloomberg.
El Gobierno también anunció USD 8.000 millones para más de 200 líneas de transmisión hasta 2030. Desde el año pasado aprobó al menos cuatro grandes centros de datos, con una inversión prevista cercana a USD 10.000 millones.
El ministro de Economía, Marcelo Ebrard, dijo a Bloomberg que para algunos de esos proyectos se construyen ahora centrales eléctricas y líneas de transmisión junto con el sector privado. Sobre la inteligencia artificial, afirmó que solo hay dos opciones: “o se dispone de ello, o no”.
Ninguna instalación alcanza la escala que exige la IA
La directora ejecutiva de MEXDC, Adriana Rivera Cerecedo, afirmó en una entrevista con la revista Industry & Energy Magazine que la IA no puede operar con menos de 250 megavatios y que hoy ningún centro de datos del país llega a esa potencia. El mayor, en Pedro Escobedo, Querétaro, opera con 149 MW.
Según la asociación, el país tiene 279 MW instalados y 205 MW en construcción. Sus estudios proyectan una demanda de 1.730 MW en 2031. Bloomberg señaló que MEXDC espera inversiones directas de algo más de USD 20.000 millones en cuatro años.
Rivera Cerecedo dijo a Energía Estratégica que MEXDC espera que esos 205 MW entren en operación a finales de 2026 y que otra cantidad igual reciba energía en el primer trimestre de 2027.
El desafío posterior a 2027 será habilitar la infraestructura necesaria para cubrir los 1,320 MW que todavía separarían al sector de la proyección de 1,730 MW para 2031. Esa expansión requerirá nuevas fuentes de generación, refuerzos en las redes de transmisión y distribución, además de procesos de interconexión que permitan a los desarrolladores asegurar el suministro para sus instalaciones.

articles.title: Karnataka aims to become a global hub for frontier tech; Fadnavis’ vision for a new Maharashtra
articles.text:
Karnataka aims to become a global hub for frontier tech; Fadnavis’ vision for a new Maharashtra
Karnataka aims to become a global hub for frontier technologies such as AI, deeptech, and biotech, said CM DK Shivakumar at Bengaluru Tech Summit. Meanwhile, Maharashtra CM Fadnavis has shared his roadmap for a trillion-dollar, drought-free, deeptech Maharashtra by 2035.
Dear Reader,
The best of AI is yet to come.
The potential of artificial intelligence still remains unexplored, and it can help create solutions with population-scale impact, said panellists during a discussion at Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026.
Karnataka Home and IT Minister Priyank Kharge, Infosys Co-founder S Gopalakrishnan, Biocon Group Chairperson Kiran Mazumdar Shaw, and Accel India Founding Partner Prashanth Prakash stressed the opportunities in areas such as drug development, cybersecurity, IT solutions, governance and services.
At another conference across the world, Union Minister Jayant Chaudhary spoke about India’s robust startup story.
India has around 300,000 registered startups, many of which are led by women, the Minister of State for Skill Development and Entrepreneurship told global tech leaders at the TIECON 2026 conference in Singapore. “Our seeds are sown throughout the country,” he said. Highlighting the market potential, he pointed out that Indian farmers are keen to use technology, and the IITs are launching deeptech funds.
Moving on, ecommerce giant Amazon plans to invest an additional $7 billion in renewable energy projects in India by 2030, as it seeks to meet growing electricity requirements and reduce the carbon intensity of power across its operations.
In other news, Pragya Misra, OpenAI’s head of strategy and global affairs in India, is taking on a new role. She will lead the firm’s business development for India and South Asia, with a focus on building partnerships that help businesses transform with AI.
In today’s newsletter, we will talk about
- Karnataka’s aim to become a global hub for frontier tech
- Fadnavis’ vision for a new Maharashtra
Here’s your trivia for today: What cloud-based gaming service did Google launch in 2019, only to shut it down in 2023 due to lack of adoption? (Scroll down for the answer)
Technology
Karnataka aims to become a global hub for frontier tech
Karnataka aims to become a global hub for frontier technologies such as artificial intelligence, deeptech, semiconductor, robotics, and biotech, said Chief Minister DK Shivakumar at the inaugural of Bengaluru Tech Summit (BTS) in Bengaluru on Tuesday, citing the state government’s enabling policies.
BTS, now in its 29th edition, is themed around ‘AI and Beyond’. Addressing the event, the chief minister highlighted that Karnataka has consistently been at the forefront of technology and is well placed to lead the next phase of global innovation, backed by a strong IT and startup ecosystem.
Key takeaways
- Karnataka, the CM said, accounted for two out of every five dollars earned by India through software and services exports, which amounted to around $173 billion last year.
- The state attracted $9.4 billion in FDI equity inflows in the first half of FY26, accounting for 26.7% of India’s total inflows during the period. Karnataka is home to more than 24,000 recognised startups, and nearly two out of every five Indian unicorns originate from the state, Shivakumar said.
- AI is another main focus of Karnataka’s technology ambitions, with Bengaluru accounting for nearly 50% of India’s AI and machine learning talent.
Roadmap
Fadnavis’ vision for a new Maharashtra
Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis spent nearly five hours judging student presentations at the summit of The Governance Challenge 2026 in Mumbai. Six finalist teams pitched their answers to one question: what can the Government of Maharashtra do to make the state an innovation hub by 2035? The teams presented ideas on healthcare, education, farming and access to credit.
Thereafter, the chief minister, the finalists of the challenge, and Gaurav Goel, Founder & CEO of Samagra, which runs the challenge, joined Shradha Sharma, Founder & CEO, The Bharat Project and YourStory Media, for an open conversation.
Key takeaways:
- Fadnavis shared his roadmap for a trillion-dollar, drought-free, deeptech Maharashtra by 2035. The CM called Gen Z the first generation born entirely into technology, constantly connected to global best practices. Properly channelled, he said, this exposure produces bright ideas. But he stressed the need for balancing new ideas with mentoring, oversight and experience. “Innovation is a simple solution for a very complex problem,” he stressed.
- Goel explained that The Governance Challenge (TGC) was created to fill the gap in management education. Business school case studies, campus events, internships and placements all lean heavily towards the corporate and startup world, leaving students with little exposure to governance or social impact. TGC tries to change that through immersion, in the hope that the experience stays with students and later draws them towards nation building.
- Shradha Sharma called the day a glimpse of what a Viksit Bharat could look like: a chief minister who listens, and young people ready to do the work.
News & updates
- Social media curbs: Meta Platforms has fine-tuned Instagram's content recommendation systems in India to curb the visibility of sexually suggestive material and violent content, deploying more advanced AI models to identify and filter unwanted posts before they reach users.
- Funding: Redbrick Offices, which provides managed office spaces and workspace solutions, has raised about $72 million in equity across its Series A and A1 funding rounds. The company plans to use the capital to expand its managed offices portfolio and invest in technology, design and service delivery to cater to enterprise and GCC clients.
- Data centre curbs: The Trump administration plans to press ahead with efforts to block imports of Chinese data centre equipment despite pushback from Amazon, Google, Meta and other US technology companies, according to people briefed on the matter, Reuters reported.
What cloud-based gaming service did Google launch in 2019, only to shut it down in 2023 due to lack of adoption?
Answer: Google Stadia
We would love to hear from you! To let us know what you liked and disliked about our newsletter, please mail [email protected].

articles.title: La Voyager 1 llegará mañana a un día luz de la Tierra: sus señales tardarán 24 horas en llegar hasta nosotros
articles.text:
La NASA está a punto de recibir por primera vez un mensaje enviado desde un día luz de distancia. Tanto esta como otras agencias espaciales están más que familiarizadas con recibir señales mucho más lejanas que esa, gracias a los avances de la tecnología espacial. Sin embargo, será la primera vez que alguien recibe un mensaje tan lejano emitido por un objeto creado por el ser humano. Dicho objeto es la sonda Voyager 1, lanzada en 1977.
Los datos. El 18 de noviembre, 10:16 UTC (11:16, hora peninsular española), la Voyager 1 enviará señales de telemetría a los científicos de la NASA como lleva haciendo casi 50 años. Sin embargo, en esta ocasión el mensaje tardará justo 24 horas en llegar, ya que la sonda estará a 1 día luz de nuestro planeta. Esto no supone nada a nivel práctico, pero es un gran hito que está siendo muy celebrado tanto por la comunidad científica como por toda la sociedad.
Un saludo simbólico. Aunque la Voyager 1 no nos enviará ningún mensaje especial, nosotros sí podemos hacerlo. La NASA ha preparado para la ocasión una web con la que los móviles y tablets pueden parpadear simbólicamente en “VGR”, la señal de llamada de la sonda en código Morse. Esperan que muchas personas se unan a la iniciativa para que haya un anillo de luces saludando a Voyager 1 a lo largo de todo el mundo.
Medio siglo de viaje. En 1965, un estudiante de posgrado de Caltech llamado Gary Flandro estaba estudiando una rara alineación que se da entre Júpiter, Saturno, Urano y Neptuno cada 175 años cuando se dio cuenta de algo interesante. Si se aprovechaba la alineación que tendría lugar en 1977, se podría impulsar una nave hacia todos esos planetas en un tiempo récord, ya que la gravedad de cada uno de ellos le daría un impulso hacia el siguiente. Esta fue la semilla de la que nacieron las misiones Voyager, con las que se enviaron 2 sondas al espacio en 1977. La Voyager 2 se lanzó primero, el 20 de agosto de 1977, y la Voyager 1 despegó 16 días después, el 5 de septiembre. La Voyager 2 visitó los cuatro planetas, mientras que la Voyager 1 pudo observar de cerca tanto Júpiter como Saturno.
Ambas cumplieron sus cometidos y continuaron vagando por el espacio, más allá del Sistema Solar. Actualmente siguen funcionando, con la Voyager 1 más adelantada. De hecho, se calcula que la Voyager 2 alcanzaría el día luz en 2035, aunque posiblemente deje de funcionar antes.
Apagado de instrumentos. Poco a poco, las dos sondas se van quedando sin energía. Tanto la Voyager 1 como la Voyager 2 funcionan con un generador nuclear de plutonio, y la energía disponible baja unos cuatro vatios al año en cada sonda. Para aprovechar esa energía al máximo, se han ido apagando instrumentos poco a poco. De los diez instrumentos que llevaban inicialmente, la Voyager 1 ha apagado ocho y la Voyager 2 siete, así que trabajan bajo mínimos. En este tiempo, la NASA ha exprimido a la perfección la energía de las sondas, pero llegará un momento en el que esta se acabará. Mientras tanto, siguen batiendo récords como el que le espera a la Voyager 1 mañana mismo.

Black Friday 2026 – L'aspirateur robot Dyson Spot+Scrub Ai à 649,00 € (-17%)
L'aspirateur robot Dyson Spot+Scrub Ai passe sous les 650 € chez Amazon et Dyson soit une baisse d'environ 17% sur le prix habituellement constaté. C'est actuellement l'un des meilleurs produit de notre comparatif.
Dernier modèle sorti des lignes de production de Dyson, le Spot+Scrub AI a la lourde tâche d'imposer enfin le britannique comme un fabricant d'aspirateur-robot crédible. Et pour cela, cet appareil lancé à 1199 € compte sur l'IA et un bac à poussière dépourvu de sac.

articles.title: Govern and discover records with common metadata in AWS Agent Registry | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Govern and discover records with common metadata in AWS Agent Registry
As organizations build more agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and skills, they need a consistent way to describe, govern, and find them. AWS Agent Registry provides a catalog for registering, approving, and discovering these resources and custom records. Each record carries a name, a description, a protocol descriptor, and an approval status. However, every organization has attributes and facts that it wants to track, and some are unique to that organization, such as its business units, resource owners, risk classifications, and development environments. Organizations want one common definition for each of these attributes, and they want every agent, MCP server, and skill in the registry to carry these facts. Until now, organizations had no way to define these facts in AWS Agent Registry and store them on each record.
Custom metadata schemas are now available in AWS Agent Registry. A custom metadata schema is a set of organization-defined key-value pairs that records in an AWS Agent Registry carry. An administrator defines the schema and applies it to the registry, and all records within the registry must then adhere to the schema. When publishers create or submit records, they supply values for the fields specified in the applicable schema, and AWS Agent Registry validates those values against the schema set by the admin. Approvers can rely on the validated values when reviewing a record, and consumers and agents can use them to discover and filter records. Administrators, publishers, security and governance teams, approvers, consumers, and agents all work from a shared set of facts to govern, discover, and understand the resources in their agentic fleet.
In this post, we follow the AnyCompany organization publishing an MCP server with custom schema definition, enriching that record, and making it available for discovery by humans or agents. We use an MCP server as the example, but the same steps apply to other record types.
How custom metadata works
With custom metadata, an organization can use standardized vocabulary for describing its resources. The registry administrator defines the custom metadata schema: field names, types, allowed values, and whether each field is required or optional. The registry enforces the schema on every record, so a field such as environment has the same name and the same allowed values whichever team publishes the record.
The schema has common attributes that apply to every record type, and you can add dedicated fields that only apply to specific record types. Each field is Text, Enum, URL, or Boolean.
- When a record is created or updated, the registry validates the custom metadata against the schema set up by the admin. 
  - If a record is created without any custom metadata, AWS Agent Registry saves it as NON_COMPLIANT. A team can save work in progress this way, but it can’t submit the record for approval until it has the required fields and values.
  - If a record includes custom metadata with an unknown field, a missing required field, or an invalid value, AWS Agent Registry rejects it with a ValidationException.
- GetRegistryRecord returns the record’s custom metadata values and its compliance status. (COMPLIANT means that the values match the administrator’s schema. It is not an approval. The approvers make that decision.)
- Discovery APIs also allow filtering records based on custom attributes.
What custom metadata makes possible
Because teams can describe the AWS Agent Registry records with the same fields and values, the registry can support and scale governance and compliance.
Ownership and operations
Fields such as environment (prod, staging, or dev), businessUnit, ownerTeam, supportContact, and costCenter record where a resource runs, who is responsible for it, and who pays for it. A configuration management database (CMDB) ID links the record to your existing inventory, and a support-tier field sets expectations for anyone who depends on the resource.
Security and compliance
Data classification, compliance scope such as Payment Card Industry (PCI) or Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), risk tier, scan status, and a scan report URL turn an approval into a check of structured evidence. Your existing scanners, CMDB sync jobs, and classification tools write these values through the API before a record is submitted. You can build your record approval process or automation using these values, as this post shows.
Better discovery
Custom metadata values are indexed for search. A consumer or agent can combine a natural-language query with specific metadata filters, such as environment=prod AND businessUnit=payments AND securityScanStatus=PASSED. Only approved records are returned, so a record that matches the filters but hasn’t been approved stays out of the results. Figure 1 shows how each role, from administrator to consumer, moves a record through schema definition, registration, enrichment, approval, and discovery.
Walkthrough of an MCP record from registration to discovery
AnyCompany operates anycompany-governed-registry, an AWS Agent Registry without auto-approval. Its payments team publishes an MCP record, payments-ledger-mcp, a read-only server for ledger lookups. Existing security and inventory systems enrich this MCP record before an approval function decides whether consumers can discover it.
The five numbered steps in Figure 2 match the walkthrough: define, register, enrich and submit, review, then discover.
Prerequisites
To follow the walkthrough, you need:
- An AWS account in a supported AWS Region.
- AWS credentials available to Boto3 and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions for AWS Agent Registry.
- Python 3.11 or later and boto3 1.43.113 or later.
- The sample implementation is in the GitHub repo.
The snippets are shortened: cp and dp are the agent-registry-control and agent-registry boto3 clients. The sample repository has the complete code.
Step 1: AWS Agent Registry admin defines the custom metadata schema for the registry
AnyCompany’s admin creates a registry with a custom metadata schema that every record must follow.
- Every record must have its environment, businessUnit, and securityScanStatus fields.
- Records can also carry optional fields that the publisher or automation fills in later: ownerTeam, cmdbId, dataClassification, and securityScanReportUrl.
- MCP servers also record their networkEgress, which is optional.
Figure 3 shows this schema and the values payments-ledger-mcp will carry once enrichment completes in Step 3. The empty autoApprovalRules list means that the registry approves nothing on its own. Every submitted record stays in Pending approval until someone or something approves it. You decide whether that is done by automated checks you build (Step 4 uses an AWS Lambda function), a human approver, or both.
Administrators can also review the schema in the AWS Agent Registry console. Figure 4 shows the common attributes and the MCP-specific field as they appear on the registry’s details page.
Step 2: The publisher registers the server
The payments team’s pipeline registers payments-ledger-mcp with its custom metadata. Its first attempt uses production instead of one of the administrator’s allowed values.
The registry rejects the record. After the pipeline sends prod, the record is created as a compliant draft. This is how the schema keeps every team using the same values.
Step 3: Automation adds additional metadata and submits
Next, AnyCompany’s automation adds what its own systems know: the result from its security scanner, the asset ID from its CMDB, and the approved data classification. It then submits the record for approval.
An update replaces the whole metadata map, so the automation reads the current values, adds its own, and writes them back together. In the sample, the scanner and CMDB calls are stubs that you replace with your own tools. The registry sends a pending-approval event to Amazon EventBridge. In Step 4, a rule that you create passes the event to your approval function.
Step 4: The approval automation decides from the evidence
When the record moves to Pending approval, AWS Agent Registry sends an event to Amazon EventBridge, and an Amazon EventBridge rule is set to invoke a custom AWS Lambda function. Figure 5 shows the console view of payments-ledger-mcp, with the custom metadata values that the approval function reads for its check.
The function reads the record’s custom metadata and compliance status to check that the record is COMPLIANT, the scan PASSED, a cmdbId is present, and the data is public or internal. payments-ledger-mcp passes all four, so the function approves. A record that fails a check is rejected, and the reason names the failed check. In your production systems, you can choose to route records that need a human review, such as those with confidential or restricted data, for manual review instead of being rejected.
Step 5: Consumers find the records from AWS Agent Registry with custom metadata fields as filters
A developer looking for a ledger tool searches the registry and filters on the same fields the administrator defined.
The search returns payments-ledger-mcp because it’s approved and matches all three filters. Agents can run the same search through the registry’s MCP endpoint, https://agentregistry.<region>.api.aws/registry/<registryId>/mcp, which offers search, list, and get as MCP tools. In the GitHub sample, a Strands agent connects to the AWS Registry MCP endpoint and uses a model on Amazon Bedrock. Its system prompt lists the custom metadata fields to filter records on. The agent turns a plain-language request, such as “a production MCP server for payments ledger lookups that passed its security scan”, into a filtered search. It answers with payments-ledger-mcp.
Developers and agents query the same fields the administrator defined, and the approval function checked, so both find only servers that meet your governance rules.
Design the schema for long-term use
Treat the schema as your organization’s shared vocabulary:
- Agree on the vocabulary first. Settle field names and allowed values with the teams that publish and approve records before you create the schema. Schema changes are additive: you can add fields, add allowed values, or make an optional field required, but you can’t rename, remove, or retype a field.
- Expect existing records to lag behind schema changes made after the records were added to the registry. Existing records aren’t rewritten. A record that no longer matches the schema is reported as NON_COMPLIANT and keeps its approval status. The record stays approved, but its next update must meet the new schema. Editing an approved record creates a draft that must be submitted for approval again, and the submit fails until every required field has a value. Until a curator approves the new revision, consumers keep seeing the approved one.
- Put each field at the right level. Use common attributes for questions that apply to every record type, and record-type fields for record-specific facts such as autonomy level for agents.
- Pick the type that fits the field. Use Enums for decision fields that need consistent spelling, Text for external identifiers, and URL for evidence stored behind the source system’s access controls.
- Make a field required only when the publisher can assign a value at registration. For a value that your continuous integration (CI) or automation provides after the record is published, allow an interim value, for example PENDING. In this post, the scan runs after registration, so securityScanStatus has three values: PENDING, PASSED, and FAILED. The publisher writes PENDING, and the enrichment automation replaces it.
- Keep sensitive details out. Leave secrets, internal endpoints, and detailed findings out of broadly readable metadata.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how to add custom metadata in AWS Agent Registry to give every record a common set of facts, such as its environment, owning business unit, data classification, and security scan status. Using one MCP server, we showed an administrator defining the schema, a publisher and existing automation filling in the values, an approval function that you build in AWS Lambda deciding approval, and a consumer finding the approved server with metadata filters. Because the administrator owns the schema, every team uses the same fields and values, and that consistency is what makes approvals and searches in AWS Agent Registry dependable.
- Try it yourself: Use the sample at GitHub repo.
- Go deeper: Read the AWS Agent Registry Developer Guide and custom metadata API reference.
- Availability: See supported AWS Regions.

articles.title: Trmnl Frame is a $1,300 ePaper display designed to look like real artwork
articles.text:
In a nutshell: The holidays are just around the corner and gift giving is on a lot of minds, but what do you get for the person who has everything? It's an age-old question and one that Trmnl hopes to answer with its latest ePaper display... that is, if you've got deep wallets and don't mind waiting until early 2027.
The Trmnl Frame, not to be confused with a similarly named Samsung product, is a 31.5-inch full color digital picture frame enclosed in a wooden frame. The company's third release, it features a Spectra 6 ePaper display with a resolution of 2,560 x 1,440 (~16:9 aspect ratio). Inside is a 10,000mAh battery (upgradeable to 20,000mAh) that's reportedly good for between two to six months between charges, based on refresh rate settings.
There is also a USB-C port for always-on connectivity, discrete physical control buttons, and a microSD card slot for offline use. Trmnl additionally includes lifetime access to its web platform with no subscription fees required, and the device's firmware is open source for those that like to tinker.
The display is mounted in handmade wooden frames in your choice of white oak, cherry, sapele, or walnut woods. Trmnl literally opened its own woodworking shop a few miles from its headquarters, so the "handmade" description couldn't be further from the truth.
Frame can be hung in portrait or landscape orientation using the unit's built-in mounting points and included hanging hardware. There's also an optional wooden kickstand for an extra $25, and there's nothing stopping you from crafting your own stand.
Trmnl says Frame is ideal for displaying photos, art, calendars, and weather reports. Really, usage is limited only by your imagination.
Trmnl is now accepting pre-orders for Frame, with pricing starting at $1,299. According to the pre-order page, 197 of the initial batch of 475 units have already been spoken for. The company said it will be able to ship some orders by the end of 2026 but to expect most purchases to go out in early 2027.

articles.title: Civilization studio Firaxis Games lays off a third of staff
articles.text:
Firaxis Games, the studio behind the Civilization and XCOM franchises of computer strategy games, last week laid off about a third of its staff, totaling around 60 people. That’s according to a recent report in Bloomberg.
The report cites people “familiar with the cuts,” saying that the flagship game the studio is currently working on, a new entry in the XCOM series, “has faced development struggles and missed a significant milestone.” The departures also include the studio head, Heather Hazen.
A Firaxis spokesperson released the following statement:
Firaxis is restructuring and recentering around the studio’s core strength—designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years. As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis. These decisions are never easy, but they’re essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis.
The storied studio has had a rough run of things of late. Its most recent game, Civilization VII, launched to solid enough sales but divided players in terms of reception. Players have long criticized new Civilization titles for being barebones compared to immediate predecessors that have seen multiple post-launch updates and expansions, but the response was sharper this time.

articles.title: Por fin: WhatsApp tendrá almacenamiento propio para tus chats y será gratis
articles.text:
WhatsApp está por implementar uno de los cambios más importantes en la gestión de copias de seguridad de su aplicación para Android. La plataforma comenzó a probar un sistema de almacenamiento en la nube propio, el cual permitirá guardar tus chats en los servidores de WhatsApp. Una vez que se despliegue, los usuarios podrán olvidarse de Google Drive como opción para respaldar sus conversaciones.
La beta más reciente de WhatsApp para Android incluye una función conocida como WhatsApp Cloud Storage. De acuerdo con WABetaInfo, esta nueva opción ofrece hasta 2 GB de almacenamiento gratuito para guardar copias de seguridad de chats en la nube. La cantidad sería más que suficiente para el usuario promedio, aunque algunos tendrían que hacer ajustes para dejar fuera algunas fotos o vídeos en su respaldo.
Actualmente, WhatsApp depende de Google Drive para realizar las copias de seguridad en Android. Además de servir como espacio de almacenamiento, la función también nos facilita la vida cuando cambiamos de dispositivo. Solo necesitamos configurar nuestra cuenta de Google en el móvil y WhatsApp se conectará al Drive para restaurar nuestras conversaciones en el nuevo móvil.
El nuevo almacenamiento en la nube de WhatsApp ofrece las mismas funciones que el de Google Drive. La compañía confirmó que las copias almacenadas en sus servidores estarán protegidas por cifrado de extremo a extremo. Esta medida será obligatoria para utilizar el servicio, por lo que los usuarios tendrán que activar el cifrado de copias de seguridad y configurar una passkey o clave como método predeterminado de protección.
WhatsApp regala 2 GB de almacenamiento en la nube gratis
A juzgar por las imágenes, los usuarios podrán elegir entre su proveedor favorito para gestionar las copias de seguridad de sus conversaciones. WhatsApp ofrece la opción de usar el almacenamiento propio o cambiar a Google Drive en cualquier momento.
Si tus respaldos pesan menos de 2 GB, la opción más indicada sería configurar el almacenamiento propio, ya que esto ayudaría a liberar espacio en tu cuenta de Google para usarlo en otros servicios. No obstante, si tienes muchos vídeos o imágenes, lo mejor sería configurar por defecto la opción de Drive para no dejar fuera nada cada que se activa la copia de seguridad.
WhatsApp solo ofrecerá 2 GB a los que tienen una cuenta gratuita, aunque si pagas por WhatsApp Plus, podrás aumentar la cuota hasta 100 GB. La plataforma también ofrece la opción de obtener hasta 4 TB de almacenamiento, aunque deberás suscribirte a un plan de Meta One. En caso de que dejes de pagar la suscripción a Plus o One y tu copia de seguridad exceda los 2 GB, WhatsApp te dará hasta cuatro meses para que la renueves antes de borrar el archivo de su sistema.
Por el momento, el almacenamiento gratuito en la nube solo está disponible en la versión 2.26.46.4 de la beta de WhatsApp para Android. La compañía no ha confirmado si hará lo mismo en iPhone, que actualmente depende de iCloud para subir y guardar nuestras copias de seguridad. Conociendo a la compañía, es probable que esta característica llegue a todos en algún futuro no muy lejano.

articles.title: Nvidia board establishes National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee in wake of Jensen Huang scandal — group to work with independent law, national security, and trade compliance experts
articles.text:
Nvidia board establishes National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee in wake of Jensen Huang scandal — group to work with independent law, national security, and trade compliance experts
It's like closing the corporate barn door after the horse has bolted.
Less than a week after Jensen Huang resigned from the company, Nvidia's board has created its own National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee. According to its announcement, the new standing committee will provide high-level oversight of Nvidia’s “national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risk management,” with its National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team reporting directly to the group and to interim CEO Colette Kress.
“Nvidia recognizes that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security,” Nvidia chairperson Harvey Jones said. “As the world’s leading advanced computing company, Nvidia has both a responsibility and an opportunity to lead the industry in addressing these challenges. We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation.”
The rumors of Jensen Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy, have thrown the company into turmoil, especially after his admission and subsequent apology. People have begun digging into details about Ms. Huang, revealing that she was at the center of a tangled web of companies and was reportedly instrumental in importing around $7.5 billion of banned Nvidia chips into China. A deeper investigation also revealed that her husband, Kang Wei, was behind her rise to prominence and seemingly accepted her relationship with the billionaire. It remains unclear if the couple made these shrewd business moves purely for profit or if they were under the control of a hidden third party, but it has certainly exposed the company to additional scrutiny.
The chairpersons of the House committees on China, Foreign Affairs, and Intelligence have since invited Jensen to a closed-door briefing to discuss Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage,” while President Donald Trump mentioned that the FBI is looking into Jensen Huang’s relationship with Ms. Huang. The U.S. first applied export controls to Nvidia’s most advanced chips, the A100 and H100, in 2022, forcing the company to create the China-market A800 and H800 GPUs that complied with Washington’s performance limitations.
However, the White House lowered the bar once more in 2023, which resulted in the even more watered-down H20, which, nonetheless, remained in high demand. Even though the Trump administration did not implement Biden’s AI diffusion rule, which threatened to outright ban several countries from buying Nvidia AI chips, the president eventually banned the export of H20 chips to China from April to June 2025.
Even before Trump’s total Nvidia AI GPU ban, there have already been multiple reports of smuggling, with one semiconductor analysis firm tracking more than 1.5 gigawatts of banned AI chips exported to China and estimating that up to 1.5 million Nvidia GPUs were smuggled in recent years. Despite that, the former Nvidia chief has always denied the allegations, saying that “There’s no evidence of any AI chip diversion.” Whether the allegations are true or not, it seems that the company is taking the situation seriously and taking steps to plug any leaks. As for Jensen Huang, he may be out of the company, but he still has to face Congress and all ongoing investigations.

articles.title: New study shows how school phone bans help with learning
articles.text:
A new U.S. study has shown how banning cell phones from schools can improve student learning.
The findings were released by Harvard’s Center for Education Policy Research (CEPR) in partnership with researchers at NWEA and Dartmouth. According to the researchers, this is the first national analysis “comparing achievement growth for individual students, before and after strict cell phone bans.”
They say that as smartphones became widely adopted between 2013 and 2024, eighth-grade math and reading achievement fell by roughly one grade equivalent. This worked out to losing “the equivalent of two to three weeks of learning every year,” which the researchers acknowledged is “small on an annual basis” but nonetheless “accumulated” over time. Ultimately, they found that banning phones in schools worked out to restoring the equivalent of one to two weeks of lost learning each year, or about half of the annual decline in achievement since 2013.
To conduct the study, the researchers analyzed data from 3.3 million students attending 4,600 schools nationally during the 2021–22 through 2025–26 school years. Specifically, they examined schools that implemented strict cellphone bans that required students to store their devices in lockable pouches for the day.
Overall, these were some of the key findings:
- Lockable pouches had a “modest yet steady positive impact on student achievement” that lasted the four years
- Lockable pouches had a “consistent effect” across school and student demographics, with not significant differences across the grades, poverty levels of prior academic achievement
- Storing phones in lockable pouches appeared to “reduce the share of students suffering large drops in reading achievement”
- Bell-to-bell bans and instructional time bans boosted student achievement
With this study focusing on schools, researchers said next steps involve looking beyond the classroom. In particular, they encouraged social media restrictions that are already implemented by Meta to be extended to platforms like YouTube, TikTok and Snapchat, produce “baseline” measures to track social media use and regular monitoring of student engagement and mental health.
This study comes amid increased scrutiny around the globe on youth technology use. Earlier this year, Ontario said it was considering a ban on phones in schools, while Canada is planning to ban kids under 16 from using social media.
