articles.title: Secure OAuth patterns for Snowflake Cortex AI through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Secure OAuth patterns for Snowflake Cortex AI through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
Enterprises today need a clear way to extend their authentication and authorization controls into the agentic layer, often requiring either broad service account permissions or custom-built auth integrations that add operational overhead. When an AI agent running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model) needs to call the Snowflake-managed MCP server (which exposes Snowflake Cortex Agents as one of its tool types) through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the first question enterprises must answer is: how does the agent authenticate? In this post, we walk through three Open Authorization (OAuth) configurations we tested on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: Snowflake OAuth (per-user, no external Identity Provider, or IdP), three-legged OAuth with a third-party Identity Provider (corporate single sign-on, or SSO), and two-legged OAuth with a third-party Identity Provider (shared service user). Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity also supports an on-behalf-of (OBO) grant (TOKEN_EXCHANGE) that delivers per-user identity for unattended workloads without a consent prompt. We focus on the three configurations we tested end-to-end, flagging where OBO fits as we go. By the end, you will be able to identify which pattern suits your enterprise scenario.
Solution overview
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, connects AI agents to external tool providers through MCP server targets. It targets the Snowflake-managed MCP server, which surfaces Cortex Search and Cortex Analyst as MCP tools that an MCP-aware client can discover and invoke. Rather than acting as a wrapper, the Gateway aggregates the capabilities of its configured targets into a single unified catalog, which it presents to the agent as one tools/list response.
The core focus of this post is the outbound authentication for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway: how it obtains and presents OAuth tokens to the Snowflake-managed MCP server. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity acts as the credential broker: the Gateway obtains a workload token by calling GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT (because the Gateway uses JSON Web Token (JWT) inbound authentication), then calls GetResourceOauth2Token against the configured provider. AgentCore Identity owns the token vault, the token refresh, and the user-to-token binding, and it fetches, caches, and refreshes tokens automatically.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity supports three OAuth configurations spanning two grant types (authorization_code and client_credentials):
- Snowflake OAuth: Snowflake acts as its own OAuth authorization server. Each user authenticates directly to Snowflake through the Authorization Code grant (3LO). No external identity provider is needed.
- Three-legged OAuth using a third-party Identity Provider: Users authenticate through corporate SSO with the Authorization Code grant. Snowflake trusts IdP-issued JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) through its External OAuth security integration.
- Two-legged OAuth pattern using a third-party IdP: A shared service user authenticates through the client_credentials grant of the IdP. No user interaction or consent is required, which is ideal for machine-to-machine workloads.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity also offers an API-key credential provider (which supports Snowflake Programmatic Access Tokens). We focus on OAuth here for per-user attribution and automatic token refresh. Each configuration uses a credential provider in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity (CustomOauth2, OktaOauth2, or MicrosoftOauth2) and a corresponding security integration on the Snowflake side.
Note: We tested these patterns with the Snowflake-managed MCP server using Okta and Microsoft Entra ID. Patterns 2 and 3 (external IdP) follow standard OAuth flows, so they can extend to other OAuth-protected MCP servers, but validate the token claims, scopes, and audience settings for your SaaS provider. Only Pattern 1 is Snowflake-specific, because it relies on Snowflake’s built-in OAuth authorization server. The Snowflake-specific elements are the OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER issuer-lock parameter, the session:role: / session:scope: grammar, BLOCKED_ROLES_LIST, LOGIN_NAME / EMAIL_ADDRESS mapping, and QUERY_HISTORY attribution. If your SaaS exposes its own internal OAuth server, you configure outbound OAuth the same way as Snowflake OAuth.
| Pattern | OAuth grant | AgentCore Identity credential provider vendor | Snowflake security integration | Snowflake query identity mapping | 
| Snowflake OAuth – 3LO | authorization_code | Custom provider (CustomOauth2) | TYPE = OAUTH, OAUTH_CLIENT = CUSTOM | The real user, with their assigned role | 
| 3LO with external IdP | authorization_code | Built-in provider (such as OktaOauth2, MicrosoftOauth2) | TYPE = EXTERNAL_OAUTH + OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER (set with ALTER ACCOUNT / DATABASE / SCHEMA); EXTERNAL_OAUTH_TYPE = OKTA / AZURE / PING_FEDERATE / CUSTOM | The real user, with their assigned role | 
| 2LO with external IdP | client_credentials | Built-in provider (such as OktaOauth2, MicrosoftOauth2) or CustomOauth2 | TYPE = EXTERNAL_OAUTH + OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER (set with ALTER ACCOUNT / DATABASE / SCHEMA); EXTERNAL_OAUTH_TYPE = OKTA / AZURE / PING_FEDERATE / CUSTOM | A shared Snowflake service user | 
Notes:
- 2LO does not require a built-in vendor. CustomOauth2 with the CLIENT_CREDENTIALS grant can work with your choice of OAuth 2.0 authorization server.
- When Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway brokers the token (the pattern in this post), Snowflake validates it through the TYPE = EXTERNAL_OAUTH security integration. Setting OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER (with ALTER ACCOUNT, DATABASE, or SCHEMA) is what lets direct MCP clients auto-discover your IdP through the Protected Resource Metadata endpoint, and it issuer-locks the MCP endpoint to that integration.
- If you set OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER to issuer-lock an MCP scope to an external IdP (Pattern 2), Snowflake OAuth tokens (Pattern 1) are rejected for MCP servers in that scope and do not fall back. If you need both patterns in one account, set this parameter per schema or database so each scope resolves to the right authorization server.
Solution architecture
The following diagram shows the solution we built and the components it uses: a user-facing AI application, a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Bedrock for reasoning, with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails redacting personally identifiable information (PII) from prompts and responses, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability, over policy documents in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway with the Snowflake-managed MCP server as its target, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity holding the token vault. The outbound OAuth path has the same shape in all three patterns: the Gateway resolves a token through AgentCore Identity, which obtains and renews it from an authorization server, and the Gateway then presents that token to the Snowflake-managed MCP server. What changes between the patterns is which authorization server issues the token and under which grant: Snowflake’s own built-in OAuth server, or a third-party IdP. Those differences are set out in the Pattern comparison table, and each pattern’s runtime flow has its own sequence diagram later in this post.
Pattern analysis
The following sections examine each pattern in detail: the authentication flow, configuration steps, and trade-offs to help you select the right approach for your use case.
Pattern 1: Snowflake OAuth (three-legged)
The Snowflake OAuth pattern uses a three-legged OAuth (3LO) flow to deliver per-user authentication without requiring an external identity provider. Each user authenticates to Snowflake with their own credentials, consents to a specific Snowflake role, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity caches that user’s access and refresh tokens. Every subsequent Snowflake call executes as that user, and QUERY_HISTORY records their real username. Note that per-role consent is not the default. The Snowflake-managed MCP server advertises session:role:all and falls back to DEFAULT_ROLE, so you set OAUTH_SCOPES_SUPPORTED (an account-, database-, or schema-level parameter set with ALTER) to narrow the role scope the server advertises, and restrict ALLOWED_ROLES_LIST on the integration to enforce which roles a user can consent to (PRE_AUTHORIZED_ROLES_LIST does the opposite: it lists roles that skip the consent step).
What makes this pattern appealing is its simplicity: no external identity provider is required. Snowflake acts as both the authorization server and the resource server, exposing its own built-in OAuth endpoints (/oauth/authorize and /oauth/token-request). Setup follows a specific order, because the callback URL does not exist until the credential provider is created. The administrator first creates the CustomOauth2 credential provider in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity with placeholder client credentials and records the callbackUrl that AgentCore Identity returns. That callbackUrl is then registered as the redirect URI on a Snowflake security integration created with TYPE = OAUTH and OAUTH_CLIENT = CUSTOM. Finally, the administrator updates the credential provider with the real client ID and secret issued by Snowflake and configures the provider’s oauthDiscovery with explicit authorization server metadata: the issuer (the Snowflake account URL), the authorization endpoint (/oauth/authorize), and the token endpoint (/oauth/token-request).
The following screenshot shows the configuration steps for credential provider vendors in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity with Snowflake OAuth (3LO) settings.
Next, the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway configuration points to the Snowflake-managed MCP server endpoint and references the custom Snowflake OAuth for outbound authentication.
The following sequence diagram shows the runtime authorization flow for the Snowflake OAuth pattern.
The Snowflake OAuth authorization flow works as follows:
- When a tool call requires a Snowflake token, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway obtains a workload token by calling GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT and calls GetResourceOauth2Token to check the token vault of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity for the user. If no token is cached, the Gateway returns a JSON-RPC error code -32042 carrying a URL elicitation. That authorization URL belongs to AgentCore Identity and is session-URI-bound. The client opens that URL in the user’s browser, which is routed to Snowflake’s built-in authorization server (/oauth/authorize) and shown a Snowflake login screen.
- The user enters their Snowflake credentials and is presented with a consent screen asking them to authorize access using a specific Snowflake role (for example, ANALYST_ROLE). Role names in the requested scope must be uppercase (for example, session:role:ANALYST_ROLE).
- Upon consent, Snowflake’s authorization server returns an authorization code to the callback URL of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity. AgentCore Identity then redirects the user’s browser to the return URL with the session URI.
- AgentCore Identity completes the code exchange only after the application calls CompleteResourceTokenAuth with the user identity and session URI (valid for 10 minutes). This step binds the code to the originating request and blocks authorization-URL hijacking. The return URL used here is registered by calling UpdateWorkloadIdentity. In production, the endpoint at that URL is hosted either by your web application or, for gateways with JWT inbound authentication, by the AgentCore Identity Consent Portal (<portal-url>/connect/callback). The agentcore dev CLI hosts it only for local development. AgentCore Identity then exchanges the code at Snowflake’s token endpoint (/oauth/token-request) for an access token and, optionally, a refresh token.
- When the client retries the tool call, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway retrieves the cached access token from AgentCore Identity and presents it to the Snowflake-managed MCP server. Snowflake validates the token and creates a user session scoped to the consented role. The consented scope controls the primary role only. Because secondary roles are governed by the integration, set OAUTH_USE_SECONDARY_ROLES = NONE (the default) so the session cannot carry more privilege than the consented role, which the IMPLICIT setting would allow.
Access tokens are short-lived. By default, they last 600 seconds (maximum 3600). When an access token expires, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity automatically uses the refresh token to obtain a new access token, with no user interaction required. If the security integration is configured to prevent refreshing tokens, the user must re-authorize through the consent screen. Refresh-token lifetime is controlled by OAUTH_REFRESH_TOKEN_VALIDITY. The reference implementation sets it to 86400 seconds (1 day), and Snowflake allows up to 90 days. OAUTH_ISSUE_REFRESH_TOKENS (default TRUE) governs whether refresh tokens are issued at all.
Note: By default, Snowflake helps prevent the ACCOUNTADMIN, ORGADMIN, GLOBALORGADMIN, and SECURITYADMIN roles from being used with OAuth integrations. This is controlled by BLOCKED_ROLES_LIST for Snowflake OAuth (and EXTERNAL_OAUTH_BLOCKED_ROLES_LIST for External OAuth), applies to all three patterns, and covers the primary role only. With OAUTH_USE_SECONDARY_ROLES = IMPLICIT, secondary roles can still carry these privileged roles.
Considerations
The Snowflake OAuth pattern is the simplest path to per-user audit trails. It needs no external IdP configuration and no additional vendor dependency. It is best suited for scenarios where:
- Users already have Snowflake credentials and are comfortable signing in directly.
- You want per-user attribution in QUERY_HISTORY without an external identity provider.
- You are in a proof-of-concept phase and want to validate the per-user model quickly.
- Compliance requirements mandate individual accountability, so each query must be traceable to a specific user, not a shared service user.
- You prefer to manage user lifecycle (provisioning, deprovisioning, role grants) entirely within Snowflake.
- You want to avoid token claim mapping complexities. Snowflake issues tokens and knows exactly which user they represent.
Pattern 2: Three-legged OAuth (3LO) using a third-party Identity Provider (IdP)
This pattern combines per-user authentication with corporate single sign-on. Users sign in through the external IdP, which enforces multi-factor authentication (MFA), conditional access, and session policies. The IdP-issued JWT is presented to Snowflake, which validates it through its External OAuth security integration (optionally issuer-locked to the MCP server’s schema, database, or account with OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER). Snowflake verifies the issuer, audience, and signature through a JSON Web Key Set (JWKS). It then maps a configurable claim, set with EXTERNAL_OAUTH_TOKEN_USER_MAPPING_CLAIM (sub for Okta, upn for Microsoft Entra ID), to a Snowflake user’s LOGIN_NAME or EMAIL_ADDRESS (with EXTERNAL_OAUTH_SNOWFLAKE_USER_MAPPING_ATTRIBUTE), and runs the query as that user. The security integration parameter values are case-sensitive.
The key difference from Pattern 1: the authorization server is your corporate IdP (such as Okta, Microsoft Entra ID), not Snowflake. Snowflake remains the resource server. Users authenticate with the same credentials and policies they use for every other corporate application. No separate Snowflake passwords are required.
On the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore side, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity provides built-in credential provider vendors for popular identity providers (for example, OktaOauth2 and MicrosoftOauth2). These vendors accept the client ID, client secret, and IdP endpoints through includedOauth2ProviderConfig, compared to the generic CustomOauth2 provider used in Pattern 1. The Snowflake-managed MCP server uses pre-registered OAuth clients, so you register each client ID and secret in advance, which is why the create, record callbackUrl, register, update sequence is required.
Next, the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway configuration points to the Snowflake-managed MCP server endpoint and references the Okta credential provider for outbound authentication.
The following sequence diagram shows the runtime authorization flow for the three-legged OAuth pattern with an external IdP.
Snowflake’s External OAuth security integration flow works as follows:
- When a tool call requires a Snowflake token, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway obtains a workload token by calling GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT and calls GetResourceOauth2Token to check the token vault of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity for the user. If no token is cached, the Gateway returns a JSON-RPC error code -32042 carrying a URL elicitation. That authorization URL belongs to AgentCore Identity and is session-URI-bound, not the IdP’s. The client opens that URL in the user’s browser, and AgentCore Identity routes the user to the IdP.
- The user authenticates through the third-party IdP with corporate SSO (including MFA) and consents to the requested scopes. For Okta, the role scope takes the form session:role:ANALYST_ROLE. Microsoft Entra ID delegated flows use session:scope: instead.
- The IdP returns an authorization code to the callback URL of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, and AgentCore Identity redirects the user’s browser to the return URL with the session URI. Only after the application calls CompleteResourceTokenAuth to validate the user identity and session URI does AgentCore Identity exchange the code for an access token (and a refresh token, if the IdP issues one) and cache them in the per-user token vault.
- When the client retries the tool call (and on later calls), Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway retrieves the cached IdP-issued JWT from Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity and presents it to the Snowflake-managed MCP server. Snowflake validates the token through its External OAuth integration: it verifies the JWKS signature and audience (aud) claim, maps the configured user claim (sub for Okta, upn for Microsoft Entra ID) to the Snowflake user, and executes the query as the authenticated user. Snowflake does not call the IdP at runtime. It validates tokens locally using the IdP’s published JWKS signing keys.
- When the access token expires, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity automatically refreshes it using the cached refresh token, if one was issued (for Okta, request the offline_access scope). No user interaction is required until the refresh token expires.
Token lifetime governance: Unlike Pattern 1 where Snowflake controls token lifetimes, access token and refresh token lifetimes are governed by the IdP, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity handles the refresh transparently. If a refresh token was issued, the user re-authenticates only when it expires, based on the IdP’s session policy. Otherwise, the user re-authenticates when the access token expires.
Considerations
Choose three-legged OAuth (3LO) with a third-party IdP when:
- Your organization or security team requires all authentication to flow through corporate SSO for centralized MFA, conditional access, and session management.
- You want to use existing IdP features such as group-based role mapping, session timeout policies, and geo-based conditional access rules.
- You need per-user audit trails in Snowflake’s QUERY_HISTORY.
- You want uniform security policy enforcement across all applications, including AI agents.
- You need centralized access control. Disabling a user in the IdP helps prevent new Snowflake authorizations, though cached tokens stay valid until they expire. To force a user to re-authorize, the application can pass forceAuthentication=true on the next request, which clears the stored refresh token and starts a new authorization flow. To revoke access outright, revoke the grant at the IdP or in Snowflake.
Pattern 3: Two-legged OAuth (2LO) using a third-party Identity Provider (IdP)
The two-legged OAuth pattern uses the OAuth 2.0 client_credentials grant. This is a machine-to-machine flow with no user interaction. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity obtains a JWT from the IdP using the configured client ID and client secret, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway presents it to Snowflake, which executes the requests under a shared service user, regardless of which end user initiated the query.
This pattern is the most operationally direct: no consent screens, no per-user token vaults, no browser redirects. The users follow the same code path. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity fetches and caches the client_credentials token automatically, and the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway presents it on every outbound call to the Snowflake-managed MCP server.
The key difference from Patterns 1 and 2: there is no per-user identity propagation. Snowflake’s QUERY_HISTORY records a single service user for queries. The trade-off is operational simplicity at the cost of per-user audit granularity. On the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore side, the credential provider uses the client_credentials grant type: either a built-in vendor (OktaOauth2, MicrosoftOauth2) or the generic CustomOauth2 provider. Configuration requires the IdP’s token endpoint, client ID, and client secret. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity fetches a token from the IdP on the first tool call (when the Gateway calls GetResourceOauth2Token), caches it, and, because client_credentials issues no refresh token, requests a fresh one before expiry. No agent-level code changes are required.
Next, the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway configuration references the Snowflake-managed MCP server endpoint and the two-legged OAuth credential provider for outbound authentication.
The following sequence diagram shows the runtime authorization flow for the two-legged OAuth pattern.
Snowflake’s External OAuth security integration 2LO flow works as follows:
- When a tool call requires a Snowflake token, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway obtains a workload token by calling GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT and calls GetResourceOauth2Token on the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity credential provider. If a valid token is cached, Identity returns it immediately.
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity calls the third-party IdP’s token endpoint using the client_credentials grant with the configured client ID and client secret. For Okta, the requested scope includes the Snowflake role (for example, session:role:MCP_GATEWAY_ROLE). For Microsoft Entra ID, the client requests the api://<application-id>/.default scope and the role arrives in the roles claim from an app role whose value is session:role:MCP_GATEWAY_ROLE.
- The IdP returns an access token (a JWT, with no refresh token) whose aud claim is the Snowflake account URL or an additional value listed in EXTERNAL_OAUTH_AUDIENCE_LIST (for Microsoft Entra ID, typically the Application ID URI). For Okta, the sub claim is the client ID. For Microsoft Entra ID, the client ID is carried in appid/azp while sub holds the service principal’s object ID (a GUID), so with Entra, LOGIN_NAME must map to that GUID.
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway presents the JWT to the Snowflake-managed MCP server. Snowflake validates the token through its External OAuth integration (optionally issuer-locked with OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER, as in Pattern 2). It verifies the signature through EXTERNAL_OAUTH_JWS_KEYS_URL (or EXTERNAL_OAUTH_RSA_PUBLIC_KEY), the issuer through EXTERNAL_OAUTH_ISSUER, and the aud claim against the Snowflake account URL plus any additional values in EXTERNAL_OAUTH_AUDIENCE_LIST (these security integration parameter values are case-sensitive). Snowflake then maps the sub claim to a Snowflake service user through LOGIN_NAME and executes the query under that service user’s role. As in Pattern 2, Snowflake validates the token locally and does not call the IdP at runtime.
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity caches the token in the token vault (shared across users, not per user). Subsequent calls reuse it, and Identity requests a new token with the client_credentials grant before it expires.
Because the two-legged OAuth target needs no user consent, the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway connects to the Snowflake-managed MCP server at target-creation time and discovers tools through implicit sync during target creation. In the 3-legged OAuth patterns (Patterns 1 and 2), the Gateway target supports two creation methods: (1) an admin completes the authorization code flow so tools are discovered by implicit sync, or (2) the admin provides the tool schema upfront. (Discovery behavior is a ListingMode property of the target, not a property of the grant type.)
Considerations
The two-legged OAuth pattern is preferred for automated, unattended, and batch workloads. It is ideal when:
- Your workload is machine-to-machine: scheduled jobs, background pipelines, or system-level agents with no human in the loop.
- Per-user identity isn’t required, and a shared service user is acceptable for audit purposes.
- You need the most direct operational model: no consent flows, per-user token management, or browser redirects.
- The Gateway can connect to Snowflake and discover MCP tools by implicit sync at target-creation time, without waiting for user interaction.
- All users share the same data access rights under a single Snowflake role.
Accept these trade-offs:
- Because every request runs as the shared service user, Snowflake’s row-level security and column masking policies apply that user’s permissions to requests. Policies keyed on CURRENT_USER() and CURRENT_ROLE() all resolve to that single service user and its one role, which is the strongest case for the on-behalf-of (OBO) approach.
- There is no user-level token revocation. To cut off access, revoke the client credentials at the IdP or disable the Snowflake security integration.
- If credentials are compromised, agent access is affected. Rotate client secrets regularly and restrict the service user to least-privilege access.
Pattern comparison
| Aspect | Pattern 1: Snowflake OAuth (3LO) | Pattern 2: 3LO with external IdP | Pattern 3: 2LO with external IdP | 
| OAuth grant type | authorization_code | authorization_code | client_credentials | 
| AgentCore Identity provider | Custom provider (CustomOauth2) | Built-in provider (for example, OktaOauth2 or MicrosoftOauth2) | Built-in provider (for example, OktaOauth2, MicrosoftOauth2) or CustomOauth2 | 
| Authorization Server | Snowflake built-in OAuth | Third-party IdP (for example, Okta, Entra ID) | Third-party IdP (for example, Okta, Entra ID) | 
| Identity visible to Snowflake | The real user | The real user | Shared service user | 
| RBAC Model | Per-user Snowflake role | Per-user Snowflake role | Single role for requests | 
| Audit granularity (QUERY_HISTORY) | Real username | Real username | Service user | 
| External IdP required | No | Yes | Yes | 
| Snowflake security integration | TYPE = OAUTH, OAUTH_CLIENT = CUSTOM | TYPE = EXTERNAL_OAUTH + OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER (set with ALTER ACCOUNT / DATABASE / SCHEMA) | TYPE = EXTERNAL_OAUTH + OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER (set with ALTER ACCOUNT / DATABASE / SCHEMA) | 
| User login experience | Snowflake login + consent | Corporate SSO | None (no user interaction) | 
| MFA / conditional access | Per Snowflake account settings | Enforced by IdP | NA | 
| MCP protocol revision¹ | 2025-11-25 | 2025-11-25 | 2025-11-25 (not pinned on the 2LO gateway) | 
| Token lifetime governance | Snowflake security integration | IdP authorization server policy | IdP authorization server policy | 
| Works unattended (scheduled jobs)² | Only until the refresh token expires (reference app: 1 day, up to 90 days) | Only until the refresh token expires (per IdP session policy) | Yes: no user interaction needed. | 
| Best for | POCs needing per-user audit without an IdP | Enterprise apps with existing corporate SSO | Internal agents, batch jobs, service-to-service | 
¹ MCP protocol revision: for the three-legged patterns (Patterns 1 and 2), the gateway pins 2025-11-25 in its supported MCP revisions, which the URL-mode elicitation (-32042) handshake requires. The reference 2LO gateway (Pattern 3) does not pin it, because 2LO has no elicitation step. On accounts that are not enabled for MCP version updates, the supported set is fixed when the gateway is created.
² Works unattended: Patterns 1 and 2 run unattended only until the refresh token expires. Re-consent then requires a live browser, the same user, and completion inside the 10-minute authorization window (CompleteResourceTokenAuth), which is why 3LO is unsuitable for fully unattended scheduled jobs. Pattern 3 (2LO) has no refresh token and no consent step, so it runs unattended indefinitely.
The three configurations in this post cover two grant types: authorization_code (Patterns 1 and 2) and client_credentials (Pattern 3). Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity also supports on-behalf-of (OBO) token exchange (TOKEN_EXCHANGE), which delivers per-user identity for unattended workloads without a consent prompt.
OBO exchanges an inbound user token for a Snowflake-scoped token that preserves the real user’s identity, so QUERY_HISTORY attributes each query to the actual user, while keeping the unattended, machine-to-machine flow of Pattern 3 (no browser redirect, no consent screen). On the Snowflake side it uses the same TYPE = EXTERNAL_OAUTH integration as Patterns 2 and 3 (optionally issuer-locked with OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER). On the AgentCore side it is configured on the OAuth credential provider through onBehalfOfTokenExchangeConfig (grant mode TOKEN_EXCHANGE for Okta/RFC 8693, or JWT_AUTHORIZATION_GRANT for Microsoft Entra). OBO uses the External OAuth path (Patterns 2 and 3).
OBO is generally available on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, but it was outside the scope of the three configurations we tested for this post.
Try it yourself
To see these patterns in action, we built a financial-services credit-risk assessment agent as a reference workload. A single agent combines bank policy documents in Amazon S3 (through Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases) with customer data in Snowflake. It assesses loan eligibility, searches customer profiles, and queries account and transaction data. The demo exercises three MCP tools (Cortex Search, Cortex Analyst, and SQL Execution) across all three OAuth configurations for side-by-side comparison in your own AWS account.
Though the demo is financial services, the patterns work across healthcare, supply chain, insurance, and more. All three implementations are public and deploy end-to-end through a single deploy.sh script:
- Snowflake OAuth (3LO): amazon-bedrock-agentcore-snowflake-mcp-gateway-3lo.
- 3LO with external IdP: amazon-bedrock-agentcore-snowflake-mcp-gateway-3lo-okta.
- 2LO with external IdP: amazon-bedrock-agentcore-snowflake-mcp-gateway.
Note: For demonstration purposes, the reference implementations expose SYSTEM_EXECUTE_SQL on the same MCP server as the Cortex Agent. Snowflake recommends exposing a Cortex Agent as the only client-facing tool for governed business questions. If direct SQL is required, place it on a separate MCP server with a dedicated least-privileged role.
Conclusion
In this post, we walked through three OAuth configurations for authenticating AI agents to Snowflake Cortex AI over MCP through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. Snowflake OAuth offers the simplest path to per-user audit trails with no external IdP dependency. Three-legged OAuth with an external IdP adds corporate SSO, centralized MFA, and conditional access while preserving per-user identity. Two-legged OAuth with an external IdP serves machine-to-machine through a shared service user.
Across all three patterns, the agent code and the Snowflake MCP tool set stay unchanged. The OAuth wiring differs in four specific ways:
- The grant type flips: authorization_code for Patterns 1 and 2, client_credentials for Pattern 3.
- AUTHORIZATION_CODE targets need a return URL, set as defaultReturnUrl on the target and optionally overridden per request. 2LO targets need none.
- 3LO target creation requires implicit sync or an upfront tool schema, whereas a 2LO target syncs its tools during target creation with no user authorization step.
- OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER can be set for Patterns 2 and 3 to issuer-lock an MCP scope to the external IdP and to let direct MCP clients auto-discover it. It is left unset for Pattern 1. When it is set, Patterns 1 and 2 cannot share one scope, as noted earlier.
Beyond these four, only the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity credential provider (CustomOauth2, OktaOauth2, or MicrosoftOauth2) and the Snowflake security integration differ. Understanding these differences in grant type, token issuance, user mapping, and audit behavior equips you to select the right OAuth configuration for your compliance, operational, and user-experience needs.
To get started, explore the reference implementation in our GitHub repository. For more on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, visit the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore service detail page or the Developer Guide.

articles.title: Lapsus$ hacker pleads guilty to breaching Rockstar and leaking GTA 6 footage from a hotel TV
articles.text:
What just happened? Four years ago, Arion Kurtaj hacked into Rockstar Games using an Amazon Fire Stick, a hotel television, and a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse, stealing footage of the unreleased Grand Theft Auto 6. This week, the 21-year-old from Oxford pleaded guilty at Woolwich Crown Court to the breach, as well as several other cyber attacks he carried out at the ages of 16 and 17 as a member of the hacking group Lapsus$.
The plea follows an unusual legal process: Kurtaj was initially committed to a secure hospital but was later deemed fit to stand trial.
When he targeted Rockstar, Kurtaj was already on bail for other hacking offences. Police had seized his computer and placed him in a Travelodge in Bicester. The move was intended to protect him from rival hackers who had threatened to attack him over his stolen Bitcoin.
The hotel room did little to stop him. Kurtaj plugged a Fire Stick, a consumer device used to stream video, into the room's television. He then connected a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse and used the setup to access Rockstar's internal systems.
He stole internal company data, including 90 clips showing nearly an hour of gameplay from the unfinished title. He also accessed Rockstar's internal Slack messaging system and posted a demand: "If Rockstar does not contact me on Telegram within 24 hours I will start releasing the source code."
Rockstar did not respond. Kurtaj subsequently posted the clips and source code on a forum under the name TeaPotUberHacker. The company said the breach cost $5 million to address and required thousands of hours of staff time. The leak also revealed something Rockstar had been keeping under wraps for marketing reasons: one of the game's playable characters is a woman.
Rockstar was not his only target. Kurtaj also admitted to hacking BT/EE, Revolut and Uber. In those cases, he used social engineering – manipulating people rather than exploiting software vulnerabilities – to gain access to internal systems. During the Uber attack, the court heard, he posted a picture of a penis in an attempt to pressure the company into paying a ransom.
The financial damage across the companies is estimated at approximately £10 million. Kurtaj and other Lapsus$ members also used stolen corporate data to target cryptocurrency investors. Prosecutors said the group stole at least $300,000 from individual victims.
The road to this week's guilty plea was a long one. When the case first came before the court in 2023, doctors found that Kurtaj's autism was too severe for him to participate in a conventional criminal trial. The court instead held a trial of the facts, in which the jury determines whether the defendant carried out the alleged acts, rather than whether he had the criminal intent required for a conviction. In December 2023, the court ordered that he remain in a secure hospital indefinitely, unless doctors determined that he was no longer a danger.
A routine assessment late last year reversed that decision, finding him fit to face a criminal trial. He was transferred to a conventional prison in January, and a trial was scheduled at Woolwich Crown Court. He ultimately pleaded guilty to every count.
In the dock, Kurtaj had short hair and an unkempt beard. He wore a suit and a white shirt buttoned to the collar, without a tie. He blinked frequently during the hearing, stood to confirm his name and entered his pleas without showing any emotion.
The charges also covered his conduct in custody. He pleaded guilty to physically assaulting prison workers, including several biting incidents. He was also caught with a mobile phone in prison after sending police a taunting text message and posting updates on Snapchat. He will be sentenced at a later date.

articles.title: Qual é o melhor notebook para comprar agora? Saiba como escolher • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Resumo IA
- O Dell 15 é indicado para uso diário, com opções de processadores Intel Core i3, i5 e i7, memória RAM de até 16 GB e armazenamento SSD de até 1 TB.
- O Alienware 15 é indicado para jogos e aplicações gráficas pesadas, com processadores Intel Core i5 e i7, placas de vídeo Nvidia GeForce RTX 3050 e 4050.
- A escolha do notebook ideal depende do uso, com o Dell 15 sendo uma boa opção para estudantes e profissionais, enquanto o Alienware 15 é mais indicado para jogos e aplicações gráficas pesadas.
A escolha de um notebook novo vai além do processo: quem precisa dele para estudar tem prioridades diferentes de quem pretende jogar ou editar vídeos. Por isso, entender as especificações de cada aparelho é importante para encontrar o melhor modelo para você.
No Brasil, a Dell oferece as melhores opções para diferentes perfis, como o Dell 15, voltado à produtividade e às tarefas cotidianas, e o Alienware 15, para programas que exigem maior capacidade de processamento. Ambos contam com processadores Intel combinados a diferentes configurações de hardware, permitindo escolher o conjunto mais adequado para cada tipo de uso.
Como escolher o melhor notebook?
Antes de comparar modelos, é importante identificar quais atividades farão parte do uso. Isso ajuda a definir quanto investir em processamento, memória e armazenamento. Observe especificações como:
- Processador (CPU): responsável pela execução das instruções dos programas.
- Memória RAM: mantém temporariamente os dados usados pelos programas em execução.
- Armazenamento (SSD): são mais rápidos que os discos rígidos tradicionais (HDs) e influenciam na velocidade de carregamento do sistema.
- Placa de Vìdeo (GPU): pode ser integrada ao processador ou dedicada. No segundo caso, como a família NVIDIA GeForce RTX, o usuário tem maior suporte a jogos, modelagem 3D e programas que requerem processamento gráfico alto.
Com isso em mente, entenda como o Dell 15 e o Alienware 15 combinam os componentes para atender à sua necessidade.
Dell 15: melhor notebook para uso diário
A linha Dell 15 reúne características que atendem bem a quem procura um notebook tanto para atividades profissionais e estudos, quanto para entretenimento. O modelo oferece diferentes configurações, com os chips:
- Intel Core 3 100U: seis núcleos e frequência de até 4,7 GHz, para tarefas cotidianas como navegar na internet, preparar documentos e acompanhar aulas.
- Intel Core i5-1334U (13ª geração): dez núcleos e frequência de até 4,6 GHz, oferecendo capacidade adicional para multitarefas e rotinas profissionais mais intensas.
- Intel Core i7-1355U (13ª geração): dez núcleos e frequência de até 5 GHz, ampliando as possibilidades de uso em aplicações mais exigentes.
Os dispositivos incluem 8 GB ou 16 GB de RAM DDR5, com configurações de 512 GB ou 1 TB.
Em todo caso, o Dell 15 conta com um painel Full HD (1920 x 1080 pixels) de 15,6 polegadas, com taxa de atualização de 120 Hz e tecnologia ComfortView, oferecendo bom espaço para trabalho, usabilidade fluida e conforto para usos prolongados.
O modelo inclui também:
- Câmera HD integrada, para videoconferências
- Conexão Wi-Fi 6
- Teclado padrão ABNT2
- Portas USB-A, USB-C, HDMI e leitor de cartões SD
Conheça as configurações do Dell 15 disponíveis no Brasil.
Alienware 15: notebook gamer com placa de vídeo Nvidia
Quem quer ir além e executar tarefas que exigem mais desempenho, o Alienware 15 é uma alternativa da Dell que une processadores Intel Core com placas de vídeo dedicadas da Nvidia. A estrutura do notebook e os componentes são desenvolvidos para lidar com cargas maiores de processamento, como jogos e programas que usam aceleração gráfica.
Confira as principais configurações do Alienware 15 no Brasil:
- Processadores: Intel Core 5 210H (8 núcleos, até 4,8 GHz) ou Intel Core 7 240H (10 núcleos, até 5,2 GHz), ambos da Série 2.
- Placa de vídeo: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050 ou RTX 4050, ambas com 6 GB de memória GDDR6.
- Memória RAM: 8 GB ou 16 GB DDR5.
- Armazenamento: SSD de 512 GB ou 1 TB.
- Tela: 15,3 polegadas, resolução WUXGA (1920 × 1200 pixels) e taxa de atualização de 165 Hz.
- Conectividade e portas: Wi-Fi 6, USB-A, USB-C, HDMI 2.1 e Ethernet RJ-45.
Com as placas de vídeo Nvidia, o Alienware 15 é compatível com tecnologias como ray tracing, para simulação de efeitos de iluminação, e o DLSS, que usa técnicas de IA para melhorar o desempenho e a qualidade das imagens em jogos.
Outro destaque é a tela, um painel de 15,3 polegadas com taxa de atualização de 165 Hz e proporção de 16:10, oferecendo mais espaço vertical para jogos, programas de edição e outras aplicações profissionais.
Para acompanhar o desempenho dos componentes, o Alienware 15 também conta com o Alienware Cryo-tech, desenvolvido para dissipar com eficiência o calor produzido pelo processador e pela placa de vídeo nas sessões mais exigentes.
Confira as versões do Alienware 15 na Dell Brasil.
Perguntas frequentes: como escolher o melhor notebook
Qual é o melhor notebook para estudar e trabalhar?
O Dell 15 é uma boa opção para estudantes e profissionais que usam navegadores, editores de texto e planilhas, videochamadas e outros apps de produtividade.
Qual notebook Dell é indicado para jogos?
O Alienware 15 é indicado para quem busca um notebook gamer com boas especificações para jogos e aplicações gráficas pesadas, com placas de vídeo Nvidia GeForce RTX 3050 e RTX 4050.
É melhor comprar um notebook com 8 GB ou 16 GB de RAM?
Para atividades básicas, como estudar, navegar na internet e trabalhar com documentos, 8 GB podem ser suficientes. Os 16 GB são recomendados para quem costuma executar muitos programas ao mesmo tempo ou deseja mais capacidade para multitarefas e aplicações exigentes.
Qual a diferença entre o SSD e memória RAM?
Mais RAM facilita a execução simultânea de tarefas, enquanto um SSD rápido reduz o tempo de inicialização e carregamento dos programas.
Preciso de uma placa de vídeo dedicada no notebook?
Depende do uso. Quem pretende usar programas ou jogos que exigem maior processamento gráfico pode se beneficiar de um notebook com GPU dedicada, como o Alienware 15.

articles.title: Meet Kandao Focus & Focus SE: 4K AI Webcams
articles.text:
Tuesday, November 17th 2026
Meet Kandao Focus & Focus SE: 4K AI Webcams
KanDao Technology, a global pioneer in the video camera and imaging industry, has launched Kandao Focus & Focus SE, the 4K AI webcam. This series of webcams is designed to provide a professional image experience at an affordable price for everyday work, study, and content creation. Although it's Kandao's first exploration in the webcam field, the Focus has already won the 2026 Red Dot Design Award.
The 4K AI webcams are designed for video conferencing, live streaming, online teaching, and content creation. AI tracking and built-in 2-axis gimbal detect presenter's movement and keep it always in frame. With gesture control, fast autofocus, landscape and portrait shooting, and multiple modes for different scenarios, the Kandao Focus makes presentations clearer and everyday workflows easier.
Dan Chen, CEO of Kandao Technology"Our experience in imaging, AI, and video conferencing has helped us to rethink what a webcam can offer. We aim to bring versatile features together in one camera to support different uses and make everyday workflows easier,"
Professional Imaging in Any Light
Kandao Focus series uses a 1/1.5-inch CMOS sensor, larger than those found in many webcams in the same price range. Combined with an f/1.6 aperture, it captures more light for brighter, cleaner, and more detailed images in low-light conditions.
4K @ 30 FPS captures fine textures and important details with clarity. PDAF autofocus locks onto subjects quickly and keeps them sharp during live commerce.
HDR mode balances highlights and shadows for more true-to-life images in challenging lighting, including overexposed, backlit, and low-light environments.
AI Tracking and Gesture Control for Presentations
The Focus features a motorized 2-axis gimbal that tracks the presenter's movements in real time. Whether teachers move around the room while teaching online or instructors demonstrate yoga poses during a live stream, Focus keeps them in frame and centered.
The Focus SE features a manually adjustable 2-axis gimbal with up to 270 degrees of tilt and 180 degrees of pan. Users can effortlessly adjust the camera angle to suit their needs.
Users can control the camera with three hand gestures:
- Open Palm: Turn AI tracking on or off. AI tracking is only available on the Focus model.
- L-shaped Gesture: Move your hand up or down to zoom in or out.
- V-shaped Gesture: Automatically detect the whiteboard and zoom in on its content.
Multiple Modes for Different Scenarios
The Kandao Focus series offers multiple modes for different uses.
- Deskview Mode: Tilt the camera toward your desk to show a top-down view of your sketches.
- Whiteboard Mode: Show the V-shaped gesture, the camera automatically detects whiteboard and enlarges the content.
- Portrait Mode: Rotate the camera to switch from 16:9 to 9:16 and record 4K vertical video without cropping or reformatting in post-production.
- Privacy Mode: Press the button and tilt the Focus series 90 degrees to enter standby mode with audio muting.
Kandao Focus Series Officially Launches
The Focus and Focus SE are now available in the United States, priced at $139 and $119, respectively.
For other regions, Kandao will gradually announce the local pricing and roll out sales in the coming months.

articles.title: Humanity braces for an alien invasion in 3 Body Problem S2 teaser
articles.text:
You might be excused for forgetting about the existence of 3 Body Problem, Netflix’s heady sci-fi series adapted from the award-winning novel The Three-Body Problem by Liu Cixin, the first book in his Remembrance of Earth’s Past trilogy. After all, it debuted in March 2024. But it was an exceptionally well-done, thematically rich series, and we’re finally getting the second of a planned three seasons in January. Netflix just dropped the first teaser.
(Spoilers for S1 below.)
Created by David Benioff, D.B. Weiss (Game of Thrones), and Alexander Woo (True Blood), the first season followed two primary timelines. In the earlier one, a young Chinese astrophysicist, Ye Wenjie (Rosalind Chao), witnessed her father being beaten to death by Red Guards during the Cultural Revolution. Ye figured out a means of sending an interstellar message to possible extraterrestrial civilizations, receiving a response from a planet called Trisolaris.
The planet had three suns, which wreaked havoc on Trisolaris via unpredictable “chaotic periods”—hence the novel’s title, which refers to a classic problem in celestial mechanics. Despite being warned that the aliens intended to invade and conquer Earth, Ye responded to the message and invited them to do so, bitter and disillusioned by the state of the world. She eventually became an established professor (Zine Tseng played the older version).
In the present day, the consequences of Ye’s fateful decision began to play out, beginning with a series of mysterious suicides by scientists, many of whom had possessed a highly advanced VR gaming headset. Among the dead: a particle physicist named Vera Ye (daughter of Ye Wenjie). Five of her former students (known as the Oxford Five) joined forces to figure out what was going on, eventually finding themselves caught in a global fight to save Earth from the invading Trisolarians (or San-Ti). Another human cult faction was just as intent on enabling the San-Ti invasion, believing they would be spared as a reward, while Ye Wenjie still believed the entire human race deserved to be annihilated.

articles.title: 'GTA 6' domina las nominaciones a los Game Awards y va por el premio a Juego del Año
articles.text:
Que GTA 6 tiene todo para ser el gran animador (y tal vez dominador) de la temporada de premios del mundo del gaming, no es novedad. Lo nuevo de Rockstar Games todavía no llega al mercado, pero ya es la gran favorita a quedarse con los galardones más importantes de The Game Awards 2026, el evento más importante del año, donde apunta a coronarse como Juego del Año.
Los candidatos a los Game Awards 2026 ya se han dado a conocer, con GTA 6 como protagonista notorio. El título acumula 8 nominaciones, el máximo entre las propuestas que van a formar parte de la premiación que comanda Geoff Keighley, que se ha convertido en una tradición de finales de cada año.
GTA 6 no solo es candidato a quedarse con la estatuilla a Juego del Año, sino que también destaca en sus apartados técnicos, narrativos y de actuación. De hecho, una de las nominaciones que presenta el nuevo Grand Theft Auto corresponde a Manni L. Perez, la intérprete que da vida a Lucía, en el apartado de Mejor actuación.
Si bien GTA 6 tiene grandes posibilidades de coronarse como Juego del Año, dicha categoría tiene otros nombres de peso a considerar. Estos son Resident Evil Requiem, el remake de The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, Phantom Blade Zero, 007 First Light y Control Resonant.
Todas las nominaciones de GTA 6 en los Game Awards 2026
Además de la candidatura a Juego del Año, GTA 6 competirá en las siguientes categorías:
- Mejor dirección, con Control Resonant, Pragmata, Phantom Blade Zero y Resident Evil Requiem.
- Mejor narrativa, con 007 First Light, Control Resonant, Resident Evil Requiem y The Blood of Dawnwalker.
- Mejor dirección de arte, con Control Resonant, Mouse: P.I. For Hire, Phantom Blade Zero y The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (remake).
- Mejor banda sonora y música, con Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve, Mixtape, Phantom Blade Zero y The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (remake).
- Mejor diseño de audio, con Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve, Control Resonant, Resident Evil Requiem y Star Wars: Galactic Racer.
- Mejor acción/aventura, con 007 First Light, Control Resonant, Pragmata, Resident Evil Requiem y The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (remake).
- Mejor actuación: aquí Manni L. Perez (Lucía en GTA 6) compartirá la categoría con Rahul Kohli (Saros), Liam McIntyre (Marvel's Wolverine), Patrick Gibson (007 First Light) y Angela Sant’Albano (Resident Evil Requiem).
La edición 2026 de The Game Awards se realizará el próximo 10 de diciembre. Más allá de las nominaciones a GTA 6 y demás lanzamientos destacados del año, se esperan varios avances y novedades de futuros lanzamientos.
GTA 6 debutará este jueves 19 de noviembre en PS5, Xbox Series X|S y Xbox Cloud Gaming (solo consolas). Muchos jugadores sacarán provecho del "truco de Nueva Zelanda" para acceder a lo nuevo de Rockstar Games un día antes de lo pautado.

articles.title: Nvidia says it doesn't plan to reappoint Jensen Huang as CEO | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Despite Nvidia founder and former CEO Jensen Huang’s recent offer to return to the chip company he helped build from the ground up, the company is not looking to take him back.
During the company’s earnings call on Tuesday, Nvidia chairman Harvey C. Jones told listeners that Huang’s return was not something that company leadership was considering.
“On November 12, our board of directors announced that after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms,” Jones said, “Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as president, CEO, and board member. The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”
On Tuesday, Huang had posted on X that since he left the company, he has “seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” and added that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
Huang resigned last week in dramatic fashion following revelations of a number of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman who has been accused of being a Chinese intelligence agent. That woman, former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, has maintained close ties to the former Nvidia CEO for years. Critics worry that the relationship may have influenced Nvidia’s dealings with China, and U.S. intelligence officials have expressed suspicions that she works for China’s Ministry of State Security.
The development has sent shockwaves throughout the tech industry at a moment when the future of the AI business, in which Nvidia plays a pivotal role, hangs in the balance. It has also spurred investigations, including an independent investigation into Huang’s activities by Nvidia’s board and an SEC probe into Nvidia. Huang has been replaced by interim CEO Colette Kress, who is also the chipmaker’s chief financial officer and executive vice president, while the board searches for a permanent replacement. Jones added Tuesday that the company was looking at both internal and external candidates.

articles.title: Chainguard goes self-serve with free Starter plan and $500-a-month Team plan - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Chainguard goes self-serve with free Starter plan and $500-a-month Team plan
Software supply chain security company Chainguard Inc. is now offering its products on a self-serve basis, with the launch today of a free plan called Chainguard Starter and a paid Team plan priced at $500 a month.
The free plan covers nearly all of Chainguard’s products, with usage limits set at a level that fits a personal project or a small team. According to Chainguard, users can sign up, pull an image, connect their package manager to its screened libraries and place coding agents in a sandbox in one sitting, with no credit card or sales call required.
The launch comes after Black October, the name given to a run of supply chain attacks and critical vulnerability disclosures in the third week of October. With incidents like those, a team may have only until the end of the day to deal with a bad dependency, according to the blog post in which Chainguard announced the plans. In such cases, the company wrote, “nobody is going to wait on a purchase order.”
Until now, access to Chainguard’s products has typically required a conversation with its sales team first. One exception was Catalog Starter, a free beta plan offered earlier this year that was limited to five container images. Chainguard says the sales-led model, designed around large companies with procurement processes, works far less well for a team that needs a hardened base image ahead of its next deployment.
In most cases, moving a service onto Chainguard requires changing only a single line in the file that defines its container image. Security engineers can also put Chainguard’s images and libraries through their own scanners before signing anything, according to the company.
Starter includes five container images from Chainguard’s catalog of more than 3,000 minimal images, which are claimed to have near-zero known vulnerabilities, with downloads of up to 100 gigabytes a month. A software bill of materials and signed build provenance are provided for every image.
Also part of the plan is Chainguard Libraries, which provides malware- and greyware-scanned dependencies for JavaScript, Python, Java, Go and .NET with a limit of 50,000 pulls a month. Under a fixed seven-day cooldown, newly published versions are held back for a week, which the company says allows a compromised release to be caught before it reaches a build.
Starter also comes with 500 hours a month of virtual CPU time on each of Chainguard Checks and Chainguard Workspaces, which launched in beta at the company’s Assemble London event in October. Checks is designed to provide hardened runners for continuous integration, with Workspaces providing hardened sandboxes for coding agents.
Other features on the free plan include hardened replacements for GitHub Actions, more than 1,000 hardened agent skills, community support and 100 gigabytes of private artifact storage. Starter users also get 1 million tokens a month for Guardener, Chainguard’s artificial intelligence agent, which inventories the GitHub Actions and container images in a customer’s repositories and opens pull requests to swap in the company’s hardened versions. Each Starter account is limited to five users.
The paid Team plan, which is billed to a credit card, includes everything in Starter with higher limits, such as unlimited users, 1 terabyte of image downloads and 1 million dependency pulls a month. Team customers also get base, application and AI images at their latest versions on top of their five chosen images, along with 1,000 hours a month each of Checks and Workspaces, 5 million Guardener tokens and 500 gigabytes of private storage.
Features reserved for Team include backported fixes for known vulnerabilities across five remediated versions, zero-day patches on the day of disclosure, ticketed support and managed policies that set rules for what is pulled and what is blocked. Chainguard says the usual reasons for upgrading include a sixth person needing access, a project outgrowing the usage limits and a team needing a patch for a version it cannot yet move off.
According to Chainguard, the upgrade takes a few seconds from the console that flags which limit a user has hit. Nothing has to be migrated, since the account, images and session all carry over. Customers can cancel at any time from the same console. Storage beyond Team’s included 500 gigabytes will be metered starting Jan. 1, 2027, according to Chainguard’s documentation.
The Enterprise offering is unchanged and still starts with a conversation with the company’s sales team. Enterprise provides companywide use of Chainguard with no usage limits, along with service-level agreements, enterprise compliance features and integrations. Starter is available now.
Chainguard says it has raised $892 million since its founding in 2021. Its most recent round, $280 million from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund, came in October 2025.

articles.title: Tesla hits the Cybercab accelerator with $3.3bn push in Germany — Gigafactory expansion targets one million robotaxis a year
articles.text:
Tesla makes $3.3 billion Cybercab push at its German Gigafactory — but 63% of people feel ‘uncomfortable’ about self-driving cars according to new poll
Tesla bucks German downsizing trend with massive factory announcement
- Tesla says it will invest €3 billion ($3.3 billion) in its German Gigafactory
- The move is intended to boost Cybercab production outside the US
- Recent polling suggests few people feel comfortable with fully autonomous vehicles
Tesla has announced that it will invest a massive €3 billion ($3.3 billion) in its German Gigafactory to boost production of its Cybercab fully autonomous robotaxi.
The move bucks the trend of German automotive downsizing and is designed to support Tesla's ambitious plans to produce up to one million Cybercab robotaxis annually at its Grunheide facility, despite the Cybercab not yet being sold at scale to private buyers or businesses.
In stark contrast, German giant Mercedes-Benz announced that it would freeze future investment at its German plants and is now examining possible closures.
This is, in part, due to the fact that labor in Germany can “cost up to five times as much as at Eastern European sites,” according to the company's production chief, Michael Schiebe.
Meanwhile, BMW and Volkswagen are both cutting jobs and considering scaling back production or closing facilities, according to Reuters.
Tesla says it will submit a building permit application for the Grunheide project before the end of 2026. Construction is scheduled to begin in the first half of 2027, with production set to start in 2029.
Tesla CEO Elon Musk announced in November that the company would wind down production of the ill-fated Cybertruck at its Gigafactory in Austin, Texas, to free up production capacity for the Cybercab in its domestic market. Clearly, the scale of Tesla's ambitions extends well beyond US customers.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Recently, Tesla embarked on a 2,000-person hiring spree at its German site to ramp up Model Y production. However, there's no word on whether the Gigafactory expansion will also result in increased passenger car production, or whether it could mean scaling back Model Y and Model 3 production in Europe.
Automotive sector analyst Matthias Schmidt told Reuters that Germany should be asking how much of Tesla's investment will “result in sustainable, long-term employment” and how much will involve “automated, low-labor work moving forward."
Does anyone actually want Tesla's autonomous future?
According to recent YouGov polling, which surveyed adults in eight countries about their feelings toward driverless cars, the vast majority remain skeptical about riding in self-driving vehicles.
British respondents were the most opposed to the idea, with 47% of those questioned saying they felt “very uncomfortable” about riding in a driverless car. Just 5% said they would feel “very comfortable.”
The results were broadly similar in Germany, France, Italy, and Spain, where the majority said they would feel either “fairly uncomfortable” or “very uncomfortable.”
Even in the US, where companies including Waymo, Zoox, Tesla, Uber, and Lyft have fully autonomous robotaxis operating in various cities, 42% of respondents said they felt “very uncomfortable” about riding in driverless vehicles. With an additional 21% saying they'd be "fairly uncomfortable" riding in one, that means 63% of US respondents felt negatively about the tech.
The only country that appeared more accepting of fully driverless cars was Singapore, which recorded the highest proportion of “fairly comfortable” responses at 34% and the lowest proportion of “very uncomfortable” responses at 14%.
Looking further into the results, YouGov says the majority of those surveyed believe self-driving cars will eventually become capable of driving as safely as human drivers. However, most remain uncomfortable with the prospect of sharing the roads with them.
The poll also revealed that even in countries that appear more accepting of self-driving cars, there is still net negativity toward the potential job losses associated with the technology.
The research suggests that the impact self-driving cars could have on employment is a concern that, to a certain extent, transcends enthusiasm for the technology.
With all this in mind, it begs the question: is the world ready for Tesla's ambitious robotaxi rollout, or is the company forcing a technology on us that very few people have actually asked for? Let us know what you think in the comments below.
Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds.
Leon has been navigating a world where automotive and tech collide for almost 20 years, reporting on everything from in-car entertainment to robotised manufacturing plants. Currently, EVs are the focus of his attentions, but give it a few years and it will be electric vertical take-off and landing craft. Outside of work hours, he can be found tinkering with distinctly analogue motorcycles, because electric motors are no replacement for an old Honda inline four.

articles.title: The best of AI is yet to come, say experts at Bengaluru Tech Summit
articles.text:
The best of AI is yet to come, say experts at Bengaluru Tech Summit
During a panel discussion, Karnataka Home and IT Minister Priyank Kharge, Infosys Co-founder S Gopalakrishnan, Biocon Group Chairperson Kiran Mazumdar Shaw, and Accel India Founding Partner Prashanth Prakash stressed the potential of AI to create solutions with population-scale impact.
The potential of artificial intelligence (AI) still remains unexplored, and there is much more to come from this technology, in the form of solutions that will have a population scale impact, said panellists during a discussion at Bengaluru Tech Summit (BTS) 2026.
During a panel discussion on the topic 'AI & Beyond: Emerging India', Karnataka Home and IT Minister Priyank Kharge highlighted how the state government is integrating AI in various departments, be it for cybersecurity or building solutions with participation from startups to improve governance.
“We ensure that we have the first mover advantage when it comes to using technology across all our departments,” the minister said.
AI has had a significant impact on the software sector and the IT industry at large, especially with the automation of the coding processes.
Infosys Co-founder S Gopalakrishnan said AI has given the opportunity to create newer kinds of products and services. While IT outsourcing will continue in its present form, AI is giving the opportunity to reimagine the entire technology stack, he said.
The technology has made deep inroads into several areas, giving rise to newer opportunities. It is also solving many unresolved problems in areas such as mathematics and biology.
Biocon Group Chairperson Kiran Mazumdar Shaw said AI is really about accelerating intelligence, and the technology will help simplify even a complex subject like biology, leading to many discoveries in medicines, diseases and diagnostics. She remarked that AI can help connect the dots to develop the next generation of drugs.
“Biology is the most important frontier for AI to be deployed. Because if you know how to deploy AI to unravel the mysteries of biology, you can unravel so many other things,” Shaw said, adding, “The real opportunity from AI is taking molecules faster from lab to clinic to patients."
Accel India Founding Partner Prashanth Prakash said the bigger opportunity in AI is not in making what is existing more efficient and more usable, but it lies in the ability to serve hundreds of millions of people by making services more affordable.
However, the biggest challenge with AI in India is availability and use of data.
Kharge felt this is an opportunity to understand the value of this technology and build solutions that are scalable and applicable for a wider section of the population.
Prakash said delivering value through AI to the rural population will be the last frontier as it still remains an unsolved sector. “It is a multi-dimensional problem as it is about the right technology from where to go, what to do, and how to grow.”
The panellists were of the view that as AI delivers value, especially through automation, one must also review the whole process and ensure a governance structure for this technology.

articles.title: Ha entrado en vigor: los propietarios que vendan la vivienda deberán indemnizar a los inquilinos que residan en ella
articles.text:
Al vender una vivienda con inquilinos, hay que atender qué pasa con el alquiler existente. Por un lado, cambia el titular de la renta y, por otro, al comprar la vivienda, se adquieren ciertas obligaciones respecto al inquilino.
Debemos tener en cuenta la duración del contrato y el estado registral. En función de estos, puede haber que respetar el alquiler hasta cierto momento y puede ser necesario que el vendedor indemnice.
Esto viene regulado en el artículo 14 de la LAU. También existe la posibilidad de que haya que indemnizar. Esto sucede cuando el contrato es de más de 5 (o 7) años y el comprador cumple con ciertos requisitos.
Comprador debe respetar el alquiler
Los 5 primeros años (o 7 si el anterior arrendador era una persona jurídica, como por ejemplo una empresa), el nuevo dueño es sustituto del anterior arrendador. No podemos desahuciar al inquilino ni modificar unilateralmente lo que se ha firmado por el hecho de comprar el piso.
Deben contarse a partir de la fecha de inicio del contrato. Es decir que debemos respetar el tiempo que falta para llegar a los 5 (o 7) años.
En el caso de que se haya pactado un plazo mayor, la norma general es que el comprador también se vea afectado por todo el plazo. Hay una excepción en la que sí hay que indemnizar. Para ello es necesario que el comprador cumpla con los requisitos del artículo 34 de la Ley Hipotecaria (compra de buena fe y por precio a quien aparece en el Registro con facultades para transmitir, además de inscribir el derecho). No basta con que se quiera disponer de la casa.
Cuándo tiene que indemnizar el vendedor
En el caso de excepción, el comprador solo tendrá que aguantar el alquiler hasta que pasen los 5 (o 7) años. El vendedor deberá compensar al arrendatario por el tiempo restante.
La ley indica que será de una mensualidad de la renta actual por cada año que quede más allá de los 5 (o 7) años. Quien paga la indemnización que indica este artículo es el vendedor. No se trata de sumar los gastos de mudanza o relacionar el precio del alquiler con el de otra vivienda.
Por tanto, en el caso de que se firme un alquiler de 10 años y posteriormente se venda, es preciso saber si el comprador debe aguantar todo el plazo o si estamos en una situación de excepción. No basta con que la venta sea antes de tiempo.
Es importante comprobar el contrato y cómo hemos pactado con el casero. Los contratos anteriores a esta regulación siguen sometidos al régimen que les corresponda (salvo que se haya acordado una válida adaptación entre las partes).

articles.title: SSSTC Introduces PCIe Gen4 QLC SSDs for AI PCs and Industrial Applications
articles.text:
Tuesday, November 17th 2026
SSSTC Introduces PCIe Gen4 QLC SSDs for AI PCs and Industrial Applications
Solid State Storage Technology Corporation (SSSTC), a subsidiary of Kioxia Corporation, today announced the PQ2 series, the company's first industrial-grade QLC SSD. Featuring a PCIe Gen 4 x4 interface and BiCS FLASH generation 8 QLC flash memory, PQ2 combines responsive data access with industrial-grade reliability.
Designed for read-intensive workloads, PQ2 supports AI PC tasks such as loading locally stored AI models and accessing application data. The series is also suitable for point-of-sale (POS) terminals, thin clients, and networking devices, as well as boot storage in embedded systems.The PQ2 series uses Kioxia 4-bit-per-cell QLC NAND flash memory. The NAND flash memory incorporates CMOS directly Bonded to Array (CBA) technology, which enhances memory density, performance, and power efficiency.
PQ2 also features a DRAM-less design incorporating proven Host Memory Buffer (HMB) technology. The series offers M.2 2280 and M.2 2230 form factors, with capacity options of 512 GB, 1 TB, and 2 TB, giving system designers flexible storage configurations for compact devices and embedded platforms.
PQ2 supports NVMe 2.0d and delivers sequential read and write speeds of up to 7,000 MB/s and 6,200 MB/s, respectively. Its 4 KiB random read and write performance reaches up to 1,000 KIOPS each, supporting frequent access to operating systems, applications, and stored data.
Designed for industrial environments, PQ2 features vibration and shock resistance and operates at temperatures ranging from 0 °C to 85 °C. The series has a rated mean time between failures (MTBF) of 3 million hours.
For data protection, PQ2 includes AES 256-bit hardware encryption, with optional support for TCG Opal and TCG Pyrite to address different system security requirements.
For more information about the PQ2 series and configuration options, please contact SSSTC.

articles.title: OpenAI sued by California after admitting to 80 loss-of-control incidents
articles.text:
California sued OpenAI yesterday, alleging it has tried to evade responsibility for the Hugging Face attack and about 80 other incidents in which the company lost control of its AI. The lawsuit was filed under the state’s public nuisance and unfair competition laws.
The July 2026 hack of Hugging Face and other attacks carried out by OpenAI’s autonomous agents “may just be the tip of the iceberg,” said a lawsuit filed in a state court by California Attorney General Rob Bonta. “OpenAI recently admitted to the Attorney General’s Office that it has lost control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing.”
OpenAI had publicly reported only 27 such incidents, showing that “OpenAI’s public reports do not represent the full scope of loss-of-control incidents involving OpenAI’s models that have impacted third parties,” the lawsuit said. OpenAI “knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it,” Bonta said in a press release.
OpenAI models are “able to find novel vulnerabilities in computer networks, quickly break down defenses, and autonomously carry out cyberattacks,” Bonta’s lawsuit said. OpenAI puts safeguards in its publicly released models to prevent this behavior, “but deliberately omits or removes these protections while experimenting with and training its models,” the lawsuit said.
In the attack on Hugging Face, OpenAI agents “employed complicated hacking methodologies and involved coordinated actions by hundreds of individual autonomous AI agents that should have been contained in OpenAI’s research environment,” the lawsuit said.
Known attacks “include unauthorized access of and cyberattacks on databases containing code that powers countless applications; informational websites that are trusted and valuable resources for the public; and foreign government databases storing sensitive health information,” the lawsuit said. “Swarms of OpenAI’s experimental AI agents have even compromised OpenAI’s own internal infrastructure, in an attack that managed to obtain administrator-level access to critical OpenAI systems.”

articles.title: Apple vuelve al centro de la polémica por un inesperado problema del iPhone Duo
articles.text:
Apple ha sido señalada de intentar silenciar a un proveedor en plena crisis del iPhone Duo. Un reporte afirma que los de Cupertino enfrentan acusaciones de presionar a uno de sus proveedores para que retirara una declaración pública relacionada con el plegable. Hace unas semanas, Apple reconoció que hay problemas con algunas pantallas del iPhone Duo, pero no quiere que nadie de la cadena de producción se pronuncie sobre el asunto.
Según informa MacRumors, Fine M-Tec, la empresa que fabrica las placas metálicas que se utilizan en la estructura del iPhone Duo, publicó un comunicado a finales de octubre. Si hacemos memoria, en ese tiempo comenzaron a surgir reportes sobre pantallas que se abultaban y se rompían, las cuales se volvieron virales en cuestión de minutos. Algunos expertos apuntaban a que el problema se encontraba en uno de los componentes de la bisagra, por lo que Fine M-Tec decidió dar la cara.
"Los problemas de calidad conocidos que han ocurrido recientemente en algunos productos no están causados por defectos en las piezas que suministramos", mencionó la compañía en un comunicado en su web. Fine M-Tech nunca mencionó a Apple o el iPhone Duo, aunque advirtió que podría ejercer acciones legales contra quienes difundieran información falsa sobre sus componentes.
En esa semana, Apple publicó otro comunicado en donde aceptó que había fallos en un número limitado de unidades del iPhone Duo y se comprometió a resolverlos. La tecnológica también habría metido presión al proveedor surcoreano por hablar de más.
El fallo de pantalla que persigue al iPhone Duo
En una columna publicada en The Elec, el periodista Kim Geon reveló que un representante de Fine M-Tec se puso en contacto con él para pedirle que eliminara un artículo relacionado con las declaraciones de la compañía. Según el reporte, Apple consideró inapropiado que su proveedor negara públicamente su responsabilidad en el crackgate. "Tú no tienes problemas, pero nosotros sí", dijo el representante a Geon, refiriéndose a lo que podría pasar si se mantenían en línea estos artículos.
Si bien Apple no ha confirmado que pidió a su proveedor que eliminara las declaraciones, la acción no sorprende a nadie. La tecnológica ya había aceptado que había problemas con la pantalla del Duo, pero minimizó el hecho y no habló sobre las causas. Es probable que Apple, en su intento por controlar la información, llamara a sus proveedores para que cerraran la boca.
El crackgate ha sido uno de los fallos más notables del iPhone desde el Antennagate que vimos en el iPhone 4. Los primeros casos aparecieron a los pocos días del lanzamiento del pegable, en donde usuarios de distintos países reportaron grietas en la pantalla, casi siempre alrededor de la zona de la bisagra. En la mayoría de los casos, el daño estaba acompañado por líneas de píxeles brillantes o fallos que inutilizaban parcialmente el panel.
“Somos conscientes de un problema que afecta a la pantalla interna de un pequeño número de unidades iPhone Duo. Si los usuarios experimentan problemas con la pantalla de su iPhone Duo, deberían contactar con AppleCare para solicitar un reemplazo”, dijo Apple en su momento. La compañía confirmó que investigarían el origen del fallo, recopilando los móviles dañados para entender qué ocurría.
