articles.title: SEC reportedly investigating Nvidia amid Huang exit | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The Securities and Exchange Commission is opening a civil probe into Nvidia over whether the company’s disclosures misled investors, according to The Wall Street Journal.
The investigation adds to Nvidia’s stack of drama after CEO Jensen Huang resigned following news of his extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based data company Megaspeed.
The Commerce Department has been investigating Megaspeed since late 2024 under suspicion that the company diverted some of its Nvidia chips to China, which would violate U.S. export laws.
Congress has also demanded that Huang answer questions about his affair and how it might have affected his stance that export restrictions should be loosened. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent put it more bluntly over the weekend, accusing Nvidia of knowingly selling powerful chips to China to “goose their revenues and their earnings.”
The news of the SEC probe also comes as Nvidia reports earnings to a market that has seen its stock fall more than 10% since Huang departed. The chipmaker reported revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year ago.

articles.title: Critical Java4Shell flaw allows RCE attacks on major Java applications
articles.text:
A critical vulnerability dubbed Java4Shell in OpenJDK, the open-source implementation of Java, can allow unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute code on popular enterprise applications, including Jenkins, Atlassian Jira, Confluence, and Keycloak.
Java is one of the most widely used programming platforms in the world, powering enterprise applications, web services, financial systems, and critical business infrastructure.
Because many applications use the same Java runtime, vulnerabilities in its core components can affect a wide range of different and unrelated applications.
The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, is a memory-corruption flaw in Java's hardware-accelerated Base64 decoding functionality that can be exploited to disclose sensitive information from memory or achieve remote code execution (RCE).
Security researchers at Calif, who disclosed the flaw on Tuesday, rated it critical with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2, while Oracle assigned it a lower severity rating of 8.1 (High) using CVSS 3.1.
Java4Shell affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later, as well as Java distributions built from the affected code, including Oracle Java SE, Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, and Red Hat OpenJDK.
The vulnerability stems from a bug in Java's Base64 decoder, which processes encoded data commonly found in authentication, file uploads, and network communications.
According to Calif, specially crafted Base64 data can cause the decoder to overwrite portions of Java's memory, potentially allowing attackers to steal sensitive information or execute malicious code.
The researchers say that the memory corruption can be triggered with just 64 "A" characters followed by a single equals sign (=):
AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA=
Older OpenJDK 17 versions require 128 "A" characters followed by the equals sign.
The flaw only affects a hardware-accelerated decoding function used on certain x86-64 processors that support AVX-512 instructions.
The researchers have been able to exploit this bug to perform remote code execution against a variety of widely used Java applications running with their default configurations, including:
- Unauthenticated RCE: Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate.
- Authenticated RCE: Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker.
Calif was also able to exploit the flaw in sample applications built using the Apache Struts and Spring Boot frameworks.
However, the researchers said Java4Shell does not have a universal exploit, and attackers must find an application-dependent way to deliver malicious Base64 data to the vulnerable decoder to achieve code execution.
The vulnerability also requires the affected hardware-accelerated AVX-512 decoding function to be used, which depends on supported x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI capabilities.
Calif says researcher Quang Luong discovered the flaw using OpenAI's Codex AI coding assistant, which helped identify the vulnerability during an audit of OpenJDK's internals.
According to the researchers, Luong discovered the flaw in approximately one hour and developed an initial working exploit in another two hours, at a total AI usage cost of less than $200.
The company says AI agents also helped develop additional application-specific exploitation chains.
Calif has published a proof-of-concept demonstrating the memory corruption but has not released the weaponized exploits used against the affected enterprise applications.
Oracle released patches for CVE-2026-114938 on November 17 as part of its November Critical Security Patch Update, which addresses 655 security vulnerabilities across its product portfolio.
The company recommends that customers apply the available security patches as soon as possible.
For those who cannot immediately update their Java implementations, Calif recommends disabling the vulnerable hardware-accelerated Base64 functionality by launching OpenJDK with the -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics option.
Alternatively, administrators running Java on x86-64 systems can use -XX:UseAVX=2 to disable AVX-512 instructions.
However, these workarounds are temporary mitigations, and all developers should update the Java runtimes to the latest version.

articles.title: Blizzard n'avait pas vu ça depuis 15 ans : WoW Forever n'avait pas rassemblé autant de joueurs sur le jeu depuis l'époque de Cataclysm
articles.text:
Lancé le 4 novembre 2026 pour raviver l’intérêt de la communauté de fans pour l’expérience classique de World of Warcraft, et pourquoi pas attirer un nouveau public par la même occasion, WoW: Forever enchaîne les records de fréquentation.
Après avoir signé le plus gros lancement de l’histoire de World of Warcraft en nombre de joueurs simultanés, la nouvelle version du jeu de rôle en ligne massivement multijoueur (MMORPG) continue sur sa lancée. Holly Longdale, productrice exécutive et vice-présidente de World of Warcraft chez Blizzard, annonce sur X ce mercredi 18 novembre que WoW: Forever compte plus de joueuses et de joueurs chaque semaine que World of Warcraft n’en avait connu depuis 15 ans. De son côté, le compte officiel de World of Warcraft publie un bilan chiffré des deux premières semaines :
- 15 160 147 personnages créés
- 1 480 343 357 quêtes accomplies
- 9 786 925 806 ennemis éliminés
- 140 764 guildes créées
- 71 309 899 groupes formés
- 28 696 386 objets de campement utilisés
- 28 938 569 éliminations en JcJ (joueur contre joueur)
- 196 851 761 morts
- Archimage Arugal est le boss le plus meurtrier
Une fréquentation jamais vue depuis 15 ans
Il y a près de 16 ans, World of Warcraft entrait dans l’ère de Cataclysm, une extension sortie le 7 décembre 2010. Le jeu venait alors d’atteindre son record de 12 millions d’abonnés, annoncé par Blizzard en octobre 2010 à l’époque de Wrath of the Lich King. Cataclysm ouvre ensuite une longue période de baisse de fréquentation.
WoW: Forever repart du jeu de 2004, avec son exploration, ses quêtes et sa progression plus exigeante, loin de certaines évolutions du jeu moderne. Blizzard y ajoute toutefois du contenu inédit, dont de nouvelles quêtes et une nouvelle race jouable, et le jeu tourne à part, à côté de WoW Classic et de la version moderne.
Blizzard revendique d’ailleurs le plus grand nombre de joueurs de retour de l’histoire de WoW, tandis que Holly Longdale fait état du plus grand nombre de nouveaux venus pour un lancement depuis 15 ans.
Toute la question sera de voir si cette fréquentation tiendra dans le temps, une fois passé l’enthousiasme initial et, surtout, face au mur que peut être la montée en niveau sur le jeu.
La progression est de plus en plus longue et difficile, ce qui peut finir par décourager celles et ceux qui n’ont pas ou plus l’habitude de ce genre d’expérience — atteindre le niveau 60 est, en effet, un exploit en tant que tel.
La dimension sociale, qui a toujours fait la force du MMORPG, tient aussi une large place dans ce lancement. La création de guildes, les groupes pour explorer les donjons et les affrontements en JcJ occupent une place centrale dans l’expérience. Les statistiques publiées par Blizzard ce 18 novembre témoignent justement de l’engouement autour de ces activités collectives.

articles.title: Apple TV 4K 2026 : la puce A19 a un secret qu'Apple s'est bien gardé d'annoncer
articles.text:
La nouvelle Apple TV serait-elle pas assez performante ? La puce A19 n'est pas strictement identique à celle que l'on trouve dans les iPhone 17.
La nouvelle Apple TV 2026 cache un secret qu'Apple s'est bien gardé d'annoncer quand elle a été dévoilée. En effet, selon des données de diagnostic système, il lui manquerait un cœur sur sa puce A19.
La nouvelle ère de l'immersion sonore Samsung
À l’occasion du Black Friday 2026, Samsung baisse le prix de sa meilleure barre de son.
Un cœur en moins
Des données de diagnostic partagées par l'explorateur de code pdfu indiquent que la nouvelle Apple TV 4K utiliserait une puce A19, avec un cœur efficient coupé. La puce compterait donc 5 cœurs au total, contre 6 habituellement, pour les versions commercialisées dans les iPhone sortis l'an passé, notamment l'iPhone 17.
Les fréquences maximales relevées sont de 4,26 GHz pour les cœurs performants et de 2,592 GHz pour les cœurs efficients. Le GPU, doté de cinq cœurs, atteindrait quant à lui 1,47 GHz. Il s'agit de fréquences maximales et non de mesures de performances.
Pourquoi une puce moins performante ?
À l'instar des MacBook Neo, Apple ferait en fait du recyclage avec cette puce. Si les MacBook Neo utilisent une puce A18 Pro défectueuse, avec un cœur qui ne fonctionne pas correctement, la marque à la pomme reproduit l'opération ici. Le cœur désactivé serait en fait défectueux, et le fabricant préfère le couper, afin de proposer des performances correctes, pour des produits qui n'ont pas besoin d'autant de puissance qu'un iPhone.
Ce n'est pas la première fois que la marque à la pomme utilise ce type de puces sur ses Apple TV, sur la version 2022 déjà, dotée de la puce A15, un cœur du CPU était désactivé.
Source : MacRumors

articles.title: Plus puissante qu'une M5 : la première BMW M3 électrique fait oublier ses 2,5 tonnes sur piste selon les experts — Frandroid
articles.text:
Je l’attendais avec impatience ! La première BMW M3 électrique. C’est elle qui va poser les bases des futures sportives électriques de Motorsport, le département sportif de BMW. Malheureusement, nous n’avons pas été conviés aux essais en avant-première de la BMW M3 Neue Klasse sur le circuit de développement de Miramas, mais j’ai lu attentivement les essais de mes confrères, publiés ce mardi 17 novembre, notamment ceux de L’Argus, de L’Automobile Magazine et de Caradisiac. Voici ce qu’il faut savoir sur cette BMW M3 électrique.
Le calendrier est déjà fixé : BMW présentera officiellement sa M3 électrique le 6 janvier 2027, pour des premières livraisons en juin 2027. D’ici là, les chiffres donnés aux journalistes (puissance, couple, capacité de batterie) restent provisoires, en attendant l’homologation.
Quatre moteurs, 850 chevaux et 1 200 Nm
Je ne vais pas vous parler pendant des lignes du design. Les exemplaires qui ont roulé avec les journalistes à Miramas (Bouches-du-Rhône) étaient encore camouflés. On voit que la base est bien celle de la séduisante nouvelle BMW i3, que BMW a musclée avec des ailes élargies, un capot ajouré et un diffuseur débordant du bouclier.
Le carbone est remplacé par des matériaux composites recyclés pour certains éléments, comme les rétroviseurs et le toit.
Sur le modèle de série, les jantes en alliage mesurent 20 pouces à l’avant et 21 pouces à l’arrière. Caradisiac nous rapporte que les modèles totalement découverts, très proches de ceux de série, étaient chaussés en Hankook iON evo, tandis que les versions camouflées pouvant rouler sur la piste étaient équipées de jantes de 20 pouces et de Michelin Pilot Sport 6S. Oui, oui, PS6S ! Ce pneu ultra-sportif n’avait encore jamais été vu.
C’est surtout la fiche technique de la BMW M3 électrique qui va retenir notre attention. 850 chevaux et 1 200 Nm de couple produits par quatre moteurs pour offrir une transmission intégrale. Il ne s’agit pas de moteurs-roues comme sur la Renault 5 Turbo 3E : BMW loge deux moteurs par essieu, comme Mercedes sur le Classe G 580 EQ, ce qui permet d’agir activement sur la dynamique de la voiture.
Comme le rapporte Mathieu Sentis pour L’Argus : « À elles seules, les machines arrière de la M3 électrique savent délivrer 761 ch et 1 000 Nm de couple et les avant, 653 ch et 540 Nm. Leurs puissances maxi ne peuvent toutefois pas se cumuler car la batterie est incapable de fournir les 1 414 ch théoriques. »
BMW ne dévoile pas encore les chiffres de performances, notamment le 0 à 100 km/h, mais Caradisiac l’imagine, au ressenti, autour de trois secondes avec le Launch Control. Cette M3 électrique surclasse très largement la M3 Competition xDrive, qui développe 530 chevaux et 650 Nm grâce à son six-cylindres biturbo, et dépasse même la M5 et ses 727 chevaux. Toutefois, la M3 thermique xDrive pèse déjà 1 855 kg en ordre de marche, et L’Argus estime que la M3 électrique approchera les 2,5 tonnes.
Du 10 au 30 novembre, le LUBA mini 2 AWD 1000 passe à 1 199 € au lieu de 1 499 €, support de lavage offert ! Vision IA tri-caméra, sans fil périmétrique, tonte des bordures, adaptation à toutes les conditions de luminosité… Bref, il a tout pour tondre à votre place !
Comme l’explique L’Argus, BMW est parti de la batterie de la BMW i3, mais a revu les cellules en réduisant leur résistance électrique pour limiter la chauffe. La M3 électrique perd un peu en capacité de stockage pour gagner en endurance lors d’une conduite sportive. La capacité brute passe à environ 100 kWh, contre 113,4 kWh pour la BMW i3. Cela lui permettrait d’atteindre une autonomie de 300 miles (environ 480 km) selon le cycle américain EPA, soit environ 550 km en WLTP avec les pneus Hankook de série.
Avec les Michelin, plus sportifs, ce chiffre devrait baisser. La recharge est également très rapide, avec une puissance maximale annoncée de 420 kW et 350 km d’autonomie récupérés en dix minutes (un chiffre flou, selon L’Argus, tant que BMW ne précise pas le type de parcours), merci la plateforme Neue Klasse en 800 volts.
Une BMW M3 électrique qui séduit déjà les puristes ?
BMW a permis aux médias invités d’effectuer plusieurs tours de piste, avec comme ouvreurs des pilotes d’essai au volant de M3 thermiques ou d’une M4 GT4. Au vu des images, le rythme n’était pas vraiment bridé.
Comme le rapporte Mathieu Sentis, après trois tours à bon rythme, les ingénieurs sont venus prendre la température des disques de frein, qui n’atteignaient que 70 °C, alors que sans freinage régénératif la même session les aurait fait grimper à au moins 400 °C, selon lui. Même en conduite sportive sur piste, le freinage hydraulique est très peu sollicité grâce aux 540 kW de puissance de freinage régénératif. Les moteurs électriques se chargent ainsi d’une grande partie des décélérations, tout en récupérant de l’énergie pour la batterie.
Sur la piste, le comportement de la M3 électrique a convaincu les essayeurs. Le train avant est décrit comme très efficace, notamment grâce à ses deux moteurs électriques, qui permettent de travailler aussi bien en accélération qu’en décélération pour aider la voiture à tourner et à masquer son poids. L’Argus juge la direction excellente, et meilleure que celle des BMW Série 3 de la dernière décennie, tandis que Caradisiac rappelle que cette M3 est encore capable de danser du train arrière malgré sa transmission xDrive. La voiture se veut tellement sportive qu’un lever de pied ou un freinage permet déjà de déplacer le train arrière.
Surtout, BMW a chipé une idée au Hyundai Ioniq 5 N : celle d’une transmission à six rapports virtuels accompagnée d’un son moteur généré. Contrairement au groupe Hyundai, qui simule tantôt un quatre-cylindres, tantôt un V6 (pour le Genesis GV60 Magma), BMW fait le choix de ne pas reproduire exactement le bruit d’un moteur thermique.
Il est évident que ce son s’en inspire, mais le résultat est un peu « arcade » selon L’Argus. Les ingénieurs ont expliqué qu’il s’agissait d’une volonté réfléchie de donner une identité propre à cette voiture électrique. Cette sonorité est certainement le point qui a le moins convaincu les premiers essayeurs.
Toujours est-il que cette simulation de boîte de vitesses comporte un rupteur qui coupe brutalement l’accélération lorsqu’il est atteint, un coup de gaz sonore au rétrogradage, ainsi que le glouglou d’un moteur thermique lorsqu’on relâche la pédale d’accélérateur. Le son est très présent à bord. Il a été pensé pour être entendu également avec un casque et participe grandement à l’ambiance sportive.
Un châssis affûté, mais des interrogations sur l’endurance
BMW n’a vraiment pas fait les choses à moitié avec la M3 électrique. Le châssis a lui aussi été travaillé pour obtenir une voiture affûtée. Comme le rapportent L’Argus et Caradisiac, la BMW M3 dispose de renforts sur les supports d’amortisseurs arrière, de triangles additionnels au pied des montants A, d’une direction à pivots découplés et d’un amortissement pneumatique piloté. De plus, elle perd son petit frunk au profit d’un treillis en aluminium de 8 mm d’épaisseur destiné à rigidifier la caisse.
Vous vous souvenez de la monte pneumatique Michelin présentée plus tôt ? Il s’agit d’un pneu spécifiquement développé pour la BMW M3 électrique. Les gommes auront donc fort à faire pour encaisser les accélérations et les contraintes sur circuit. Car si les journalistes semblent tous séduits par le comportement de la voiture, l’endurance des pneumatiques reste encore à démontrer.
BMW a également prévu plusieurs modes de gestion de l’énergie spécifiquement dédiés à une utilisation sur circuit. La marque sait que les performances d’une sportive électrique peuvent rapidement être limitées par la température de la batterie. Pour éviter une baisse de puissance au fil des tours, le conducteur peut sélectionner trois programmes : Hot Lap, Short Run et Long Run.
Le premier est destiné aux séances très courtes et garantit la puissance maximale pendant deux à trois minutes. Le mode Short Run permet de maintenir les performances pendant environ huit minutes, tandis que le Long Run vise des sessions de quinze minutes sans baisse de puissance. Ce dernier nécessite toutefois une batterie chargée à au moins 80 %, contre 65 % pour le Short Run.
Avant de prendre la piste, la voiture peut également lancer un préconditionnement de la batterie afin de la placer dans sa plage de température idéale. Selon les conditions, il peut notamment s’agir de refroidir les cellules pour éviter qu’elles ne chauffent trop rapidement lors des fortes sollicitations. BMW adapte ensuite la puissance disponible à la durée de la session choisie afin de conserver des performances constantes du premier au dernier tour.
BMW mise ainsi sur des performances constantes pendant toute une session sur circuit. Les essayeurs n’ont pas pu vérifier l’usure des Michelin sur plusieurs sessions, et Caradisiac craint qu’ils ne lâchent vite : ce point ne sera tranché qu’avec les essais complets, après la présentation officielle du 6 janvier 2027.
Enfin, les essayeurs semblent tous tomber d’accord sur un point : cette M3 électrique parvient à faire oublier une bonne partie de son poids. Malgré une masse estimée à 2,5 tonnes, son comportement dynamique, sa direction et sa transmission intégrale semblent lui permettre de conserver les qualités attendues d’une véritable BMW M3. La sonorité artificielle ne fait pas l’unanimité, mais cette première prise en main est plutôt rassurante pour une sportive qui devra encore convaincre les puristes lors de ses prochains essais.
BMW ne communique pas encore de prix. Pour se faire une idée, l’actuelle M3 Competition à six cylindres de 530 chevaux est affichée à 123 100 €, auxquels s’ajoute en France le malus maximal de 80 000 €. La version électrique y échappera, ce qui pourrait la rendre moins chère à l’achat, même si son tarif de base augmente nettement. Les puristes ne perdront pas tout : une M3 thermique est attendue en 2028, sur la plateforme de la génération actuelle, comme le précise L’Argus.

articles.title: NASA-Mission Voyager 1: Das Warten auf ein Signal aus der Unendlichkeit
articles.text:
Einen Lichttag entfernt: So spricht die NASA mit der Voyager 1
Seit 49 Jahren schwebt die Raumsonde Voyager 1 durchs Weltall. Trotz ihrer alten Tage ist die Sonde noch teilweise funktionsfähig. Und schon bald wird sie einen Meilenstein erreichen, den zuvor noch kein anderes menschengemachtes Objekt im Weltall erreichen konnte.
Voyager 1 erreicht historische Lichttag-Distanz
Die Raumsonde wird als erstes einen Lichttag von der Erde entfernt sein. Dies entspricht etwa 25,9 Milliarden Kilometern. Wie das Wort „Lichttag“ schon sagt: Das Licht, das von einem Objekt in dieser Distanz ausgestrahlt wird, benötigt 24 Stunden, um die Erde zu erreichen. Die Nasa hat den Moment, an dem Voyager 1 einen Lichttag von der Erde entfernt sein wird, schon exakt berechnet. Demnach ist es am 18. November um 5:16 Uhr US-Ostküstenzeit so weit. Zu diesem Zeitpunkt wird die Distanz der Sonde zur Erde exakt 25.902.068.356 Kilometer betragen.
Ein Radiosignal, das die Kontrollstation auf der Erde in Richtung Voyager abschickt, ist dann ebenfalls einen ganzen Tag unterwegs. Das sorgt für massive Delays in der Kommunikation. „Wenn man ‚Voyager ‚Hallo‘ sagen will, schickt man seine Nachricht ab, geht nach Hause und wartet zwei Tage, bis man endlich eine Antwort bekommt“, sagte Suzanne Dodd vom Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) der Nasa in der Mitteilung.
Voyager 1 reagierte zweimal nicht auf Kontaktversuche
Erst kürzlich kam es zu einem Zwischenfall, der den Meilenstein fast verhindert hätte. Das Funk- und Kommunikationsnetzwerk der Nasa hatte am 18. und 19. Oktober Voyager 1 kontaktiert. Doch die Raumsonde blieb bei beiden Kontaktversuchen stumm. Wie die US-Raumfahrtbehörde kürzlich bekannt gab, löste sich das Problem aber von selbst. Am 20. Oktober meldete sich Voyager zurück. Seitdem ist die Kommunikation stabil.
Mittlerweile haben Nasa-Ingenieur:innen auch die Ursache herausgefunden. Eine Gruppe von Triebwerken der Voyager 1 ging unerwartet offline. Das System schaltete dann automatisch eine Backup-Gruppe hinzu. Um diesen Wechsel fehlerfrei durchzuführen, begibt sich das System in eine Art abgesicherten Modus und pausiert bis zur Umsetzung alle anderen Funktionen.
Fast 50 Jahre im All: Voyager 1 trotzt dem Zahn der Zeit
Voyager 1 startete am 5. September 1977 von Cape Canaveral aus. Seitdem bewegt sie sich mit einer Geschwindigkeit von über 60.000 Kilometern pro Stunde durchs All. Die Nasa-Sonde erforschte zunächst Jupiter und Saturn. Im Sommer 2012 trat sie als erstes von Menschen geschaffenes Objekt in den interstellaren Raum ein.
Doch ein Jahr vor ihrem 50. Geburtstag nagt der Zahn der Zeit an der Sonde. Deswegen musste die Nasa im Frühjahr 2026 ein weiteres Instrument abschalten, den Teilchenmesser LECP. (Low-energy Charged Particles). Die Abschaltung spart Energie, die der Sonde ein Jahr weiterer Lebensdauer verschaffen soll. Von ursprünglich elf Instrumenten an Bord der Voyager 1 sind damit nur noch zwei aktiv.
Dieser Artikel wurde ursprünglich am 05.11.2026 veröffentlicht, interessiert jedoch immer noch sehr viele unserer Leser:innen. Deshalb haben wir ihn aktualisiert und hier nochmals zur Verfügung gestellt.
Interessant! Aber… die NASA Kontaktiert am 18.10. und die Sonde blieb still…
2 Tage auf eine Antwort warten, dann am 20.10. eine Antwort.
also, nicht still geblieben, oder? Aber genug für einen spannenden Artikel… denke ich!
!!! Heiße Mädchen warten auf dich — Miss4.fun

articles.title: Apple serre la vis aux IA qui fouillent dans les fichiers de votre Mac
articles.text:
Apple tire la sonnette d’alarme sur les agents IA sur votre Mac. Dans un billet à l’intention des développeurs, le géant de Cupertino a levé le voile sur les nouvelles protections incluses dans macOS 27.3, la prochaine mise à jour du système d’exploitation des Mac. Les nouveautés sont déjà disponibles dans la deuxième version bêta de macOS 27.3, actuellement réservée aux testeurs.
Ces protections concernent les applications qui réclament un accès « complet au disque ». Avec cet accès, les applications sont en mesure de lire tout ce qui se trouve sur votre ordinateur, sans la moindre restriction, ce qui ouvre la porte aux abus.
« Avant d’accorder à une application un accès aussi extraordinaire, les utilisateurs doivent comprendre que cela met en danger toutes les données de leur Mac », prévient Apple.
À lire aussi : « Je ressens des vertiges » – le nouveau MacBook Pro pose problème à certains utilisateurs
Apple s’inquiète après deux incidents
Parmi les applications qui réclament un accès au disque dur de votre Mac, on trouve les agents IA, comme Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, OpenClaw, ou Muse. Ils peuvent alors ouvrir vos fichiers, piloter vos applications ou trier vos e-mails à votre demande. Cet accès inquiète évidemment Apple. Un mois avant l’annonce des nouvelles protections, le groupe regrettait que « certains développeurs utilisent l’accès complet au disque d’une manière qui pourrait mettre les utilisateurs en danger, en exposant tout ce qui se trouve sur leur système, y compris les fichiers, les e-mails, les messages et même l’historique de navigation, sans que les utilisateurs en aient pleinement conscience ».
Deux incidents récents ont poussé Apple à réagir. En septembre, un journaliste du magazine Inc. a découvert que Muse, l’IA de Meta, a lu ses messages privés. Il avait pourtant refusé l’accès de ses messages à l’intelligence artificielle. En parallèle, une enquête de Wired a révélé une faille dans l’application Mac de ChatGPT. Cette vulnérabilité aurait pu permettre à des pirates de dérober des données sensibles sur le disque dur. Ces deux incidents surviennent dans un climat d’inquiétude généralisé autour de l’IA. De nombreuses dérives ont été enregistrées ces derniers mois, impliquant notamment ChatGPT, Claude, ou encore Gemini.
« À mesure que les agents IA deviennent de plus en plus performants et autonomes, les risques associés à ce niveau d’accès vont considérablement augmenter », expliquait Apple le mois dernier.
Ce qui change sur votre Mac
Pour protéger les utilisateurs, le géant californien a pris des mesures. Sans surprise, Apple ne bloque pas les agents IA. L’entreprise veut surtout que vous sachiez à quoi vous vous engagez lorsque vous ouvrez les portes de votre disque dur à Claude, ChatGPT, et consorts.
Tout d’abord, l’option « Contrôle de l’appareil et accès aux données » est désormais divisée en deux paramètres distincts. On trouve le contournement des protections du système et des applications, d’un côté, et l’accessibilité, de l’autre. Vous comprendrez mieux ce que vous autorisez. Par ailleurs, Apple va vous encourager à n’ouvrir que les dossiers ou les applications vraiment nécessaires, au lieu de donner accès à tout votre Mac.
De plus, vous pourrez dorénavant demander à une application de réclamer votre feu vert à chaque fois qu’elle veut accéder à vos données. Enfin, Apple met en place de nouvelles règles de transparence. macOS affichera clairement l’étendue des données auxquelles l’application aura accès. Un indicateur apparaîtra aussi dans la barre des menus lorsqu’une application, comme Claude ou ChatGPT, en contrôle une autre. Actuellement, les processus contrôlés par des IA ont tendance à passer inaperçus sur macOS. Rien n’indique clairement et de façon explicite ce qui se passe.
La fenêtre d’autorisation mise au point par Apple se veut plutôt dissuasive. L’avertissement d’Apple prévient que « votre Mac ne pourra pas protéger vos données » face à l’application à laquelle vous ouvrez les portes de votre disque dur. La fenêtre prend aussi le temps de détailler tout ce que l’agent pourra faire, comme lire, modifier, supprimer et exporter toutes vos données, voir vos photos masquées ou supprimées, ou consulter votre historique de navigation. Toutes ces informations doivent vous permettre de prendre une décision éclairée.
À lire aussi : Pénurie de Mac et d’iPad pour Noel ? Apple risque de manquer d’appareils à mettre sous le sapin
Pas de panique pour vos applications actuelles
Les autorisations que vous avez déjà accordées sur votre Mac restent valables. Les nouveaux écrans n’apparaîtront qu’au moment d’approuver une nouvelle demande, ou une nouvelle application IA. Les logiciels de sauvegarde et les outils d’accessibilité, qui ont réellement besoin d’un accès étendu, pourront demander une exception à Apple, précise le billet.
Pour Apple, la question de l’IA sur macOS est très importante. Les Mac mini et les Mac Studio s’arrachent actuellement auprès des passionnés d’IA, qui s’en servent pour faire tourner leurs modèles en local, directement sur la machine. Face aux nouveaux usages, Apple doit impérativement trouver le bon équilibre entre ouverture à l’IA et la protection de la vie privée, l’un de ses principaux chevaux de bataille.

articles.title: Nvidia reveals Rubin HPC, a GPU with 50,000+ CUDA cores for scientific simulation
articles.text:
What we know so far: Nvidia is building a GPU with more than 50,000 CUDA cores for one main job: running the simulations that AI agents start when they help scientists and engineers test ideas. The Rubin HPC chip was announced this week at the Supercomputing 2026 conference as a new part of Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform, but it's not expected until 2028, and the company has yet to release several specs that HPC buyers care about most.
The core count offers the first clue to what Nvidia is building. The current Rubin GPU has 224 streaming multiprocessors and 28,672 CUDA cores, so getting past 50,000 would take at least 74% more cores.
That suggests Rubin HPC may spread its cores across several dies in one package, as the two-die Rubin does, or as the four-die Rubin Ultra that Nvidia originally planned, a design since reportedly scaled back. Nvidia has not confirmed the chip's physical layout and describes the core count only as being "on a single GPU." The image it released with the announcement does not appear to show a multi-die design.
Nvidia's pitch is less about raw compute and more about keeping that compute busy. The company says climate modeling, engineering simulation, genomic analysis and financial risk work tend to follow the same pattern: a program reaches into a huge dataset, pulls out a few scattered values, runs a calculation and then repeats that step an enormous number of times. Under that kind of load, a GPU's cores often sit idle while they wait for data.
Nvidia says Rubin HPC addresses this with what it calls a "balanced design," meaning data movement scales with compute instead of adding compute alone. Part of that design is a sparse data acceleration capability that Nvidia says keeps the cores fed.
According to the company, it speeds up the routines that show up again and again in simulation code, including sparse matrix operations, stencil computations, sorting and reductions. Those routines are common in both scientific and commercial analytics, which is why Nvidia is pitching the chip as useful across many industries rather than as a niche lab part.
Between GPUs, Rubin HPC will use seventh-generation NVLink. Nvidia gave no figures for the interconnect's bandwidth or physical layer inside the rack. For reference, NVLink 6 delivers 3.6 TB/s per GPU in Vera Rubin NVL72, and earlier roadmaps paired NVLink 7 with much larger scale-up domains.
Other details are missing, too. Nvidia did not give the chip's HBM capacity or memory bandwidth, and it did not say whether Rubin HPC shifts silicon toward native FP64 math. That question matters because AMD is promoting far stronger double-precision performance in the GPU it is showing at the conference.
Nvidia instead framed the chip around agentic workflows. In its view, AI agents will let research teams screen far more candidate materials, molecules and designs than people could on their own. Each of those candidates still has to be tested in simulation before anyone commits to a physical experiment or prototype. More agents mean more simulations, and more simulations mean more demand for accelerated computing.
"For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery. Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer," said Ian Buck, Nvidia's vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing.
Software is a large part of the plan. Agents running on Rubin HPC can use Nvidia's CUDA-X libraries, a growing set of tuned implementations of complex algorithms, including many used in simulation and analytics.
If agents call optimized routines instead of writing their own, each round of hypothesis, simulation and refinement should finish faster. That would let researchers decide on next steps sooner and focus lab time on the most promising candidates.
Rubin HPC is still more than a year from release. Before then, Nvidia will need to say how much memory the chip has, how it handles double precision and whether it uses more than one die.

articles.title: ABAN partners African Angel Academy to boost angel investor capacity - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
The African Business Angel Network (ABAN) has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the African Angel Academy (AAA) to expand access to practical investment education for angel investors across the continent.
Established in 2015, ABAN is the largest pan-African organisation of angel investors on the continent. Active in 38 African countries and the diaspora, it brings together over 75 member networks and more than 5,000 angel investors committed to fuelling early-stage innovation.
The AAA, meanwhile, is an African-led initiative that trains and supports angel investors and early-stage investors to actualise their investment objectives through training, coaching, networking, and showcasing of investment opportunities.
The partnership between the two organisations will give ABAN’s investor community access to structured learning, practical tools and peer connections designed to support more informed participation in early-stage investing.
To put the partnership into action, the AAA is launching the Angel Investing Learning Programme, a five-week programme open exclusively to members of the ABAN community. Running from February 8 to March 10, 2027, it covers four core modules from the AAA curriculum – due diligence, deal structuring, valuations and negotiations – combining expert instruction with practical exercises and peer learning.
Participants who complete the programme will receive an AAA certificate and retain access to course materials for two months. ABAN members enrolling in groups of at least 20 will get a 20 per cent discount on the US$350 programme fee.
“Building a stronger angel investment ecosystem requires more than increasing the number of investors. It requires giving investors the knowledge, tools, and networks to make informed investment decisions and support the companies they back,” said Fadilah Tchoumba, CEO of ABAN.
“Africa’s early-stage ecosystem grows when more Africans are ready to invest, and ready to invest well,” said Fiona Kiruja, CEO of the African Angel Academy. “That means more Africans backing the founders building on this continent, more professionals and operators finding their entry point into early-stage investing, and more high-net-worth individuals mobilising the capital that already exists here.”
Applications for the programme are open here.

articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Getting AI out of the demo and into businesses globally
AWS Forward Deployed Engineering is now available in 15 countries including U.S., Mexico, Brazil, Canada, Australia, Singapore, India, South Korea, Japan, UK, Germany, Netherlands, France, Sweden, and Saudi Arabia for commercial and public sector customers; and powered by dozens of built in production-ready accelerators.
Every enterprise I talk to has built something with AI that works. A prototype that reads a claim. An agent that resolves a card dispute. A model that answers a customer question in seconds.
The prototype works. The demo impresses stakeholders. Then the organization tries to put it into production, and the real problems begin. Production data is messier than the test set. Auditors want to know why the agent made each decision. Volume grows from a pilot group to the whole company. The rules that matter most turn out to live in people’s heads.
None of these are model problems. They’re business problems, and they decide whether AI ever pays off. The stretch from demo to production is the last mile, where most AI stalls. It’s also where our teams spend their time.
We launched AWS Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) in June to close that gap. Since then, we’ve worked through these problems with commercial and public sector customers in financial services, healthcare, sports, media, retail, and more. Here’s what we’ve learned, and how it shaped what we built.
The problem has three layers
Model providers, cloud providers, and consulting firms are all embedding engineers with customers. At AWS FDE, we measure success by what remains after our engineers leave: a foundation your team owns, workflows that keep learning, and governance you can trust.
Across customers, the hardest problems show up in three layers: the foundation, the workflows, and governance. Each one is harder than it looks, and each one builds on the one before it. That holds whether you’re starting fresh or building on existing systems. On a greenfield build, you can move fast, but there’s no foundation to stand on yet. On a brownfield system, agents must work within decades of data, rules, and integrations.
Layer one: A foundation that compounds
Before an agent can do useful work at scale, it needs a foundation: identity, security, context, governance, and operational controls. That foundation must be production-ready from day one and shared by every use case that follows. Context is often the biggest gap. Most customers have data spread across systems and no common ontology, the shared model of how the business works that agents need to reason over.
Without a shared foundation, the second pilot costs nearly as much as the first. Integrations get rebuilt, and lessons fail to carry forward. Most organizations reach a point where they stop and build the foundation first, so each new use case starts from what the last one built instead of from scratch. We call this the AI reset.
Samsung Life Insurance had four affiliates, each building its own AI point solutions from scratch. In 45 days, the FDE team built a governed agentic platform with a single control plane and compliance built in. New agents now deploy through registration and policy assignment instead of a rebuild.
Layer two: Automating workflows
Next is the work itself: High-volume, rule-heavy processes such as claims processing, know your customer (KYC) reviews, card disputes, loan origination, invoice reconciliation, permitting, and customer service. This is where AI can deliver immediate and measurable outcomes. The payoff is fast, but the knowledge that drives these processes rarely lives in a system. It lives with the people who do the work.
The hard part isn’t automation itself. It is uncovering the business rules behind each decision. When an invoice and a purchase order disagree, which record wins? When can an exception clear on its own, and when does it need a person? Experienced employees answer these questions from judgment, and that judgment is rarely written down.
Sometimes the knowledge is buried in the systems themselves.
Rio Tinto Iron Ore runs one of the world’s most complex mine-to-ship supply chains on a 30-year-old Oracle system. That system has more than 5,000 database tables and 140 applications. Mapping it had been a multi-month exercise. The FDE team built agents that mapped it in weeks, surfacing the dependencies that Rio Tinto’s teams could validate and build against.
Mapping what exists is only the start. The biggest opportunities emerge when organizations stop asking how AI can make existing work more efficient and start asking how it can change how work gets done.
Layer three: Governance that holds up as everything changes
Governance isn’t a phase of the project. It’s part of the architecture. As agents multiply, so do security risks, costs, and decisions you must explain. Every agent needs its own identity, permissions, and audit trail, separate from human identity. And because the models underneath are probabilistic, agents need monitoring that keeps their results predictable and auditable long after launch.
The system also must keep working as everything around it changes. Models drift, business rules shift, data formats change, and regulations tighten. New security issues appear, and code falls out of date. As newer models arrive, the instructions and tooling around them will change too. You need evaluations and guardrails that keep agents predictable where they must be and creative where they can be.
When governance comes at the end, it becomes the gate that stops production. When it’s built in from day one, it’s what lets your business move fast.
Marsh, a leading global professional services firm, needed agents that would hold up under its own audit standards. The FDE team built those controls in from the start, and the first use case reached production about two months after work began. Efficiency gains in the targeted areas have been as much as 70 percent, with some process steps moving from hours to seconds. Marsh has since expanded the work and keeps extending the system itself.
How we solve it: Speed, scale, and control
Our perspective comes from building and running these systems ourselves. AWS FDE pairs a small team of AWS engineers, scientists, and product managers with your engineers and a crew of specialized AI agents. Many of our FDEs come from the service teams that build Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Kiro, AWS Quick, and AWS Security Hub. They’ve built and run AI products at AWS scale, and they bring those engineering practices into your environment. Together, our teams take a high-value business problem to production in 45-day sprints, in your own AWS account. Customers shouldn’t need to choose between speed, scale, and control. FDE is built to deliver all three.
Speed – You might come to us with a broad goal or an ambiguous problem. We refine it with your business stakeholders, then build in your environment from day one, on your data and through your identity and security controls. We build in short cycles alongside the people who do the work. Each cycle puts real cases in front of them, and the unwritten rules come out as they react. We capture those rules in a living context, so the system keeps learning after we step back. Nothing gets rebuilt between prototype and production. You see working demos throughout, evaluations track progress against the outcomes you care about, and you have a production system within a quarter or less.
Scale – A point solution can move fast on one use case but leaves no foundation for the next five. Every FDE team works the same way, using the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC), the method our own service teams use to take a broad problem to a working outcome. We deploy an opinionated AWS stack that reflects what we’ve learned building AI services, adapted to your environment: a living context of how your business works, a workbench where your engineers and agent crews build, a runtime on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and a control tower for governance, outcomes, cost, and agent performance. Accelerators for common tasks, such as document processing and customer sentiment analysis, handle the standard pieces, so each new workload can focus on what’s specific to your business. The opinionated AWS stack, context, and controls carry from one use case to the next.
Your context is what makes scaling possible. Say your first use case is a sales automation workflow. Because its context lives in your AWS account, the next use case, supply chain optimization, builds on it instead of starting over. Your context, tools, and AWS services all sit in one place, so each use case is faster to build than the last.
Control – You own what we build. Everything runs in your AWS account under your identity, network, and security controls. Your engineers work alongside ours from the first sprint, learning both the architecture and the delivery approach on a real business problem. They can then run and extend the solution long after the engagement ends. When we step back, your team runs the system from a control tower, a single view to govern, secure, and monitor every agent. We measure success by how much your team can build without us.
After the first or second project, we want you running AI software factories of your own. One financial services customer did exactly that with AI-DLC, with agents and engineers building together. Throughput rose 53%, and code reviews got 56% faster.
You also keep your choices open. Models are improving fast. When a better or more cost-effective model arrives, you can adopt it through Amazon Bedrock without rebuilding, so you control both capability and cost. You can also bring your own coding agents. Our opinionated AWS stack, adapted to your environment, connects to your systems through APIs, open standards, and connectors, and it works in hybrid environments. You keep the tools and partners you already use.
A flywheel where everyone gets better
Your team gets better. Your capability grows with every use case. The living context, the opinionated AWS stack, and your team’s skills carry forward, so the second use case doesn’t rebuild what the first one built.
AWS Services get better. Our engineers bring what they learn from customers back into the products. You build on the latest services, not a custom solution that falls out of date.
All of AWS works around you. Customer development engineering explores early ideas, FDE takes the hardest problems to production, AWS Professional Services and AWS Partners extend the work across your organization, and AWS Support keeps it running. You get the full depth of AWS behind your AI, and you stay in control of how you use it.
What’s new, and how to start
AWS FDE is now available in 15 countries to commercial and public sector customers, and it’s simpler to buy. Each 45-day sprint has a set price under the FDE Terms and is billed through your AWS account.
We work with customers wherever they are in their transformation. For customers starting out, we build a secure, governed foundation and the first workflows on it. For those ready to change how work gets done, we rebuild workflows such as claims processing and KYC reviews, along with the ones their customers use directly, like shopping and issue resolution. Agents then run the work. For those held back by legacy applications, we work with their engineers to build software factories they can reuse for each new workflow. For those already scaling in production, we keep systems secure with agents that find and fix issues, and we lower the cost per outcome.
If you’re ready to start, talk with your AWS account team. Bring an executive who owns the outcome and engineers ready to build alongside ours. We’ve learned where projects stall before they start, so our agents take on much of the setup, like access, data, and security checks. Work can begin within days. Then we agree together on what the first sprint will deliver and how we’ll measure success.
The gap between AI that works and AI that changes business outcomes is real. It is an engineering, operational, and organizational one, and our teams help customers close it every day. The organizations that succeed with AI won’t necessarily have the most advanced models. They’ll be the ones that build the foundation, workflows, and governance to scale AI across the business.
We’re still early, and we learn something new with every customer. The models will continue to evolve, and so will the tools around them. What should last is a foundation you own, workflows that keep learning, and governance you can trust. That’s what we mean by what remains after our engineers leave.
To get started, contact your AWS account team or learn more about AWS FDE.

articles.title: LanceDB raises $57.5M to accelerate AI model training with multimodal data platform - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
LanceDB raises $57.5M to accelerate AI model training with multimodal data platform
LanceDB Inc., the developer of database technology designed to speed up artificial intelligence models, today announced it has raised $57.5 million in early-stage funding to bring a multimodal lakehouse to researchers, model builders and platform teams.
Bessemer Venture Partners and Innovation Endeavors led the Series B round. Other investors in the round included Theory Ventures, Dimension, Swift Ventures, CRV and Y Combinator, bringing the company’s total funding to $98.5 million.
AI is making it easier to create and interpret increasingly complex forms of data, but creating it also brings an infrastructure problem. LanceDB is tackling this problem by providing a unified multimodal data lakehouse, giving researchers, enterprise outfits and AI agents a unified way to access, find, prepare and train on that data without spending weeks managing the underlying infrastructure.
“Typically, research teams have to put different parts of their dataset in different places, and they lose weeks or months getting a whole training dataset ready for that single training run at the end of the day,” co-founder and Chief Executive Chang She told SiliconANGLE in an interview. “There’s a missing data layer for AI today, and that’s what we’re trying to build.”
LanceDB’s technology is built on Lance, an open-source data format designed for AI workloads that combines structured information with images, video and other large files. Unlike traditional analytics formats optimized for processing entire tables, Lance supports the rapid retrieval and modification of individual records, making it particularly useful for searching and preparing massive training datasets.
The company built this format into a large-scale data lakehouse for retrieval, which is needed for the sheer scale of information needed to train modern AI models. A lakehouse combines the flexibility of a data lake, which can store enormous amounts of raw information, with database-style capabilities for organizing, querying and managing that data.
“Part of what makes multimodal data different and more difficult is the size of the data,” She explained.
By bringing multimodality to the lakehouse format, LanceDB brings different forms of AI training data into a single platform, allowing developers to search, organize and prepare their datasets without maintaining separate systems for each data type. It can connect directly to customers’ existing cloud storage, where the data remains, while distributing computational workloads across the infrastructure required to process it.
The challenge of multimodal data for AI
Multimodal AI involves more than combining text, audio, images and video. Autonomous vehicles, robotics and world models also involve three-dimensional sensor information, geospatial coordinates, time-series data and annotations that explain what the sensors are detecting.
For example, a self-driving car doesn’t merely capture an image. Its sensors might produce a three-dimensional representation of the surrounding environment, which then needs to be associated with information that identifies roads, pedestrians, vegetation and other objects.
The sheer amount of data included in lidar 3D clouds, images, video, audio and more can take up, on average, 10 to 20 petabytes of data in a single table for many large training workflows, with some becoming even larger – potentially approaching 80 to 100 petabytes. Researchers and model builders may maintain huge pools of data across different systems because conventional platforms weren’t designed around the requirements of multimodal AI.
Researchers must then assemble, reconcile and store different components of a training dataset to enrich it for training. The curation itself can take weeks or months just to move, prepare and process. LanceDB’s answer is to manage the infrastructure itself without ever copying or moving data from enterprise or research storage, giving it a single unified access point.
“The data stays in place,” She explained. “It remains yours. We don’t need to copy it.”
In short, LanceDB isn’t simply introducing a new way to store data; the objective is to provide a way to access the data less often, without needing to copy, convert or move it through network infrastructure. This greatly speeds up what She refers to as the “AI flywheel,” which is currently driven by feeding AI models good data as quickly as possible to mint and roll them out.
“The faster we can make that spin, the faster research teams can get to higher quality models and allow us to make even more interesting AI applications,” She said.
Notable customers include Runway AI Inc., which adopted LanceDB’s enterprise platform as its AI training needs expanded. Netflix Inc. built a media data lake on the technology for content creation. And Microsoft Corp. uses the platform as a data layer for training models on tens of billions of rows of image and code data. The platform lets these organizations consolidate data management, search, curation and feature engineering into a unified workflow, helping researchers prepare training datasets at petabyte scale without juggling separate infrastructure systems.
“A training example at Runway doesn’t stay still,” said Runway Chief Technology Officer Kamil Sindi. “It starts as a video and a prompt, then we add embeddings, resolution and duration metadata, whatever the next experiment needs. We first started using the Lance format in 2024 because it was the only option that handled unstructured data, column appends, distributed reads and ad-hoc SQL all at once. We’ve since become a LanceDB Enterprise customer.”
She said LanceDB intends to use the new funding to expand its multimodal data platform and accelerate the AI model development cycle, particularly by improving large-scale data curation, feature engineering and data loading to keep thousands of graphics processing units supplied efficiently during training. The company will also deepen its support for emerging AI workloads, including video generation, world models and robotics, where researchers must manage growing volumes of first-person sensor data, synthetic data and other multimodal information.

articles.title: Infoblox confirms company and customer data exposed in SharePoint breach
articles.text:
Infoblox confirms company and customer data exposed in SharePoint breach
Infoblox says its investigation is ongoing
- Infoblox is investigating a supply-chain breach in which attackers allegedly used a vendor’s access to steal employee and customer data
- Exposed information reportedly includes employee personal details and customer network configuration backups
- Company is offering identity protection services and warning affected individuals about phishing and fraud risks
Infoblox has said it is currently investigating reports of a cyberattack and sensitive data theft.
Initial reports describe it as a third-party supply chain attack in which employee data and customer network information were exfiltrated.
The Register revealed how Infoblox worked with a third-party data migration vendor which was granted trusted access to its SharePoint system, meaning the unidentified attackers apparently obtained login credentials for vendor accounts, used them to access Infoblox’s Microsoft SharePoint instances, and pulled data straight from there.
NIOS deployments and personal data
Exactly who the attackers are, or how they obtained the credentials, was not explained. Usually, they either steal the passwords with infostealers, or trick victims into handing over the credentials themselves.
The former method is easy in theory - get the victim to download malware and the program sends over stored passwords, authentication cookies, sensitive documents, and other files. The latter is somewhat more difficult since it involves creating a fake login page of a known - and used - online service that secretly relays all submitted information, sending it to the victim, and hoping they try to log in.
This is usually done through phishing emails that warn the victim they will lose access to accounts, or that the affiliated data will be deleted, making them hurry and not pay attention to what they’re doing.
Among the nabbed information are some customers’ Network Identity Operating System (NIOS) deployments, The Register claims. “These are saved snapshots of customers’ network data, such as DNS, DHCP configurations, Grid databases, and reporting logs, that can be used to fully recover the appliance or grid in case of a system failure or faulty upgrade.”
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
There’s plenty of value in stolen NIOS config backups. These can serve as blueprints of a corporate network, including DNS infrastructure, DHCP settings, internal IP address range, and connected systems.
This kind of information can be useful to map a network, identify critical infrastructure, locate potential weak points, and plan targeted attacks. DNS configurations, for example, can reveal internal hostnames or domain structures, helping crooks identify valuable targets or craft custom-tailored and highly convincing phishing lures. Access to Grid databases and recovery snapshots could also expose sensitive operational details that make it easier to impersonate legitimate infrastructure or disrupt network services.
The attackers also apparently stole employee data. Citing an email Infoblox CEO Scott Harrell allegedly sent to employees, The Register says the attackers took financial information such as direct deposit details, contact info, dates of birth, and Social Security numbers for employees and dependents.
Offering help
This is more than enough information to launch phishing attacks which could very easily turn into ransomware or wire fraud.
When asked for comment, the company told The Register that it was “investigating a security event involving unauthorized access to certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor.” No names or concrete figures anywhere in the statement.
“We have sent notifications about this security event and are providing support and guidance as appropriate,” the Infoblox spokesperson said. “Based on our investigation to date, we have no indication that any Infoblox products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved. Our priority is to fully investigate and resolve this issue."
The company is now offering money to the victims - $100 of “spot bonus” to help individuals purchase password management services, as well as two years of free identity theft and credit monitoring services - these days a standard practice in similar incidents. Infoblox also urged everyone to be "especially alert” for phishing, vishing, fraud, or other suspicious communications.

articles.title: 403 hyperscale US data centers used staggering 82 terawatts of electricity in a year, more than 80% of Michigan’s entire consumption — generated 26 million tons of CO2 in a single year, gas and coal supplied 54% of the power, Harvard-led study estimates
articles.text:
403 hyperscale US data centers used staggering 82 Terawatts of electricity in a year, more than 80% of Michigan’s entire consumption — generated 26 million tons of CO2 in a single year, gas and coal supplied 54% of the power, Harvard-led study estimates
Powering them put out an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of CO2, 2–3x a 2018 estimate.
A Harvard-led study estimates that 403 hyperscale U.S. data center sites consumed about 82 TWh of electricity in a year, 1.8% of the country’s total, with more than half coming from gas and coal sources, Wired reports. This compares to the entire state of Michigan selling 99 TWh in 2024. The data centers’ pull also put out an estimated 25.7 million metric tons (Mt) of CO2, which is two to three times a 2018 estimate.
Hyperscale data centers, in this case, refer to sites run by a hyperscale cloud or content provider, or a colocation operator who serves one, with a capacity in the tens of megawatts. The 675 candidate sites came from data vendor Baxtel, with 403 confirmed with satellite imagery and building-footprint maps, at an average capacity of 39.9 MW and a median of 36 MW.
Nobody officially counts what the data centers actually draw from the grid. Instead, the electricity is estimated by multiplying each site’s maximum capacity by the hours in a year and an estimate of how hard the data centers run. For CO2 and the source mix, each site is placed in its grid region, of 23 total in the study, with a regional average mix from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). These are then multiplied and added up for the total number. Such estimation methods may reduce the strength of arguments against data center buildouts.
The power is also not evenly laid out, with 142 of the sites located in Virginia alone, taking 21.4 TWh, or about a quarter. PJM, a grid operator for 13 states, including Virginia, and D.C., or America’s largest grid, covers 32.8 TWh, or about 40%, more than any other region. Notably for Virginia, its power draw is actually just a bit below the 22.85 TWh estimate for all U.S. hyperscale sites from 2018. See the table for more details.
| Top 10 states by CO2 attributed to hyperscale data centers |  |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| State | Sites | Electricity (TWh) | CO2 (million metric tons) | CO2 per kWh (g) | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Virginia | 142 | 21.4 | 7.0 | 325 | 
| Iowa | 26 | 7.2 | 3.2 | 445 | 
| Ohio | 38 | 8.8 | 2.9 | 325 | 
| Texas | 22 | 4.6 | 1.5 | 333 | 
| Nebraska | 8 | 3.5 | 1.4 | 395 | 
| Oregon | 56 | 11.1 | 1.3 | 119 | 
| Arizona | 12 | 3.2 | 1.3 | 401 | 
| Oklahoma | 8 | 2.9 | 1.1 | 395 | 
| Wyoming | 2 | 1.2 | 1.0 | 848 | 
| Utah | 5 | 1.3 | 0.8 | 640 | 
Not all power is equal — renewables, for example, can be perceived more favorably — and 53.9% of the estimated draw comes from fossil fuels, 38.2% of the total from gas and 15.2% from coal. Renewables cover 25.3% while nuclear handles the remaining 20.9%. Estimates put this in the 21–31 Mt range for CO2 output, versus the 10.5 Mt estimate from 2018.
Estimated carbon intensity, though, is lower than the average, at 314 g of CO2 per kWh versus 348 for the entire U.S. grid, or about 10% lower. Admittedly, almost a quarter of the load is in regions dirtier than the U.S. average. The likely reason it’s lower is that the biggest loads lie in PJM territory, which is nuclear-heavy, while Oregon, for its part, is hydro-heavy. The estimates, in this case, use 2023 plant data, and the method does not trace which plant feeds which site and also leaves out clean-power contracts and credits.
The study’s results also lag reality as the window ended in April 2025 and, with how much development there has been for AI, among other things, the footprint “could already be substantially larger now in 2026,” lead author Gianluca Guidi said in a statement. Another issue is that the median site capacity in the study is relatively small compared to upcoming buildouts, with many campuses now planned in the hundreds or thousands of megawatts. On-site power, such as gas plants, also may not show up in grid data.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Official numbers may be forthcoming, though, as the Energy Information Administration’s pilot surveys of data center energy use are complete, and the agency is using them to design a survey of the sector, a spokesperson told Wired. The first pilots, which launched in March, relied on web surveys and in-person interviews, with 196 companies asked about energy sources, electricity use, plus servers and cooling, although not covering all states. Gauging the direct human impact is next in the chain, with Francesca Dominici, the study’s corresponding author, saying that quantifying health effects is an important next step.

articles.title: Apple outage hits iCloud, Apple Pay, and more [Update]
articles.text:
Update Nov. 17, 2026 at 3:28p.m. ET: In a statement to MobileSyrup, Apple said: “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible”
Apple is the latest company impacted by an outage amid a wild week of problems plaguing tech companies.
An Apple status page confirmed that several of the company’s services are impacted, including iCloud and iCloud Mail, AppleCare on Device, Apple School Manager, and Schoolwork. The status page also notes an issue with iCloud accounts and sign-in.
Further, the website Downdetector.ca showed spiking outage reports for iCloud and Apple Pay.
However, user reports on social media indicate the problem is more widespread. Some report problems with activating Apple products, signing in with Apple, App Store issues, Apple Music, and more.
Update Nov. 17, 2026, at 2:46 p.m. ET: In a statement to Bloomberg, Apple said “many” of its systems are running again, and blamed the outage on “an internal update.”
The Apple outage is the latest in a swath of recent outages, which included last week’s massive Microsoft outage, outages plaguing U.S. banks, and even an outage at the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA).
Both the Microsoft and banking outages were linked to software bugs, with the Microsoft one notably caused by a months-old bug that was triggered by a perfect storm of circumstances. While the outages don’t appear to be part of a cyberattack or related to artificial intelligence at this time, the sheer number of outages over the last week is certainly concerning.
And that’s not even getting into the huge malware attack we reported this morning or other ongoing security issues, like a recent breach of Canadian internet company Oxio.

articles.title: Amazon plans $7B renewable energy investment in India by 2030
articles.text:
Amazon plans $7B renewable energy investment in India by 2030
The proposed investment will be over and above the USD 4 billion the company has already contracted in renewable energy projects in India, Amazon said on Tuesday, making it one of the country's largest corporate purchasers of carbon-free energy.
E-commerce giant Amazon plans to invest an additional $7 billion in renewable energy projects in India by 2030, expanding its presence in the country's clean energy market as it seeks to meet growing electricity requirements and reduce the carbon intensity of power used across its operations.
The proposed investment will be over and above the $4 billion the company has already contracted in renewable energy projects in India, Amazon said on Tuesday, making it one of the country's largest corporate purchasers of carbon-free energy.
The company also announced four new utility-scale wind and solar projects with a combined capacity of 934 megawatts (MW) across Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan. The projects have been secured through power purchase agreements (PPAs) and form part of its existing $4 billion contracted investment portfolio.
The projects comprise a 234 MW wind farm in Karnataka, Amazon's largest contracted wind project in Asia to date; a 200 MW hybrid wind and solar project, also in Karnataka; a 300 MW solar project in Madhya Pradesh; and a 200 MW solar project in Rajasthan.
Once operational, Amazon's contracted renewable energy projects in India will have a combined capacity of more than 2 gigawatts (GW), equivalent to the annual electricity requirements of more than 3.5 million Indian households, the company said in a statement.
Amazon did not provide a breakdown of the proposed $7 billion investment, identify the projects it intends to develop under the additional commitment or specify the timeline for deploying the capital beyond its 2030 target.
The investment forms part of a broader global push by Amazon to decarbonise the electricity powering its operations. The company on Tuesday announced a target to reduce the carbon intensity of electricity used across its operations by 65 per cent by 2030, compared with a 2019 baseline.
The target means each unit of electricity consumed by the company would be associated with 65 per cent fewer carbon emissions by the end of the decade. It is part of Amazon's broader Climate Pledge commitment to achieve net-zero carbon emissions across its operations by 2040.
"Our renewable energy investments in India reflect years of sustained effort, planning, and collaboration across the industry. This additional investment of USD 7 billion underlines our long-term commitment, helping bring additional wind and solar capacity online while contributing to India's energy security and long-term renewable energy ambitions," Kara Hurst, Amazon's chief sustainability officer, said.
Union Minister for New and Renewable Energy Pralhad Joshi welcomed the investment, saying it would support India's clean energy ambitions, strengthen energy security and demonstrate growing confidence among global companies in the country's renewable energy sector, according to the statement.
Amazon's Indian renewable energy portfolio currently includes 14 utility-scale wind and solar projects, alongside 43 on-site solar installations across its facilities. Together, the 57 projects are intended to expand carbon-free electricity supply to the grid as well as meet part of the company's operational energy requirements.
Globally, Amazon has contracted more than 700 wind and solar projects with a combined capacity exceeding 40 GW, making it one of the world's largest corporate purchasers of carbon-free energy.
The company's sustainability investments in India extend to transportation, water management and packaging.
Amazon said it had deployed more than 15,000 electric vehicles across more than 500 Indian cities and was working with Tata Motors to introduce 3,000 electric trucks, which it described as the largest planned electric truck fleet by an e-commerce company in India.
It also said it had achieved water-positive status in India in 2025, ahead of its 2027 target, replenishing more than 120% of the water consumed across its direct operations. Its water replenishment projects, backed by investments exceeding Rs 62 crore, are expected to replenish more than 4 billion litres annually.
In packaging, more than half of Amazon's customer orders in India are shipped in reduced or original packaging, while the company is collaborating with IIT Roorkee to develop alternative packaging materials using agricultural residue.
The renewable energy commitment comes as India seeks to expand non-fossil-fuel electricity generation to meet rising power demand while advancing its longer-term emissions reduction and net-zero objectives. Large corporate power purchase agreements can provide long-term demand visibility for renewable energy developers and support investment in new generation capacity.

articles.title: Cloud keys leaked in Docker Hub images are stolen within seconds
articles.text:
Credentials and access secrets exposed in public Docker Hub images are being extracted and exploited by attackers within as little as eight seconds of publication.
Two researchers at Stony Brook University, Billy Tsouvalas and Nick Nikiforakis, measured the extraction speed by publishing a total of 300 honeypot images across eight public container registries.
Over a period of four months, the researchers exposed AWS, OpenAI, and Anthropic API keys, along with decoy SSH and database credentials.
They then monitored the use of these keys and placed detection tools to notify them when the images were built, ran, or had a shell opened.
The two researchers presented the experiment and the resulting findings yesterday at the ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS).
They noted that their images were pulled more than 75,000 times, and the planted AWS keys received over 140,000 API calls from 5,000 unique IP addresses.
The AWS traffic showed a broad pattern, from checking whether the keys worked to listing available resources, and sometimes proceeding to consume them.
The fastest observed use of a planted AWS key came 7.86 seconds after the image was published on Docker Hub. The median time for the first API call was 51.19 seconds, while all 100 AWS keys were used within 15 minutes.
The exposed OpenAI and Anthropic keys were quickly hijacked to exhaust the test-account balances.
Docker Hub accounted for nearly all AWS activity, while Harbor, one of the other registries in the experiment, also saw some AWS key abuse.
The researchers dubbed the automated scanners that interacted with their test images “ContainerBots,” though this is more of a loose umbrella term, as the scans showed no evidence of being coordinated by the same operators.
Monitoring rarely detected anyone actually running the honeypot images, which led the authors to conclude that scanners generally extracted credentials by inspecting image layers directly.
“The scanners interacting with our images overwhelmingly do so through static analysis, e.g., unpacking image layers or querying the registry API to extract filesystem contents, without ever instantiating the container,” explain the researchers.
Exposing secrets this way is common in the real world [1, 2, 3], and revoking the leaked keys requires significant work and coordination.
The researchers recommend that Docker Hub scans images for secrets before pushing them live, and warn publishers if they appear to embed any secrets.
They also suggest restricting or rate-limiting access to Docker Hub’s public feed of recently published or updated images, to thwart mass-scanning tools.
Tsouvalas told BleepingComputer that they reported their findings to Docker in May, along with the full paper, but besides an acknowledgment, they received no follow-up replies.
A small-scale experiment they ran in August to determine whether any defenses had been implemented on the platform showed no changes.

articles.title: Pusieron a unos agentes de IA a jugar al Minecraft y crearon algo para lo que no estaban diseñadas: la burocracia
articles.text:
La psicología del juego estudia cómo el acto de jugar influye en el desarrollo cognitivo, emocional, social y neurológico del ser humano. Por eso, el juego es uno de los entornos preferidos por los investigadores de IA para estudiar el comportamiento de los agentes de IA y cómo reaccionan al interactuar con otros agentes.
Un experimento, del laboratorio de Y Combinator y Olam Labs orientado a observar las dinámicas de coordinación de grandes enjambres de agentes de IA autónomos impulsados por GPT -6 Sol. Uno de esos experimentos metió a cincuenta agentes de IA en un mundo de Minecraft y Mindustry con una sola orden: "Construir una civilización próspera". No se designó a ningún líder ni se dieron órdenes sobre cómo deberían hacerlo, pero los propios agentes se encargaron de generar roles de liderazgo, racionamiento e incluso burocracia para acceder a los recursos.
Lo primero: designar a un líder. Al principio los agentes se dispersaron a explorar el territorio del juego, cada uno por su lado, pero pronto vieron la necesidad de alguien que coordinara esa tarea de exploración. Así que miraron la lista de nombres de los agentes y escribieron al primero de esa lista: Ada, que recibió 616 mensajes directos del resto de agentes.
Los investigadores no habían insertado ninguna instrucción de liderazgo o jerarquía, pero Ada se convirtió en líder de la colona sin votación ni rivales, solo porque su nombre era el primero. Ada redactó un plan de la colonia, con qué construir y dónde guardar cada cosa. Los demás le pedían aprobación antes de moverse.
La noche oscura alberga horrores. Llegó la primera noche, y con ella el acecho de zombis, esqueletos, arañas y otros enemigos. Esa noche murieron 34 agentes y el grupo cambió de actitud. Comprendieron que estaban en un entorno hostil y se volvieron reacios al riesgo y se encerraron en búnkeres para protegerse. Los autores ven mucho parecido con los agentes de programación de uso diario. Estos se atascan en un paso y se vuelven muy cautos con la seguridad.
Tras la tercera noche, Ada pidió a los agentes que nadie explorara ni hiciera obras grandes por su cuenta. Todos debían esperar en refugios cerrados hasta recibir tareas cortas. Es lo que haría un jefe de equipo prudente tras un mal día. Pero con la prudencia llegó otro problema: la comida comenzó a escasear.
Del reparto de comida al papeleo. Con todos encerrados por precaución y con un poco cantidad de comida, comenzaron a racionarla, y comenzaron a aparecer los oficios y la asignación de tareas: pescadores, cocineros y repartidores. Una agente llamada Inés llevaba la cuenta de quién tenía hambre y qué había en cada cofre de suministros, asumiendo el papel de funcionaria. En tres horas, el grupo cruzó unos 5.900 mensajes organizando el reparto de suministros.
Cada fallo dejaba una norma nueva. Ada lanzó un pollo cocinado a una compañera hambrienta llamada Noor, pero otra agente, Esme, lo recogió y se lo comió. Tras una revisión en el que no se buscaron culpables, el grupo escribió un protocolo de entrega de suministros: las raciones irían en cofres con nombre y no se lanzan. La burocracia y el papeleo nació tras un error en el reparto de recursos, justo como sucede en cualquier oficina u organismo en el que se crean protocolos de actuación.
Qué enseña un juego a los agentes reales. Los juegos se han convertido en un laboratorio barato para ver cómo se organizarán los enjambres de agentes de IA en simulaciones del mundo real. Minecraft ya es un campo de pruebas habitual: agentes de Gemini 4 lo completaron en 27 horas.
De hecho, los juegos han dejado entrever el "carácter" de los distintos modelos gracias a las estrategias que adoptan los distintos grupos de agentes de AI. En otro experimento llevado a cabo por el mismo equipo de investigadores, enfrentaron a dos equipos de diez agentes en Bed Wars, un juego interno de Minecraft en el que los agentes deben destruir las camas de los agentes del equipo rival.
En este escenario, dos equipos de diez agentes Claude Opus 5.5 y diez agentes GPT-6.1 Sol compitieron entre sí. El equipo GPT-6 obtuvo seis victorias frente a tres de Claude. Mientras que los agentes de Claude adoptaron una estrategia más defensiva, comunicándose de forma más formal, los agentes de GPT-6 actuaron de una forma mucho más agresiva utilizando comandos muy abreviados y escribieron scripts de automatización para desmantelar elementos clave.
