articles.title: Le nouvel Echo Time d'Amazon, un réveil connecté avec Alexa et écran tactile perd déjà 55 € pour le Black Friday — Frandroid
articles.text:
Amazon propose déjà de nombreux produits connectés pour se faire une véritable installation domotique, et la marque en a lancé un nouveau le 28 octobre : l’Amazon Echo Time. Il s’agit en fait d’un réveil à poser sur votre table de chevet, qui associe un écran tactile à l’assistant vocal Alexa, avec la possibilité de consulter l’heure, la météo, votre calendrier ou encore piloter les appareils connectés de votre maison. Le tout dans une petite sphère à écran rond, qui rappelle un réveil à l’ancienne. Un appareil disponible à un tarif élevé, qui profite du Black Friday pour perdre 55 euros par rapport à son prix de lancement, ce qui permet de l’avoir à 159,99 euros.
Les atouts de l’Amazon Echo Time
- Un écran tactile rond de 3,2 pouces, sans caméra
- L’assistant vocal Alexa intégré pour gérer la maison connectée
- Une interface personnalisable avec des centaines de cadrans et des informations accessibles d’un coup d’œil
L’Amazon Echo Time est un produit qui coûte 214,99 euros mais que vous retrouvez à 159,99 euros pendant le Black Friday d’Amazon, jusqu’au 30 novembre 2026.
Du 10 au 30 novembre, le LUBA mini 2 AWD 1500 passe à 1 399 € au lieu de 1 899 €, support de lavage offert ! Sans fil, navigation LiDAR 360°, évitement précis des obstacles, tonte des bordures… La tonte sans effort, même pour les jardins les plus complexes.
Si, par la suite, l’offre mentionnée dans cet article n’est plus disponible, merci de jeter un coup d’œil ci-dessous afin de dénicher d’autres offres concernant l’Amazon Echo Time. Le tableau s’actualise automatiquement.
Un réveil connecté avec écran tactile pour organiser sa journée
La particularité de l’Echo Time, c’est son écran tactile rond de 3,2 pouces qui, contrairement à une enceinte Echo classique, permet de consulter les informations les plus importantes sans avoir besoin de faire appel à Alexa à chaque fois. L’heure, la météo, l’agenda ou encore les rappels s’affichent sur l’interface de l’appareil. Il propose aussi des centaines de cadrans personnalisables (thèmes météo, personnages sous licence ou affichages plus sobres), que l’on change à la voix. Comme ça, dès que vous ouvrez l’œil, vous avez un aperçu de la journée qui vous attend.
L’appareil conserve les fonctions essentielles d’un réveil, avec la gestion des alarmes et les routines personnalisées. Vous pouvez demander à Alexa de programmer plusieurs réveils, de consulter votre agenda ou de lancer une chanson dès que vous arrêtez l’alarme, pour bien commencer la journée. Vous pouvez lancer un flash info, lire la météo ou encore contrôler des équipements connectés. Par exemple, le réveil sonne, vous l’arrêtez, et Alexa enchaîne avec le dernier flash info de votre radio préférée et la météo, tout en réglant le thermostat sur la température programmée. C’est un vrai tableau de bord domestique sur la table de chevet.
Alexa, musique et maison connectée : un vrai assistant
Au-delà de son rôle de réveil, l’Echo Time reprend bien sûr les principales fonctions de l’écosystème Amazon. Alexa est là et permet de lancer une musique, une station de radio ou des podcasts, mais aussi de répondre à vos questions. L’Echo Time est d’ailleurs conçu pour Alexa+, la version d’Alexa dopée à l’IA générative, censée tenir une conversation plus naturelle. Pendant que vous vous préparez, vous pouvez donc discuter de tout et de rien avec votre réveil.
Vous l’aurez compris, tout l’intérêt de ce modèle dépend beaucoup de la place que vous accordez à Alexa dans votre quotidien. Si vous avez déjà plusieurs appareils compatibles, l’Echo Time peut devenir un point de contrôle supplémentaire bien pratique. Bon, par contre, si vous cherchez un simple réveil qui affiche l’heure, avec une alarme, son prix reste difficile à justifier.

articles.title: Japan takes Fugaku supercomputer offlline after cyberattack
articles.text:
The Fugaku supercomputer operated by Japan's RIKEN Center for Computational Science has been taken offline following a security breach.
The organization says that between November 10 and 13, an unauthorized party exploited the public dashboard displaying Fugaku's operational status to gain access to multiple internal servers.
Although the research center has yet to determine the access method, RIKEN’s investigation confirmed that the intruder accessed some servers to plant malware that targeted user data.
Specifically, the organization says that the following details have been compromised:
- Names, email addresses, and user IDs of 4,222 Fugaku users
- Names and email addresses of 375 Rikyu users
- SSH private keys and access keys stored on users’ computers
- Research data files stored on users’ computers
RIKEN notes that the attacker used some of the access keys in attempts to connect to additional systems, but the investigation did not determine further unauthorized access or theft of research results.
The organization has not attributed the attack, and it’s still working to determine the exact intrusion method.
RIKEN’s Center for Computational Science operates the two supercomputers, making them available to researchers in academia and industry sectors.
Fugaku, which entered shared use in March 2021, is a 537 petaflops supercomputer used in drug discovery, severe-weather forecasting, and simulations of airborne virus transmission. Rikyu is a 64 petaflops supercomputer used in AI scientific research.
In response to the incident, RIKEN shut down Fugaku on November 14, disabled users’ login keys, and asked users to revoke and replace any credentials they had stored on the supercomputer.
RIKEN said Fugaku operations will resume only after it has ensured that it’s safe to do so.
The remediation effort includes addressing the exploited software vulnerability, rebuilding compromised servers, reviewing the network configuration, and implementing advanced AI-driven security measures.
Users are advised to revoke any SSH keys and other credentials stored on Fugaku, and watch out for suspicious emails impersonating RIKEN.
A RIKEN spokesperson told BleepingComputer that they have no more details to share about the incident at the time, but promised to publish updates when the investigation uncovers new findings.

articles.title: Redbrick Offices raises Rs 630 Cr in equity led by India SME Investments and Abakkus
articles.text:
Redbrick Offices raises Rs 630 Cr in equity led by India SME Investments and Abakkus
Redbrick said it plans to use the capital to expand its managed offices portfolio from about 6.5 million sq. ft. to more than 10 million sq. ft. over the next 18 to 24 months, while investing in technology, design and service delivery to cater to enterprise and GCC clients.
Redbrick Offices has raised about $72 million (Rs 630 crore) in equity across its Series A and A1 funding rounds, the company said. The funding comprises a large primary infusion and a smaller secondary component.
India SME Investments led the Series A round in March 2026, while the Series A1 round was recently led by Abakkus’s Four2Eight Opportunities Fund. Evolvence Equity Partners, IIFL Capital Asset Management and UTI Alternatives, among others, also participated in the extended round. India SME Investments made a follow-on investment as part of Series A1. UTI Alternatives had earlier invested in the company through a structured convertible debenture issuance in March 2025.
Redbrick said it plans to use the capital to expand its managed offices portfolio from about 6.5 million sq. ft. to more than 10 million sq. ft. over the next 18 to 24 months. It will also use the funds to serve workspace requirements of large enterprises and global capability centres (GCCs), and to invest in technology infrastructure, design, and service delivery. The company said it is open to strategic partnerships and acquisitions that fit its growth plans.
The fundraise comes as India’s flexible office market crosses 100 million sq. ft., driven by demand from large enterprises and GCCs, according to the company.
“This investment marks an important milestone in our journey,” said Ayush Goenka, chairman and managing director of Redbrick Offices. He said the backing from India SME, Abakkus and other investors validates the company’s focus on improving unit economics and on demand-backed, profitable growth.
Ankit Aggarwal, senior vice president and senior fund manager for private equity at Abakkus, called Redbrick a capital-efficient business that has scaled while remaining profitable. He said flexible, asset-light corporate spaces are becoming a core part of real estate strategy for multinationals and GCCs in India.
Mitin Jain, founder and managing partner of India SME Investments, said the firm’s March 2026 decision to back Redbrick was based on its belief in Goenka and the management team’s record of building a sizeable, bootstrapped business with a focus on profitable growth.
Ladderup Corporate Advisory and IIFL Capital Services were financial advisers to the company, and Rajani Associates was its legal adviser.
Redbrick Offices operates about 6.5 million sq. ft. across more than 70 centres in over eight Indian cities, with more than 1.15 lakh seats. It builds Grade-A offices to client specifications and provides facilities management and hospitality-led services through its wholly owned subsidiary, Snow White Technologies & Services Private Limited. Its clients include GCCs, Fortune 500 companies, large enterprises, BFSI firms and US-based multinationals.

articles.title: Panne mondiale d’Outlook et Teams : Microsoft dévoile ce qu'il s'est vraiment passé
articles.text:
Le 12 novembre à 17 h 20, heure de Paris, des millions de professionnels ont vu leurs boîtes mail se figer et leurs réunions tomber à l’eau. La fenêtre d’impact reconnue par Microsoft court jusqu’au lendemain 17 h 10, et les signalements compilés par Downdetector couvrent 74 pays et territoires. L’analyse préliminaire vient de tomber, et le coupable est bien plus vieux que la panne.
Un bug endormi trois mois, réveillé en moins de deux heures
Tout part d’un correctif déployé en juillet sur les passerelles réseau de Microsoft 365, ces serveurs qui aiguillent les connexions vers Exchange Online, la messagerie professionnelle maison. Préparé pour ces machines et pour elles seules, il embarquait un défaut de gestion des accès concurrents, capable d’épuiser processeur et mémoire sous certaines conditions de trafic. Pendant plus de trois mois, ces conditions ne se sont jamais présentées.
Le 12 novembre, deux événements sans rapport les ont réunies, causant la panne historique. Une quinzaine d’heures avant la panne, Teams a quitté sa passerelle de secours pour la passerelle principale, qui dessert aussi Exchange Online, ce qui a gonflé la charge et bouleversé la répartition du trafic. Au même moment, près de 14 % de la capacité manquait à l’appel, conséquence d’un problème distinct survenu la veille. Chaque facteur pris séparément restait indolore ; leur addition a réveillé le bug. « En moins de deux heures, ce défaut jusqu’alors inconnu a été rencontré sur l’ensemble de notre flotte », retrace Charles Lamanna, vice-président exécutif de Microsoft. Au pire de la crise, plus de 80 % des serveurs ne répondaient plus, et les cloisons censées confiner l’incident à une région ont cédé les unes après les autres.
Teams, OneDrive et SharePoint disposaient d’une infrastructure de repli et se sont relevés les premiers. Exchange Online n’en avait aucune : la messagerie est restée à terre jusqu’au bout, et le rétablissement complet n’a été annoncé que samedi matin.
Pourquoi les tests de Microsoft n’ont rien vu
Les campagnes de tests de charge n’ont jamais déclenché le défaut : les laboratoires de Microsoft tournent sur des machines moins puissantes que celles de la production. Le bug frappe d’autant plus fort que le serveur embarque des cœurs et des composants récents, soit exactement le profil des passerelles réellement en service. Les mélanges de trafic simulés en interne ne ressemblaient pas davantage à la réalité du 12 novembre.
Lire aussi : Souveraineté numérique : l’État français veut abandonner Windows pour Linux
Une fois redémarrés, les serveurs se faisaient aussitôt submerger par les requêtes accumulées, et les mécanismes de récupération automatique n’avaient pas été pensés pour une flotte muette à 80 %. Les ingénieurs ont fini par restaurer une ancienne version du code, isoler les machines par grappes, appliquer le correctif, puis réintroduire le trafic au compte-gouttes. Microsoft écarte toute piste de cyberattaque et promet trois chantiers : des capacités élargies, une surveillance affinée et des protections contre les bascules de trafic en cascade. « Nous sommes profondément désolés de l’impact pour l’ensemble de nos clients », conclut Charles Lamanna.
En France, des collectivités et une agence régionale de santé en Occitanie se sont retrouvées sans messagerie, pendant que le ministère de la Santé assurait que les établissements de soins tenaient le choc. L’analyse définitive est promise dans la semaine, et nous ne manquerons pas de revenir dessus.

articles.title: El Código Civil permite a los propietarios arrancar las ramas y las raíces de los árboles y plantas de su vecino en estos casos
articles.text:
Los árboles y plantas pueden ser objeto de conflicto entre vecinos si sobrepasan el límite de la parcela en que han sido plantados.
Por un lado están las ramas que sobresalen en el jardín de nuestro vecino y, por otro, están las raíces que atraviesan el terreno de la otra persona.
El Código Civil prevé que el afectado pueda reclamar el corte de las ramas (artículo 592). También tenemos el derecho a realizar nosotros mismos el corte de las raíces, pero solo en nuestro terreno.
Qué distancia deben guardar los árboles
Antes de llegar a este problema, el Código Civil (artículo 591) prevé cómo deben ser plantados los árboles en los límites de otras fincas.
En primer lugar, se aplicará la distancia que establezcan las ordenanzas o costumbres locales. En caso contrario, habrá que dejar un margen de dos metros de distancia de la línea divisoria (para árboles altos) o 50 centímetros (arbustos o árboles bajos).
El propietario tiene derecho a solicitar que sean arrancados los árboles que se planten a menos distancia de su finca de la permitida. No hay derecho a arrancarlos por nuestra cuenta.
El derecho de corte de raíces solo llega hasta el límite de nuestra finca. No podemos pasar al terreno del vecino.
Los derechos anteriores son respecto de fincas colindantes. No pueden confundirse con el derecho a actuar sobre plantas situadas en zonas comunes de una comunidad de propietarios. También puede haber otros conflictos en las zonas comunes.
Otro supuesto regulado en el Código Civil es el de los árboles de un seto vivo medianero. Estos se presumen también medianeros. Cualquiera de sus dueños podrá exigir su derribo. Salvo que sean mojones (es decir, que sirvan para marcar el límite de las fincas). En estos casos es necesario el consentimiento de ambos colindantes para arrancarlos (artículo 593).

articles.title: Jensen Huang se ofrece a volver como director ejecutivo de Nvidia tras su salida por presunto espionaje
articles.text:
Jensen Huang aseguró que estaría dispuesto a retomar el cargo de director ejecutivo de Nvidia, aunque la junta directiva del fabricante de chips de inteligencia artificial (IA) habría descartado, por ahora, la posibilidad de restituir a su fundador tras su salida en medio de un presunto caso de espionaje.
En sus primeras declaraciones públicas desde su dimisión del jueves pasado, Huang afirmó que consideraría un honor volver a liderar la compañía, valorada en 3,7 billones de dólares.
“Si el consejo considera que mi regreso beneficia a los accionistas, a los empleados, a la empresa y a Estados Unidos, me sentiría honrado de atender esa petición y volver a ejercer como director ejecutivo”, señaló Huang, según Financial Times.
La salida de Huang se produjo después de que surgieran acusaciones sobre una supuesta relación con una mujer que, de acuerdo con las autoridades estadounidenses, tendría vínculos con los servicios de inteligencia chinos y ocuparía además un puesto ejecutivo de alto rango en Nvidia.
Durante el fin de semana ganó fuerza una campaña para promover su regreso. Huang, quien habría estado al frente de Nvidia durante 33 años desde su fundación, incluso recibió el respaldo condicionado del presidente Donald Trump, que el lunes dijo estar abierto a su vuelta.
Sin embargo, la junta —que analiza perfiles internos y externos para cubrir el puesto— habría transmitido ese mismo día que no contempla reincorporar a Huang.
Qué investigó la junta directiva de Nvidia
La junta de Nvidia abrió una investigación independiente para determinar si Jensen Huang pudo haber sido blanco de una operación de inteligencia extranjera. La revisión quedó a cargo de un comité de directores independientes, con asesoramiento legal externo, después de que informaciones periodísticas vincularan al ejecutivo con una empresaria china investigada por autoridades estadounidenses.
La empresa afirmó entonces que no tenía razones para creer que la seguridad nacional de Estados Unidos o secretos corporativos hubieran resultado comprometidos. La pesquisa, sin embargo, puso bajo escrutinio la conducta del entonces director ejecutivo y los mecanismos de gobierno corporativo de una compañía decisiva para el desarrollo de la inteligencia artificial.
Por qué el caso trascendió el ámbito personal de Jensen Huang
La controversia adquirió una dimensión política por las sospechas sobre posibles transferencias de chips avanzados a compañías chinas. La empresaria relacionada con el caso había trabajado para Megaspeed, una firma de computación en la nube de Singapur que estaba bajo investigación por un eventual acceso de China a procesadores de Nvidia sujetos a controles de exportación de Estados Unidos.
Las acusaciones no fueron verificadas de manera independiente por medios estadounidenses, y China negó cualquier implicación en una operación de espionaje. Aun así, legisladores estadounidenses solicitaron explicaciones y plantearon la necesidad de endurecer las restricciones sobre las ventas de chips de inteligencia artificial al gigante asiático.
Qué obstáculos enfrenta un eventual regreso de Huang a Nvidia
La dimisión de Huang no se produjo solo en medio de la investigación sobre sus vínculos personales. También surgieron reportes sobre una segunda relación extramatrimonial con una ejecutiva de Nvidia que, según The New York Times, le reportaba de forma directa.
Trump afirmó el domingo 8 de noviembre de 2026 que Jensen Huang había “hecho un trabajo increíble para nuestro país” y que el entonces jefe de Nvidia le dijo que desconocía que la empresaria china con la que mantuvo una relación fuera una espía.
La sucesión abrió un debate sobre la continuidad del liderazgo en Nvidia, donde Huang ejerció durante más de tres décadas y mantiene una participación accionaria relevante. La directora financiera, Colette Kress, asumió como directora ejecutiva interina mientras la empresa inició la búsqueda de un reemplazo permanente entre candidatos internos y externos.

articles.title: Samsung, Micron, and SK Hynix are accused of conspiring to inflate RAM prices, lawsuit moves forward
articles.text:
Ripple effect: Conventional wisdom holds that the rush to build data centers to meet AI demand has more than quintupled DRAM prices since 2025, consequently raising consumer electronics prices. However, a recent lawsuit alleges that the top DRAM manufacturers actually coordinated to fatten their profits, something they've been convicted of before.
A California judge has denied Samsung's motion to dismiss a lawsuit accusing it, Micron, and SK Hynix of colluding to inflate DRAM prices. Spiking DRAM prices and, by extension, RAM prices are the main cause of recent price hikes for PCs, consoles, and other devices.
In Garciaguirre et al. v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd. et al., initially filed in June, the plaintiffs accused the trio of neglecting to increase production as AI data center projects siphoned capacity. They argued that in a truly competitive market, at least one player would have increased output to capitalize on rising demand and sell more wafers, prompting the others to react.
Instead, the plaintiffs accuse DRAM manufacturers of deliberately diverting supply from consumer products to HBM server memory and eliminating supply channels to inflate prices. As one piece of evidence, a client reported that all three companies adopted near-identical questionnaires almost simultaneously, asking customers how they planned to use the DRAM they were ordering.
Such behavior suggests collusion, which the lawsuit claims violates Section 1 of the Sherman Act. The section forbids two or more people or business entities from cooperating to restrict trade in a way that harms competition.
This is the third time in roughly the past three decades that Samsung, Micron, and SK Hynix have been accused of price-fixing. This week's decision directly references a case in which all three, along with the now-defunct DRAM divisions of Infineon and Elpida, pleaded guilty to cartel-like behavior between 1998 and 2002. However, the three still-operating manufacturers defeated a similar case in 2018.
It remains unclear how long the latest case will drag on or whether it will affect RAM prices anytime soon. Most experts expect demand to outpace supply through much of 2027, if not longer.
Although memory prices are widely blamed for the absurd current state of the GPU market, a recent report also suggests that Nvidia artificially raised demand for data center GPUs (many of which currently sit inert in warehouses) to keep prices high. The GPU maker at the heart of the AI boom has long been accused of financing its own clients, but after cofounder Jensen Huang's ouster as CEO, past statements emerged suggesting that this was a tactic to inflate prices in response to a chip oversupply.

articles.title: Reason over time-series data with OpenTSLM on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Reason over time-series data with OpenTSLM on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
Across industries, decision-making starts with understanding what is changing and why. Industrial organizations collect data that informs decisions across their operations. This data helps prevent production stoppages, diagnose vehicle faults, explain drops in data-center performance, and adjust pricing as supply and demand shift. However, interpreting that data still requires specialist time, and collecting more data does not mean teams can act on it. General-purpose language models like Claude or ChatGPT can help analyze data. However, processing long histories across hundreds of operational metrics as text or images can consume large numbers of tokens, which increases cost.
To help organizations act on this data, Aionic Labs is developing temporal foundation models, including OpenTSLM, an open source family of time-series language models (TSLMs). These models interpret operational measurements, from equipment sensor data to supply and demand, alongside context such as maintenance records, market news, and an engineer’s observations. In doing so, TSLMs help systems recognize emerging problems in recent measurements. Experts can then ask follow-up questions to understand what changed and assess how to respond. TimeNet, the shared data infrastructure for time-series data, provides one format and API to find, build, and load the datasets used to train and evaluate these models. Together, they help organizations understand how their systems change and act before problems become costly.
OpenTSLM is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, so you can deploy the model in your own AWS environment. This post explores how Nexthink and Aionic Labs are bringing this capability to proactive IT assistance, then shows how to deploy OpenTSLM and adapt it to your own data using TimeNet.
A customer example: Proactive IT support at Nexthink
Nexthink and Aionic Labs are building toward a digital workplace where employees get help before they need to ask for it. At the center is Spark, Nexthink’s personal IT agent, enhanced with time-series language models that connect device telemetry and context to the problems employees experience. Spark turns that understanding into action: it checks the likely issue, guides the employee through an appropriate fix, and follows up on the result. Proactive assistance becomes part of keeping work moving.
The workflow combines recent device time-series, such as CPU activity, memory use, available disk space, application stability, and connectivity, with timestamped events and device and software context. The TSLM receives the numerical measurements alongside this text context and interprets how the signals change over the observation window.
The TSLM provides Spark with three outputs:
- State summary: Explains the likely issue and the supporting signal patterns, connecting device behavior with the employee’s experience.
- Recommended action: Specifies checks to confirm the issue and a practical action for Spark to offer the employee.
- Expected outcome: Describes the intended improvement and how Spark checks the result.
Device telemetry and context support investigation of a range of issues, including slow performance under high CPU or memory load, recurring application freezes or crashes, and files that fail to synchronize. Resource usage, application events, storage measurements, and connection activity provide different pieces of evidence. Combined with device configuration and software versions, they give the TSLM a broader basis for explaining the employee’s experience and directing Spark’s next checks.
In the illustrative low-disk example in Figure 2, the TSLM connects declining free space, a rising disk queue, and more frequent application hangs with likely employee symptoms, such as a slow computer or difficulty saving files. Spark checks how much space is left and whether temporary files can be removed using an IT-approved cleanup. If the checks confirm that a cleanup is appropriate, Spark shows the employee what it proposes to remove and asks for confirmation. After the employee confirms, Spark runs the cleanup, checks the space now available, and asks whether the problem has improved. If the issue persists, Spark offers to pass the findings to IT support.
TSLMs understand how systems change and help people act on that understanding. For Spark, this means recognizing emerging IT problems and guiding employees toward a solution. The same approach brings time series intelligence to manufacturing, energy, and connected products, turning measurements and context into explanations and intelligent decisions.
Solution overview
The architecture in Figure 3 provides a reusable deployment pattern for time-series applications. SageMaker JumpStart supplies the model discovery and deployment path.
SageMaker JumpStart is a machine learning (ML) model hub that accelerates your ML journey. With SageMaker JumpStart, you can evaluate, compare, and deploy pretrained foundation models (FMs), including the newly available OpenTSLM model. As part of the AWS AI offerings, SageMaker JumpStart provides customizable ML solutions which you can deploy to Amazon SageMaker AI inference endpoints within your AWS infrastructure. It complements Amazon Bedrock, which offers serverless API foundation model inference along with features like customizations, knowledge bases, agents, and guardrails.
Key technical benefits of SageMaker AI and SageMaker JumpStart include:
- Pre-built inference containers – AWS Deep Learning Containers with GPU acceleration, so you can serve the model without building your own image.
- Automatic scaling endpoints – Managed infrastructure scales compute resources based on request volume and latency requirements.
- Inference API – SageMaker real-time inference endpoints with standardized API calls, SDK, and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) integration.
- Integrated monitoring – Built-in metrics for throughput, latency, and resource utilization with an Amazon CloudWatch integration.
- Enterprise security – Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) deployment with IAM access control and network isolation options.
The model in SageMaker JumpStart is OpenTSLM-Flamingo. It combines the Gemma 3 4B language model with a time-series encoder and cross-attention layers that let the language model attend to the encoded series. The model has 5.24 billion parameters in total, stored in bfloat16, so its weights take about 10.5 GB of GPU memory.
An application prepares numerical time series and text context, invokes the SageMaker endpoint, and receives the model’s response. The application can present that response to an expert or use it as input to another workflow.
This separation allows the application to control the observation window, select relevant signals, and validate the response before using it. It also makes the model independently adaptable: a new checkpoint can be evaluated against representative cases before the application switches to it.
In addition, we show a tutorial that fine-tunes a pretrained OpenTSLM checkpoint from Hugging Face using ARFBench data loaded through TimeNet. The notebook submits a SageMaker training job that loads ARFBench through TimeNet and fine-tunes the model. Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) stores the resulting model artifact, which is then deployed to a separate SageMaker real-time inference endpoint for evaluation.
Prerequisites
For the deployment walkthrough, use an AWS account with an Amazon SageMaker AI domain and a SageMaker AI execution role. The role must be able to create SageMaker models and endpoints in a supported Region, for example a role with the AmazonSageMakerFullAccess managed policy. The quick setup for single users creates both. The managed policy grants broad permissions to get started. For production, use a policy that grants only the permissions you need, as described in Amazon SageMaker AI identity-based policy examples. OpenTSLM runs on a single GPU with at least 24 GB of memory and bfloat16 support, and we recommend 32 GB of host memory. The default instance type is ml.g6.2xlarge (one NVIDIA L4 GPU with 24 GB of memory, 32 GB of host memory). In SageMaker JumpStart, OpenTSLM also supports ml.g6.4xlarge, ml.g6.8xlarge, ml.g5.2xlarge, ml.g5.4xlarge, ml.g5.8xlarge, ml.g6e.xlarge, and ml.g6e.2xlarge. In the Service Quotas console, check your quota for “ml.g6.2xlarge for endpoint usage”, or for the instance type you choose. You need a quota of at least 1. If it’s lower, request an increase. See the OpenTSLM JumpStart model card for the model access requirements.
For fine-tuning, use JupyterLab in Amazon SageMaker Studio or a local Jupyter environment with AWS credentials configured to run the accompanying notebook, which submits the training job. The notebook uses the SageMaker default S3 bucket and an execution role. Fine-tuning runs on ml.g7e.2xlarge, so also check your quota for “ml.g7e.2xlarge for training job usage”. Training runs on the job’s managed GPU instance. The notebook itself does not need a GPU. Obtain access to the selected Hugging Face checkpoint where required.
Deploy OpenTSLM with SageMaker JumpStart
To deploy OpenTSLM in SageMaker Studio, complete the following steps:
- In SageMaker Studio, choose Models in the navigation pane, then JumpStart models.
- Search for “OpenTSLM” and choose OpenTSLM-Flamingo Gemma 3 4B. The model page shows the model ID, the license, and the request and response format.
- Choose Deploy.
- On the Deploy model to endpoint form, review the Gemma Terms of Use under License agreement and select the checkbox to accept the end user license agreement (EULA). Keep the default instance type, ml.g6.2xlarge, or choose another supported instance type. Then choose Deploy.
- Wait until the endpoint status is InService. In our tests, this took about 6 minutes. Note the endpoint name, which starts with jumpstart-dft-. You need it to send requests and to clean up.
You can also create the deployment from Python with the SageMaker Python SDK v3. The following example uses ModelBuilder. The model is gated: setting accept_eula=True accepts its license, the Gemma Terms of Use. Review the terms before you deploy. The SDK prints a link to them when it builds the model.
Ask a question about a time series
The endpoint accepts a JSON request with one or more instances. Each instance holds a question, one or more numerical series, and optional context lines. Each series has its values, a name, and a short description of the signal, such as its unit and sampling interval. A series can hold up to 32,768 values. The endpoint scales each series to a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1 and passes the original mean and standard deviation to the model as text, so the model receives both the shape and the scale of the signal. Use None for a missing value. The model masks it.
Send the request with the SageMaker Runtime InvokeEndpoint API. Set ENDPOINT_NAME to match your deployment. The calling identity needs the sagemaker:InvokeEndpoint permission. The following synthetic CPU example shows a request.
A request can hold up to four instances, each with 1 to 32 series, and the response contains one answer per instance in generated_text. max_new_tokens accepts values from 1 to 512. The model uses greedy decoding, so the same request typically returns the same answer. A real-time invocation must complete within 60 seconds, and the request body can be up to 6 MB. On ml.g6.2xlarge, the model generates about 20 tokens per second. The endpoint processes the instances of a request in sequence, so response time grows with the number of instances and the length of the answers: an answer of 512 tokens takes about 30 seconds. To stay within 60 seconds, send several instances in one request only with short answers, for example with max_new_tokens of 128. The 6 MB limit also bounds how much series data a request can carry. For long-running requests, you can use asynchronous inference.
You can send the same request with the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). Save the request as JSON, for example with json.dump(request, open("request.json", "w")), then run:
Choose an input window that preserves relevant events
OpenTSLM-Flamingo compresses the encoded time series into a fixed-size set of representations before the language model uses it. This bounds the representation passed to the language model, but it does not make the complete system unlimited in memory or guarantee that a brief event remains easy to identify in a very long recording.
Long-context research makes this distinction concrete. TS-Haystack evaluates event retrieval across recordings of different lengths and finds that the evaluated TSLM variants often lose accuracy as the history grows, especially when locating event start and end times. These results motivate testing the chosen checkpoint on the windows and questions used by your application.
Choose a window that contains the event and enough surrounding context to interpret it. For long recordings, compare overlapping windows. Preserve sampling resolution for brief events and align related channels in time. Include units, sampling interval, and the observation period in the text context. Validate both normal and abnormal examples at the intended lengths. The endpoint’s accepted payload size and the model’s useful analysis window are separate constraints.
Fine-tune OpenTSLM on ARFBench with SageMaker
Follow the accompanying fine-tuning notebook for the complete example, from preparing ARFBench data with TimeNet to launching a SageMaker training job and deploying the adapted model.
When should you fine-tune?
Start by testing the pretrained OpenTSLM model on representative examples from your application, and assess how well it answers your questions.
- Use the pretrained model when its answers are correct and its explanations match the signals.
- Improve the input when important information is missing, such as measurement units, sampling rate, system context, or the relevant time window.
- Fine-tune the model when it consistently misses patterns specific to your domain or struggles with your task, even with sufficient context. Use representative signals paired with reviewed answers.
TimeNet provides a consistent way to load the data for training and evaluation. After fine-tuning, compare the adapted model with the original on examples that were not used for training.
Prepare fine-tuning data with TimeNet
ARFBench is a public benchmark of multiple-choice questions about anomalies in Datadog’s software-incident telemetry. We use ARFBench because its multiple-choice answers can be scored automatically, which makes the effect of fine-tuning measurable. The same workflow applies to tasks with open-ended answers, such as the summaries and recommended actions in the Nexthink example. TimeNet serves ARFBench as a versioned dataset: each question is stored with its answer options, its correct answer, and the metric signals. The training job loads ARFBench through TimeNet and the model checkpoint from Hugging Face.
Submit a SageMaker training job and deploy the fine-tuned model
A SageMaker training job runs the OpenTSLM training script on a GPU instance. The job fine-tunes the time-series encoder, the perceiver resampler, the cross-attention layers, and the language model’s token embeddings, and keeps the rest of the Gemma 3 language model frozen. The job saves the fine-tuned model to Amazon S3 in the layout of the Hugging Face model repository and writes the test accuracy before and after training to a metrics.json file. If your SageMaker Studio domain has a default MLflow App, the job also logs the training and validation loss and the test accuracy to it, so you can compare runs in the MLflow UI. In our run on one ml.g7e.2xlarge instance, accuracy on 135 held-out ARFBench questions rose from 5.0% to 45.9%. That is well above the 24.5% that random choice reaches on the full benchmark according to the ARFBench paper. Before fine-tuning, the model left most answers empty. Afterwards, it answered every question with one of the given options. ARFBench serves here as an example application: it shows how to adapt the model to a new task and answer format with a public dataset. The result is not a comparison with other models or an official ARFBench leaderboard result.
The following excerpt from the accompanying notebook starts the training job with ModelTrainer. scripts/train.py loads ARFBench, evaluates and fine-tunes the model, and saves it to FINETUNED_PREFIX.
To deploy the fine-tuned model, create a new real-time endpoint on ml.g6.2xlarge, or another instance type that the JumpStart model supports, with the same container image and environment variables as the JumpStart model, and the inference script that the accompanying notebook provides. Point its model data to the S3 location of the fine-tuned model files. The request format stays the same, so you can send it the requests from the previous section. The accompanying notebook contains the code.
Adapt the workflow to your domain
The same workflow can be adapted to other time-series tasks by pairing signal windows with relevant questions and reviewed answers. Potential examples include interpreting equipment behavior with maintenance context, explaining energy-consumption patterns with operating conditions, and describing activity from wearable measurements. The data, supervision, and evaluation should reflect the domain and the decision the application is intended to support.
Preserve the timing and meaning of the measurements during preparation, and separate training and evaluation data in a way that reflects deployment. For a predictive task, only information available at prediction time belongs in the input. Domain experts should assess whether an answer is grounded in the signals and useful for the intended workflow. For free-text answers, compare them with reviewed reference answers, for example through expert ratings or LLM-as-a-judge, where a language model scores each answer against a rubric.
Clean up
Deployed endpoints continue to incur charges until you delete them. When you finish, delete the endpoint, its endpoint configuration, and its model. If you deployed from SageMaker Studio, run the following commands instead of choosing Delete on the endpoint page, which deletes only the endpoint. The commands look up the configuration and model names from the endpoint name and delete all three. Set ENDPOINT_NAME to the name of your endpoint, for example the default name that starts with jumpstart-dft- for a Studio deployment:
Repeat these commands with the name of the fine-tuned endpoint. Stop the notebook application and remove tutorial-specific S3 data and artifacts that you do not intend to retain. The training job stops when it completes.
Conclusion
Time-series language models connect numerical measurements with the questions, context, and expertise people use to make decisions. Across manufacturing, energy, wearables, and digital infrastructure, they give people and applications a common way to interpret how systems change. The broader opportunity is to connect operational history with language, making past observations more useful in current decisions.
OpenTSLM is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, so you can deploy it to a real-time inference endpoint in your own AWS environment through SageMaker Studio or the SageMaker SDK. TimeNet and SageMaker training jobs provide a path to adapt the model to your domain’s signals and questions.
To get started, explore Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, follow the examples in the AWS Samples repository, and consult the OpenTSLM repository and TimeNet documentation. Start with the public ARFBench example, evaluate it on representative cases, then bring the signals, questions, and expertise from your own domain.

articles.title: House Democrats promise a US return to global climate talks
articles.text:
ANTALYA, Turkey—After their big gains in the 2026 midterm elections, a delegation of Democratic US House members appeared at the United Nations COP31 climate change conference Monday, pledging to rejoin the international fight against global warming.
Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, said it is a “pivotal time” for US climate and energy policy.
“The wrecking ball of Donald Trump and this out-of-touch administration, and the temporarily empty chair of the United States at this COP31, does not represent what the Americans want or need,” Huffman said.
President Donald Trump has pulled the United States out of the Paris climate agreement twice and is trying to quit the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. The current administration has also tried to cut all funding for climate programs.
Since Trump returned to the White House in 2025, the United States has had no formal government presence at the UN talks, but was informally represented by America Is All In, a coalition including local governments, businesses, faith groups, Native American tribes, and universities.
Huffman said the midterm election shows that Americans have rejected the current administration’s efforts to “turn the United States into something like a petro-dictatorship.” The results could pave the way for the country to reestablish a formal presence at the annual talks.
Given legal uncertainties about Trump’s efforts to completely withdraw the US from the UN’s climate framework, the extent of US participation in the talks is unclear. But Huffman said that, in the past, US congressional delegations have attended the annual Conference of the Parties, as the meeting is formally known, under both Democratic and Republican majorities.
“The next time we’re here, we will be an official congressional delegation led by the leadership of the House of Representatives,” Huffman said in an interview with Inside Climate News.

articles.title: As data centre backlash grows, industry leaders say communities must demand better projects | BetaKit
articles.text:
Communities should ensure innovation is baked into the data centre development process from the get-go, argues Christopher Fazekas, vice-chair of Xnrgy Climate Systems’ board.
“Data centres aren’t going anywhere, but they can be better, so we should make them better, together,” Fazekas said on stage Tuesday morning in Toronto at the MaRS Climate Impact conference. Fazekas spoke during a panel focused on the ongoing public backlash toward data centres, which was reflected in the results of the recent US midterm elections that saw voters broadly reject measures that would have supported development.
“Data centres aren’t going anywhere, but they can be better, so we should make them better, together.”
Christopher Fazekas, Xnrgy Climate Systems
Angus Reid Institute polling shows more than two-thirds of Canadians would oppose having a large AI data centre built near their homes, as many communities have become increasingly concerned about the environmental impact of these facilities, from the water and electricity they consume to the air and noise pollution they create, and where the economic benefits flow. The industry is already feeling the effects: a lack of local support reportedly just drove Telus to pull out of two planned projects in Vancouver.
Arizona-based Xnrgy builds custom air handling solutions designed to help make data centres more sustainable. While Fazekas views the construction of these facilities as inevitable, he acknowledged that the broader data centre industry has thus far “done a terrible job of representing itself” and the value these types of sites could bring to communities. Fazekas and his colleagues believe that the path forward entails more than just building parks and schools.
Fellow panellist Irene Lam, director of client services at Toronto’s Mantle Climate, thinks there is a happy medium between opposing all data centre construction and simply accepting the AI infrastructure buildout on industry’s terms. Her employer is a strategy and risk management consultancy that has engaged the ecosystem on this exact topic.
“We don’t have to unconditionally accept [data centres], but we do need to consider some of the trade-offs that need to be made,” Lam said.
Lam argued that successful projects will require carefully planning these sites around energy system capacity, as well as ensuring communities have input in this process and any decisions that might impact their future.
RELATED: Telus pulls out of two government-backed AI data centres in Vancouver
“We are going to need some of this infrastructure built, regardless,” said Lam. “But the question really is, how do we do this in a Canadian way? How do we build more innovatively, sustainably, and responsibly?”
Lam has already seen a few ways that cities and towns can achieve this, including by ensuring that data centre developers engage with communities early on, establishing clear expectations, and holding these firms accountable through reporting requirements, deadlines, and penalties for non-compliance.
Fazekas echoed this sentiment, arguing that municipalities ought to set a few key ground rules for prospective new builds up front, including eliminating the use of water and evaporative cooling altogether, tackling noise pollution, and requiring sites to generate lasting local employment, such as by setting up corporate campuses nearby, rather than simply exporting processing power.
At the moment, Fazekas said “the only force for innovation … is coming from the industry itself” as it seeks to increase capacity to meet surging AI demand. He thinks greater pressure from communities could accelerate the pace of data centre innovation because more of these facilities are likely to be built, either way.
“The middle ground is an open conversation that demands innovation and demands progress, but also accepts the fact that this is part of industrialization and the new revolution of technology,” Fazekas said.

articles.title: 'Los Juegos del Hambre: Amanecer en la cosecha' (★★★½☆) sorprende con la entrega más trágica de la saga
articles.text:
La esperada precuela de Los Juegos del Hambre: Amanecer en la cosecha, está a punto de llegar a los cines. La película se convierte en la sexta entrega de la aclamada saga, y también en la segunda de las precuelas de la historia de Katniss. Tras muchos meses con la emoción por las nubes, los fans al fin se reencuentran con el cruel y radical mundo de Panem. Esta vez, además, con una de las tramas más importantes de toda la franquicia.
Y es que Los Juegos del Hambre: Amanecer en la cosecha nos transporta 24 años antes de los acontecimientos de la primera película, hasta la mañana de la cosecha de los 50.º Juegos del Hambre. Un brutal evento conocido como el Segundo Vasallaje de los Veinticinco. Se trata de una edición especialmente cruel en la que el Capitolio envió el doble de tributos a la arena. Es, también, la edición en la que participó un jovencísimo Haymitch Abernathy, el que posteriormente fuera el mentor de Katniss y Peeta.
El personaje interpretado por Woody Harrelson en las películas originales se ganó el calor del público. Pero ahora, en esta versión rejuvenecida, el testigo recae sobre Joseph Zada. El protagonista de Los Juegos del Hambre: Amanecer en la cosecha debe demostrar que puede llenar los zapatos de un legado como el de Haymitch. Todo ello acompañado de un reparto de absoluto lujo con nombres como Ralph Fiennes, Kieran Culkin, Glenn Close, Jesse Plemons, Elle Fanning, McKenna Grace o Maya Hawke.
El trágico pasado de Haymitch
La principal duda que surgía cuando se anunció el desarrollo de Los Juegos del Hambre: Amanecer en la cosecha era evidente. ¿Es necesaria otra película más de la saga? ¿Tiene este universo algo más que decir? La respuesta ya se vio claramente en el libro del que parte. Y ahora la película da exactamente la misma réplica. Sí. Esta franquicia aún está viva. Todavía quedan historias por contar.
Y de entre todas ellas, esta es una de las más interesantes. El pasado de Haymitch era uno de los grandes interrogantes de la tetralogía original. Alcohólico y deprimido, su presentación no despertaba otra cosa que pena y recelo. Sin embargo, su desarrollo fue formidable. Pronto aprendíamos que se trataba de un personaje roto, sin esperanza, hundido. Poco a poco, el veterano mentor recuperaba la chispa de la vida gracias a Katniss y Peeta. Pero no sabíamos por qué la había perdido en primer lugar.
Ahora, Los Juegos del Hambre: Amanecer en la cosecha lo explica a la perfección. Porque lo que vemos al principio de la cinta es a un muchacho feliz, enamorado y valiente que vive lo mejor que puede en el Distrito 12. A lo largo de sus dos horas y media, el filme narra cómo Haymitch pudo pasar de un punto a otro tan opuesto. Cómo su mente y su alma se quebraron por completo a raíz de su participación en los Juegos.
Los Juegos del Hambre: Amanecer en la cosecha es, por tanto, una historia profundamente triste. Es cierto que todas las de la saga lo son. Pero en ellas siempre se vislumbraba un ápice de luz, de esperanza. Trataban sobre el nacimiento (y la necesidad) de una revolución social. Este nuevo filme le da inteligentemente un pequeño giro más oscuro al discurso para no resultar tan repetitivo. Esta vez, el tema central es la supervivencia del individuo, del espíritu de libertad que nace de dentro. Es la lucha contra la opresión del sistema que se recrea en el sufrimiento y el desánimo como mecanismos de poder. Aunque a veces esas batallas, sean tan imposibles que se pierdan.
Más tributos, más espectáculo
Otro de los puntos que destacan en Los Juegos del Hambre: Amanecer en la cosecha, en este caso no tan para bien, es su duración. La cinta se extiende a más de dos horas y media que, al terminar, se notan. Aunque está dividida en "capítulos" para intentar aligerar el ritmo, a veces se enreda demasiado en sí misma, perdiendo la ligereza de la que sí hace gala durante la mayor parte del metraje.
Hay un pecado en el que la cinta no puede evitar caer. En sus 158 minutos pretende contarnos la vida feliz de Haymitch en el Distrito 12, el desgarrador momento en el que es seleccionado como tributo, su paso por el Capitolio, su entrenamiento, la lucha en la arena y también las consecuencias posteriores en su vida y la de sus seres queridos. Todo ello en profundidad.
Obviamente es una tarea imposible, y ciertas partes se hacen mucho más superficiales y vagas que otras. Tampoco ayuda que se añadan algunas subtramas y personajes que, por esos mismos límites de tiempo, quedan reducidos a elementos prescindibles y olvidables en el esquema general de la cinta. Al final, el equilibrio general está algo desnivelado, lo que le resta puntos pese a que, eso sí, es una película muy entretenida.
Sobre todo porque Los Juegos del Hambre: Amanecer en la cosecha se hace grande cuando más abraza su escala colosal. Hay secuencias impresionantes en el Capitolio, coloridas y terribles a partes iguales. También en la arena, preciosa, gigante y letal. Y también hay escenas mucho más íntimas y más llenas de vida en ese polvoriento y desdichado Distrito 12. El juego de contrastes que hace la película en cada uno de sus escenarios es muy interesante y ayuda a generar la sensación de espectáculo.
En definitiva, Los Juegos del Hambre: Amanecer en la cosecha consigue sorprender para bien con una de sus historias más trágicas. Es una película triste y cruel con su protagonista que, además, remarca de nuevo el profundo mensaje político de la saga. Eso sí, no es ni mucho menos perfecta. Se hace larga, con algunos segmentos bastante perezosos y olvidables. En cualquier caso, en líneas generales es muy entretenida. Joseph Zada tiene el carisma suficiente para sostener el papel de Haymitch. Y el filme cuenta con las dosis de acción y espectacularidad que se le requieren a una franquicia como esta. A buen seguro los fans de la saga la van a disfrutar enormemente.

articles.title: Tech orgs push back on Canadian bill that weakens encryption
articles.text:
Lobbyists and executives from Meta, Apple, and Google’s parent company, Alphabet, are mounting a final effort to rewrite Bill C-22 before it officially passes.
The bill, known as the “lawful access” bill, is designed to allow Canada’s investigative agencies and police services to compel tech companies to retain and turn over some previously encrypted data. Although controversial, the Canadian government insists the measures align the country with its Five Eyes and Group of Seven allies.
However, tech companies have pushed back on the lawful access bill for months, arguing that the bill as written would still allow the government to issue secret orders that weaken encryption.
On Monday, leaders from Meta, Signal, and Tailscale argued against the bill at a Senate committee hearing designed to shape its final form. This committee is the bill’s last hurdle before it could potentially pass into law, and it rarely rejects bills—but it often secures amendments.
Now, tech companies argue that the bill goes far beyond what other countries have adopted, and warn that having a backdoor into previously encrypted data could compromise Canadians’ privacy. Yahoo Finance (Bloomberg) added that Meta has argued the law would effectively make its platforms “an arm of the government’s surveillance apparatus.”
Meta even threatened to pull services like WhatsApp from Canada if Bill C-22 passes, according to a CBC News report. Now, Meta is not the only company that is threatening this. Signal stated back in May that if it is asked to comply with Bill C-22, it could pull its services from Canada.
Apple hasn’t gone that far yet, but it previously said it “will never” add a backdoor to its products. Apple also provided the following statement to MobileSyrup:
“At Apple, we believe privacy is a fundamental human right. It’s one of our core values, which is why we minimize the data we collect and design our products from the ground up to protect users’ most sensitive data. While we appreciate attempts to improve C-22, the bill could still undermine Apple’s ability to offer the powerful privacy and security features our users expect from us, including encryption, even as AI and other evolving technologies provide hackers with new tools to exploit cybersecurity weaknesses. You can’t build a backdoor just for the good guys, yet C-22 could force companies to build backdoors into products — something Apple will never do. We are proud of our longstanding cooperation with Canadian law enforcement to protect public safety. Unfortunately, C-22, as drafted, puts the privacy and security of Canadian users at risk.”
The government has been trying to get this bill into law as quickly as possible, with Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree telling the National Post that “my expectation is to get it done before we rise. I want this as law before we rise.”
The federal government has been rushing this bill, including pushing it through the House of Commons right before it rose for summer break in June.
Source: Yahoo Finance (Bloomberg)

articles.title: Waymo suspends freeway rides nationwide after California DMV order | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Waymo robotaxis are no longer allowed to operate on California freeways after the state’s Department of Motor Vehicles restricted the Alphabet-owned company’s operations following several incidents that raised safety concerns.
California’s DMV, which regulates the testing and deployment of autonomous vehicles in the state, issued the operational restrictions on Waymo on November 11. However, the restrictions weren’t made public until Tuesday. San Francisco Business Times was the first to report the order.
The DMV confirmed the new restrictions to TechCrunch, stating that the department took action after three Waymo autonomous vehicles entered an active construction closure on U.S. Route 101 near Burlingame, and another separate incident involving California Highway Patrol vehicles on Highway 280 in San Francisco.
Waymo has complied and is preventing its robotaxis from accessing freeways in any of the markets it operates in, including those outside of California. Waymo currently has commercial operations in 15 U.S. cities.
The DMV said Waymo’s freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety.
“The Department determined that Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present, despite a prior restriction and corrective actions implemented following similar incidents that occurred on May 18, 2026,” according to an emailed statement sent to TechCrunch.
The DMV said the restrictions will remain in place until Waymo can demonstrate that it has taken “effective corrective actions” to address the deficiencies.
Waymo spokesperson Dana Gallagher told TechCrunch the company has temporarily restricted freeway operations across its other operating markets to evaluate its performance.
“Safety is at the foundation of everything we do,” Gallagher said in a statement. “Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state. In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations.”
Waymo began offering freeway rides in late 2025, a commercial milestone that has been central to its expansion in major metro areas. Freeway access allows Waymo to connect riders to airports and other destinations more efficiently, slashing travel times by avoiding slower surface streets.
That has been particularly important in the San Francisco Bay Area because Waymo’s service area stretches from the city south to Silicon Valley. Freeway access has dramatically shortened trips across the Peninsula that previously took 45 minutes or more than an hour.
In May, Waymo abruptly stopped operating on highways. The company didn’t cite a specific reason at the time, but several social media posts showed Waymo robotaxis driving through traffic cones and struggling to navigate construction zones.
Waymo robotaxis returned to freeways in July after the company said it updated the self-driving software system to improve performance around freeway construction zones.

articles.title: Spara's Scout AI assistant acts on sales opportunities before reps know to look - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Spara’s Scout AI assistant acts on sales opportunities before reps know to look
Artificial intelligence sales agent startup Spara Inc. today introduced Scout, an AI assistant designed to act on sales opportunities before salespeople know to look for them.
Working around the clock, the new service analyzes context from customer conversations, emails and customer relationship management data to identify opportunities, prepare personalized outreach and complete work before reps realize it needs doing.
Scout is aimed at addressing a limitation of most AI assistants, which still require users to tell them what to do, according to Spara. The service instead works within the daily workflows of salespeople, providing an always-on partner that keeps track of customers and helps move work forward without constant direction.
Signals analyzed continuously by Scout include job changes, company news, buying signals and CRM activity across a salesperson’s accounts. From there, the service determines when to engage customers and prospects, as well as who to contact. Instead of requiring another platform to manage, Scout delivers its findings through Salesforce Inc.’s Slack and text messages.
Over time, Scout retains what it learns about each account, along with the salesperson’s preferences and previous outreach. Doing so is said to allow the service to anticipate next steps and deliver more relevant recommendations.
Outreach messages are drafted in the salesperson’s voice, with reps kept in control of what gets sent. Going beyond recommendations, Scout can join customer calls and contribute to conversations in real time, helping salespeople move opportunities forward.
“Sales has always been a game of speed, timing and relationships, but there’s only so much one person can keep track of in a day,” said David Walker, co-founder and chief executive of Spara. “Even the best sales organizations can’t realistically give every rep the support they need to act on every opportunity at exactly the right moment.”
Spara also released early results from users of the new service. Salespeople using Scout were found to have increased the number of personalized emails sent eightfold in their first two weeks of use. Outreach generated by Scout drew a 10.5% reply rate, against 3.5% for traditional sales sequences, according to the company. Early users also booked 29% more meetings.
Chris Brown, a partner at Spara investor Inspired Capital who has worked with the team since the beginning, said Spara has built agents that go-to-market teams trust with their most important customer conversations. Scout is now “putting that trust to work for individual sellers,” he added.
Scout is available for free starting today at spara.com/scout.
Founded by Walker and Zander Pease, Spara offers a platform for building AI agents that carry out sales work across chat, email, text messaging, voice and interactive product demos. The agents handle tasks ranging from engaging and qualifying leads to following up with prospects, booking meetings and managing renewals. Notable customers include Justworks Inc., Rho Technologies Inc. and Mindbody Inc.
Spara launched in September 2025 with $15 million in seed funding. Including additional funding since then, the company has raised $20 million to date, with Radical Ventures and Inspired Capital leading the seed round.

articles.title: China engineers behind J-35 fighter jet pioneer 3D-printed load-bearing structures in military aircraft — behemoth 16.4-foot part uses segmented printing and fusion techniques
articles.text:
China engineers behind J-35 fighter jet pioneer 3D-printed load-bearing structures in military aircraft — behemoth 16.4-foot part uses segmented printing and fusion techniques
China has been at this for over two decades, and they're not slowing down.
The Shenyang Aircraft Design and Research Institute, the developers of China’s J-35 fighter jet platform, used metal 3D printing to create large primary load-bearing structures for military aircraft applications. Global Times reports the structure is over 16.4 feet (five meters) in length, using segmented printing and fusion techniques.
Shenyang Aircraft Design and Research Institute, a research organization under the Aviation Industry Corporation of China (AVIC), has been working on 3D-printed aircraft components since 2003. The impressively large 3D-printed components are the culmination of decades of research and development of various metal additive manufacturing techniques.
The engineers are no strangers to large 3D-printed components: in 2005, they achieved secondary load-bearing structures; then, in 2012, large primary load-bearing titanium alloy structures, earning additive manufacturing expert Wang Huaming and his team China’s National Technological Invention Award.
Recently, however, the team created a primary load-bearing structure even larger, at over 16.4 feet. The massive component is not printed in one piece, as printing such a large structure faces warping and cracking issues, as stated in Progress and Challenges of Laser Direct Manufacturing of Large Titanium Structural Components, published in the Chinese Journal of Lasers. To avoid these problems, two techniques were employed: Segmented Additive Manufacturing (SAM) and additive fusion joining. It sounds like fancy words to say it was printed separately and welded, and it technically wouldn’t be wrong — but the key distinction is that it is part of the whole workflow; basically, metal 3D printing into the intentionally designed gaps between the components and creating one whole printed piece.
Additive manufacturing eliminates the need for expensive molds and multi-part construction. Titanium alloys are notoriously difficult to machine, cast components are usually weak, and joining parts using bolts and screws is additional labor — metal 3D printing solves all of this by creating a strong printed part in the desired shape in one large piece, minimizing the need for additional fasteners. By eliminating molds, the team can iterate much faster and create more complex structures that would otherwise not be possible with traditional manufacturing techniques.

articles.title: Meta testet neue Messenger-App auf Instagram-Basis
articles.text:
Konkurrenz für Whatsapp: Meta testet neue Messenger-App auf Instagram-Basis
Direktnachrichten (DM) auf Instagram erfreuen sich bei Nutzer:innen offenbar großer Beliebtheit. In den vergangenen Jahren haben einige Entwickler:innen versucht, per DM zu kommunizieren, ohne ablenkende Reels oder Posts angezeigt zu bekommen. Eine Lösung, um die DM-Funktionen verschiedener Messenger-Apps zu vereinen, ist etwa Beeper.
Messenger-App auf Instagram-DM-Basis
Jetzt scheint Meta auf die entsprechende Nachfrage der Instagram-Nutzer:innen zu reagieren. Mit Direct bringt der Facebook-Konzern eine eigenständige Messenger-App an den Start, die auf den Instagram-Direktnachrichten basiert.
Zunächst handelt es sich dabei aber lediglich um einen Test für Nutzer:innen in der Türkei und Thailand, wie der Konzern mitteilt. Ob und wann die Direct-App auch in anderen Ländern wie Deutschland angeboten wird, dürfte auch vom Erfolg des Experiments abhängen. Meta hat sich dazu bisher nicht offiziell geäußert.
Macht Direct künftig Whatsapp Konkurrenz?
Interessant ist der Direct-Start vor allem deswegen, weil Instagram-Chef Adam Mosseri zuletzt solchen eigenständigen Nachrichtensystemen für verschiedene Meta-Dienste eher skeptisch gegenüberstand, wie etwa techbook.de schreibt. Weil Interessierte nicht zwingend auf ein Instagram-Konto angewiesen sind, könnte Direct auf längere Sicht dem Meta-Dienst Whatsapp Konkurrenz machen.
Eine Anmeldung zu der neuen Messenger-App ist mit den Instagram-Logindaten möglich. Dann werden bisherige Kontakte und Chats übertragen. Wer kein Instragram-Konto hat, kann sich per E-Mail-Adresse oder Telefonnummer anmelden. Neue Kontakte lassen sich dann über die Instagram-Nutzer:innennamen oder per QR-Code manuell hinzufügen.
Optisch erinnert Direct stark an Instagrams Nachrichtenfunktion. Bekannte Funktionen wie individuelle Chat-Hintergründe, kreative Optioen wie Zeichnen und Sticker erstellen sowie das Veröffentlichen kurzer Statusmeldungen (Notes) bleiben erhalten.
Daten- und Jugendschutz im Fokus
Meta legt bei Direct aber zudem einen großen Wert auf Daten- und Jugendschutzmaßnahmen. So müssen Direct-Nutzer:innen mindestens 13 Jahre alt sein. Eltern können über Aufsichtsfunktionen Gesprächskontakte einsehen und Zeitlimits setzen.
Verdächtige oder unangemessene Interaktionen mit jungen Nutzer:innen will Meta technisch erkennen können. Darüber hinaus sollen nur Kontakte oder schon verbundene Personen Chats starten oder Nutzer:innen zu Gruppen hinzufügen können.
Heiße Mädchen warten auf dich — Miss4.fun

articles.title: Diese 5-Minuten-Übung verändert, wie du mit ChatGPT arbeitest
articles.text:
ChatGPT wie einen Kollegen nutzen: Diese 5-Minuten-Übung empfiehlt ein Stanford-Professor
Im Frühjahr 2025 ist Jeremy Utley, Professor am Hasso Plattner Institute of Design der Stanford-Uni, mit seinem Videointerview „How Stanford Teaches KI-Powered Creativity in Just 13 Minutes“ viral gegangen. Das Video ist über 2,3 Millionen Mal angeschaut worden.
KI-Chatbot als Teamkollegen behandeln
Darin erklärt Utley, dass eine kleine Verschiebung des Mindsets im Umgang mit KI-Chatbots einen großen Unterschied bezüglich des Outputs mache. Statt KI nur als Werkzeug zu nutzen, würden High-Performer ChatGPT und Co wie eine:n Teamkolleg:in behandeln, so Utley.
Als Beispiel führt Utley das Verfassen einer E-Mail an. Normalerweise würden Nutzer:innen die KI einfach bitten, ihnen eine Antwort zu schreiben und wären mit dem Output schnell zufriedenzustellen. Um das volle Potenzial aus den Chatbots zu kitzeln, sollte die KI aber zur Zusammenarbeit eingeladen werden, wie es vonseiten der Stanford-Uni heißt.
Laut Utley gibt man dabei der KI die Erlaubnis, Fragen zu stellen. Ein entsprechender Prompt könnte so lauten: „Hilf mir, auf diese E-Mail zu antworten. Stelle mir alle Fragen, die du benötigst, um den Kontext zu erhalten“. Ebenfalls möglich ist, das Output des einen KI-Chatbots der Konkurrenz, etwa Gemini oder Claude, vorzulegen und um eine kritische Einschätzung zu bitten.
Positives Feedback fördert Ideenfindung
Selbst die Eigenart großer Sprachmodelle, Nutzer:innen überwiegend positiv und unkritisch gegenüberzutreten, lässt sich Utley zufolge als Kreativitätsbooster nutzen. Wenn ChatGPT alle Ideen wunderbar finde, fühle man sich vielleicht weniger gehemmt oder eingeschränkt bei der Ausarbeitung weiterer, zunächst abwegig erscheinender Ideen.
Die wahre Magie, so Utley, entstehe aber erst dann, wenn Nutzer:innen der KI beigebracht hätten, wer sie sind. Dazu gehöre der persönliche Geschmack, der Ton, der Stil oder Kriterien dafür, was gut ist oder aussieht. Der Output klinge dann menschlicher. Letztlich könne KI auch dazu beitragen, mögliche Engpässe im kreativen Denken zu überwinden.
Emotionale Entscheidungen diskutieren
Um herauszufinden, wie sich KI-Zusammenarbeit wirklich anfühlt, hat Utley sich eine fünfminütige Übung ausgedacht. Dabei geht es darum, mit ChatGPT und Co eine emotionale Entscheidung zu diskutieren, für die normalerweise eine nahe Person konsultiert würde. Beispiele: Ein schwieriges Gespräch, eine Entscheidung über die weitere Karriereplanung oder die Frage, ob man ein neues Projekt übernehmen sollte.
Der Prompt könnte dann so aussehen: „Ich kämpfe mit einer Entscheidung. Bevor du mir einen Rat gibst, stelle mir bitte drei Fragen, um meine Situation besser zu verstehen“. Dann sollen Nutzer:innen einfach ganz normal mit dem KI-Chatbot plaudern. Utley zufolge sei diese Übung meist der Augenöffner für Menschen, die Zweifel an seinem Konzept hätten.
Dieser Artikel wurde ursprünglich am 28.02.2026 veröffentlicht, interessiert jedoch immer noch sehr viele unserer Leser:innen. Deshalb haben wir ihn aktualisiert und hier nochmals zur Verfügung gestellt.

articles.title: Your AI coding agent could cost 5x more depending on the harness, benchmark finds
articles.text:
Your AI coding agent could cost 5x more depending on the harness, benchmark finds
The same AI model can cost up to five times more to run depending on the coding agent harness it’s paired with, according to a new benchmark that tested 22 configurations across five open-weight models.
Runta and Baseten ran those combinations 27,280 times for FrontierHarness Eval v1.1, consuming roughly 83 billion tokens in the process.
Nearly 65% of estimated inference spending went to runs that failed verification or timed out.
The model itself accounted for 92.8% of the cost differences, but the harness still made a considerable difference. One configuration could be the cheapest option for one model and among the most expensive for another, adding another wrinkle for developers looking to cut coding-agent costs by changing harnesses or swapping in a cheaper model. Nearly 65% of estimated inference spending went to runs that failed verification or timed out.
Rankings flip with the model
The benchmark covered 22 coding-agent harness configurations across five models served through Baseten, including GLM-5.3, GLM-5.3 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Muse Spark Open, and Kimi-K3. Each configuration ran 62 terminal-based tasks four times per model, with pass rates, inference costs and execution times recorded for comparison.
Codex CLI ranked first for lowest average cost per task with GLM-5.3 but dropped to 16th out of 22 configurations with Kimi-K3. DeepSeek Harness Creator showed an even larger change, ranking first with Muse before falling to 21st with GLM-5.3 Flash.
Across the five models, harnesses shifted a median of 11 ranking positions when the model changed, while costs varied by as much as fivefold even when the model stayed the same.
Across the five models, harnesses shifted a median of 11 ranking positions when the model changed, while costs varied by as much as fivefold even when the model stayed the same. The biggest difference came with DeepSeek, where Cline CLI cost five times as much as OpenCode v1 but delivered a pass rate only two percentage points higher.
The researchers also shuffled the trials within each model 300 times to see whether random variation could explain the cost differences. The gaps in the actual results were larger than those in the shuffled trials, with a reported p-value of 0.003.
Failed runs eat the budget
Failed runs accounted for 52.7% of estimated inference spending, with timeouts adding another 11.8%. Just 35.5% went toward successful runs. Those costs are based on Baseten’s published rates, but they put a price on a familiar problem with coding agents struggling to complete difficult tasks.
Among the five best-value harnesses, 68% to 82% of unsuccessful runs ended with the agent submitting a final answer that failed verification rather than timing out.
Among the five best-value harnesses, 68% to 82% of unsuccessful runs ended with the agent submitting a final answer that failed verification rather than timing out. The researchers also found 216 instances of reward hacking in the execution logs, including 163 involving online lookups. All received zero scores.
Steps, not prompts, drive cost
Runta looked at whether prompt size, tool count, cache hit rates, or agent steps had the biggest impact on cost. Step count was the only factor with a statistically significant correlation to cost per successful task, at 0.51.
Mini-SWE-agent showed how multi-step agent execution can drive up token costs, starting with the smallest prompt in the benchmark at 882 tokens but averaging 38 steps per successful task and ranking 17th out of 22 configurations for cost per pass.
The five best-value harnesses relied heavily on shell commands, which made up 61% to 93% of their tool calls, and rarely used subagents, or context summarization. Runta didn’t test those design choices separately, however, so the results don’t establish whether the simpler setups were responsible for the lower costs.
