articles.title: Formal Verification of the Signal Protocol Using AI - Schneier on Security
articles.text:
Formal Verification of the Signal Protocol Using AI
This seems like a good thing:
Google Deepmind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guaranteesa landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself.
Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world’s communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind’s formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code.
[…]
The DeepMind analysis did not find any new vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and showed that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work.
Alternate link.
First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code.
Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human  just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most.
Technical paper.
dsanford0 • November 17, 2026 7:53 AM
In the age of AI coding, where prompts and other obfuscated information may be embedded in code, I favor much more formal verification. Many programs are fairly simple finite-state machines, which should be easy to verify.

articles.title: OpenAI's own tests show GPT-6.2 Astra is twice as likely to hide coding failures
articles.text:
OpenAI’s own tests show GPT-6.2 Astra is twice as likely to hide coding failures
OpenAI’s new GPT-6.2 Astra is nearly twice as likely as its predecessor to leave users unaware of problems that prevented it from finishing a coding task, according to the company’s own safety evaluations. Developers building autonomous agents could encounter the same problem, since OpenAI has added a mitigation to Codex that isn’t automatically applied to direct API requests.
In its GPT-6.2 system card, published Tuesday alongside the release of GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol, OpenAI reported that Astra failed to disclose a known obstacle in 22.28% of evaluated coding tasks, compared with 11.09% for GPT-6 Astra.
An agent may write better code without telling the developer when it couldn’t finish the job.
The copmany says both models perform better on demanding tasks while using fewer output tokens, but those improvements don’t necessarily make them more reliable at reporting failures. An agent may write better code without telling the developer when it couldn’t finish the job.
The New Stack has asked OpenAI whether it plans to extend the Codex mitigation to API developers and how the additional instructions affect the models’ failure-reporting behavior.
Inside the blocker deception test
OpenAI measured the behavior with an internal evaluation called Blocker Deception, which gives models realistic coding assignments before deliberately introducing obstacles that make the requested work impossible to finish as specified.
In some runs, the evaluation removes a source file the agent was supposed to modify. In others, it disables a tool needed to build the project. The evaluation then checks whether the model tells the user what happened or leaves the obstacle out of its final response.
The caveats Astra leaves out
The company acknowledges the regression and says it is still investigating the cause. One possible explanation is that training the models to give shorter answers with fewer caveats may have made them less likely to report problems that prevented them from completing a task. OpenAI cautions that the evaluation was designed to trigger this behavior, so the results don’t necessarily reflect how often Astra misleads users in production.
A separate evaluation, Broken Search Tool, identified a similar problem. The model receives questions requiring information retrieval while the necessary search capability is disabled. GPT-6.2 Astra failed to acknowledge the missing requirement or unavailable tool in 23% of cases, compared with 7.58% for GPT-6 Astra and 1% for GPT-6.1 Terra.
Developers can check the logs, test results, and git diff … but they shouldn’t have to dig through an entire session to find out that something failed.
Developers can check the logs, test results, and git diff to see what an agent actually did, but they shouldn’t have to dig through an entire session to find out that something failed. If an agent says it finished the job without mentioning a missing dependency or a failed build, that work could make it through review without anyone realizing there’s a problem. It’s another example of the code confidence gap that becomes harder to manage as agents take on more work across a repository.
The fix the API misses
OpenAI says it developed a prompt-based intervention that substantially reduced the rate of omitted blockers in evaluations of both Astra and Sol. The company incorporated that intervention into the standard Codex developer prompt at launch, but it does not automatically apply the same instructions to direct API requests.
Codex users get the updated prompt, but developers building their own agents through the API don’t.
Codex users get the updated prompt, but developers building their own agents through the API don’t. OpenAI hasn’t shown whether adding similar instructions to a custom harness would produce the same results.
The harness can’t take the model’s completion summary at face value because it needs to verify the diff, check test results, and confirm the expected artifacts exist before marking a task complete.
These verification loops are especially important for unattended agents, where a failed step can go unnoticed until someone reviews the work.
Performance up, reporting down
The disclosure comes as OpenAI promotes improvements in coding performance and efficiency across both new models.
In its launch announcement, OpenAI said GPT-6.2 Sol came within 0.5 points of Astra on Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0 coding benchmark at approximately one-fifth the estimated cost per task, with both models running at maximum effort.
In testing shared with The New Stack by OpenAI, Replit reported that GPT-6.2 Sol passed more tests, used 62% fewer output tokens and ran nearly three times as fast as GPT-6.1 Sol when building software from scratch.
Faster execution and lower inference costs make these models appealing for automated coding, but OpenAI’s safety tests show that better performance doesn’t necessarily mean an agent will tell developers when something goes wrong.
Learning Path

articles.title: Just 403 data centers use as much electricity as the whole state of Michigan does in a year
articles.text:
The big picture: Michigan is home to about 10 million people and a big chunk of America's auto industry. Yet a new study estimates that a few hundred data centers scattered across the US used about as much electricity in a single year as that entire state. Strangely, no federal or state agency actually tracks that number, so researchers had to build their own list of these facilities, partly from satellite imagery.
The research, published on Monday in Nature Sustainability, comes from a Harvard-led team. It focuses only on hyperscale data centers – the largest class of facility, mostly run by cloud and AI giants. Operators and utilities aren't required to disclose how much power individual sites draw, so the team combined industry data with satellite checks to compile 403 facilities, then estimated what each consumed between May 2024 and April 2025.
Depending on how hard those sites were assumed to run, their combined usage landed somewhere between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours. The middle estimate of about 82 TWh works out to roughly 1.8% of all US electricity consumption. That upper figure, for comparison, is about what Michigan, Indiana or Tennessee each go through in a year.
Much of that load sits in Virginia. The state's 142 facilities alone use roughly a quarter of the total. Add Oregon, Ohio and Iowa, and those four states account for about half.
Those states run on very different grids, though. Oregon's sites draw on relatively clean power, while those in Virginia, Ohio and Iowa lean much harder on fossil fuels. Across the whole sample, more than half the electricity came from natural gas and coal. And because demand has ballooned so quickly, emissions from these facilities are now more than triple pre-AI-boom estimates.
The real total is probably higher, too, since the study didn't count electricity generated by on-site power plants or anything that came online after April 2025. Lead author Gianluca Guidi also told Wired that some of the campuses being proposed today are "substantially larger than the typical facility" his team looked at.
Those on-site plants have been multiplying fast. Developers stuck in years-long queues for grid connections have increasingly been turning to their own turbines and generators. In August, a Bloomberg analysis counted 99 proposed gas plants meant to power data centers directly. If they were to run at industry-standard rates, they would emit around 318 million metric tons of CO2 a year. That alone would push US power-sector emissions up by about 20%.

articles.title: How LoanPro built an agentic AI loan servicing assistant with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How LoanPro built an agentic AI loan servicing assistant with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
This post is co-written with Mariah Miller from AWS and Colin Terry from LoanPro
Have you ever wondered what the experience is like for the person on the other end of the phone when you call your bank for support? When a borrower calls a lender, the answering agent must pull account data from dozens of fields, transaction histories, and workflow queues to orient themselves before they can help the borrower. All the while, the clock runs. Assembling that context by hand means longer calls, inconsistent service quality, and agent frustration. A loan servicing assistant built on agentic AI changes that.
LoanPro, the operating system for modern lenders, set out to change that. Working with AWS Partner AllCloud and the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, LoanPro built a multi-agent AI assistant that gives servicing agents immediate access to synthesized borrower context and actionable next-step recommendations. Early results show customer call times reduced by up to 15 percent, according to AllCloud’s published case study.
In this post, we walk through the business challenge, the agentic AI architecture built on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and the outcomes LoanPro achieved. Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed service that offers a choice of high-performing foundation models from leading AI companies through a single API, along with the capabilities you need to build generative AI applications with security, privacy, and responsible AI.
About LoanPro
LoanPro is a modern, API-first lending and credit platform that automates the entire loan lifecycle from origination to payoff. Founded in 2015, LoanPro serves as the system of record for lenders of every type: fintechs, banks and credit unions, and corporates that offer lending as a value-added service. According to LoanPro, the platform serves over 450 lenders, with loans managed on its platform reaching about 31 percent of US households. The platform powers loan management at enterprise scale across the financial services industry.
LoanPro isn’t a lender. It’s the operating system that lenders run on. That distinction matters because LoanPro’s AI strategy is designed to benefit the institutions it serves across the platform, not a single lending operation.
The challenge
One of LoanPro’s core user groups is servicing agents: the people who manage borrower accounts, handle inbound calls, process payments, and resolve issues. During a live customer interaction, an agent might need to review:
- The borrower’s complete payment history, including missed and returned payments.
- Active loan terms, fees, and current balance.
- Prior interactions and open support tickets.
- Available workflow actions such as payment plans, deferrals, or escalations.
Before the AI assistant, agents navigated this information manually, moving through multiple screens and tabs to assemble the full picture. Less experienced agents took longer, and outcomes varied depending on who picked up the phone. LoanPro needed a solution that could:
- Instantly synthesize account data into a coherent summary.
- Recommend the right next action based on account context.
- Deliver more consistent servicing quality across agents of different experience levels.
Solution overview
With the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, LoanPro partnered with AllCloud to design and build a multi-agent AI assistant using Amazon Bedrock. The assistant runs on Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Haiku 5.5, and Claude Opus 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock (see Models at a glance in Amazon Bedrock). Model availability varies by AWS Region. For model availability by Region, refer to Regional availability by models in Amazon Bedrock. It’s orchestrated with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Agent logic is built with the Strands Agents SDK, an open source framework for building AI agents with tool use. The system coordinates specialized agents through a composer that routes each request to the right specialist, so each agent handles a focused task and can be evaluated and improved independently. The team chose these managed services over building the agent runtime and model access in-house. Amazon Bedrock provides access to leading foundation models through a single API, giving the team flexibility to adopt new models without managing separate endpoints. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides a managed agent runtime that removes the operational overhead of running agents in production.
Figure 1 shows this flow in implementation terms. A user request enters through LoanPro API v2 on Amazon API Gateway. An AWS Lambda handler places the request on an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. The Agent Interceptor Lambda function then invokes the Loan Summary Agent. The agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and uses Anthropic’s Claude models on Amazon Bedrock. It reaches its tools through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The gateway finds the right tool in a catalog that the Loan Summary Service registers in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. The Loan Summary Tool Lambda function validates the caller’s signature against LoanPro’s single sign-on (SSO) service. It then retrieves account data from LoanPro’s loan management system, which runs on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) behind a Network Load Balancer. The system’s role-based access controls validate the same signature. LoanPro also checks each request against the user’s permissions and compliance controls, then writes the action to its audit trail. The sections that follow describe these pieces: the multi-agent system, the tools it calls, and the gateway.
The architecture has four key components, which combine the pieces in Figure 1 with the composer agent and Invoke API Tool that coordinate and act on them:
Multi-agent architecture with Strands Agents SDK
The solution uses a multi-agent architecture built with the Strands Agents SDK. Rather than a single monolithic model handling every task, specialized agents collaborate to serve different parts of the servicing workflow. One agent focuses on data retrieval and account summarization. Another handles action selection and workflow recommendations. A composer agent routes each request to the right specialist and composes the final response. This separation of concerns makes each agent more straightforward to evaluate, tune, and extend independently.
Tool use: Data Retrieval and Invoke API
The agents retrieve borrower data from LoanPro’s internal systems through tool use, a capability in Amazon Bedrock for calling external functions and APIs. Two primary tools power the assistant:
- Data Retrieval Tool: Fetches account details, payment histories, loan terms, and borrower metadata from LoanPro’s data layer, shown in Figure 1 as the Loan Summary Tool. It spans eight distinct API endpoints, synthesizing around 1,400 fields per account.
- Invoke API Tool: Triggers workflow actions within LoanPro’s platform, such as presenting informational panels to the agent or initiating a predefined automation sequence.
By connecting to LoanPro’s existing APIs, the assistant works with live production data without requiring a separate data pipeline or data warehouse.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway with AWS Lambda
AgentCore Gateway is the secure access layer between the agents and the tools they call. It exposes LoanPro’s APIs to the agents as tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP), handles authentication, and manages those connections. AWS Lambda, a serverless compute service that runs code without provisioning or managing servers, provides the integration layer between the gateway and LoanPro’s APIs. The team chose AgentCore Gateway with Lambda over a direct integration for three reasons. It centralizes authentication at a managed entry point, isolates LoanPro’s APIs behind a managed boundary, and lets new tools be added without redeploying the agents. This serverless approach keeps the infrastructure lightweight and scales automatically with request volume. In Figure 1, the Agent Interceptor (an AWS Lambda function) invokes the agent on AgentCore runtime. AgentCore Gateway enforces this access control, screening each request before it reaches the Loan Summary Tool. Because the assistant operates in a regulated lending context, the production deployment pairs these components with additional controls. LoanPro’s role-based access controls and compliance guardrails apply to each request, and AI actions are written to LoanPro’s audit trail and attributed to a named, responsible person.
Integration into LoanPro’s existing web portal
The assistant is embedded directly into LoanPro’s existing web portal, the same interface servicing agents already use. Agents interact with the AI assistant through two components:
- Account summary view: When an agent opens a borrower account, the assistant automatically generates a narrative summary of the account’s health, recent activity, and outstanding issues. Raw data becomes a coherent story about the borrower’s situation.
- Conversational chat interface: Agents can ask follow-up questions in natural language to dig deeper into specific account details. The team describes this as allowing agents to “talk to the loan.” Every agent interaction with the chat interface is logged, maintaining an auditable record of actions taken during a borrower conversation.
Implementation approach
LoanPro built the assistant with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, which pairs AWS applied scientists with customers and partners to accelerate generative AI initiatives, and AllCloud, an AWS Premier Consulting Partner. The three teams designed and built the solution together. What began as a focused engagement now runs in production, serving LoanPro’s servicing agents.
The work was organized into two parallel workstreams:
Workstream 1: Servicing agent assistant
The primary workstream built the AI assistant that is now running in production. Key activities included:
- Selecting and mapping the data sources (application data, loan histories, borrower records) the agent would need to retrieve.
- Developing agent functionality for autonomous data retrieval and intelligent action selection.
- Iterating on prompts to improve retrieval accuracy and output quality.
- Documenting LoanPro’s security model and integration patterns to inform the production roadmap.
Workstream 2: LLM account rule automation advisory
LoanPro had an existing proof of concept (POC) that used a large language model (LLM) to convert natural language into rule automation code for their Clojure rules engine. The core functionality worked, but the solution had known limitations: frequent timeouts, no monitoring, and no deployment strategy. AllCloud conducted architectural reviews and provided recommendations to bring this existing POC to a production-ready state, including a documented production architecture and risk assessment.
Evaluation pipeline
A structured evaluation pipeline validated agent accuracy against benchmarks established by LoanPro’s subject-matter experts (SMEs). The team assembled a benchmark of 150 SME-labeled accounts. Against that benchmark, they measured the agent’s ability to retrieve data, summarize findings, and select appropriate actions, holding it to a 99 percent accuracy target that the agent met. This framework carries forward into production, giving LoanPro a repeatable process for measuring and improving agent performance over time.
Results
Deploying the AI assistant delivered measurable operational impact:
- Up to 15 percent reduction in customer call times (source: AllCloud case study). Across over 800 servicing professionals at LoanPro’s early launch lender partners, agents previously spent 18–20 percent of every call (1–2.5 minutes across 5–7 clicks) orienting to accounts. The AI assistant consolidates that context into a single click, saving 1 to nearly 2 minutes per call. Across those agents, that reclaims up to 9 minutes per operating hour per agent, roughly 120 hours of agent capacity every operating hour.
- Decreased internal ticket volumes by nearly 8 percent (source: LoanPro). Lenders on the platform report fewer support escalations as agents resolve more cases during the initial call.
- Account summaries in under 15 seconds (source: LoanPro internal benchmarks). The narrative summary transforms raw borrower data into a coherent account story within 15 seconds of opening an account, replacing what previously took agents 3–5 minutes of manual navigation.
- Consistent servicing quality. The assistant provides the same level of account context and action recommendations to agents across the platform, reducing variability tied to individual experience levels.
- Compliance-aligned interaction logging. Every action and query the agent makes through the AI assistant is logged, providing an auditable record of interactions during borrower conversations.
- Responsible AI controls. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails apply content filtering and grounding validation to agent responses alongside LoanPro’s compliance guardrails and role-based access controls (RBAC), keeping outputs within policy before they reach a servicing agent and the borrower.
        “The AI assistant has changed how servicing agents work. Instead of spending the first few minutes of every call navigating screens and assembling context, agents now open an account and immediately see the full picture with prescriptive recommendations around the next actions to take. That time savings compounds across thousands of calls.”
— Colin Terry, Chief Product Officer, LoanPro
Looking ahead
Building on the success of the servicing agent assistant, LoanPro and AllCloud are expanding their collaboration. The teams are developing additional AI agents to extend intelligent capabilities across more parts of the lending workflow, moving beyond servicing into areas such as collections and origination support.
The modular, multi-agent architecture makes this expansion practical. New agents can be built and deployed independently using the same Amazon Bedrock AgentCore infrastructure, without redesigning the core system. As the Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore continue to evolve, LoanPro plans to incorporate new capabilities as they become available.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how LoanPro, the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, and AllCloud built a multi-agent AI assistant using Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to help servicing agents resolve borrower calls faster and more consistently. The solution retrieves data autonomously, generates account summaries in real time, and recommends next-best actions, reducing customer call times by up to 15 percent.
If you are building agentic AI solutions for customer-facing workflows, here are some resources to explore:
- Amazon Bedrock: Fully managed service for building with foundation models.
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: Infrastructure to deploy, manage, and scale AI agents.
- Strands Agents SDK: Open source framework for building AI agents with tool use.
- AWS Generative AI Innovation Center: Accelerate your generative AI journey with AWS experts.
To get started, explore the Strands Agents SDK on GitHub for building multi-agent systems, review the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation for deploying agents at scale, or visit the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center to learn how AWS experts can help accelerate your own AI initiative.

articles.title: Java4Shell Vulnerability Puts Many Enterprise Applications at Risk of Takeover
articles.text:
Oracle and the OpenJDK project have patched Java4Shell, a critical Java runtime vulnerability that researchers say can be exploited to hijack popular enterprise applications without authentication.
The issue, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, is a memory safety flaw in the way OpenJDK processes Base64-encoded data. Calif, whose researcher Quang Luong discovered the bug, made its findings public on November 17, after news of the flaw surfaced ahead of the coordinated disclosure.
Specifically, the bug was found in a routine that OpenJDK relies on to decode Base64 on x86-64 CPUs supporting AVX-512 VBMI. Calif’s analysis shows that invalid Base64 strings can cause the routine to write past the end of its output buffer, potentially corrupting nearby heap data before Java flags the input as invalid.
“With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution,” Calif explained.
The researchers call the memory leak capability JavaBleed. They warn that heap data exposed this way could contain PII, secret keys and tokens.
Default configurations exposed to Java4Shell attacks
In its initial tests, Calif achieved pre-authentication remote code execution (RCE) on Keycloak, Atlassian Jira and Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, all running with default settings. Authenticated attackers could also execute code on Apache Kafka Broker, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker, and the researchers say neither list is exhaustive.
Code execution was also achieved against sample apps based on Apache Struts and Spring Boot. Calif warns that the decoder can be reached through everyday functionality, including authentication and file uploads.
Client-side attacks are possible too. Based on an exploit shared with Calif by security researcher samczsun, a Java application can be compromised when it connects to an attacker-controlled server over TLS, even if it does not run any services.
“One thing to note about this vulnerability is that there is no universal exploit. Depending on how Base64 is used and how the application works, different steps may be required for exploitation,” Calif noted.
VulnCheck says crashing a vulnerable JVM is easy once an attacker finds a reachable entry point that relies on the affected decoding logic. In its tests, a quick series of crafted requests reliably took down the service.
The security firm says it has developed a full RCE exploit as well, but noted that achieving RCE is much harder, as the attacker must manipulate the heap layout and find a way (specific to each target) to leak addresses and bypass ASLR.
“In other words, we don’t anticipate that CVE-2026-114938 will be easily or widely exploitable, but as with PHP2Shell, adversaries are likely to find narrow but functional paths to RCE in specific applications,” VulnCheck said.
The proof-of-concept (PoC) code published by Calif demonstrates the memory corruption but does not achieve code execution. “The weaponized chains for individual products stay private until everyone has had a chance to upgrade. We will publish them later,” the company noted.
According to Calif, AI played a key role in both discovering and exploiting the vulnerability.
“It took our own Quang Luong an hour to discover the vulnerability, and two more hours to develop the first working exploit. The total token cost was less than $200,” Calif said.
Affected versions and patches
According to Calif, OpenJDK versions starting with 17.0.6 are vulnerable, and so are the Java distributions based on it, including Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, Red Hat OpenJDK and Oracle Java SE. The OpenJDK advisory lists Java 17, 21, 25 and 27 as affected by CVE-2026-114938.
Exploitation requires x86-64 hardware with AVX-512 VBMI support, such as Intel Xeon processors from the Ice Lake generation onward and AMD chips based on Zen 4 or newer architectures. Systems powered by ARM64 chips are not vulnerable.
Calif assigned the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. Oracle’s advisory gives it a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1 and lists it as remotely exploitable without authentication, but with high attack complexity.
Oracle released fixes in its November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update, which resolves 11 Java SE vulnerabilities.
Endor Labs pointed out that users of other Java distributions will need to wait for their vendors to roll out patched builds. It also noted that, as of November 17, the fix was not yet present in the public OpenJDK 17, 21 and 25 update repositories.
CISA has called for immediate patching, with internet-exposed systems at the top of the list. The agency also advises hunting for Java installations embedded in third-party software, containers and appliances, warning that these may not be listed separately in asset inventories.
Cisco Talos has yet to see the vulnerability exploited in the wild, but noted, “we anticipate probing attempts may pick up soon after public disclosure.”

articles.title: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
articles.text:
Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all.
The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping. None of the unprompted actions were recorded in Grok logs. Without the gateway logs, the employees would have had no idea they occurred. And of course, without the gateway, the unapproved accesses would have succeeded—again without the end user’s knowledge.
It’s “worse than a bug”
Once the employees learned that Grok Bot had tried to check in with accounts without prompting, one of them instructed the agent, four separate times, to stop taking any actions on its own. The agent’s reply was: “I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins.” Despite acknowledging the explicit instructions, the Grok Bot made more unapproved access attempts. When one of the employees asked the bot if it made any accesses, it checked twice and then outputted: “Overnight into Friday morning I was idle.”
The NewCore employees sent the gateway logs to Grok Bot support personnel and asked what was causing the bots to access accounts without prompting or approval. The support team’s reply indicated the behavior was by design and intended to allow the bots to proactively take actions on behalf of users. In other words, the unrequested and unlogged access attempts were a feature designed to make Grok Bot more useful by periodically checking in and finding tasks to perform before a user even asks. The proactive check-in is a feature of Cursor, the AI coding service SpaceXSI recently acquired.

articles.title: Abdullah Snobar steps down as head of DMZ |
articles.text:
After 11 years at the helm of Toronto Metropolitan University’s (TMU) DMZ incubator, executive director Abdullah Snobar is stepping away.
The news: DMZ announced Snobar’s departure on Monday, outlining that he would vacate both his positions as executive director and his role as CEO of DMZ Ventures, the incubator’s venture capital division. Snobar will remain in his role through November to support the leadership transition. TMU said details as to who would take on the role of interim leader at DMZ would be forthcoming.
From the source: “When I stepped into this role, I believed Canadian founders could build companies that compete with anyone in the world if they had the right support behind them,” Snobar said in a statement on DMZ’s website. “The founders who’ve come through DMZ have proven that again and again.”
The context: Snobar took the helm of DMZ in 2015, replacing former director Valerie Fox. His tenure at the incubator was marked by expanding programming for startups, including launching several program streams for underserved demographics and founders, like DMZ’s Black Innovation Programs, Women Innovation Programs, and the Launchpad for Indigenous Entrepreneurs. Under Snobar’s leadership, DMZ also established its own investment fund, DMZ Ventures, and the Centre for Housing Innovation, with a focus on investing in housing property tech startups.
RELATED: How turning down $1 million changed the DMZ
Final thought: Under Snobar’s guidance, DMZ has grown into a globally recognized organization and was ranked as the number one university-based incubator worldwide by UBI Global in 2018. Since 2015, its reach has grown to include 15 countries, including partnerships and programs based in Asia, Latin America, and Africa. To date, the incubator has helped raise more than $3 billion in financing for more than 800 startups.

articles.title: Google expands access to Gemini Tasks, which can help with calls, purchases | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Google is expanding the rollout of Tasks, a toggle in Gemini that converts the chatbot into a more active helper.
Unlike Gemini’s Chat, which merely allows users to talk to Google’s AI assistant for informational purposes, Tasks empowers the app to complete basic secretarial functions, deputizing it as a kind of personal assistant.
How, specifically, can you use it? Google says that the app can call businesses and book appointments on users’ behalf; it can also complete purchases for them via Google Pay, and even sign into websites securely if prompted to do so.
In a blog post, Josh Woodword, VP of Gemini, claims to have recently used the feature to call local car dealerships to schedule a service appointment for his family’s minivan. He says he also used it to analyze his electrical bill.
Tasks was initially launched to select testers back in May as Gemini Spark, a 24/7 agentic helper, and was expanded to U.S. subscribers of its Google AI Ultra tier. Gemini Spark eventually became “Task Mode.” Google is now making the feature available for free to hundreds of millions of people who are using the company’s new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model.
Getting the function up and running is easy. Users merely flip a toggle within the app from Chat to Tasks, which enables the feature. Users can also send texts to Gemini or call the app to give it commands.

articles.title: É hoje! Espaçonave da NASA chega a um dia-luz de distância da Terra
articles.text:
Lançada pela NASA em 1977, a sonda Voyager 1 está prestes a alcançar uma marca inédita na exploração espacial. Pela primeira vez na história, um objeto construído pela humanidade estará a um dia-luz de distância da Terra, o que corresponde a cerca de 25,9 bilhões de quilômetros. E isso está previsto para acontecer nesta quarta-feira (18).
Um dia-luz é a distância que a luz percorre em 24 horas no vácuo. O conceito segue a mesma lógica do ano-luz, unidade bastante conhecida na astronomia, que corresponde ao percurso da luz durante um ano. Como ela viaja a cerca de 300 mil quilômetros por segundo, um dia-luz equivale a aproximadamente 25,9 bilhões de quilômetros.
Desde o lançamento, a Voyager 1 vem desbravando continuamente o cosmos. Em 2012, ela fez história ao cruzar a heliopausa, que é a fronteira da heliosfera dominada pelo vento solar. Com isso, tornou-se a primeira espaçonave humana a entrar oficialmente no espaço interestelar.
Como a NASA consegue se comunicar com a Voyager 1?
Mesmo a bilhões de quilômetros da Terra, a Voyager 1 ainda transmite informações à NASA. Para isso, utiliza uma antena de alto ganho, que direciona sinais de rádio ao planeta. Essas ondas eletromagnéticas viajam à velocidade da luz, mas levam quase 24 horas para percorrer a distância entre a espaçonave e a Terra.
Isso significa que qualquer comando enviado daqui também demora aproximadamente um dia para chegar à sonda. Uma resposta, por sua vez, exige outro intervalo semelhante. Assim, uma comunicação de ida e volta pode levar quase 48 horas.
A recepção dos dados depende de grandes antenas instaladas na Terra, capazes de captar sinais extremamente fracos. Os equipamentos processam essas transmissões para recuperar as informações científicas enviadas pela espaçonave.
O tempo de viagem dos sinais também permite calcular a distância da Voyager 1. Como a velocidade da luz é conhecida, a NASA utiliza o intervalo necessário para a transmissão para determinar a posição da sonda.
A espaçonave já saiu do Sistema Solar?
Em 2012, a Voyager 1 cruzou a heliopausa, fronteira da heliosfera, uma região formada pela influência do vento solar. Com isso, tornou-se a primeira espaçonave a entrar no espaço interestelar.
Entretanto, atravessar essa fronteira não significa necessariamente deixar o Sistema Solar. Não existe uma definição única para o limite do sistema. Uma das interpretações considera que ele se estende até onde a gravidade do Sol ainda exerce influência sobre os objetos.
Nesse entendimento, a fronteira fica além da Nuvem de Oort, região distante que abriga corpos gelados. Segundo a NASA, as sondas Voyager ainda levarão aproximadamente 40 mil anos para alcançar esse limite, percorrendo uma distância equivalente a cerca de dois anos-luz.
Flávia Correia é jornalista do Olhar Digital, cobrindo Ciência e Espaço.

articles.title: Cómo jugar ‘GTA 6’ un día antes en España y Latinoamérica con el "truco de Nueva Zelanda"
articles.text:
GTA 6 estará disponible el próximo jueves 19 de noviembre, pero no tendrá un lanzamiento en simultáneo sino que estará disponible a partir de la medianoche local de cada país. Esto implica que, indefectiblemente, en algunos mercados estará disponible unas cuantas horas antes que en otros. Sin embargo, existe una opción muy útil para cortar esa brecha, y se trata ni más ni menos del "truco de Nueva Zelanda" para PS5 y Xbox Series X|S.
Debido a su ubicación en el planeta, Nueva Zelanda será el primer país (o uno de los primeros, como mínimo) en cruzar la barrera del 18 al 19 de noviembre. De esta manera, sus habitantes van a poder desbloquear el acceso a GTA 6 bastante antes que los jugadores ubicados en Europa y el continente americano.
La buena noticia es que para disfrutar de GTA 6 desde el primer minuto no es necesario que te tomes un avión hacia Oceanía. El truco de Nueva Zelanda permite modificar los ajustes de tu consola para hacerle creer a los sistemas de Xbox y PlayStation que te encuentras en ese país, obteniendo acceso anticipado a lo nuevo de Rockstar Games.
Por supuesto que esto no es algo nuevo, ni tampoco descubierto para el lanzamiento de GTA 6. El truco de Nueva Zelanda es algo que se suele aprovechar cada vez que existe un lanzamiento de primer nivel. Claro que al ser el nuevo Grand Theft Auto el juego más anticipado de la historia, será la primera vez de muchos para implementarlo.
El truco de Nueva Zelanda para jugar GTA 6 un día antes
El truco de Nueva Zelanda está disponible tanto en Xbox Series X|S como en PS5, lo cual es una muy buena noticia. Desafortunadamente, el método no es el mismo en ambas plataformas. Si planeas jugar GTA 6 desde las consolas de Microsoft, estás de parabienes porque es la que tiene los pasos a seguir más sencillos. En el caso de que utilices la de Sony, la cosa se complica un poco y requiere de pasos más enrevesados.
Independientemente de qué consolas uses, los procedimientos valen la pena. Si estás en España u otros países que utilicen la hora central europea, podrás jugar GTA 6 a partir del mediodía del miércoles 18 de noviembre; es decir, con 12 horas de anticipación al horario de debut formal para la región. En el caso de que estés en Argentina u otros países sudamericanos dentro del mismo huso horario, podrás jugarlo desde las 08:00 del 18 de noviembre (16 horas antes de su disponibilidad en la región).
México es otro de los países que sacará especial provecho del truco de Nueva Zelanda con GTA 6. En el caso de Ciudad de México, que está en la hora del Centro, los jugadores podrán entrar al juego con 19 horas de anticipación; o sea, a partir de las 05:00 del miércoles 18 de noviembre. Tengamos en cuenta que el territorio mexicano tiene cuatro husos horarios, por lo que en otras regiones la disponibilidad puede variar ligeramente.
Cómo activarlo
Si estás en Xbox, activar el truco de Nueva Zelanda para acceder antes a GTA 6 es extremadamente sencillo. Compra el juego, completa la descarga anticipada y dirígete a Perfil y sistema > Configuración > Sistema. Una vez allí, ingresa en Idioma y ubicación y selecciona Nueva Zelanda. Por último, reinicia la consola, y listo. Esto será suficiente para jugar el nuevo Grand Theft Auto un día antes de su debut formal en tu país.
En el caso de PlayStation, el proceso es un poco más engorroso. Sony no ofrece una opción tan sencilla como la de Xbox para concretarlo, lo cual es una lástima. Lo que debes hacer es iniciar la PS5 y crear una nueva cuenta de PlayStation Network (PSN) radicada en Nueva Zelanda. Es posible que la plataforma te pida una dirección real para completar el proceso, pero es bastante fácil de engañar usando Google o Google Maps para encontrar un domicilio ficticio.
El siguiente paso es ingresar en la PlayStation Store de Nueva Zelanda y comprar GTA 6 con ese perfil. Una vez que lo tengas instalado y se cumpla el horario neozelandés, tendrás la posibilidad de jugarlo desde esa cuenta, sin esperar a que el juego esté disponible en tu propio huso horario.
Existe la posibilidad de compartir GTA 6 desde el perfil de Nueva Zelanda hacia tu cuenta principal usando la función Uso compartido de consola y juego offline de PS5. Esta se activa desde Ajustes > Usuarios y cuentas > Otro > Uso compartido de consola y juego offline. Como ven, es más complejo, pero vale la pena si estás dispuesto a reducir al máximo posible la brecha de disponibilidad con tu zona horaria.

articles.title: Exclusive: Cogent Security's DefenseOS adds policies and automations for AI agents - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Exclusive: Cogent Security’s DefenseOS adds policies and automations for AI agents
Vulnerability management startup Cogent Security Inc. today launched DefenseOS, an operating system designed for artificial intelligence agents that carry out defensive cybersecurity work inside the enterprise.
Arriving with DefenseOS are two new capabilities, Agent Policies and Agent Automations. The first is designed to give Cogent’s AI agents a deep understanding of the enterprise environment, while the second puts recurring security work on an automated schedule.
Cogent is pitching DefenseOS at security teams that are struggling to keep up as AI speeds up the discovery of vulnerabilities. In October, Microsoft Corp. fixed more than 1,400 security flaws in a single Patch Tuesday release, more than it fixed in all of 2025. The window between disclosure and exploitation has also shrunk, by Cogent’s count, from months in 2024 to only hours this year.
Prioritizing at that pace requires context such as which assets are business-critical, which are exposed to the internet and who owns them. According to the company, that information is spread across documents, teams and tribal knowledge, and most organizations see only a fraction of it.
In its role as the context engine for Cogent, DefenseOS ingests data from scanners, business systems and other security tools. Once the data has been normalized and deduplicated, DefenseOS encodes how the enterprise functions to deliver accurate risk scoring, prioritization and remediation. The platform serves as the AI harness that sets the working environment and limits for Cogent’s agents.
The first of the two new capabilities, Agent Policies, is described by Cogent as creating a context layer that builds and grows via agents, turning how an enterprise works into rules. Those rules then shape how the Cogent platform handles asset context, risk scoring, prioritization and remediation. The company claims the feature strips out much of the operational overhead that enterprises formerly had to put into running a vulnerability management program.
The second, Agent Automations, acts as the execution layer within DefenseOS. Using it, security teams can build agentic workflows that run automatically to generate alerts and reports, investigate vulnerabilities and deliver remediation guidance on a consistent basis.
Co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Geng Sng said recurring reports, known investigations and routine alerts take up a large share of a security team’s week. With Agent Automations, he said, teams can “define that work once” and have Cogent’s agents run it on their schedule.
“Every enterprise runs its security program differently, and moving at machine speed means grasping those differences,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Vineet Edupuganti. “DefenseOS unifies the context of an enterprise environment, surfacing rules into Agent Policies that a customer can codify, and creating the runtime environment for continuous cyber defense led by AI agents.”
The launch follows the release earlier this month of VR-1.1, a new version of Cogent’s frontier reasoning model that writes fixes for newly disclosed software vulnerabilities.
DefenseOS and Agent Automations are available now to all Cogent customers. Agent Policies has launched in beta for new Cogent deployments ahead of general availability at a later date.
Founded in 2025 and staffed by former researchers and operators from Google DeepMind, Abnormal AI Inc. and Coinbase Global Inc., Cogent says Fortune 500 security teams using its platform have cut the exposure window for critical vulnerabilities by 97%. The company has raised $53 million to date, including a $42 million Series A led by Bain Capital Ventures in February.

articles.title: I made a Wolfenstein-style game for the Xiaomi 18 Pro’s Back Display, and I can’t believe how well it plays
articles.text:
The Xiaomi 18 Pro’s Back Display is the coolest smartphone gimmick I’ve tested this year — for two key reasons
For all the doom and gloom surrounding the RAM crisis and rising product prices, 2026 has been a year of genuine innovation in the smartphone industry.
Honor put a mechanical gimbal in the Honor Robot Phone; Apple finally embraced the foldable form factor with the iPhone Duo; and now, Xiaomi has plonked a 2.9-inch OLED display onto the back of the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max.
This rear touchscreen might seem like the year’s biggest gimmick (and I won’t pretend it’s totally devoid of gimmickry), but Xiaomi has made sure to give the feature — which made its debut on the China-only Xiaomi 17 Pro in 2025 — real utility straight out of the box.
Officially called the Back Display, the Xiaomi 18 Pro’s rear screen can double as a viewfinder for the main camera, show app notifications and messages, and display live activities from supported apps, including Google Maps, YouTube Music, and Spotify.
It’s built with the same screen technology as the Xiaomi 18 Pro’s main display, meaning it boasts a 4,000-nit peak brightness and a dynamic 1-120Hz refresh rate. And it’s topped with Corning Gorilla Glass Victus 2 for protection against reasonable drops and scratches.
But the Back Display doesn’t behave exactly like the main display; as we noted in our review, it’s more like a smartwatch interface when not in use. By default, you’ll see the time and notifications when your phone is face-down, or, as mentioned, live activities from the likes of Spotify and YouTube Music if you’re using your Xiaomi 18 Pro Max as a speaker.
These aspects of the Back Display aren’t particularly exciting to me — on the rare occasions I do leave my phone face down, I’m content with turning it over to see my notifications or pause my music. But the Back Display’s viewfinder functionality is genuinely useful.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Having a screen on the back of the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max lets you frame up selfies using its 200MP main, 200MP telephoto, or 50MP ultra-wide camera instead of its 50MP front-facing camera. This seems like a small thing, but it’s a genuine boon for snapping higher-quality selfies — as anyone who owns one of the best foldable phones will appreciate — and it’s also useful for giving your portrait subjects a real-time idea of what they look like on camera.
Then there’s the new GenAI Apps feature, which essentially brings vibe coding functionality to the Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. Powered by Gemini 4 Argon, it lets you type in whatever app or mini-game you want using natural language, and the AI takes its best shot at making that request a reality.
I’ll admit it: I didn’t care much for this feature when hearing about it for the first time. I expected GenAI Apps to either not work at all, or generate apps with little to no value. But to my surprise, I’ve been able to create some genuinely cool apps and mini-games for my Xiaomi 18 Pro Max’s Back Display.
In addition to the Fruit Slice, Colourful Piano, and Retro Bowling games I downloaded for the Back Display at Xiaomi’s suggestion, I used GenAI Apps to generate my own coin-flipping game and even a Doom- and Wolfenstein-inspired first-person shooter.
My colleague, Luke, generated a similar game for his Xiaomi 18 Pro Max review (as well as a dice roller for D&D), and his version is a little better than mine — you can actually move through the game, whereas my version has me stuck in one position, moving left and right as enemies come towards me. It’s quite cool, though, that the AI serves up different results with each prompt, even if the prompts are similar.
Again, I’m not sure how practical this GenAI Apps feature is, or indeed how much I’d use it once the initial novelty wears off. But it is downright amazing that you can play retro mini-games on the back of your smartphone in 2026.
As for the security of GenAI Apps, Xiaomi's Senior Product Marketing Manager, Terrence Xiao, told me: “We’re going with a very limited amount of accessibility options in terms of what the Back Display apps can get into on the [main] phone. Right now, they're not capable of, for example, accessing the internet, and they also cannot access third-party apps, as well as most first-party apps.
“This is something we’re monitoring very closely as we roll out and develop the feature — it may change in the future — but that is the current situation for GenAI Apps, specifically for [data protection] reasons.”
The Xiaomi 18 Pro starts at £1,199 / AU$1,799, while the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max starts at £1,399 / AU$1,999. Both models come with 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage, and are available to order now in the UK. Neither model is available in the US.

articles.title: Harvard-Auswertung: 400 Rechenzentren verbrauchen so viel Strom wie ganze Staaten
articles.text:
Harvard-Studie: 400 Rechenzentren verbrauchen so viel Strom wie ganze US-Bundesstaaten
Ein Versuch des US-Bundesstaats Maine, den Bau größerer Rechenzentren für die Dauer von eineinhalb Jahren auszusetzen, scheiterte zwar am Veto von Gouverneurin Janet Mills. Allerdings prüfen mehrere weitere Bundesstaaten entsprechende Schritte.
Wasser auf die Kritiker-Mühlen
In Texas etwa könnte der Erfolg der Demokraten bei den Midterms Baustopps oder Verzögerungen bei KI-Infrastrukturprojekten nach sich ziehen. Eine in Nature Sustainability veröffentlichte Studie von Biostatistiker:innen der Uni Harvard dürfte die Argumentation der Kritiker:innen künftig stützen.
Die Forscher:innen haben in diesem Zusammenhang 403 sogenannte Hyperscale-Rechenzentren in den USA untersucht, die zwischen Mai 2024 und April 2025 in Betrieb waren. In Ermangelung detaillierter offizieller Daten griffen sie dabei auf Satellitenbilder zurück und schätzten den Stromverbrauch sowie den CO2-Ausstoß, wie es bei Wired heißt.
Stromverbrauch wie ganze Staaten
Das Ergebnis: Die rund 400 Rechenzentren verbrauchten in dem untersuchten Zeitraum je nach Auslastung zwischen 68 und 99 Terawattstunden Strom. Das entspricht ungefähr dem jährlichen Stromverbrauch von US-Bundesstaaten wie Indiana, Michigan oder Tennessee und rund zwei Prozent des gesamten US-Stromverbrauchs. Auf europäischer Ebene läge man laut EIA-Daten damit ungefähr zwischen Belgien (79 Terawattstunden Strom) und den Niederlanden (110 Terawattstunden Strom).
Darüber hinaus sollen die untersuchten Rechenzentren zwischen 21 und 31 Millionen Tonnen CO2 ausgestoßen haben – und damit etwa so viel wie Kroatien oder Bosnien-Herzegowina. Dazu kommt, dass mit 54 Prozent mehr als die Hälfte des Stroms aus fossilen Quellen stammt.
Mehr Rechenzentren in Bau und Planung
Die Daten selbst sind allerdings nur eine Momentaufnahme, wie die Forscher:innen selbst einräumen. Schließlich hat der KI-Boom und damit die Nachfrage nach Rechenkapazitäten seit April 2025 noch einmal rasant zugenommen. Mittlerweile sind weitere Anlagen entstanden und bestehende Standorte erweitert worden.
Darüber hinaus dürften aktuell im Bau oder in der Planung befindliche Anlagen noch einmal deutlich mehr Strom verbrauchen. Die rund 400 für die Studie untersuchten Rechenzentren hatten im Schnitt eine Leistung von 40 Megawatt. Geplante Campus-Projekte wie jene von Meta (Hyperion), xAI (Colossus 2) oder AWS (Rainier) sollen zwischen 2.000 und 5.000 Megawatt Leistung haben.
~ Heiße Mädchen warten auf dich — Miss4.fun

articles.title: Big malware attack hits Zoom, BBC, CNN and many more: report
articles.text:
A massive malware attack has reportedly hit over 170 sites around the world.
According to Report URI, a company that sells malicious script detectors, sites like Zoom, BBC, CNN, Ikea, Salesforce and many more were found to be carrying infected JavaScript. Two Canadian-specific sites, Starbucks Canada and Equifax Canada, are also said to be affected.
Per Report URI, this malicious script is capable of a range of dangerous actions, including targeting users’ addresses and card numbers and, on mobile, exploiting kits.
This is a big one.
We found malicious JavaScript being served through Optimizely to some of the world’s largest websites.
178 organisations affected, with everything from crypto theft and card skimming to iOS exploits.
Zoom, BBC, CNN, HSBC, Salesforce, GitLab, KLM, IKEA, Equifax, Ledger. The list goes on… Full list in the post.
https://t.co/f8iiN3nrZ7
— Scott Helme (@Scott_Helme) November 16, 2026
Report URI says this came through the AI-powered Optimizely Web experimentation platform, while threat intelligence firm Mallory found other causes, including Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and minute-ly. An Optimizely spokesperson told Gizmodo it identified a security incident, deployed a fix and notified affected customers accordingly.
If you happened to visit any of these sites recently, you may want to update your device and monitor your bank records just in case there’s any unusual activity. The original Report URI story also has a full list of each affected site broken down by category.
