articles.title: Sudanese fintech startup Cashi raises $660k from Proparco - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Sudanese fintech startup Cashi has raised US$660,000 in funding from Proparco, marking the French development finance institution’s first investment in Sudan.
Founded in 2022 by the team behind alsoug.com, which became Sudan’s leading online marketplace, Cashi is building a digital payments ecosystem for underserved markets, working around the limits of the country’s traditional payment infrastructure.
Users can deposit and withdraw cash, pay bills and transfer money through a network of local merchants, so they rely less on banks. Its MyCashi digital wallet has 2.2 million registered users, and it is especially popular with young people.
Network disruptions are common in Sudan, so Cashi has also built USSD, SMS, offline card and other non-app products. These keep transactions going and help aid organisations get humanitarian assistance to people in areas where connectivity is poor.
The funding from Proparco will support Cashi’s work in fragile markets, mainly its mission to provide reliable financial services in Sudan. The country is in a severe humanitarian and economic crisis, with limited access to banking, ongoing cash shortages and frequent outages of telecoms and payment systems.
“In Sudan today, being able to send, receive or withdraw money can decide how a family gets through the month, or whether a small shop stays open. When the banks were unavailable during the war, Cashi stayed open and available. We built it to keep working when cash runs short and the network drops,” said Nina Saeed, CEO of Cashi.
“Today, millions of consumers and merchants use Cashi. Millions more across Sudan still have no bank account and no ATM nearby. Where you live should not decide whether you can get paid, pay a bill or send money home. They are the people we are building for.”
The deal is part of Proparco’s wider push to back African businesses meeting critical development needs, especially in fragile and conflict-affected countries.
“In fragile contexts such as Sudan, access to reliable financial services is not only a driver of economic development, but also an essential means of supporting livelihoods and strengthening resilience,” said Guillaume Barberousse, global head of investment at Proparco.
“This first operation in Sudan reflects our commitment to supporting entrepreneurship and financial inclusion, including in the most challenging environments.”

articles.title: Responsible AI for agentic AI: A phased roadmap for platform and application teams | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Responsible AI for agentic AI: A phased roadmap for platform and application teams
Companies build agentic AI platforms to govern the applications, tools, skills, models, and storage that agents use. The nondeterministic nature of generative AI models introduces a complexity that previous software development practices didn’t anticipate. Consider a real estate app that generates property listings from retrieved data: does it accurately reflect the property, or hallucinate features that don’t exist? Or a customer service agent grounded on internal knowledge bases: can you verify that it doesn’t surface confidential information?
Until recently, responsible AI (RAI) was model-centric, scoped to the machine learning development lifecycle: training, testing, and inference. Models didn’t reason, use tools, or take actions. When the conversation extended to model-powered systems, it covered statistically bounded situations you could test against known inputs. Generative AI powered applications and agents changed this. The systems now reason, act, compose tools dynamically, and interact over multiple steps, expanding both the scope and the depth of what responsible AI must cover.
Organizations are turning Responsible AI, which includes the pillars of security and privacy, veracity and robustness, fairness, safety, controllability, explainability, transparency, and governance into a growth strategy by addressing its expanding scope early. When enterprises adopt agentic AI at scale, the positive and negative impacts come hand in hand. As Wade and Wirtz observe in the Harvard Business Review, trust is becoming a competitive differentiator. The same capabilities that personalize at scale can also surveil and discriminate, and organizations that govern them earn stakeholder confidence. Robinhood, for example, built a generative AI financial crimes agent on Amazon Bedrock with strict data governance. They achieved a 20% efficiency gain while maintaining regulatory compliance. Structuring these practices across platform maturity is the next step. In this post, we refer to the team that manages the platform as the Platform team, and to the teams that build on it as Application teams. Application teams, sometimes called Workstream teams, build and own agents on the platform.
This post provides a condensed, actionable roadmap for the Platform team and Application teams building on agentic AI. It’s designed to be read together: the Platform team sets up the guardrails. Application teams build within them. Both need a shared language for where they are and what good looks like. We provide a Responsible AI Assessment Skill, that maps the AWS Responsible AI Lens pillars to a three-phase maturity model: governance foundations, pilot deployment, and evaluation and hardening. For each phase, it shows which responsible AI pillars are critical and when to revisit them. An accompanying scorecard lets both application teams and the platform team assess where they are today and iterate as their applications mature.
Note: This post covers the key questions to ask at each phase. It leaves out step-by-step implementation details. This post also doesn’t provide legal or compliance advice. Always consult your legal team.
The challenge
In conversations with customers building agentic AI platforms, four challenges surface consistently.
- Unpredictable runtime behavior: nondeterministic outputs, goal drift, and cascading failures where one agent error propagates across services. A financial services company in Germany found that multi-agent orchestration amplified a single misclassification into policy violations across three downstream services.
- Data exposure and authority boundaries: Scope every agent to its intended tenants, data, systems, and actions. Isolate session context so each session starts with data residency at the access layer, and grant privileged access through least-privilege, task-bound permissions that agents can’t modify themselves. Agents then act only in the systems and with the authority they were explicitly given.
- Regulatory velocity: EU AI Act, ISO 42001, NIST AI RMF, and upcoming legislation are creating compliance requirements faster than governance can adapt. Proving compliance for nondeterministic systems requires continuous evaluation, which should be monitored and revisited with a predefined cadence (for example, daily, weekly, or monthly).
- Team collaboration: organizations lack a shared framework defining who owns what across the agent lifecycle. A media company in the UK flagged that segregation of duty between developer and deployment teams is undefined for agent workloads. The Platform team builds guardrails that application teams work around, and application teams defer responsibility they assume the platform handles.
Solution: A three-phase responsible AI maturity framework
In this post, we define an agentic AI platform as described in AgentOps: Operationalize agentic AI at scale with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a system for building, deploying, and operating AI agents securely at scale, covering governance, build and operations, evaluation, and observability. Your responsible AI posture should mature progressively alongside this platform. We break the journey into three phases and present prioritized responsible AI pillars across a customizable 12-week implementation timeline, allowing the platform team to establish a solid responsible AI foundation while their first use cases take shape.
Phase 1: Governance foundation
Focus pillars: Governance, security and privacy
In this phase, assess project fit, risks, and ethics, secure legal and compliance approvals, and define the trust model for AI agents. The application teams classify risks for each planned use case using a risk rubric. The Platform team focuses on establishing the core landing zone infrastructure, for example, setting up the overarching monitoring and access control, and governing newly onboarded agents and use cases from the start.
Critical tasks to consider in this phase include:
Security and privacy
- Evaluate access to data and systems needed by each agent and assess potential impact. This lays the foundation for the knowledge grounding strategy.
- Implement foundational data security and data exfiltration protection with data classification, data access control, logging, data integrity, and data access monitoring.
- Build a map of the data that is shared between agents like organizational knowledge bases and the subjective data like context graphs which individual agents might need. Then establish access boundaries and assign read/write permissions accordingly.
Governance
- Define a risk classification rubric aligned to your regulatory obligations (EU AI Act risk tiers, financial services industry requirements, and so on). Assign Low / Medium / High / Unacceptable risk levels to each planned use case and document the control requirements each risk level triggers. Gather relevant documentation and traceability requirements.
- Before onboarding agents, the underlying models need to go through a vetting procedure. The procedure covers a series of evaluations with safety and reliability criteria. Catalog approved models based on capability, latency, and cost.
- Implement a process to centrally register and govern products like agents, shared tools and skills deployed in your organization for centralized visibility and consumption. Every product gets registered with owner, risk tier, and regulatory scope. If a resource (agent, tool, skill) isn’t in the registry, it can’t be discovered and managed by the organization.
Phase 2: Pilot deployment
Focus pillars: Safety, veracity and robustness, controllability, security and privacy
Deploy your first agent that serves measurable business value. With the template and developer guidance provided from the Platform team, application teams implement orchestration patterns, memory, guardrail baselines, knowledge grounding, and tool use patterns. Risks identified in the foundation phase must now be addressed through a set of concrete controls in a pilot implementation.
In this phase, application teams consider the following concerns:
Safety
- Guardrails. Platform team establishes foundational personally identifiable information (PII) redaction filters for model I/O and tool calls. Provide a set of guardrails rules ready to be applied. Application teams then set content moderation thresholds explicitly based on the use case the agent serves. Configure human escalation for low-confidence responses.
- Policies. Define which agent can access what tool and how. Augment with fallback scenarios in case of policy violations.
Veracity and robustness
- Knowledge grounding with checks: Even with the right context, models can still hallucinate or misrepresent the provided sources. Therefore, configure contextual grounding checks to verify every response is correctly grounded in relevant data. For regulated use cases, activate automated reasoning for verifiable outputs. Implement a process to curate and update your knowledge sources. Define how out-of-domain requests are classified and handled.
Controllability
- Implement a process for Human-in-the-loop approval for high-risk or on-behalf-of actions as circuit breakers. Define criteria for when an agent must defer to a human approver/reviewer (for example, confidence below threshold, safety guardrail triggered, or a high-stakes decision). Log escalation events for later audit and analysis.
- Provide permission audits to the end-user to grant/revoke access provided by human users or agents that granted permissions to sub-agents to gain transparent control.
- Activate end-to-end observability with session-level, trace-level, and span-level telemetry. Emit structured traces for agent decisions, guardrail invocations, and tool calls. Implement distributed tracing across multi-agent and multi-tool workflows to support full reconstruction of agent reasoning paths. Add dashboards for 360-degree observability and cost-control.
Security and privacy
- Establish least-privilege access controls. Define policy-based authorization rules for tool-level access using declarative policy languages. Apply granular access policies for agent actions and per knowledge source.
Phase 3: Evaluation and hardening
Focus pillars: Fairness, explainability, transparency, security and privacy
You have seen your first agent deliver business value. But how can you demonstrate it to a regulator, an auditor, or a board? How do you detect and help prevent unauthorized events on the system? In the third phase, evaluation stress-tests the fairness thresholds, and bias benchmarking. Hardening turns those findings into fixes.
This phase includes the following workstreams:
Fairness
- Model-level fairness testing: Check model cards for fairness metrics and restrict model access to a list of pre-approved models tested for common biases. In case there is no metric provided, test bias and alignment yourself using established benchmark sets such as Compositional Evaluation Benchmark (CEB) or Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM). Monitor whether outputs and routing treat demographic groups equitably.
- Agent-level fairness testing: Evaluate whether end-to-end agent routing, including tool selection, and resource allocation treats user groups equitably.
- Fairness regression monitoring: Set up automated pipelines to detect fairness drift over time as models are updated or new data sources are added.
Transparency
- Enforceable transparency for machine generated content: Attach machine-readable provenance labels to every reusable output, so downstream consumers can verify origin. Enforce mandatory AI-presence disclosure in user-facing interactions.
- Decision audit trails: Each agent action is logged with enough detail to reconstruct the reasoning path for a given outcome. For instance, what did the agent access, when and with which identity.
Explainability
- Compile an audit report for a fictional audit or appeal: Make sure you can quickly assemble the relevant data and understand how a decision was made.
- User-facing explanations: Provide end-users with on-demand, plain-language summaries of why an agent took a specific action or made a recommendation.
Security and privacy
- Continuous evaluation: Set up evaluation pipelines and evaluate before and after deployment. Document the results. Implement alerting mechanisms to be notified when metrics fall below a predefined quality threshold.
- Conduct penetration testing and red-team evaluations targeting agent-specific threat models: prompt injection, tenant isolation under concurrent access, token exchange with misconfigured profiles, and long-running async agent tasks. Define a Security Incident Response runbook specific to AI agent safety events. Configure automated alerting for safety-critical events.
- Fine-tune release criteria (evaluation scores, security scan results, fairness metrics) iteratively based on production feedback. Build deployment gates into your continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline. Nothing reaches production without meeting the release criteria for its risk tier.
When to revisit
Responsible AI isn’t a one-time implementation. As the platform evolves, each dimension must be periodically reassessed. The following table gives some examples to define both standing review cadences and event-driven triggers for re-evaluation.
| Standing Cadence | 
|  | 
| Triggers | 
|  | 
Example use case and implementation
Consider the following case: A bank builds a multi-agent loan processing platform. The platform features an intake agent, risk scoring agent, compliance agent, and customer communication agent.
Phase 1 (Governance foundation): The platform team gathers legal requirements for their use case, for example those stemming from the EU AI Act and financial regulation, and registers agents at High-risk tier (financial decisions affecting individuals) using the AWS Agent Registry. They use a secure landing zone built with AWS Control Tower with foundational logging and access control active and configure tenant isolation to help prevent cross-customer leakage. The team documents residual risk and scope for each agent: for example, if the intake agent produces unexpected data, the risk scoring agent processes its output without independent verification.
Phase 2 (Pilot deployment: Validation and rollout): Risk scoring uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases grounded in regulatory lending documentation. Automated Reasoning checks verify denial decisions conform to documented criteria (conformance, not causal explanation). Amazon Bedrock Guardrails redact PII data before customer communication. To address the multi-agent trust gap: the scoring agent confirms key applicant data from source systems rather than solely relying on the intake agent’s extraction. Each agent is bounded to required tools through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions, and the team uses Policies in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to further restrict the risk scoring agent to read-only access on the customer segment the agent is approved for. A case where the Automated Reasoning check returns a result other than VALID (for example, SATISFIABLE or TRANSLATION_AMBIGUOUS), or where the applicant’s risk score falls within the marginal band (for example, ±5 points of the threshold), is automatically escalated to a human credit specialist (human-in-the-loop review) before the decision is communicated. Escalation events are logged with the triggering condition for audit.
Phase 3 (Evaluation and hardening: Continuous monitoring): Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, run on every pipeline push. CI/CD blocks deployment if an evaluation result is below releasing criterion or per-subgroup fairness metrics drifts beyond threshold. Red-team exercises (independent security team) test realistic security threats on the intake agent to verify that it can’t influence scoring. Human review of denial decisions, moving to after-the-fact review through an appeals process after 2,000 aligned decisions over 60 days. AI usage in the decision process is disclosed transparently to customers. Every automated decision is traced end-to-end using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. It captures OpenTelemetry spans that can be automatically aggregated into a single distributed trace ready for auditing and appeals.
How to measure maturity
Frameworks serve as aspirations, while measurements provide accountability. Questions like “Can you list the risk tier for a use case?” will necessarily arise when the platform is operational from stakeholders like CISOs or auditors. To leave you prepared, we provide a repository with a set of questions that you can use to gauge your current posture and identify improvement areas before your system goes live.
We also package the questionnaire as a portable skill for AI Agents like Amazon Quick, and AI coding assistants like Kiro, Claude Code, and Codex. The AI walks you through each phase and assesses your responsible AI posture along the dimensions on a scale from 1–5. Scores below 4 indicate substantial risks that should be remediated. Scores of 4 or higher indicate residual risk that might be acceptable when acknowledged on a case-by-case basis. The AI also provides actionable recommendations for improving your Responsible AI posture.
Conclusion
Responsible AI (RAI) is a continuous, evolving effort. We recommend organizations implement RAI pillars through the AgentOps journey. These best practices cover governance policies, evaluation gates, and production telemetry into agentic AI platforms. This creates the feedback loop that keeps fairness, safety, and transparency continuously measured and improved.
This framework is a starting point, not an exhaustive compliance checklist. RAI practices vary by industry, use case, and requirements. Organizations should consult their own legal, compliance, and ethics teams to tailor these recommendations to their specific regulatory obligations and risk profiles.
For a comprehensive treatment of responsible AI across workload types, refer to the AWS Well-Architected Responsible AI Lens, which provides detailed best practices, design principles, and evaluation criteria for each of the eight pillars discussed in this post. For industry-specific guidance, consult the Financial Services Industry Lens and the Healthcare Industry Lens, which address sector-specific regulatory and ethical requirements. Get started today by installing the RAI assessment skill from this repository and evaluating your organization’s RAI posture with your preferred AI agent.

articles.title: Karnataka aims to become global hub for frontier technologies: DK Shivakumar
articles.text:
Karnataka aims to become global hub for frontier technologies: DK Shivakumar
Karnataka Chief Minister DK Shivakumar said the strong technology ecosystem in the State gives it the advantage to lead in areas such as AI, biotech, semiconductor and robotics.
Karnataka aims to become a global hub for frontier technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), deeptech, semiconductor, robotics, and biotech, said Chief Minister DK Shivakumar at the inaugural of Bengaluru Tech Summit (BTS) in Bengaluru on Tuesday, citing the state government's enabling policies.
BTS, now in its 29th edition, is themed “AI and Beyond”. Addressing the event, the Chief Minister highlighted that Karnataka has consistently been at the forefront of technology and is well positioned to lead the next phase of global innovation backed by strong IT and startup ecosystem.
The Chief Minister said Karnataka accounted for two out of every five dollars earned by India through software and services exports, which amounted to approximately $173 billion last year.
The state also attracted $9.4 billion in foreign direct investment (FDI) equity inflows in the first half of FY26, accounting for 26.7% of India's total inflows during the period. Bengaluru is home to more than 1,000 Global Capability Centres (GCCs), while over 30 new GCCs brought investments of more than $1 billion into Karnataka in 2025.
Shivakumar said Karnataka was home to more than 24,000 recognised startups, with nearly two out of every five Indian unicorns (startups valued at $1 billion or more) originating from the state.
Bengaluru ranked eighth among the world's startup ecosystems and second in Asia for AI-native startups. Startups in Karnataka have collectively raised approximately $79 billion, while women founders in Bengaluru have secured $13.4 billion in funding.
The state government is also extending financial support to startups working on emerging technologies. Through its ELEVATE initiative, it has supported nearly 1,500 startups with equity-free grants worth $41 million over the past decade.
Under ELEVATE NxT, deeptech startups are eligible for grants of up to Rs 1 crore. Since last year, 33 startups have received equity-free funding totalling Rs 30 crore.
The government has also announced Innoverse, a deeptech accelerator that will support 35 growth-stage ventures over the next five years. The programme aims to help startups move beyond product development and scale up to industrial-level operations.
Another initiative, Government First, aims to make the state government an early customer for startups. A dedicated fund of Rs 25 crore has been earmarked to procure innovative solutions developed by these companies.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is another main focus of Karnataka's technology ambitions. Shivakumar said Bengaluru accounted for nearly 50% of India's AI and machine learning talent.
The state is also building what he described as India's first government-led AI university, alongside an AI Hub that will bring startups, researchers and industry stakeholders together.
An additional Centre of Excellence at IIIT Raichur will focus on expanding AI applications across 13 districts of North Karnataka, particularly in sectors such as agriculture, healthcare, education and small businesses.
Karnataka is also looking to strengthen its position in the semiconductor industry. The state is home to more than 100 fabless chip companies, while Bengaluru accounts for three out of every five engineers working in India's semiconductor capability centres, Shivakumar said.
The state currently accounts for one-fifth of India's electronics exports. Its next priority is to expand beyond chip design and build manufacturing capabilities.

articles.title: Seattle police bomb squad buys $360,000 Spot robot dog, already planning to get a second
articles.text:
What just happened? Boston Dynamics' quadrupedal robot, Spot, continues to find work in law enforcement. Rather than a Black Mirror-style machine of mass destruction, the robotic dog is now being used by Seattle police's arson/bomb squad. It cost the department $360,000, and it plans on buying another one.
The Seattle Police Department (SPD) writes that Spot was purchased with Federal Emergency Management Agency grant funding approved by the Seattle City Council in April 2026. The approval was granted after the robot was assessed for potential privacy and security risks.
The SPD notes that Spot is a lot lighter, nimbler, and easier to maneuver than the bomb squad's five other robots, which traverse on treads. Spot's ability to climb stairs is going to be a big advantage over the older robots.
Using Spot's robotic arm, an operator can locate a door handle, open the door, and send the robot into a room containing a suspected explosive without anyone having to enter. The operator can then manually control the arm to lift the device and place it in a safe container. The entire process can be carried out from nearly a mile away, keeping both the operator and the public at a safer distance.
The introduction of Spot, which also packs a 360-degree camera and a microphone, has raised familiar concerns about weaponized robots and AI making life-or-death decisions. But Seattle police said Spot can't be equipped with weapons, doesn't use AI to make independent decisions, and doesn't use facial recognition tech.
Police spokesperson Detective Shane Weatherford said the plans to buy a second Spot robot were already in the works. The SPD never said how many times the current Spot has been deployed, why it needs a second unit, or how it will pay for the next robot.
Police officials said the device would address unspecified "critical gaps" in equipment needed for detecting dangerous objects and preventing terrorism, according to a city record.
The Seattle Times highlights the $360,000 this Spot model costs and the apparent lack of specifics from the SPD about why the price was justified or how often it's being used. Buying another of these robots, which will push the total bill to almost three-quarters of a million dollars, will likely raise plenty of eyebrows.
This isn't Spot's first deployment in a law enforcement setting. In 2019, the Massachusetts State Police bomb squad leased one of the robots for use as a "mobile remote observation device."
The NYPD deployed a heavily modified Spot known as Digidog in 2020. It led to plenty of backlash, so the NYPD terminated its $94,000 lease in 2021, only to bring Digidog back two years later.
More recently, it was reported that ICE wants to spend up to $2 million on Spot robots.

articles.title: Artist brings old Space Shuttle tank back to life
articles.text:
Fine art sculptor Natalie Rosen is seen at work for the California Science Center, shaping space shuttle Endeavour's external tank and other foam-covered components that are now debuting on display in the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center in Los Angeles.
Credit:
California Science Center/collectSPACE.com
Fine art sculptor Natalie Rosen is seen at work for the California Science Center, shaping space shuttle Endeavour's external tank and other foam-covered components that are now debuting on display in the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center in Los Angeles.
Credit:
California Science Center/collectSPACE.com
Natalie Rosen is not the type of specialist you immediately associate with being one of the key people behind the new exhibit of the space shuttle Endeavour.
She is not a former NASA technician or engineer, as many of her colleagues have been for the past several years, nor is she a curator or conservator. Before this job, she had no experience working on any aircraft or spacecraft, as the new Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center, an extension of the California Science Center, opened in Los Angeles on November 13.
Without her expertise and artistry, however, the largest component of Endeavour‘s “stack” would look nothing like it did when the shuttle was flying.
The only fully authentic display of a space shuttle in its launch configuration opens to the public at the California Science Center in Los Angeles on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026.
Credit:
California Science Center / ZGF Architects/Mike Kelley
The only fully authentic display of a space shuttle in its launch configuration opens to the public at the California Science Center in Los Angeles on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026.
Credit:
California Science Center / ZGF Architects/Mike Kelley
“My background is in the fine arts. I have my bachelor’s and my master’s in fine arts from Cal State Long Beach,” Rosen told collectSPACE.com. “When I came in on this project, they were looking for a sculptor, and I had been sculpting.”
Rosen had been working with mixed media for her thesis project and had experience sculpting foam. As it happened, the California Science Center had a lot of foam that needed shaping.
ET-94
For those unfamiliar, the space shuttle was assembled from three primary launch components. The orbiter and its solid rocket boosters were reusable, given the time needed to inspect, service, and, in the case of the solid-fuel motors, refurbish and refill between flights.
The 154-foot-tall (47-meter) external tank was the only major part of the stack that was disposed of with each launch. After providing propellant for the orbiter’s three main engines, the tank was jettisoned and disintegrated while reentering the atmosphere.
To protect the orbiter from the extreme cold of the cryogenic liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen in the external tank and to keep the propellant and oxidizer from boiling off too quickly, the ET was covered in insulating foam. (Some of that foam became liberated during ascent and was what caused the loss of the space shuttle Columbia and its crew in 2003.)
The only flight-worthy tank to remain at the end of the program was ET-94. A so-called lightweight tank, it was built at a time when NASA was transitioning to a super-lightweight model and was therefore set aside. Originally slated to support a science mission on Columbia, it instead became a testbed after the tragedy, having its foam stripped off and tested to better understand what had happened.
After the program ended, NASA donated ET-94 to the California Science Center. It arrived by way of a transoceanic barge and a road trip, then sat at Exposition Park for nearly a decade.
Natalie Rosen shapes a foam ice frost ramp that was later installed in a series of ramps along the outside length of external tank ET-94 for the display of space shuttle Endeavour at the California Science Center’s Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center in Los Angeles.
Credit:
California Science Center
Natalie Rosen shapes a foam ice frost ramp that was later installed in a series of ramps along the outside length of external tank ET-94 for the display of space shuttle Endeavour at the California Science Center’s Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center in Los Angeles.
Credit:
California Science Center
“So much of the foam on the ET had been dissected and removed during its time as a test article that they [the California Science Center] were trying to figure out how to put it back on and blend it in to the original foam in a convincing way,” said Rosen.
“Orange” peel
There has been a longstanding debate among shuttle enthusiasts and modelers about exactly what color the external tank is, and the answer resides in the foam.
“It’s orange. It’s cream. It’s burnt sienna. It just depends on the original foam, when you’re seeing it and how it’s aging. Because it starts as a kind of very ice cream-white almost color, and then depending on how long it sits out in the Sun, it turns orange,” said Rosen.
By the time she had come on staff, the decision for the most part had already been made. Dennis Jenkins, the leader of the Endeavour project, had blended a special paint called “ET Orange” that was used to cover the existing acreage “bumpy” foam. Separately, a mocha-like color was picked out for the intertank.
“And then the latest foam to be installed, which would have looked the newest on all of the closeout hardware—the feed lines, the ice frost ramps, the flanges around the intertank and the intertank rings—those were all the lightest color that we custom mixed. That was what we called the ice cream color,” Rosen said.
Sculptor Natalie Rosen, poised atop a high platform in 2024, works on touch-ups to the foam on the forward intertank stringers for the external tank on vertical display with the space shuttle Endeavour in the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center in Los Angeles.
Credit:
California Science Center
Sculptor Natalie Rosen, poised atop a high platform in 2024, works on touch-ups to the foam on the forward intertank stringers for the external tank on vertical display with the space shuttle Endeavour in the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center in Los Angeles.
Credit:
California Science Center
It was not only about color matching, though. For multiple reasons, the original aerospace-grade foam could not be used, so a commercial substitute had to be found that could match what Rosen described as the “orange peel.”
“If you look at the tank very closely, there’s this bumpy texture, and there is a pattern from the original manufacturing and how it was sprayed on. There’s this overlapping line, a subtle-like stripe to it,” she said.
Replicating that pattern was not easy.
“There was a lot of trial and error in the beginning of what we could do to try and get it to match what was already there,” Rosen told collectSPACE. “We tried taking impressions off of the real foam and making molds and casting, but that didn’t really work. I then suggested we put in a dense urethane, like plain urethane foam, and I hand-sculpt the top of it to match what was around it. That ended up becoming the best solution for fixing the acreage foam that had an orange peel-like texture.”
Jenkins, who had worked as a space shuttle engineer and led NASA’s delivery of the orbiters to their museum homes, had high praise for Rosen and her work.
“She had to come up with a lot of new processes because we couldn’t apply foam the same way they did at Michoud. It’s not flightworthy by any means, but just coming up with how to make it look real took a lot of imagination on her part, and she was pretty much a one-woman show for most of it,” he said.
In the vertical
Some of the repair work to the external tank was finished before it was lifted by crane into the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center and mated with the boosters and Endeavour. From then on, Rosen had to climb scaffolding to get to her worksites.
“It’s definitely the largest art project I’ve ever worked on, and, I mean, I touched every inch of it,” Rosen said. “Once it went vertical, I was going up and down stairs. Probably the scariest was the point in the scaffolding where it just became ladders. So I had to be very, very careful and calculated in what I was doing.”
Even after the scaffolding was removed in preparation for the museum opening, Rosen’s ascents were not over. A couple of weeks ago, she had to install a final component on the aft dome of the liquid hydrogen tank. To reach that, she needed a scissor lift.
External tank restoration specialist Natalie Rosen applies close-out foam on external tank ET-94’s aft longeron area, preparing it for display with the space shuttle Endeavour at the California Science Center’s new Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center in Los Angeles.
Credit:
California Science Center
External tank restoration specialist Natalie Rosen applies close-out foam on external tank ET-94’s aft longeron area, preparing it for display with the space shuttle Endeavour at the California Science Center’s new Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center in Los Angeles.
Credit:
California Science Center
Now that the entire Endeavour stack has made its public debut, Rosen is not parting ways with the California Science Center. Her work on ET-94 has launched her career into a new frontier.
“In this last year, I have been working on different artifacts with the team. I have been helping leading up to the opening. I’ve helped in ways with the different aircraft, with their assembly, their disassembly, and reassembly. I’ve done some repairs in certain areas. I’ve worked with our satellite and probe collection to do repairs and also contacted specialists outside of my realm to clean and repair thermal blankets,” said Rosen.
“So I’m planning on staying with the museum for now. They’ve offered me another position, and I’m happy to stay,” she said.
The California Science Center’s Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center is now open to the public. Admission is free, but timed entry tickets are needed due to the high demand. Reservations can be made online or at 213-744-2019.
Robert Pearlman is a space historian, journalist and the founder and editor of collectSPACE, a daily news publication and online community focused on where space exploration intersects with pop culture. He is also a contributing writer for Space.com and co-author of "Space Stations: The Art, Science, and Reality of Working in Space” published by Smithsonian Books in 2018. He is on the leadership board for For All Moonkind and is a member of the American Astronautical Society's history committee.

articles.title: Physical AI company Promise Robotics announces $40-million Series B round | BetaKit
articles.text:
A Toronto startup using AI and robotics to accelerate homebuilding has attracted $40 million CAD in Series B funding.
The news: Promise Robotics, which uses a combination of AI software and robotics to build modular, prefabricated homes, announced the closure of its Series B round on Tuesday. The round was led by White Star Capital, with additional participation from Horizons Ventures, Radical Ventures, and Public Sector Pension Investment Board (PSP Investments).
From the source: “Homebuilding can’t scale on trade labour alone,” said Promise Robotics CEO and co-founder Ramtin Attar in a press release. “We’re building the production infrastructure the industry can scale on; a network of intelligent factories … this round lets us extend that network.”
The context: Promise Robotics uses AI to take building designs, break them into modular pieces, and then fabricate them via AI-controlled robotics. Those prefabricated pieces are then delivered to a construction site and assembled by crews of human workers. The company has factories in Calgary and near Edmonton in Nisku, Alta. It’s also planning an expansion south of the border in Phoenix and has signed deals with Texas’ D.R. Horton, a major residential developer in the US.
Promise Robotics plans to use the funding to expand its production infrastructure and research and development capacity. It also has plans to expand its workforce from 85 to more than 100 employees, according to reporting from The Globe and Mail.
Final thought: Access to affordable housing has been a persistent issue in Canada for decades, with the Canadian Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) estimating that an undersupply of housing has driven up prices. Canada has reacted to that forecasting by pledging to build 500,000 new homes per year, though reporting from the Canadian Housing Research Network pegs the current rate of construction at closer to 200,000. Promise Robotics has pitched its model as a way to improve productivity, increase capacity, and accelerate construction timelines.
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.
Feature image courtesy of Promise Robotics.

articles.title: Xiaomi trae a Europa algunos de sus nuevos electrodomésticos inteligentes
articles.text:
Además de la nueva gama alta con el Xiaomi 18 Pro y 18 Pro Max, y la puesta a punto de sus wearables, Xiaomi también ha presentado sus nuevos electrodomésticos inteligentes para el mercado global, lo que quiere decir que llegarán a España. En total, son 4 electrodomésticos nuevos: la lavasecadora Mijia Tri-Drum Washer Dryer Pro 12 kg, el frigorífico Mijia Refrigerator Pro Multi-Door 546 L, el robot aspirador Xiaomi Robot Vacuum 6 Max y la aspiradora vertical Mijia Vacuum Cleaner 4 Max, coincidiendo con el anuncio de la IFA de que Mijia iba a ser marca global.
De esta forma, la Mijia Tri-Drum Washer Dryer Pro 12 kg llega con tres tambores de funcionamiento independiente como seña de identidad, y con la eficiencia con bandera: reduce un 48 % el consumo de agua, un 49 % el de energía y un 68 % el tiempo necesario.
Además, según la compañía, su tecnología Xiaomi Oxygen Care es capaz de eliminar 20 tipos de manchas habituales y ayuda a evitar la transferencia de color, y su función Smart Infusion ofrece un lavado inteligente de 32 minutos en el tambor principal o un ciclo rápido de 12 minutos en los secundarios.
Tiene limpieza con vapor a alta temperatura y lavado con agua caliente para erradicar el 99,99 % de las bacterias, todo controlable desde su app. ¿Su precio? Todavía por confirmar.
Su nevera, por otro lado, destaca con su suministro constante de hielo para bebidas: según Xiaomi, su sistema automático puede almacenar hasta 180 cubitos de hielo en el modelo de puerta francesa y 140 en el de cuatro puertas cruzadas. Y hacemos distinción porque llega en dos modelos: el formato French-door, con un cajón congelador para alimentos voluminosos; y el formato Cross-door, con 18 compartimentos (seis de ellos en el congelador). Tampoco tiene precio fijado para su lanzamiento en España, de momento.
Más aspiradoras, tanto robóticas como manuales.
Además de la lavadora y la nevera, Xiaomi también ha presentado dos aspiradores: uno robot y otro de mano. El Xiaomi Robot Vacuum 6 Max tiene un sistema de patas mecánicas biónicas dobles que le permiten sortear desniveles y escalones individuales de hasta 6 cm, y un perfil ultradelgado de 9 cm y radar dToF retráctil inteligente para limpiar bajo muebles con apenas 9,3 cm de altura libre. Usa un sistema de triple cámara panorámica con IA para evasión de obstáculos y reconoce 200 tipos de objetos comunes y 80 clases de muebles.
Tiene potencia de succión de 35.000 Pa, y una base omnidireccional autolimpiable reduce al mínimo el mantenimiento manual mediante el lavado con agua caliente (a más de 85 °C) del rodillo y la mopa. Todo a un precio todavía por confirmar.
Por su parte, la Mijia Vacuum Cleaner 4 Max ofrece aspiración de alta potencia; con su nuevo modo Turbo ofrece hasta 280 AW de potencia de succión, un sistema de detección de polvo mediante luz azul con un ángulo de 180º, que permite ver el polvo microscópico magnificado hasta 30 veces y una base inteligente con vaciado automático por empuje 4 en 1 (Push-in Smart Dust Emptying Base Station). ¿Su precio? A partir de 559,99 €.

articles.title: Blog Review: Nov. 18
articles.text:
PCIe and trust; rack-scale co-design; heterogeneous scaling; AI data center primer; on-device balancing; EU semi trends.
Cadence’s Rajesh Pamujula considers how to establish trust when sensitive data, proprietary models, cryptographic keys, and confidential workloads increasingly traverse PCIe links.
Synopsys’ Neeraj Paliwal argues that extreme co-design, where silicon, interface IP, memory, cooling, and power are designed together as one system, is needed for efficient racks that are capable of running increasingly demanding AI workloads.
Siemens’ Kevin Rinebold and Andras Vass-Varnai examine the evolving semiconductor design landscape shaped by the shift from monolithic scaling to heterogeneous architectures and consider how to navigate the complexities of AI-driven 3D-IC and chiplet technologies.
Keysight’s Linas Dauksa provides a primer on the technologies that power AI data centers, how they handle training and inference workloads, and why they’ve become the backbone of modern AI.
Arm’s Michael Gamble checks out how to enable gaze-based interactions in lightweight smart glasses by running fast, sensor-dependent AI on-device while larger workloads stay where more compute is available.
SEMI’s Sitong He chats with Patrick Vandenameele of imec about the trends reshaping the semiconductor industry, why collaboration matters more than ever, and the role Europe can play in global competitiveness.
Plus, check out blogs featured in the latest Low Power-High Performance newsletter:
Rambus’ Kushal Koolwal examines why longer contexts, higher concurrency, multimodal models, and AI agents will continue changing where memory pressure appears.
Siemens EDA’s Jim Shiely shows how to use evidence from silicon to improve the tools and decisions for next-gen hardware.
Synopsys’ Andrew Appleby observes that traditional voltage scaling is no longer sufficient to deliver real-time performance within tight energy and thermal limits.
Cadence’s Joe Chen demonstrates how to right-size the memory hierarchy around the device’s data streams, reuse patterns, latency requirements, and operating constraints.
Arm’s Siyu Mou explains the rationale behind 8-bit floating-point data formats, their ecosystem momentum, and hardware support.

articles.title: Panne Apple : iCloud, l’App Store et Apple Music ne fonctionnent plus, voici ce que l’on sait
articles.text:
Mise à jour 19h10 : Apple reconnaît désormais plusieurs pannes. La liste des services impactés s’est allongée. Apple indique deux problèmes sur « Compte iCloud et connexion » et classe l’App Store, Apple Music et AppleCare sur l’appareil en « panne », le niveau le plus grave de son échelle. L’entreprise n’a toujours donné ni cause ni délai de rétablissement.
Apple a reconnu le problème sans en donner la cause.
En fin d’après-midi, les signalements ont brusquement grimpé sur les sites de suivi de pannes. À 18 h 42, Apple Support, l’App Store et iCloud occupaient les trois premières places des services les plus signalés sur Downdetector.
La connexion au compte en cause
Selon 9to5Mac, des utilisateurs ont été déconnectés d’iCloud sans prévenir, puis ont rencontré des échecs de vérification ou des erreurs inconnues en voulant se reconnecter. Comme ils reposent sur le même compte Apple, d’autres services ont été touchés. L’App Store ne se chargeait plus, et Apple Pay, Apple Music, l’activation des appareils et App Store Connect, l’outil des développeurs, connaissaient eux aussi des problèmes.
Peu avant 18 h 50, la page État du système d’Apple signalait un « problème » pour le service « Compte iCloud et connexion », mais ne donnait ni cause ni délai de rétablissement.

articles.title: SA crypto platform OVEX deploys AI fraud detection system built by DataProphet - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
South African crypto platform OVEX has gone live with a custom AI fraud detection system, built by machine learning consultancy DataProphet, that catches 98 per cent of fraudsters in testing.
Founded in 2017, OVEX offers South Africa’s largest selection of digital asset markets, and has partnered with several leading cryptocurrency companies and firms, including Invictus Capital, Hyperion, and TrueUSD.
DataProphet, meanwhile, was formed in 2014, and builds and runs custom machine learning for financial services, manufacturing, and other businesses. The two companies began working together back in April to replace OVEX’s rules-based fraud system with AI that learns how fraudsters behave.
Rather than judging an account from a snapshot, the system reads a user’s full activity history in sequence, including every login, deposit, trade and withdrawal. Two models, one trained on fraudulent behaviour and one on honest customers, assess which pattern each account more closely resembles. Accounts that lean towards the fraud model are flagged for investigation.
By late July, the model was catching 98 per cent of fraudsters in testing, compared with 75 per cent for the old system, and flagged 100 per cent of fraud cases it had never seen before. OVEX expects 99 per cent fewer false alarms and a 92 per cent reduction in undetected fraud. The platform also includes a tool showing investigators when an account’s behaviour turned suspicious, and a dashboard for retraining models.
“We partnered with DataProphet for their deep machine-learning expertise and they’ve built a system tailored to our platform, giving us a far more sophisticated way to identify fraud as it evolves,” said Jonathan Ovadia, chief executive of OVEX.
“Our partnership with OVEX proves that applied AI doesn’t have to be a black box or a heavy compliance burden,” said Ridwaan Seedat, CEO of DataProphet.

articles.title: Malware attack hits Zoom, Salesforce and IKEA-linked websites
articles.text:
Malware attack hits Zoom, Salesforce and IKEA-linked websites
A malware attack reportedly used Optimizely scripts on 178 organisation websites, including Zoom, Salesforce and IKEA, to target card details and crypto wallet addresses.
You may trust the website you are visiting. But what about the tools running behind it?
Cybersecurity researchers have uncovered a malware campaign involving websites linked to 178 organisations worldwide, including Zoom, Salesforce, IKEA, HSBC and Crocs. The attack shows how a compromised third-party tool can turn familiar websites into potential entry points for cybercriminals.
According to findings, the malicious code was injected through Optimizely Web, a platform companies use to run website experiments and A/B testing. This technique allows brands to show different versions of a webpage and measure how users respond.
The attack exploited that routine website function to deliver code capable of interfering with what users entered or copied on affected pages.
How a trusted website tool became a malware route
The attacker reportedly exploited a feature in Optimizely that allows customers to add JavaScript to projects. JavaScript is commonly used to make websites interactive and run features within a browser.
Malicious JavaScript was added to customer projects and delivered through Optimizely's trusted domain. This made the activity harder to identify as suspicious because the code came from a service already used by the affected websites.
Researchers at Report URI examined 1,611 Optimizely snippets and found 188 infected snippets linked to 178 organisations. The malware scanned webpages, form fields, links, images and clipboards for cryptocurrency wallet addresses.
When it detected a valid address, it could replace it with one controlled by the attacker.
A user copying a wallet address while an affected browser tab was open could therefore paste the wrong address without noticing. The malware could also capture card details entered directly into forms on affected websites.
Zoom, HSBC, IKEA and BBC among the names listed
The affected organisations spanned technology, finance, retail, travel, media and non-profit sectors.
Zoom, Salesforce and Bitly were among the technology companies named. The financial services list included HSBC US, HSBC Hong Kong and Equifax.
Retail and consumer brands such as IKEA, ASOS, Mattel, American Eagle, Crocs India and Levi's websites in several countries were also listed. Airlines including Air France-KLM and Alaska Airlines appeared in the findings, alongside media organisations such as BBC, CNN and Fox News.
Optimizely says it has fixed the issue
Optimizely said an unauthorised party exploited a vulnerability in its Experimentation account signup flow to inject malicious JavaScript into some customer projects.
The company said it blocked the vulnerable path, deployed a fix, removed the injected code, ended active sessions, revoked tokens and reset access for affected accounts.
The incident also exposes a security challenge for businesses that rely on third-party website tools. A website may be operated by a well-known brand, but its security also depends on the services and code it loads.
Users should keep their browsers updated, verify cryptocurrency wallet addresses before transferring funds, avoid entering payment details on suspicious pages and monitor cards for unusual transactions. A familiar brand name alone does not guarantee that every element running on its website is safe.

articles.title: Seis meses de prisión y una multa superior a 1.000 euros por presentar en el trabajo un parte de baja médico falso
articles.text:
El primer parte de baja que el trabajador recibió por gastroenteritis era solo para un día. Sin embargo, el siguiente día tampoco fue a trabajar. Cuando la empresa le pidió que justificara su ausencia, el trabajador mandó por e-mail otro parte (ficticio) que no le había dado su médico.
Los hechos ocurrieron en junio de 2017. El día 6 el trabajador tenía un parte de baja y alta (por gastroenteritis aguda), que le dio un médico y solo era para ese mismo día.
El día 7 no estaba cubierto médicamente, pero el trabajador envió un parte (que él mismo hizo u obtuvo) que justifica esta ausencia.
Fue el Juzgado de lo Penal número 3 de Granollers quien primero condenó al trabajador (por falsedad en documento oficial y por un delito leve de estafa).
El documento que querían pasar por auténtico
En la Sala de lo Penal han tenido en cuenta que, en casos en los que se trata de “reproducciones” que se quieren pasar por documentos oficiales, hay que tener en cuenta qué documento se quiere imitar.
El soporte en el que se elabora el documento no tiene relevancia. En este caso se trataba de una baja médica que no existía.
Así se resolvió la polémica sobre el parte de baja digital. Condena por falsedad documental. Los efectos de la sentencia suponen 6 meses de cárcel y 6 meses de multa (a 6 euros diarios).
Cada mes de multa son 30 días (artículo 50 del Código Penal). Esto suma 1.080 euros. Además, se le condena a pagar las costas de primera instancia. También se incluye una inhabilitación para presentarse a elecciones durante el tiempo de la condena (algo curioso).

articles.title: Obsolescence programmée : Apple renvoyé devant la justice pour entrave à la réparation de ses iPhone
articles.text:
Apple devra s’expliquer devant la justice française au sujet de l’iPhone. L’association Halte à l’obsolescence programmée (HOP) a annoncé ce mardi que le procureur de la République de Paris avait décidé de poursuivre l’entreprise devant le tribunal correctionnel pour « l’emploi de techniques, y compris logicielles, visant à entraver la réparation et le reconditionnement hors de ses circuits agréés ». Une première audience de fixation est prévue le 25 février 2027, et les plaidoiries doivent se dérouler sur quatre jours à partir du 17 juin 2027, selon une source proche du dossier citée par l’AFP et reprise par TF1 Info.
Ce procès fait suite à une plainte déposée par HOP le 7 décembre 2022, et à une enquête confiée à la DGCCRF. Il vise 24 modèles d’iPhone* vendus entre le 17 novembre 2021 et le 23 juillet 2024, parmi lesquels l’iPhone XS, les iPhone SE de 2020 et 2022, les iPhone 12, 13 et 14 ou encore l’iPhone 15 Pro Max. C’est la première fois que le parquet s’appuie sur le délit spécifique d’entrave à la réparation et au reconditionnement, inscrit en 2021 à l’article L441-3 du Code de la consommation. En cas de condamnation, Apple risque notamment une amende pouvant atteindre 5 % de son chiffre d’affaires et pourrait devoir indemniser les consommateurs lésés, rappelle HOP.
La sérialisation, au cœur des reproches
L’association reproche à Apple d’avoir recours à la sérialisation, aussi appelée appariement. Le principe consiste à associer le numéro de série de certains composants, comme l’écran, la batterie ou les caméras, à celui du téléphone. Lorsqu’une pièce est remplacée, le système le détecte, et peut restreindre certaines fonctions si l’intervention n’a pas été validée par Apple. La reconnaissance faciale Face ID a ainsi pu être désactivée après le remplacement de la caméra avant, et l’état de santé de la batterie pouvait ne plus s’afficher après un changement de batterie.
Plus grave encore aux yeux de HOP, ces dysfonctionnements se seraient produits « même quand un appareil est réparé avec une pièce identique et d’origine, dès lors que l’intervention n’est pas adoubée par Apple ». Pour l’association, la pratique limite la réparation chez les réparateurs indépendants, et donc la possibilité de faire réparer son téléphone à un prix raisonnable. HOP rappelle qu’un remplacement d’écran sur les iPhone les plus récents est facturé 489 euros par Apple, contre 161 euros en moyenne en France selon l’éco-organisme Ecosystem.
« La décision du parquet de Paris d’aller jusqu’au procès représente un signal fort pour les consommateurs et un avertissement pour ceux qui mettent en péril le droit à la réparation », se félicite Laetitia Vasseur, déléguée générale et cofondatrice de HOP. « Une condamnation pour obsolescence programmée par entraves à la réparation serait une première historique en France et dans le monde », estime-t-elle.
Apple conteste, et a déjà assoupli ses règles
De son côté, Apple « conteste fermement ces allégations infondées », a fait savoir un porte-parole de la firme de Cupertino. « Nous cherchons toujours de nouvelles façons d’offrir la meilleure expérience possible à nos clients, ce qui implique notamment de concevoir des produits durables, accompagnés de mises à jour logicielles qui permettent aux utilisateurs de conserver leurs appareils plus longtemps. Nous sommes convaincus que la meilleure réparation est celle dont on n’a jamais besoin, et nous continuerons d’innover pour proposer les meilleurs produits au monde », ajoute l’entreprise.
La marque a toutefois fait évoluer sa politique depuis le dépôt de la plainte. Elle a lancé un programme de réparation en libre-service, puis a progressivement autorisé l’utilisation de pièces d’origine d’occasion et la validation de certaines réparations directement depuis l’iPhone. Des avancées que HOP reconnaît, tout en estimant qu’elles « restent à confirmer dans le temps ». Le cadre légal a lui aussi bougé, avec la directive européenne sur le droit à la réparation, qui encadre désormais ces pratiques.
Ce n’est pas la première fois que HOP s’en prend à Apple. Une première plainte, déposée en 2017 après le scandale du ralentissement des iPhone lié à l’usure des batteries, avait abouti en 2020 à une amende de 25 millions d’euros pour pratique commerciale trompeuse par omission, dans le cadre d’une transaction pénale, sans procès. Cette fois, l’affaire sera bien plaidée devant un tribunal. Elle sera la deuxième à porter sur l’obsolescence programmée au sens large, après celle visant le fabricant d’imprimantes Epson, attendu devant le tribunal correctionnel de Nanterre en février 2027. Plus de dix ans après son inscription dans la loi, le délit d’obsolescence programmée n’a encore jamais donné lieu à une condamnation.
*La liste complète n’a pas été communiquée. En toute logique, elle devrait couvrir tous les modèles sortis de l’iPhone XS (2018) à la gamme iPhone 15, soit les iPhone XS, XS Max et XR, les iPhone 11, 11 Pro et 11 Pro Max, l’iPhone SE de 2020, les iPhone 12 mini, 12, 12 Pro et 12 Pro Max, les iPhone 13 mini, 13, 13 Pro et 13 Pro Max, l’iPhone SE de 2022, les iPhone 14, 14 Plus, 14 Pro et 14 Pro Max, ainsi que les iPhone 15, 15 Plus, 15 Pro et 15 Pro Max.

articles.title: Tor releases emergency update amid ongoing DDoS attack
articles.text:
The Tor Project has released a security update for its network relay software to increase defenses against an ongoing distributed denial-of-service attack that it says has overwhelmed relays and affected most operators.
Tor version 0.4.9.17 includes a series of security fixes, including one the project described as especially important for relay denial-of-service defenses involving IPv6 handling.
“This release comes in rapid response to the ongoing DDoS attack on the network, which has affected most relay operators,” the Tor Project said in its release announcement.
The project said a massive ongoing flood of client circuits has overwhelmed relays across the privacy network, causing a problem that has been difficult to address.
The project says this update includes a security fix to improve relay defenses against denial-of-service attacks.
"One fix in particular is especially important for relay DoS defenses related to IPv6 handling," explains the project.
Tor is working on additional defenses and expects to issue further releases in the near future.
Relay operators are urged to upgrade to version 0.4.9.17 as soon as possible. The project said no additional action is required after installing the update.
The announcement did not provide any other details as to who is behind the DDoS attacks or when they began.
The Tor Project thanked relay operators for helping respond to the attack, pointing to active discussions on its tor-relays mailing list and asking operators to continue providing support.
"Thank you to all… except our attacker(s)."

articles.title: Gigabyte prépare ses PC portables Intel Nova Lake et AMD Zen 6 : une fuite relance l’attente
articles.text:
Gigabyte aura semble-t-il de belles choses à nous montrer au CES. Une fuite en provenance de Russie nous renseigne sur la gamme pratiquement complète de PC portables gamers et créatifs attendus chez la marque taïwanaise début 2027. Voici ce que l’on apprend.
Des PC portables pour les joueurs, qu’ils soient fortunés ou qu'ils le soient un peu moins, mais aussi pour les créateurs de contenus ou les mordus d’IA locale. C’est ce que l’on retient d’une liste, a priori complète, ou presque, ayant fuité cette semaine pour les modèles Gigabyte attendus dans les prochains mois.
BenQ iScreenBar : la barre lumineuse qui s’accorde avec l’iMac
Des lignes en harmonie avec celles de l’ordinateur d’Apple, une conception rigoureuse, des matériaux sélectionnés, rien n’a été laissé au hasard, tout comme le service qu’elle rend une fois allumée !
Gigabyte exposé par l’EEC
Cette fuite nous provient en l’occurrence d’une source officielle : l’EEC (Eurasian Economic Commission). Il s’agit de l’organe de régulation de l’Union économique eurasiatique (qui réunit la Russie, la Biélorussie, le Kazakhstan, l’Arménie et le Kirghizistan).
Les appareils qui utilisent du chiffrement, comme les PC portables, les smartphones ou les tablettes, doivent obligatoirement y être déclarés avant de pouvoir être commercialisés sur ces différents marchés, ce qui explique les nombreuses fuites de produits n’ayant pas encore été annoncés émanant de cette source.
Ces précisions étant faites, on apprend que Gigabyte nous préparerait une trentaine de nouveaux appareils au total, répartis au sein de ses gammes Aorus, Eagle, Gaming et Aero. Ces modèles représente selon toute logique la prochaine génération d’appareils de la marque, attendue début 2027 lors du CES. Nous devrions donc avoir l’opportunité d’en découvrir au moins une partie à Las Vegas, en janvier.
Une trentaine de nouveaux laptops en fuite, dont un modèle RTX Spark
On vous passe le décryptage fastidieux des différents suffixes de ces appareils, renvoyant tantôt à des configuration Intel, tantôt à de possibles configurations AMD, ou carrément à de nouvelles lignées, mais l’on retient que Gigabyte ferait cohabiter de nouveau des processeurs AMD (potentiellement Zen 6) et Intel (potentiellement Nova Lake) sur ses PC portable gaming haut de gamme, dont le futur Aorus Master 16 Gen 3. Ce dernier pourrait d’ailleurs s’équiper de RTX 5070 Ti, 5080 ou 5090 côté GPU, en fonction des options choisies.
Sur le milieu de gamme, représenté notamment par la lignée « Gaming », Gigabyte miserait une nouvelle fois sur des RTX 5050 et 5060, voire 5070. En d’autres termes, il y aurait peu de changement de ce point de vue face au milieu de gamme actuel de la marque… même si l'on peut s’attendre à des évolutions côté affichage ou châssis par rapport à certains modèles comme le très bon Gigabyte Gaming 16 que nous testions l’année dernière.
Plus intéressant, certains documents de l’EEC font mention d’un « AERO AION GR6XK Copilot+ PC » basé sur une plateforme à la mode : RTX Spark. L’appareil serait donc le premier à s'équiper d’une puce NVIDIA N1X chez Gigabyte. On a hâte d’en savoir plus.

articles.title: Microsoft’s new coding model promises near-Opus performance at 5% of the cost
articles.text:
Microsoft’s new coding model promises near-Opus performance at 5% of the cost
At its Ignite conference in San Francisco on Tuesday, Microsoft announced a number of new AI models, including two new coding models.
Imaginatively named Code 2 and Code 2 Flash, these new models promise to come very close to models like GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 at less than half the cost.
As Microsoft notes, “MAI Code 2 is at the frontier of price-performance” for enterprise coding tasks. “It does all of this while also delivering changes code maintainers would merge, at a fraction of frontier cost.”
MAI Code 2 benchmarks
The promise here is that Code 2 gets to 98% of the performance of GPT-6.1 Sol at 40% of the cost and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost (which also goes to show how expensive Anthropic’s models are to run right now).
The model, Microsoft says, has also been tuned to create “great dashboards and visualizations” and that it “excels at visual coding.”
At least for the OpenAI comparison, it’s worth noting that OpenAI today released GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, with improved performance. That softens Microsoft’s claims a bit, but it’s worth noting that OpenAI, too, notes that at least on Agents’ Last Exam, GPT-6.2 Astra is now 5.5 points “ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at just 5% of the cost” (which also goes to show how expensive Anthropic’s models are right now).
MAI Code 2 Flash benchmarks
As for MAI Code 2 Flash, Microsoft argues that it can match Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna on benchmarks like DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal-Bench 2.1, and SWE Atlas at 20% and 65% of the cost, respectively.
Microsoft’s bet: specialist models vs. generalists
One interesting wrinkle here is that Microsoft specifically tuned these models for the day-to-day coding work of its users. “They’re explicitly not yet tuned for harder problems, like fundamental science research and very long horizon agentic work,” Microsoft writes.
The models Microsoft is comparing these models to are generalists. For a while, OpenAI took a similar approach with its Codex models, but it has abandoned this approach in favor of more general models.
Microsoft, meanwhile, which doesn’t build those kinds of in-house frontier models, seems to be focused on smaller specialized models that it can run more efficiently. And while they won’t match the frontier models across every benchmark, focusing on these specific tasks makes a lot of sense in this context.
Microsoft is taking this even further with models like MAI Work Flash, a model trained to work across Microsoft 365 and Fabric IQ products.
Availability
MAI Code 2 and Code 2 Flash are now available in GitHub Copilot, while Code 2 Flash is in limited preview on Microsoft Foundry. OpenRouter, Vercel, Hermes, Open Code, and Kilo will soon get support as well.

articles.title: Ask Maps: Wie du via Google Maps jetzt auch Termine buchen kannst
articles.text:
Mit neuen KI-Funktionen: So will Google Maps den Planungsstress auf Reisen reduzieren
Kurz vor Weihnachten sind die Deutschen so viel unterwegs wie zu kaum einer anderen Zeit im Jahr. Auf den Straßen führen Staus zu Verzögerungen, und auch Busse und Bahnen sind so voll wie nie. Laut einer repräsentativen Umfrage des ADAC Südbayern zum Mobilitätsverhalten in der Weihnachtszeit besuchten im vergangenen Jahr 43 Prozent der Deutschen Verwandte oder Freund:innen. Am häufigsten reisten die 18- bis 29-Jährigen. Google Maps will diesem Reisestress jetzt etwas entgegensetzen und weitet die neue „Ask Maps“-Funktion auf weitere Länder aus. Sie soll unter anderem dabei helfen, Reiserouten zu erstellen und freie Termine zu finden.
Google Maps bekommt agentische Funktionen
Google Maps ist die mit Abstand beliebteste App zum Routenplanen – in Deutschland wie international. Laut Angaben des Tech-Konzerns verwenden sie mehr als zwei Milliarden Menschen pro Monat. Im Jahr 2024 sollen Nutzer:innen eine Billion Routenkilometer geplant haben. Zusätzlich sind 250 Millionen Geschäfte und Orte eingezeichnet, die direkt in der App Informationen zu ihrem Angebot, ihren Preisen und ihren verfügbaren Terminen bereitstellen. Mit der Funktion „Ask Maps” können Nutzer:innen jetzt detaillierte Reisepläne erstellen und Echtzeit-Informationen zur Route erhalten. Das soll unter anderem dabei helfen, den anstehenden Weihnachtseinkauf zu machen. Aber auch größere Trips sollen mit der neuen Funktion planbar sein.
„Du erhältst einen Tagesplan mit Insidertipps und nummerierten Markierungen auf der Karte für jeden Halt, sodass du dir den Plan leicht vorstellen kannst“, heißt es in einem Google-Blogbeitrag. Sobald Nutzer:innen mit einem Reiseplan zufrieden sind, können sie diesen auch mit anderen Personen teilen. Bevor sie losfahren, rufen sie die App auf und wählen ihren Reiseplan aus. Er liefert Informationen zu Parkmöglichkeiten oder Ladestationen sowie Echtzeitdaten zu Wetter, möglichen Verzögerungen und Mautgebühren. Sogar die Stimmung am nächsten geplanten Stopp soll angezeigt werden. Unterwegs können Nutzer:innen den Zeitplan auch spontan anpassen und beispielsweise einen Aussichtspunkt oder ein Restaurant für das Mittagessen auf dem Weg hinzufügen.
„Ask Maps“ jetzt auch in Deutschland verfügbar
Die agentischen Funktionen von „Ask Maps“ sollen besonders nützlich sein. Nutzer:innen können damit online Termine für Kosmetik, Tierpflege oder Autoreparaturen vereinbaren. Im Google-Blogbeitrag wird erklärt, wie die App beispielsweise mit dem Befehl „Finde für mich einen Termin für eine Maniküre um 16 Uhr in meiner Nähe“ genutzt werden kann. Die Funktion soll daraufhin freie Termine bei Salons im Umkreis anzeigen, sodass Nutzer:innen schnell entscheiden können, wo sie buchen möchten. Der Google-Maps-Agent soll sogar in der Lage sein, lokale Unternehmen direkt anzurufen. Auch Restaurantreservierungen sind möglich. Dafür greift der Maps-Agent auf bestehende Listen mit Lieblingsrestaurants zu und prüft automatisch die Verfügbarkeiten.
Die Funktion war seit März 2026 in den USA und in Indien auf Android- und iOS-Geräten verfügbar. Jetzt weitet Google das Feature auf weitere Regionen aus, darunter auch Deutschland. Reisepläne und die Listensuche sollen jetzt in mehr als 200 Ländern und Regionen verfügbar sein. Nützliche Routentipps sowie die Suche nach Terminen führt Google zunächst testweise in den USA ein. Weitere Regionen sollen in Kürze folgen. Der Veröffentlichungszeitpunkt ist nicht zufällig gewählt: Google hofft, dass viele die App verwenden, um ihre Weihnachtseinkäufe zu planen. Auch sollen Nutzer:innen die neuen Funktionen verwenden, um pünktlich an Heiligabend mit ihrer Familie unter dem Weihnachtsbaum sitzen können.
