articles.title: How ArisGlobal scaled generative AI inference on Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How ArisGlobal scaled generative AI inference on Amazon Bedrock
ArisGlobal, a provider of life sciences technology spanning pharmacovigilance, regulatory, medical affairs, clinical, and quality functions, developed NavaX, an AI engine purpose-built for life sciences on Amazon Bedrock, to automate adverse-event case processing. ArisGlobal chose Amazon Bedrock for managed access to foundation models, EU geographic cross-Region inference, and managed prompt caching. As enterprise customers added distinct compliance requirements, the shared prompt prefix grew by about 150% over 6 months, while per-case inference costs increased by more than 200%.
ArisGlobal first cached each source document because it was the largest part of a request. That left the growing shared prompt prefix outside the cache. By reversing the order and caching the shared prefix instead, ArisGlobal reduced effective input cost and supported additional tenants without proportional cost growth.
Who is ArisGlobal?
ArisGlobal is the creator of LifeSphere, a unified SaaS platform for pharmacovigilance, regulatory affairs, quality, and medical information. LifeSphere serves pharmaceutical companies globally, including multiple Top 20 pharma organizations by revenue (source: ArisGlobal press release). The entire system runs on AWS.
LifeSphere NavaX is ArisGlobal’s AI engine that transforms drug safety from a system of record into a system of strategic advantage. ArisGlobal productionized their first generative AI solution on Amazon Bedrock with Anthropic’s Claude in March 2025. According to ArisGlobal’s internal production telemetry, they have processed over 1 million real transactions in regulated pharmaceutical environments, handling billions of tokens across multiple enterprise tenants. Model availability varies by Region. See Model support by AWS Region.
How NavaX processes an adverse event case
When a pharmaceutical company receives an adverse-event report, typically a multipage PDF describing a patient’s reaction to a medication, NavaX’s Dynamic Data Extraction (DDE) agent extracts around 130 fields. These fields include patient demographics, suspect drugs, reporter information, event timelines, seriousness criteria, and regulatory classifications. Because this content includes protected health information, ArisGlobal applies responsible-AI controls as a standard part of its production deployment. It draws on capabilities such as Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to filter content and detect or mask sensitive information. Extracted fields are also validated against the schema and grounded in the source document.
This extraction happens across multiple sequential requests to the model. Each request focuses on a different section of the case form, and each carries:
- System instructions — model behavior rules, output format specifications, and regulatory compliance constraints.
- Customer-specific rules — per-tenant extraction logic, field mappings, and business rules that differ by pharmaceutical company.
- Extraction schema — around 130 target fields with types, validation rules, and few-shot examples.
- The source document — the adverse event PDF (often 10–200 pages).
Two inputs repeat at different scopes. The shared prompt prefix includes the system rules, extraction schema, and few-shot examples. It repeats across requests, cases, and tenants using the same agent. The source document repeats only for the requests associated with one case.
The prompt bloat problem
When NavaX launched with its first enterprise tenant, the system prompt was lean. As ArisGlobal onboarded additional pharmaceutical companies, each brought specific requirements:
- Custom field mappings (Tenant A maps reaction onset differently from Tenant B).
- Regulatory jurisdiction rules (EU ICSR compared with FDA MedWatch and PMDA formatting).
- Company-specific business logic for seriousness assessment and causality.
- Per-tenant few-shot examples calibrated to each company’s historical cases.
Over 6 months, the shared prompt prefix grew from approximately 72,000 to 180,000 tokens, a 150% increase. With multiple sequential requests per case, per-case inference costs increased by more than 200%.
The prefix grew with every tenant and was reprocessed on every request, so prompt growth compounded with transaction volume.
Table 1 compares the original document-first request order with the production prompt-first design.
| Aspect | First approach | Production design | 
| Request order | Per-case document, cache checkpoint, shared prompt prefix | Shared prompt prefix, cache checkpoint, per-case document | 
| Cached prefix | The document, which changes for every case | The shared prompt prefix, which repeats across requests | 
| Reuse scope | Only the remaining requests for one case | Requests across cases and tenants using the same agent | 
| Cost effect | The growing prompt is repeatedly processed at the full input rate | Fleet-wide prompt reuse supports sublinear cost growth | 
| EU routing | EU geographic cross-Region inference remains unchanged | EU geographic cross-Region inference remains unchanged | 
Amazon Bedrock prompt caching strategies
Amazon Bedrock prompt caching reduces latency and input token costs by caching a contiguous prompt prefix from the start of a request through a cache checkpoint. A later request with the same prefix can read cached tokens at a reduced rate instead of processing them again. Cache entries have a time-to-live (TTL) that resets after a successful cache hit.
Caching is prefix-based rather than block-based. Request sections are evaluated in sequence—tools, system, then messages—so changing an earlier section invalidates matching content that follows it.
Cache checkpoints (explicit control)
With explicit cache checkpoints, you can choose the exact prefix boundary. Supported Claude models allow up to four checkpoints per request.
- Place each checkpoint after a stable, reusable prefix.
- Meet the model-specific minimum prefix size. For Claude Sonnet 4.5 the minimum is 1,024 tokens (see supported models and Regions).
- Checkpoints are evaluated in this order: tools, system, and messages.
- Changing an earlier section invalidates cache matches for later sections.
- The default TTL is 5 minutes. Select models support a 1-hour TTL by setting "ttl": "1h". Longer-TTL entries must precede shorter-TTL entries.
Simplified cache management (automated)
With simplified cache management, you place one checkpoint after static content. Amazon Bedrock searches backward from that point for the longest matching prefix, up to about 20 content blocks.
- One checkpoint can locate the longest matching prefix automatically.
- Use explicit checkpoints when stable content extends beyond the lookback range.
What ArisGlobal cached, and what they deliberately did not
ArisGlobal uses one explicit checkpoint immediately after the shared prompt prefix, which is sent first. The per-case document follows the checkpoint and is processed on each request.
This reverses the initial request order. Because only a prefix can be cached, ordering determines which content can be reused.
The launch design: Prioritizing document reuse
The first design put the 10–200 page source document at the start of each request and placed the checkpoint after it. The shared prompt prefix and section-specific question followed the checkpoint.
The design reused the document within one case: the first request wrote it to cache, and later requests for that case read it at the reduced rate.
The next case used a different document and required a new cache write, so reuse never extended across cases or tenants.
More importantly, the shared prompt prefix remained after the checkpoint and was processed at the full input rate on every request. The content driving the cost curve was excluded from the cache.
The evolved production design: Prioritizing shared-prefix reuse
The production design changed the order rather than adding another checkpoint: the shared prompt prefix comes first, the checkpoint follows it, and the document comes last.
The same checkpoint now creates a reusable fleet-wide cache entry:
- Before — the cached document prefix was unique to one case and the shared prompt was never cached.
- After — the cached shared prompt prefix repeats across requests, cases, and tenants using the same agent.
ArisGlobal gave up limited document reuse within one case and gained prompt reuse across the fleet. The shared prefix is also the part that grows as customers are added.
Updated implementation
For most active accounts, cases arrive about every 5 minutes per tenant and multiple tenants run concurrently. This traffic keeps the shared prefix warm during business hours because each cache hit resets the TTL.
Caching both the prompt and the document
A second checkpoint after the document would cache a combined prefix consisting of the shared prompt and that case’s document. The entry would still be unique to one case.
ArisGlobal therefore prioritized the prefix whose reads amortize across the fleet. The shared prompt prefix scales across cases and tenants. The per-case document does not.
In production, 65% of input tokens on a typical request are served from the shared prompt cache. Figure 1 shows cache reads consistently exceeding cache writes.
Results
Caching the shared prompt prefix produced the following results while the EU geographic cross-Region inference profile remained in place:
- 65% of input tokens served from cache at the reduced read rate.
- Up to 25% lower end-to-end latency on cached production requests.
- Approximately 50% lower effective input cost.
- Approximately 40% lower overall monthly inference spend at more than 19 billion tokens per month.
- Around 15% more enterprise tenants onboarded without proportional cost increases.
- EU geographic routing unchanged. Prompt caching operates within the existing inference configuration.
Based on ArisGlobal’s production billing data, serving 65% of input tokens from cache reduced effective input cost by approximately 50%. At more than 19 billion tokens per month, this produced approximately 40% overall monthly savings in inference spend.
Note: All performance and cost figures in this section reflect ArisGlobal’s production metrics as reported to AWS. Results will vary based on prompt structure, traffic patterns, and cache hit rates.
Production learnings
ArisGlobal’s experience offers guidance for many workloads with large, repeated prompt prefixes:
Cache what repeats, not what is largest. A large per-case document offers limited reuse, while a byte-identical shared prompt prefix can serve requests across the fleet.
Put stable content first. Order tool definitions, system instructions, schemas, and examples before the checkpoint. Place tenant identifiers, case data, and the per-request question afterward.
Use fleet traffic to amortize cache writes. Requests from tenants using the same agent can read the same prefix, and cache hits reset the TTL. For sporadic traffic, evaluate the 1-hour TTL on supported models.
Reduce avoidable calls. Each call still processes the uncached document, so bundle sequential questions when output limits and schema requirements permit.
Keep the prefix byte-identical. Timestamps, request IDs, tenant names, and reordered tool definitions can cause misses. Move every dynamic element after the checkpoint.
Monitor the production baseline. Track cache reads, cache writes, and total input tokens in CloudWatch. Alert on a sustained drop below the normal 65% cache-hit baseline rather than using an incompatible 80% threshold.
Check model-specific limits. Prefix minimums and TTL options vary by model. Claude Sonnet 4.5 requires at least 1,024 tokens for a cache checkpoint.
Conclusion
ArisGlobal combined EU geographic cross-Region inference with prompt caching aimed at the right content. Caching the stable shared prefix instead of the per-case document reduced effective input cost by approximately 50%, contributed to approximately 40% overall monthly inference savings, and supported around 15% more enterprise tenants without proportional cost increases.
The key lesson is that cache value depends on reuse, not size. For multi-tenant agentic workloads, a repeated shared prompt prefix can be more valuable than a larger document that changes for every case.
To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock prompt caching documentation, the cross-Region inference guide, and the AWS blog post Effectively use prompt caching on Amazon Bedrock.

articles.title: Nommé avant d'être testé : GTA 6 relance le débat sur les Game Awards 2026 — Frandroid
articles.text:
Treize ans après GTA V, Rockstar sort enfin GTA 6 ce jeudi 19 novembre sur PS5 et Xbox Series. À part une poignée de testeurs, personne n’y a encore joué. Le jeu est pourtant déjà le plus nommé des Game Awards 2026, la cérémonie de Geoff Keighley, avec huit nominations annoncées ce mardi 17 novembre, dont celle du jeu de l’année. La situation fait grincer des dents, mais elle respecte bien le règlement à la lettre.
En plus du jeu de l’année, GTA 6 est nommé pour la meilleure direction, la meilleure narration, la meilleure direction artistique, la meilleure musique, le meilleur design sonore, le meilleur jeu d’action-aventure et la meilleure performance d’acteur, pour Manni L. Perez (Lucia Caminos).
Pour le titre suprême du GOTY (Game of the Year), il affronte 007 First Light, Control Resonant, Phantom Blade 0, Resident Evil Requiem et le remake de The Legend of Zelda : Ocarina of Time sur Switch 2.
Un jour d’avance sur la date limite
Le règlement des Game Awards accepte tous les jeux commercialisés avant le 20 novembre 2026 à 21 heures, heure du Pacifique, soit le 21 novembre à 6 heures du matin à Paris.
GTA 6 passe donc avec un peu plus d’une journée de marge, au point que des joueurs ont soupçonné l’organisation d’avoir taillé ce calendrier sur mesure.
Geoff Keighley a balayé l’idée dans une interview à Variety : les dates sont les mêmes chaque année, et les éditeurs en tiennent sans doute compte pour caler leurs sorties.
Comment un jeu non sortie peut-il être nommé ?
Comment juger un jeu que personne n’a pu acheter ? Les nominations sont choisies par un jury de plus de 160 médias et créateurs de contenu, qui peuvent recevoir des versions anticipées des jeux, précise l’organisation dans un communiqué relayé par PC Gamer.
Ce sont donc des professionnels qui ont pu tester GTA 6 en avance qui ont pu voter pour nommer le jeu comme jeu de l’année. On ignore toutefois combien de jurés ont vraiment eu GTA 6 entre les mains. Rockstar n’a jamais officialisé la date de publication des tests, mais les premiers sont attendus ce mercredi 18 novembre, la veille d’une sortie qu’on suit en direct.
Les gagnants seront connus le jeudi 10 décembre à Los Angeles, dans la nuit du 10 au 11 décembre, heure française.

articles.title: He convertido una presentación en una web con Gemini Notebook. Solo tuve que pedírselo
articles.text:
Los cuadernos de Gemini son una de las mejores funciones de la IA si necesitas trabajar sobre tus propios documentos. He usado Gemini Notebook (el antiguo NotebookLM, que Google rebautizó en julio) para documentos de estudio y de trabajo: basta con meterle todos los archivos como fuentes para que la IA responda a partir de esos archivos. Sin que se vaya a buscar fuera, lo que reduce (aunque no elimina) las alucinaciones. Y si con un cuaderno no tienes suficiente, puedes convertirlo en una página web. Con sus enlaces y todo.
Tu cuaderno es una web. Google ha introducido una novedad en Gemini Notebook: la opción de convertir cualquiera de los cuadernos en una página web interactiva. Basta con pedírselo a la IA con solo escribir “Móntame una página web”. Gemini se pondrá a la tarea y convertirá el cuaderno en una página que queda guardada dentro del propio cuaderno. Google permite abrirla en local como pestaña nueva y compartirla con otras personas.
Una manera más práctica de centralizar la información. Una vez subidas todas las fuentes, ya sean documentos, archivos o enlaces, Gemini puede generar todo tipo de contenido a partir de ellas. Al crear una página web, la herramienta organiza todo el contenido para que quede más accesible, navegable y visual. Y como todos sabemos movernos por una web, consultar así el cuaderno resulta más cómodo.
El proceso de creación es sencillo y solo necesita un pequeño prompt. La generación tarda unos minutos, según el volumen de fuentes que tenga el cuaderno. Una vez terminada la página, aparece en el área de Studio de Gemini Notebook: al pulsar sobre el icono se abre la web en pantalla.
Diseño pulido y minimalista. He estado probando la nueva herramienta y he creado una página completa a partir de una presentación que tenía guardada en Gemini Notebook. La calidad del resultado ha sido realmente buena: me parece un excelente complemento a los demás formatos que ya genera, como las presentaciones (descargables en PDF o PowerPoint) o las infografías.
No es del todo nuevo. Google acaba de anunciarlo, pero, en sí misma, la creación de páginas web no era algo extraño para quien ya usaba sus cuadernos: bastaba con añadir el cuaderno como fuente en la app de Gemini y pedirle la web a la herramienta Canvas. Lo que sí es nuevo es que ahora se hace sin salir de Gemini Notebook, y que la página queda a mano en el apartado Studio. Bajo mis pruebas, Google mejoró la calidad del resultado y la forma en que la IA organiza el contenido.
Si utilizas Gemini Notebook habitualmente, ahora puedes convertir tu contenido en una web de manera más sencilla. No debes activar nada: la función se está desplegando en todo el mundo. Si aún no te aparece, toca esperar un poco. Google no aclara si hay diferencias entre la versión gratuita y los planes de pago.

Good morning ☀️️
Cape Town has a date with AI this Friday, and TechCabal’s publisher is taking the stage.
On November 20, OpenAI Academy, Andela, and Innovation City are bringing the Codex Champions Showcase to Cape Town, South Africa, with a focus on how Africans can use AI to tell their own stories.
Tomiwa Aladekomo, chief executive of Big Cabal Media, TechCabal’s parent company, will join Jessica Hope, founder of communications agency Wimbart, for a conversation about storytelling in the age of AI.
And it won’t be all talk. Five finalists from Andela’s talent network will demonstrate tools they’ve built with OpenAI’s Codex to help African creators tell better stories, reach bigger audiences, and bring their ideas to life. The showcase has already made stops in Nairobi and Lagos. Cape Town gets its turn this Friday, from 4 p.m. to 8 p.m. SAST.
If you’re in town, register here. Come for the ideas, stay for the demos, and say hello to Tomiwa.
Now, on to today’s stories.
—Emmanuel
TC Mzansi, our newsletter covering South African tech is coming on November 23.
Internet
Starlink issued notice to cease unauthorised operations in South Africa
Starlink has spent three years finding its way into South African homes without officially launching there. The country’s telecoms regulator has finally sent it a message: No licence, no Internet party.
On October 14, South Africa’s Independent Communications Authority (ICASA), the country’s telecoms regulator, issued a formal notice of non-compliance to SpaceX, Elon Musk’s aerospace company, ordering it to stop providing unauthorised Starlink services in the country.
Communications Minister Solly Malatsi disclosed the order in a parliamentary response. Starlink isn’t licenced in South Africa, but some residents haven’t stopped using it.
Explain like I’m new here: Since 2023, South Africans, particularly those in poorly connected rural areas, have used Starlink’s international roaming service to get online. The trick was to buy a Starlink dish, register it in a neighbouring country like Lesotho, and use it back home—no South African licence required.
Starlink recently tried closing that loophole. It tightened roaming restrictions, cutting the permitted stay from 60 days to 30 days, then to just seven days for users in South Africa. In October, the company introduced stricter identity and country-of-origin checks to stop customers from registering their kits abroad and using them indefinitely in South Africa.
Some users had already found creative workarounds, from temporarily switching their kits off to crossing the border to reset their roaming clocks. ICASA wasn’t amused.
Here’s the bigger problem: South Africa’s telecoms licencing rules require at least 30% ownership by historically disadvantaged groups. The government has proposed allowing qualifying investments in local businesses and skills development as an alternative, but the regulatory framework remains contested.
Zoom out: This is about more than a few satellite dishes. Starlink offers a way to reach communities that traditional broadband networks struggle to serve. South Africa also has a legitimate interest in ensuring telecoms providers follow its licencing rules.
ICASA’s investigation is ongoing, and it has yet to determine any penalties. South Africa wants Starlink to use the front door. The country is still arguing over what the key should look like.

Telecoms
MTN revives bid to take over Telkom
MTN seems to have developed a taste for big infrastructure deals. In February, the telco giant agreed to buy the remaining 75.3% of IHS Towers—one of Africa’s largest independent tower companies—that it did not already own. Now it is back knocking on Telkom’s door.
What happened? MTN Group is back in talks to acquire rival Telkom, a South African telecoms group, four years after an earlier attempt fell apart. The discussions are early, but MTN is considering a cash offer, and Telkom shareholders could potentially take MTN shares instead.
Explain like I’m new here: In 2022, the two companies held takeover discussions, but MTN wanted Telkom to consider its proposal without negotiating competing offers. Rain, another South African telecoms operator, had expressed interest in Telkom at the time. MTN eventually walked away.
Competition regulators will be circling: Combining two major mobile operators could give the merged business considerable influence over prices, infrastructure and access to customers. Regulators would want to know whether the benefits of combining networks outweigh the risk of reducing competition. In 2024, the Competition Tribunal blocked Vodacom’s proposed 30% investment in Maziv, the company housing fibre operators Vumatel and Dark Fibre Africa, for similar reasons. After a series of appeals, it secured approval in August 2025. That likely gave MTN some reason to believe consolidation is possible.
What it could mean: MTN reported 39.49 million South African subscribers in June, while Telkom had 25.67 million mobile subscribers in March. Together, that is about 65.2 million subscribers. Hurdles remain as the South African government owns 40.5% of Telkom, while the Public Investment Corporation (PIC), the state’s investment arm, holds another 11.08%. No deal has been agreed, and the companies say there is no certainty one will happen.
Capital Markets
NGX buys a piece of Kenya’s stock market
The NGX Group, the parent company of the Nigerian Exchange (NGX) and other market infrastructure businesses, has bought a 10% equity stake in the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE), the institution that operates Kenya’s main stock market.
Explain like I’m new here: In 2024, NGX Group invested in the Ethiopian Securities Exchange (ESX), the country’s first-ever bourse in decades. NGX became a 10% shareholder and secured a seat on its board. ESX launched in January 2025, and it still has a long way to go before becoming a busy cross-border investment corridor.
NGX is not alone in this strategy, as exchange operators are looking beyond their home markets for investment returns and opportunities to build regional relationships. In 2021, the NSE acquired an additional 4% stake in Tanzania’s Dar es Salaam Stock Exchange.
What could this unlock? A Nigerian investor buying shares in a Kenyan company may face different brokers, regulations, settlement arrangements, and currency-conversion requirements. NGX’s investment could help connect these markets. The Dangote Refinery share sale, which allowed regional investors to participate through local market operators, offers a glimpse of what cross-border access can look like. Companies could eventually reach investors in more than one market.
Yet, owning 10% of the Kenyan bourse does not automatically create a shared trading platform or remove the regulatory and currency hurdles between the two markets.
Fintech
Payaza secures Kenyan licence
Payaza has been collecting something more useful than passport stamps: regulators’ signatures.
Just 17 days after securing approval in Zambia, the Nigerian-founded payments company has landed another one in Kenya. In an email on Monday, Payaza announced to merchants in two words in Swahili: Ni rasmi! It’s official!
The Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) granted the company a payment service provider licence on November 5, allowing it to process online payments for Kenyan businesses.
Explain like I’m new here: Payaza provides the infrastructure that helps businesses accept payments from customers. It says it operates in more than 27 countries worldwide, including Nigeria, Ghana, Uganda, Tanzania, and South Africa.
Its latest approval lets Kenyan merchants use Payaza to accept card payments, mobile money, and bank transfers. The company also plans to support merchant settlements and cross-border collections.
Between the lines: Payaza isn’t getting permission to become another M-PESA. Its licence covers payment gateway services, not customer wallets or deposit-taking. The Kenyan approval follows an October 19 authorisation from the Bank of Zambia, which designated Payaza as a payment system operator.
Zoom out: Kenya is hardly short of ways to pay. But collecting money from customers across different African markets remains complicated by local banking systems, currencies and regulations.
Payaza is betting that businesses would rather use one payments provider than piece together a different solution in every country.
Two licences in 17 days is impressive paperwork. Getting merchants to use those payment rails is where the real business begins.

articles.title: Defect-Aware Chiplet Matching For Heterogeneous Integration Yield (ASU, Ampere)
articles.text:
Researchers at Arizona State University and Ampere Computing published “DT-MATCH: Defect- and Topology-Aware Chiplet Matching for Yield Optimization in Heterogeneous Integration.”
Abstract
“Heterogeneous integration (HI) and advanced packaging enable chiplet-based system-on-chip (SoC) designs; however, they also introduce new yield challenges arising from manufacturing defects and complex die-to-die (D2D) interconnect constraints. In particular, lane-level defects, limited spares, and strict structural compatibility requirements impede the efficient assembly of functional systems from defective but repairable chiplets. We present DT-MATCH, a defect- and topology-aware chiplet matching framework that maximizes the number of functional SoCs under realistic assembly constraints. DT-MATCH provides two complementary approaches. The integer linear programming (ILP)-based approach is implemented using a batching strategy to approximate the exact formulation. The greedy randomized adaptive search procedure (GRASP)-based approach provides substantial acceleration, but it does not guarantee yield optimality. Both approaches use a preprocessing pipeline to reduce the problem size. Experimental results on industrial designs demonstrate that, as expected, the ILP-based approach achieves superior solution quality. The GRASP-based approach leads to lower runtimes while still achieving solution quality that is comparable to the ILP-based solution. Together, these methods provide a trade-off between solution quality and efficiency for practical chiplet assembly optimization.”
Find the technical paper here. November 2026.
Xuanyi Tan, Sanmitra Banerjee, Dhruv Thapar, Sreejit Chakravarty, and Krishnendu Chakrabarty. “DT-MATCH: Defect- and Topology-Aware Chiplet Matching for Yield Optimization in Heterogeneous Integration.” arXiv:2611.19544, November 14, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19544.

articles.title: A developer got Doom to run on a USB flash drive, and file transfers are the controls
articles.text:
The takeaway: Doom now runs on a 128GB USB flash drive with its own built-in screen, and players control the game by copying files to the drive or reading files from it. The port is the work of Aaron Christophel, a German embedded software developer and hardware hacker known online as atc1441, whose earlier Doom ports include an electric toothbrush, a Xiaomi Mi Band 10 and a toy video walkie-talkie.
Keeping the whole game on the drive meant working with limited hardware. At the end, Christophel got the USB drive's display chip to handle all of the rendering, input, saves and reloads without any help from the computer it's plugged into.
Christophel says the microcontroller that drives the screen has 128KB of SRAM, 2MB of flash memory, and a measured clock speed of 40MHz. The SRAM is the chip's working memory, where the game has to keep its active state while it runs. The flash has to hold the program code and the game data. With those limits, the original DOS release of Doom was never going to fit.
Instead, Christophel turned to DMC100-DOOM, a stripped-down port by Polish developer Artur Bieniek. Bieniek wrote it for an AC/DC digital clamp meter, a handheld tool electricians use to measure current. The meter's chip has just 32KB of RAM, so Bieniek had the port draw the screen in strips instead of holding a full frame in memory. That focus on squeezing Doom into very little memory made it a natural match for a display controller in a USB stick.
The controls are the strangest part of the project. A flash drive has no buttons, no D-pad and no joystick. To the host computer, it's just storage, so Christophel used the file system as the input. Each transfer becomes a command the game understands, like moving forward or firing. The result is an unusual setup where a file manager works like a gamepad.
In Christophel's YouTube video, the game runs locally at about 13 frames per second. That's technically playable, though probably not much fun. However, the project is meant to show what the hardware can do, not to offer a better way to play a 33-year-old shooter.
The demo also says something about how capable cheap, single-purpose chips have become. When Doom came out in 1993, running it well on a typical home PC wasn't easy. Today, a chip whose job is to show status information on a USB stick's small screen can run the game at a rate that's usable, if barely. Christophel said the drive is a clear case of modern hardware having "too much processing power" for the job it was built to do.
The flash drive is the latest in a run of similar projects for the developer. Just last week, Christophel got Doom running on an Anker power bank.

articles.title: Un robot de 53 dedos sorprendió al tocar Chopin junto a un pianista en Italia
articles.text:
TeoTronico, un robot pianista de 53 dedos, compartió escenario con el músico italiano Roberto Prosseda en Prato, ciudad de la región de Toscana, en un encuentro que puso frente a frente la precisión mecánica y la expresividad humana. Ambos interpretaron piezas de Chopin, alternando solos antes de tocar juntos en una misma actuación.
Según informó Euronews, el programa incluyó también obras de Mozart y Rimsky-Korsakov, donde el autómata exhibió su capacidad de sincronización y exactitud. El evento no tuvo un ganador declarado: su propósito fue plantear una pregunta que atraviesa el mundo del arte y la tecnología, si una máquina puede transmitir emoción a través de la música.
TeoTronico tiene 53 dedos y supera los límites anatómicos del pianista humano
El robot fue creado en 2008 por el ingeniero italiano Matteo Suzzi y funciona mediante electroimanes e instrucciones informáticas que le permiten pulsar las teclas con una exactitud difícil de igualar. Sus 53 dedos le otorgan una ventaja mecánica concreta: puede ejecutar combinaciones y velocidades que están fuera del alcance de cualquier mano humana.
A lo largo de la actuación, el pianista mecánico demostró que sus interpretaciones son impecables desde el punto de vista técnico. Cada nota cayó en el momento exacto, sin vacilaciones ni variaciones, con una regularidad que ningún intérprete puede sostener durante toda una pieza. A diferencia de un músico de carne y hueso, el autómata no se fatiga, no comete errores por tensión ni reinterpreta una partitura según su estado de ánimo: ejecuta exactamente lo que se le instruyó, cada vez.
El robot también está integrado con Gemini, el chatbot de Google, lo que le permite mantener conversaciones con el público en tiempo real y responder preguntas sobre las piezas que interpreta.
Prosseda sostuvo que ninguna máquina puede reemplazar la emoción humana en la música
Frente a esa exhibición de destreza, el pianista italiano defendió que la perfección técnica no puede sustituir la emoción y la conexión humana que están en el corazón de la música. Para Prosseda, tocar no es solo reproducir notas con exactitud: es comunicar algo que surge de la experiencia, la memoria y la sensibilidad del intérprete, elementos que no se programan.
La postura del músico resume un debate que recorre el mundo del arte desde que las máquinas empezaron a imitar procesos creativos. La pregunta no es si un robot puede tocar bien, sino si puede tocar con significado. Chopin, cuya obra estuvo en el centro de la velada, es uno de los compositores donde esa distinción se vuelve más evidente: sus partituras exigen matices de dinámica y rubato que los intérpretes modulan de manera personal en cada ejecución. En ese terreno, el pianista marcó una línea clara entre ejecución y expresión artística.
Desde su creación, el robot acumuló actuaciones en festivales y espacios académicos de Europa
El autómata participó a lo largo de los años en numerosos encuentros donde musicólogos, ingenieros y artistas analizan los límites de la interpretación automatizada. Suzzi lo concibió como una herramienta de investigación musical y tecnológica, y la máquina recorrió festivales y espacios académicos en distintos países del continente.
El encuentro con Prosseda en la Toscana continúa esa línea. Lejos de presentar al robot como amenaza o al humano como víctima de la automatización, el evento funcionó como un espacio de contraste: ambos intérpretes compartieron el mismo piano, el mismo repertorio y el mismo escenario, pero con aproximaciones radicalmente distintas.
El debate sobre si los autómatas pueden expresar emoción a través del arte no tiene aún una respuesta definitiva. Lo que quedó claro en Prato es que la tecnología ya alcanzó la perfección técnica, y que la siguiente frontera —si existe— está en otro lugar.

articles.title: How Québec Tech companies are turning breakthrough technologies into global growth | BetaKit
articles.text:
For Montréal-based ChillSkyn, deciding where to sell its hardtech innovation required finding customers with an expensive heat problem. Its specialized coating is designed to keep refrigerated trucks cool in the sun, making the southern United States, Mexico, and Brazil promising places to start.
“The science may be universal, but trust is built locally.”
Patrick Racine, ChillSkyn
The company had invested heavily in third-party validation but quickly learned that prospective buyers wanted to see the technology work in their own markets before committing any dollars.
“The science may be universal, but trust is built locally,” said Patrick Racine, co-founder and CEO.
Today, as the company prepares to grow further, it’s turning to Québec Tech for help with what comes next. ChillSkyn is one of 12 companies recently awarded the Stage V distinction, which is designed to create more hyper-growth scaleups in the province through tailored guidance, specialized expertise, and financial assistance. All 12 companies have validated their business models and begun to expand outside of the province.
BetaKit spoke with three of the newly distinguished companies about what early expansion has taught them so far, and how Québec Tech’s support can help them tackle their next big goals.
Building a presence abroad
The new round of Stage V companies was announced on Nov. 11 and spans AI, robotics, healthtech, industrial innovation, and the circular economy. They share international ambitions but need different kinds of support along the way.
For Longueuil-based Rbot9, that means help finding the right partners in markets it already serves. The company—which develops industrial cable robots to handle jobs in food processing, warehousing, and industrial painting—began putting its technology to work abroad before installing a system in Québec or elsewhere in Canada.
President and founder Frédéric Vachon said the company went where labour shortages and operational challenges were creating the greatest need. Customers were willing to invest in unfamiliar technology if it could solve a pressing problem.
Winning an order, however, was only part of the work.
“Unlike software, you can’t just deploy a robot remotely. There’s shipping, installation, integration, training, and ongoing technical support to consider,” he said.
Every facility is different, too. Layouts, equipment, and operating requirements vary, and Rbot9 has to make its technology fit without having to customize every installation.
The company works with local automation specialists who understand customers’ facilities and can help install and support the equipment. That leaves it free to focus on developing and manufacturing its technology.
Through Québec Tech, Vachon wants help strengthening those kinds of partnerships and navigating local regulations as the company looks to double its sales over the next 12 to 18 months. Advice from people who have already grown hardware businesses internationally would be particularly valuable.
“We’re looking for practical guidance, strong connections, and access to networks that would otherwise take years to build on our own,” he said.
Getting closer to customers
Québec City-based Lightbeans creates digital versions of building materials such as tile, wood, and stone, helping architects and designers see how products would look before ordering physical samples. Manufacturers pay to have their materials digitized and listed on the platform, while design professionals use it for free.
Co-founder and CEO Philippe Hébert said growth depends on attracting both groups. The more materials designers can find, the more useful the platform becomes. Their participation, in turn, gives manufacturers a reason to join.
Doing business in the US has meant making that process smoother. Shipping materials can be a barrier, so Lightbeans adapted its technology to work from fewer samples. It also helps manufacturers navigate delivery.
Earning buyers’ confidence has taken time, too. Hébert described the building materials industry as conservative, with demanding sales cycles. It’s why he spends more time meeting people face to face, including at recent industry gatherings in Tennessee and Arizona.
“Those meetings build a level of trust no digital campaign can replace,” he said.
Recruiting salespeople remains one of the company’s biggest challenges. Through Québec Tech, Hébert hopes to learn from entrepreneurs who have built a successful US team or a two-sided platform. The company is also exploring a US service location to be closer to customers.
Support at the right time
For ChillSkyn, the next challenge is building a sales network to sell its technology abroad. Racine said this is new territory for his team and that he wants to connect with others who’ve done it before.
“We’ve learned a tremendous amount through our early international expansion, but we recognize that we have even more to learn,” he said.
Stage V companies can also access up to $100,000 to cover up to 65 percent of professional fees for local or international experts, plus up to $10,000 for international travel. Racine said the financial support will help the company put its sales plans into action sooner.
ChillSkyn has its sights set on becoming an established name in refrigerated transportation across North, South, and Central America, while opening new markets and industries along the way. Racine said young companies like his that start selling abroad early can struggle to find the support they need, with many international growth programs favouring more mature businesses.
“Québec Tech recognized this gap and is playing an important role in helping Québec technology companies compete internationally,” he said. “We’re grateful to be part of that effort.”

articles.title: How Shopify Orchestrates AI-Powered Mobile App Development Without Overloading Developers' Machines
articles.text:
To prevent AI development workflows from exhausting developer machines' resources, Shopify built Remote Dev, a remote mobile development environment that enables AI agents to independently build, test and maintain iOS and Android applications and in parallel.
In fact, according to Shopify engineers, running agentic workflows in parallel quickly hogs all resources available on development machines. They explain that "three or four workflows were enough to max out a laptop", on top of the resources already consumed by compilers, simulators, and emulators. Moreover, "if someone accidentally closed a laptop lid, the work stopped".
Shopify had previously built River to address the same challenge in web and backend development, but, being River a Linux-based solution, it could not be used for building iOS apps. To overcome this limitation, Shopify built Remote Dev:
With Remote Dev, we're no longer limited by how many builds and simulators our laptops can handle. Each River session gets its own environment, so we can have one agent debugging something on Android, another working on an iOS feature, and another testing a PR, all in parallel.
Remote Dev uses a fleet of remote Macs running Shopify's development environment and iOS simulators, accessible via SSH. Android emulators run on separate Linux VMs. This architecture allows developers to build and test both iOS and Android builds through the same SSH session.
Agents can work on multiple tasks in parallel, each with its own environment for maximum independence. They can also be accessed through a Slack channel backed by River. Thanks to this setup, Remote Dev can
implement changes, build the app, run tests, interact with the simulators, collect screenshots, and create a PR. If something fails, it can inspect the logs, fix the issue, and try again, all while we focus on other tasks.
The platform supports automated workflows, including overnight runs that identify bugs, implement fixes, and submit PRs. Agents can also verify that a build is functional by navigating through the app, interacting with its UI, reproducing bugs, recording current behavior, implementing fixes, and running the same interaction to verify the fix.
Shopify says that, after promoting internal adoption through demonstrations and storytelling, River's share of merged PRs increased from 6% to 61%.
Commenting on Shopify's article, LinkedIn user Raiyan Jugbhery, in charge of software infrastructure and founder at SpendMe, argued that the key advantage of Remove Dev is its Xcode and iOS Simulator integration, noting that "a PR you still have to pull and verify on a Mac isn't really autonomous". However, he pointed out that the article does not explain "how they keep builds from queuing when several agents ask for a Mac at once", which he identified as a key concern.
Junaid Raza, solutions architect at Hoboetech, raised another concern. Allowing agents to run the simulator could lead to unreliable test results, as "give [the agent] a red test and enough retries and it'll sometimes rewrite the test until it passes". To prevent this, he suggests prohibiting runner agents from modifying the tests they execute.
Shopify says it plans to expand the platform with continuous application health monitoring, automated crash detection and fixes, and PR generation for identified issues, among other capabilities.

articles.title: Xiaomi actualiza su Smart Band y su Watch y presenta los Xiaomi Clips, sus primeros auriculares abiertos
articles.text:
Junto con los nuevos Xiaomi 18 Pro y 18 Pro Max, la compañía también ha renovado algunos de sus wearables más interesantes. En este sentido, ha presentado la nueva Xiaomi Smart Band 11, el Xiaomi Watch S5 y los auriculares Xiaomi Clip. La mayoría de renovaciones de productos que ya conocemos, pero con especificaciones y precios que los siguen haciendo muy interesantes.
En el caso de Xiaomi Smart Band 11 (y su versión con NFC), vuelve a repetir con un modelo muy estilizado con pantalla AMOLED de 1,72" de 60 Hz y 2000 nits, con biseles simétricos ultradelgados y su batería de larga duración de hasta 21 días. Como es habitual, hace gala de sensores clave para la monitorización de la salud, incluyendo seguimiento de la frecuencia cardíaca de alta precisión, una gestión del sueño mejorada con orientación personalizada y más de 150 modos deportivos.
Por su parte, el modelo con NFC también tiene pantalla AMOLED de 1,72", también con biseles simétricos ultradelgados, pero con hasta 18 días de batería, con el extra de poder usar el NFC seguro para pagos sin contacto.
- Xiaomi Smart Band 11 Standard Edition (en Negro, Plateado, Rosa, Morado y Dorado) por 54,99 €.
- Xiaomi Smart Band 11 NFC Edition (en Negro, Plateado y Rosa) por 67,99 €.
- Xiaomi Smart Band 11 Unibody Edition en color morado por 75,99 €.
- Xiaomi Smart Band 11 Ceramic Edition en color Blanco Perla por 75,99 €.
Xiaomi Watch S5 41mm por fin compatible con Google Wallet
Para el Xiaomi Watch S5, la compañía ha optado por un diseño compacto de acero inoxidable de 9,9 mm de grosor que incorpora nuevas asas articuladas con una pantalla AMOLED de 1,32 pulgadas, lo que ofrece más espacio para alojar una batería de mayor tamaño, de 590 mAh, con hasta 14 días de autonomía entre cargas. Respecto a su pantalla, tiene brillo máximo de hasta 3.000 nits, por lo que garantiza muy buena lectura incluso con mucha luz.
La gran novedad de este nuevo reloj inteligente de Xiaomi es que por fin es compatible con Google Wallet para los pagos móviles NFC, que se suma a la compatibilidad con Xiaomi Pay, que es compatible con tarjetas de más de 300 bancos asociados en Europa. Ambos modelos llegan al mercado con los siguientes precios:
Xiaomi repite de nuevo con su apuesta por la salud. El S5 ofrece más de 150 modos deportivos, con algunas funciones extras como Workout Picks, que recomienda tipos y duraciones de entrenamiento en función de la meteorología, la condición física, los hábitos de ejercicio y el nivel de forma física; o Health Summary, que analiza más de 50 métricas de actividad física, sueño y salud para identificar cambios. Además de la monitorización del sueño con Sleep Algorithm 2.0, que según la compañía mejora en un 11 % la precisión al detectar el momento de conciliación del sueño y el despertar, y en un 14 % la precisión de las fases del sueño.
Sobre su precio, el Xiaomi Watch S5 41mm estará disponible en Negro, Azul o Blanco Cerámico por un precio especial de 194,99 €.

articles.title: Classified Communications Network at the National Security Agency Goes Down, Defense Official Says
articles.text:
An internal network the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline Tuesday after what the agency described as “routine maintenance.”
The problem disrupted the operations of NSANet, a classified internal network used by employees of the agency, according to a defense official who was not authorized to discuss the matter by name and spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity.
“The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the NSA said in a statement. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.”
The intelligence agency did not provide any additional details on the cause of the outage or the scope of the disruption.
The outage was first reported by CNN.
The NSA episode is among a series of cyber-related disruptions to critical government and private sector functions in the last week, including a system overload Friday that resulted in a ground stop of air traffic in the United States, a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase on Monday that caused ripple effects in the financial system and an internal systems outage at United Airlines that delayed departing flights.
On Tuesday , Apple acknowledged on its system status page that its Apple Music, App Store and AppleCare services suffered full outages after an internal update.
Top Trump administration national security officials said there was no indication that the events are related or attributable to a cyberattack or hostile activity.
“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation-state, with a malign actor of any kind,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is also Trump’s national security adviser, told reporters while traveling with the president in Asia.
Rubio acknowledged that it was “unsettling to see these reports day after day of some technical failures” and that while the government is always vigilant, each of the recent events “are distinct, and they’re different in their causation — in some cases, highly technical.”
Jay Clayton, the Trump administration’s director of national intelligence, attributed the problem to government institutions and private companies pushing through upgrades of their computer systems around the same time, resulting in periodic technological hiccups.
“Many people are patching their systems,” Clayton said in a CNBC interview Tuesday about the spate of disruptions. “They know that their legacy systems have vulnerabilities. They’re outdated, they don’t work well with new systems. It is time for an upgrade across our digital infrastructure. And as you patch and upgrade your systems — taking them down and bringing them back up — there are things like this that happen.”
Sen. Mark Warner, the Democratic vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, echoed that assessment.
“AI is making it possible to identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” Warner said in a statement. “While we still need to get to the bottom of these incidents, the evidence so far points toward legitimate efforts to secure our systems, not malicious activity.”

articles.title: Apple services, including iCloud, App Store, Apple Music, and more, hit by outage | TechCrunch
articles.text:
After a recent slew of tech outages, service disruptions, and flight chaos this week, it’s now Apple customers who are facing technical issues.
The iPhone maker’s System Status page indicates that there are issues with iCloud’s Account & Sign In services affecting “all users,” which could make the service slow or unavailable. The App Store, AppleCare on Device, and Apple Music are also experiencing issues, the page indicates.
Like all major tech companies, Apple faces outages and other technical issues affecting its cloud services at times. However, today’s issues are likely more noticeable to end users because problems with iCloud can lead to account sign-in problems. This could cause your iPhone to ask for your Apple ID and password, and you could see other attempts to sign in to services with your Apple account information fail.
On Reddit, some folks also noted that they were unable to activate a new iPhone, which is likely related to these ongoing issues.
Given the recent increase in AI-driven cyberattacks, users across social media have already begun to speculate about the cause. In particular, users are expressing concerns about the Apple outage, as it arrives only days after technical failures at Microsoft led to its cloud systems that power flagship services like Outlook and Teams failing due to cascading software issues.
Similarly, a brief outage of Chase’s banking app this week garnered attention, as did an ongoing partial outage (at the time of publication) of the National Security Agency’s internal classified network, both of which were blamed on software glitches.
So far, none of the outages in the past week have been attributed to cyberattacks, but rather to technical problems.
Apple responded to TechCrunch’s request for comment (which it initially gave to Bloomberg), noting that the outages were caused by an internal update and not a cyberattack. “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible,” the statement read.
After the initial outages were reported, Apple’s status page was updated to include other outages impacting Apple School Manager, iCloud Mail, iCloud Web Apps (iCloud.com), Schoolwork, and the Volume Purchase Program.
By 6 PM ET on Tuesday, the status page showed all the outages were resolved.
This article was updated after publication with the status of the outages.

articles.title: Why adaptability beats capacity for data centers
articles.text:
Why adaptability beats capacity for data centers
AI is reshaping data center design, density, cooling and sustainability
There’s always a quiet moment of calm in my morning that usually comes just after the 6 a.m. handover from the night team, and before meetings with customers and prospects get started. It’s time I reserve for reflecting and planning, looking at both the week ahead and working on the longer-term requirements our facility needs to meet.
It’s the latter of those priorities that’s taking more of my time these days, and it reflects the changing nature of the conversations I’m having with CIOs and technology leaders. Two years ago, most customers, especially those in regulated sectors such as finance and healthcare, were asking about uptime, certification and cost.
Today, the first question is almost always about AI.
Head of Data Centre at Ilkari.
They want to know if the facility can support the capacity they’re going to need, and whether it can do so on a timeline that matches how quickly their workloads are scaling. These are fair and important questions, and, in all honesty, they are not always easy to answer.
The increase in demand, driven by AI, means decisions we previously had years to make, now need to be made in a matter of months. Not impossible, but it fundamentally changes the way we think about designing and running facilities longer term.
Density, not just capacity, is what matters for AI workloads
Around the world, capacity challenges dominate headlines, but the infrastructure story underneath it is almost entirely about power density, cooling, and grid capacity. Historically, infrastructure was designed for low power density, whereas today, AI needs much more power per rack as well as more advanced cooling.
A good example is a rack that housed standard enterprise workloads at 5 to 10 kVA two years ago is now being asked to support 15 kVA within the next 18 months, and we’re already planning to support 25 to 30 kVA within the next few years. That is not an incremental change. It requires a different physical design that provides more density in an efficient way, often through modular Performance Optimized Data Centre (POD) architecture and in-row cooling. This allows us to add power and cooling gradually, controlling investment, improving efficiency, and ultimately, allowing us to increase capacity as demand grows.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The lack of density for AI workloads is why many established markets, including some of Europe's data center hubs, are struggling to add capacity at the pace required by demand.
For CIOs evaluating a provider, the useful question isn't “do you have any capacity today?” it's “how does your design accommodate the density I'll need in three years?” because a facility built for yesterday's power needs can quickly become an operational risk if it can't be reconfigured without a lengthy rebuild.
A good example of this is a POD we recently reconfigured within 30 days to meet a customer’s changing requirements, changing 40 racks at 5 kVA, to 20 racks at 10 kVA to support high-density demands. It was a significant project, and the kind of turnaround that's only possible when a facility is designed for change and adaptability, rather than attempting to bolt flexibility on afterwards.
Cooling design has to keep pace with density
Managing excess heat caused by the increased processing demands of AI workloads is becoming an increasingly important part of infrastructure design and customer consideration.
The good news is that cooling technology is improving all the time, making high density possible without needing to prioritize colder climates.
We mostly use air cooling with in-row technology, and because our design is modular, we can increase cooling as the IT load grows. For example, our customers typically join with an initial setup and gradually scale their capacity as their requirements grow.
As the customer’s IT load increases, we progressively activate the in-row cooling units, ensuring that cooling capacity is only deployed when and where it is needed. We also use a refrigerant-based cooling system rather than a water-based one, which keeps our water consumption low to begin with
This approach allows us to operate more efficiently when it comes to both energy and water use, which, as we know, is under increasing scrutiny from regulators and communities alike, and as a limited resource, needs to be used responsibly.
Local footprint must be part of the design conversation, too
It’s been hard to escape the recent tranche of negative media coverage about data centers taking valuable resources (land, water and power) from local communities. It’s true that they have an impact on the local community, but it’s unfair to frame this as entirely negative.
In my experience, a site's economic footprint is much larger than the building itself. Beyond the direct operational jobs, data centers support a much wider chain of indirect employment in sectors such as security, maintenance, cleaning, logistics, and transport. They also drive investment in the surrounding energy and connectivity infrastructure.
The ability to serve the local community and economy, as well as our customers, is an integral part of my role. It’s also something I encourage technology leaders to consider as a legitimate part of their due diligence. After all, banks, government services, cloud providers, and now AI, all depend on the same underlying capacity, and the locations that can offer credible, well-designed and well-run infrastructure, also attract more technology investment, digital skills, and the surrounding ecosystem that a growing digital economy needs.
Sustainability has to be operational, not aspirational
The scrutiny on data centers' environmental footprint is only intensifying as AI-driven demand grows, and rightly so. When it comes to managing a facility, this means building sustainability into daily operations, rather than treating it as a future aspiration or initiative that is bolted on after the fact.
In practice, this means ensuring efficient cooling design, transparent community engagement, and genuine investment in the skilled engineering talent needed to run higher-density infrastructure safely. At Ilkari, we do this through our POD-based design and in-row cooling architecture, which allow us to scale cooling capacity efficiently as IT load grows, and maintain efficient and sustainable data center operations.
It also means working with local governments to make sure the right investments are being made in local power and energy infrastructure to allow us to operate in a way that is sustainable for the local community.
The infrastructure design questions CIOs should be asking
The reality of running a data centre as AI demand increases means a fundamental shift in how facilities need to be designed and built.
For CIOs thinking about what infrastructure requirements their AI workloads need, my advice is not to start with a capacity spreadsheet, but with a short list of broader questions, including:
- How does this provider's design scale with density, not just floor space?
- Can it demonstrate its ability to meet your requirements under real conditions, not just on paper?
- Is sustainability built into day-to-day operations (cooling design, community engagement, skilled engineering talent), or is it a separate initiative?
- As density increases, has the provider planned for the point where air cooling is no longer sufficient, and what alternative cooling technologies and infrastructure would that require?
In my experience, the organizations getting this right aren't the ones with the flashiest AI roadmap, they are the ones designing and building for change from the outset.

articles.title: SiMa.ai's Palette 3.0 runs many AI models on one chip and lifts throughput up to 3.5 times - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
SiMa.ai’s Palette 3.0 runs many AI models on one chip and lifts throughput up to 3.5 times
Physical artificial intelligence chip startup SiMa Technologies Inc. today released Palette 3.0, a new version of its Palette software suite intended to allow many AI models to run concurrently on one chip.
According to the company, the release, which builds on the Palette Neat agentic development environment launched in June, can raise model throughput by as much as 3.5 times.
Developers building drones, robots and other autonomous machines, which need to run AI models on the device rather than in a data center, are a primary focus of the release. SiMa.ai argues that while industry incumbents rely on adapting legacy data center technology, it builds its software and silicon exclusively for physical AI.
Leading the new capabilities in Palette 3.0 is improved concurrent model execution on SiMa.ai’s Modalix MLSoC. Maintaining what the company describes as a low-power profile, a single chip can handle complex reasoning and multimodel workloads at the same time. The platform can also run separate Docker containers on the chip. Supported workloads include large language models and vision-language models.
Perception, depth and reasoning models used by drones and robots are also said to run faster on the new version. Working with ecosystem partners, SiMa.ai has added unified sensor fusion, dense neural depth fields and closed-loop digital twin simulation to the platform. The goal of the additions, SiMa.ai says, is to remove the integration and validation bottlenecks that slow down autonomous development.
Performance figures for those models are published in a new Model Registry, which SiMa.ai says measures every result within real-world power constraints. The company is offering competitive benchmarking details on request.
Also new in the release is a set of open-source capabilities for generative AI application development. Behind the 3.5-times throughput figure is speculative decoding, using the EAGLE3, DFlash and Gemma 4 MTP algorithms. Support has also been added for large mixture-of-experts models such as OpenAI Group PBC’s GPT-OSS-20B, which can now run on the Modalix MLSoC 16GB system-on-module.
Developers are free to adapt the open-source code, which is available on GitHub. Documentation for Palette 3.0 is provided through SiMa.ai’s Developer Center.
Founded in 2018 by Chief Executive Krishna Rangasayee, SiMa.ai offers a platform that combines purpose-built silicon with software for AI on physical devices. Notable customers and partners include Robert Bosch GmbH, Emerson Electric Co. and Synopsys Inc.
SiMa.ai raised $150 million in a Series C round at a $1.45 billion valuation in September. Fidelity Management & Research Co. and Amplify Partners co-led the round. The company has raised $500 million to date.

articles.title: Votre Mac va vous faire réfléchir avant de laisser une IA prendre les commandes
articles.text:
Apple teste de nouveaux contrôles pour mieux encadrer l’accès des applications aux fichiers et aux autres logiciels du Mac. Avec la deuxième bêta de macOS 27.3, l’utilisateur est davantage invité à limiter les permissions plutôt qu’à donner les clés de toute sa machine.
L’IA s’installe sur nos ordinateurs, mais Apple n’entend pas lui dérouler le tapis rouge sans quelques contrôles à l’entrée. Le constructeur, qui fait de la protection des données un argument de vente, voit les assistants réclamer des accès toujours plus larges pour travailler à notre place. Avec macOS 27.3, il commence à mettre en œuvre le durcissement annoncé début octobre. Les utilisateurs pourront toujours accorder ces permissions, mais le système fera davantage pour leur expliquer ce qu’ils s’apprêtent à autoriser.
Donner accès à un dossier plutôt qu’à tout le disque
Apple détaille aujourd’hui les changements introduits avec macOS 27.3 bêta 2. Deux catégories sont concernées : l’accès complet au disque et les permissions permettant de contrôler l’ordinateur et d’accéder aux données.
Le système encourage désormais à sélectionner uniquement les dossiers ou les applications nécessaires au travail demandé. Il propose aussi de configurer une application pour qu’elle sollicite l’autorisation à chaque accès, plutôt que de lui accorder une permission permanente.
La distinction est importante : consulter des fichiers et prendre la main sur un autre logiciel ne sont pas la même opération. Apple sépare ainsi le réglage « Device Control and Data Access » en deux sections, « System & App Protection Override » et « Accessibility ». Un indicateur signale également lorsqu’une application en contrôle une autre.
L’objectif est de mieux montrer la portée des autorisations avant leur validation. Pour un assistant chargé de ranger un dossier de factures, un accès limité peut suffire. Lui permettre de consulter beaucoup plus de données mérite une décision distincte.
Un nouveau réglage pensé pour les agents IA : Apple prépare-t-elle le terrain pour le sien ?
Ces changements apparaîtront lors de nouvelles demandes de permissions. Les accès accordés avant macOS 27.3 restent valables : installer la mise à jour ne retirera donc pas automatiquement les droits déjà confiés à des applications.
Les agents IA sont particulièrement concernés par les risques d’un accès étendu, mais les nouveaux contrôles s’appliquent aussi à d’autres logiciels. Des dispositions spécifiques sont prévues pour les applications de sauvegarde et les technologies d’assistance, dont certaines fonctions nécessitent justement des permissions importantes.
Est-ce qu’Apple prépare le terrain avant le lancement de son propre agent IA ? Rien n’est moins sûr, mais Siri AI, lancé cette année, pourrait progressivement évoluer vers l’IA agentique et aider l’utilisateur en effectuant de nombreuses tâches sur le Mac, tout en préservant la confidentialité de ses données.
Quoi qu'il en soit, les développeurs devront adapter leurs écrans de configuration et prévoir que leur logiciel fonctionne avec un accès limité. Une application ne devrait pas se retrouver inutilisable simplement parce que son propriétaire refuse de lui ouvrir tous ses dossiers.
Ces nouveautés restent pour l’instant en bêta. En attendant leur arrivée en version stable, les autorisations existantes peuvent déjà être vérifiées dans Réglages Système > Confidentialité et sécurité. Le nouvel avertissement ne reviendra pas sur les clics que l’on a déjà faits, mais mieux vaut jeter un œil de temps en temps, histoire de vérifier qu’une app que l'on n'utilise plus ne se montre pas un peu trop curieuse.

articles.title: « Je serais honoré de revenir » : Jensen Huang sort du silence après le scandale chez Nvidia
articles.text:
Jensen Huang parle enfin ! Mardi 17 novembre 2026, l’ancien CEO de Nvidia a pris la parole publiquement pour la première fois depuis sa démission. Elle était survenue le jeudi 12 novembre, à la suite d’un scandale géopolitique qui a fait le tour du monde. Quelques jours auparavant, on apprenait que Jensen Huang avait eu deux relations extraconjugales, dont l’une avec une dirigeante soupçonnée d’espionnage pour Pékin.
Dans une lettre publiée sur X, il remercie ses soutiens, reconnaît de « graves erreurs » dans sa vie personnelle et ouvre la porte à un retour à la tête de l’entreprise qu’il a fondée en 1993.
La lettre tombe quelques heures avant la présentation des résultats trimestriels par Colette Kress, la CEO par intérim, et le jour même où le conseil d’administration a annoncé la création d’un comité chargé de superviser le respect des contrôles américains à l’exportation de puces.
La lettre de Jensen Huang, traduite en français
Voici la lettre de Jensen Huang, traduite en français :
Au cours de la semaine écoulée, j’ai été submergé par l’amour et le soutien d’amis, de collègues de l’industrie et de personnes que je n’ai jamais rencontrées. Merci à tous ceux qui ont fait preuve de bienveillance envers ma famille et moi. Cela compte énormément pour moi.
Je suis arrivé aux États-Unis il y a 53 ans, et devenir citoyen américain est l’un des plus beaux cadeaux et l’une des plus grandes fiertés de ma vie. Nvidia est l’œuvre de ma vie. La bâtir aux côtés de mes collègues pour en faire l’entreprise qu’elle est aujourd’hui a été un privilège et un honneur. Une entreprise comme Nvidia n’aurait été possible nulle part ailleurs qu’en Amérique. J’aime notre pays, et j’aime Nvidia.
Je n’ai pas été à la hauteur des exigences attendues de chacun chez Nvidia, et j’ai commis de graves erreurs dans ma vie personnelle. J’ai créé des problèmes au conseil d’administration, ce que je regrette profondément. J’assume entièrement mes erreurs et je m’engage à coopérer avec l’enquête indépendante du conseil.
Depuis mon départ, j’ai vu affluer les appels des salariés, des investisseurs, des partenaires commerciaux et des clients de Nvidia pour que je revienne en tant que CEO. Beaucoup continuent de me contacter directement, alors que l’entreprise fait face à des dynamiques technologiques, commerciales, concurrentielles et géopolitiques complexes. Nvidia est une entreprise comme il n’en naît qu’une par génération. Si le conseil d’administration estime que mon retour est dans le meilleur intérêt de nos actionnaires, de nos salariés, de l’entreprise et de l’Amérique, je serais honoré de répondre à ces appels et de revenir en tant que CEO.
Merci encore à tous ceux qui m’ont adressé leurs vœux. Votre soutien me touche profondément. À ma famille : je vous aime, et je passerai le reste de ma vie à me montrer digne de votre amour.
Jensen
Faut-il faire revenir Jensen Huang ? Deux camps se déchirent
Depuis la démission, une pétition baptisée « Stand with Jensen » réclame son retour le temps que l’enquête indépendante établisse les faits. Elle dépasse les 190 000 signatures, dont celles d’Elon Musk, de Garry Tan (Y Combinator) ou de Tim Sweeney (Epic Games).
Plus de 9 000 signataires se présentent comme des salariés de Nvidia sans que l’on puisse le vérifier. Les fonds Altimeter et Atreides, actionnaires de Nvidia, ont aussi demandé au conseil de garder « toutes les options sur la table ». Donald Trump, lui, a assuré lundi qu’il ne verrait pas d’inconvénient à son retour, estimant que Jensen Huang avait retenu la leçon.
Mais tout le monde ne partage pas cet avis : Jensen Huang a apporté beaucoup d’instabilité chez Nvidia et une partie de la confiance est rompue. Le conseil d’administration de Nvidia n’envisagerait pas de réintégrer Jensen Huang pour l’instant, ni comme CEO ni à un autre poste, et se concentre sur son enquête et sur la recherche d’un successeur, avec un cabinet spécialisé.
Nvidia veut éviter d’avoir à sa tête un patron accusé d’avoir aidé à la Chine à obtenir des informations préciseuses sur la technologie américaine. La pression politique joue aussi contre Jensen Huang : une partie des élus des États-Unis souhaitent comprendre ce qu’il s’est passé et mettent pour l’instant le patron de Nvidia en liste noire.
Une soirée décisive pour Nvidia, qui va présenter ses résultats sans Jensen
En Bourse, l’action Nvidia a perdu environ 24 % depuis le début du mois de novembre et enchaîne six semaines consécutives de baisse, une première depuis 2012. Lundi, elle a encore reculé de plus de 4 % pour clôturer à son plus bas niveau depuis juillet 2025. Le tweet de Jensen Huang a provoqué une légère hausse, mais l’action est redescendue quelques minutes plus tôt.
Pour Nvidia, tout se jouera ce soir. L’entreprise publiera ses résultats du troisième trimestre vers 22h20, heure de Paris, avant une conférence avec les analystes à 23h. De bons résultats pourraient mettre fin à une semaine de doutes sans pour autant rassurer tout le monde : sans Jensen Huang, Nvidia perd le visionnaire qui l’a toujours dirigé.
