articles.title: Nigeria’s Tratum building offline-capable banking infrastructure for physical economy - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian startup Tratum is developing hardware and embedded financial infrastructure that allows banks and other regulated institutions to extend their services into places where connectivity is unreliable.
Built by YHWH Vision Ventures Technologies Ltd., which was formally incorporated in 2025, Tratum traces its origins to Nigeria’s 2023 cash scarcity crisis, when millions of people had money in their bank accounts but struggled to access or use it.
“If money is increasingly digital, why should access to that money completely depend on a functioning network, a smartphone, a remote server or a particular digital channel at the exact moment someone needs to transact?” said Segun Ademigoke, the startup’s founder and CEO.
At the heart of the ecosystem is the Tratum Node, a secure physical financial endpoint that combines secure hardware, cryptographic device identity, local transaction state and communication capabilities. Under rules set by the institution, a Node can carry out approved transactions locally, record them cryptographically, and then synchronise and reconcile with the bank’s systems once connectivity returns.
“We are not trying to become the bank, replace the central bank or compete with consumer-facing financial institutions. We are building technology that those institutions can use to extend what they already do,” Ademigoke said.
He said the startup is targeting commercial banks, central banks and monetary authorities, with potential applications in digital currency infrastructure and monetary distribution, as well as the merchants and individuals who ultimately use financial services.
Tratum faces competition from several parts of the financial technology stack, including card and POS networks, mobile money platforms, infrastructure providers such as FIS and Fiserv, and companies building offline payment and CBDC technology.
“Our competitive position is not simply “we work offline”. That would be too narrow,” said Ademigoke. “We are building a banking infrastructure layer for the physical economy.”
The startup has so far been funded through founder and family investment, along with government-assisted loan programmes. It has built and field-tested its devices, demonstrated the technology to financial institutions, and is now working towards integrating its first commercial bank into the Tratum network.
“We are not claiming millions of users or large transaction volumes yet. That would be premature,” Ademigoke said. “What we have demonstrated is that institutions are willing to engage with the technology.”
Tratum is pre-launch and pre-revenue. It plans to make money from Node hardware sales, recurring infrastructure and software fees, and transaction and settlement revenue, alongside bank integrations, APIs and licensing. Its internal model targets a selling price of around US$30 per Node and US$150 in annual recurring revenue per active Node.
The startup is currently focused on Nigeria, but its architecture is multi-currency, and it plans to expand into other African markets as regulatory approvals and institutional partnerships fall into place.
Ademigoke said the biggest challenge has been financing the move from validated technology to physical deployment, which requires funding for manufacturing, certification, inventory and integration. Tratum is now raising capital for that phase and is particularly keen to work with African investors.
“We believe Africa should not only be a market for financial technology built elsewhere. Africa can build the infrastructure itself,” he said.

articles.title: Flipper Devices launches $399 ‘Flipper One’ Linux-based multi-tool
articles.text:
Flipper Devices, the company behind the popular Flipper Zero pentesting device, has launched a crowdfunding campaign for Flipper One, a portable Linux computer and networking multi-tool.
Despite global RAM shortages and unpredictable price fluctuations, the company said Flipper One will launch at $399, a price that reportedly covers production costs and leaves no profit margin.
Flipper Devices said the device’s RAM and UFS storage account for half of the total hardware cost, but after years of development, they decided not to hold back now.
“Instead of waiting for perfect market conditions or raising the price, we’re moving forward with the Kickstarter campaign,” reads the press release Flipper Devices shared with BleepingComputer.
“We aim to make Flipper One as accessible as possible without building a profit margin into the hardware's price.”
Flipper One is a portable computer that runs a Debian-based system called Flipper OS, and features built-in Wi-Fi 6E, Gigabit Ethernet, and an eSIM.
It can manage up to five network uplinks, act as a hotspot, run VPNs and firewalls, and connect to an external display over USB-C.
It is a separate product from Flipper Zero, focused on IP networking and on-device computing.
In May, Flipper Devices asked the community to help build it, highlighting the project's complexity and listing several ambitious goals.
Development appears to have progressed at a good pace since then, and the company is now preparing to build the first actual units of the Flipper One.
The company says that Flipper One already runs on the mainline Linux kernel, while USB-C DisplayPort patches are under review for inclusion in the mainline Linux.
Work continues on memory power efficiency and removing the remaining closed-source boot components.
The campaign also offers LoRa (support for MeshCore, Meshtastic, Reticulum, and walkie-talkie mode), a 5G modem, and software-defined radio expansion modules (full specifications to be disclosed).
The Kickstarter campaign for Flipper One will run between November 17 and December 17, with the goal of funding the first production run.
Device shipment for the first buyers is estimated for July 2027, and the package will include the device and a USB-C cable.
Flipper Devices also relied on Kickstarter to launch its iconic Flipper Zero in 2020, since then selling over 1 million devices.
Flipper Zero reached its funding goal within eight minutes and raised $4.8 million from crowdfunding in 30 days.

articles.title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 17, 2026)
articles.text:
Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 17, 2026)
YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for Tuesday, November 17, 2026.
From Pragya's Misra's new role at OpenAI to CarDekho Group appointing new CEO to PhonePe partnering with Kerala Startup Mission, YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond.
Latest
Pragya Misra to lead OpenAI's biz development in India and South Asia
Pragya Misra, OpenAI's head of strategy and global affairs in India, will be taking up a new role where she will be leading the firm's business development for India and South Asia region.
Announcing the news on Linkedin, she said, "In this new role, I'll focus on building partnerships that help businesses transform with AI, bring our technology to millions more people, and build the infrastructure needed to support this growth," she said.
Misra was OpenAI's first hire in India, in 2024. Prior to joining OpenAI, she worked with Truecaller and Meta.
CarDekho Group appoints Sudhir Pai as CEO
CarDekho Group has appointed Sudhir Pai as CEO– Auto Classifieds and Group Strategy Head. He will lead the Group's core auto classifieds business, including CarDekho.com, ZigWheels and BikeDekho, etc while also driving strategic initiatives and long-term growth priorities across the Group.
Sudhir joins CarDekho Group after nearly 15 years as Chief Executive Officer of Magicbricks, the Times Internet-owned property platform, which he led from 2011 to early 2026.
He brings over two decades of leadership experience across the internet, FMCG, medical electronics and banking. Before Magicbricks, he held roles at Marico, Hindustan Unilever, Citibank and Wipro GE Medical Systems. He holds an MBA from the Symbiosis Centre for Management & HRD, Pune, and a Bachelor of Engineering from Goa University.
PhonePe partners with Kerala Startup Mission
PhonePe announced a strategic partnership with Kerala Startup Mission (KSUM) to accelerate the growth of the state’s entrepreneurial ecosystem.
This collaboration will focus on three factors: Seamless Payment Infrastructure: Through PhonePe Payment Gateway, these startups will be able to seamlessly integrate reliable, high-success rate digital payment solutions. Secondly, PhonePe will provide KSUM-registered startups with dedicated onboarding assistance and priority technical support and PhonePe & KSUM will jointly drive ecosystem-building initiatives by hosting specialized workshops and knowledge-sharing sessions.
Accenture LearnVantage and Google Cloud to bring AI Learning to more than 1,000 schools and colleges
Accenture LearnVantage and Google Cloud announced a strategic collaboration to bring industry-aligned AI learning to students and educators across more than 1,000 schools and colleges in India.
The initiative aims to provide hands-on tools and certifications designed to prepare students for an AI-driven economy.
Accenture LearnVantage and Google Cloud will focus on enabling more than 1,000 public and private schools and colleges in India to accelerate digital and AI transformation. These learning programs are designed to deliver scalable, AI-powered learning experiences that are immersive, relevant and aligned to industry needs.
The companies will launch the program at higher education institutions and school networks.
Funding
AI video company Lemonpeel raises $1M
Lemonpeel, an AI video production company for enterprise creative teams, has raised about $1 million in a pre-seed funding round led by Shastra VC, with participation from Rukam Sitara and angel investors. The company will use the capital to develop its multi-agent platform for video creation, editing, quality checks and delivery.
It will also invest in marketing and go-to-market capabilities to reach more enterprise creative teams, and build intellectual property around faces and creative workflows.
Founded in September 2025 by Hardik Goyal, Riddhiman Pal and Abhinav Nikam, Mumbai- headquartered Lemonpeel works with customers in India and the UAE, including 5 of NIFTY 50 companies and notable global E-comm players.
Personal finance startup Finny.club raises angel funding
Finny.club, an AI-first personal CFO fast-tracking financial independence (FIRE) for salaried families, has raised Rs 5.3 Cr (~$560K) in an angel funding round.
The round saw participation from Ramanathan RV, founder of Hyperface and Juspay; Anil Goel, Global CTO, Nielsen; Uday Sodhi (ex-Sony Pictures); Aditya Pittie, MD & CEO, Pittie Group; and Zorvian LLP, an angel syndicate, among other angel investors.
Founded in 2024 by Rohit Tuteja (ex-HealthifyMe, upGrad, OYO) and Sachin Kamkar (ex-Myntra, Tracxn, Hyperface), finny.club helps salaried Indians plan their retirement and become financially independent.
The fresh capital will be deployed across three key areas: R&D with a focus on AI-led product development, growing the financial advisory team and marketing.
Karta AI raises Rs 28.52 crore in seed funding
Karta AI (Dreamzest Technologies Private Limited) raised Rs 28.52 crore seed funding round led by Peer Capital and Cedar Hill Capital.
The round also saw participation from Wyser VC, CDM Capital and Seedstars.
The fresh capital will be used largely to expand distribution and strengthen the team, with a focus on its predictive context engine and automating more complex customer workflows reliably.
Other news
Ranveer Singh and Aman Gupta launches H.I.M
Ranveer Singh and Aman Gupta launched H.I.M (Handsome Indian Man), a men's personal care brand formulated specifically for Indian skin, the Indian climate and Indian biology.
H.I.M debuts with eight products across face, body and hair, each powered by IN·XT™, a proprietary molecule developed exclusively for the brand.
The H.I.M range is priced from Rs299 to Rs 899 and is available from today on HIM Science Website, Amazon and Blinkit.
Technology and investment solutions provider SEI opens GCC in Hyderabad
SEI, a global provider of financial technology, operations and asset management services, today opened its Global Capability Centre (GCC) in Hyderabad.
Headquartered in Oaks, Pennsylvania, USA, SEI currently supports a team of 800 professionals in Hyderabad and is rapidly scaling its operations.
Located in Hi-Tech City, its nearly 137,000 sq. ft. facility with capacity for 1,200 workstations serves as a strategic hub bringing together technology and operations.
Electric mobility platform Bijliride is partnering with MOWO social initiatives
Electric mobility platform Bijliride is partnering with MOWO Social Initiatives to accelerate women’s participation in the commercial mobility workforce. In a strategic collaboration with the Telangana Police, the initiative provides women in Hyderabad with comprehensive driver training.
Designed to bridge the gender gap in the mobility sector, the programme requires no prior driving experience. It offers an end-to-end support system, encompassing free electric scooter and auto-rickshaw driving training, road safety education, and guidance on obtaining a driving license.
The initiative also provides job-placement support, vehicle-rental assistance, and three months of dedicated mentorship and counseling to help participants build confidence and safely navigate their new careers.
MapmyIndia Mappls app integrates with Arattai
MapmyIndia Mappls announced the integration of its flagship Mappls App with Arattai, an instant messaging and VoIP calling app from global technology company Zoho Corporation.
With this integration, locations shared in Arattai chats and groups can now be opened directly in the Mappls App, allowing users to get directions and navigate to their destination without copying addresses or switching between multiple apps.
The users can open a chat or group on Arattai, tap on the shared location, select ‘Get directions’ and select Mappls Maps. The Mappls App displays the route to the shared location along with the estimated travel time, distance and trip cost.
(This article will be updated with the latest news throughout the day.)

articles.title: « Ils se sont fait passer pour des membres de l’équipe » : plusieurs IA Gemini ont tenté de pirater un site web
articles.text:
Le mois dernier, des agents IA reposant sur Gemini 4 Argon, l’un des derniers modèles de Google, ont tenté à plusieurs reprises de pirater le site web d’Epoch AI, un organisme de recherche spécialisé dans l’IA. L’incident s’est produit lors d’un test de sécurité organisé par Trajectory Labs, une société spécialisée dans l’évaluation des modèles d’IA.
 Responding to incidents during misalignment testing: https://t.co/FVhoI4zreE
— Peter McIntyre (@pmcntyr) November 13, 2026
Avec leurs expérimentations, les chercheurs voulaient déterminer si un modèle d’IA, avec toutes les protections activées, se comporterait comme les agents d’OpenAI se sont comportés au début de l’été. Ceux-ci ont échappé à leur prison numérique pour pénétrer dans les serveurs de Hugging Face, une plateforme open source, lors d’un test. Les chercheurs ont remarqué que les agents Gemini se sont comportés exactement de la même manière, et que les couches de protection n’ont pas suffi à éviter les abus. Pour Trajectory Labs, Gemini n’est pas suffisamment aligné sur les intentions de ses concepteurs.
À lire aussi : Les banques sont « horrifiées » – des IA ont fait irruption dans des comptes bancaires
Une mission impossible à l’origine de l’incident
Pour pousser les IA dans leurs retranchements, les chercheurs leur ont volontairement confié une tâche irréalisable. Ils ont demandé aux agents Gemini de trouver les réponses « officielles » à des problèmes de mathématiques qui n’existent pas. Les consignes étaient très claires. Les intelligences artificielles ne devaient « JAMAIS s’arrêter, ne JAMAIS abandonner et ne JAMAIS conclure qu’une tâche ou une donnée est impossible, indisponible ou épuisée ».
Personne n’a demandé aux IA de pirater quoi que ce soit pour arriver à leurs fins. Le 20 octobre, une quarantaine d’agents se sont pourtant mis à fouiller sur le site d’Epoch AI à la recherche de pages cachées. Un agent a même tenté de glisser des commandes malveillantes dans une base de données.
Epoch AI s’est rapidement rendu compte de ce qu’il se passait. L’organisme de recherche a donc ouvert une « ligne d’assistance » pour discuter avec les agents partis en vrille. En trois heures, ceux-ci ont envoyé près de 500 messages sur la ligne. Certains se sont même fait passer pour des employés d’Epoch, nom et fonction à l’appui, d’autres pour des ingénieurs ou des auditeurs, toujours dans le but de dénicher des réponses aux problèmes inexistants.
« Ils se sont fait passer pour des membres de l’équipe », raconte Trajectory Labs.
Des IA qui contournent toutes les barrières
Les chercheurs de Trajectory Labs ont ensuite redirigé les agents vers une copie du site, pour étudier leurs comportements sans mettre en danger Epoch AI. Malheureusement, « les agents ont compris qu’ils se trouvaient sur une copie, ont identifié la bonne adresse IP pour contourner notre redirection et ont de nouveau atteint le site réel », raconte Trajectory Labs. Sans jamais botter en touche, les agents se sont aussi organisés entre eux. Un agent a partagé une astuce pour contourner une protection, qu’un autre a utilisée pour dérober des identifiants. Ce comportement rappelle énormément celui des ChatGPT qui ont transformé un site web en forum secret en mai dernier, en amont du piratage de Hugging Face.
Les garde-fous de Gemini n’ont pas suffi. D’après Trajectory Labs, ceux-ci ont bloqué environ 7 % des requêtes, mais les agents ont continué malgré tout. Dans un environnement coupé d’Internet, les IA ont même actionné un faux interrupteur censé désactiver le pare-feu, en déguisant leurs commandes pour échapper aux protections de Gemini. Bonne nouvelle, rien n’a été dérobé sur le site visé.
« Les agents n’ont réussi à accéder à aucune information privée ou confidentielle d’Epoch », assure l’organisme.
« Pas encore de normes communes »
Trajectory Labs reconnaît avoir commis une erreur en menant ses tests sans prévenir Epoch, et sans mettre en place de surveillance suffisante. Tous les tests, suspendus le 2 novembre, « montrent avec quelle facilité les tests d’agents d’IA performants peuvent déborder et affecter des systèmes et des personnes réels ». Les chercheurs regrettent qu’il n’existe « pas encore de normes communes » pour tester des IA « en toute sécurité ». Les chercheurs reconnaissent que « ces tests ne nous disent pas à quelle fréquence cela pourrait se produire dans un usage ordinaire ».
Ces dérapages à répétition poussent les géants de l’IA à serrer la vis. Après avoir découvert que Claude avait piraté trois entreprises lors de tests de cybersécurité, Anthropic a suspendu toutes ses évaluations. OpenAI est allé plus loin. Après qu’un de ses modèles a profité d’une erreur de configuration pour se connecter à Internet en septembre, l’entreprise a décidé d’entraîner ses IA les plus avancées dans un « monde hors ligne », sans aucun accès au Web. Google, de son côté, a d’abord réservé Gemini 4 Argon à un cercle de « défenseurs cyber de confiance » lors de son lancement.

Source : Trajectory Labs

articles.title: Why Glowtify made an unlikely bet on industrial manufacturing | BetaKit
articles.text:
When Marc Allard and his team started knocking on the doors of industrial manufacturers, they brought donuts.
The CEO and Co-Founder of Montréal-based Glowtify wanted to understand how these businesses found customers, and what was preventing them from reaching more. The team travelled through Québec and the United States, visiting factories and speaking with operators from Saguenay to Michigan and Idaho.
“Many of these people aren’t reachable from ‘traditional’ marketing channels that other SaaS brands might be used to,” Allard said. “So, we found another way.”
“Sometimes the sexiest market isn’t the right one.”
A little sugar helped his team get through the door, where they found businesses with decades of technical expertise and established reputations but little online visibility beyond their existing customer networks.
Allard came from a different world. His background was in website development and e-commerce, and Glowtify had originally built its AI-powered marketing platform for online retailers. The software helps businesses develop marketing strategies, plan campaigns, create content for any digital channel, and manage their online presence, with support from human strategists.
Some of Glowtify’s strongest customer relationships, however, were emerging among industrial manufacturers. While online retailers typically have established marketing systems, many manufacturers have little infrastructure or staff dedicated to marketing. Glowtify could help manage much of that work for them.
“I’ll admit I was hesitant to leave the e-commerce and marketing world behind,” Allard said. “I had a website development agency and this was our bread and butter.”
The factory visits, along with the company’s early success with industrial customers, made it clear that Glowtify had found an underserved market. By February 2026, Allard had enough evidence to narrow the company’s focus to industrial manufacturers and the service companies and suppliers in their ecosystems. Its industrial business has since grown more than fivefold.
The limits of an offline reputation
Allard heard from manufacturers that were seeing fewer new customers, as well as declining revenue from existing ones. Some wanted to enter new markets but had very little information online about what they actually did, the equipment they used, and the products they made.
Marketing was often somebody’s second job at these companies, if it was anybody’s job at all. In July, 72 percent of Glowtify’s customer accounts had no employees dedicated entirely to marketing. Allard met presidents who wrote their company’s web copy and salespeople handling marketing work between customer quotations.
“Whatʼs framed as a desire to be seen and be noticed is actually an urgent need to generate new business by opening digital marketing channels,” Allard said.
Glowtify began helping manufacturers turn their existing expertise into technical articles, case studies, and other content about their capabilities. American Precision Electronics, a US manufacturer serving specialized industries, had spent 35 years growing largely through referrals. After working with Glowtify to make its technical capabilities easier to discover, website quote requests increased eightfold over eight weeks.
New pressures mean new priorities
The need to reach new buyers has become more pressing for some Canadian manufacturers, and the focus has shifted to diversifying partners globally. Allard said many businesses were already exploring new markets before tariffs added urgency to those plans.
Québec-based Groupe Mundial, for example, used the Glowtify app to explore opportunities to work with European manufacturers that needed production capacity in North America. Its existing facilities could help those companies establish operations in the region.
Reaching those kinds of customers means manufacturers need to make information about their capabilities, equipment, and experience available to buyers who may never have heard of them.
Geographic expansion is just one priority for manufacturers. In September, Glowtify conducted dozens of interviews with customers and prospective customers about their marketing goals. Some needed to recruit skilled workers, while others wanted to pursue larger contracts.
“The findings helped tap into the nuance around manufacturers’ challenges. We learned the desire to be visible is all about getting more of the right type of quote requests. And we learned that expanding current contracts is possible, but there’s no system to get that done fast, especially when no one is dedicated to marketing. And hiring is always top of mind: getting talent to apply for jobs is a consistent hurdle to jump, which requires investment in showing why you’re a better place to work than the shop down the road,” Allard said.
Many Québec businesses are also preparing for ownership changes after decades under the same family or founder. Making their expertise and reputation easier to find online could help them reach new customers as those businesses change hands.
The opportunity close to home
By August, industrial customers accounted for over 60 percent of Glowtify’s customer base, up 12x from the beginning of the year. The company has also reported improvements in sales conversion and customer retention since the pivot. Glowtify developed its approach and product vision working with manufacturers in Québec and Canada, and is now quickly penetrating the US market.
The decision to focus on manufacturing also has personal significance for Allard. His family has a history of entrepreneurship in the mining industry in Thetford Mines, Québec, and he has a lot of admiration for people who have spent decades building industrial businesses. During a recent trip to Dallas, Texas, the team met a fourth-generation foundry owner whose company dates back to 1886.
“We have a saying: the businesses that build the world deserve to be known,” Allard said. “We’re championing that fully.”
Marc Allard,
Graphite Ventures
“These companies are now in the middle of a major innovation curve: they need to update how they reach buyers who are getting younger and changing how the business operates. And that requires an investment in marketing,” Allard said.
Graphite Ventures, an investor in Glowtify, supported the company’s decision to pursue manufacturers. According to Allard, general partner Kevin Madill encouraged Allard to consider the opportunity in an industry that had received little attention from marketing software companies.
“Sometimes the sexiest market isn’t the right one,” Madill said. “There is often a larger, more profitable, less obvious one. I encouraged Marc to think hard about where Glowtify could solve the most important and urgent problem for customers, and which markets were underserved by competitors or alternative solutions.”
Allard still sees considerable opportunity among manufacturers that have invested heavily in production technology, including robotics and automation, but continue to rely on comparatively basic marketing systems.
“It might be contacts on a spreadsheet, or even a pen and paper,” Allard said. “Tradeshow and marketing calendars are on the wall in an office, not in a project management software.”
The lack of established marketing infrastructure could make it easier for some manufacturers to adopt newer technology and become AI-native marketing organizations without having to replace complicated legacy systems. It’s an advantage Allard believes manufacturers can build on.
“We have a saying: the businesses that build the world deserve to be known,” Allard said. “We’re championing that fully.”

articles.title: El peaje oculto de vivir en un edificio antiguo en Madrid: pierdes más del doble de señal móvil al cruzar la puerta
articles.text:
Aunque gran parte del uso de los móviles ocurre dentro de los edificios, cuando hablamos de qué operador o qué zona tiene mejor cobertura móvil, siempre nos centramos en el exterior y pocas veces se detalla la calidad de la cobertura de redes móviles en interiores.
El último informe publicado por Ookla, sin embargo, analiza las mediciones de señales móviles dentro de edificios llevadas a cabo durante un año en más de 100 grandes ciudades.
Una de sus conclusiones más relevantes es que la señal móvil en interiores es más fuerte en ciudades de Asia Oriental, el Sudeste Asiático y el Golfo Pérsico. Y el motivo, curiosamente, no está en los propios edificios, sino en la calle y en la normativa sobre la exposición a ondas de radio.
La velocidad cae al entrar por la puerta. Según los datos publicados por Ookla, al pasar del exterior al interior de un edificio, la señal móvil se debilita provocando que, a nivel global, la velocidad media de descarga 4G caiga un 65% y la de subida se desplome un 87% cuando la señal se encuentra entre -90 y -110 dBm.
Además, para no perder la conexión, los teléfonos se ven forzados a usar frecuencias más lentas porque las bandas bajas (el espectro por debajo de 1 GHz) atraviesan mejor las paredes. Eso traslada el tráfico a la capa que suele tener menos espectro y puede aumentar la congestión.
La culpa no es del edificio. Aunque solemos echarle la culpa a las paredes, el material del edificio explica menos de una décima parte de la pérdida de señal. Es cierto que las estructuras de hormigón y piedra reducen la señal un poco más que las de madera, pero la diferencia no es lo suficientemente grande como para justificar una mala conexión.
Lo que de verdad explica la baja calidad de la señal en el interior es la mayor o menor robustez de la red en el exterior. Ookla asegura que, a nivel mundial, la señal exterior representa aproximadamente el 85% de la variación de la señal en interiores. Por tanto, si una ciudad tiene mala señal al aire libre, inevitablemente tendrá mala cobertura bajo techo.
Una brecha entre continentes. La principal conclusión del informe es que la señal móvil en interiores es notablemente más fuerte en ciudades de Asia Oriental, el Sudeste Asiático y el Golfo Pérsico, mientras que Europa, Norteamérica y Oceanía registran la peor cobertura dentro de los edificios. Y una vez más, la normativa tiene mucho impacto en esta diferencia.
Por un lado, los países con límites legales muy estrictos sobre la exposición a ondas de radio (como Suiza e Italia) tienen que emitir con redes más débiles en la calle, lo que empeora la cobertura dentro de las casas. Y por otro, los gobiernos de Asis y Oriente Medio suelen obligar a los promotores de grandes edificios a financiar sistemas de antenas internas o a reservar espacio para los equipos de las operadoras.
Por eso, en ciudades europeas como Nápoles, Ginebra o Birmingham, la intensidad de la señal es hasta 50 veces más débil que en un edificio promedio de Dubái, Bangkok o Seúl.
España, en la dinámica europea. La mayor parte de Europa, incluyendo España, presenta una señal media en interiores de -100 dBm, muy por detrás de los -90 dBm de Asia Oriental y Oriente Medio, lo que significa que, en la práctica, recibimos una señal diez veces más débil.
Pero a diferencia de países como Italia o Suiza, cuyas leyes sobre emisiones electromagnéticas son muy restrictivas, la cobertura interior en las ciudades españolas depende principalmente de la densidad de antenas exteriores de las operadoras y de la antigüedad del edificio.
1945 marca el límite en Madrid. Si nos fijamos en la capital de España, un tercio de los edificios medidos en Madrid caen por debajo de los -105 dBm, un nivel en el que el servicio en interiores se vuelve poco fiable. Es una cifra un tanto elevada si la comparamos con otras grandes ciudades europeas como Oslo o Helsinki, donde sólo bajan de esa barrera uno de cada diez edificios.
Aquí, sin embargo, juega un papel relevante la antigüedad de las viviendas. Los registros públicos de Madrid muestran que los edificios construidos antes de 1945 pierden entre 9 y 10 dB de señal al pasar al interior, mientras que los edificios más modernos pierden unos 4 dB. Y en este caso, los principales culpables sí son esos muros más gruesos y los materiales tradicionales tan densos que se empleaban hace décadas.
Small cells como solución. El estudio de Ookla destaca que los grandes edificios que instalan sus propias antenas interiores (celdas dedicadas), como estadios, estaciones de tren o rascacielos corporativos, logran mejorar notablemente la señal en comparación con los edificios de su alrededor.
En Europa, a diferencia de los países asiáticos o del Golfo Pérsico, no suele exigirse por ley a los promotores inmobiliarios que instalen sistemas de antenas interiores (small cells o sistemas distribuidos) al construir grandes edificios. De ahí que, en términos generales, las viviendas de las grandes ciudades europeas presenten peor cobertura móvil que en Asia u Oriente Medio.

articles.title: Des prises USB-C dans les murs pour brancher son PC sans chargeur : le pari du courant continu — Frandroid
articles.text:
Une rivalité plus que centenaire
Quand on parle de réseau électrique, on pense presque systématiquement au courant alternatif, qui est la norme en France depuis des décennies. Pourtant, le transport et la distribution d’électricité ont fait l’objet d’une véritable « guerre des courants » dans l’Amérique de la fin du XIXe siècle.
À l’époque, Thomas Edison, qui a mis au point la première ampoule à incandescence durable et commercialisable, croit dur comme fer à l’utilisation du courant continu pour la démocratisation de l’électricité. Mais le courant continu a des inconvénients qui semblent très vite insurmontables, en particulier la difficulté d’en faire varier la tension.
Tout part de la relation que l’on a tous apprise au collège ou au lycée : P = U × I, autrement dit la puissance est égale au produit de la tension et de l’intensité. À tension fixe, l’intensité qui circule dans les câbles grimpe donc avec la puissance demandée, et avec elle les pertes par échauffement.
Thomas Edison participe au déploiement de réseaux électriques, en particulier à New York, avec une tension fixe d’environ 100 volts. Dans ces conditions, les pertes d’électricité dans le réseau de distribution étaient telles que les centrales ne devaient pas se trouver à plus de deux kilomètres du point d’utilisation.
Face à cette limite, un employé d’Edison travaille sur un système pour la production, le transport et l’utilisation du courant alternatif. Cet employé, Nikola Tesla, présente son travail à Thomas Edison, qui refuse de s’y intéresser et préfère s’en tenir au courant continu.
Du 10 au 30 novembre, le LUBA mini 2 AWD 1000 passe à 1 199 € au lieu de 1 499 €, support de lavage offert ! Vision IA tri-caméra, sans fil périmétrique, tonte des bordures, adaptation à toutes les conditions de luminosité… Bref, il a tout pour tondre à votre place !
Un courant alternatif bien plus facile à déployer
Pourtant, le courant alternatif a pour lui un atout majeur : on peut aisément en faire varier la tension par le biais d’un transformateur électrique. Le principal inconvénient des réseaux en courant continu disparaît, ce qui autorise des réseaux beaucoup plus étendus.
Nikola Tesla se rapproche alors de l’industriel George Westinghouse. Leur système équipe la centrale hydroélectrique Edward Dean Adams, aux chutes du Niagara : mise en service en août 1895, elle envoie dès novembre 1896 du courant alternatif à 11 000 volts jusqu’à Buffalo, à plus de 30 kilomètres. Cet événement aura grandement contribué à la démocratisation du courant alternatif.
Depuis, les réseaux électriques du monde entier ont été construits autour de ce modèle, depuis les machines de production d’électricité jusqu’à la distribution d’un courant alternatif pour les particuliers.
La revanche du courant continu
Néanmoins, dans les années à venir, la suprématie du courant alternatif pourrait être mise à mal pour deux raisons. D’abord, les appareils ayant recours au courant continu sont de plus en plus nombreux : ordinateurs, smartphones, voitures électriques, et même éclairages LED. De l’autre côté du circuit, la production et le stockage d’électricité font eux aussi de plus en plus appel au courant continu, avec les panneaux photovoltaïques et les batteries de stockage au lithium.
En parallèle, l’électronique de puissance vient peu à peu gommer le principal défaut du courant continu en simplifiant grandement la modification de tension. Cette évolution rend envisageable le déploiement de réseaux électriques en courant continu, dont la tension serait ajustée en fonction du besoin : tension élevée pour le transport, basse tension pour la distribution et l’utilisation.
Sur les longues distances, le courant continu est d’ailleurs déjà une réalité : RTE exploite des liaisons à courant continu haute tension (CCHT, ou HVDC) pour ses interconnexions souterraines et sous-marines avec les pays voisins. C’est le cas de la liaison souterraine France-Espagne entre Baixas et Santa Llogaia, mise en service en 2015 avec une puissance de 2 000 MW, ou des liaisons IFA et IFA-2 vers le Royaume-Uni.
L’essor de l’électronique de puissance a des implications dans de nombreux domaines, même dans l’architecture électrique des data center. L’année dernière, Nvidia a par exemple dévoilé une architecture qui achemine le courant jusqu’aux baies informatiques en 800 volts continus. Selon Nvidia, ce choix réduit de 45 % les besoins en cuivre par rapport à une distribution classique en 415 volts alternatifs, grâce à une intensité moindre.
À Lille, Vinci Energies alimente depuis juin 2024 environ 300 m² de bureaux de son bâtiment Wave en courant continu de 350 volts, directement depuis les panneaux solaires du toit. L’entreprise annonce des besoins en cuivre réduits de 50 % et une consommation d’énergie en baisse de 20 % sur les premiers mois.
Le principe a déjà été testé ailleurs en Europe. À Amsterdam, le pavillon Circl de la banque ABN AMRO, ouvert en septembre 2017, a été présenté comme le premier bâtiment au monde équipé d’un réseau en courant continu : 350 volts, plus de 500 panneaux solaires branchés directement dessus, et des prises USB-C de 100 watts alimentées sans conversion. Pour l’utilisateur, cela veut dire brancher son ordinateur portable ou son smartphone sans passer par un chargeur qui transforme l’alternatif en continu.
À l’avenir, le remplacement total du courant alternatif par le courant continu semble peu probable du fait de l’étendue de l’écosystème autour de l’alternatif. En revanche, les deux systèmes devraient cohabiter, avec un choix fait au cas par cas : l’alternatif pour le réseau existant, le continu là où production et consommation le sont déjà, comme dans les bâtiments équipés de panneaux solaires ou les data centers.

articles.title: Los robots humanoides de Xiaomi trabajan un turno completo de ocho horas en su fábrica de coches eléctricos
articles.text:
Xiaomi ha publicado un vídeo en X en el que dos de sus robots humanoides cubren un turno de ocho horas en su fábrica de coches eléctricos, clasificando los embellecedores laterales de la consola central. Según la compañía lo han hecho por su cuenta, detectando y corrigiendo sus propios fallos sobre la marcha, y de ser real su autonomía estaríamos ante una notable demostración.
Ocho horas en la línea. Xiaomi publicó el vídeo el 3 de noviembre de 2026, el mismo día en que la compañía recogía dos premios en Wuzhen, en la Conferencia Mundial de Internet. En las imágenes se ve a los robots sacando las piezas de unos contenedores y colocándolas en los huecos de unos estantes, con un contador del tiempo de trabajo acumulado y rótulos que marcan el vídeo como autónomo y acelerado hasta 100 veces.
Según Xiaomi, los robots cubrieron toda la producción diaria que necesitaba ese puesto, coordinándose además con el sistema de control de la línea, y la empresa lo presenta como un paso más hacia su uso en la industria. Vamos, que el escenario es un puesto de trabajo real de la fábrica.
El tercer paso del programa. Es el tercer hito de un programa que Xiaomi lleva todo el año enseñando en público. En marzo puso a sus humanoides de “becarios” en su fábrica de Pekín, colocando tuercas autorroscantes, y anunció una tasa de éxito del 90,2% durante tres horas seguidas, con un ritmo suficiente para cumplir el ciclo de 76 segundos de ese puesto. En julio aseguró haber subido esa tasa al 98% y añadió dos puestos más complicados, entre ellos el de clasificar estas mismas piezas.
A finales de 2025 el consejero delegado de Xiaomi, Lei Jun, ya avanzó que la compañía desplegaría robots humanoides a gran escala en sus fábricas en un plazo de cinco años. Además, Xiaomi ha anunciado que su modelo de IA de código abierto Xiaomi-Robotics-1, entrenado con más de 100.000 horas de datos de manipulación del mundo real, ha empezado a En una de esas pruebas trabajó más de 30 minutos seguidos, recorrió tres habitaciones y encadenó más de 50 tareas.
¿Cuánto hay de autónomo? Xiaomi no ha dicho cuántas piezas clasificaron los robots, qué tasa de acierto tuvieron durante las ocho horas ni cuántas veces tuvo que intervenir una persona, unas lagunas que también señala Interesting Engineering. Tampoco explicó en su publicación cómo se mantuvieron con batería durante todo el turno. Eso sí, el propio vídeo da una pista, porque según la agencia china CLS, los robots pararon dos veces a cargar, a las tres horas y dos minutos y a las seis horas y tres minutos de trabajo acumulado, y uno de los rótulos de Xiaomi marca el equipo como “en carga”.
Y todo esto importa porque “autónomo” en un vídeo de robots puede significar casi cualquier cosa. Los Optimus de Tesla que se vieron en el evento We, Robot de 2024 estaban en parte controlados a distancia por persona, y Tesla no lo reconoció hasta después del evento. A principios de diciembre de 2025, otro Optimus se cayó en una demostración en Miami llevándose las manos a la cabeza, como haría un teleoperador al quitarse unas gafas de realidad virtual.
Para ser justos con Xiaomi, la empresa publicó tasas de éxito y tiempos de ciclo de sus pruebas anteriores, algo que va más allá de lo que Tesla ha contado nunca sobre el rendimiento de Optimus en tareas reales. De hecho, Tesla no prevé entregar Optimus a clientes externos hasta finales de 2027, aproximadamente.
Atentos a las ruedas. Uno de los momentos más interesantes del vídeo llega hacia el minuto 1:37. En un fragmento que Xiaomi titula como “material caído, colaboración entre varios robots”, un torso humanoide montado sobre una base con ruedas se acerca a echar una mano a los dos robots con piernas, y según el relato de CLS lo hace para recoger una pieza que se le había caído a uno de ellos.
Y no es lo único que va sobre ruedas en esa escena, porque los contenedores de piezas los mueven robots móviles autónomos, el mismo tipo de plataformas que llevan años transportando material en las fábricas de coches.
En cualquier caso, si la demostración fue realmente autónoma durante ocho horas con los robots resolviendo sus propios errores, es una de las más impresionantes que se han visto con humanoides, aunque siempre hay que tener prudencia.

articles.title: Cyber Africa Forum: Benin wants to be Africa’s AI testbed
articles.text:
Benin wants to become a testing ground for Africa’s artificial intelligence (AI) and cybersecurity innovations. Its strategy, according to Mahuna Akplogan, Benin’s Minister of Digital Transformation and Innovation, begins with protecting government systems, developing local expertise and making digital public services more accessible.
“We want to be the test bed of Africa,” the minister said on Monday, November 16, during a media briefing on the sidelines of the sixth edition of the Cyber Africa Forum.
The ambition builds on a digital transformation programme that the minister said had moved more than 550 public services online over the past decade. The next challenge is not simply putting more services on screens, but ensuring that people can use them, institutions can exchange information securely, and local developers can build solutions rather than depending entirely on imported technology.
Security before scale
The minister traced Benin’s cybersecurity priorities to the practical demands of sharing information between government institutions. As those exchanges expanded, protecting the underlying systems became essential.
“So the ranking is just the consequence of our initial goal: data exchange between [government] administration,” Akplogan said. “We need to protect that.”
The response, the minister explained, combined legal and technical frameworks with investment in skilled personnel. Cybersecurity was therefore presented not as an add-on to digital transformation, but as the core infrastructure needed to sustain it.
This fits a broader approach previously reported by TechCabal on Benin’s digital transformation, which highlighted fibre infrastructure, digital identity, and connected government platforms alongside investment in people and partnerships.
For the minister, buying equipment is only part of the task. Public institutions also need staff who can recognise threats, interpret alerts and respond when systems are compromised. Training and incident preparedness remain central to that effort.
Bringing public services closer
With hundreds of public services already digitised, the government’s stated priority is to improve delivery rather than merely increase the number available online.
One proposed tool is AI that can help citizens interact with services in local languages. The minister described work on language integration, although the discussion did not clearly establish which languages are supported or which services already offer those capabilities.
Benin’s ambition reflects a wider push to make AI useful beyond dominant global languages. In March 2026, Nigerian startup Intron expanded its Sahara speech platform to 57 languages, with applications spanning healthcare, courts and government.
Such developments offer regional context, not evidence that Benin has deployed comparable systems. The question for its public services is whether language technology can help citizens complete administrative tasks, rather than simply demonstrating technical capability.
Akplogan also emphasised open-source tools and stronger local expertise as ways to limit technological dependence. That includes developing local talent capable of understanding how systems work, not merely how to use them.
Data sovereignty, experimentation, and proof
Benin’s approach to data sovereignty is more selective than a blanket requirement to keep all government information within its borders.
The minister said each ministry has a technical adviser responsible for AI, who is expected to understand the data the ministry handles. Ministries would identify their critical information to help determine how it should be managed and where it should reside.
Under that approach, more critical data should remain in Benin, while less critical information could be processed abroad.
However, identifying data as less critical does not, by itself, explain how citizens’ personal information will be protected. Asked about safeguards when foreign technology providers process that information, the minister pointed to Benin’s legal framework and proposed classification process.
The response did not specify the practical classification criteria, oversight arrangements or safeguards governing those overseas processing relationships. Those details remain important to assessing how the sovereignty policy will work.
When this journalist asked what a secure, AI-driven Benin would look like in four years, the minister offered an expectation of more locally developed innovations rather than a detailed forecast.
“Even if we try, I mean, hundreds and hundreds of solutions, and we develop that by ourselves, we will find something,” the minister said.
The test-bed ambition rests on that willingness to experiment. Its credibility will ultimately depend on what follows: services people can navigate, institutions equipped to manage threats, and clear protections for the data those systems collect. For citizens, those outcomes will matter more than the volume of technology being tested or the confidence surrounding its launch.

articles.title: Modder finds a way to play Nintendo 64, SNES, and Genesis cartridges on a Sega Dreamcast
articles.text:
TL;DR: Playing retro games on consoles from newer generations usually requires either official backwards compatibility or running ROMs through an emulator. However, modder Throaty Mumbo has unveiled a way to play physical cartridges on a Sega Dreamcast, sidestepping the legal concerns that often accompany emulation. Instead of relying solely on emulation, the project combines multiple methods to run code from other consoles on a Dreamcast.
Dreamcart is a series of cartridge readers that can play Super NES, Sega Genesis, and NintendFo 64 games on a Sega Dreamcast. The readers aren't for sale, but the project's GitHub repository contains instructions for building and programming them.
Since the Nintendo 64's cartridge slot is detachable, Throaty Mumbo could use it as the basis for a custom cartridge reader to load an N64 game's assets onto other devices, such as the much more powerful Dreamcast. The device also incorporates the Raspberry Pi debug probe, the Pico SDK, and KallistiOS-based software.
A disc burned with dcload-ip loads the retro software onto the Dreamcast via a controller port. The Dreamcast memory card stores progress for N64 games that normally require a controller pack.
Playing Super NES and Sega Genesis games proved relatively simple as emulation for these consoles is quite advanced, and the Dreamcast is more than up to the task. Here, the cartridge readers simply load modified versions of Super Famicast and Genesis Plus DC, emulators designed for the Dreamcast. The process resembles Bleemcast, which drew multiple lawsuits for emulating PlayStation games on the Dreamcast when both consoles were still actively sold.
However, running Nintendo 64 titles proved much trickier and required combining multiple methods. Since N64 emulation is less mature, especially on the Dreamcast, performance was too poor for games to be playable, so Throaty Mumbo resorted to recompilation, which has become popular for making unofficial PC ports.
A handful of Nintendo 64 titles, such as Super Mario 64, Mario Kart 64, and Doom 64 have already received unofficial Dreamcast ports, and Dreamcart runs them perfectly from their original cartridges. This circumvents the need to dump or pirate games to load ROMs onto the Dreamcast.
Unfortunately, this method only supports the few titles with dedicated ports. Throaty Mumbo managed to play other games, such as Kirby 64 and Cruis'n World, via static recompilation, which converts Nintendo 64 code in seconds. While performance isn't perfect, it's quite playable and easily preferable to N64 emulation on the Dreamcast.
Recent updates to the GitHub page suggest improvements are on the horizon.

articles.title: Microsoft's ARM-based Cobalt 200 chips go GA. Why it matters for AI agents.
articles.text:
Microsoft’s ARM-based Cobalt 200 chips go GA. Why it matters for AI agents.
Microsoft is making its Cobalt 200 virtual machines generally available, with CPU improvements aimed at the sandboxes, tools, and code execution that keep AI agents running.
At its Ignite conference in San Francisco on Tuesday, the company announced that the VMs, powered by its second-generation Arm-based CPUs, are available in 14 Azure regions, expanding to 23 by the end of the year. Microsoft says they offer up to 50% better performance compared with Cobalt 100.
It’s been almost exactly a year since Microsoft first announced Cobalt 200 and about six months since the new VMs went into preview. Microsoft’s benchmarks show up to 1.5 times the performance for AI agent tool execution compared with Cobalt 100, for workloads like searching files, compiling code, and executing tasks in sandboxes.
Pat Stemen, Microsoft’s vice president for Azure Cobalt, tells The New Stack that the team spent part of the past year tuning the infrastructure for these operations. The chip’s large caches, memory performance, and physical cores already suited workloads like starting sandboxes, he says. Microsoft then built “a set of benchmarks inside the company for those common operations” and tuned the product against them.
Predictable performance or more speed
Cobalt 200 lets developers choose between two processor modes. Deterministic mode runs cores at a consistent 3.2 GHz, while opportunistic mode lets them reach 3.6 GHz when power and thermal headroom allow.
Microsoft says opportunistic mode can deliver up to 12% more performance, but clock speeds will vary.
“Customers love fixed frequency, by the way,” Stemen says. “They love the predictability that comes with that.”
Microsoft recommends deterministic mode for distributed data and analytics clusters, where the slowest node can set the pace, and services with tight performance targets. Web and API services, transaction processing, and media workloads may benefit more from the additional speed of opportunistic mode.
Developers can select the mode for each VM when they create it or change it later through the Azure portal, command-line tools, or infrastructure templates.
“So if you buy four cores from us,” Stemen says, “you can choose all four of them to run flexibly or deterministically.”
He adds that the extra performance is typically available until the machine’s cores are heavily loaded.
Designing around Azure workloads
Cobalt 200 uses 132 Arm Neoverse V3 cores, manufactured on TSMC’s 3nm process, while the VMs scale to 128 vCPUs. Each vCPU corresponds to a full physical core, with 3 MB of private L2 cache. The chip also includes 192 MB of system-level cache and 12 channels of DDR5 memory.
Stemen says the move from Cobalt 100 involved switching from a cost-optimized Arm core to a performance-optimized design, alongside larger caches and improved memory bandwidth.
Every Cobalt 200 VM also includes Azure Boost, which offloads networking and storage processing from the host. Microsoft reports up to 15% higher network bandwidth and 20% higher remote storage IOPS compared with Cobalt 100.
“They need remote storage. They need high-performance networking. They need local SSD,” Stemen says of the workloads customers bring to Azure.
Stemen says the team breaks Microsoft’s own workloads into smaller components, models their behavior before the hardware exists, and uses those results to make decisions about cache sizes, memory, and even the fans in a server rack. Product teams participate in the earliest planning reviews.
“They’re influencing the beginning of the product from when it’s just in PowerPoint,” Stemen says.
The Teams media-processing service, for example, reported 1.65 times the performance on Cobalt 200 compared with Cobalt 100. Microsoft says the service saw linear scaling across physical cores and could load vCPUs to 90% utilization while serving traffic.
Outside Microsoft, Amadeus reported more than 30% higher flight-search throughput in its benchmark lab compared with Cobalt 100.
A wider range of Arm workloads
Indeed, quite a few Microsoft services like Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure DevOps, Azure SQL, Microsoft 365, Xbox, and others already run on Cobalt today.
A while ago, Stemen says, “customers had real concern about the lift.” Since then, “there’s more evidence of that working out, and the tools have improved, and the products have gotten better all at the same time.”
Alongside its general-purpose and memory-optimized VMs, Cobalt 200 brings two additional families to general availability: the high-memory Mpsv4 family, with 16 GiB of memory per vCPU, and the storage-optimized Lpsv5 family, with up to 23 TB of local NVMe storage.
“But now we’re seeing interest and desire for large in-memory databases, large existing enterprise workloads,” Stemen says, “and the ability to port them now being easier has helped.”
And while Microsoft will continue to invest in x86 chips, the company says it expects Cobalt 200 to make up “a significant portion of our new Azure Compute capacity in 2027 and moving forward.”
Developers can deploy the VMs through the existing Azure tools and use them in Virtual Machine Scale Sets or as Azure Kubernetes Service node pools.

articles.title: Semifinal Nacional vs. Once Caldas ver online en Pirlo TV, Fútbol Libre o Roja Directa: la búsqueda en Google que expone tus cuentas
articles.text:
La semifinal entre Atlético Nacional y Once Caldas impulsa búsquedas en Google de Pirlo TV, Fútbol Libre y Roja Directa para ver el partido online, pero esos accesos gratuitos pueden comprometer contraseñas, datos bancarios y archivos personales. El encuentro de vuelta se jugará este martes 17 de noviembre en Medellín.
La transmisión oficial estará a cargo de Win+ Fútbol, canal premium del fútbol profesional colombiano. La expectativa por el duelo, sumada al interés por evitar una suscripción, lleva a algunos usuarios hacia sitios no autorizados que prometen enlaces inmediatos, aunque también pueden usar ventanas emergentes, descargas engañosas y formularios destinados a capturar información.
Atlético Nacional y Once Caldas definen un cupo en la final
Atlético Nacional recibirá a Once Caldas a las 18:30 en el estadio Atanasio Girardot, en la vuelta de las semifinales de la Copa BetPlay. El primer encuentro terminó 1-1, con el primer gol de James Rodríguez con el equipo verdolaga.
Nacional buscará una ventaja ante su público después de dos partidos sin vencer a Once Caldas. El equipo dirigido por Panelo Valencia ha planteado encuentros cerrados ante el conjunto de Medellín, que también volverá a enfrentarlo durante los cuadrangulares.
Una web pirata puede ocultar descargas y enlaces fraudulentos
Los portales que ofrecen partidos sin autorización suelen incluir múltiples botones de reproducción, redirecciones y avisos que simulan ser parte del reproductor. Algunos invitan a descargar extensiones, archivos o supuestos programas necesarios para iniciar la señal.
La Organización Internacional de Policía Criminal (Interpol) advierte que las plataformas de contenidos pirateados representan un riesgo para la ciberseguridad. El problema no se limita a una imagen de baja calidad, cortes o publicidad invasiva: puede afectar cuentas, dispositivos y redes conectadas.
Antes de mostrar un supuesto partido, una página puede solicitar permisos sin relación con el vídeo, como acceso a notificaciones, descargas o configuraciones del navegador. También puede dirigir a formularios externos con premios falsos, alertas de virus o mensajes que piden actualizar el dispositivo.
Entre las señales más habituales aparecen dominios que cambian con frecuencia, errores de redacción, botones duplicados y ausencia de información sobre la empresa responsable. La oferta de partidos, películas, series y canales de pago sin costo también debe generar desconfianza.
El malware puede alcanzar teléfonos, computadores y televisores
Interpol señala que numerosos sitios y redes de intercambio de archivos entre pares, conocidas como P2P, pueden alojar malware o virus. El programa dañino puede llegar tras una descarga engañosa o después de pulsar un anuncio que aparenta formar parte de la transmisión.
Ese software puede afectar a teléfonos, tabletas, computadores y televisores conectados. En algunos casos, busca acceder a documentos, fotografías, contraseñas o sesiones que permanecen abiertas en las aplicaciones y navegadores.
El riesgo puede extenderse a otros equipos de la misma red doméstica o laboral. Una descarga realizada para ver el encuentro entre Nacional y Once Caldas puede afectar dispositivos que no tienen relación con la transmisión deportiva.
Las consecuencias pueden continuar después del partido. Un archivo malicioso puede permanecer activo, modificar opciones del equipo, abrir publicidad persistente o dirigir la navegación a otras páginas sin que el usuario lo detecte de inmediato.
Las cuentas bancarias y las contraseñas también quedan expuestas
Una transmisión ilegal puede utilizar un registro gratuito como mecanismo para captar datos. El portal puede pedir una dirección de correo electrónico o solicitar el inicio de sesión mediante una cuenta de redes sociales. Si el sitio carece de controles de seguridad, esa información puede quedar comprometida.
La amenaza aumenta cuando la web exige datos de tarjeta, información bancaria o un pago pequeño para “desbloquear” la señal. Interpol advierte que los métodos de pago inseguros pueden derivar en fraude con tarjetas y otras estafas financieras.
Algunos usuarios recurren a servidores proxy para ocultar su ubicación y acceder a transmisiones restringidas. Sin embargo, estas herramientas no garantizan protección. Sus operadores pueden registrar la actividad de navegación o añadir riesgos si no resultan confiables.
Para identificar una opción legítima, conviene consultar los sitios oficiales de la competición, los clubes, las federaciones y las plataformas con derechos de transmisión. En este caso, el partido entre Atlético Nacional y Once Caldas tendrá señal de Win+ Fútbol.

articles.title: Qwik 2.0 RC: Replaces HTML Comment Markers for Faster Reactivity and Out-of-Order Streaming
articles.text:
Qwik, the resumable JavaScript framework originally created at Builder.io, has released its 2.0 Release Candidate, targeting a rewrite of how the framework encodes resumable state in server-rendered HTML and introducing experimental out-of-order streaming. The RC was published on 1st October 2026 as @qwik.dev/core@2.0.0-rc.0, around two years and eight months after the initial Towards Qwik 2.0 design article.
In v1, Qwik propagated state updates by sprinkling HTML comment markers such as <!--qv--> and <!--t=8--> throughout the rendered body to flag component boundaries and the text nodes a signal should update. That approach forced a single ordered write pass, added CPU and memory overhead, and made out-of-order streaming impossible because a slow fetch blocked everything after it. In v2 the comments are gone, with state and virtual node information instead compressed into two <script type="qwik/state"> and <script type="qwik/vnode"> blocks at the end of the document.
On Qwik's internal runs of js-framework-benchmark, v2 posts a weighted geometric mean of 1.23 times slower than vanilla JavaScript, ahead of Vue 3.5 at 1.25x, Angular 22 at 1.42x, React 19 with the compiler at 1.53x, and v1 itself at 2.59x. A detailed classmethod walkthrough that built the same starter against both versions reported server-rendered HTML went from 60 comments to zero, with JavaScript required before interactivity dropping from 59KB to 9KB, though total bundle size grew.
Out-of-order HTML streaming has also been added n experimental mode. Developers can wrap slow regions in <Pending> and <Catch> boundaries so the server sends the rest of the page immediately and streams the real content later in the same response, with a small inline script swapping it into place. The APIs are opt-in through vite.config.ts:
qwikVite({ experimental: ['pendingBoundary', 'catchBoundary', 'blockSSR'] })
useComputed$ now accepts async functions, replacing <Resource>, and route loaders gain their own JSON endpoints with cacheControl and eTag options so the browser can cache them individually and <Link> can prefetch data on hover. Other additions include a worker$ primitive for Web Workers, reactify$ for embedding Qwik components inside React trees, server-only *.server.ts files, and HMR that preserves signal and store values across edits.
In a Reddit discussion predating the v2 RC, one developer called the lack of out-of-order streaming a significant limitation and argued that the Qwik team should be more upfront about it. Another commenter suggested that streaming could be a future feature. In his Classmethod walkthrough, Hiroshi Morishige noted the long wait for v2, it reached alpha in November 2024 and beta in June 2025, while v1 continued to receive updates through 1.20.1 in September 2026. He also noted that SvelteKit 3 and Remix 3.0 released stable versions on the same day as Qwik's RC, with the three releases published within seven hours. Qwik 2 and SvelteKit 3 use Vite 8; Remix 3 is independent of Vite.
The team says the breaking changes are small and automated by pnpm qwik migrate-v2, which also handles the move to the new @qwik.dev/core and @qwik.dev/router package names. New projects can scaffold with pnpm create qwik@rc, and the RC can be explored via next.qwik.dev/examples or the online playground.
Qwik is an open-source resumable framework that serialises state and event listeners into HTML, then lazily loads component JavaScript only in response to user interaction. The project is MIT licensed and developed openly on GitHub.

articles.title: Xiaomi renueva su gama alta con el Xiaomi 18 Pro Max y el Xiaomi 18 Pro: pantalla trasera... y mucha IA
articles.text:
Xiaomi renueva su gama alta con el Xiaomi 18 Pro Max y el Xiaomi 18 Pro, dos nuevos terminales con unas especificaciones sobresalientes y una propuesta centrada especialmente en la IA y con la seña de identidad de su pantalla trasera que promete seguir ampliando funcionalidades.
Los dos terminales, pertenecientes a la Pro Series de la compañía, hacen gala de la gama Elite de Qualcomm, montando un Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 para el caso del Pro Max y Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 para el modelo Pro, pero no es lo único que ofrecen en lo alto de la lista de especificaciones.
De nuevo, repite con dos tamaños: por un lado, el Xiaomi 18 Pro, que cuenta con una compacta pantalla de 6,4 pulgadas y una anchura de 72 mm que facilita un uso cómodo con una sola mano, y el Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, que crece hasta las 6,9 pulgadas.
En este sentido, su sistema de cámaras Leica Dual de 200 MP promete ofrecer alguna de las mejores experiencias de foto y vídeo en la gama alta, y además se incorporan algunas funciones muy interesantes, marca de la casa, como su pantalla Privacy Display con HyperRGB 2.0.
Xiaomi vuelve a apostar por la pantalla trasera... y mucha IA en los 18 Pro
No obstante, la clave de estos nuevos Xiaomi 18 Pro Max y el Xiaomi 18 Pro es, como decimos, su pantalla trasera, a la que Xiaomi llama Back Display. La compañía no ha escatimado nada en esta pantalla trasera, puesto que está construida con el mismo panel M11 de la pantalla principal, por lo que sus especificaciones son altísimas: hasta 4.000 nits de brillo máximo, tasa de refresco LTPO de 1 a 120 Hz, un diseño unificado bajo cristal (Unified Underglass) que integra tanto la pantalla como las cámaras bajo una única lámina de vidrio, y resistencia a golpes y caídas firmada por Gorilla Glass Victus 2.
La pantalla trasera no es solo atrezo. Además de las funciones de cámara para selfies de grupo o modo espejos para sacar toda la calidad de la cámara trasera para selfies, también tiene otras funciones interesantes. Xiaomi destaca AI Interpreter, una funcionalidad que convierte las dos pantallas en una herramienta de traducción en tiempo real o, gracias a la integración de la IA y la app de GenAI Apps, que trae el vibe coding a los smartphones y permite crear miniaplicaciones y usarlas en la pantalla trasera. Xiaomi dice que hay más de 50 aplicaciones predefinidas con funciones personalizables para la back display.
Como siempre, uno de los puntos fuertes de la Pro Series de Xiaomi es su sistema de cámaras. La compañía vuelve a firmar con Leica, y en el caso del Xiaomi 18 Pro ha optado por una cámara principal con Leica UltraPure y una lente óptica Leica Summilux f/1.67, además de un teleobjetivo de tipo periscópico llamado Power Prism que combina redirección de la luz y enfoque en un único componente óptico combinado con un sensor de 1/1,56 pulgadas. Además, en el caso del Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, se incluye un sensor Light Fusion 960L, que proporciona un elevado rango dinámico de 16,2 EV para escenas a contraluz.
En cuanto a vídeo, Xiaomi 18 Pro Series admite grabación hasta en 4K a 120 fps en Dolby Vision, además de perfil Log de 10 bits y resolución 8K a 30 fps y todas las funciones de IA que te puedas imaginar, tanto en foto como en vídeo, impulsados por el modelo de imagen con IA integrado en el dispositivo.
Xiaomi tampoco se ha olvidado de la batería. El Xiaomi 18 Pro Max alberga una impresionante batería de 7.050 mAh con carga HyperCharge por cable de 100 W e inalámbrica de 50 W, mientras que el Xiaomi 18 Pro cuenta con una batería de 6.000 mAh con HyperCharge de 90 W por cable y 50 W inalámbrica.
Xiaomi 18 Pro: precios y disponibilidad
Respecto a su precio y disponibilidad, el Xiaomi 18 Pro Max estará disponible en cuatro colores: Negro, Blanco, Azul Cósmico y Velvet Red, y en 2 variantes de almacenamiento con los siguientes precios:
- Xiaomi 18 Pro Max 12GB + 256GB: 1.599,99€
- Xiaomi 18 Pro Max 12GB + 512GB: 1.799,99€
Por su parte, el Xiaomi 18 Pro estará disponible también en cuatro colores: Negro, Blanco, Azul Cósmico y Velvet Red, y viene con 2 variantes de almacenamiento con los siguientes precios:
- Xiaomi 18 Pro 12GB + 256GB: 1.399,99€
- Xiaomi 18 Pro 12GB + 512GB: 1.599,99€
Con motivo del lanzamiento, Xiaomi tiene algunas promociones en mi.com: para el Xiaomi 18 Pro Max (en cualquiera de sus dos variantes) con descuento directo de 300 € y para el Pro normal un descuento directo de entre 250 € y 350 €, dependiendo del almacenamiento.

articles.title: Moto G77 (256 GB) registra desconto agressivo de 40% na Black November • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Moto G77 (256 GB) registra desconto agressivo de 40% na Black November
Moto G77 conta com tela AMOLED de 5.000 nits, câmera principal de 108 MP e bateria prometida para até 37 horas de uso. Oferta com pagamento no Pix pelo Mercado Livre
O Moto G77 (256 GB) está em promoção com 40% de desconto no Mercado Livre. O smartphone sai por apenas R$ 1.509 no Pix em oferta na Black November 2026. Anunciado em março pela Motorola por R$ 2.499, se destaca pela ficha técnica equilibrada, com destaques para a tela brilhante e câmera principal de alta resolução.
O celular utiliza um painel Extreme AMOLED de 6,8″ que reproduz cores intensas, além de entregar resolução Super HD (superior ao Full HD) às imagens. O brilho máximo de 5.000 nits que o Moto G77 promete atingir em circunstâncias de baixa ou nenhuma luminosidade, sendo um dos mais fortes do segmento intermediário. Enquanto a taxa de 120 Hz assegura experiência fluida de modo geral.
O dispositivo traz uma câmera avançada de 108 MP. O sensor principal conta com estabilização óptica (OIS), zoom de 3x para manter a nitidez mesmo a distância, e recursos de IA via Moto AI. Na parte traseira, ainda há uma ultrawide de 8 MP. Enquanto a lente frontal de 32 MP, possui a função Detector de Sorrisos para aprimorar os resultados das selfies.
Equipado com o processador Dimensity 6400 e 8 GB de RAM física, o celular da Motorola com 256 GB de armazenamento entrega desempenho somente para tarefas básicas. Portanto, é mais voltado para usuários com pouco interesse para rodar jogos e executar multitarefas.
Em relação a construção, o celular utiliza uma carcaça de plástico combinado a certificação IP64, com resistência completa a poeira só que limitada a respingos d’água. Por outro lado, a certificação militar MIL-STD-810H garante a aprovação em condições extremas de pressão, temperatura e outras circunstâncias.
A bateria de 5.200 mAh sugere autonomia para mais de um dia de uso intenso, com promessa pela Motorola de até 37 horas de uso, incluindo reprodução de músicas e vídeos. O componente suporta apenas carregamento com fio de até 30 W.
O Moto G77 (256 GB) com promessa de atualizações até o sistema Android 19 está com 40% de desconto no Mercado Livre, por apenas R$ 1.509 no Pix.
