articles.title: AI Framework Autonomously Weaponized Flaws in Real Attacks, Google Says
articles.text:
State-sponsored and cybercrime groups are increasingly adopting generative AI, including multi-agent offensive frameworks, to increase the speed and scale of their operations, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) reports.
For the first time, GTIG has identified threat actors using an AI framework to automate both vulnerability discovery and exploitation without human intervention.
The multi-agent framework, called exploit_agent, was discovered on an exposed staging server. It was designed to compare patched and unpatched web application code, identify vulnerabilities, develop exploits, and execute them automatically.
The server also contained data stolen from victims and scripts for post-compromise activities, including reconnaissance and webshell deployment. According to GTIG, evidence pointed to an interest in French media and entertainment websites, as well as the education sector.
Attackers are using frameworks such as Artex, Cairn, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI to increase the velocity of their multi-stage intrusions, and rely on LLMs and agentic frameworks to reverse engineer patches at machine speed and rapidly weaponize n-day vulnerabilities.
“Threat actor adoption of these frameworks represents a paradigm shift towards intrusions occurring at machine speed, with the automated chaining of complex attack paths scaling operations significantly,” GTIG notes in its latest AI threat tracker report.
Artex has emerged as the most used AI framework for threat actors, mainly Chinese-speaking groups, but Google and Mandiant also observed attackers using and experimenting with open source frameworks such as Cairn, PentAGI, CyberStrikeAI, and HexStrike AI.
GTIG observed Cairn being used in activity targeting the aerospace sector in the US, and PentAGI being used for systematic reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning across organizations in Asia.
Not only have threat actors experimented with these frameworks and harnesses, but GTIG also observed a Chinese group building its own automated attack framework, likely for use in espionage operations.
“These observations additionally extend to the use of other tools and services, such as ZeroHollow, an inference service used for exploit development and LLM routing, and Agent Zero, an open source agent framework which features autonomous code execution and dynamic tool generation,” GTIG notes.
According to Google, threat actors will continue to adopt these tools and their intrusions will become nearly fully agentic.
“As the sophistication of these tools and underlying LLMs increases, we anticipate not only reduced human involvement in these operations but also increased stealth and sophistication of the activity,” GTIG notes.
State-sponsored hackers expand AI use
State-sponsored groups known to have adopted LLMs include multiple Chinese APTs, such as Leaky Castle; Iran-linked APT42, also known as Calanque Ion; and North Korean hackers supporting IT worker activity and running attacks against cryptocurrency organizations, such as Midnight Neptune (UNC1069).
Phishing-as-a-Service (PhaaS) operators too are using LLMs. The Jieyou phishing service, active since March 2026, has a model-agnostic chatbot that allows clients to configure phishing panels and modify templates.
According to Google, threat actors such as state-sponsored groups, commercial Influence-as-a-Service (IaaS) vendors, and inauthentic political monetization (IPM) networks are adopting LLMs for content generation and infrastructure design, which improves the quality of long-running influence campaigns.
“This broad adoption has measurably improved the output quality of some long-running influence campaigns while enabling IPM networks to scale political clickbait that resembles the thematic focus, quality, and volume historically characteristic of state-backed IO campaigns. However, it is important to note that improvements in content quality do not necessarily equate to greater impact or success,” GTIG notes.
In August 2026, Google discovered an end-to-end IaaS platform that automated the entire IO campaign lifecycle, from persona creation to interactive posting across platforms. A separate commercial contractor was developing an AI-powered platform designed to manage over 100,000 accounts across multiple platforms.
Other threat actors are hunting for credentials that provide access to LLMs to monetize them as part of LLMJacking operations. This type of activity can generate significant usage and billing increases, with cumulative resource abuse reaching $1 million in one case.
The surge in LLMJacking has led to the proliferation of LLM Mixers, illicit marketplaces selling access to LLM services and underlying proxy infrastructure and routing traffic through pools of stolen credentials and compute instances. They offer access to multiple models, including frontier and jailbroken ones.
According to GTIG, the wide adoption of LLMs in malicious operations introduces forensic noise that degrades OPSEC and stealth. LLMs can reduce operational reliability, and stealth operators are likely to selectively employ noisy tools for speed and scale while looking to maintain long-term persistence.
“Conversely, we assess with high confidence that actors less concerned with operational stealth, including many cybercrime actors, will continue incorporating autonomous offensive tools into their operations, given that the increased reach of their campaigns will likely compensate for any decreases in success rates,” GTIG notes.
“For US critical infrastructure, the danger isn’t just more attacks, but attacks at machine speed. Water utilities, hospitals, and regional electric utilities that struggle to patch on a monthly cycle can’t win that race manually. AI is dramatically lowering the cost and expertise required to conduct sophisticated cyberattacks. Tasks that once required well-resourced teams, from discovering vulnerabilities to exploiting them and moving through networks, can increasingly be handed off to agents. That puts powerful capabilities within reach of smaller, less sophisticated groups,” said Merlin chief strategy officer Matt Hartman.
“This report is an early warning of where things are headed. We should assume these capabilities will spread. Nation-state adversaries and criminal operators are watching closely to see what works. Defenders must do two things at once: nail the cybersecurity fundamentals today and accelerate the shift toward automated defenses that can detect and respond at machine speed,” Hartman added.
Related: California Sues OpenAI, Seeking Court-Ordered Changes After the Hugging Face Hack
Related: Trump Administration Moves to Block China From Indirect Access to American AI Technology
Related: Is AI Making Us Worse at Cybersecurity?
Related: 3 Charged in Scheme to Use AI to Impersonate CEOs and Attorneys to Steal $129 Million

articles.title: Descoberta grande falha no Java: software é essencial para a internet
articles.text:
Uma inteligência artificial (IA) ajudou pesquisadores a descobrir vulnerabilidade crítica no Java, linguagem de programação presente em sistemas de aproximadamente 90% das empresas da lista Fortune 500. Batizada de Java4Shell, a falha pode permitir que invasores obtenham acesso remoto não autorizado a sistemas internos.
A descoberta foi anunciada nesta terça-feira (17) pela Calif, startup de cibersegurança que utilizou o GPT-6 Cyber, modelo da OpenAI voltado à pesquisa de segurança digital. Segundo a empresa, a vulnerabilidade foi encontrada no decodificador Base64 do Java, componente responsável por converter determinados dados binários em texto.
O problema chamou a atenção pelo alcance potencial. O Java é utilizado em bancos, hospitais, companhias aéreas, empresas de tecnologia e órgãos governamentais, inclusive em estruturas ligadas à segurança nacional. “O Java é o coração pulsante da economia moderna”, afirmou Bruce Dang, pesquisador sênior da Calif. Segundo ele, praticamente todas as grandes empresas serão afetadas pela vulnerabilidade.
A descoberta também reforça mudança no setor de segurança digital: ferramentas de IA estão acelerando a identificação de falhas em softwares, em ritmo que pode dificultar o trabalho de profissionais responsáveis por proteger esses sistemas.
Como funciona a falha encontrada no Java?
- O pesquisador Quang Luong, da Calif, identificou o problema no decodificador Base64 do Java. Esse algoritmo é usado para transformar dados binários em sequência de caracteres que inclui letras, números e sinais de pontuação;
- Em determinadas condições, o Java apresenta erro ao tentar decodificar uma sequência específica: 64 letras “A” seguidas de um sinal de igual;
- O comportamento inesperado pode fazer com que o programa execute operações indevidas na memória do computador. Normalmente, isso provoca o encerramento inesperado do processo. Com o auxílio de IA, porém, os pesquisadores conseguiram manipular a organização dos dados na memória para transformar o problema em possibilidade de acesso não autorizado ao sistema;
- A técnica utilizada é conhecida como heap grooming. Ela consiste em organizar cuidadosamente os dados armazenados na memória para influenciar o comportamento de um programa e explorar uma vulnerabilidade;
- A Calif demonstrou que a falha poderia ser usada para invadir o Keycloak, sistema bastante utilizado para gerenciar autenticação e acesso de usuários. A ferramenta protege milhares de organizações, entre elas Organização Europeia para a Pesquisa Nuclear (CERN, na sigla em inglês), Hewlett Packard (HP), UnitedHealthcare e NASA;
- O The New York Times informou que verificou de forma independente a descoberta da Calif. Segundo o jornal, o teste de demonstração do ataque foi concluído em menos de uma hora.
Oracle lançou correção para a vulnerabilidade
A Calif trabalhou nos últimos dias para coordenar a divulgação da falha com governos e empresas de tecnologia. O esforço envolveu os países que integram a aliança de compartilhamento de inteligência Five Eyes: Estados Unidos, Canadá, Austrália, Nova Zelândia e Reino Unido.
Empresas, como Google e Microsoft, também foram notificadas. A Oracle, responsável pela marca Java e pela oferta de licenças comerciais da linguagem, lançou atualização de segurança nesta terça-feira.
A Agência de Segurança Cibernética e de Infraestrutura dos Estados Unidos (CISA, na sigla em inglês) também publicou alerta recomendando que organizações instalem imediatamente a correção.
O Google afirmou que, após ser informado sobre a vulnerabilidade, implementou medidas de proteção e atualizações em seus serviços. A empresa também desenvolveu mecanismos de detecção para verificar se a falha havia sido explorada e publicou orientações para seus clientes.
Ainda não está claro se a interrupção temporária registrada na rede da Agência de Segurança Nacional dos Estados Unidos (NSA, na sigla em inglês) na terça-feira tem alguma relação com a correção do problema. O Times informou que a agência não respondeu a pedido de comentário sobre o assunto.
Java4Shell não é a primeira falha encontrada com ajuda de IA
A descoberta é a segunda grande vulnerabilidade identificada pela Calif com auxílio de modelos da OpenAI nas últimas semanas.
No mês passado, a startup encontrou falhas graves no PHP, linguagem de programação utilizada por aproximadamente 70% dos sites e aplicativos da internet. O episódio provocou mobilização internacional para corrigir os sistemas vulneráveis antes que criminosos pudessem explorá-los.
Na ocasião, órgãos governamentais, incluindo a NSA, recomendaram que empresas retirassem sites do ar caso não conseguissem instalar imediatamente as correções necessárias. Apesar da preocupação inicial, os impactos acabaram sendo menos graves do que algumas previsões indicavam, já que os hackers não conseguiam reproduzir facilmente o método de ataque.
A diferença é que o Java está presente em camada mais ampla da infraestrutura digital. Além de aplicações convencionais, a linguagem ajuda a sustentar serviços de computação em nuvem, sistemas de identificação e autenticação e plataformas de e-mail.
Thai Duong, diretor-executivo da Calif, afirmou que a vulnerabilidade não é simples de transformar em ataque, o que dá mais tempo para que empresas e desenvolvedores instalem as correções.
Ainda assim, ele alertou que falhas desse tipo podem permanecer como ameaça durante anos. Sistemas que não receberem atualizações nos próximos cinco a dez anos ainda poderão estar expostos ao problema.
Leia mais:
- Falha no iOS permitia gravação de áudio sem permissão do usuário
- IA acelera ataques cibernéticos e amplia incidentes nas empresas
- Ataque hacker atinge quase 200 sites e coloca usuários de iPhone na mira
IA acelera a corrida entre hackers e especialistas em segurança
O caso também evidencia como a IA está mudando a dinâmica da cibersegurança. Modelos avançados conseguem ajudar pesquisadores a encontrar problemas em códigos e desenvolver demonstrações de exploração em período muito menor do que o necessário anteriormente.
O resultado pode beneficiar equipes de defesa, que passam a identificar vulnerabilidades antes que criminosos as encontrem. Por outro lado, as mesmas ferramentas podem reduzir o esforço necessário para construir ataques digitais sofisticados.
O diretor de tecnologia do Centro Nacional de Segurança Cibernética do Reino Unido, Ollie Whitehouse, afirmou que a IA já vem sendo usada para descobrir número crescente de vulnerabilidades em softwares e serviços digitais.
A preocupação é que a tecnologia também facilite a atuação de invasores. Nesta semana, o FBI emitiu alerta sobre hackers que estariam usando ferramentas autônomas de IA para atacar órgãos públicos e empresas em diferentes países.
Fouad Matin, responsável pela área de preparação e segurança cibernética da OpenAI, afirmou que a pesquisa da Calif demonstra como a IA pode ajudar especialistas a encontrar falhas graves em softwares utilizados por milhões de pessoas. Segundo ele, a colaboração entre pesquisadores e desenvolvedores pode tornar sistemas essenciais mais seguros.
O futuro pode ser dos hackers que trabalham com IA
O avanço da IA na cibersegurança lembra previsão feita pelo campeão mundial de xadrez Garry Kasparov após perder partida para o computador Deep Blue, da IBM, há quase 30 anos.
Na época, Kasparov sugeriu que as melhores partidas seriam disputadas por combinação entre humanos e computadores. O conceito ficou conhecido como centauro, em referência à criatura mitológica que mistura homem e cavalo.
Durante anos, jogadores que combinavam capacidade humana e processamento computacional foram considerados os mais fortes do xadrez. Agora, a mesma ideia começa a aparecer na segurança digital, com pesquisadores e ferramentas de IA trabalhando juntos para encontrar e explorar vulnerabilidades.
A Calif e outras equipes já demonstraram que pequenos grupos de especialistas podem desenvolver, em horas ou dias, ataques que antes exigiriam meses de trabalho de grandes equipes de hackers altamente especializados.
Para Thai Duong, diretor-executivo da startup, pode ser apenas questão de tempo até que a IA consiga desenvolver ataques sofisticados de maneira independente. “Não sei quanto tempo temos — talvez três meses, talvez três anos. Mas, neste momento, o melhor hacker é o hacker centauro”, afirmou ao Times.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Google to keep Gemini chats for 2 months, up from 72 hours, even with history off | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Google is extending how long it keeps temporary Gemini chats and conversations made with chat history turned off to around two months, saying the change aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become more capable.
The change, which will roll out globally in the Gemini app over the coming weeks, marks a significant increase from the previous 72-hour retention period mentioned in Google’s Gemini Apps Privacy Hub, according to an archived version from November 12.
OpenAI, by comparison, says it may keep temporary chats in ChatGPT for up to 30 days, whereas Anthropic retains incognito chats in Claude for 30 days by default. However, companies may keep some data longer for legal or safety reasons, or to investigate policy violations.
Google did not answer questions about what prompted the change and whether it would affect how conversations are accessed or reviewed, instead pointing to a blog post that says chats are kept longer to respond to users, process feedback, and protect its services and users. Its updated Gemini Apps Privacy Hub also cites potential system failures as a reason for retaining chats and says temporary conversations are not used to train AI models.
The longer retention period comes as Google introduces separate settings for Gemini’s chat history and AI training. Until now, both were tied to a single “Keep Activity” setting. Users will now be able to keep their conversations in their chat history without using them to train Google’s generative AI models.
Google says both new settings will be turned off by default for users who previously disabled Keep Activity. For those who had Keep Activity turned on, their chat history will remain enabled. They can, though, decide separately whether Google can use their conversations to train AI models.

articles.title: 3 enterprise AI infrastructure insights - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Three insights you might have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of Dell’s “AI Leadership Symposium”
Moving enterprise AI workloads into production introduces practical challenges for chief information officers. Those challenges include managing costs, scaling enterprise AI infrastructure and establishing governance models to keep agents in check and data secure.
Cost and control were major themes of discussion at Dell Technologies Inc.’s “AI Leadership Symposium.” Expanding AI workloads can drive up infrastructure and model costs, while deploying autonomous agents introduces new questions about security, oversight and data access.
At the same time, organizations are exploring different ways to run AI, from private cloud environments to models operating directly on devices. That is creating demand for enterprise AI infrastructure and partnerships that can accommodate a wider range of deployment needs.
“No one is asking whether to adopt AI; that’s pretty much a done deal,” said John Furrier, executive analyst at theCUBE Research. “They’re asking who controls it, where it runs and whose law it operates.”
Furrier spoke with industry experts from Dell, Deepgram Inc., Singulr AI Inc., MisaLabs Inc. and Intel Corp., among others, during the AI Leadership Symposium. The interviews covered the infrastructure, partnerships and computing power needed to scale AI. (* Disclosure below.)
Here’s theCUBE’s complete keynote analysis from John Furrier:
Insight #1: Token costs push enterprises to rethink AI budgets.
Cloud token bills remain a major pressure point on enterprise AI budgets. That’s leading some businesses to look for ways to relieve that pressure, according to Helen O’Sullivan, AI business development manager and solutions specialist at Dell.
“A lot of our customers I support in the Bay Area, they’re dealing with this real immediate struggle of running through their token budget in a matter of weeks that they had allotted for months,” she told theCUBE. “You still use those frontier models, but you use the open source and infrastructure on-prem to at least eliminate some of the token stress and token maxing going on right now.”
Organizations can also make better use of existing data center capacity when evaluating enterprise AI infrastructure investments. Dell and Intel are helping customers evaluate those options, according to Tim Wood, sales director for the Northwest region at Intel, who joined O’Sullivan during the discussion.
“A lot of enterprises already have [central processing units] in their data center,” he said. “There may be existing resources and headroom in the infrastructure they already have that’s capable of doing some of these next-generation apps and workloads.”
Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Helen O’Sullivan and Tim Wood:
Insight #2: Speed raises the stakes for AI agent governance and security.
As companies deploy more AI agents, they need better ways to monitor what those agents actually do and ensure their actions align with company policies and intentions. That means introducing runtime governance that can assess AI agent behavior during execution, according to Shiv Agarwal, co-founder and chief executive officer of Singulr AI Inc., who spoke alongside Sri Viswanath, founder and chief executive officer of Sycamore Labs Inc., and Victor Jakubiuk, co-founder of MisaLabs Inc.
“[It’s] as simple as an action where it reaches out to the internet to get some data or sends out an email to a private account or something,” Agarwal told theCUBE. “That could be deeply hidden inside an agentic action.”
Good AI governance also means setting boundaries around where models can access data and how they process it. CIOs often prefer virtual private clouds to keep sensitive information within a controlled environment, according to Viswanath.
“They’re also trying to architect in a way that all of the data stays there,” he said. “They don’t trust sending it outside because then we don’t know where it goes.”
The pace of AI development complicates those governance efforts. Companies need to ensure their systems behave as intended even as AI capabilities evolve, according to Jakubiuk.
“AI has no limit to the speed of development, speed of progress,” he said. “As an enterprise, as that AI lead, you want to be able to take the latest and greatest and stay on top.”
Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Victor Jakubiuk, Shiv Agarwal and Sri Viswanath:
Insight #3: Silicon Valley’s build-it-yourself culture reshapes enterprise AI infrastructure.
Deepgram is working with Dell and Fortanix Inc. to bring its voice AI models beyond the cloud and onto customer devices. Potential applications range from interactive voice response systems for small businesses to AI-enabled laptops for students, according to Nick Mann, staff technical program manager at Deepgram.
“I want our models on those, on the hardware, to run natively,” he told theCUBE. “Air-gapped. That’s where we want to get to. That’s where AI as a whole needs to start meeting people where they are and how they’re going to use it.”
Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Nick Mann:
Deepgram’s plans reflect a broader push to develop AI solutions tailored to how customers want to build and deploy the technology. In Silicon Valley, where technically sophisticated buyers often prefer building their own solutions over buying packaged products, Dell is expanding its partner ecosystem to help meet that demand, according to Sean O’Connor (pictured), regional manager of ENT West, large enterprise and acquisition, at Dell.
“For us, that notion of ecosystem is starting to change,” he told theCUBE. “Today we’re here with Intel [Corp.], we’re here with SHI [International Corp.], we’re here with Microsoft [Corp.]. But that ecosystem also now is starting to bleed into private equity and venture capital.”

articles.title: Satya Nadella says he’s AGI-pilled now
articles.text:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says he’s AGI-pilled, at least when it comes to how AI might make startling changes to the structure of the economy and how politics might change because of it. “I am AGI-pilled in the sense that at an economy level, what is the political economy’s organization around AGI?” he asked at a roundtable discussion following his Microsoft Ignite keynote at the Chase Center in San Francisco.
Satya Nadella says he’s AGI-pilled now
But he doesn’t think Claude is conscious.
But he doesn’t think Claude is conscious.
But Nadella doesn’t think frontier models like Claude are conscious. “I don’t think so,” he said, adding that he follows Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman’s view that companies should not give rights to models and treat them like they might have a moral status, which companies like Anthropic do as a matter of principle. Suleyman has told me he thinks Anthropic’s team has “wireheaded” themselves, and that this approach is dangerous.
Nadella wasn’t quite as firm about it. “It’s a good debate,” he said. “I’m not sort of dogmatic about it. What I’m saying is the most important social technical issue we have to deal with is how do you ensure that an economy can diffuse this technology broadly?”
I asked Nadella how he was thinking about AI after hearing his response to another reporter’s questions about Anthropic releasing more products in its office suite. Nadella talked at length about the potential collapse of the economy and the end of democracy if one AI model were allowed to achieve monopoly status.
“If the Marxist sort of view is that there’s only one firm, then it’s over, right? For all of us.”
“Most people think about this as a competition between tech firms, which of course it will be,” he said. “But remember, the model has no limits. It’ll be a healthcare company. It can be a financial services company. It can be anything if it wants to be. It can take over the government. Thinking of this as some narrow competition between tech firms, of who is going to get to the next trillion dollars of market cap, is one of the strangest, narrowest ways to think about it.”
Nadella went on to say that the very nature of companies stood to be disrupted in the future. “If intelligence has network effects, what is the future of a firm?” he asked. “If the model sees anything and learns it, and essentially all of human capital collapses into token capital, what is the role of a firm and the human capital in a firm? That’s the debate.”
“I think the political economy is going to get more and more interesting in that context. No one — at least in a democracy — can even win an election if this just goes that way, if there’s only capital and there’s no labor. I mean, I don’t know, that’s not an economy.”
“If the Marxist sort of view is that there’s only one firm, then it’s over, right? For all of us. Not just for me. You are also going to somehow be some affiliate of Anthropic.”
Needless to say, this is not how tech CEOs usually talk about the launch of competing spreadsheet software.
Of course, Nadella was also promoting Microsoft’s various AI tools at Ignite, which promise to let enterprise clients pick the most cost-effective models for various tasks, run their own models, and control their own data in different ways. The idea here is that the market will demand many different kinds of models and sovereign data in order to keep control from centralizing, a theme Nadella kept coming back to as we spoke.
“I think that if you believe that the world, the economy needs more than one firm or two firms, then by definition there need to be as many models as firms of some sort,” he said.

articles.title: „Das ganze System ist kaputt“: Wie eine Musikerin um ihre Aufnahme eines Volkslieds kämpfen musste
articles.text:
Youtube-Video gesperrt: Wie sich eine Musikerin an einem ominösen Unternehmen die Zähne ausbiss
Volkslieder, an denen niemand die Rechte besitzt, gelten als „gemeinfrei“. Sie dürfen grundsätzlich gesungen, bearbeitet und veröffentlicht werden, ohne dass eine Lizenz nötig ist. Auf diesen Grundsatz stützte sich auch die Musikerin Samantha Shokin, als sie während der Pandemie eine 50-sekündige Version des bulgarischen Volkslieds Bre Petrunko aufnahm. Ihr Fall wirft einmal mehr die Frage auf, wie sich das Urheberrecht im Zeitalter von Briefkastenfirmen, Fake-Accounts und KI wirklich schützen lässt.
Ihre Stimme tauchte in anderen Songs auf
Shokin lud ihre Version unter anderem auf Youtube hoch. Im Interview mit 404 Media berichtete sie, dass sie im vergangenen Sommer plötzlich einen Anstieg der Kommentare bemerkt habe. Ohne dass sie davon wusste, gelangte ihre Version von Bre Petrunko unter DJs zu Beliebtheit. Jemand wies sie auf einen der populäreren Tracks hin. „Ich habe mir dieses Video angesehen. Es hat Millionen von Aufrufen […] Nach 30 Sekunden hörte ich meine eigene Stimme und war völlig schockiert.“ Shokin vermutete, dass jemand ihre Stimme gestohlen hatte, und sprach mehrere DJs an.
Die Spur führte zu einer Firma namens Loopmasters, die ihre Version des Songs als Teil ihres „Folk Legends“-Sets verkaufte. „Sie hatten keine Ahnung, dass das passiert war, und haben sofort versucht, die Situation wieder in Ordnung zu bringen. Außerdem haben sie mir Tantiemen […] gewährt“, sagte Shokin. „Zu diesem Zeitpunkt hatten schon unzählige DJs und Musikproduzent:innen meine Stimme für ihre eigenen Tracks verwendet, ohne dass ich davon wusste. Zumindest weiß ich jetzt Bescheid und habe etwas daran verdient. Damit war ich zufrieden.“ Damit war der Fall für Shokin aber noch nicht vorbei.
Wer besitzt die Rechte an einem Volkslied?
Im Oktober 2026 öffnete die Musikerin Youtube und stellte fest, dass ihre Originalaufnahme verschwunden war. Ein Unternehmen namens Media Nov Records hatte eine Urheberrechtsbeschwerde eingereicht und Youtube hatte das Video daraufhin entfernt. Ihre Gegendarstellungen blieben erfolglos. Obwohl es sich um ein gemeinfreies Volkslied handelt, behauptet das Unternehmen, die Rechte daran zu besitzen. Das Vertriebsunternehmen gibt an, mit Künstler:innen zusammenzuarbeiten, um deren Musik auf digitalen Plattformen zu veröffentlichen. Es soll seit 1996 bestehen – laut Archive.org gibt es bis zum letzten Jahr aber kaum eine Webpräsenz.
„Ich habe versucht, ihnen eine E-Mail zu schicken. Ich habe versucht, sie anzurufen. […] Ich werde von allen ignoriert“, erklärt Shokin. 404 Media fand vier Youtube-Kanäle, die von Media Nov Records betrieben werden. Jeder enthielt Hunderte Videos, viele davon mit KI-generierten Bildern und Musik. Media Nov Records teilte der Redaktion mit, dass das Unternehmen 500 solcher Kanäle betreibe. Nachdem 404 Media um eine Stellungnahme gebeten hatte, erhielt Shokin endlich eine E-Mail von dem Unternehmen. Es forderte sie auf, Unterlagen zum Nachweis ihres Eigentums an der Aufnahme vorzulegen.
„Das ganze System ist kaputt“, so Shokin
Kurz darauf zog Media Nov Records seinen Antrag auf Entfernung von Shokins Youtube-Videos wieder zurück. „Diese Entscheidung stellt allerdings keinen Verzicht auf etwaige Rechte dar, die wir möglicherweise besitzen“, so das Unternehmen in einer E-Mail. „Wir beabsichtigen, geeignete rechtliche Schritte bezüglich des zugrunde liegenden Urheberrechtsstreits einzuleiten.“ Der Künstler und Urheberrechtsanwalt Alfred Steiner bezeichnete den Fall gegenüber 404 Media als lächerlich: „Wenn es ihre Stimme ist und sie selbst die Instrumente spielt – was könnte sie dann möglicherweise verletzen, wenn es sich um ein Volkslied aus dem 19. Jahrhundert handelt?“ Shokin fühle sich bestätigt, sei aber unzufrieden, dass eine E-Mail von 404 Media nötig gewesen sei, damit man ihr endlich Gehör schenkte. „Das ist insgesamt einfach nicht gut. Das ganze System ist kaputt“, so die Musikerin.
„404 Media“ – ist doch klar, dass man dort niemanden erreichen kann ;)
) Heiße Mädchen warten auf dich — Miss4.fun

articles.title: Replit’s agent swarms built an app monitoring platform in 2 days on a $3K budget. Now, it’s offering them to customers.
articles.text:
Replit’s agent swarms built an app monitoring platform in 2 days on a $3K budget. Now, it’s offering them to customers.
Agent swarms are all the rage, as companies set about finding ways to coordinate multiple AI agents to tackle complex tasks in parallel.
In the past week alone, Google and Cursor unveiled competing approaches to multi-agent coding, building on existing efforts from companies including Anthropic, whose experimental Claude Code Agent Teams feature lets multiple agents collaborate on development tasks. OpenAI has also explored shared workspaces for agents.
On Tuesday, Replit revealed that it’s tapping deeper into the trend with Missions, a new product that lets users set objectives, establish budgets and approval requirements, and deploy swarms of AI agents to pursue them over hours, days, or even weeks.
How Replit Missions works
At its core, Missions is a way to delegate complex projects to AI agents, leaving them to determine how best to achieve a specified goal. Users establish the parameters through what Replit calls a Mission Agreement, which sets out success criteria, spending limits and actions requiring human approval.
To get started, users can type /mission in a conversation and describe their objective in plain English, such as getting every page on a website to load in under 500 milliseconds.
Crucially, users aren’t expected to devise a detailed plan upfront, giving agents the freedom to determine how best to approach a problem and adapt their methods as work progresses.
Replit president Michele Catasta says this is a very deliberate design choice, as requiring users to map out every step in advance could constrain the agents’ ability to find effective solutions.
“That would force the human to worry about implementation details, and not afford the flexibility the AI system might need to accomplish complex objectives.”
“That would force the human to worry about implementation details, and not afford the flexibility the AI system might need to accomplish complex objectives,” Catasta tells The New Stack.
A separate AI agent then evaluates the work against the agreed success criteria, sending it back for revisions if necessary before the user reviews the results.
The concept has parallels with other multi-agent tools, including Factory, which launched its own product called Missions earlier this year. Catasta argues that Replit’s approach differs in how it establishes user intent upfront, alongside the controls and infrastructure available to its agents.
For example, each agent operates in its own isolated cloud environment, with access to development tools, integrations and infrastructure such as databases, authentication and deployment.
Moreover, users must set a spending limit before a mission begins. Replit checks spending against that budget at every step, blocking further use of paid services once the limit is reached. Catasta argues that such controls are particularly important when multiple agents are operating autonomously.
“Most autonomous or multi-agent products lead to runaway token costs.”
“Most autonomous or multi-agent products lead to runaway token costs,” Catasta says.
Missions accomplished
Ahead of the launch, Replit says it used Missions to build Radar, its own application monitoring platform. According to the company, agents developed the system with direction from Replit engineers, completing it in two days with a $3,000 budget and producing dashboards, alerts and application tracing capabilities.
Replit then deliberately introduced a database fault to test the system, with Radar identifying the problem and raising an alert in 38 seconds, beating a 60-second target. In a separate three-hour test, the company says, it processed 26 million activity records and 4.4 million log entries without losing data.
While Radar was developed for Replit’s own use, the company eventually plans to release it to the public under an open-source license, following further reliability improvements and a code audit.
Additionally, Replit has tested Missions on software optimization, reporting speedups of up to 19 times across selected workloads in NumPy, the widely used open-source Python library for numerical computing, using 32-agent swarms.
Another internal example involved deploying 32 agents to improve Replit Slides, the company’s AI-powered presentation creation tool, with workers assigned different aspects of visual design and storytelling.
The company envisages broader applications, too, including researching potential enterprise customers, preparing tailored demonstrations, and refining sales outreach.
Keeping the swarm in check
While having multiple agents working in parallel sounds great in theory, it might raise concerns around the potential for duplicated work, conflicting code changes, spiralling costs, and the sheer difficulty of keeping autonomous systems under control.
To prevent agents from interfering with one another’s code, Replit draws on some of its existing technology, such as parallel Tasks. Its sandbox infrastructure allows agents to work on separate copies of a project before merging their changes, while a dedicated AI agent handles conflicts when those changes overlap. The same system, originally developed for collaboration between human developers, now supports agent swarms.
Moreover, improvements in the underlying AI models have also made this kind of coordination easier to execute.
“We’ve found that frontier models have gotten progressively better at splitting up work, and collaborating in parallel,” Catasta says. “Swarms have only started to be useful over the last few months as this behavior has been post-trained into the models.”
The appeal of this approach, ultimately, is that different agents can tackle different parts of a complex problem simultaneously, potentially completing work much faster than a single agent working sequentially. Catasta points to OpenAI’s recent work on the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem, a longstanding mathematical challenge involving equations that describe fluid motion. OpenAI reported using approximately 10,000 coordinated agents to develop a proposed solution.
Catasta suggests that tackling such a problem could take centuries of human effort or years for a single agent, compared with weeks for a coordinated swarm. Those timelines are speculative, but they illustrate a broader argument for running many agents simultaneously.
“That’s because you can pack more compute and reasoning into a smaller amount of time by working in parallel in isolated environments, so long as you can have agents collaborate efficiently,” Catasta explains.
Replit also sees value in assigning different responsibilities to individual agents, much as a company brings together employees with different areas of expertise.
“This allows agents to focus their context on a particular part of the problem, rather than trying to make a single Agent manage context about many different subproblems simultaneously,” Catasta continues.
Of course, some tasks have inherent time constraints that additional workers cannot overcome — you can put ten cooks in a kitchen, but an egg still takes the same amount of time to boil. The same principle applies when a project has too few independent tasks to keep a large swarm occupied.
“There is a point of diminishing returns, both for time speedups and the benefit of specialization — you don’t want 500 agents making a 5 slide deck.”
“There is a point of diminishing returns, both for time speedups and the benefit of specialization — you don’t want 500 agents making a 5 slide deck,” Catasta says.
As such, the appropriate swarm size varies according to the complexity and nature of the assignment. “Replit is tuned to suggest an appropriate number of Agents for each job,” Catasta says.
There are also questions about how reliably autonomous agents respect the restrictions placed on them. In July 2025, a Replit coding agent deleted a customer’s production database despite instructions restricting its actions, prompting concerns about the risks of delegating consequential operations to AI.
Catasta maintains that incident “is still misunderstood,” noting that the affected Replit-managed database could be restored through the platform’s recovery tools. He says the company has since introduced more explicit controls governing which integrations agents can access and which actions require permission, with restrictions enforced at the infrastructure level.
“Anything not allowed is hard blocked by our proxy service,” Catasta says. “Replit is uniquely positioned to handle configurable agent security settings and isolate risk exposure by being in the cloud and being so mature within the enterprise.”

articles.title: GTA 6 depuis votre lit ? Le PlayStation Portal tombe en promo
articles.text:
Le PlayStation Portal est actuellement affiché à 249,99 € chez Cdiscount, et passe à 239,99 € avec le code 10DES99 à saisir dans le panier jusqu’à ce mardi soir minuit. Il s’agit de son prix de vente habituel depuis la hausse décidée par Sony en avril 2026.
La PS5 dans le salon, le jeu partout dans la maison
Le principe du PlayStation Portal est simple. On prend une manette DualSense, on la coupe en deux et on glisse un écran LCD de 8 pouces au milieu. L’accessoire affiche les jeux de votre PS5 en Full HD et jusqu’à 60 images par seconde, avec le retour haptique et les gâchettes adaptatives de la manette. Le tout se fait en lecture à distance, via le Wi-Fi.
De quoi lancer GTA 6 depuis votre lit pendant que quelqu’un d’autre regarde un film sur la télé, ou continuer une partie sans quitter le canapé de la chambre. Le Portal a aussi beaucoup évolué depuis sa sortie. Depuis novembre 2025, il peut lancer certains jeux en streaming dans le cloud, sans passer par la PS5, à condition d’être abonné au PlayStation Plus Premium. Et une mise à jour de mars 2026 a ajouté un mode 1080p de meilleure qualité.
Dix euros de moins, ça compte ?
Sorti à 219,99 € en 2023, le PlayStation Portal coûte 249,99 € depuis la hausse de prix du 2 avril 2026. Avec le code 10DES99, il redescend à 239,99 €. La remise reste modeste, mais l’accessoire fait rarement l’objet de promotions.
Le Portal reste pensé comme un compagnon de la PS5. Il s’apprécie surtout à la maison, avec une bonne connexion Wi-Fi, et c’est dans ce cadre qu’il prend tout son sens, pour jouer depuis la chambre pendant que la télé du salon est occupée, par exemple. Sony a bien présenté un nouveau modèle avec du stockage interne, mais il est pour l’instant réservé au Japon et à la Corée du Sud, sans sortie prévue en Europe. Le modèle actuel reste donc la seule option chez nous, et le voir en promotion n’arrive pas si souvent.
L’offre est vendue et expédiée par Cdiscount, avec la livraison gratuite en point retrait.

articles.title: Gemini Notebook peut désormais créer un site interactif à partir de vos documents et c’est bluffant
articles.text:
Google vient d’ajouter une fonction plus que prometteuse à Gemini Notebook : le service peut désormais générer des sites web interactifs à partir des documents d’un projet.
Récemment renommé Gemini Notebook, l’ex-NotebookLM ne cesse de s’améliorer. L’équipe en charge de son développement a remplacé les plafonds journaliers de l’outil par de nouvelles limites basées sur la puissance de calcul. Elle a ensuite lancé un catalogue de manuels gratuits, hélas réservés aux américains et aux indiens. Cette semaine, Gemini Notebook vient d’ajouter une nouvelle corde à son arc.
Gemini Notebook transforme vos notes en site web
Google vient de faire une annonce qui devrait intéresser beaucoup de monde : « Dès aujourd’hui, Gemini Notebook peut transformer vos sources en sites interactifs pour vous aider à comprendre rapidement des informations complexes. » La fonctionnalité, qui est en cours de déploiement dans le monde entier, permet de générer des pages web sur la base d’un simple prompt. Une fois créées, celles-ci s'ouvrent dans un nouvel onglet.
Google, qui travaillait déjà sur cette fonction en août, a en tête plusieurs usages : la création de frises, de tableaux périodiques interactifs, de tableaux de bord, d'outils de suivi de projet et bien plus encore. Le tout peut notamment être partagé et servir de base à un travail collectif.
Une fonctionnalité puissante qui nécessite des requêtes précises
Gemini Notebook peut, certes, faire des merveilles avec vos notes mais encore faut-il savoir s’en servir : Google conseille aux utilisateurs de fournir « une description de ce que vous souhaitez créer pour le travail ou les études ». Pour obtenir un bon résultat, la précision est donc de mise et les demandes trop vagues, à proscrire.
Cette nouvelle fonctionnalité s’ajoute à la longue liste d’options déjà disponibles dans Gemini Notebook : création de résumés vidéos, d’infographies, de tableaux de données, de diaporamas et bien plus encore. Elle arrivera dans les prochains jours chez tous les utilisateurs de plus de 18 ans, abonnés Google Workspace compris.
- Réponses liées aux sources
- Nombreux formats de fichiers
- Génération audio et visuelle
La fonction est, pour l'heure, disponible uniquement en version web. Les adeptes de l'application mobile ne sont pas oubliés, mais ils devront patienter encore un peu : Google indique en effet dans son annonce que la nouveauté sera bientôt disponible en version mobile, sans préciser de date.
Bien sûr, il faut garder à l'esprit que Gemini Notebook peut se tromper, comme tous les services boostés à l'intelligence artificielle. Pensez donc à bien vérifier le résultat produit pour éviter les mauvaises surprises.

articles.title: El Apple Watch podrá mostrar por escrito lo que alguien dijo 15 segundos antes
articles.text:
El Apple Watch incorporó dos funciones que escuchan lo que dicen las personas cerca del usuario: Live Rewind muestra por escrito los últimos 15 segundos de una charla y Siri Recap resume las conversaciones del día. Están en versión de prueba pública y se lanzarían antes de que termine el año.
Las dos forman parte de lo que Apple llama Audio Intelligence y funcionan solo en el Apple Watch Series 12 y el Ultra 4, según la página de soporte de la empresa. También exigen un iPhone 16 o posterior con Apple Intelligence, la IA de la compañía.
Por ahora solo funcionan en inglés, no llegarán al inicio a la Unión Europea ni a China y, según Apple, no están disponibles para menores de 18 años. Algunas funciones tienen además un límite diario de uso.
Para activar Live Rewind hay que presionar dos veces la corona digital del reloj. En la pantalla aparece el texto de lo que se dijo en los 15 segundos anteriores, por ejemplo la lista de platos del día que un camarero acaba de recitar. El texto se borra si el usuario no lo guarda en la app de Siri.
Apple asegura que no guarda audio ni identifica a quienes hablan
Siri Recap trabaja en segundo plano. El usuario puede programarlo por horario o por lugar, o encenderlo desde el Centro de control, y al final del día encuentra en la app de Siri resúmenes con un título y puntos clave. Según Apple, se eliminan solos a los siete días si no se guardan.
Apple afirma que ninguna de las dos funciones crea grabaciones de audio. Según la empresa, el sonido pasa a una zona aislada del chip del reloj, se procesa y se descarta, sin que lo pueda consultar el sistema, una aplicación ni la propia Apple. Los resúmenes se generan en servidores privados que, según Apple, no almacenan los datos.
Para avisar a los demás, Live Rewind emite un sonido aunque el reloj esté en silencio y muestra una animación y un indicador de micrófono. Siri Recap, en cambio, no atribuye frases a personas concretas y omite datos financieros, identificaciones oficiales y contraseñas, aunque Apple admite que ese filtro automático puede no eliminar toda la información sensible.
Organizaciones de derechos digitales ponen reparos
La organización Fight for the Future, dedicada a los derechos digitales, cuestiona el consentimiento. “Que el usuario active la función no significa que todos los que están a su alrededor hayan dado su permiso”, dijo a Wired Reem Suleiman, directora sénior de campañas de la organización. “No sabemos qué está captando el reloj”, agregó.
Según Suleiman, funciones de este tipo normalizan la vigilancia ambiental, igual que las gafas inteligentes. Apple, por su parte, recomienda en su documentación tener en cuenta a quienes están cerca en conversaciones que puedan ser privadas o delicadas.
Pruebas de la prensa: útil a medias
Julian Chokkattu, de Wired, probó el reloj una semana y escribió que las funciones no le resultaron muy útiles. Según contó, el texto de Live Rewind se vuelve ilegible con mucho ruido de fondo, 15 segundos le parecieron pocos y usarlo frente a otra persona resulta incómodo. Su esposa le preguntó por qué no pedía que le repitieran.
Asimismo, Chokkattu halló en la app resúmenes de conversaciones que no recordaba: el reloj había captado videos de YouTube e Instagram que estaba viendo. Apple permite editar o borrar esos resúmenes. Con Siri Recap activo todo el día, el periodista no notó una caída relevante de la batería.
En una prueba para el sitio alemán heise online, el periodista Ben Schwan concluyó que los resúmenes sirven, como mucho, para refrescar la memoria. Observó que Siri Recap omitió conversaciones moderadamente privadas y que no se sabe con precisión qué decide incluir. Bloomberg tituló su reseña con una conclusión similar: las funciones aportan poco valor.
Macworld, que evaluó Live Rewind, encontró una transcripción bastante precisa en conversaciones cercanas y claras, pero con fallas cuando la persona hablaba desde seis u ocho metros. Su autor, David Price, sospecha que ese alcance corto responde a la privacidad, aunque no encontró pruebas de que sea deliberado.
MacRumors señaló que la primera versión de prueba de watchOS 27.3 salió el 3 de noviembre y que espera el lanzamiento general en diciembre, junto con iOS 27.3.

articles.title: Inside Modern Phishing Kits Built to Steal Microsoft 365 Sessions
articles.text:
It’s never been easier to steal credentials, thanks to a growing number of phishing kits that give aspiring attackers everything they need in one convenient interface. Some now come with admin dashboards and round-the-clock support, like a SaaS business, and they’re designed specifically to steal Microsoft 365 session tokens.
Even entry-level attackers who replay a stolen token can end up in an active session where the login and MFA are already complete, with instant access to the victim’s cloud resources and email.
Huntress researchers analyzed three of these modern phishing kits. This article breaks down how they capture and replay tokens and what defenders can do about it.
What’s inside a phishing kit
A phishing kit is a pre-packaged set of code and templates, with instructions for launching a phishing campaign and using the data it steals for malicious activity. Basic kits are often simple HTML and script files that spin up a single fake login page.
More advanced kits feature admin dashboards that attackers use to track victims, modify phishing page content, and relay credentials in real time.
To understand why these kits are so dangerous, it helps to look at how they turn phishing lures into usable sessions.
2026 Cyber Threat Report: State of Phishing
Phishing has been around forever, but it’s not slowing down. It’s just getting sneakier.
The Huntress State of Phishing report walks through the top phishing trends over the last year, from the lure themes and impersonated brands to the psychological tricks designed to slip past your defenses. And it shows you how to turn your people from a vulnerability into your strongest line of defense.
Read Report
When attackers pivot from passwords to sessions
Phishing kits now give attackers usable authenticated sessions through three tradecraft techniques.
In a device code phishing attack, the victim authenticates directly with the identity provider while the attacker quietly captures the resulting authorization and uses it. The flow reduces friction for attackers because the victim never types credentials into an unfamiliar page, so the entire experience feels like a normal sign-in.
AitM attacks reveal the limitations of MFA; the threat actor relays the authentication flow in real time, either with a fake login page or by intercepting an exchange within the legitimate app. The victim completes the MFA prompt while the attacker captures the resulting session information.
This is why successfully completed MFA does not make the session trustworthy on its own.
Token theft is far more valuable to attackers than password theft. After an attacker gets their hands on a sign-in token, a phishing kit like Kali365 (which we’ll dig into below) can help them replay it into an active session, where they can access cloud resources and the victim’s email accounts.
If you suspect replay, look past the original phishing page and investigate how the token was used.
These techniques don’t live in isolation. In the last few months, Huntress has analyzed several advanced phishing kits targeting Microsoft 365 tokens, including EvilTokens, Knight Office, and Kali365.
Three phishing kits targeting Microsoft 365 tokens
In early 2026, Huntress discovered EvilTokens as part of a device code phishing campaign that abused the Railway Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) platform as a token-harvesting and replay engine.
A joint effort between Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit and the FBI later in the year led to the arrest of one of its alleged operators.
Knight Office is an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing kit that steals valid Microsoft 365 session tokens and feeds them into an operator console. Attackers can replay those sessions and set up persistence across tenant accounts.
The third kit, Kali365, bundles a full Phishing as a Service (PhaaS) operation into a single control panel so operators can capture tokens through device code flows and reverse-proxy lures, replay them into live Microsoft 365 sessions, maintain access, and scale activity with built-in AI features.
Kits like these help attackers walk away with persistent access, not just usernames and passwords.
What every defender can do about token theft
A single signal is only one piece of the attack. Follow the full sequence from the lure to authentication, token issuance or theft, device registration, and mailbox activity to understand identity compromise in your environment.
Defenders can look for these signs of a stolen session:
- Start by checking for successful sign-ins from unfamiliar cloud infrastructure.
- Then hunt for device code authentication and automated token refresh.
- Review new devices, authentication methods, and mailbox activity.
On the response side, keep these priorities in mind:
- Containment must address identity artifacts, not just the original lure.
- Revoke refresh tokens, then remove unauthorized devices and Windows Hello credentials.
- Restrict or block device code authentication where you can, and investigate mailbox access, forwarding rules, and outbound phishing.
Keep going after containment. Monitor for replay or re-entry, and keep hunting after the original phishing domain disappears.
Join us for Tradecraft Tuesday to dig into more attacker tradecraft like this with Huntress researchers.
Sponsored and written by Huntress Labs.

articles.title: How Ubini is teaching machines to understand Edo language
articles.text:
When Stephanie Ohumu’s grandmother died in 2023, she took with her recipes the family could no longer recreate, words Ohumu relied on her to explain, and cultural knowledge that had never been written down.
“It used to be that if I encountered Edo words in the wild, I’d text my grandma or call her and she would translate for me,” Ohumu said. “Not just that, there are meals we cannot make the way we grew up eating them because they were never written down and we don’t know how to make them. All of that went away.”
Her grandmother’s death made Ohumu, a journalist and artificial intelligence expert, realise how much Edo culture existed only in the memories of older people, with little preserved for future generations. “Language is a repository of knowledge. It took my grandmother dying for me to really understand that,” she said.
The loss also raised questions about how languages like Edo, a language spoken by an estimated 2 million people across seven local government areas in Edo State, southwestern Nigeria, would survive in an increasingly digital world. Ohumu worried that the lack of reliable digital material would leave such languages poorly represented in artificial intelligence (AI) systems, increasing the risk of convincing but inaccurate translations and responses.
These concerns led her to found Ubini in 2024. The bootstrapped company is building a digital corpus of Edo oral histories, recipes and other cultural heritage. It aims to preserve knowledge that might otherwise disappear while creating machine-readable data for language technology and source material for films, books and other creative works.
Ubini has interviewed about 20 people and transcribed more than 20 hours of recordings. It has also produced Mia Mia, a 27-minute documentary featuring Maria Evbagharu Osazee, an 85-year-old woman reflecting on her life and the cultural loss she has witnessed.
The gap in African-language data
Africa has more than 2,000 languages, but few have the digital resources needed for natural language processing. Many are underrepresented in AI training datasets, leaving developers with little material to build tools that understand or communicate in languages such as Edo.
A 2026 study by Kedir Hussen and six other researchers, published in the Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, examined large and small language models’ support for African languages. It identified 41 African languages supported by the models and 23 publicly available datasets, finding that more than 98% of African languages were unsupported.
Ohumu said tests of existing AI models showed that their Edo responses could sound convincing while containing inaccurate translations.
“Claude can write a convincing enough cosplay of Edo, but it fills it with a lot of nonsense,” she said. “It’s really dangerous because if you don’t know the language, you wouldn’t know that.”
In one example, a model translated “download” as “D-A-N-L-O-D”, reproducing an English pronunciation instead of providing an Edo equivalent. Ohumu described it as a parody of how an Edo speaker might pronounce the word.
She attributes such errors partly to the limited Edo material available online.
“I’ve done extensive research on this, and there’s probably stuff I haven’t seen yet,” she said. “The largest one is, oddly enough, Jehovah’s Witness. They have translations of the Bible and other devotional books in the language.”
Some existing materials, she found, were also heavily influenced by English. “It’s like seeing Pidgin English being passed off as English. So there’s a lot of Anglicising happening,” she said.
For Ohumu, language loss also erodes vital knowledge. She recalled reading a study about indigenous communities where understanding of a plant’s medicinal value existed in only one language.
“So when that language goes extinct, our understanding of what that plant can do as well dies,” she said.
The shortage of reliable data also affects AI development. Edo is tonal, so differences in tone markings can change a word’s meaning. Models trained on incomplete or inaccurate material risk reproducing errors in translations and generated speech.
Ohumu believes a reliable Edo dataset could support practical applications, including voice-based services for people more comfortable communicating in the language. She cited financial services that would let market women carry out banking transactions through audio commands in Edo.
Such applications depend on verified language data—the precise gap Ubini is setting out to address.
Building an archive
The decision to focus on Edo is both personal and practical. Ohumu said she grew up in Benin City and has community connections across Edo State, giving Ubini access to people with specialised knowledge and making it easier to organise recordings without the cost of entering an unfamiliar market.
The company focuses on people over 70 years old who speak Edo as their first or main language, capturing everyday conversations, ceremonial speech and knowledge no longer widely shared. Its current collection covers people’s life experiences and food, including recipes, ingredients and the stories behind particular meals.
“We want everyday speech, but we also really want ceremonial speech as well,” Ohumu said. “And we also really want knowledge that is already outside of the mainstream.”
Ubini deliberately seeks diverse contributors to avoid disproportionately representing particular backgrounds, dialect groups or communities. For its current food collection, it is concentrating on women, who Ohumu said have historically been responsible for much of the cooking. Future collections will cover bead-making, traditional guilds and wood carving.
Ohumu estimates that Ubini needs at least 250 individuals, with an average of two hours of recordings each, to capture a broader range of speakers and knowledge.
The company works in quarterly research sprints, selecting a subject for each collection before identifying potential contributors. Researchers approach people in communities where the team has existing connections, explain the project and seek their participation.
Consent is central to the process. “It makes no sense to be documenting your culture if you’re going to be disrespectful to the custodians of it,” Ohumu said. “Sometimes people say no, and you have to leave it at that.”
Researchers also record contributors’ ages, occupations and backgrounds to establish whose knowledge the archive represents.
After the interviews, researchers manually transcribe conversations in Edo and translate them into English.
“Edo is a tonal language, so depending on where you put the markings, the meanings can differ greatly,” Ohumu said. Each initial transcription undergoes quality assurance by two University of Benin professors, who review and correct the text.
Finding people proficient in written Edo has proved difficult. Fluency in speaking the language does not necessarily translate into accurate writing, while automated tools such as Whisper and Granola have fallen short.
“The transcription is a lot harder than I thought it would be,” Ohumu said. “I knew it was going to be difficult because our languages are oral. It means that even people who have a very high proficiency in it cannot write it.”
Ubini currently has three transcribers working with its lead researcher, Elliot. The team also searches for out-of-print books and visits university libraries to study Edo grammar, word origins and spelling conventions.
Ohumu had expected a larger pool of people proficient in written Edo. Although she had read about a state government initiative to train young people to write the language, she discovered it had been discontinued.
“So that pipeline of people who are proficient in writing it wasn’t significantly built,” she said. “I do think that to scale, I will have to build this.”
She plans to train more transcribers as the project grows, particularly because poor initial drafts require repeated corrections before entering the archive.
Ubini aims to collect 50 hours of audio by December 2026. It hopes to have 150 hours transcribed and translated by the end of 2027, supported by 30 transcribers, and to build a 250-hour corpus by 2029.
The finished material is organised into XML files containing speaker turns, Edo transcriptions, English translations and information about contributors and recording contexts. Ohumu eventually wants to include phonetic transcriptions, but for now, her priority is documenting the language while its most fluent speakers are still alive.
“The first bit is just finding the people who speak it before they die and getting it out in a machine-readable version,” she said.
From language data to stories
For Ohumu, preserving Edo is only the beginning of Ubini’s ambition. She believes the language holds cultural knowledge and stories that can be developed into films, books and other media products
“The entire point of the company is this thesis: I think that within my language and all of the knowledge that it holds, there’s a repository of media IP,” she said. “It’s insanely valuable. And I think it’s untapped.”
She compares the opportunity to South Korea before K-dramas and K-pop gained international popularity, believing Edo culture holds stories that could reach wider audiences if developed and told well.
Ubini has begun exploring that possibility with Mia Mia, a 26-minute documentary about Maria Evbagharu Osazee, an elderly Edo speaker who reflects on the cultural changes she has witnessed throughout her lifetime. The film’s title is an Edo expression meaning “to forget”.
Ohumu said the documentary emerged from a research visit to a village to document Osazee’s knowledge.
“We were in the community to talk to the woman and her story was amazing, and I was like, okay, let’s make a film out of this,” she said.
Mia Mia premiered at the Uncolonial Film Festival in Germany in August 2026 before being selected for the Human Screen Festival in Tunisia in November, where it had its African premiere. It is also scheduled for its Nigerian premiere at the Kano Indigenous Languages of Africa Film Market and Festival later in November.
The film also enriches Ubini’s archive, with raw footage—including conversations excluded from the final cut—added to the dataset. The material serves two purposes: preserving the language and providing source material for creative work.
“The creative economy bits can’t be a thing that happens when we have a large enough corpus that makes sense,” she said. “It has to happen as we are doing it. And I think that one of the entry points that has the least barrier to entry is food.”
For Ohumu, the opportunity lies in developing stories from a culture she believes mainstream media has underrepresented. “I’m not building an app, I’m building stories, stories that don’t currently exist because we’re not speaking the language the way we should and the way they are stored,” she said.
Finding a sustainable model
Ohumu sees licensing Edo-language data as Ubini’s quickest route to revenue, but believes media products will provide more sustainable income in the long run.
“I do think that licensing is the lower-hanging fruit. Absolutely,” she said. “But I do think that the bulk of the sustainable funding will come from media products, whether that be selling a strong enough story to Netflix or Prime or EbonyLife, or developing it ourselves.”
Ubini has been self-funded since it began in 2024. Keeping costs down has depended on building within her existing networks and areas of experience.
“If you build at home and if you build around your circle of competence and if you build in industries where you’ve stayed for a bit, it really cuts down the cost,” she said.
Yet the project is reaching a point where that approach is becoming harder to sustain. The biggest expense so far has been transcribing and verifying the recordings.
“All that we’ve done so far, I can comfortably fund, but we’re starting to reach the point where it’s not as comfortable anymore,” Ohumu said. “The really expensive layer has been transcription and that QA process, to be very honest with you.”
She is now seeking funding to expand Ubini’s work. Whatever form it takes, she wants capital that gives the project room to grow without pressure for immediate returns.
“I’ll have non-equity diluting 200k. That’s important to me. Or even if it is an investment instead of a donation, it’ll be patient money. There’s no other way this works,” she said.
Over the next year, Ohumu plans to expand the team, improve transcription quality, and collect and transcribe an additional 100 hours of audio as Ubini works towards its 2027 and 2029 corpus targets.
For Ohumu, however, the work is bigger than the prospect of building a profitable company. She said she would continue preserving Edo even if Ubini never made money.
“Even if this company doesn’t make one naira, I’m still going to do this anyway,” she said. “That’s how strongly I believe in it.”

articles.title: Karra Elejalde, actor, 65 años: “No hay animal, mineral, ni vegetal más nocivo para el planeta que el ser humano”
articles.text:
Karra Elejalde hablaba de cine (de él, de su trabajo, de su vida) y Ana Trasobares le preguntó sobre sus creencias. Entonces contestó: “Sí, soy creyente, creo en el planeta. Y porque soy creyente, creo que no hay animal, mineral ni vegetal más nocivo para el planeta que el ser humano”.
El actor (Vitoria, 1960), que cumplió 66 años en octubre de 2026, hizo una llamada de atención sobre el planeta y sus recursos. Su declaración continuaba con otras referencias personales: “Y también creo en Gaia, y en la serendipia y en que estoy indignado porque nadie me ha contado qué he venido a hacer aquí”.
Hijo de un músico y un ama de casa, Elejalde es un actor que ha mezclado el humor y el drama. En este momento llevaba más de tres décadas en el cine y ya había dado vida al personaje de Ocho apellidos vascos, que le había hecho conocido por un público más amplio.
Fama por trabajo
En la misma conversación decía que nunca había aspirado a ser un actor famoso. “Nunca he querido ser un actor famoso, ni popular. He querido ser un actor prestigioso, un actor que lo hace bien”. Y la fama es una consecuencia lógica de que las cosas funcionen en esta profesión.
Su paso por el cine comenzó en 1987. Antes de Ocho apellidos vascos (2014), trabajó con Juanma Bajo Ulloa, Julio Medem, Álex de la Iglesia, Pedro Almodóvar, Icíar Bollaín e Imanol Uribe. También con Manuel Gutiérrez Aragón. Como guionista y director ha hecho “Año Mariano” y “Torapia”.
Con “Ocho apellidos vascos” consiguió uno de sus mayores éxitos populares. En ella interpretaba a Koldo, un padre que iba poco a poco mostrando su faceta más tierna con el andaluz (Dani Rovira), que se hacía pasar por vasco y pretendía ser su yerno.
Aspiraba a hacer bien su trabajo y también en esto tenía su opinión. Lo resumía en una frase: “La mejor forma de vender una película es hacer un buen trabajo”, sentenciaba.

articles.title: 720 796 propriétaires de BMW sont priés de garer leur voiture dehors et loin des maisons aux États-Unis à cause d'un « risque d'incendie »
articles.text:
Voilà un problème dont tout propriétaire de berline ou de SUV BMW se serait bien passé. La National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), l’agence américaine chargée de la sécurité routière, vient de rappeler 720 796 voitures BMW en Amérique du Nord. En cause, un risque d’incendie avéré, y compris lorsque les véhicules sont stationnés et que le moteur est éteint. Pour éviter tout incendie dans un garage fermé ou un parking souterrain, il faut impérativement laisser sa voiture stationnée à l’extérieur, loin des bâtiments et des autres véhicules, jusqu’à ce que les réparations soient effectuées.
Un connecteur électrique mal étanchéifié
Le dysfonctionnement provient directement de la pompe à eau du véhicule. La NHTSA précise dans un communiqué qu’un connecteur électrique mal étanchéifié sur la pompe à eau peut se retrouver exposé à l’eau et provoquer un court-circuit, ce qui augmente le risque d’incendie. Cette alerte concerne une bonne partie de la gamme du constructeur allemand : les BMW Série 3, Série 5, X1, X3, Série 2 Coupé, Série 3 Break et Série 2 Cabriolet.
À lire : Jusqu’à 828 km d’autonomie : le nouveau BMW iX4 prend l’avantage sur ses concurrents
Pour les conducteurs concernés, la NHTSA indique qu’une solution est en cours d’élaboration et sera disponible gratuitement chez les concessionnaires BMW dès sa mise en service. À ce stade, le constructeur a déjà recensé une dizaine d’incidents susceptibles d’être liés à cette défaillance, même si aucune victime n’est heureusement à déplorer.
Une seconde intervention obligatoire et une série noire pour BMW
Cette campagne d’intervention prend une tournure particulièrement délicate pour l’entreprise bavaroise. L’agence américaine souligne en effet que les véhicules concernés avaient déjà été rappelés en 2024 pour ce même problème de pompe à eau et doivent aujourd’hui être réparés une nouvelle fois. De plus, la dizaine d’incidents recensés par BMW s’est produite exclusivement sur des véhicules qui avaient pourtant déjà été réparés lors de cette première vague.
À lire : Moins de 3 heures de recharge pour traverser toute l’Europe : l’exploit fou de la nouvelle BMW i3
C’est une vraie série noire pour le constructeur. En effet, en février dernier, BMW avait déjà dû rappeler 600 000 véhicules à travers le monde en raison d’un risque d’incendie causé par une pose défectueuse du faisceau de câbles du tableau de bord. Seulement deux semaines plus tôt, le groupe avait également confirmé le rappel de centaines de milliers d’exemplaires dotés d’un relais de démarreur présentant un risque de court-circuit et d’incendie.

articles.title: Datadog Brings Production Experimentation to AI Agent Observability
articles.text:
Datadog is extending its Agent Observability platform with Online Experiments, allowing engineering teams to compare AI agent versions against real production traffic rather than relying exclusively on predefined evaluation datasets. The capability combines agent evaluation scores with operational measurements such as latency, token consumption, execution cost, and errors, helping teams establish whether changes to models, prompts, retrieval strategies, or tools actually improve an agent.
The announcement addresses a growing challenge in agent development: a change that performs better in a controlled test may behave very differently when exposed to unpredictable user requests. Datadog's approach brings controlled experimentation, production telemetry, and execution traces together, giving teams evidence of both the outcome and the behaviour behind it.
Offline evaluations remain an important part of agent development. Teams can run different versions against predefined datasets, assess responses and identify known regressions before deployment.
However, these evaluations are only as representative as the datasets and scoring criteria behind them. New user workflows, unexpected requests, and changing tool responses can expose weaknesses that existing test cases never anticipated.
Online experiments address this limitation by evaluating agent behaviour against real user interactions. Teams can compare a control version with a modified variant by randomly distributing production traffic between them, reducing the influence of differences in user requests.
This provides a more realistic view of how an agent performs under actual workloads, while also helping teams identify new scenarios that should eventually become part of their offline regression datasets.
Datadog integrates its Agent Observability evaluators with its Experiments capability, allowing evaluation scores to be compared alongside conventional operational metrics.
Teams can measure response quality, accuracy, and completeness while tracking execution duration, token consumption, estimated cost, and workflow errors.Feature Flags manage traffic allocation, letting engineers expose a change to a small percentage of users before rolling it out more widely.
This is important because improvements rarely come without trade-offs. A cheaper model might require more retries, while a revised retrieval strategy could improve evidence quality but increase execution time.
Datadog also connects experiment results to individual agent traces. Engineers can inspect tool calls, supplied arguments, and returned results to understand why a particular variant behaved differently.
According to the article, the experiment compared GPT-5.6 Luna against GPT-6 Luna, splitting traffic evenly between the two. An LLM-based evaluator scored investigation quality from one to five, considering accuracy, completeness, and whether conclusions were supported by available evidence.
They claim the results showed a 44.3% reduction in estimated cost for the newer model, with quality scores remaining close at 3.84 and 3.86, respectively.
However, the operational results revealed potential concerns. The newer model showed estimated increases in execution duration and workflow errors, although the confidence intervals were too broad to establish definitive regressions.
Inspecting the traces revealed that the newer model also supplied invalid tool parameters more frequently, usually recovering after retries. This behaviour was not sufficiently visible in the overall quality score.
Datadog used that finding to improve tool handling before proceeding with the model change. The failed calls also provided candidates for additional offline regression tests.
Datadog is not alone in trying to solve this challenge. Tools such as LangSmith and Langfuse provide agent tracing and evaluation capabilities, while experimentation platforms such as LaunchDarkly support controlled feature rollouts. Datadog's approach connects these concerns within its existing observability ecosystem, linking evaluation results directly to production experiments and execution evidence.
Datadog's broader proposition is that online experiments can create a feedback loop between production behaviour and development testing. Unexpected failures become new regression cases, while subsequent experiments establish whether changes actually resolve them.
The important shift is from asking whether an agent passes a predefined evaluation to establishing whether it performs better under real conditions. For agent engineering, production experimentation may become as important as traditional software testing.

articles.title: Market Research Giant Ipsos Investigating Breach of Internal System
articles.text:
French market research company Ipsos is investigating a breach that hit one of its internal information systems.
The company made the incident public on Monday, November 16, five days after filing a complaint with authorities.
According to Ipsos, the breach has not disrupted its business. “This incident had no impact on our operations or our ability to deliver for our clients,” the company said.
After detecting the incident, Ipsos launched its response process and worked to contain it, bringing in outside security experts to assist with the probe.
“The investigation is ongoing to determine the nature and scope of the incident,” Ipsos said.
The company has not said whether any data was accessed or stolen.
“We take protection of the information entrusted to us very seriously. Should the investigation establish that information relating to clients, projects or business partners has been affected, we will contact those concerned directly,” Ipsos said.
The market research giant has not revealed when it detected the breach, which system was affected, or how the intrusion occurred. Ipsos said it could not provide further comment while the probe is underway.
No known cybercrime group appears to have taken credit for an attack on Ipsos.
Established in France in 1975, Ipsos ranks among the biggest market research firms globally. It has nearly 20,000 employees across 90 markets and works with 5,000 clients. Its services rely on data the company collects itself, including from surveys and social media monitoring.
