articles.title: Si tu iPhone está desactualizado, hay un motivo urgente para ponerlo al día: pudo infectarse desde la web de IKEA o Zoom
articles.text:
Un ciberataque contra la plataforma web Optimizely permitió la distribución de malware a través de sitios de empresas y marcas genuinas como IKEA, Zoom, CNN, HSBC, BBC, Ledger y Air France-KLM. De acuerdo con Report URI, fueron 178 las organizaciones que se vieron impactadas por esta situación que tuvo lugar ayer, lunes 16 de noviembre. Entre los dispositivos apuntados se encuentran los iPhone y iPad que todavía corren versiones antiguas de sus sistemas operativos, por lo que se está recomendando ponerlos al día.
Según menciona Bleeping Computer, el ataque se produjo a través de una vulnerabilidad en el proceso de creación de cuentas de Optimizely. Esto abrió la puerta a que los piratas informáticos cargaran código JavaScript malicioso en las webs de varias empresas que usan la citada plataforma para personalizar sus sitios.
El malware en cuestión era capaz de realizar varias tareas y podía infectar los dispositivos que visitaran los portales pertenecientes a medios de comunicación, tecnológicas, aerolíneas o tiendas de retail, sin que estas empresas se dieran cuenta de qué sucedía. Si bien los iPhone y iPad no eran los únicos blancos de este ataque, sí se detectó la presencia de malware adicional para los dispositivos de Apple.
Respecto de las capacidades del software malicioso oculto en las webs en cuestión, se indica que podía interceptar datos de tarjetas de crédito, cambiar direcciones de carteras de criptomonedas, tomar capturas de pantalla y más. En el caso de los iPhone o iPad, se detectó la presencia de dos malware adicionales: Coruna y Darksword.
Tu iPhone o iPad pudo infectarse con malware en las webs de IKEA, Zoom o HSBC
Coruna y Darksword son malware que en el pasado ya hicieron estragos en modelos de iPhone o iPad que no ejecutan la última versión de sus sistemas operativos. En el caso de Optimizely, el primero habría apuntado a equipos que todavía usan iOS 13 a iOS 17, mientras que el segundo se habría enfocado en los que corren iOS 18 o superior. Incluso se menciona la aparición de referencias a móviles con iOS 26, aunque solo para listar sus características técnicas.
Vale aclarar, no obstante, que todavía no se han encontrado evidencias de que el hackeo a Optimizely haya permitido que los malware Coruna y Darksword infecten de forma efectiva los iPhone o iPad apuntados. La plataforma web atacada ya eliminó el código malicioso de los sitios de sus clientes y aplicó un parche a la vulnerabilidad que permitió el ingreso de los atacantes en primer lugar.
Los expertos que descubrieron el ciberataque con malware recomiendan actualizar tu iPhone o iPad a iOS 26.3/iPadOS 26.3 o superior. En el caso de que tengas un modelo que no admita dicho software, se sugiere instalar al menos iOS 18.7.3 o iPadOS 18.7.3.

articles.title: Amazon e Google terão quase 30% da Anthropic após IPO; entenda acordo
articles.text:
A abertura de capital da Anthropic deve consolidar duas das maiores empresas de tecnologia do mundo como acionistas importantes da desenvolvedora do Claude. Amazon e Google terão, juntas, 28,4% do capital da companhia após a oferta pública inicial de ações (IPO, na sigla em inglês), segundo informações divulgadas pela empresa em documento atualizado enviado à Comissão de Valores Mobiliários dos Estados Unidos (SEC, na sigla em inglês).
A Amazon ficará com 14,7% da Anthropic, enquanto a participação do Google será de 13,7%. Os números foram detalhados em registro apresentado nesta terça-feira (17), um dia antes da estreia planejada da companhia no mercado de ações.
As participações, porém, terão particularidade: as duas gigantes receberão ações de classe sem direito a voto. Isso significa que elas terão fatia expressiva do valor econômico da Anthropic, mas não poderão usar esses papéis para participar das votações comuns dos acionistas.
Amazon poderia ter fatia ainda maior
A participação da Amazon poderia ser mais expressiva. Quando investiu bilhões de dólares na Anthropic em 2023 e 2024, a companhia também recebeu notas promissórias conversíveis em ações.
A empresa decidiu converter parte desses títulos durante o processo de abertura de capital. Com isso, ficará com 14,7% da desenvolvedora de inteligência artificial (IA).
No entanto, a Amazon optou por manter parte das notas promissórias. Caso convertesse todos esses títulos imediatamente, sua participação poderia chegar a 23,8% da Anthropic, de acordo com o documento enviado à SEC.
A decisão também está relacionada a um limite de participação acionária previsto nos acordos entre as empresas. A Amazon não abriu mão dessa restrição para a operação.
Google também amplia participação na Anthropic
- O Google terá 13,7% da Anthropic após a operação;
- A participação resulta da conversão de títulos anteriores e da compra de ações em colocação privada realizada paralelamente ao IPO;
- Essa colocação privada envolve um grupo de grandes empresas de tecnologia que concordou em comprar US$ 26 bilhões (cerca de R$ 150,3 bilhões) em ações sem direito a voto. Entre as participantes estão AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia e TSMC Partners;
- Google e Nvidia se comprometeram, cada uma, a comprar US$ 10 bilhões (aproximadamente R$ 57,8 bilhões) em ações;
- A operação é parte importante da estratégia de financiamento da Anthropic. No prospecto, a empresa estima que poderá levantar cerca de US$ 84,6 bilhões (R$ 489 bilhões) líquidos com a oferta pública e a colocação privada, considerando o preço intermediário estimado das ações.
Leia mais:
- Anthropic inicia IPO histórico com avaliação de até US$ 1,4 trilhão
- Anthropic lança rival do Excel com IA; veja como funciona
- Fala AI: Anthropic diz que IA resolveu problemas sobre buracos negros
Amazon também é uma das principais fornecedoras de infraestrutura
A relação entre Anthropic e Amazon vai além da participação acionária. A desenvolvedora do Claude também é grande cliente da infraestrutura de computação em nuvem da Amazon Web Services (AWS).
Em acordo firmado em abril de 2026, a Anthropic se comprometeu a gastar pelo menos US$ 110 bilhões (cerca de R$ 635,5 bilhões) com serviços da Amazon entre maio de 2026 e abril de 2036, independentemente do uso efetivo da capacidade contratada, conforme o registro enviado à SEC.
Isso coloca a Amazon em posição dupla: a empresa participa do capital da Anthropic e, ao mesmo tempo, é uma das fornecedoras de infraestrutura necessárias para o desenvolvimento e a operação dos modelos de IA.
O Google também ocupa posição semelhante. Além de acionista, a companhia fornece capacidade computacional para a Anthropic por meio de sua infraestrutura de nuvem e de seus chips especializados.
Cofundadores manterão o controle das decisões
Apesar da participação expressiva de Amazon e Google, o poder de decisão da Anthropic terá estrutura própria. Os sete cofundadores da empresa manterão, por meio de classe especial de ações, 50,1% do poder de voto em deliberações gerais dos acionistas.
Além disso, a companhia possui fundo de benefício de longo prazo, o Long-Term Benefit Trust, que tem poderes para eleger e remover os integrantes de uma classe de diretores que formará a maioria do conselho de administração.
A estrutura busca preservar a missão declarada da Anthropic de desenvolver IA de maneira responsável, equilibrando os interesses financeiros dos acionistas com os objetivos de benefício público da companhia.
A oferta pública prevê ações com preço entre US$ 70 e US$ 78 (aproximadamente R$ 405 a R$ 451 por papel), e a empresa foi aprovada para negociar na Nasdaq sob o código ANT.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Pedestal AI raises $4.7 million to agentify the supply chain | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Delivery supply chains are the lifeblood of contemporary businesses — and a new startup is betting that purpose-built AI agents can make them run a lot more smoothly.
On Tuesday, Pedestal AI emerged from stealth with $4.7 million in seed funding. The company’s goal is to use agentic AI to make supply chains faster and more reliable — a plan that’s already brought them together with Fortune 500 companies and some of the largest shipping firms in the world.
The seed round was led by Eclipse, with participation from RRE, Converge VC, Timescale Ventures, and VitalStage. Pedestal says the funding will be used to expand its product and engineering time, grow the marketing organization, and support additional deployments.
In practice, much of Pedestal’s work is about removing friction from the shipping process — with agentic technology used as a means to that end. In one case, the company reduced missed deliveries for a major furniture company by 20% by deploying agents to take on some of the work that drivers were supposed to do. The agentic system they built would call customers 30 minutes before a delivery and collect any special instructions; if the call didn’t go through, a text would be sent from a separate system. Along the way, the deployment collected a wealth of data about friction points in the process, which could be used to optimize the system even further.
CEO Raj Aggarwal says contemporary AI systems are particularly useful for dealing with that data. “The challenge is that the data is messy and it’s constantly changing,” Aggarwal told TechCrunch. “It’s disparate because it sits in so many legacy systems. That’s what makes it hard.”
Supply chain AI has become a particularly hot space in recent months as alumni from autonomous driving teams look to launch their own startups. The supply chain startup Atomic, launched by a team of Tesla alumni, came out of stealth in 2025 with an emphasis on streamlining inventory. Another venture called Loop was launched by Uber alums to focus on predictive analytics.
As Aggarwal sees it, deliveries are particularly well-suited to training reinforcement learning systems. Because of their high volumes and easily measured outcomes, it’s easy to fine-tune contemporary AI systems toward what’s working and away from what isn’t.
Perhaps most importantly, it’s the kind of problem that can have an immediate effect on a client’s bottom line, making it easy to justify the expense.
“If you can get it right,” he told TechCrunch, “you can have really big impact.”

articles.title: EcoFlow Stream 5000 Review: Less than a year after the Stream Ultra X, the new Stream delivers more capacity and greater safety in a smaller footprint
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Stream 5000 is EcoFlow's worthy successor to the Ultra X. It packs 5 kWh of storage into a smaller-than-expected unit, accepts up to 5,000W of solar, and delivers up to 3,000W of AC power. It also costs less per kWh than the Stream Ultra X. The catch is that it is not a plug-in kit and requires an electrician for installation.
Reasons to buy
- + 5 kWh of capacity at a lower cost per kWh than the Ultra X
- + Four MPPT inputs that accept up to 5,000W of solar
- + Up to 3,000W AC output, with installer sign-off or a Stream Gateway
- + Ten-year warranty and a claimed 10,000 cycles
- + Mixes with older Stream units, for up to 90 kWh in total
Reasons to avoid
- - Needs professional installation
- - Heavy at 45.4 kg
- - Not a whole-house backup system
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
EcoFlow Stream Ultra X: 30-second review
The Stream 5000 is the second generation of EcoFlow's modular Stream family. It follows the Ultra X I reviewed not long ago. Except that in many ways this is a very different proposition.
The Ultra X was sold on a plug-and-play promise. In the UK, that promise came with small print, and had the rug pulled from under it just before the regulations changed. The Stream 5000 drops the pretence, making it a home battery designed for professional installation, and its price reflects that.
Inside is a 5 kWh battery, a hybrid inverter and four MPPT solar trackers. Each tracker takes up to 1,250W, so the total solar input reaches 5,000W. That is two and a half times the Ultra X. This unit can output up to 3,000W of AC power once an approved installer signs it off or it is connected to a Stream Gateway. That is enough for a washing machine, a dishwasher and a tumble dryer, though not all at the same time.
Where the previous Stream hardware came in five different flavours, with the Ultra X at the top, this generation has boiled it down to just two options. The Stream 5000, reviewed below, and the Stream 5000 AC. The main difference is that the Stream 5000 has four MPPT inputs for solar, while the AC model omits them but keeps the same battery capacity and inverter. You can add extra battery capacity to both in 5kWh chunks. The Stream 5000 and extra batteries stack physically to connect seamlessly, rather than using an external cable like the previous design.
EcoFlow says you can combine the new units with earlier Stream products to reach up to 90 kWh, if you have somewhere to store that many devices.
The app does the thinking, as before. It watches tariffs, weather and usage, then decides when to charge and when to discharge.
The only disconcerting part is that the Ultra X and the 5000 came out about a year apart, which makes me wonder what they’ll release this time next year.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
That thought aside, the Ultra X was a brilliant piece of hardware that EcoFlow continues to sell, but for a modest amount more, the Stream 5000 goes that extra mile.
EcoFlow Stream 5000: Price & availability
- How much does it cost? £1,599 early bird, for the Stream 5000. £1,499 for the Stream AC 5000
- When is it out? Available now across most of Europe
- Where can you get it? EcoFlow official website and selected European retailers
EcoFlow launched the Stream 5000 with early-bird pricing, which is still active.
In the UK, the Stream 5000 is £1,599, and the Stream 5000 AC is £1,499, which is only £100 more than the launch price of the Ultra X, which had less battery capacity than either of these new batteries.
In Germany, the Stream 5000 starts at €1,399, and the AC version is €1,299.
The maths is where this gets interesting. At £1,599, the Stream 5000 works out at about £320 per kWh. The Stream AC 5000 comes in under £300 per kWh. My Ultra X costs £1,599 for 3.84 kWh, or about £416 per kWh. The smaller Stream Ultra, at £799 for 1.92 kWh, is exactly the same cost per kWh as the Ultra X.
So the bigger battery is the better buy, even if that is not always the case with premium kit.
Extra batteries cost £1299, and each adds the same 5kWh as the base units.
Competition is thin at this size. The Anker Solix Solarbank 4 E5000 Pro is the same capacity solar input and price in the UK and Europe. It stacks like the Stream 5000, but the maximum capacity is 40 kWh.
At the other end of the spectrum is the Tesla Powerwall 3, which offers from 13.5 kWh up to 54 kWh, though installed prices start at around £7,000.
A cost not included in EcoFlow's headline price, and it applies to all these products: the electrician. Retrofit installs of home batteries are often quoted in the thousands, though a unit this size should come in well under that if you have a relatively recent consumer unit.
- Value: 4 / 5
EcoFlow Stream 5000: Specs
| Category | Spec | 
|---|---|
| Battery capacity | 5 kWh (LFP) | 
| Max AC output | 3,000W (installer sign-off or Stream Gateway needed) | 
| Solar input | 5,000W max (4 x MPPT, 1,250W each, 60V max) | 
| Max charging power | 4,000W (Stream AC 5000: 3,000W) | 
| AC charging input | 3,000W | 
| Expandable capacity | Up to 90 kWh (with previous generation Stream units) | 
| Cycle life | Up to 10,000 cycles | 
| Claimed lifespan | Up to 15 years | 
| Warranty | 10 years | 
| IP rating | IP65 | 
| Low temperature charging | Activated below 10°C | 
| Noise level | 30 dB maximum | 
| Dimensions | 295 x 489 x 298 mm | 
| Weight | 45.4 kg (Stream AC 5000: 44.6 kg) | 
| Connectivity | WiFi, EcoFlow app, Gateway for larger systems | 
EcoFlow Stream 5000: Design
- Heavy but more compact than before
- Battery and microinverter in one
- Application controlled
The Stream 5000 follows a new, refined, and functional look. The curved black-and-silver plastic panels of the first Stream generation are gone, replaced by a metal exterior that is undoubtedly more resilient and noticeably more compact.
At 295 x 489 x 298 mm, it is physically smaller than the Ultra X, which measured 420 x 294 x 460 mm. By my sums, that is about 43 litres against 57 litres, even though the Stream 5000 holds 30 per cent more energy. EcoFlow claims it is up to 40 per cent smaller than comparable home batteries, but it’s also a good bit heavier too.
The Stream 5000 weighs 45.4 kg, or a fraction over 100 imperial pounds. That is 6.6 kg heavier than the Ultra X, and I thought that unit needed two people to easily move it.
One annoyance is that the cardboard box it arrives in has hand slots to help you lift it, but they aren’t remotely strong enough, and using them will undoubtedly tear the box.
Personally, I’d keep a dolly handy to move the box to where you intend to deploy it, especially if you are working alone or waiting for help to get it out of the box.
The unit has handholds that can withstand use, but extraction from the box is much safer with a second person around.
Like the Ultra X, the Stream 5000 is IP65 rated. That means it resists dust and water jets from any direction. A label on top suggests that, instead of just dumping it outside, you need a small lean-to roof above the battery for the heaviest deluges, which seems sensible.
My view is that for the winter, you definitely want this unit inside, if only to warm the room it lives in when it gets warm while charging. Conversely, in the summer, outside might be better.
If the weather gets exceptionally cold, when the polar vortex comes to visit, typically batteries don’t do well below certain temperatures.
Therefore, a battery that heats itself before it charges in the cold is a very good idea in a British winter. EcoFlow says low-temperature charging kicks in below 10°C, and the small amount of power that it uses to stay warm makes the cells perform that much better.
The Stream AC 5000 is the same box without the solar inputs. That makes it slightly lighter, at 44.6 kg. It also makes it simpler.
Two things stand out from the Ultra X design. First, the solar side is far more generous. Four inputs at 1,250W each is serious capacity. Second, there is no longer any hint of a socket-in-the-wall approach. This is a unit for a wall bracket, a clean installation and a tidy cable run.
Here’s the breakdown of what each Stream model offers for comparison.
|  | Battery Capacity | Solar Inputs | Solar Input | Max Expansion | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stream 5000 | 5kWh | 4 | 5000W | 90kWh | 
| Stream 5000 AC | 5kWh | 0 | N/A | 90kWh | 
| Stream Ultra X | 3.84kWh | 4 | 2000W | 22kWh | 
| Stream Ultra | 1.92kWh | 4 | 2000W | 12kWh | 
| Stream Pro | 1.92kWh | 3 | 1500W | 11.52kWh | 
| Stream AC Pro | 1.92kWh | 0 | N/A | 11.52kWh | 
| Stream Max | 1.92kWh | 2 | 1000W | N/A | 
The older Stream and the new 5000 designs diverge massively in their interconnection philosophy. On the Stream Ultra X, there are two special inputs that were designed to couple the battery to the mains and to other batteries, in an up-and-down chain.
But the Stream 5000 and its AC brother only have one of these connections, and EcoFlow subtly changed the design so you can hook up prior batteries using the same cable.
The single port on the 5000 is meant to connect it directly to a consumer unit or power gateway, and the batteries stack vertically to integrate electrically.
With just a single unit, unless you are concerned about theft, the bracket isn’t needed, but should you buy additional battery capacity that is added under the Stream 5000 to create a stack, using the bracket would be advisable to stabilise the assembly.
So how do you mix and match older hardware? Well, when you add a Stream 5000 to an existing solution, the EcoFlow software detects the new hardware and defines a ‘system’ where the independent parts work in unison. It’s not necessary for the older batteries to be physically connected to be used, and that also allows them to have their own rules regarding discharge and recharge.
One other change worth noting is that the Ultra X had two AC outputs, whereas the Stream 5000 has just one. But the total power delivery of the Ultra X over AC was only 1200W, and 2300W if you cabled two units together. But the single AC port on the Stream 5000 can output 2500W, making it much more useful.
- Design: 4 / 5
EcoFlow Stream 5000: Features
- 5000W of solar input
- Ten-year warranty
- Up to 90 kWh
Initially, I assumed the solar inputs on the Stream 5000 would be the same as those on the Ultra X, but they aren't.
On the Ultra X, each MPPT port could handle 500W and a maximum of 14A and 60V, with all four handling a maximum of 2000W, or about four 500W solar panels.
These specifications got a major overhaul on the Stream 5000, with each MPPT capable of accepting 1250W, 40A and 60V of input. Therefore, you can much more easily connect solar panels in series without overloading the system.
For testing, EcoFlow sent me two SUNPRO 500W panels with a maximum voltage of 33.38V and a maximum current of 14.98A. I couldn’t connect those panels to the Ultra X because of the amps limit, but I could connect them to the Stream 5000. And using a parallel configuration where the amps double but the volts stay the same, I could hook at least two of these to each MPPT pair.
Looking at these numbers, the sweet spot for panels on the Stream 5000 is 400W or 200W panels with an arrangement where the total watts is less than 1250W, under 40 amps, and volts are under 60. EcoFlow sells a 400W rigid solar panel which is rated at 13.79A and 37.1V, and each MPPT on the Stream 5000 could handle three of those in parallel, to hit 1200W of solar input in total, and 4800W in total with all four MPPTs used with 12 panels.
The panels cost about £150 each, so the panel investment would be £1800, but on a sunny day the system should be able to fully recharge the Stream 5000 in around 90 minutes.
That’s a game changer, certainly, but probably even more significant is the 3,000W output to the grid.
The Ultra X could manage 2,300W on its sockets, but only 800W back into the house.
Having given up the pretence that this is a plug-in solution, although you can run it plugged in with 800W output, either directly wired or via a gateway, this unit can output 3000W into the home electrical system.
There is, however, a condition. EcoFlow says the full 3,000W needs sign-off by an approved installer, or a connection to a Stream Gateway. Without either, expect 800W, just like the Ultra X.
The battery chemistry is LFP, as before. EcoFlow claims up to 10,000 cycles and a life of up to 15 years. That is a big jump over the Ultra X, which was rated for 6,000 cycles to 70 per cent capacity. The warranty remains ten years, but the chemistry of LFP should still offer 60% of the capacity after 10,000 cycles.
For those curious, 10,000 cycles equals 27 years of daily use. This unit is meant to have a product life of around fifteen years, according to EcoFlow, so two full recharge and discharge cycles per day.
EcoFlow has been smart about expansion. The new unit works with the previous generation of Stream products. That means anyone who bought an Ultra X can add a Stream 5000 later, up to a claimed 90 kWh in total. A 5 kWh expansion battery is also available, and for larger systems the Stream Gateway handles the supervision. EcoFlow says it can cope with an EV charger and heat pump too. I don’t have the gateway, an EV charger or a heat pump, but there is clearly some headroom in this system before you need to consider EcoFlow’s Ocean range.
Software is the other half of the story. The EcoFlow app is still the best in this part of the market. It tracks usage, tariffs, and forecasts, and adjusts the battery accordingly. A new Local Mode was released in September, which should keep the system running and controllable if the internet drops.
- Features: 4.5 / 5
EcoFlow Stream 5000: User Experience
- A great app now with free AI
- Get an electrician
- Add Solar later
My usual disclaimer applies. I am not an electrician. Anything here about wiring is my understanding, not a rule, or anything you can take to an insurer after your house burns down.
The key difference from the Ultra X is that EcoFlow is upfront about this. It says the Stream 5000 is professionally installed. There is no pretence of a plug-in option, and there is none of the grey area I had to wade through last time.
That also matches where the law is heading. Plug-in solar has become legal in the UK from 27 August, but the new rules do not cover batteries. You still cannot simply connect a battery to a spare three-pin socket and start storing energy.
Well, you can, but it wouldn’t be covered by current regulations.
Installation is relatively painless if you are a qualified electrician, which I’m not, and involves wiring the provided cable into a fused spur connected to a bi-directional RCD in the consumer unit.
I already had this facility in place from my Ultra X installation, but even if they look the same, they’re subtly different, and I also wanted to retain my two Ultra Xs, so I had an electrician make the changes.
The cost of doing that can vary massively, and is highly dependent on how old your consumer unit is. Before I got the Ultra X, I had an old consumer unit where circuits didn’t have their own dedicated RCDs, but I had that swapped out for a new design where each has an RCD, making this installation much easier and within regulations.
Once everything was wired, the EcoFlow Stream 5000 and both of my EcoFlow Ultra X units wanted firmware updates. And, after those changes were made, the EcoFlow mobile app registered lots of changes and new items which weren’t there previously.
With the Stream 5000 at the helm, the hardware was reorganised around a defined ‘system’ where the Ultra X hardware was merged into the collective solution. Although not physically tied to anything but the house electrics, this allowed the battery capacity across all three batteries to be synced, providing a system of approximately 12,5 kWH.
There are lots of minor changes in the app, but the one that most interested me was that where it used to need a subscription, the AI+ functions are now included for free. In theory, this should mean I can let AI decide when to charge and discharge each day, without having to guess. If you have spare time and love to tinker, then you aren’t forced to use it.
Like the Ultra X, the Stream 5000 follows anti-islanding rules. If the mains fail, it must stop feeding the property to avoid sending electricity to the grid, where someone might be working to restore power.
Those who want a fail-over mode where the home switches to internal power need to consider installing a gateway with that capability. However, the Stream 5000, even with a gateway, can only output 3000W of power, so you need to be careful about the loads if you are cooking.
There is a UPS mode that automatically kicks on the AC power during a power loss, but it can only output 2500W. There is a local mode now, but that's only for when the internet fails, not the power grid.
My system is missing solar, but the plans are in place, and the Stream 5000 is a big part of that. With the solar input on that unit, combined with those on my two Stream Ultra X devices, I have 12 inputs and the potential for 9000W of solar once I’ve deployed the panels to achieve that.
This is where the Stream 5000 becomes a critical component in this scheme. Five kilowatts of solar input means a decent roof array is on the table, and a larger array means more free power, and the 12.5 kWh of total batteries is big enough to carry my household through the more expensive times of the day.
My total daily usage is around 16 kWh, so that’s enough to consider exporting some to the grid between 4 pm and 7 pm, and I’ll certainly consider that once my solar panels are in place.
- User Experience: 4 / 5
EcoFlow Stream 5000: Final verdict
The Ultra X was a clever product held back by a regulatory grey area. Or rather, the government went soft on the plug-in part of the deal just before the regulations changed, unhelpfully.
EcoFlow has stopped trying to sell a home battery as a plug-in gadget. With the Stream 5000, it has built a compact, quiet, well-specified battery that does the job properly. It then priced it attractively and designed it to grow. It also works with the earlier Stream range to an extent, which is a nice touch for anyone who has already bought in, like me.
The weaknesses are few, but I need to mention them. It is heavy, needs an electrician to install it safely, and that adds to the cost. And if you want the whole house to stay on during a blackout, then this probably isn’t the right equipment for you, even with a gateway.
If you want a plug-in system with no electrician involved, none of this applies, and the Ultra X era products remain the nearest fit, with their own caveats. For everyone else, this is the better battery.
My only concern is that the leap from the Ultra X to the 5000 took less than a year, and what EcoFlow will release a year from now. I’m hoping their new compact model doesn’t change dramatically, and that we get a larger 10 kWh extra battery, or the 3 kWh pack mentioned at launch.
The arrival of the Stream 5000 could have made all my previous investments redundant, but it hasn’t. And, given how much of it EcoFlow has sold, the brand seems determined to keep customers on board with each new release. Which, considering how some others operate in the tech space, is a breath of fresh air.
EcoFlow Stream 5000: Report card
| Value | Excellent cost per kWh, before installation | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Design | Compact for its capacity, but heavy | 4 / 5 | 
| Features | Big solar input, strong expansion and more power output | 4.5 / 5 | 
| User Experience | Easy to configure and now has AI management | 4 / 5 | 
| Overall | The best got even better in most respects | 5 / 5 | 
Should I buy a EcoFlow Stream 5000?
Buy it if...
You want a proper home battery without a giant price tag
At about £320 per kWh before installation, it undercuts most of the market, and it still comes with a ten-year warranty.
You plan to add solar
Five kilowatts of solar input and four independent trackers give you room to grow. You can start with the battery and add panels later.
You already own Stream kit
It works with the previous generation, so you can expand an existing system rather than start again.
Don't buy it if...
You want plug-and-play
This is not that. It needs a qualified installer, and the UK rules are clear that plug-in batteries are not yet covered.
You need a full home UPS
Check the specification carefully before you commit, because this system isn’t built to handle all electricity needs should the grid fail.
You have a tired old consumer unit
Budget for an upgrade. It is a cost that will not show up on the EcoFlow price tag, but you still need to pay it.
Mark is an expert on 3D printers, drones and phones. He also covers storage, including SSDs, NAS drives and portable hard drives. He started writing in 1986 and has contributed to MicroMart, PC Format, 3D World, among others.

articles.title: SuperDial revamps its healthcare voice agent platform to stop AI bots wasting time calling each other - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
SuperDial revamps its healthcare voice agent platform to stop AI bots wasting time calling each other
SuperDial Inc., the creator of voice-first artificial intelligence agents for automating healthcare workflows, is overhauling its platform with a new Agent-to-Agent RCM architecture.
The goal is to eliminate the compute inefficiencies that have arisen as autonomous workers become more prevalent in the industry.
The startup, which raised $15 million in a Series A funding round last year, is best known for its voice agents that automate payer operations, revenue cycle management and administrative outreach. It aims to alleviate the time-consuming burden of having to call health insurance providers, waste time on hold, navigate phone trees and check online portals for information. Traditionally, SuperDial has seen itself as a voice-first platform that’s focused on call automation, but the shift to its Agent-to-Agent RCM architecture suggests it wants to deemphasize phone calls as much as possible.
The company is addressing the friction that has emerged from the slightly dystopian reality that both healthcare providers and insurance payers have largely replaced humans with AI agents in order to automate routine calls. But the fact that agents are handling the calls on both sides creates huge inefficiencies, resulting in those bots wasting time and compute resources as they engage in unnecessary robotic conversations. Rather than streamline insurance eligibility checks, claim follow-ups and prior authorizations, those agents find themselves stuck in multi-minute phone exchanges to relay structured data verbally that both sides already possess.
SuperDial founder and Chief Executive Sam Schwager refers to these scenarios as the “bot wars,” and says they’re increasingly engaging in relentless and destructive battles with one another that cost both healthcare providers and insurance companies money.
“One side deploys AI to secure approvals and payment for care,” he said. “The other deploys AI to review those requests and, at times, deny them. Neither has a reason to stop. Every extra round costs more in AI spend, pulls in staff on both sides to handle what the bots can’t settle, and can delay payment and care. The result is more friction, not less.”
Calling a truce
With Agent-to-Agent RCM, SuperDial is trying to sidestep the bot wars by no longer defaulting to outbound calls. Instead, it acts as a kind of omnichannel orchestration layer, where success is determined by the number of requests resolved, rather than completed phone calls. When a revenue cycle team initiates a request, SuperDial’s agents will first check the relevant electronic data interchange feeds and application programming interfaces to find the information they need.
If they find it, great, but if not, they will then try the payer’s web portals. If they’re still out of luck after exhausting all options for digital retrieval, only then will they proceed to place a voice call. Those calls are more efficient too, since SuperDial’s agents will retain all of the context from their initial search, so they only need to query the agent on the other side of the line for the information that’s missing.
Schwager said Agent-to-Agent RCM puts more emphasis on resolution, allowing a provider’s agent and a payer’s system to connect and work together to resolve administrative requests with less work on both sides.
“The difference between this and the bot wars is the definition of done,” he said. “Two agents were optimizing for their own side of the exchange, but now those two agents are optimizing for a usable answer — that is, the information the provider needs to move the account forward, delivered in response to a request the payer can actually answer.”
For customers, life becomes much simpler. All they have to do is tell SuperDial what it needs to know, and its agents will work to get the answers in the fastest time and most efficient manner possible. “How we get the answer is our problem, not theirs,” Schwager said.
Schwager said the industry needs to move away from the idea that healthcare administration can be improved by having two bots argue with each other faster. “If an agent already has the information, that context should travel with the request,” he explained. “If a digital channel can answer it, there should be no call. The goal is fewer exchanges, not faster ones.”
The company’s long-term goal is to create an AI-native network that facilitates seamless, automated payer-provider communications. The goal is to eliminate repetitive inquiries and cut down on the administrative delays that can negatively impact patient outcomes, Schwager added.
SuperDial says it’s already having a big impact. Since it founded its platform in 2021, it has handled more than 10 million automated calls between healthcare providers and insurance firms – interactions that would once have been made by humans. Had humans made those calls, it would have been much slower, because SuperDial says its agents average about four minutes per call when dealing with insurers’ automated voice systems, compared with 17 minutes or more when reaching a human representative.
With its architectural overhaul, SuperDial is now targeting insurers, in addition to the healthcare providers it already serves. Earlier this year, it announced it had signed a key deal with Guardian Life Insurance Co. of America to modernize its dental provider data attestation workflows.

articles.title: Read everything that Nvidia’s board chair had to say about Jensen Huang
articles.text:
Nvidia’s quarterly earnings call on Tuesday was its first with CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress at the helm alongside the company’s first board chair, Harvey C. Jones. The leadership change followed Jensen Huang’s resignation last week after reports he had multiple affairs – including one with former Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese asset Alice Huang and one with a direct report, Kimberly Powell. Nvidia is investigating whether Huang’s relationship with the former compromised national security or company secrets. Huang will also testify before lawmakers on December 1st.
Read everything that Nvidia’s board chair had to say about Jensen Huang
Harvey C. Jones said the company would not be addressing or taking questions ‘regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation.’
Ahead of Tuesday’s earnings, Huang said he would be willing to return as CEO. However, during the company’s earnings call, Jones stated that “the Nvidia board unanimously accepted [Huang’s] resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” Jones also said that during the call, the company would not be addressing or taking questions “regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation and the ongoing investigation.” He added that, “the Board is proactively dealing with the immediate consequences facing the company, as well as enhancing our oversight capacity going forward.”
In Tuesday’s earnings Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, continuing years of skyrocketing revenue driven by the AI industry.
Jones shared the following update on the company:
As Chairman of NVIDIA’s Board of Directors, I want to say a few words on the Board’s behalf. NVIDIA is an exceptionally strong company. Its strength comes from its extraordinary people, groundbreaking technology, and exemplary track record of execution. Our financial performance speaks for itself.
On November 12th, our Board of Directors announced that after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as President, CEO, and board member. The NVIDIA Board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO. The Board appointed Colette Kress, NVIDIA’s longtime and well-respected CFO, as interim CEO. In addition, the Board announced it was initiating a search for a permanent chief executive, and we have since retained Heidrick and Struggles to lead the search.
While this was an unexpected transition, the Board acted deliberately and in the best interest of the company’s employees, customers, partners, and shareholders. This morning, the company announced that our Board has established a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee that will include a select group of our independent Board directors, senior external advisors, and legal counsel.
This committee will enhance— will– excuse me, will enhance our engagement with the U.S. government, including all relevant agencies. We will not be addressing or taking questions on today’s call regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation and the ongoing investigation. Our Board will communicate further when appropriate. On behalf of our shareholders, the Board is proactively dealing with the immediate consequences facing the company, as well as enhancing our oversight capacity going forward.
We have an incredibly talented leadership team, and we have every confidence in Colette’s leadership, integrity, and ability to deliver as interim CEO. Colette has been at the center of this company’s extraordinary growth for the last— growth for the last 13 years, instrumental in executing strategy, and with a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations, and financial position. The Board and the entire leadership team remain laser-focused on driving NVIDIA forward. Our commitment to generating value for shareholders, customers, and partners remains unchanged.
Kress responded to a question about the company’s leadership transition, saying “the most important thing that we think through right now is our employees.” She added, “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual.”
Jones also gave an update on Nvidia’s search for a new permanent CEO:
From the board’s point of view, we take the search very seriously. We’re going to look into internal candidates as well as external candidates. The Board appreciates that we’re living in a world where the advanced silicon technologies and national security dynamics are making major changes in our marketplace. Our new CEO will have to navigate those waters very carefully. So, the search will be thorough and we want to install the CEO, the permanent CEO, as quickly as possible, but we won’t expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person.

articles.title: Xiaomi 18 Pro und 18 Pro Max vorgestellt: Wo der Hersteller bei der globalen Version Abstriche macht
articles.text:
Xiaomi 18 Pro und 18 Pro Max vorgestellt: Wo der Hersteller bei der globalen Version Abstriche macht
Schon seit September 2026 sind das Xiaomi 18 Pro und 18 Pro Max in China erhältlich. Bislang mussten interessierte Käufer:innen in anderen Regionen noch auf eine globale Version warten. Doch diese Wartezeit ist jetzt vorbei. Xiaomi hat offiziell die globale Version der beiden Xiaomi-18-Pro-Modelle enthüllt. Über die Navigation gelangst du schnell zu den Themen rund um die Smartphones, die dich am meisten interessieren.
Xiaomi 18 Pro (Max): Hardware im Detail
Die globalen Versionen des Xiaomi 18 Pro und 18 Pro Max stimmen weitestgehend mit der chinesischen Variante überein. Lediglich beim Akku hat Xiaomi Änderungen vorgenommen.
Prozessor
In beiden Xiaomi-Smartphones kommen Snapdragon-8-Elite-Chips zum Einsatz. Das Xiaomi 8 Pro setzt auf den Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, während das Max-Modell den Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 und damit etwas mehr Leistung bekommt. Bei beiden Chips hat Qualcomm die Leistungsaufnahme durch eine Gate-All-Around-Transistorarchitektur verbessert. Die Chips verbrauchen dadurch weniger Energie unter Volllast und werden auch nicht zu warm.
Für die reine Rechenleistung im Alltag verbaut Xiaomi zudem eine Qualcomm-Oryon-CPU mit insgesamt acht Kernen. Im Vergleich zum Vorgänger soll die CPU-Leistung bis zu 13 Prozent besser ausfallen, die GPU-Performance um etwa 44 Prozent besser. Und auch bei der NPU-Leistung, die für die KI-Features zuständig ist, verspricht Xiaomi eine deutliche Verbesserung von 35 Prozent. Wie sich das im Alltag bemerkbar macht, müssen aber noch Tests zeigen.
Kamera
Für die Kameras des Xiaomi 18 Pro und 18 Pro Max hat sich der Smartphone-Hersteller mit Leica zusammengetan. Als Hauptkamera dient ein 200-Megapixel-Sensor mit einem lichtstarken Objektiv (f/1,67). Dazu kommt ein Teleobjektiv mit einer äquivalenten Brennweite von 75 Millimetern, das ebenfalls auf einen 200-Megapixel-Sensor setzt. Optisch kann der Zoom sogar auf 150 Millimeter angehoben werden. Ergänzt wird das Setup durch eine Ultraweitwinkelkamera mit 50 Megapixeln sowie einer Selfie-Kamera auf der Front mit derselben Auflösung.
Wer KI beim Fotografieren nutzen möchte, kann auf drei Bildstile zurückgreifen. „B&W Film“ soll Schwarz-Weiß-Aufnahmen mehr Tiefe verleihen, während „Iconic CCD“ dem Bild sattere Farben verleiht. „Modern Vintage“ soll die Details der Aufnahme herausstellen. Bei Porträts und Gegenlicht sorgt die KI dafür, dass Gesichter aufgehellt werden, um die Sichtbarkeit zu erhöhen. Nach der Aufnahme kann die Künstliche Intelligenz zudem das Bild analysieren und Bildzuschnitte für eine bessere Komposition vorschlagen.
Für Videoenthusiasten bieten beide Geräte Aufnahmen mit maximal 8K bei 30 Bildern pro Sekunde. Wer sich mit 4K zufrieden gibt, kann bis zu 120 Frames pro Sekunde aufnehmen. Zudem bieten Xiaomi 18 Pro und 18 Pro Max die sogenannte Log-Videoaufnahme mit bis zu 120 Bildern pro Sekunde. Die logarithmische Aufnahme sorgt für ein kontrastarmes Bild, das sich im Nachgang besser mit Videoschnittprogrammen an die eigenen Farbwünsche anpassen lässt und mehr Dynamik einfängt.
Display
Das Xiaomi 18 Pro und 18 Pro Max bieten jeweils zwei Displays. Auf der Frontseite sitzt der Hauptbildschirm mit einer maximalen Helligkeit von 4.000 Nits und einer maximalen Bildwiederholfrequenz von 120 Hertz. Die beiden Panele sind bei den Modellen technisch identisch und unterscheiden sich nur durch ihre Größe. Das Max-Modell setzt auf ein 6,9 Zoll großes Display, das Standardmodell hingegen auf 6,4 Zoll.
Das Hauptdisplay der Xiaomi-Smartphones bietet einen Privacy-Modus. Wird dieser aktiviert, wechselt das Display auf Privacy-Pixel, die einen engeren Betrachtungswinkel mit sich bringen. Das Ergebnis: Neugierige Blicke von rechts und links schauen lediglich auf ein dunkles Display. Der Privacy-Modus lässt sich dabei auch nur für bestimmte Apps und Benachrichtigungen aktivieren.
Neben dem Hauptbildschirm bieten Xiaomi 18 Pro und 18 Pro Max aber auch noch ein Display auf der Rückseite. Das „Back-Display“ nutzt dasselbe Panel wie der vordere Bildschirm, ist aber deutlich kleiner. Es zeigt Benachrichtigungen, Kartenansichten oder Inhalte, die von User:innen selbst dort angepinnt werden. So können etwa QR-Codes angezeigt werden, die von anderen gescannt werden können. Das Back-Display kann aber auch in Kombination mit der Hauptkamera genutzt werden, um Selfies und Videos im Vlog-Stil aufzunehmen, ohne jemanden mit dem Bildrand abzuschneiden.
Akku
Beim Akku des Xiaomi 18 Pro und 18 Pro Max müssen Käufer:innen außerhalb Chinas geringfügige Abstriche machen. Während das chinesische Pro-Modell eine Akkukapazität von 7.000 Milliamperestunden bietet, sind es bei der internationalen Version „nur“ 6.000 Milliamperestunden. Ähnlich gestaltet es sich beim Xiaomi 18 Pro Max. Hier ist der Akku der internationalen Version von 8.500 auf 7.050 Milliamperestunden geschrumpft.
Und auch beim Laden setzen sich die Änderungen fort. Die chinesischen Modelle lassen sich beide mit maximal 100 Watt per Kabel laden. Bei den globalen Versionen erreicht nur das 18 Pro Max diese Geschwindigkeit. Das normale Pro-Modell kann aber immerhin noch mit maximal 90 Watt kabelgebunden geladen werden. Beim kabellosen Laden unterscheiden sich die Versionen nicht. Hier sind jeweils 50 Watt möglich.
Die Software des Xiaomi 18 Pro (Max)
Beide Xiaomi-Modelle werden mit HyperOS 4 ausgeliefert, das auf Android 17 basiert. Features wie Xiaomis Hypercore-Technologie sollen dafür sorgen, dass die Arbeitslast gleichmäßig auf die Prozessorkerne verteilt wird und Daten vorzeitig geladen werden, um das Betriebssystem insgesamt schneller und responsiver zu machen. Wer weitere Xiaomi-Geräte besitzt, kann über den sogenannten Smart Hub Haushalts- und andere smarte Gadgets vom Smartphone aus bedienen.
Wie es bei einem modernen Smartphone fast schon Pflicht ist, ist auch KI mit an Bord des Xiaomi 18 Pro und 18 Pro Max. Hier übernimmt Googles Gemini die Aufgaben als digitaler Assistent. Dadurch können User:innen etwa auf Features wie „Circle to Search“ zurückgreifen, um schnell nach Objekten auf dem Bildschirm im Netz zu suchen. Xiaomi setzt mit HyperAI aber auch noch eine eigene KI ein. Sie kommt etwa bei AI Voice Note zum Einsatz und verwandelt Sprachnotizen in strukturierte Texte.
Xiaomi verspricht bei beiden Modellen eine lange Support-Zeit. Die Geräte erhalten insgesamt fünf neue Android-Generationen per Update. Danach unterstützt Xiaomi die beiden Geräte immerhin noch ein Jahr mehr mit Sicherheitsupdates. Das Xiaomi 18 Pro und 18 Pro Max sollten also mindestens sechs Jahre softwareseitig sicher bleiben.
Xiaomi 18 Pro (Max): Speicher und Preise
Das Xiaomi 18 Pro und das 18 Pro Max erscheinen beide in vier Farbvarianten: Velvet Red, Black, White und Cosmic Blue. Zudem sind die beiden Modelle in je zwei Speicherkonfigurationen erhältlich:
Xiaomi 18 Pro: Speicher und Preis
- Zwölf Gigabyte Arbeitsspeicher und 256 Gigabyte freier Speicher: 1.399 Euro
- Zwölf Gigabyte Arbeitsspeicher und 512 Gigabyte freier Speicher: 1.599 Euro
Xiaomi 18 Pro Max: Speicher und Preis
- Zwölf Gigabyte Arbeitsspeicher und 256 Gigabyte freier Speicher: 1.599 Euro
- Zwölf Gigabyte Arbeitsspeicher und 512 Gigabyte freier Speicher: 1.799 Euro
Wer direkt zum Marktstart zugreift, bekommt von Xiaomi noch einige Boni geboten. Dazu zählen etwa eine dreimonatige Testversion von Google AI Pro, Youtube Premium und vier Monate Spotify Premium. Interessierte Käufer:innen können sich ihr Smartphone schon jetzt reservieren. Über den Onlineshop von Xiaomi bietet der Hersteller noch Goodies wie Smartwatches und Lautsprecher für alle Vorbesteller:innen.

articles.title: Après 50 ans dans l'espace, Voyager 1 s’apprête à franchir une première historique : 1 jour-lumière de la Terre
articles.text:
Ce 18 novembre, Voyager 1 deviendra le premier objet humain à atteindre une journée-lumière de la Terre. Une véritable prouesse pour la sonde lancée en 1977, malgré ses forces déclinantes.
Années 70, cinq ans après le programme Apollo. La NASA envoie dans l’espace deux sondes jumelles, Voyager 1 et Voyager 2, à deux semaines d’intervalle. À leur bord, un disque d’or, gravé de sons et d’images de la Terre, comme un message de l’humanité adressé à d’éventuels visiteurs.
Leur mission officielle est alors limitée : étudier de près les plus grosses planètes du Système solaire, Jupiter et Saturne. Mais l’agence spatiale décide ensuite de prolonger leur voyage. Près de 50 ans plus tard, elles poursuivent inlassablement leur route.
Une distance qui défie l’imagination
Et ce mercredi 18 novembre à 11h16 en France, Voyager 1 se trouvera exactement à une journée-lumière de la Terre, c’est-à-dire la distance que parcourt la lumière en 24 heures. Cela représente environ 26 milliards de kilomètres, une distance qu’aucun objet construit par l’humain n’a atteint. Un message envoyé à la sonde met donc un jour entier à lui parvenir, et sa réponse autant pour revenir.
Car pour rappel, la lumière file à 300 000 kilomètres par seconde : il lui faut 1,3 seconde pour rejoindre la Lune, un peu plus de 8 minutes pour venir du Soleil, et entre 3 et 22 minutes pour relier la Terre à Mars, selon la position des deux planètes. Neptune, la plus lointaine du Système solaire, n’est qu’à 4h10 de lumière, soit près de six fois moins que Voyager 1.
Son trajet est sensationnel : la sonde a survolé Jupiter en 1979, puis Saturne l’année suivante, où elle a observé les anneaux et Titan, la plus grosse lune de la planète. En 1990, depuis les confins du Système solaire, elle prend la célèbre photo « Pale Blue Dot », sur laquelle la Terre n’est plus qu’un minuscule point bleu. Elle pénètre dans l’espace interstellaire en 2012, la région au-delà de l’influence du Soleil. Voyager 2, elle, a emprunté un chemin plus long via Uranus et Neptune. Elle n’atteindra la journée-lumière qu’en novembre 2035.
Un travail monstre pour les maintenir en vie
Mais à bientôt 50 ans, les sondes sont à bout de souffle. Alimentées par une source nucléaire, elles perdent 4 watts de puissance chaque année alors qu’elles en produisaient 470 chacune à leur départ. Le froid extrême du vide spatial n’aide pas, puisqu’elles évoluent à quelques degrés seulement au-dessus du zéro absolu.
Pour faire des économies d’énergie, les ingénieurs du Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) de la NASA n’ont donc pas eu d’autre choix que d’éteindre peu à peu leurs instruments. « Ceux qui consomment le moins d’énergie, mais qui donnent quand même de bonnes données scientifiques, remontent forcément en haut de la liste », explique Jeffrey Hayes, chercheur de l’agence spatiale. De même, l’hydrazine, carburant qui alimente les sondes, risque de geler. Dans ce cas, ce serait « game over », prévient-il. Si les engins poursuivront leur route respective, ils ne pourront plus transmettre aucun signal.
Voyager 1 se dirige désormais vers Gliese 445, une étoile de la Petite Ourse, à la vitesse de 61 000 kilomètres par heure. Elle la frôlera à 1,7 année-lumière dans 40 000 ans.

articles.title: Co-Designing Sparse Attention for Efficient Long-Context Inference | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Agentic workloads, long documents, and large codebases are pushing context lengths from tens of thousands of tokens to hundreds of thousands. At those lengths, attention becomes the most expensive part of a transformer layer. Dense attention scores every query against every key, so its cost per query grows with the context length N, and at 128K tokens it can take most of the prefill time in a layer.
The model-level solution is sparse attention, a transformer technique in which each query attends to only a small subset of the context, chosen per query, instead of all of it. This cuts both the compute and the memory traffic of attention on long context.
This post is a practical primer for model developers designing sparse attention that runs well on NVIDIA GPUs. It focuses on model-level sparse attention, where sparsity is trained into the model, rather than drop-in methods applied after training such as BLASST, MInference, or Quest. A production FP8 kernel is used to sweep the indexer’s design knobs (query heads, key heads, head dimension, compression ratio, and speculative-decoding depth), measure how Top-k cost scales, and compare token-level with block-level core attention.
Each section explains what the hardware rewards and why, and ends with a guideline you can apply to your own design. This post follows the same co-design approach as the earlier posts on dense attention and hardware-friendly LLM design.
What is sparse attention and why does it matter?
Sparse attention is an AI optimization technique that limits which prior tokens each query attends to. Instead of attending to the entire context, each query attends to only the \(k\) most relevant keys, typically a few thousand. Core attention then stops scaling with context. But those \(k\) keys have to be found, and the component that finds them, the indexer, still scores all \(N\) keys. The cost does not disappear; it moves into the indexer. In Figure 1, the indexer and Top-k take 47% of the DeepSeek V3.2 prefill layer.
Sparse attention has three stages (Figure 2). An indexer scores every key, Top-k keeps the \(k\) highest scores, and core attention runs softmax attention over those \(k\) keys and values. The last two stages scale with \(k\), the indexer with \(N\).
The indexer design space
An indexer is a small attention-like block. Query heads score the current query against a cache of indexer keys, and post-processing operations (such as a ReLU and weighted sum) turn the scores into one logit per key. Table 1 shows how recent models fill that in. Table 2 provides a key to the notation used in this post.
| Model / method | \(Q\) heads | \(K\) heads | Hsz | Post-processing | CR | Selection granularity | Notes | 
| Dense attention | None | None |  | None |  | All keys | Baseline. No indexer, every query attends to every key | 
| DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) | 64 | 1 | 128 | ReLU + weighted sum | 1 | Token | Separate FP8 index cache | 
| GLM 5.2 | 32 | 1 | 128 | ReLU + weighted sum | 1 | Token | Index shared across layers | 
| GLM 5.3 Flash | 32 | 1 | 128 | ReLU + weighted sum | 4 | Block of 4 + tail |  | 
| LongCat LSA-Flash | 32 | 1 | 128 | ReLU + weighted sum | 1 | Token | Hierarchical, index shared | 
| CSA | 64 | 1 | 128 | ReLU + weighted sum | 4 | Compressed token |  | 
| Qwen QSA | 4 | 1 | 128 | ReLU + sum | 4 | Block of 4 + tail |  | 
| MiniMax MSA | 4 (1 per group) | 1 | 128 | MaxPool over scores | 1 | Block of 128 | Scores every token, pools scores per block, no cross-head reduction | 
| NSA | 64 | 4 | 192 | Softmax | 16 | Block of 16 |  | 
| MoBA | 32 | 8 | 128 | MeanPool on \(K\) | 4096 | Block of 4096 | Pools keys before scoring, no cross-head reduction | 
| Symbol | Meaning | 
| \(N\) | Context length: ISL in prefill, KVSL in decode | 
| PB, DB | Prefill and decode batch size | 
| QH, KH | Indexer query heads and indexer key heads | 
| \(G\) | Group size = QH / KH: query heads scoring against one shared K head | 
| Hsz | Indexer head dimension | 
| ISL, KVSL | Input sequence length (prefill), KV cache length at the current decode step | 
| CR | Compression ratio of the indexer key cache (one indexer key per CR tokens) | 
| \(D\) | Draft tokens per decode step (speculative decoding), query rows per step = \(D\) + 1 | 
| B, B_out | Bytes per input element (1 for FP8), bytes per output logit (4 for FP32) | 
Most designs use KH = 1, 32 to 64 query heads reduced to one score with a ReLU and weighted sum, Hsz = 128, and token or small-block selection. The measurements in the next five sections, one per design knob, show which of these are efficient on NVIDIA GPUs and which should change.
How does the indexer compute?
The indexer is one batched matmul with a fused epilogue (Table 3). Prefill scores all ISL query tokens at once, so the matmul is large and compute-bound. Decode scores only \(D\) + 1 query tokens per KH per step and streams the whole key cache from HBM for a few rows of logits.
| Operation | Phase | Prefill shape | Decode shape | Runs on | 
| Scoring BMM (Q · Kᵀ) | Main loop | [PB·KH, ISL·G, ISL/CR, Hsz] | [DB·KH, (D+1)·G, KVSL/CR, Hsz] | Tensor Cores | 
| Post-processing (ReLU) | Epilogue | [PB·KH·ISL·G, ISL/CR] | [DB·KH·(D+1)·G, KVSL/CR] | CUDA cores | 
| Cross-head reduction (weighted sum over G) | Epilogue | [PB·KH·ISL, ISL/CR] | [DB·KH·(D+1), KVSL/CR] | CUDA cores | 
| Logit store | Epilogue | [PB·KH·ISL, (ISL/CR)] | [DB·KH·(D+1), KVSL/CR] | HBM write | 
Counting FLOPs, \(Q\) and \(K\) reads, and logit writes gives each phase’s arithmetic intensity. In prefill the \(Q\) and \(K\) terms shrink as 1 / ISL, so at long context only the logit write survives.
Three observations follow from Equations 1 and 2 shown in Figure 3:
- Sequence length (ISL, KVSL) and CR appear in neither equation: they scale total work but not the ratio of FLOPs to bytes.
- Both intensities are proportional to \(G\) = QH / KH. Reducing the \(G\) heads of a group to one logit gives \(G\) times more FLOPs per logit written. Designs without this reduction (MSA, MoBA) lose that factor.
- Decode intensity grows almost linearly with \(D\) + 1 and is nearly independent of Hsz, as long as all \(D\) + 1 query tokens fit in one pass over the key cache.
Unless noted, measurements use an FP8 indexer kernel with 64K indexer keys (CR = 4), Hsz = 128, KH = 1, PB = 1, and DB = 128.
Query heads, group size, and speculative draft length
Intensity is proportional to group size, but prefill and decode respond differently. Prefill is compute-bound, so more query heads mean proportionally more time. Decode is memory-bound: reading the key cache is the main bottleneck. More query heads add FLOPs but no new bytes, so runtime stays the same. Figure 4 confirms both.
Decode runtime moves only 2% while \(G\) grows 16x, because the single key cache read sets the runtime. Prefill runtime grows more slowly than \(G\) at small \(G\): doubling \(G\) from 8 to 16 costs 1.66x, not 2x. This is because the FP32 logit write happens once per logit regardless of G, and at small G it dominates. Above about \(G\) = 16, the matmul dominates and runtime grows with \(G\).
Equation 2 has a second lever on decode intensity: \(D\) + 1, the query tokens scored per step. Without speculative decoding, it is 1. With speculative decoding, the model drafts \(D\) tokens and verifies them with the new token in one step. This means that the indexer scores \(D\) + 1 query tokens against the same key cache. Like extra query heads, the extra query tokens add FLOPs but no new bytes, so the draft tokens are nearly free while they fit in one pass. Figure 5 shows where this process stops.
One Tensor Core tile holds up to 256 query rows. With an FP32 epilogue, register pressure limits the practical tile to about 200 rows, so one pass over the key cache can score \(G\) x (\(D\) + 1) up to about 200: six query tokens at \(G\) = 32 and 26 at \(G\) = 8. Up to that point, runtime rises only 1.37x and 1.87x while the work grows 6x and 26x. Beyond that point, the rows no longer fit in one tile, so the kernel launches more CTAs, and runtime steps up.
Group size and speculation depth compete for the same tile. An FP16 epilogue widens the tile to 256 rows and gives 1.31x at \(G\) = 64, \(D\) + 1 = 4 (Figure 6). Accumulating the matmul in FP16 as well reaches 1.45x, but only if the indexer QK scaling keeps the matmul outputs within FP16 range.
Guideline 1: Keep \(G\) x (\(D\) + 1) within one Tensor Core tile, about 200 rows (256 with an FP16 epilogue).
Guideline 2: Run the indexer epilogue in FP16. Use FP16 for accumulation too, as long as the indexer’s QK scaling keeps the matmul outputs within FP16 range.
Key heads (KH)
Increasing KH at a fixed QH shrinks \(G\), lowering intensity in both prefill and decode, but the two pay differently.
In decode, each additional KH means one more full read of the key cache and one more set of logits to write. The key read is most of decode’s traffic, so runtime grows linearly with KH: 7.6x from KH = 1 to 8 (Figure 7). The FLOPs stay the same, but KH times the bytes move.
Prefill is less sensitive: 1.3x to 1.6x from KH = 1 to 8. The FLOPs do not change, and the extra key reads are small next to the logit write that dominates prefill traffic. What grows is the per-logit work, because each key head writes its own logit for every key. A reduced-precision epilogue (Guideline 2) and Top-k fusion (Guideline 6) both shrink this work.
Guideline 3: Use KH = 1 with a cross-head reduction over the \(G\) (=QH) query heads, so one logit per key is written.
Head dimension (Hsz) and the epilogue
Hsz enters Equation 1 directly, so a wider head raises prefill intensity. It enters Equation 2 minimally, so decode just pays for the extra key bytes.
Prefill has a second effect Equation 1 does not capture. The epilogue (ReLU and weighted sum) works on the scores, whose count does not depend on Hsz. Only the matmul FLOPs grow with Hsz. At small Hsz, prefill is bound by the epilogue on the CUDA cores and the Tensor Cores wait. Widening the head adds matmul FLOPs that fit within that waiting time, so runtime grows much more slowly than Hsz until the two balance at about Hsz = 128.
Figure 8 confirms this. In prefill, Hsz = 64 to 128 costs only 1.1x to 1.2x, not 2x, and beyond 128 runtime grows with the FLOPs. In decode, runtime grows with Hsz throughout, since every extra key byte is read from HBM.
Guideline 4: Use Hsz = 128 or 256. Hsz = 64 leaves the Tensor Cores waiting on the epilogue. Narrower heads cut decode bytes, so most designs settle at 128.
Compression ratio (CR)
With CR = 4, one indexer key stands for four tokens. CR here is the indexer’s compression ratio. Core attention can compress its own KV cache separately, which mainly saves memory capacity, while indexer CR sets runtime. CR does not appear in Equations 1 or 2, so it does not change what limits the kernel. It changes the total work, linearly in 1/CR in both prefill and decode.
Figure 9 shows prefill runtime doubling with every halving of CR, since every key removed takes its share of matmul, epilogue, and logit write. Decode doubles with every halving as well, except at the smallest cache (8K keys, 1.8x), where the key read is too short to reach full HBM bandwidth.
Scoring fewer keys is the only way to reduce indexer work. Table 1 shows three ways: compressed indexer keys (CSA, GLM 5.3 Flash, QSA, NSA, MoBA), hierarchical indexing (LSA-Flash), and index sharing across layers (GLM 5.2, LSA-Flash).
Guideline 5: Reduce the keys the indexer scores, with compression, hierarchical indexing, and index sharing. None of these changes arithmetic intensity, so use them alongside Guidelines 1 to 4, not in place of them.
Top-k selection
The indexer produces one logit per indexer key. Top-k scans those logits and keeps the \(k\) largest for each query, on CUDA cores in both prefill and decode. Figure 10 shows how its cost depends on how many keys are scored and kept.
Scoring more keys costs more (Figure 10, left): each doubling of the key count costs about 1.7x in prefill and 1.5x in decode, because every logit is compared. Keeping more keys costs little (Figure 10, right): 64x more \(k\) raises Top-k time under 2x in prefill and 1.7x in decode. So the lever on Top-k is the same as on the indexer, the number of keys scored, and Guideline 5 helps both.
Two kernel techniques reduce Top-k cost further. First, the selected keys change little from one decode step to the next. NVIDIA Guess-Verify-Refine Top-k in TensorRT LLM uses the previous step’s result as a guess and verifies it in one pass over the logits. On DeepSeek V3.2 and DeepSeek V4 decode it is 2.1x to 2.4x faster than a standard radix select.
Second, fusing Top-k into the indexer removes the logit write and read-back between them, which saves time, frees the HBM that held the logits, and saves the energy of moving them. An open source example is the selective Top-k path in FlashInfer, which scores, reduces, and filters inside one kernel and never writes the full logits matrix.
Guideline 6: Treat Top-k as part of the indexer’s budget. Its cost follows the keys scored, not \(k\). Fuse it with the indexer, and in decode reuse the previous step’s result.
Token-level versus block-level selection
Selection granularity (refer to Table 1) indicates whether the indexer selects single tokens or blocks. This choice matters most to the core attention kernel.
With token-level selection (DSA, GLM 5.2, LSA), the \(k\) selected keys and values are scattered across the KV cache. The kernel looks up an address for every selected token and fetches each one separately. Since every query token selects different tokens, two queries rarely share a fetch.
With block-level selection (GLM 5.3 Flash, QSA, NSA, MSA, MoBA), the selected keys and values come in contiguous blocks. One address serves a whole block, fetched in bulk, and queries that select the same block share the fetch: the kernel works block by block, fetching each block once, computing for every query that selected it, then combining each query’s partial results.
Block size then sets the cost. In Figure 11, the budget is 2,048 selected keys per query and the block size varies: 16 blocks of 128 keys, 32 of 64, or 64 of 32. FLOPs and KV bytes are the same, but every block adds a query load, a partial result, and a merge step, so the kernel’s time follows the number of blocks it processes. Halving the block size nearly doubles runtime in both prefill and decode.
Head sharing matters for the same reason. In dense attention, every query token attends to every block, so a fetched block is reused across all query tokens. In sparse attention, each query token picks its own blocks, so reuse is limited to the query heads of one token that share a KV head. With a large group size, where many query heads share each KV head, a fetched block serves all of them.
Guideline 7: Prefer block-level selection with large blocks. Token-level selection also works, but blocks let core attention fetch keys in bulk and share them across queries.
Guideline 8: Use a large core attention group size, so that many query heads share each KV head.
Get started with sparse attention co-design
Sparse attention makes core attention cost-effective, but the indexer that selects the keys still touches the whole context, so that is where a sparse model’s long-context cost now lives. The eight guidelines below are the design choices that keep the indexer, Top-k, and core attention efficient on NVIDIA GPUs.
Apply the eight guidelines presented in this post to your own design:
- Guideline 1: Keep \(G\) x (\(D\) + 1) within one Tensor Core tile, about 200 rows (256 with an FP16 epilogue).
- Guideline 2: Run the indexer epilogue in FP16. Use FP16 for accumulation too, as long as the indexer’s QK scaling keeps the matmul outputs within FP16 range.
- Guideline 3: Use KH = 1 with a cross-head reduction over the \(G\) (= QH) query heads.
- Guideline 4: Use Hsz = 128 or 256. Most designs settle at 128.
- Guideline 5: Reduce the keys the indexer scores, with compression, hierarchical indexing, and index sharing.
- Guideline 6: Treat Top-k as part of the indexer budget. Fuse it with the indexer, and in decode reuse the previous step’s result.
- Guideline 7: Prefer block-level selection with large blocks. Token-level selection also works, but blocks let core attention fetch keys in bulk and share them across queries.
- Guideline 8: Use a large core attention group size, so that many query heads share each KV head.

articles.title: L'éditeur de GTA 6 licencie un tiers des développeurs de son studio Firaxis, deux jours avant GTA 6 — Frandroid
articles.text:
Chez l’éditeur américain Take-Two, tout le monde attend Grand Theft Auto VI, qui sort ce jeudi 19 novembre chez son studio Rockstar. Un autre studio du groupe passe pourtant une semaine bien plus sombre. Firaxis Games, connu pour Civilization, XCOM et Marvel’s Midnight Suns, a licencié environ 60 personnes ce mardi 17 novembre, selon des sources du journaliste Jason Schreier, de Bloomberg. Cela représente environ un tiers des salariés du studio, et sa dirigeante, Heather Hazen, quitte aussi l’entreprise.
Du 19 au 30 novembre, le Plaud Note Pro passe à 149 € au lieu de 189 € ! Il enregistre vos réunions, les transcrit et les synthétise pour vous, il suffit d’appuyer sur un bouton. Les Plaud Note, NotePin et NotePin S sont aussi à -20 %. Bref, c’est le moment d’arrêter de perdre du temps au travail !
Un porte-parole de 2K, le label de Take-Two qui gère Firaxis, a confirmé son départ. Dans une déclaration envoyée aussi au site spécialisé Game Developer, il justifie les coupes par un recentrage sur des jeux de stratégie.
Dans le cadre de ces changements, la taille du studio est réduite afin de se concentrer sur la conception, la technologie et l’expérience joueur, ce qui implique de dire au revoir à des collègues talentueux qui ont contribué à bâtir Firaxis. Ces décisions ne sont jamais faciles à prendre, mais elles sont indispensables pour écrire le prochain chapitre de l’histoire de Firaxis.
Un studio déjà fragilisé par Civilization VII
Firaxis sortait déjà d’une période compliquée. Son dernier jeu, Civilization VII, a reçu un accueil mitigé à sa sortie en 2025, et le studio a enchaîné les mises à jour depuis. Surtout, le prochain XCOM a connu des difficultés de développement et a raté une échéance importante cet été, toujours d’après les sources de Bloomberg. Le projet continue, mais les licenciements pourraient le bousculer.
Côté finances, Take-Two a publié le 9 novembre ses résultats du deuxième trimestre. Strauss Zelnick, CEO de Take-Two, y promet pourtant une année « historique », portée par des précommandes de GTA VI qui dépassent largement les prévisions. En coupant un tiers d’un studio historique deux jours avant ce lancement, Take-Two montre très clairement où passent ses priorités.
Grand Theft Auto VI sort ce jeudi sur PS5 et Xbox Series X|S. Côté Firaxis, 2K n’a pas encore nommé la personne qui remplacera Heather Hazen, et le prochain XCOM n’a pas été officialisé.

articles.title: Un ciberataque alcanzó a 178 sitios de todo el mundo, incluidos BBC, CNN, Zoom e IKEA, para robar criptomonedas e infectar iPhones
articles.text:
El 16 de noviembre, un código malicioso se ejecutó en las páginas de 178 organizaciones, entre ellas Zoom, BBC, CNN, Salesforce, IKEA, HSBC y Equifax, según la empresa de seguridad Report URI. El ciberataque intentaba robar criptomonedas, copiar datos de tarjetas e infectar iPhones y iPads.
El investigador Scott Helme, fundador de Report URI, explicó que los atacantes no vulneraron cada sitio por separado. Escribieron su código en Optimizely Web, una plataforma que las empresas usan para probar distintas versiones de sus páginas. Como el script llegaba desde el servidor de Optimizely, los sitios lo trataban como confiable.
Helme dijo que no se sabe cómo los atacantes obtuvieron acceso a tantas cuentas de clientes sin relación entre sí. Precisó que el servidor de Optimizely entregó exactamente lo que recibió, por lo que no se trató de una alteración de su red de distribución.
Qué hacía el código en cada visita
El programa buscaba direcciones de billeteras de criptomonedas en el texto de la página, en los formularios y en el portapapeles, y las reemplazaba por las del atacante. Quien copiaba una dirección para hacer una transferencia podía pegar otra distinta.
También registraba los números de tarjeta, la fecha de vencimiento y el código de seguridad que el usuario escribía en los formularios propios del sitio. Según Report URI, los pagos hechos en ventanas de procesadores externos quedaban fuera de su alcance. El código además enviaba cookies y capturas de pantalla.
En los dispositivos de Apple, el script cargaba dos conjuntos de herramientas de ataque llamados Coruna y DarkSword. Según Report URI, apuntan a versiones antiguas de iOS. Una página de iPhone con iOS 18.6 o anterior que se recargaba cada 60 segundos era un síntoma visible.
Reuters informó que no pudo confirmar si el código funcionó en cada caso ni cuántas víctimas dejó. El análisis de MATT Research indica que se demostró que los kits se entregaron, pero no una infección exitosa de un dispositivo real.
188 archivos infectados en nueve horas
Report URI revisó 1.611 archivos de Optimizely y encontró 188 infectados, que pertenecían a 178 organizaciones. Por sector, el informe cuenta 32 de banca y finanzas, 23 de tecnología, 20 de comercio minorista, 12 de streaming y 10 de medios. Helme advirtió que la cifra real probablemente sea mayor, porque solo pudo revisar los archivos que encontró a tiempo.
La primera inyección que detectó apareció a las 04:21 (hora UTC) del 16 de noviembre en la página de la BBC. A las 19:25, las billeteras de los atacantes habían recibido unos USD 7.040, casi todos en bitcoin. Los atacantes reconstruyeron el programa 26 veces durante el día.
La limpieza masiva comenzó cerca de las 20:40 UTC. A las 23:11, Report URI observó que todos los archivos estaban limpios. El servidor principal de los atacantes dejó de responder el 17 de noviembre, según el mismo informe, y Optimizely reconoció el incidente en su página de estado.
Las empresas respondieron de forma desigual
Salesforce dijo a Reuters que investigaba cambios no autorizados en los scripts de Optimizely y que los desactivó como medida de precaución. Equifax dejó de usar la plataforma y afirmó que no encontró pruebas de que sus sistemas hubieran sido comprometidos. IKEA indicó que evaluaba el posible impacto en sus servicios y clientes.
El informe midió además las defensas de los sitios afectados. Entre 256 servidores revisados, 68 no tenían una política de seguridad de contenido, la regla que limita qué scripts puede cargar una página. Solo 24, el 15%, bloquearon el código malicioso.
Report URI recomendó a quien visitó alguno de los sitios afectados ese día actualizar el iPhone o iPad, verificar que las transferencias de criptomonedas llegaron a la dirección prevista y revisar los resúmenes de tarjetas. La firma señaló que no puede saber cuántas tarjetas, cookies o capturas se robaron, ni cuántos dispositivos iOS se infectaron antes de que el ataque se detuviera.

articles.title: Court clears brothers of $25 million Ethereum crypto heist charges
articles.text:
US District Judge Jessica Clarke has acquitted two brothers accused of stealing $25 million in cryptocurrency in about 12 seconds through a scheme that exploited a bug in the Ethereum blockchain.
Clarke's decision comes one year after a mistrial in the same case, after jurors failed to agree on whether to convict or acquit former Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) students Anton Peraire-Bueno and James Peraire-Bueno in this first-of-its-kind scheme, as Reuters first reported.
"The question before the Court is not whether the Peraire-Buenos' conduct was right or moral, or even whether it violated uncharged crimes. It is simply whether the evidence at trial, construed in a light most favorable to the Government, could support wire fraud and related convictions in this case," the federal judge said.
"Because the Government failed to prove that the Peraire-Buenos made any material misrepresentations in the execution of their scheme, the motion is granted, and a judgment of acquittal is entered for Anton Peraire-Bueno and James Peraire-Bueno."
The Peraire-Bueno brothers were arrested in Boston and New York in May 2024 on wire fraud and money laundering charges and were facing 20 years in prison for each count if convicted.
According to prosecutors, the brothers allegedly manipulated blockchain transaction validation processes by accessing pending private transactions, altering them, obtaining victims' cryptocurrency, and rejecting requests to return the stolen funds.
The indictment claimed they learned their victims' trading behaviors while preparing the attack (starting in December 2022) and took measures to hide the stolen proceeds and their identities.
They were also accused of using multiple cryptocurrency addresses and foreign exchanges and setting up shell companies. After the attack, they also allegedly moved the stolen crypto assets through a series of transactions to obscure their source and ownership.
The prosecutors also said that, while planning and executing the attack, the brothers deployed a series of "bait transactions" designed to identify "victim traders," exploited a vulnerability in the MEV-Boost relay code, causing the relay to release the full content of a proposed block prematurely, and reordered the proposed block to their advantage.
In the next stage of the scheme, they allegedly reordered the block on the Ethereum blockchain, which resulted in the theft of approximately $25 million in cryptocurrency from the victim traders.
Throughout the process, the brothers also allegedly searched online for information on carrying out the attack, concealing their involvement in the Ethereum exploit, and laundering the criminal proceeds through cryptocurrency exchanges with lax verification procedures.
Prosecutors also said they hired attorneys with expertise in cryptocurrency, extradition procedures, and the crimes outlined in the indictment.
