articles.title: Los fontaneros expertos avisan: si abres el grifo y cae un chorro de agua débil, el problema ya ha comenzado y puede ser peor de lo que parece
articles.text:
Que el agua salga del grifo con menos fuerza de la habitual puede parecer una molestia menor, pero también puede ser el primer aviso de que algo no funciona en la instalación de tu casa. Y detrás de este problema puede haber muchas cosas, desde un aireador sucio hasta una fuga. Aquí, los fontaneros advierten que no siempre se trata de una avería grave, aunque tampoco conviene dejar pasar semanas antes de mirarlo.
Un grifo o toda la casa. Lo primero es averiguar hasta dónde llega el problema, si es cosa de la fontanería de tu casa o de la red. Por ejemplo, si es solo un grifo ya sabes que el problema está en casa, pero si afecta a toda la vivienda pueden ser más cosasa, desde una llave de paso mal abierta a unas tuberías envejecidas, pasando incluso por un problema en la red pública. Y también importa si el bajón se nota sólo con el agua caliente o en todo.
La cal del aireador. Cuando el culpable es un único grifo, lo más probable es que la pieza que tiene en la boca, el aireador, se haya ido llenando de cal y otras partículas. Lo mismo pasa si el problema sucede solo en las alcachofas de la ducha. La solución es bastante sencilla, y basta con desenroscarlo, dejarlo un rato en vinagre, frotarlo con un cepillo de dientes viejo, aclararlo bien y volver a colocarlo. Eso sí, si el chorro sigue flojo toca revisar la llave de paso de ese grifo, que puede haberse quedado medio cerrada tras una reparación o un golpe accidental.
Cuando falla toda la casa. Las tuberías antiguas, sobre todo las de acero galvanizado, van acumulando depósitos por dentro que acaban estrechando el paso del agua, que también recuerda que la llave general tiene que quedar abierta del todo después de cualquier trabajo de fontanería. Vamos, que el tubo se va estrechando por dentro. Otra posibilidad es que falle la válvula reductora de presión, y en ese caso lo recomendable es que lo revise un fontanero.
La fuga que no se ve. Pero lo complicado llega cuando tenemos una fuga, porque puede manifestarse como una pérdida de presión antes de que aparezca ningún charco. Hay otras pistas, como una factura que sube sin que hayas cambiado tus hábitos, manchas de humedad o pintura que se levanta. Y las paredes que siguen húmedas también son un aviso, algo que la Agencia de Protección Ambiental de Estados Unidos pide vigilar en su lista para detectar fugas.
Agua caliente y pozos. ¿Y si sólo pierde fuerza el agua caliente? Pues entonces conviene mirar el termo o el acumulador, donde se van depositando sedimentos. En las viviendas con pozo, el fallo puede estar en la bomba o en el presostato, que puede quedarse atascado y dejar la casa sin presión, o en un filtro sucio, que también puede restar presión.
Y antes de llamar a nadie, merece la pena preguntar a los vecinos. Si ellos tienen una presión normal, el problema está en tu casa, pero si les pasa lo mismo puede deberse a una rotura en una conducción principal o a un pico de consumo en la zona, o incluso trabajos de mantenimiento en la red. En estos casos, lo que toca es consultar a la compañía de abastecimiento, porque por mucho que revises las tuberías de casa no vas a encontrar nada.

articles.title: L’iPhone Duo aura finalement droit à la reconnaissance faciale
articles.text:
Après des années d’attente, l’arrivée du tout premier iPhone pliant il y a quelques mois a ravi les fans d’Apple. Et bien que l’iPhone Duo soit un excellent smartphone, cette première mouture n’est pas exempte de quelques défauts. À la surprise générale, le premier smartphone pliant d’Apple a fait l’impasse sur l’une des fonctionnalités les plus pratiques qu’Apple ait intégrée à ses iPhone au cours des dernières années : Face ID.
Le système de reconnaissance faciale d’Apple, présent depuis l’iPhone X et redoutable d’efficacité, a été remplacé par Touch ID sur l’iPhone Duo. Une régression pour beaucoup d’utilisateurs qui voyaient dans cette absence le principal défaut de l’appareil. L’absence de Face ID sur l’appareil fait en effet partie des concessions qu’Apple a dû faire, faute de place suffisante dans l’appareil pour y accueillir le capteur TrueDepth indispensable au fonctionnement de Face ID.
En attendant qu’Apple corrige le tir dans une prochaine version de l’iPhone Duo, la firme de Cupertino vient de bricoler une solution de secours pour offrir un semblant de reconnaissance faciale à son iPhone Duo.
Une reconnaissance faciale limitée
Dans la deuxième bêta développeur d’iOS 27.3, Apple vient d’introduire une option de reconnaissance faciale 2D reposant sur la caméra frontale de l’appareil. Mais celle-ci, bien loin de Face ID (qui fournit une reconnaissance faciale en 3D), s’accompagne de quelques contraintes.
Concrètement, cette reconnaissance faciale ne fonctionne que lorsque l’iPhone Duo est fermé, depuis l’écran de verrouillage. Moins sécurisée que Touch ID, l’option reste facultative, mais les données de reconnaissance faciale restent enregistrées dans la Secure Enclave de l’appareil.
Cette nouvelle option de reconnaissance faciale qui intègre l’iPhone Duo est par ailleurs restreinte dans son utilisation. Vous ne pourrez pas vous en servir pour accéder aux mots de passe, ni pour valider des paiements avec Apple Pay, Touch ID restant obligatoire pour ce cas précis. Autre limitation, et pas des moindres, cette reconnaissance faciale ne fonctionne pas dans le noir, contrairement à Face ID.
Surtout, au-delà de 45 minutes d’inactivité sur l’iPhone Duo, le déverrouillage de l’appareil par reconnaissance faciale n’est plus disponible. Il faudra impérativement utiliser Touch ID pour s’authentifier de nouveau.
Enfin, Apple a ajouté une nouvelle fonction « Fermer pour verrouiller » qui permet de verrouiller automatiquement l’iPhone Duo dès lors que vous le fermez, plutôt que de transférer le contenu affiché sur l’écran intérieur vers l’écran extérieur.

articles.title: Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution
articles.text:
Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution
- Date:
- November 16, 2026
- Source:
- University of Innsbruck
- Summary:
- Scientists have developed a new way to determine whether quantum simulations can be trusted, solving a growing problem as quantum computers become too powerful for conventional machines to check. Demonstrated on a 51-qubit system, the technique measures uncertainty and provides verifiable error margins that could help unlock the full potential of quantum computing.
- Share:
As quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them? Scientists have now developed a promising new method that could help overcome this challenge by measuring the accuracy of quantum simulations and identifying how much uncertainty their predictions contain.
The technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results. Researchers successfully demonstrated the approach using a quantum simulator with up to 51 qubits in Innsbruck, Austria.
Quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all. However, this progress creates a verification problem. When a simulation is small enough, scientists can compare its results with calculations performed on a conventional computer. As quantum systems grow beyond those limits, that direct comparison becomes impractical, making alternative ways to assess their reliability essential.
A New Way to Measure Quantum Computing Accuracy
The breakthrough comes from an international research team led by Tristan Kraft at the Technical University of Munich and Peter Zoller at the University of Innsbruck and the Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, working alongside Barbara Kraus of the Technical University of Munich. The researchers developed a method for experimentally determining how a quantum simulator operates and translating uncertainties in its behavior into measurable limits on the accuracy of its results.
Quantum simulators are specialized physical systems designed to reproduce the behavior of other quantum systems. They are especially useful for investigating situations involving large numbers of interacting particles, where the calculations required can quickly overwhelm even powerful conventional computers.
But quantum experiments are never entirely free from errors. "But no real experiment is perfect," says Tristan Kraft. "Interactions may turn out differently than expected, the system is influenced by its environment, and measurements are also subject to uncertainties."
Rather than assuming a quantum simulator behaves exactly as intended, the new approach examines experimental data to determine what is actually happening inside the system. This allows researchers to identify important interactions and account for disturbances such as fluctuations and noise.
"From this data, we determine the relevant interactions as well as key influences from fluctuations and noise. We then calculate how the uncertainties in this model affect the simulation results," explains Tristan Kraft. "The quantum simulator thus provides not just a single value, but a result with error margins that quantify its accuracy."
Successfully Tested on a 51 Qubit Quantum Simulator
To evaluate the method, the researchers began with a relatively small quantum system containing ten trapped ions. Because conventional computers can still calculate the behavior of a system of this size, the team could test its reconstructed models and calculated error limits against independent measurements.
After this initial validation, the researchers expanded their experiments to a chain of 51 trapped ions. The larger demonstration, carried out by a team led by Manoj Joshi and Christian Roos using an ion trap quantum simulator, showed that the technique could also work with substantially more complex quantum systems.
This represents an important step toward establishing how trustworthy quantum simulation results are, particularly as quantum devices advance into territory where direct verification with traditional computing methods becomes increasingly difficult.
Extending the Breakthrough to More Complex Quantum Systems
The next challenge is to bring the technique to two-dimensional quantum simulators. These systems can model more complicated interactions among particles, making them valuable for exploring quantum physics. At the same time, their growing complexity makes their results particularly difficult to confirm using conventional calculations.
"This is particularly important because classical calculations for such systems become significantly more difficult as the number of particles increases," explains quantum computing pioneer Peter Zoller. "This also makes independent verification of the results increasingly complex, making the question of experimentally determined error limits all the more important."
The researchers are now adapting their method for the newest generation of two-dimensional quantum simulators, which offer improved precision and can investigate systems containing larger numbers of particles.
Looking further ahead, the approach could help scientists establish a more meaningful way to measure quantum advantage, the ability of quantum systems to outperform conventional computers. Instead of comparing machines based only on their processing speed or the size of the problems they can handle, researchers could also examine how accurately each system produces its answers.
"After all, when a classical computer and a quantum simulator tackle the same problem, it's not just a matter of which one delivers a result faster. What's also crucial is which one can solve the problem with a smaller, verifiable margin of error," says Peter Zoller.
This shift could change how progress in quantum computing is evaluated. Future breakthroughs may be judged not simply by how many particles a simulator can model or how quickly it performs calculations, but by its ability to solve increasingly difficult problems with demonstrably reliable results.
The findings were published in Physical Review X. The research received support from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), the German Ministry of Research, Technology and Space, the European Union, BMW, and other funding organizations.

Lam, Tobias Olsacher, Florian Kranzl, Johannes Franke, Lata Kh Joshi, Rainer Blatt, Augusto Smerzi, Daniel Stilck França, Benoît Vermersch, Barbara Kraus, Christian F. Roos, Peter Zoller. articles.title: Scaling LLM-Based Ranking Systems for Latency-Critical Search & Recommendation Workloads
articles.text:
Transcript
Sundara Raman Ramachandran: I'm Sundara. I'm a tech lead at LinkedIn. My current focus is on LLM inference and using LLMs for ranking and recommendation workloads. I'm also an open-source contributor in SGLang where I have primarily contributed to the scoring API where we use LLMs for ranking. I have close to 10 years of industry experience. I have worked with Microsoft in different products like Microsoft Office and Azure. Today I'm going to talk about how we scale the LLM based ranking systems at LinkedIn, what were the challenges we encountered, and what are some learnings and takeaways you can take from the talk.
LinkedIn Search
I hope all of you would have used LinkedIn at some point, that you might have used it for searching for some job or you're looking for someone in a network. The reason I ask is LinkedIn Search operates at a massive scale. If you haven't read it already, maybe after the talk you can take up the LinkedIn app and maybe search about me. LinkedIn right now has close to 1.3 billion members worldwide across 200 countries, and we are operating a very high QPS for the ranking and recommendations. Search itself is evolving. Earlier we used to search based on specific keywords, and there were specific search filters that you put when you're entering any search query. Nowadays we are moving into more of a natural language to specify our intent. In LinkedIn's use case, you might be searching for a job where you enter, find me design roles in the entertainment industry.
Or you're searching for someone in your network where the search query could be, who in my network can help me file a patent for my business? All these are raw natural language texts which are complex to understand. If you think about this, this is where LLMs can be really powerful. They help us understand the user intent and then help us provide them better results. Search and ranking at LinkedIn scale is already a complex enough problem, and if you bring LLMs into the mix, it makes it even harder. For engineers like me, it's a really fun problem to solve.
Architecture
Let's look at the high-level architecture of how these things work end-to-end. It all starts with a search query where you have the find me design roles in the entertainment industry, and the search query goes through the first layer called query understanding layer. This is where we help figure out what the user intent is, what they're actually looking for. Then comes the retrieval layer. LinkedIn has millions of jobs posted in this platform. The job of the retrieval layer is to figure out the top-K most relevant jobs for your search query. Then all these results go to the ranker layer, which ultimately decides the order in which we want to show the results to you guys. In this talk, I'm going to quickly give an overview of the query understanding and the retrieval layer to add more context to the overall talk. My specific talk is going to be focused on the ranking layer.
Let's look at the query understanding layer first. The goal of the query understanding layer is to turn the raw, ambiguous natural language text that the user has entered and convert that into more of a structured, normalized format, which the further systems can understand. Let's take this example where we have a member who's a software engineer in the Bay Area with 5 years of experience. The search query they have entered is, find software engineer jobs near my location. We take this query and then the first step here is the query planner, which identifies the search criteria here. In this case, it's a job title and location, and figures out a plan on how to execute it. The next comes the query tagger. This step enriches the query with more rich information, which we can pull from the member profile, like what is their job title, what is their location, and also some search filters they might have in their LinkedIn.
Next comes the query rewriter, which is essentially the important piece here. If you look at a search query, we have something like a self-referencing, ambiguous text there, find me software engineer job near my location. Someone has to go and really understand what the user location is. That's where the query rewriter comes into play. It's going to replace the near my location with Bay Area, which is the user location. All of this gets packaged into a nice format, normalized enough, and then passed on to the retrieval layer.
Now when we move on to the retrieval layer, the goal here is for the user query, we have to find the top-K semantically relevant jobs. We have millions of jobs posted out there. We cannot go take every job and rank them. That's where the input starts with the query understanding layer output, and we take that and convert that into a query embedding. We then do a vector search with the embedding and do a KNN search on the index, which was pre-built using all the pre-computed embeddings from the jobs out there. From this step, we get the top-K most semantically relevant jobs for the search query. In this step, we primarily focus on optimizing for recall rather than precision. What we exactly mean by that is we would rather have a few extra candidates out of the retrieval layer than discarding something which is highly relevant.
The output from the retrieval layer then is passed on to the ranking layer. As mentioned about previously, this is where we figure out what order we want to show the results to the user. We want to show the highly relevant one as the first item. If you haven't already guessed, in LinkedIn right now, we are employing LLMs to do this job for us. As with any LLM, the first step is to provide enough context for the LLM to make the right decision. That's where the output from the previous two layers, the query understanding and the retrieval layer becomes the context for this LLM. Then comes the system prompt. You have to build the prompt. You have to tell the LLM to do a specific job. You'll be surprised what we have in production. It goes by this, like we prompt the LLM, given a search query and given the member profile description and a job, can you output yes or no if the job matches the query?
It's literally that. That's what we really have in production. At the end of this, we take the probabilities of model predicting yes or no token, and use that to compute the final scores. We do this for all the candidates provided by the retrieval layer, and then finally do some business logic to show what is the first result we want to show to you.
Part Zero - LLM Ranking is a Different Problem
When you're operating systems at this scale and you're serving billions of members out there, you want to optimize all the layers underneath. That's where we have three main levels. Before going to that, I'm going to specify why LLM ranking is a very different problem. Usually, when we think about LLMs, we associate with chatbot text generation. Ranking is a very different problem all together. If you look at the generative LLM workloads, you have a prompt which you give to the LLM and it goes through a phase called prefill phase. Prefill phase is the one that the LLM understands the context you have given to it. Next comes the decode phase, and we call it decode loop here because we are generating text token by token. It goes through several steps like sampling, next token prediction. You want to get the probabilities of all the token and the vocabulary and figure out what is the token you want to output to the user, which ultimately gives you the generated text token by token.
The latency here scales with the number of output tokens required. If you take a ranking use case, let's take the job ranking scenario. We talked about the query here is software engineer jobs in Bay Area, and the system prompt is simple, like output yes or no based on a job match. The list of candidates or the list of items to be ranked here is the job description. The main difference here, let's say we want to rank 50 items, we are constructing 50 prompts to the LLM for each item. You'll have a query item 1, query item 2, like that, 50 items. All of this goes through a single batched prefill phase. Another important difference here is all of this share a common long shared prefix in terms of the query, in terms of the system prompt, and all other context you feed to the LLM.
These are shared among all the jobs you want to rank. The third one here is there is not necessarily a decode phase. We are not generating any text per se. All we need is the final probabilities of the yes or no token. The major challenges when serving a system like this is we are dealing with strict P99 latency SLAs. Imagine you go to LinkedIn and search something and we take 10 seconds to show the result. That is not a good experience. We are also dealing with high concurrency where it's not enough if we just show one job or one person in a network, we have to show a bunch of candidates, usually in the hundreds. These challenges require us to optimize on all possible trends. That's where these three come into play. In an LLM system, we have the model, we have the context, and we have the inference.
Whenever you're working with these kinds of systems, you want to make the model as small as possible and you want to make the context as short as possible, because token here is the currency. Inference, you have to make it as efficient as possible. In the rest of the talk, I'm going to dive deep into each of these sections where I'm going to share what we did, what worked for us, and what are some learnings that you could take away from us.
Part One - Model Optimizations
Let's start with the model optimizations. The goal is simple. Like you have a model, you want to make it as small as possible. What are the techniques we can employ for this? The first thing we did is something called multi-teacher distillation. We started with the larger model, around 7-billion parameter size. This model is really good in understanding the context. It can understand the product policies and it can understand the relevance between the query and item, but it was never intended to be deployed in production. The whole purpose of this teacher model or the larger model is to provide high quality training signals. We then transfer this knowledge into two separate smaller teacher models by a process called knowledge distillation. We have two models which are optimized for separate metrics, one for relevance, another for engagement. These are metrics in ranking and recommendation workloads. The relevance here basically denotes how relevant is the search result for the query.
The engagement here basically specifies, if I show this result to the user, how likely it is to drive engagement, whether the user will click, whether the user will read, and all those things. Now we have two smaller teacher models, we call it, which is optimized on these two metrics. We then use this and then train another small model, SLM ranker is what we call it, small language model, which learns the objectives from both of these teacher models. We essentially started with a larger 7 billion model and we were able to knowledge distill all this in a multi-step, in a multi-teacher way, and then compress all the context into the smaller model. You will have some quality loss, but it should be acceptable for the business use case you're solving. We didn't stop there. We looked into how to make this model even smaller. That's where a technique called pruning comes into play.
It's essentially, you take the model and you do some trial and error and figure out, can I remove some layers? Can I remove some MLP layers or any attention heads? Then see if there is an acceptable quality loss that you can still serve. Obviously, pruning doesn't come for free. Whenever you're removing something from the model, there will be some quality loss. That's why we have to again re-distill, re-train and fine-tune the model so that the loss is within the acceptable range. Just to recall the model optimizations, we started with the 7 billion larger model with the multi-teacher distillation. We got it to 0.6B. We took the 0.6B and then removed some layers and finally got this in the size of 400 million parameters. Now the model is super small that we can now already serve this in production.
Part Two - Context Optimizations
Next, I want to talk about the context optimization. If we take the job ranking scenario and a particular job description can easily be 2000 tokens. When you want to serve a ranking request, so you have a request and you have 100 jobs you want to rank. This could easily be 100 into 2000, like 200K tokens that you want to process in one shot. If we have very few members, let's say in the order of thousands, we can serve this easily. At LinkedIn scale, when you have 1.3 billion members, this is not possible. That's where we started looking into how can we compress this context. The first step we came up with is to use a summarizer, use another LLM to summarize this job description from 2000 tokens to 150 tokens. We do all this work offline. We never compute all this in the online path.
In the online, we just fetch the summarized text from the database and then pass it as input to the ranker. This helped us to bring the item prompt length all the way from 2000 tokens to 150 tokens, which is a 16x reduction in the prompt length. The interesting thing to note here is we were able to get all this thing done with a less than 2% quality loss. This is where we took prompt engineering serious. Prompt is the currency, you have to make them as small as possible. In the next question, we didn't stop there. We were looking into opportunities, how we can make the item representation even smaller. Is it possible to just have one token instead of 150 tokens? Literally not one token. Can it just be one dense vector representation? Or in simple terms, can it just be one embedding? That's where our research comes into play, where we take the full text description and then pass it to an LLM, which basically compresses into just one embedding.
LLM does a really good job. It can also be used as an embedding model, where you can pass in a full text and you can get one embedding out of it. Now for all compute purposes, we have compressed the item token length from 2000 to just one token. Then, again, we do all this offline. Nothing happens in the online path. We just come up, fetch this from the database and then pass it to the ranker.
Now you can ask me, "Sundara, this is really great. You have context compressed, went all the way from 2000 to one token. How does it perform quality-wise? Does it give you relevance result?" That's where I'm going to discuss about this graph. On the y-axis, we have the ranking quality. On the x-axis, I have the throughput measured in terms of items per second per GPU. The leftmost data point over there is the baseline metric where we use the full job description to get the results. This is the one which gives the highest-ranking quality and also lowest throughput. We were able to get only 290 items per second. The second data point is the data point for summarized text. When we use summarizer to bring down the token size from 2000 to 150. This helped us to almost increase the throughput from 290 to 2200, close to 8x, 9x, with a less than 2% acceptable quality loss.
The third data point on the right is the one I talked about in the previous slide, where we take the full job description and then context compress into just one embedding. You can see the x-axis where the numbers run from 2200 to almost 22k. This is like a 10x improvement in the throughput which you can serve. Even more interesting thing to note here is, if you see the quality, you were able to get a slightly better quality compared to the summarized text. The key takeaway here is, the best representation for your workload is not necessarily the longest one. It's the smallest one that can give you the acceptable quality your use case needs. It can be the full text, or it can be a summarized text, or it can just be even one embedding. My biggest recommendation for people serving models in production is to get the model and context really tight. Make it as short as possible. Before even you do any hardware estimates or capacity planning, get your model and context right.
Part Three - Inference Optimizations
In our use case, once we got both of them right, we started looking into inference. Inference is a really interesting problem. We already have great open-source engines out there like SGLang, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and they already provide state-of-the-art throughput for most of the use cases. It doesn't necessarily mean that for your use case, it's going to work very well. That's how we approach the problem. We didn't treat inference as a solved problem. We started looking into what is different in our workload and what are all the optimization opportunities we can look out for. In the next few slides, I'm going to dive deeper into the inference side of things. The whole idea here is there are a lot of bottlenecks, not inference related, but system related, runtime related, maybe related to the engine you are serving, maybe related to the language you are serving, which I am going to call out.
These might be hiding in your stack as well. The first bottleneck was on the CPU side. When you are serving production systems using LLMs, the first step is something called a tokenizer. In our code, what we had was we were taking the batch of items. Let's go back to the ranking workload. You have a request where you want to rank 50 items, let's say. You have like 50 prompts as a batch input to the LLM. In our code, what was happening was the tokenizer was happening sequentially on the CPU side. Basically, this was happening in the for loop one by one, it was stalling the GPU and the CPU was just sitting idle. In order to fix this, we replaced this with a batch tokenizer. What it means is Hugging Face APIs provide a fast tokenizer API, where you can send a batch of prompts and then it will parallelize the work across multiple codes.
Internally, it's implemented using REST, but for our use case, all this is available in open source. You just have to leverage these APIs. A natural extension of this was, can we do something on the server side so that we don't have to repeat this client-side batching for workloads where clients cannot naturally batch and send a batch request. We did have a lot of embedding generation workloads where either the client was not able to batch on the client side, or we had a shared model where we had multiple clients. If you want to do this batching on the client side, you have to repeat this logic across multiple clients. That's where we introduced something like server-side batching, which is going to batch across the request and then do one batch tokenization using the same fast tokenizer API, which I mentioned before. The important callout here is, if you are having any production systems, make sure you are doing batch tokenization. All these APIs are available out there in open source. Just make sure you are leveraging them.
The next bottleneck was even more subtle. When you are having an LLM based system, as I mentioned, you will have the tokenizer process, which is going to take the prompt and then figure out the token IDs. There will also be a scheduler process, some sort of scheduler, which is the one which is preparing the work and then dispatching the work to the GPU. When we looked into our system, we were sending a batch of 50 prompts. All of this can fit into the model context. What we saw in the logs was, this was getting split into smaller batches. Then we profiled the system and then figured out the root cause here to be the inter-process communication between these two processes. Essentially, from the tokenizer process to the scheduler process, we were sending the prompts one by one in a separate ZMQ message. In order to fix this, again, the fixes here are really simple.
You just want to maintain the batch integrity throughout. You just send all of them in a single ZMQ message, so that the entire batch is passed on from the tokenizer to the scheduler in one shot. A key takeaway from this slide is, if you are having production systems based in Python, you are definitely leveraging multiprocessing for some reason. I'll discuss about why in the next few slides. Make sure when you are using multiprocessing, you are using the right set of communication protocol between them. Make sure you're maintaining the batch integrity when you're sending the request.
On to the next one, I talked about this in the initial part of the slides, where ranking is completely different from text generation. Let's walk through it again. Text generation goes through the prefill phase, and a decode phase that is where we are going to generate token by token, and we predict the probabilities of all the tokens out there in the vocabulary and we are going to pick the one which is the top or based on some heuristic. That's the sampling phase. In order for that to happen you are copying all these probabilities, all these floats from GPU to CPU. There is a lot of work that is happening which are not required for ranking. If you think about the ranking or the scoring use case, you just have to do one large prefill, and then you have to copy the yes or no probabilities at the end.
This motivated us to introduce the dedicated scoring API in open source where we bypass all this unnecessary work and then just get the logits at the end. The scoring API was already really good for us, we were able to solve most of the CPU side bottleneck. Then we deploy the system in production and we see the GPU utilization metrics, and the metrics were not good. We were scratching our heads like, what is happening? Then we go profile it, use the PyTorch profile and everything, and then what we see here is there was a lot of idle gaps between the GPU kernel launches. I am going to walk you through this graph here. On the first line we have the tokenizer, as with any LLM you will first have to tokenize it. This is happening on the CPU side. Next comes the scheduler process which is again on the CPU, and this is the process which is preparing the batches to dispatch to the GPU.
The third line is the GPU compute where you have the kernel launches, all the matrix multiplications happening. In our case, for ranking, we are scoring 50 prompts at the same time. What we were doing in our code was we are copying the yes or no probabilities one by one for each request for each prompt in a synchronized blocking way. This essentially stall the scheduler from launching the next kernel launch for the next request. In order to fix this, we replace this synchronous blocking call into an asynchronous non-blocking copy, and also instead of copying the yes or no probabilities of each and every item, we replace with a batched copy. This helped us to better overlap the CPU work of the previous request while we dispatch the GPU work of the next request. The key takeaway from this slide is if you have Python systems and if you are working with tensors and all sorts of things, just make sure you are using asynchronous non-blocking copies. For example, like when we are using some tensor and copying the tensors from GPU to CPU, a simple dot to list Python call made the copy blocking. All these are subtle things which can affect your overall GPU utilization, and we have not even gotten into kernel yet, everything is happening on the CPU side.
The next thing, once we solved all the CPU side, and all the CPU bottlenecks were handled, we were looking into what work we were doing redundantly and trying to figure out if we can optimize for it. Let's revisit the ranking use case where you have the query and the items. When you are ranking 50 items you are constructing 50 prompts. If you look at the query path, the query path is repeated across all items. We are redoing the query work every time. That is where we researched a bit and trying to see how we can reuse that work, and that is where we come up with an idea to concatenate all the prompts into just one single prompt to the LLM. The blue blocks here denote the query and the green is the first item followed by a delimiter followed by item 2. We just concatenate all of them, and it is just the one single prompt to the LLM.
The key challenge here is, let's say we have a query job 1 and job 2, when the LLM is processing the job 2 and making a decision for it, it should not bring the context of job 1, or else it is going to give you wrong results. That is where we went a little bit into the kernel and then we introduced the custom Item-Aware Attention Mask, inside the flash into the kernel, so that when the LLM sees job 2 it is going to forget about job 1. By doing this optimization we were able to score n items in single pass, and we were able to naturally reuse the query KVs because we only have it once in the prompt.
I know I went a little bit deeper into the kernel and all, but the next few slides will be really interesting because these are something we didn't expect when we deployed in production, and these are brought by Python. We might have a lot of Python code. The first interesting thing that we encountered in production was, we deploy the system, we make it fast enough, and we deploy in the model server. We go see the production metrics, we were seeing spikes every few seconds in P99 latency. Just to reiterate, for search and recommendation, we are operating at a very strict latency. Usually, the P99 has to be less than 500 milliseconds. We go see the graph and we see every few seconds the P99 spikes by 300 milliseconds or so. The reason here turned out to be the Python garbage collector. Before we even got to that, we spent some time, the usual suspects would be like, there was a surge in QPS, or there was one request that had a longer prompt.
These are like user culprits. You go rule them out, and then you have to spend more time debugging what's happening, and the root cause turned out to be the garbage collector. In model server, when you load the model and there are a lot of long-lived Python objects that get created that lives through the lifecycle of the overall process. What was happening is this Python garbage collector was kicking in every few seconds and was scanning each of these objects to figure out which one it should free. This contributed to almost 300-millisecond spike every now and then. In order to fix this what we did was we started the model server. We warmed it up using some warm-up request. Then Python gives you a beautiful API called gc.freeze, which tells the garbage collector, up until this point, all the objects that got created are going to live throughout the life cycle of the model server, just to ignore it.
After this, whatever temporary object that gets created during the request path is the one the garbage collector will be interested in. With this fix we were able to get the P99 in a stable way. The next bottleneck was Python's infamous Global Interpreter Lock, which effectively makes Python bytecode executable by single thread only once at a time. It's different from how Java and C++ and all those things can give you true parallelism when you are working with threads. Python is a different thing all together. In LinkedIn's system, we take the open-source engines we have, and we take the SGLang engine, and then put it behind a gRPC servicer process. The request comes as a gRPC protobuf and the servicer process is the one which is going to deserialize the request. It's also going to do some observability, logging, metrics, and other stuff, and then dispatch the request to the SGLang worker process.
Because of the Global Interpreter Lock, and when we send large QPS the single servicer process became the bottleneck. In order to fix this, we replaced a single process with multiple processes, so that all of them can do this work in parallel in separate CPU cores. Once we solve the bottleneck on a servicer with multiprocessing, the SGLang worker process which is effectively preparing the work and dispatching the work to the GPU became the bottleneck. The fix here is again the same, instead of one process you will have multiple processes. The callout here is, each process has its own model copy and it's going to have its own CUDA stream and do the kernel launches and MemSync and whatnot, and it's effectively going to time slice the GPU. In our case we were able to do it because the model was smaller. Nowadays I think we get enough HBM in the GPU, so you should be able to deploy this as well. The callout again here, in production systems based on Python, is, worry about this Global Interpreter Lock and this can be your single fix which can help improve the throughput.
Part Four - Learnings at LinkedIn Scale
I know I went a little deeper into the inference side of things. I'm going to keep it really simple in the last four slides. It's pretty simple. These are the major learnings that you could take away from this talk and from our work. The first one is what I call benchmark what you serve. You will be like, "Sundara, that's so obvious. What are you doing otherwise?" I will tell a small story of what we did. We do all these beautiful optimizations in model, context, inference, and then we go and do an offline benchmark. We figure out the throughput we were able to get out of a GPU and then we know how much QPS we want to serve. We do the estimates, and we go inform our leadership, this is the amount of GPUs we need. They were happy and we were happy they were happy.
We go deploy this in production and we send some dark traffic, that's where we see an entirely different result. We were not able to realize the offline benchmark numbers we were able to get. We are scratching our head like, what is wrong here? Is there anything wrong with the hardware? Is there anything wrong with the specific GPU, or is there any communication bottleneck between the client and server? Something happening over the network. It turned out, we were doing our benchmarks incorrectly. When we are simulating synthetic traffic, we were effectively using even distribution to send the request. What it means is within a second interval, you are estimating based on QPS. You're going to say that my throughput is 1000 jobs per second, 1000 items per second, or something of that sort. When you're simulating the synthetic traffic, the requests are getting sent in an equally spaced manner.
All of them arrive in a uniform distribution with equal spaces. In production, when you're serving real time user traffic, you cannot expect the users to follow the same patterns. Within a second interval, you might have a surge in requests so the queue depth increases. After that, there could be some quieter periods. The major takeaway from this here is if you are serving systems in production, the closest possible result you can get is if you can record and replay your production traffic. If you don't have that option, the second closest thing you could get is if you can simulate the synthetic traffic using a Poisson distribution instead of an even distribution. Just make sure you're doing the right thing there. The second learning is what I call offline must match online. What do we mean by this? When you're working with a model-based system in production, there is an engineer who's going to work on fine-tuning the model.
There'll be prompt engineers who are designing the prompts, and they have their own set of code. The system that gets deployed in production is entirely different. You might be leveraging an open-source system, or you might be leveraging your own model server. There are a set of defaults which is different from both these. Like for example, a simple tokenization config like add end of sequence or beginning of sequence config, can change the entire prompt in itself. You have to make sure there is absolute parity between the offline and the online system. Don't discover all these disparities or discrepancies in production. Disparity has to be a gate without which you cannot launch in production at all.
The third learning is the crux of the talk. There is no single fix here when you are serving systems in production, models, LLMs, anything of that sort. You have to squeeze in throughput from all the possible places. You have to make the model as small as possible, and you have to make the context as short as possible and make the inference as efficient as possible. The final learning, if there are any tech leads, managers, and leaders, this is for you guys. When you are dealing with production systems, there are multiple actors here. You have the inference engineers. You have the model engineers. You have the prompt engineers. You have the product managers who are defining the product policies. It's very important that we bring all of these actors into one setup, one meeting which is recurring. You can have a standup or a meeting every week so that each of them can share their idea, cross check, cross validate everything.
You will be surprised how many issues you can catch in these meetings before even you get to production. We often think about optimizations as, if we have to optimize the code, we have to optimize the CPU, GPU, Python, Java, C++, Rust, and all those things. The first and foremost optimization we had to do is with respect to bringing the right people together, you remove the communication barrier and make sure you allow them to share their ideas, and then effectively improve the overall system in play.

For example, when we are working with people search or member profile, we're going to mask all the public information data or the private data, which is not exposed in their LinkedIn profile already. If there is something, for example, the date of birth or something, that's going to get masked out there. It's not even fed into the model at all. Only the publicly available information goes as input to the model.
Participant 5: Since you're saying this is in production, and I believe there's millions of requests every second happening for this kind of request search, I was wondering how this LLM infrastructure integrated with the existing service or server to handle this huge amount of requests?
Sundara Raman Ramachandran: I believe the people search and job search is right now rolled out to all premium users. It, I think, gradually will get rolled out to all users by end of this year. In terms of the actual server in production, I show a block diagram in the end. This is what we actually have in production. This is the entire model server high-level architecture. We are using a Python-based gRPC server, and we are leveraging an open-source engine, SGLang. It sits behind the Python gRPC servicer. It's all part of one application per se. It's not split into multiple, I believe. It's not like a multi-servicer and all, it's just one Python application. All these are just Python processes in the end. This is the model server. Essentially, this model server is the one which will fit into the ranker block, which we saw in the architecture diagram. This is the piece which is taking the query and the list of candidates, and it's going to give the scores for each of the candidates.

articles.title: Pretxt Emerges Stealth With $5M Seed and an AI Supervision Tool
articles.text:
Pretxt, with offices in Aspen, CO, and Dublin, Ireland, has emerged from stealth with $5 million seed funding raised from Deciens Capital, Howdy Partners and Service Provider Capital. Pretxt enters the emerging category of firms providing technology to prevent AI agents escaping their guardrails and causing unintended harm.
AI is more like a person than like traditional computer code: it doesn’t simply run; it receives, interprets, misinterprets and responds to ambiguous instructions. It is the combination of misinterpretation and wide agency of response that results in AI agents going rogue and potentially causing harm.
Since it is impossible to categorically exclude ambiguity in language (which is how we instruct the agents), our only alternative method of controlling them is to limit their agency. But too stringent a limitation of agency could become an unacceptable restriction on a potentially huge business benefit.
So, without a new category of supervision control, it is likely that we cannot have beneficial AI agents without also having potentially dangerous rogue agents. This requirement for a new control is leading to the emergence of a type of cybersecurity product that attempts to recognize a potentially harmful agentic action at runtime and control it before it can cause harm.
Pretxt is announcing just such a product which it describes as AI Supervision, “a purpose-built runtime technology to supervise AI agents as they work, guiding them back on course before mistakes become business consequences.”
Rather than neutering the capability of an agent, explains Aaron Costello, Pretxt co-founder and CTO, “We say, ‘Okay, you give an AI agent the same level of access as an authorized employee, and we will continuously monitor the manner in which it interacts with systems and other people. We will validate and ensure that all such interaction conforms with your business standards and operates in the same way that you expect your employees to operate.”
If the agent exceeds its expected authority or deviates from its authorized purpose, Pretxt doesn’t simply shut it down – it ‘steers’ the offender back on track. It’s a bit like having an experienced supervisor permanently on the shoulder of a trainee, who just steps in when necessary, with, “Don’t do it like that, do it like this instead.”
‘Steering’ is governed by context, continues Costello. “We ask new customers to onboard and connect their AI agent to our product, so we can immediately see the agent’s instructions and understand its purpose. As we watch it in operation, we learn how it speaks. We see what tools it can access, and we learn what abilities it has been given – such as ‘send’ an email, ‘post’ to LinkedIn, or ‘update’ a database.”
The customer then explains to Pretxt, I never want my AI agent to do x, or I only want my agent to do y, or see this kind of data. “It could be anything,” adds Costello. “The information is imported into Pretxt’s own AI. It becomes the context for acceptable behavior and is hooked into anywhere within the agent that could potentially violate the agent’s intended purpose and constraints.”
He gives the example of a customer service agent used by a medical practice to help patients book an appointment. Pretxt may have been told by the medical practice, ‘I never want this agent to give medical advice.’ “What we do,” he continues, “is hook into every single occasion the AI agent interacts with the user. Our own agent will look at this interaction and check whether it contains medical advice. This is done in real time. If it does contain medical advice (which we know should not be offered), we prevent it. But not by shutting down the agent, because that would leave patients unable to book appointments. We use a different approach that we call ‘steering’. If we detect medical advice, we invisibly talk back to the agent and effectively tell it, ‘You tried to give medical advice. Please continue to help the user with their booking request, but do not attempt to give medical advice again’.”
This is the purpose of Pretxt’s AI supervision app – not to shut down wanton AI agents, but to keep them safe, and prevent them straying from their predefined constraints.

articles.title: Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer
articles.text:
Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer
Drought conditions and low reservoir levels are affecting the renewable power source.
The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.
Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. The water can be released through turbines, generating electricity on demand. But an extreme, prolonged drought in the Colorado River Basin has resulted in dangerously low water levels in the Southwest’s two largest reservoirs, affecting the availability of this power source.
Residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases. Snowfall in the Rocky Mountains provides about 85% of the annual flow of the Colorado River. And in recent years, the river has seen record-low flows.
Two reservoirs along the Colorado River, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, have struggled to stay above the minimum level required for hydropower plants. At the end of September, Lake Powell’s depth was 3,518 feet, less than 1% above the level required to run the water through turbines that produce electricity at the Glen Canyon power plant. The Hoover Dam power plant requires 950 feet in Lake Mead, and that reservoir was 9% above the minimum in September.
Together, the two plants produced nearly seven terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to serve over 2 million people.
Low water levels have been an ongoing struggle for the region, which has been in a drought for 27 years. Meanwhile, climate change is continuing to shift rainfall and snowfall patterns across the region and around the world.
The effects of climate change on hydropower aren’t entirely straightforward globally—some regions will see more rain and snow because of shifting weather patterns, while others are likely to see less.
But it’s playing a role for hydropower availability, according to one 2022 review study. Rising temperatures bring more droughts, warmer winters means less snow and ice to fill the reservoirs, and more variability in precipitation can lead to alternating floods and droughts, making the power source less reliable.
Hydropower production is likely to be at its lowest level in over a decade in 2026 and tick even lower in 2027, according to projections from the EIA.
El Niño could provide some temporary relief. Sometimes this weather pattern can mean cooler, wetter conditions for the southern US. Heavy rains brought floods to the region in October and early November, and the water levels in Lake Powell rose more than 20 feet from their mid-September low. But the water is still quite low, and it’ll take much more to help reservoirs recover from decades of drought conditions.
Even as a changing climate complicates the availability of hydropower, the decline in capacity could push greenhouse-gas emissions higher. In 2023, energy-related greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 1.1% globally. A worldwide shortfall in hydropower generation accounted for about 40% of that rise, according to a report from the International Energy Agency.

articles.title: iFixit’s Apple HomeView teardown reveals a device that will be difficult to repair
articles.text:
After finding recent versions of Apple’s iPads and HomePods much easier to disassemble for battery replacements or other repairs, iFixit assumed it would be the same story for Apple’s new HomeView hub that looks like a seven-inch tablet stuck to a smart speaker. The reality was much different and by the time they got the HomeView apart iFixit’s skilled techs had “ripped a connector, snapped a speaker in two, and put more force on the poor logic board than any of us were comfortable with.”
iFixit’s Apple HomeView teardown reveals a device that will be difficult to repair
Apple’s inroads on designing repairable devices seems to have been abandoned with the HomeView.
The tablet section of the HomeView proved to be the bigger challenge to disassemble as a result of some questionable decisions with Apple’s design. The glue used to secure the display in place “held on harder than on any Apple product we’ve opened recently,” iFixit says. And while Apple’s decision to turn the HomeView’s entire aluminum chassis into a heat sink was clever, the thermal bond between a heat shield and the device’s logic board made separating the two a “remarkably risky operation.” While these design decisions possibly streamlined assembly at a factory, the extensive use of glue makes servicing the HomeView incredibly difficult.
In an accompanying teardown video iFixit also reveals how much smaller the speaker drivers are in the wall-mounted version of the HomeView versus the tabletop option. Although both versions are priced at $299, the wall version costs a little more when you factor in the required mount that’s not included, leaving iFixit feeling that you’re getting less performance while spending more money.

articles.title: DB Info: Die neue Bahn-App soll alles wissen – kennt aber keine Ticketpreise
articles.text:
DB Info: Bahn startet neue App für Informationen – darum kennt sie keine Ticketpreise
Eine neue Bahn-App will Fragen Reisender vor ihrer Fahrt, unterwegs und am Ziel beantworten. Mit DB Info sollen sich zum einen unabhängig vom Anbieter Verbindungen planen lassen.
Zum anderen informiert die Anwendung auch über Verspätungen, Gleiswechsel, Bauarbeiten, bevorstehende Abfahrten, Ankünfte, Gleise sowie Wagenreihungen – und das „konsistent und in Echtzeit zu den Anzeigen im Bahnhof“, wie die Deutsche Bahn mitteilt.
Keine Fahrkarten kaufen – aber den nächsten Kaffee finden
Preisinformationen oder einen Ticketverkauf gibt es in der für iOS und Android verfügbaren und barrierefrei konzipierten App hingegen nicht, weil diese Reisende neutral informieren soll. Zum Informationsumfang gehören aber auch Orientierungshilfen und Angebotsübersichten an Bahnhöfen – etwa zu Bahnsteigen, Schließfächern, Toiletten, Shops und Gastronomie samt Öffnungszeiten.
Aufzüge im Fokus – Lost & Found integriert
Auch Hilfe für mobilitätseingeschränkte Reisende gibt es in der Anwendung, darunter Angaben zu verfügbaren Aufzügen sowie direkten Kontakt zur Mobilitätsservice-Zentrale. In Zügen oder an Bahnhöfen Verlorenes und Vergessenes kann man direkt in der App melden.
Regelmäßig genutzte Bahnhöfe lassen sich ebenso in einer Merkliste speichern wie Aufzüge, auf die man vielleicht angewiesen ist. Dann erhält man bei Ausfällen eine Benachrichtigung.
KI‑Assistent kommt – ebenso wie streckenbezogene Reiseinfos
Die App soll den Angaben zufolge in den nächsten Monaten weiter ausgebaut werden, etwa um einen KI-Assistenten, eine barrierefreie Reisebegleitung von Tür zu Tür sowie streckenbezogene Reiseinformation für Pendelnde und Vielfahrende.

articles.title: Uber notifies drivers of data breach affecting nearly 150,000 people
articles.text:
Ride-hailing company Uber is notifying nearly 150,000 drivers that attackers stole their data after breaching AI infrastructure provider Fireworks in early October.
In breach notification letters sent to affected individuals on November 10, Uber said threat actors accessed their personal information after breaching an Uber account with a third-party service provider.
While Uber didn't share the total number of affected drivers in these letters, it revealed in a filing with Maine's Office of the Attorney General that the data breach has exposed the information of 149,346 drivers, including their names, driver’s license numbers, dates of birth, and addresses.
After being informed of the breach, Uber launched an investigation and severed data connections with the service provider to block further malicious access to its data.
"On October 9, 2026, a service provider notified Uber that an unauthorized third party had compromised the service provider's internal credentials and used them to access Uber's account with the service provider," Uber said. "After being notified of this incident, Uber immediately severed data connections with the service provider and launched an investigation. On October 13, 2026, our investigation determined that the unauthorized party had used the compromised credentials to access Uber data connected to the service provider."
Although the company didn't directly name the hacked service provider, TechCrunch first reported that the Uber data breach stems from an October 24 security incident at AI training provider Fireworks, which was hacked after a third-party cloud provider hack.
Fireworks has attributed the attack to a financially motivated cybercriminal threat actor group linked to a series of large language model hijacking (LLMjacking) attacks.
The Fireworks breach also led to security incidents at AI coding platform Cursor and digital workspace platform Notion, which also reported that the attackers stole data from a limited number of customers and (in Cursor's case) infected users' devices with backdoor malware.
An Uber spokesperson was not immediately available for comment when BleepingComputer reached out for more information about the data breach.
The company disclosed another data breach in December 2022 after a threat actor leaked IT asset information, employees' email addresses, and corporate reports stolen from third-party service provider Teqtivity.
Uber previously confirmed that hackers who breached some of its systems in October 2016 stole data from 50 million users and 7 million drivers, and that the Lapsus$ extortion group also hacked it in September 2022 in an MFA fatigue attack using the stolen credentials of an Uber EXT contractor.

articles.title: SFR rattrape enfin ses concurrents avec sa nouvelle Box 10 en Wi-Fi 7
articles.text:
SFR a lancé ce mardi la Box 10, une box Wi-Fi 7 bi-bande désormais incluse dans l'offre SFR Fibre Power à 36,99 euros par mois. Petite sœur de la Box 10+, elle promet le meilleur du Wi-Fi sans le tarif premium.
D'abord annoncée en février, puis trahie début octobre par des pages d'assistance publiées trop tôt, la SFR Box 10 est enfin officielle et équipe dès ce mardi 17 novembre 2026 l'offre SFR Fibre Power. Au programme, on retrouve du Wi-Fi 7 certifié, de la fibre jusqu'à 2 Gb/s, deux ports Ethernet 2,5 Gb/s et un écran E-ink tactile façon liseuse. Reste à savoir ce qu'elle laisse à la Box 10+, son aînée premium, et si elle pèse assez lourd face à des concurrents qui n'ont pas attendu l'opérateur au carré rouge pour faire descendre le Wi-Fi 7 en milieu de gamme. Décortiquons cette nouvelle box !
La SFR Box 10 mise sur un Wi-Fi 7 bi-bande et la fibre à 2 Gbit/s
La SFR Box 10 a pour premier argument le Wi-Fi 7, certifié par la Wi-Fi Alliance, dans une version bi-bande qu'on peut donc regretter limitée aux fréquences 2,4 et 5 GHz. SFR annonce un débit théorique cumulé de 6,8 Gbit/s, contre 5,4 Gbit/s pour la Box 8 qu'elle remplace dans l'offre Power, soit 25 % de mieux. Un plafond théorique, à partager entre tous les appareils de la maison, mais qui donne de l'air aux foyers bardés d'écrans. Côté fibre, elle repose sur la technologie GPON, avec jusqu'à 2 Gbit/s partagés en téléchargement et 1 Gbit/s en envoi. Un pari cohérent, alors que la qualité de connexion est devenue un critère de choix majeur d'un opérateur.
Au niveau des branchements, on note quatre ports Ethernet, deux à 1 Gbit/s et deux à 2,5 Gbit/s, qui accueillent les PC et consoles récentes sans brider la ligne. Comme la Box 10+, la Box 10 intègre un module Thread, un protocole basse consommation qui relie capteurs de mouvement, prises et interrupteurs connectés. Autre parti pris, l'accessibilité, travaillée avec l'association HandiCaPZéro. SFR vante un marquage en braille et une connectique placée pour être plus intuitive. La box soigne aussi son bilan carbone, avec la certification TÜV Rheinland Green Mark, une coque en plastique 100 % recyclé et des pièces métalliques recyclées à 46 %. Son mode éco, activable depuis l'écran ou l'appli SFR & Moi, abaisse sa consommation de 9,4 à 5,9 W, soit près de 40 % d'économie.
Venons-en au prix ! L'offre SFR Fibre Power, qui rappelons est, des trois grandes offres internet fixe proposées par l'opérateur, celle dite de « milieu de gamme », reste à 36,99 euros par mois, avec douze mois d'engagement et 49 euros de frais d'ouverture. SFR rembourse en revanche, sur demande, jusqu'à 100 euros de frais de résiliation facturés par l'ancien opérateur.
Le salon n'a pas été oublié, avec le décodeur SFR Box 8 TV (4K HDR, Dolby Vision, Dolby Atmos et enceinte connectée), 200 chaînes et, pour une deuxième télé, un décodeur secondaire ou l'appli sur TV connectée. Le téléphone fixe appelle en illimité les mobiles de métropole et les fixes de plus de 100 destinations. En prime, l'offre retire 3 euros par mois sur une option Netflix, Disney+, HBO Max ou Ciné+ OCS, et SFR Multi jusqu'à 8 euros par forfait mobile rattaché. Chose à savoir également, le répéteur Wi-Fi 7 est bien accessible, mais il se demande depuis l'Espace Client, contre 10 euros de frais d'activation.
SFR Box 10 : moins que la 10+, assez pour bousculer la concurrence ?
Quand on la place face à sa grande sœur, la Box10+, la nouvelle Box 10 assume ses renoncements. Souvenez-vous, lancée en septembre 2025 et proposée avec l'offre SFR Fibre Premium, la Box 10+ s'appuie sur la fibre XGS-PON, qui grimpe jusqu'à 8 Gb/s, avec un Wi-Fi 7 tri-bande. Sa troisième bande, celle des 6 GHz, offre des débits très élevés mais porte moins loin à la maison. Alors un tout petit peu plus compacte, la Box 10 fait l'impasse sur les deux. Pour un foyer classique, 2 Gbit/s laissent tout de même de la marge, même si vous rêvez de GTA 6. C'est tout le pari de Pierre Clément, le directeur exécutif Grand Public et Entreprises de SFR, qui entend « démocratiser l'accès aux technologies les plus avancées du marché ».
Sur ce terrain maintenant, SFR, dont la vente prochaine aux concurrents est toujours étudiée et discutée, n'a pas réinventé l'histoire. Dès le mois de janvier, Bouygues Telecom a ajouté à son offre Bbox Must une Bbox Wi-Fi 7 bi-bande au profil presque jumeau, avec 2 Gbit/s en téléchargement, 900 Mbit/s en envoi, mais un seul port 2,5 Gbit/s, contre deux chez SFR. Son modèle premium tri-bande a été rebaptisé Bbox Wi-Fi 7 XT pour l'occasion. Et pour le Black Friday, l'opérateur dégaine même jusqu'au 30 novembre une Bbox à 29,99 euros par mois la première année, plus abordable mais sans Wi-Fi 7 et plafonnée à 1 Gbit/s.
Orange et Free avaient même ouvert la voie dès avril 2025. L'opérateur historique a lancé la Livebox S, une box Wi-Fi 7 de cœur de gamme plafonnée à 2 Gbit/s, en même temps qu'une nouvelle Livebox 7 capable d'atteindre 8 Gbit/s. Le second a dégainé la Freebox Pop S, déclinaison sans décodeur TV de la Freebox Pop, en Wi-Fi 7 et jusqu'à 5 Gbit/s pour 24,99 euros par mois. Dans ce paysage, la SFR Box 10, qui arrive quelques mois après la Box 5G Wi-Fi 7 de l'opérateur, ne renverse pas la table. Elle comble surtout le vide entre la Box 8 et la Box 10+, avec une fiche technique soignée et un vrai souci d'accessibilité. Les budgets serrés regarderont plutôt la RED Box Fibre de RED by SFR, en Wi-Fi 5, à 22,99 euros par mois sans engagement.
Selon nous, c'est à chaud l'une des offres TV et Wi-Fi 7 les plus équilibrées sur la durée, pour un foyer qui garde sa box plusieurs années. Ce n'est pas la meilleure affaire pour la première année, ni le meilleur choix pour qui cherche seulement de la fibre rapide au plus bas prix.

articles.title: Argentina vs. Costa Rica ver online en Xuper TV, Roja Directa y Fútbol Libre: el truco gratuito que pone en riesgo tu seguridad
articles.text:
Argentina vs. Costa Rica concentrará este martes 17 de noviembre de 2027, búsquedas de enlaces gratuitos en Xuper TV, Roja Directa y Fútbol Libre, pero esos accesos pueden exponer teléfonos, computadores y otros equipos a aplicaciones fraudulentas, robo de contraseñas y programas maliciosos. El amistoso se jugará a las 20:00 en el estadio Mario Alberto Kempes de Córdoba.
La selección argentina cerrará su calendario de 2026 ante Costa Rica después de la derrota por 2-1 frente a Uruguay en La Bombonera. El partido tendrá transmisión por TyC Sports, aunque la expectativa por seguirlo sin pagar suele dirigir a parte de los usuarios hacia webs que modifican sus dominios, imitan servicios conocidos o exigen instalar archivos antes de mostrar un supuesto reproductor.
El partido se jugará a las 20:00 en Córdoba
La Albiceleste buscará despedir el año con una victoria ante su público, antes de volver a competir en marzo de 2027. Argentina llega tras caer ante Uruguay, mientras que Costa Rica perdió frente a Ecuador en el inicio de la ventana de noviembre. El árbitro del encuentro será Bruno Arleu.
La probable alineación argentina incluye a Dibu Martínez; Agustín Giay, Leonardo Balerdi, Lisandro Martínez y Nicolás Tagliafico; Enzo Fernández y Alexis Mac Allister; Nico Paz, Matías Soulé y Gianluca Prestianni; Julián Álvarez.
Costa Rica podría formar con Patrick Sequeira; Kenay Myrie, Juan Pablo Vargas, Francisco Calvo y Joseph Mora; Celso Borges, Roan Wilson, Carlos Mora y Josimar Alcócer; Kenyel Michel y Manfred Ugalde. El técnico será Bryan Ruiz.
Los enlaces ilegales pueden llevar a descargas fraudulentas
Las búsquedas para ver Argentina vs. Costa Rica online suelen derivar en portales que prometen una transmisión inmediata. Algunas de esas páginas solicitan instalar una APK, descargar un supuesto reproductor o añadir extensiones al navegador con la excusa de desbloquear el partido, eliminar anuncios o mejorar la imagen.
Una plataforma destinada a reproducir fútbol no necesita permisos para acceder a contactos, mensajes, cámara, ubicación ni funciones de accesibilidad. Si una aplicación vinculada con Fútbol Libre, Roja Directa, Tarjeta Roja o Xuper TV pide ese tipo de autorizaciones, puede incorporar funciones ajenas a la transmisión.
El Instituto Nacional de Ciberseguridad de España (Incibe) advierte que muchas aplicaciones maliciosas circulan mediante enlaces directos, repositorios externos y sitios sin controles verificables. Las APK descargadas fuera de las tiendas oficiales pueden ser copias alteradas, programas falsos o archivos con herramientas ocultas.
Los permisos de accesibilidad pueden comprometer el dispositivo
Los permisos de accesibilidad requieren especial atención porque permiten observar lo que aparece en pantalla e interactuar con otras aplicaciones. Un servicio de vídeo no necesita esas capacidades para reproducir un partido.
También resulta prudente evitar extensiones que prometen acceso a contenidos bloqueados. Algunas pueden registrar la navegación, insertar publicidad o redirigir a páginas diseñadas para capturar datos personales.
El problema puede continuar después del pitazo final. Una aplicación instalada desde una fuente desconocida puede mantenerse activa en segundo plano, cambiar configuraciones, abrir ventanas emergentes o llevar al usuario a otros sitios sin que lo advierta.
Entre las señales de alerta figuran anuncios persistentes, aplicaciones desconocidas, cambios en la pantalla de inicio, mayor consumo de batería y un descenso en el rendimiento del teléfono o computador. Que una transmisión funcione no significa que el equipo esté protegido.
Una APK fraudulenta puede robar claves y códigos bancarios
Un archivo malicioso puede incorporar un keylogger, un programa que registra las pulsaciones realizadas en el teclado o en la pantalla. Si después se accede al correo electrónico, las redes sociales o la banca digital, contraseñas y credenciales pueden quedar expuestas.
El riesgo aumenta si la aplicación obtiene permiso para leer mensajes SMS. Muchas entidades bancarias envían por esa vía códigos de un solo uso para validar transferencias, recuperar claves o confirmar accesos.
También existe la amenaza del ransomware, un software que cifra fotografías, documentos y otros archivos para exigir un pago. No hay garantía de recuperar la información aunque se entregue dinero.
Tabletas, TV Box y computadores conectados a la misma red doméstica también pueden quedar expuestos. Revisar el origen de cada aplicación y evitar descargas externas reduce riesgos que pueden persistir mucho después de Argentina vs. Costa Rica.

articles.title: Apple to add Face Unlock to iPhone Duo in future software update - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Apple is adding facial unlock for the new iPhone Duo in the next iOS 27.3 update which will use the front-facing camera when the device is in the closed position.
Many iPhone Duo customers were surprised to find out the device did not have Face ID but instead used Touch ID for security.
We know many customers, most coming from a previous iPhone, found it jarring not to have the instant unlock that Face ID provides.
READ TECH GUIDE’S iPHONE DUO REVIEW HERE
Apple has responded to these reactions and decided to remedy the situation with this new facial unlock feature which is only available on the lock screen.
Facial unlock will still require Touch ID to authenticate.
Touch ID will be required again after 45 minutes of inactivity.
The new feature needs to be enabled in the settings under Touch ID and Passcode.
Touch ID will still be required to authorise Apple Pay and access your passwords folder.
Apple has also added Close To Lock feature, which, as its name suggests locks the iPhone Duo when you close it.
Closing the iPhone Duo without this setting just transfer what you’re viewing to the front screen.
This feature can be activated in the Display & Brightness settings.
These features have just been released to developers in the beta for the iOS 27.3 software update.
Customers can expect the update to be available in early December.

articles.title: Plus de 1 000 km d’autonomie à 37 000 € ? Ce SUV BYD n’arrivera pas chez nous de sitôt
articles.text:
La voiture électrique aux 1 000 km d’autonomie ? C’est un fantasme aussi inutile qu’ancien qui deviendra très bientôt réalité. Chez Mercedes, l’EQS peut aujourd’hui parcourir 925 km. Chez Lucid, la Air pousse même le délire à 960 km. De bien jolies valeurs provenant néanmoins de modèles hors de prix. Avec ses 912 km d’autonomie, la BMW i3 joue déjà dans une gamme tarifaire inférieure, sans se montrer encore accessible, entendons-nous.
Et puis, tout le monde ne veut pas faire de compromis sur la praticité. Mauvaise nouvelle, les véhicules précités sont tous des berlines qui ne sont naturellement pas les reines du déménagement. BYD dégaine donc une solution au problème avec le Denza N8, un SUV électrique aussi habitable qu’endurant. Avec 5,15 mètres de long, 1,99 mètre de large et 1,82 mètre de haut, l’engin est capable de tout engloutir, ou presque.
Jusqu’à 1 003 km d’autonomie et une recharge éclair en 9 minutes
Contrairement au N8L rallongé, le N8 se limite à cinq occupants pour privilégier un volume de coffre grimpant à 1 046 litres. Le tout est complété par un rangement avant de 205 litres, ce qui devrait largement suffire pour ranger les câbles de recharge. Côté technique, le N8 s’octroie des batteries de 105,8 et 130,2 kWh offrant entre 800 et 1 003 km d’autonomie sur le cycle CLTC. Les valeurs dépendront largement de la version choisie.
Car le Chinois propose deux variantes en propulsion de 435 et 503 ch, accompagnées d’une déclinaison trimoteur développant en cumulé 1 210 ch, ce qui n’a pas grand sens, nous sommes d’accord. Côté recharge, les batteries équipées de la technologie Blade 2.0 admettent un 10 à 70 % en 5 minutes et un 10 à 97 % en 9 minutes sur une borne appropriée. Vraiment remarquable vu la taille des batteries, et pas illusoire.
Un tarif équivalent à 37 000 €… mais interdit d’Europe
Les premières stations Flash Charging de BYD sont en cours de déploiement en Europe pour fournir une puissance de charge en courant continu DC de 1 500 kW. Vous pourrez alors y brancher votre Denza Z9GT ou votre BYD Atto 8, mais pas ce Denza N8. Et pour cause, il n’est pas vendu chez nous. On se doute bien que le tarif qui équivaut à 37 000 € est surtout destiné aux Chinois…
Frustrant, mais de plus en plus proche de nous, tout de même… L’équipement peut aussi faire jaser, avec un écran tactile de 30 pouces surmonté d’un bandeau numérique de 1,1 mètre de large, des suspensions pneumatiques intelligentes, quatre roues directrices et la conduite autonome God’s Eye 5.0. Une version hybride rechargeable offrant 435 km d’autonomie en mode électrique suivra.
