articles.title: How friends from Coimbatore built GOAT Robotics into an Rs 8 crore business with global reach
articles.text:
How friends from Coimbatore built GOAT Robotics into an Rs 8 crore business with global reach
Starting from a rented 2BHK in Coimbatore, GOAT Robotics grew from Rs 10 lakh in turnover to over Rs 8 crore. Discover how nine engineering graduates pivoted from hotel robots to industrial automation and expanded internationally.
GOAT Robotics, a startup founded by friends who studied B.E. Robotics and Automation Engineering at a private engineering college in Coimbatore, a Tier 2 city, has achieved success by providing robotic services to several countries.
What began with a turnover of just Rs 10 lakh has now grown into a large company that spends Rs 40 lakh every month on salaries alone.
Muthu Vangaliappan, one of the Managing Directors and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of GOAT Robotics, shared the company's success story with us.
The nine founders of GOAT Robotics come from different districts, including Coimbatore, Erode, and Salem. All of them graduated in 2015 with a B.E. in Robotics and Automation Engineering from PSG Engineering College in Coimbatore. After securing jobs through campus placements, they moved to different companies across various states.
“During our college days, the nine of us were a close-knit group. We shared the same dream of studying well and achieving great heights in life. As time passed and we continued working, we began thinking about starting our own business. In 2015, Naveen, Dharmaraj, Mugesh, and I came together to establish a company called Katomaran Technologies Pvt. Ltd.,” said Muthu.
In the initial days, the four friends conducted seminars at colleges and provided robotics-related training to students and aspiring entrepreneurs.
To expand their business, they rented a 2BHK house in Coimbatore in 2018 and formally started operating Katomaran Technologies Pvt. Ltd. This beginning has now grown into a large company generating a turnover of more than Rs 8 crore.
Friends Who Started Their Journey Amid Severe Setbacks
Muthu says they faced several serious challenges and setbacks during the initial stages of their business before recovering.
“While we were providing automation and robotics services to small companies in India, we got an opportunity to work for a few companies in Singapore. We realised that there was always a shortage of around 40% of security personnel there. This led us to start using robotics and automation technology in the security sector.
“We made their work easier and addressed the manpower shortage by introducing various automation technologies, including automated toll gates and cameras, for people traffic, vehicle traffic, utility management, and surveillance. This project gave us good profits and valuable experience.
“We also began introducing robots in hotels. As the years passed, we started thinking about why we couldn't use the same technology in India. With that idea, in 2019, we continuously visited major hotels across India and submitted proposals for using robots,” Muthu shared, recalling the company's early days.
“However, we did not achieve the same level of success that we had experienced in Singapore. This was because the use of robots in India was very limited, and many people were unwilling to adopt them.
“While our business was doing well in Singapore, we faced setbacks when we shifted our focus to India.
Nevertheless, we continued working in hotels, not just with robots but also in areas such as 3D gaming and gaming simulators,” he said.
The Story Behind the Formation of GOAT Robotics
From 2019 to 2022, the team focused extensively on manufacturing specialised robots for hotels. They developed various robots, including room-service robots, hotel room-cleaning robots, bellboy robots, and dispensers, supplying them to five-star and seven-star hotels.
However, during the COVID-19 pandemic, they faced severe difficulties as they stopped receiving orders.
“While our business was progressing this way, five other friends who had studied with us were already running a company called Dotworld Technologies Pvt. Ltd.
“In 2023, their company and ours merged, and we established GOAT Robotics in Coimbatore. GOAT stands for Greatest of All Technologies,” he explained.
“When we started this company, we already had extensive experience in manufacturing, while the new group of friends had significant experience in marketing. Combining the expertise of both teams, we planned to provide automation and robotics-related services to major hotels in India.
“We frequently approached hotels and hospitals, conducted demonstrations, and submitted proposals. That was when we realised an important truth: this business model would work in foreign countries such as Singapore and Malaysia, but it would be difficult in India.
“We realised that we were running fast in the wrong direction. As we reached a point where we risked losing our business, we decided to develop a different category of robotics.”
They first began manufacturing and supplying lifting robots capable of carrying heavy loads. They developed robots for several companies to lift and move heavy objects. Later, they began manufacturing packing robots and providing automation solutions.
“We continued working with small companies through contracts. Within a few months, we received a good response. We then decided to pitch our idea to a major company for the first time.
“We sent our idea to Toyota, and they liked it and signed an agreement with us. Our journey with Toyota began in December 2023,” said Muthu.
From Coimbatore to Serving Countries Across the World
Muthu shared that getting an opportunity to work with a major company like Toyota, despite having started as an ordinary business in Coimbatore, became a major turning point for them.
He continued:
“Although we began our journey with GOAT Robotics in December 2023, we recorded a turnover of just Rs 10 lakh during 2023–2024.
“After that, we recognised our strengths, addressed our weaknesses, and began providing services to companies using various technologies in the robotics and automation sector.”
“During 2024–2025, the GOAT Robotics team began working not only with Toyota but also with several major and multinational companies, including Volvo, Maruti, Suzuki, Pricol, and Timken.
“Our turnover, which was just Rs 10 lakh, increased to Rs 6 crore in 2024–2025.
“Today, we are providing services across several countries, including India, the United States, Australia, Middle Eastern countries, Singapore, and Malaysia,” he said.
“All the members of our team come from middle-class family backgrounds and have faced considerable financial difficulties.
“Therefore, we have started an initiative to make robots accessible not only to large companies but also to small businesses.
“We are manufacturing and supplying robots at affordable prices to entrepreneurs like us,” he added.
From a 2BHK House to a Company Paying Rs 40 Lakh in Monthly Salaries
The company has robots capable of lifting or moving loads weighing 100 kg. It also manufactures robots capable of handling weights ranging from 100 kg to 5,000 kg.
To make robots accessible to ordinary entrepreneurs and micro, small, and medium enterprises, the company manufactures and sells robots priced between Rs 12–13 lakh and Rs 45 lakh, as well as robots valued between Rs 45 lakh and Rs 2 crore.
“Our journey, which began in a simple 2BHK house, has grown to the point where we established our own dedicated 6,000 sq. ft. office in 2024.
“Our company, which started with just nine people in Coimbatore, now employs 77 people.
“We provide opportunities to engineering graduates who are eager to learn and develop their knowledge after completing their education.
“We offer a minimum salary of Rs 30,000. Every month, we spend a total of Rs 40 lakh on salaries alone for the staff and interns working at GOAT Robotics,” Muthu proudly shared, describing the company's growth.
“There are nine of us. This success has been possible because each of us works in teams of two.
“We have divided ourselves into teams based on our experience in manufacturing, communication, service, marketing, and research and development. This division of responsibilities has made it easier for us to achieve success.”
“Every year, the Central Government encourages micro, small, and medium entrepreneurs by presenting awards.
“In 2025, we won the Central Government's Make in India Excellence Award 2025 and received a cash prize of Rs 10 lakh from the government.
“So far in the current financial year alone, we have achieved a turnover of Rs 8 crore.
“Our target is to reach a turnover of Rs 25 crore during this financial year,” he said.
In March 2025, the company raised Rs 2.66 crore (approximately $311K–$320K) in a funding round led by Campus Angels Network, with participation from TiE Coimbatore, NativeLead Angels, Pontaq Ventures, and others.
“Deep Affection Is What Will Make Us Successful”
Muthu also offered some advice to people planning to start a new business and those considering starting a business with partners.
“Those who run businesses with friends or other partners can achieve great success only if they always have deep affection and care for one another.
“When failures occur, they must be willing to make compromises, support one another, face problems positively, and overcome difficult times together. By doing so, they can achieve success more easily.
“Similarly, when starting something worthwhile, we should not wait for the right time. We must understand the risks involved and start the business immediately.
“If we simply watch from the sidelines or hesitate, time will leave us behind, and we may not even be able to begin what we had planned.
“If we lose time, we will neither be able to take risks nor grow,” Muthu Vangaliyappan said, sharing the lessons he had learned from his entrepreneurial journey.

articles.title: No pagó el alquiler casi cuatro años y la casera no reparó las humedades: la Audiencia rebaja la deuda en un tercio
articles.text:
La inquilina había denunciado los problemas de humedad de su vivienda. Sin embargo, sin que la propietaria hubiese subsanado estos problemas, dejó de abonar el alquiler. Finalmente, la dueña le reclamó 31.340,07 euros por las rentas pendientes (de mayo de 2020 a marzo de 2024). En la Audiencia Provincial de Barcelona se ha confirmado el deber de pago de la inquilina. Sin embargo, han rebajado la cuota a pagar en un tercio. La arrendadora también tuvo algunos problemas de incumplimiento.
El contrato se firmó en noviembre de 2017 y duraba tres años. La renta era de 650 euros inicialmente. En el momento de este proceso era de 666,81 euros.
La propietaria (Patrimonis Bersach, S.L.) ha reclamado los impagados y, por su parte, la inquilina pidió 6.000 euros por daños. En primera instancia, el juzgado ha fallado a favor de la empresa. Las costas las pone a cargo de la arrendataria.
Los problemas de humedad eran insuficientes para dejar de pagar toda la renta
Los técnicos han manifestado las deficiencias, aunque hay algunas discrepancias. El perito de la propiedad ha constatado la presencia de hongos en la pared de la fachada. Ha hablado de “ambiente muy cargado”. Además, ha señalado que falta ventilación. La empresa para la que trabaja ha presupuestado la obra por 1.800 euros.
Por otro lado, la arquitecta técnica (que actuó a petición de la inquilina) hizo un análisis visual. Indicó que había filtraciones del baño de arriba. También destacó que existían humedades por condensación (en sala y dormitorio) y concluyó que no estaba en condiciones mínimas de habitabilidad.
La Audiencia ha considerado que no estaba en condiciones de inhabitabilidad. La inquilina siguió viviendo en el piso y, por eso, no puede quedar liberada de su obligación de pagar.
Asimismo, está comprobado que la propietaria tenía la obligación de subsanar los problemas. En la Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos (artículo 21) se establece que corresponderá al arrendador efectuar todas las obras y reparaciones que sean precisas para mantener la vivienda en estado de habitabilidad, excepto aquellas que sean atribuibles al inquilino.
El magistrado que no está de acuerdo propone una indemnización
Roberto García Ceniceros coincide en que debe pagar la inquilina. Sin embargo, no acepta la rebaja. En su voto particular considera que el deber de reparar “no es mesurable”. Es decir, o se cumple o no. Considera que la ley permite resolver el contrato y pedir una indemnización; sin embargo, no debe cambiar el precio.
Propondría mantener los 31.340,07 euros. Asimismo, aceptaría los 6.000 euros de daño moral. Ambos se compensarían. Quedarían en 25.340,07 euros. Señala que la rebaja (de 10.446,69 euros) es superior a la indemnización solicitada.

articles.title: Sauvegarde WhatsApp : tout savoir sur le nouveau cloud Meta — Frandroid
articles.text:
Si votre espace de stockage iCloud ou Google est saturé à cause de WhatsApp, bonne nouvelle, vous n’aurez bientôt plus à confier vos sauvegardes à ces deux géants. Meta est en train de déployer une option de sauvegarde des discussions sur ses serveurs maison, note WABetaInfo.
En plus de permettre de libérer un peu d’espace sur votre cloud de choix, cela devrait aussi faciliter la vie de celles et ceux qui jonglent d’iPhone à Android et inversement. Malheureusement, Meta est un peu pingre sur l’espace de stockage.
Le Black Friday est lancé sur l’univers Apple. Sur Back Market, profitez de promotions sur les iPhone, MacBook, iPad, AirPods et Apple Watch. Chaque appareil est soumis à jusqu’à 100 points de contrôle qualité et est livré avec une garantie de 12 mois. De quoi profiter de performances comparables à celles d’un produit neuf.
2 Go de stockage seulement
Concrètement, un nouveau menu va faire son apparition dans les paramètres de sauvegarde des discussions. Ce dernier vous permettra de choisir votre fournisseur de stockage cloud préféré entre Google, iCloud ou WhatsApp. Le premier choix continuera d’envoyer vos données chez Google ou Apple tandis que le second vous permettra de tout sauvegarder sur le cloud de Meta. De quoi faciliter la migration entre les différents écosystèmes mobiles.
Malheureusement, la version gratuite de WhatsApp n’offre que 2 Go d’espace de stockage. Pas exactement de quoi mettre toutes vos données à l’abri si vous avez plusieurs années d’historique de conversations et autant d’années de photos du petit dernier partagées sur le groupe familial. L’abonnement WhatsApp Plus fait grimper cette limite à 100 Go et, si vous avez besoin de plus, les abonnements Meta One proposent jusqu’à 4 To de stockage en ligne.
Pour ce qui concerne la vie privée, les sauvegardes sur le cloud maison restent bien évidemment chiffrées de bout en bout pour éviter que des personnes indiscrètes chez WhatsApp ne puissent farfouiller dans vos discussions. Cela veut dire qu’il reste obligatoire d’accompagner sa sauvegarde à l’aide d’un mot de passe ou d’une clé d’accès, comme c’est le cas aujourd’hui. Perdre cette méthode d’authentification signifie donc perdre ses données.
Uniquement en bêta pour le moment
La fonctionnalité n’est pour le moment déployée que sur les versions bêta de WhatsApp sur Android. Cependant, les conseils d’utilisation du cloud WhatsApp étant déjà disponibles sur le site web de l’entreprise, il y a fort à parier que l’option devrait débouler chez tous les utilisateurs et utilisatrices du service très bientôt.
    Pour aller plus loin
WhatsApp : comment désactiver la sauvegarde automatique des photos ?
            
En attendant, si vous souhaitez faire une sauvegarde locale de vos discussions WhatsApp, c’est également possible. Renseignez un compte Google, passez l’option de sauvegarde automatique sur « Jamais », puis cliquez sur « Sauvegarder ». Le dossier com.whatsapp au sein de votre téléphone gardera une trace de vos discussions, prête à être restaurée.
Votre café et votre dose de tech vous attendent sur WhatsApp chaque matin avec Frandroid.

articles.title: Why BitLipa thinks fragmentation hurts stablecoins
articles.text:
Stablecoins—blockchain-based digital tokens pegged to fiat currencies—have made it possible to move dollar-denominated value across borders in seconds, offering businesses an alternative to international bank transfers that can take days. Yet, moving a digital dollar between wallets is not the same as delivering money to someone who needs it in their local currency.
That distinction is becoming increasingly critical as payment companies turn to stablecoins to settle international transactions.
A business moving money from Kenya to South Africa can convert Kenyan shillings into USDT—the dollar-backed stablecoin—transfer the tokens across a blockchain, and convert them into South African rand. The blockchain transfer may take seconds, but the transaction still depends on finding counterparties willing to buy the shillings, supply the stablecoins, and provide enough rand to complete the payout.
Your money crossed the blockchain. Why hasn’t it arrived?
Follow a payment from Kenya to South Africa. Watch where the money moves—and what happens when the destination runs out of local-currency liquidity.
No actual funds are transferred.
Tap to remove or restore liquidity.
Your payment begins in Kenya
You fund the transaction in Kenyan shillings. The payment provider must collect the funds before arranging the cross-border transfer.
A liquidity provider converts the money
A provider supplies the stablecoins needed for the cross-border leg. A blockchain cannot create a missing buyer or seller of local currency.
USDT crosses the blockchain
The digital-dollar transfer may settle in seconds. But a successful blockchain transfer is not the same as a successful local-currency payout.
The payment needs South African rand
A local provider must have enough rand available to fund the payout. With destination liquidity available, the payment can continue.
Payment blocked: no rand liquidity
The USDT transfer succeeded, but the recipient cannot be paid through this route because the destination provider has no usable rand. Restore liquidity to continue.
The recipient gets paid
When destination liquidity is available, the recipient can be credited. Institutions may still need to settle and reconcile their balances afterwards.
Illustrative simulation, not a live payment or exchange-rate quote. Actual routes depend on payment providers, counterparties, currency availability, compliance and settlement arrangements.
In markets where those counterparties are scarce, the transaction can remain expensive or difficult to complete, regardless of how quickly the stablecoins move.
This exposes the core limitation of stablecoins as cross-border payment infrastructure. While they can reduce the time and cost of transferring value between financial institutions, they do not automatically resolve liquidity shortages, disconnected payment networks, or regulatory barriers that make cross-border transfers complex.
The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) reached a similar conclusion in its 2026 Annual Economic Report, finding that stablecoin payments perform unevenly once currency conversion spreads and the costs of entering and exiting digital assets are included.
Where the payment breaks
Apollo Eric, the chief executive officer and founder of BitLipa, a Kenyan payment infrastructure company, has encountered this problem while building a business that connects local payment providers through stablecoin settlement.
Founded in 2019, BitLipa initially operated a peer-to-peer (P2P) crypto remittance platform before pivoting to infrastructure for businesses. It now connects payment companies, banks, mobile money operators (MMOs), and liquidity providers to facilitate collections, payouts, and cross-border settlement.
According to Eric, the company processes roughly $100 million a month. Around 70% of its transaction volume involves mobile money collections, with payouts accounting for the remaining 30%.
The more revealing aspect of its operation is what happens between collection and settlement.
When a business needs to move money from Kenya to South Africa, BitLipa’s system identifies available liquidity providers, compares their rates, and selects a route to convert and deliver the funds. The recipient can be paid before the underlying balances between the institutions are fully settled, Eric told TechCabal in an interview.
He noted that actual settlement and reconciliation can take a further one to two days. That creates two distinct measures of payment speed: the time required to credit a recipient, and the time required to settle obligations between the institutions involved.
Stablecoins can accelerate the latter process where both parties hold sufficient digital assets. However, when a transaction begins and ends in local currencies, access to domestic liquidity remains essential.
This friction is particularly pronounced in less liquid African markets.
Eric said Burundi, Malawi, Mozambique, Ethiopia, and several Central and North African markets remain difficult corridors for sourcing liquidity, despite stablecoins’ promise of rapid transfers. In Burundi, for example, the core challenge is finding buyers for Burundian francs.
A payment company holding francs cannot necessarily convert them into dollars or stablecoins at a competitive rate. While there may be strong demand to send money into Burundi, there is often insufficient demand for flows in the opposite direction.
This imbalance makes liquidity expensive to provide. Companies may need to hold local currency balances for longer, commit additional capital, or source counterparties outside their existing networks. The blockchain cannot create the missing buyer.
The fragmentation problem is bigger than blockchains
Stablecoin fragmentation operates at two levels.
The first is technical. Stablecoins circulate across multiple blockchains, including Ethereum, TRON, and Solana. Tokens issued on one network are not automatically transferable to another, even when they represent the same underlying currency. As a result, stablecoins are not technically interchangeable across chains.
Moving value between networks often requires exchanges, bridges, or issuer-supported transfer mechanisms, adding costs and operational risk.
In its 2026 report, the BIS said this is a problem, warning that the expansion of competing blockchain networks can divide liquidity and weaken interoperability.
The second, and potentially more consequential, problem is financial.
A liquidity provider holding USDT in Nigeria cannot necessarily meet demand for local currency in Mozambique. A company with enough stablecoins to settle a transaction may still lack access to the banks, mobile money networks, or local counterparties required to complete the payout.
Consequently, liquidity can be abundant globally yet remain inaccessible within a specific payment corridor.
This helps explain why adding more stablecoin issuers, blockchain networks, and payment companies does not automatically make cross-border payments cheaper. Each additional network may expand access, but it can also create another isolated pool of liquidity that cannot easily be deployed elsewhere.
For businesses, the relevant question is not how much stablecoin liquidity exists globally, but how much can be converted into the required currency, in the required location, when a payment is due.
The correspondent banking dilemma returns
Traditional international payments face a similar constraint. Banks rely on correspondent relationships to access foreign currencies and payment rails in markets where they lack a direct presence. These arrangements often require pre-funded accounts, multiple intermediaries, and additional compliance checks.
That structure can be costly, yet it also provides access to established liquidity networks, credit lines, and clearing systems that allow institutions to manage obligations.
Stablecoin-based payment companies are now building their own versions of these networks.
Rather than relying exclusively on correspondent banks, they connect exchanges, market makers, local payment providers, and businesses holding different currencies. Some providers pre-fund destination accounts to execute payouts immediately and settle the underlying obligations later.
The intermediaries have changed, but the underlying economic requirement has not: an institution or counterparty at the other end must supply the destination currency and bear the cost of holding it.
The traditional banking system has another advantage that is less visible to customers. Banks can reduce the amount of money they need to move by offsetting payments travelling in opposite directions.
Consider two businesses: one needs to send $1 million from Kenya to South Africa, while another needs to send the equivalent of $800,000 in the opposite direction.
If their payment obligations can be matched, only the equivalent of $200,000 needs to be funded externally, ignoring fees and currency movements.
Without that matching, the providers may need liquidity for both transactions.
Stablecoins make it easier to transfer the settlement asset, but they do not automatically create the relationships, liquidity-sharing arrangements, or netting mechanisms needed to reduce the amount of capital committed.
This is why payment orchestration and liquidity management may become more valuable than the stablecoin transfer itself.
The next competition is over liquidity
The challenge for stablecoin payment companies is now shifting from moving tokens to organising fragmented financial markets.
BitLipa’s approach is to connect multiple liquidity providers and payment institutions, allowing its system to compare available rates and identify counterparties capable of completing a transaction.
The company wants to make liquidity sourcing more competitive rather than depend on one provider in each market.
But this model also has limitations. Connecting more providers improves access only when those providers have usable liquidity. It cannot eliminate foreign exchange (FX) restrictions, create demand for an unwanted currency, or remove the capital required to fund one-sided payment corridors.
Traditional finance is also evolving. The BIS’s Project Agorá has tested a shared platform using tokenised commercial bank deposits and central bank reserves, demonstrating that blockchain-related technology can improve cross-border settlement without relying on privately issued stablecoins.
The competition is consequently not simply between stablecoins and banks. It is between different ways of connecting currencies, institutions, and liquidity.
Stablecoins may ultimately become a standard settlement instrument for cross-border payments. But that would not make every payment corridor equally accessible or inexpensive.
The companies best positioned to benefit may be those that can source local currencies, match opposing payment flows, and reliably deliver funds through domestic payment systems.

articles.title: AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
articles.text:
AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
- Date:
- November 14, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Berkeley
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a hidden warning sign in routine heart scans that could predict sudden cardiac death before it strikes. The AI-powered discovery outperformed conventional screening methods, potentially revealing thousands of people at risk of a fatal heart malfunction that doctors might otherwise miss.
- Share:
More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.
Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.
The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.
The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.
AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss
The results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.
Using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.
Importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.
Another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely new type of medical test.
The findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.
"Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," said Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops."
Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict
Sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.
Immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially important.
For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.
Because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.
"One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer said. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late."
The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening
Doctors currently rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.
But obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.
The approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.
At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.
"In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer said. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things."
The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.
How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns
Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.
The researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.
The AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.
This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.
"Good AI starts with good data," said Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a big part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today."
Obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.
"It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer said. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a big return when they get over the finish line."
From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments
The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.
Obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.
Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.
These longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.
For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.
Obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.
Could AI Reveal New Secrets About the Human Heart?
Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.
Rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to new insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.
Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most important contributions to medicine, opening new directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.
"There is also going to be a new way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer said, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening."
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of California - Berkeley. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Ziad Obermeyer, Alexander Schubert, James Ross, Sendhil Mullainathan, Markus Lingman. An ECG biomarker for sudden cardiac death discovered with deep learning. Nature, 2026; 655 (8121): 210 DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10674-6

articles.title: FBI warns of an open-source AI hacking tool that can breach networks in under three hours
articles.text:
What we know so far: The FBI says that hackers are using an AI-driven penetration testing tool called Artex to automate attacks that used to require skilled human operators. The software connects to large language models and handles the scanning, exploitation and lateral movement on its own, and in some cases it has gone from first targeting a system to active compromise "in under three hours."
Artex belongs to a growing category of open-source AI penetration testing platforms. Victims linked to the tool so far include IT management firm ConnectWise and thousands of its customers, security vendor Barracuda, and a group of South Korean financial institutions.
Security teams use this kind of software to probe their own defenses before attackers do the same. The FBI says attackers have taken the same capability and turned it outward against financial services firms, government agencies, technology and defense companies, telecom and internet providers, and law firms.
The tool's design explains much of its appeal. Operators can connect Artex to hosted frontier models from Anthropic and OpenAI, open-source models, or models built outside the US. Once connected, Artex usually begins by scanning a target network quickly for weak spots. It then goes after simple flaws, such as poor protections and exposed or stolen passwords, to get an initial foothold. From there it moves toward databases, mailboxes and other stores of sensitive information.
The FBI describes Artex intrusions as "noisy," meaning they produce large volumes of traffic and data that can set off a victim's defensive alerts. Speed makes up for the noise, though. The tool works faster than most human responders can investigate, so an alert may arrive while the attacker is already spreading through the network.
Artex was first released publicly in July, and the advisory ties it to several campaigns since then. In South Korea, attackers used it against a number of financial institutions, and the breaches were blamed largely on weak security, including missing multi-factor authentication. Personal data belonging to at least 68,000 people was stolen.
The biggest known operation involved ConnectWise. The FBI confirmed Microsoft's earlier finding that hackers used Artex to breach the company and reach the Microsoft 365 cloud environments of at least 2,250 of its customers.
Microsoft has said the attackers are likely Chinese, and they used the tool to steal data from the affected customers. ConnectWise did not respond to a TechCrunch request for comment on the FBI's findings.
Barracuda's breach shows how small the opening can be. The company said financially motivated criminals using Artex found an exposed credential belonging to a third-party service that Barracuda never revoked after it stopped working with that vendor.
With that credential, the attackers reached stores of credentials Barracuda uses to collect data from its customers' systems. The company said its logs were not detailed enough to rule out access, so it decided to "assume the worst" and rotated all of its customer credentials.
Arve Kjoelen, Barracuda's chief information security officer, described what this means for traditional security operations. "Defenders who rely on spotting malicious activity and then responding to it will often arrive after the attacker has finished," he wrote.
A Barracuda spokesperson told TechCrunch that the company "directly notified and advised a minority of XDR customers to revoke and recreate integration credentials." The spokesperson did not say how many customers were affected.
After the attacks, Artex's developer made the software closed source to stop further misuse. The FBI says the change came too late to prevent further misuse. The earlier open-source version is still circulating and remains "widely accessible," so anyone with a copy and access to a capable model can still run it.
The tool's own infrastructure has also proved poorly secured. Last week, researchers found hundreds of Artex systems exposed on the public internet with no password, most likely because of mistakes or misconfiguration. One of them was the system used in the South Korean attacks. Exposed instances like these could let outsiders take over ready-made hacking setups without building their own.
None of the intrusions described so far relied on new exploits. Artex succeeded by finding the same problems attackers have always used, such as missing multi-factor authentication, leaked passwords and credentials left active after a vendor relationship ended. What has changed is that an AI agent can now find and use those weaknesses faster than many defenders can react.

articles.title: Microsoft Releases .NET 11: C# 15 Union Types, Native AOT CLI Host, and CoreCLR by Default in MAUI
articles.text:
Last week, Microsoft released .NET 11, the latest version of its development platform, together with C# 15, F# 11, ASP.NET Core 11, .NET MAUI, and Entity Framework Core 11. The release is a Standard Term Support (STS) version and will be supported for two years.
As stated in the announcement, .NET 10 remains the Long-Term Support option, while .NET 8 and .NET 9 reached end of support on the same day, November 10, 2026. The release coincided with this year's .NET Conf, held from November 10 to 13.
C# 15 is the default language version for projects that target .NET 11. It adds union types, declared with the union keyword, and the compiler checks switch expressions over them for exhaustiveness. Closed hierarchies limit derivation to the declaring assembly.
The language also gains collection expression arguments, extension indexers, and labeled break and continue statements, while the memory safety work stays in preview. F# 11, according to the release, lowers compiler memory use and reduces collection allocations in FSharp.Core.
In the SDK, the CLI now starts through a Native AOT host by default and keeps the MSBuild server warm between invocations. The dotnet test command gains run-level timeouts and failure limits, and container publishing can produce reproducible digests. In the runtime, Runtime Async remains a preview and is turned on with a feature flag.
The JIT removes more bounds checks and improves devirtualization. As described in the documentation, the release also raises the minimum hardware requirements, and the x86/x64 baseline moves to x86-64-v2.
The libraries add Zstandard compression to System.IO.Compression, new Process APIs for running a process and capturing its output, and four in-memory stream adapters. System.Text.Json supports C# unions and JSON Lines output, and LINQ gains a FullJoin operator.
ASP.NET Core 11 adds asynchronous validation and generates OpenAPI 3.2 documents by default, which the release notes list as a breaking change. SignalR can refresh authentication without reconnecting.
Blazor receives a CacheView component for static server-side rendering, client-side validation for static SSR forms, and an opt-in automatic circuit pause for inactive tabs. An experimental package with AI components for Blazor is also available.
.NET MAUI now uses CoreCLR as the default runtime, with Mono still available and Native AOT as an opt-in option. As reported, XAML Incremental Hot Reload is on by default for Debug builds, XAML namespace declarations are implicit, and the Microsoft.Maui.Controls.Compatibility package no longer ships.
Entity Framework Core 11 requires .NET 11. It generates fewer unnecessary joins, translates FullJoin, supports complex types and JSON columns with TPT and TPC inheritance, and adds experimental vector search for SQL Server.
Other changes in this release are the dotnet new mcpserver template, the dotnetup toolchain manager in public preview, .NET Skills for coding agents, opt-in modern visual styles in Windows Forms, and reliability fixes in WPF.
On Reddit, the reaction was mixed. Several developers welcomed union types as a replacement for hand-written result classes, and others said that .NET 11 and .NET 10 share the same end-of-support date.
The most upvoted comments argued that AI coding tools have made new releases feel less exciting. Other users criticized the code fix for non-exhaustive switch expressions and asked for the decimal conversion change to be more visible.
For interested readers, the full release notes and the list of breaking changes are available in the official .NET 11 documentation.

articles.title: Trump minimiza onda de apagões tecnológicos que atingiu EUA
articles.text:
Uma sequência de interrupções em sistemas digitais afetou serviços essenciais nos Estados Unidos nos últimos dias, provocando atrasos em voos, problemas bancários e dificuldades em plataformas de grandes empresas. Mesmo com a chegada dos problemas à Agência de Segurança Nacional (NSA, na sigla em inglês), o presidente Donald Trump minimizou a situação e afirmou que falhas desse tipo são inevitáveis.
“É assim quando você é grande e poderoso, e tem todo o dinheiro. Coisas assim acontecem. Está tudo bem”, declarou Trump a jornalistas nesta terça-feira (17), em Manila (Filipinas), durante conferência da Associação de Nações do Sudeste Asiático (Asean).
A onda de instabilidades começou na quinta-feira (12) e passou por diferentes setores da economia estadunidense. Entre os afetados estão Microsoft, Administração Federal de Aviação (FAA, na sigla em inglês), United Airlines, JPMorgan Chase e Apple.
Na terça-feira, a própria NSA informou que sua rede havia passado por degradação temporária durante manutenção de rotina. Segundo a agência, porém, os recursos considerados essenciais para suas operações continuaram funcionando.
Falhas atingiram voos, bancos e serviços digitais
- Os episódios tiveram consequências em diferentes áreas. Na sexta-feira (13), uma falha nos sistemas de controle de tráfego aéreo levou a FAA a determinar paralisação nacional de voos que durou quatro horas e meia. Foi a interrupção mais longa do transporte aéreo estadunidense desde os atentados de 11 de setembro de 2001;
- Na segunda-feira (16), um problema tecnológico na United Airlines provocou atrasos em cerca de 150 voos. No mesmo dia, uma falha de software no JPMorgan Chase prejudicou o acesso a alguns serviços bancários;
- A Microsoft também enfrentou interrupção que afetou ferramentas como o Outlook e outros serviços de comunicação e trabalho. Já a Apple informou nesta terça-feira que uma atualização interna provocou instabilidades em seus sistemas, incluindo serviços ligados ao iCloud e ao Apple Pay. A companhia afirmou que o episódio não foi causado por ataque cibernético;
- A sequência de problemas chamou a atenção de parlamentares estadunidenses. O senador republicano Josh Hawley, do Missouri, questionou a coincidência entre tantos episódios em intervalo tão curto;
- “Se tudo isso for coincidência, será a maior coincidência da história do mundo”, afirmou.
Governo dos EUA descarta ataque coordenado
Apesar das suspeitas levantadas por alguns políticos, autoridades estadunidenses afirmam não ter encontrado sinais de que as falhas façam parte de ofensiva cibernética coordenada ou de ação patrocinada por algum governo estrangeiro.
O diretor de Inteligência Nacional dos Estados Unidos, Jay Clayton, atribuiu boa parte dos problemas a dificuldades durante atualizações e modernizações de sistemas. Segundo ele, organizações estão implementando melhorias tecnológicas, mas algumas mudanças não estão sendo concluídas como esperado.
Clayton também relacionou a instabilidade na NSA à instalação de correções para vulnerabilidade no PHP. A falha, identificada com auxílio de inteligência artificial (IA) no mês passado, poderia permitir que invasores assumissem o controle de servidores remotamente.
O cenário, portanto, não aponta necessariamente para um ataque em andamento. Ainda assim, a concentração de incidentes em sistemas importantes levantou preocupações sobre a capacidade de infraestrutura digital de suportar atualizações e mudanças sem provocar interrupções em cadeia.
Leia mais:
- Após caos nos aeroportos, meteorologia dos EUA também sofre pane
- Governo Trump avança para barrar novos equipamentos chineses
- China acusa EUA de coerção econômica por chips avançados de IA
Especialistas alertam para fragilidade da infraestrutura digital
A sequência de falhas também reacendeu o debate sobre a dependência entre sistemas tecnológicos. Em conversa com a Reuters, Cynthia Kaiser, ex-integrante de alto escalão da divisão cibernética do FBI e atual vice-presidente sênior do Centro de Pesquisa de Ransomware da Halcyon, disse que os episódios mostram como uma falha técnica ou atualização de software pode se espalhar por serviços conectados.
O contexto é acompanhado por sinais de aumento da atividade cibernética. A seguradora Marsh informou que seus clientes relataram 105 incidentes de segurança nas duas últimas semanas de outubro — mais que o dobro dos 48 registros feitos no mesmo período de maio.
Especialistas também demonstram preocupação com o uso de ferramentas de IA por criminosos para ampliar o número de tentativas de invasão realizadas simultaneamente.
Outro ponto levantado por analistas é o impacto de cortes de funcionários em empresas e órgãos públicos. A FAA passou por reduções de pessoal após o início do governo Trump, enquanto a United Airlines e a Microsoft também anunciaram cortes em suas equipes.
Não há evidências de que as demissões tenham causado as interrupções recentes. Ainda assim, a organizadora trabalhista Liz Fong-Jones argumentou que a redução de equipes experientes pode diminuir as margens de segurança necessárias para manter sistemas complexos funcionando.
O senador democrata Jack Reed também pediu que a Casa Branca apresente explicações sobre os episódios. Com falhas atingindo serviços essenciais em dias consecutivos, a pressão por transparência e por respostas sobre a infraestrutura tecnológica estadunidense tende a aumentar.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Canada’s real-time rail payment system has arrived. Here’s why most consumers will have to wait to use it | BetaKit
articles.text:
Last week, Canada’s finance minister posted a promotional video to his social media demonstrating Canada’s new real-time payment system, the Real-Time Rail (RTR).
In the video, Minister François-Philippe Champagne uses his smartphone to transfer $250 from a Wealthsimple account to a Koho account for Wainwright Tragedy Appeal, a relief effort led by the Canadian Red Cross. The demo shows a Wealthsimple-branded screen offering the option to send up to $100,000 for free, instantly, by inputting the recipient’s direct deposit details. Champagne clicks ‘Send Money’ and gets a Koho notification instantly, saying the money was deposited.
“Starting today, Canadians can send and receive money in seconds. Any hour, any day, all year round,” Champagne says.
Payments Canada says the RTR launch is a “foundational first step,” and that its phased approach will ensure the system is safe and secure.
However, the use case shown in the video is not yet broadly available to Canadians. While RTR officially launched on Nov. 9, not all of the Phase 1 participants are up and running on the new system.
First, take Champagne’s video. While the demo was a “real, live transfer,” a Wealthsimple spokesperson told BetaKit that type of transfer is currently being beta-tested with Wealthsimple employees, with plans to launch to the broader public in 2027. In an email, Koho said the RTR functionality is not yet widely available to customers because the team is still finalizing testing.
Koho and Wealthsimple (whose vice-president of payments strategy and chief compliance officer, Hanna Zaidi, sits on BetaKit’s board of directors) are not the only companies with users who will have to wait a little longer before getting to properly use RTR, a federal project that for years has held the promise of modernized payments and improved competition. The two are part of a broader list of eight participants in RTR’s first phase, alongside Questrade, DoBusiness.com, Paramount Commerce, Bank of America, Peoples Trust Company, and Digital Commerce Bank. In addition to bringing more of Canada’s financial institutions on board, there’s still work to be done for companies building payment services on top of the new infrastructure.
Questbank, for example, is the banking entity of Questrade Financial Group, which has not yet officially launched. In an email to BetaKit, a Questrade spokesperson said it will share details close to the launch of its consumer banking products.
Peoples Trust Company is participating as a settlement agent (helping settle transactions for entities without a direct settlement account) and said in an email it looked forward to “direct participation” in future phases. Paramount Commerce (which has agreed to be acquired by US company Shift4) said it is actively making real-time payouts with RTR, and Digital Commerce Bank said it was already receiving and sending funds via the payment rail. DoBusiness.com has not responded to a request for comment.
Payments Canada, the non-profit organization responsible for delivering Canada’s payments infrastructure, says the launch is a “foundational first step,” and that its phased approach will ensure the system is safe and secure. It added that since RTR is a payment infrastructure, not a consumer-facing app, “individual financial institutions manage their own customer product timelines and rollouts.”
The Department of Finance has not yet responded to BetaKit’s request for comment.
What is RTR?
The RTR system is an instant, always-on payment infrastructure for Canadians and their financial institutions to transfer funds. It first began development as a payments modernization project in 2015, with a target launch of 2019. Since then, it has been fraught with delays: Payments Canada pushed back the rollout to 2022, then later rescheduled it for mid-2023, and again to 2026, when it finally launched on Nov. 9 with eight initial participants. Notably, the system is meant to allow emergent financial companies to move money for customers without relying on banks or paying them a fee.
In Canada, existing payment infrastructure is limited by speed and transfer size. RTR is meant to support bigger transactions and settle them instantly. When making payments, Canadians typically see money leave their accounts right away, but transactions are actually settled within hours or days, which is why it can take up to three business days for a credit card payment to post.
Since Champagne’s video was posted, many social media users have expressed confusion about how the RTR differs from existing payment systems, like Interac e-Transfer.
While the video depicts a similar system, RTR is different from e-Transfer because it is an infrastructure rail that products and services can be built on. Interac is a delivery partner for RTR, whose backend infrastructure will start clearing and settling Interac’s e-Transfers over its next phases. While Interac’s e-Transfer system is faster than those traditional payment rails, it typically limits consumer transfers to $3,000, and businesses to $25,000, while RTR limits are at $100,000.
“I think the most visible advantages, perhaps, lie more in the small business segment,” Fintechs Canada executive director Adriana Vega told BetaKit last week. “That’s a segment that is super challenged with delayed payments due to batch settlement.”
Right now, only select financial institutions have direct access to Canada’s payment rails, which collectively support 99 percent of daily transactions. This includes Peoples Trust Company, which is the only settlement agent in the first cohort of RTR participants. To send and receive payments via RTR, both parties will need to be onboarded to the new system. That’s why Champagne could use Wealthsimple as the sender and Koho as the recipient in his video demo.
None of Canada’s Big Six banks are participating in this first phase, as BetaKit had previously reported, and some in the industry have criticized the lack of participation, given that these financial institutions process the vast majority of payments in Canada.
Daniel Eberhard, CEO of Koho, told BetaKit last month that a real-time system without widespread adoption would be “performative,” while Vega argued that RTR needs banks’ participation to be a success. Payments Canada has said that all major Canadian financial institutions will join in the coming months, making the RTR available to more than nine in 10 Canadians within its first year.
Despite arriving later than that of other G7 countries, Canada’s RTR was the first to launch with anti-fraud mechanisms built in. With faster payment settlement, that also means funds transferred for nefarious reasons are more difficult to claw back from fraudsters. Interac, which is the exchange solution provider for RTR, has created a central fraud scoring system and a way to confirm that funds are being routed to the correct account.
With files from Alex Riehl.
Feature image courtesy Payments Canada via YouTube.

articles.title: Así era 'Avengers: The Kang Dynasty', según Kevin Feige: un gran plotwist y su conexión con el Doctor Doom
articles.text:
A falta de un mes para el estreno de Avengers: Doomsday, el jefe máximo de Marvel, Kevin Feige, ha desvelado cuáles eran los planes originales para la quinta entrega de los Vengadores. Hace unos años, el filme iba a titularse Avengers: The Kang Dynasty. Pero todo cambió con el despido de Jonathan Majors, actor de Kang el Conquistador, tras ser declarado culpable de malos tratos a su pareja.
Durante todo este tiempo, los fans siempre han asumido que aquel hecho llevó a Marvel a tener que cambiar de planes y buscar un nuevo villano. Por eso, finalmente se decantaron por el Doctor Doom, para el que trajeron de regreso a Robert Downey Jr. Sin embargo, Kevin Feige ha confesado que no fue exactamente así como sucedió todo. Y es que, al parecer, en Marvel ya estaban maquinando cambios para Avengers: The Kang Dynasty.
"Era una situación muy delicada. No queríamos precipitarnos y tomar decisiones imprudentes en materia de empleo. La gente cree que hubo una relación de causa y efecto con los problemas de Jonathan, y es cierto que eso aceleró algunas cosas. Pero el desastre ya estaba muy avanzado antes de eso", explica el CEO de Marvel en una entrevista a Empire.
"Quantumania no tuvo la acogida que nos hubiera gustado. Hay muchos aspectos de la película de los que estamos orgullosos, y el desempeño de Kang es uno de ellos. Pero ya en aquel momento estábamos haciendo cambios [en The Kang Dynasty]", asegura entonces. "Probablemente se habría seguido llamando Avengers: The Kang Dynasty, pero habría servido como introducción para el Doctor Doom a mitad de esa película", revela.
El Doctor Doom era el villano secreto de Avengers: The Kang Dynasty
Es decir, los últimos planes de Marvel para Avengers: The Kang Dynasty pasaban por presentar un gran plotwist con su villano. En lugar de convertir a Kang en el principal enemigo, a mitad de película se revelaría que, en realidad, el Doctor Doom estaba detrás de todo. El Conquistador solo sería un personaje presentado para despistar y sorprender con el gran secreto. O, al menos, eso es lo que promete Feige, pues sus declaraciones parecen cuanto menos oportunistas.
Sea como sea, lo cierto es que Kang ya no está en el Universo Marvel. Ahora, el Doctor Doom ya ha tomado las riendas como el villano principal de la Saga del Multiverso. Y aunque de una manera rápida y apresurada, lo cierto es que en la compañía no lo están haciendo mal para convertirle en una amenaza a la que temer. Muy pronto podremos ver todo su poder en Avengers: Doomsday, que se estrena en cines el 18 de diciembre.

articles.title: MSP ScreenConnect Servers Targeted in Month-Long Campaign
articles.text:
Dozens of MSP ScreenConnect servers have been targeted in a month-long campaign exploiting a vulnerability patched in September, cybersecurity firm Huntress reports.
The attacks, ongoing since at least October 20, aim to exploit CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS score of 9.9), a critical missing authorization and improper privilege management bug that allows for files to be transmitted and executed during a connection without authorization or confirmation.
ConnectWise patched the security defect on September 8, and CISA added it to the KEV catalog on September 11. Huntress warned at the time that exploitation started on August 20.
Now, the cybersecurity firm says a new wave of attacks is targeting ScreenConnect instances, with a focus on managed service provider (MSP) servers.
The hackers exploit CVE-2026-84869 via requests to run a guest-pushed batch file that connects to a Telegram bot and installs a rogue ScreenConnect client.
“Attackers appear to be spraying servers blindly: Since October 20, we’ve seen at least 688,000 guest ‘run file’ requests for update*.bat hit 42 MSP ScreenConnect servers from 29 IP addresses, waiting for any technician to join,” Huntress says.
According to the cybersecurity firm, the activity is different from the recently observed campaigns targeting ScreenConnect instances with the SCKit malware toolkit and with unauthorized sessions from machines posing as crypto exchanges.
The exploitation of CVE-2026-84869, it explains, allows attackers to push malicious files to technicians’ machines and get their own clients to execute them when the technician joins the session. The technician sees no prompt when the files are executed.
“An MSP technician’s workstation typically holds RMM consoles, saved credentials, and access to every customer, making it an exceptionally attractive target. When a technician joins a remote session, their ScreenConnect host client and the guest machine can exchange files,” Huntress notes.
In one attack, a rogue ScreenConnect client disguised as Windows Update was installed and spawned within nine seconds of the host client running the guest-pushed bat file.
As part of another, the guest machine pushed a text file two seconds after the technician joined the session, and the technician’s client ran the file three seconds later.
In October, a targeted attack hit an MSP server: the attacker joined as a guest in three real sessions the technician had created and asked the client to execute a file designed to drop a script into the technician’s computer’s Startup folder.
Organizations should update technicians’ ScreenConnect host clients to version 26.6.5 or later, along with all the Access agents ConnectWise lists.

articles.title: Proton's Lumo, a privacy-focused alternative to ChatGPT and Claude, arrives on desktop | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Proton, the privacy-focused tech company offering alternatives to Google’s and Microsoft’s tools for email, productivity apps, password management, cloud storage, and more, is now bringing its AI app Lumo to personal computers. On Tuesday, the company launched Lumo Desktop for Windows, macOS, and Linux, allowing users to leverage its AI to carry out local tasks on their computer involving connected apps, personal files, and other automations.
The app is designed to offer users more control over their personal data, as consumer AI technology becomes focused more on AI agents that can perform tasks on users’ behalf, rather than just answering questions.
Already, the major model makers, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and others, offer desktop tools for working with their AI technologies, but doing so invites increased risk to users’ personal data. Only this week, for instance, Apple announced it was addressing those privacy concerns with tightened security settings for apps that request Full Disk Access, as the AI desktop apps do.
Proton’s idea is to offer a set of tools that let its AI access connected apps, files, and folders and automate tasks, but with more personalization over how much access the AI has. The company says users can choose which actions the AI agent takes that will need to request their approval, and it vows that the conversations and information from connected apps and files are never used to serve personalized ads or train AI models.
The new app includes a variety of connectors that support local tools, like file-system access, shell execution, and browser content fetching, as well as Proton’s email app and other third-party services, including Confluence, Dropbox, and Jira.
The connectors also support local and remote MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers, which AI agents use to access external data sources.
Proton says that users can decide for each connector which actions Lumo can perform automatically, which require approval, and which are blocked entirely. Users can also turn individual tools off from the Tools menu in their conversation.
In addition, users can set up their own scheduled tasks, where each has its own set of permissions, in terms of what can be handled automatically and what requires approval.
Proton notes that it uses encryption to ensure that only users can read their chat history, not the company. The company also says it keeps no server-side logs, and the limited data it does store is protected under Swiss privacy law. The data is hosted on European infrastructure, outside the scope of the U.S. CLOUD Act, which specifies how law enforcement agencies access data held by cloud service providers.
The company says it’s investing in its infrastructure, with its first Nvidia B300 cluster built on Open Compute Project (OCP) standards now going live in Switzerland.
Similar to other AI apps, Lumo’s desktop app supports Skills, which lets users save instructions, templates, and reference files that Lumo can reuse across their conversations. (An earlier version of this, Custom Lumos, will now be migrated to the Skills format.)

articles.title: With $5M in funding, Pretxt launches runtime oversight layer to supervise AI agents in real time - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
With $5M in funding, Pretxt launches runtime oversight layer to supervise AI agents in real time
Artificial intelligence supervision pioneer Pretxt AI is launching with $5 million in seed funding today as it tries to contain the very real risk of unleashing autonomous agents in production environments.
It has created a new kind of “AI Supervision” tool that applies oversight at runtime to ensure those agents follow a company’s rules at all times. Today’s round was led by Deciens Capital and saw participation from Howdy Partners, Service Provider Capital and NSV Wolf Capital.
The startup is pitching the idea of a continuous runtime supervision layer that monitors AI agents as they’re getting work done, contrasting their behavior with the parent organization’s rules and policies. If it spots an agent is starting to drift off-course, it will immediately intervene to put it back on the right track, before it can make a critical mistake that hurts the business.
Real-time guardrails like Pretxt has designed are likely going to become a priority for enterprises as they begin to trust AI agents with more consequential work than simply drafting emails or creating images. For instance, if agents are to be trusted with handling customer refunds and accessing mission-critical databases and modifying records within them, companies will need the strongest reassurance that they’re not going to mess up those tasks.
But those assurances are few and far between. AI is notorious for “hallucinating” responses when it doesn’t know the answer to a question, and autonomous agents have shown erratic behavior time and again. They don’t need a malicious prompt injection to start missing critical required steps in a workflow or invent policy exceptions to simplify a task they’re trying to complete. They’ve shown they can do this in both labs and in the real world.
In response, most security tools take a heavy-handed approach, blocking agents outright, but this means that work slows down. The other approach is to flag errors after the fact, but by the time that happens they could have already caused massive damage.
Pretxt’s co-founders Brian Soby (pictured, left) and Aaron Costello (right) realized that companies need a more balanced approach to agentic security and oversight. Soby, who serves as the startup’s chief executive, previously held senior security roles at Salesforce Inc. and Mitre Inc. before founding the software-as-a-service security startup AppOmni Inc.
It was there that he met Costello, who now serves as Pretxt’s chief technology officer. During their time at AppOmni, they uncovered several major vulnerabilities in AI agents developed by Salesforce and ServiceNow Inc. and began to understand what’s required to ensure those agents can still work safely.
Supervision at runtime
Many traditional agent monitoring tools use a second large language model as a “judge” to monitor the behavior of the main LLM that’s doing the work. But Pretxt’s co-founders shunned this idea because it creates latency, increases compute costs and involves too much guesswork.
Instead, their AI Supervision platform is powered by a near-deterministic engine that evaluates agent’s actions in milliseconds in order to spot those that break the rules and intercept them in progress. The company reckons it can do this up to 60 times faster than LLM-as-a-Judge-based security tools.
The approach is effective. In tests on Zapier’s AutomationBench, Pretext was able to reduce agent policy violations from around one in five to zero. The tool is designed to be easy to implement, so teams don’t need a thorough understanding of the models or agents they’re trying to supervise.
Instead, they simply choose which policies, standards and guardrails should apply to an agent, and then they can keep track of them in real time. The platform allows users to track approvals, roll back plan versions and escalate any tricky edge cases to human decision-makers.
That last capability is especially useful, because many organizations’ security plans have gaps when agents encounter situations that were not previously envisaged. In such cases, Pretxt halts the agent and asks a human to decide what the rules should be.
“Supervising an AI agent shouldn’t mean becoming an expert in everything it touches or in how it’s built,” Costello said. “Teams tell us in plain language how it should behave and where the boundaries are, and we supervise and steer the agent to stay within them. So there’s no untangling permissions or digging into the agent’s internals.”
Pretxt’s AI Supervision tool is available in early access now. It’s primarily targeting high-stakes regulated industries where mistakes and hallucinations simply cannot be tolerated.
For financial services and insurance companies, it can enforce borrower verification rules and route complex claims to humans, while in healthcare and life sciences it ensures that agents don’t step outside of strict boundaries. In customer support applications, it can prevent agents from offering unapproved discounts or refunds to customers.
AI Supervision can provide a lot of different benefits to a lot of different people. Chief information officers and other senior executives will be able to scale higher-value AI projects safely, while security teams, compliance officers and platform engineers can address gaps in risk management and ensure low-latency policy enforcement without needing to stack additional models.
Enterprise Management Associates analyst Chris Steffen said the thing that really sets Pretxt apart is its focus on the basics. Not only does it check that agents are behaving themselves, but it also makes sure they’re doing the work they’ve been assigned without breaking any rules or cutting any corners, creating what is effectively a new category of AI supervision tool.
“Most tools ask if an agent is secure, compliant or observable, but far fewer can show if the agent is correctly doing the job it was given,” Steffen said. “Most tools can only report what went wrong after the fact, when it’s too late. Pretxt intervenes while the outcome can still change to get agents back on track.”
