articles.title: Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
articles.text:
At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.
According to a blog post from the security firm Report URI, on November 16 malicious JavaScript code was served to visitors of 178 organizations through Optimizely’s platform. Report URI researcher Scott Helme wrote that the payload delivered by the malicious Javascript was rebuilt 26 times during the day, dropping a multi-purpose malware kit that could steal payment card data, cookies and screenshots, and swap any cryptocurrency payment addresses for the attacker’s.
Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “DarkSword” and “Coruna,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data.
“The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote. “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”
Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”
“We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.”
Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content.
One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files.
Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds. Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.
“So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.”
Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “Content Security Policies” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons.
“With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.”
How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload.
The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja, which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records.
Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West.
“Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.”
Internet users can control the JavaScript elements allowed to run on webpages by using simple script-blocking plugins like NoScript. But these tools have always only been effective for diehard security and privacy nerds who are willing to put up with sifting through dozens of JavaScript requests on each new website.
Happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end users was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker is your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You?

articles.title: Half of businesses run workloads in the wrong place — mainly because they can't be bothered to change their ways
articles.text:
Half of businesses run workloads in the wrong place — mainly because they can't be bothered to change their ways
Changing cloud is just too complex
- Unsuitable cloud infrastructure is adding latency and reducing performance
- Enterprises worry they'd have to re-architecture applications just to move
- IT leaders admit they'd like to move, but they just can't handle the complexity
We're already familiar with lifting workloads out of certain environments in favor of digital sovereignty, but new Akamai research has revealed that half of enterprises are running workloads in suboptimal cloud locations despite knowing that alternatives offer better performance or cost.
The report notes that traditional cloud architecture is starting to struggle with modern applications, including real-time APIs, AI and more.
In fact, four in five (82%) enterprises are now missing response time targets for business-critical interactive workloads – but they might be reluctant to change just out of pure simplicity.
Enterprises don't want the hassle of moving cloud providers
Akamai found that storing and processing data in different geographic locations (41%) and longer-than-ideal physical distances between end users and compute (38%) are to blame for these response time issues. But for many, accepting these trade-offs might be more acceptable than migrating workloads to an entirely new cloud vendor.
"As real-time interactions, conversational AI, and microservices become standard, running compute far from where data lives creates delays and inefficiencies that organizations can no longer sustain," Akamai Cloud Product Marketing VP Ari Weil explained.
Four in five (79%) worry doing this could take days, or more, but it's the investments into building applications around the current cloud provider that could be the biggest headache. Two in five (38%) say workloads would need to be re-architected before they can be relocated, with 8% worried they wouldn't even be able to move workloads at all once they've been deployed.
Half of the enterprises Akamai surveyed admitted they've left workloads in non-ideal geographic locations just because relocating them would be too expensive, complicated or disruptive. But if it were easier, three-quarters of IT leaders say they'd deploy compute resources to more geographic locations to reduce latency, improve performance and expand into new markets.

Akamai can't exactly urge enterprises to consider alternative cloud vendors and infrastructure given the circumstances, but the report certainly highlights how interconnected and dependent our tech stacks have become.

articles.title: Beste GTA-6-Alternativen: 7 Spiele für die Wartezeit
articles.text:
Warten auf GTA 6: Diese 7 Games sind das perfekte Vorprogramm
Wenn Grand Theft Auto 6 am 19. November erscheint, dürfte es wieder einige Maßstäbe setzen, wie auch schon die vorherigen Teile der Reihe. Eine gigantische Open World, lebendige NPCs – und Verkaufszahlen, von denen andere Hersteller nur träumen können. Der Hype um dieses Spiel scheint derzeit keine Grenzen zu kennen.
Die einen wollen vielleicht die Zeit bis zum Release verkürzen. Andere haben weder eine Playstation 5, noch eine Xbox Series – oder gar keine Lust auf GTA 6. Ob es nun eine interessante Open World ist, oder eine Atmosphäre und Thematik, die an Grand Theft Auto erinnern: diese sieben Spiele können als Vorbereitung auf GTA 6 dienen – oder eine gute Alternative sein.
Cyberpunk 2077 für PC, Playstation 5, Xbox Series und Nintendo Switch 2
Cyberpunk 2077 ist freilich die offensichtlichste Alternative zu Grand Theft Auto 6. Night City ist eine lebendige Open World, in der ihr mit lautem Motor durch den dichten Stadtverkehr rasen könnt und euch packende Verfolgungsjagden mit der Polizei liefert, während im Radio treibende Musik läuft. Das dürfte jedem GTA-Fan recht bekannt vorkommen. Dabei ist Cyberpunk 2077 aber kein billiger Abklatsch, sondern erzählt seine eigene, durchaus interessante Geschichte über skrupellose Unternehmen und eine Menschheit, die ihr Heil in Technologie sucht.
Schedule 1 für PC
In Schedule 1 übernehmt ihr das Management eines illegalen Drogennetzwerks. Ihr beschafft und synthetisiert Substanzen und arbeitet daran, diskrete Vertriebswege aufzubauen und das eingenommene Geld möglichst effektiv zu waschen. Neben dem reinen Ressourcen- und Zeitmanagement müsst ihr aber auch Patrouillen der Polizei umgehen, Bestechungsgelder aushandeln und euer Territorium gegen rivalisierende Dealer absichern. Ein gutes Spiel für alle, die das Verbrechen nicht nur als Kulisse, sondern als kleinteiliges und oft wenig glamouröses Geschäft erleben wollen.
Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth für PC, Playstation 4/5 und Xbox Series
Wer eine Atmosphäre sucht, die der sonnendurchfluteten Spielwelt von GTA 6 ähnelt (der fiktive Bundesstaat Leonida ist an Florida angelehnt), kann mit Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth nach Hawaii reisen. In den insgesamt drei Städten der Open World könnte man ein vergnügliches Urlaubserlebnis haben – wenn da nicht die rivalisierenden Gangs und brutalen Syndikate wären, die die Insel unter sich aufteilen wollen. Gekämpft wird hier aber nicht, wie in GTA 6, in Echtzeit, sondern in rundenbasierten Keilereien. Das gibt dem Game einen eigenen Spielfluss, der auch durch zahllose abgedrehte Minispiele aufgelockert wird.
Mafia: Definitive Edition für PC, Playstation 4/5 und Xbox Series
Wer in GTA vor allem Verfolgungsjagden, Verrat und Gangster-Geschichten liebt, dürfte in Mafia: Definitive Edition eine gute Alternative finden. Das Remake des 2002 veröffentlichten Spiels versetzt euch in die fiktive US-Großstadt Lost Heaven der 1930er-Jahre. Ihr übernehmt die Rolle von Tommy Angelos, der in seinem Clan bis ganz an die Spitze aufsteigen möchte. In Mafia: Definitive Edition steht weniger die Open World im Mittelpunkt, sondern die eher lineare Geschichte, die Einblick gibt in die Schattenseiten des organisierten Verbrechens.
Silver Pines für PC, Playstation 5, Xbox Series und Nintendo Switch 2
Silver Pines ist mehr Horror- als Actionspiel, liefert aber eine dichte Atmosphäre und eine interessante Kriminalgeschichte. Als Privatdetektiv Red Walker verschlägt es euch in eine verlassene US-Kleinstadt, um das Verschwinden des Musikers Eddie Velvet aufzuklären. Die Stadt erinnert dabei mit ihrer Film-Noir-Optik an die Serie Twin Peaks. Ihr erkundet Tatorte, sammelt Hinweise und verknüpft Indizien, um dem Verbrechen auf die Spur zu kommen. In Multiple-Choice-Gesprächen gilt es, Widersprüche bei Verdächtigen aufzudecken und moralisch heikle Entscheidungen zu treffen. Dabei sticht, ähnlich wie in GTA, der Soundtrack besonders hervor. Der changiert zwischen Jazz, Synthesizer-Klängen und treibenden Percussions und bleibt auch noch nach dem Spielen im Kopf.
Watch Dogs: Legion für PC, Playstation 4/5 und Xbox Series
Das dystopische, verregnete London von Watch Dogs: Legion fängt das Gefühl einer Metropole in der nicht allzu fernen Zukunft ziemlich gut ein. An jeder Ecke Überwachungskameras, während eine Drohne nach der anderen über die Köpfe der Bevölkerung fliegt. Also ist es besser, nicht erkannt zu werden. In Watch Dogs: Legion steuert ihr daher nicht nur eine Spielfigur, sondern wechselt ständig zwischen verschiedenen Personen – vom klischeehaften Gangster bis zur unauffällig wirkenden Oma. Mit diesen Figuren und allerlei Hacking-Equipment lehnt ihr euch gegen die autoritäre Staatsgewalt auf und erkundet dabei eine lebendige und detailreiche Open World.
As Dusk Falls für PC, Playstation 4/5 und Xbox Series
As Dusk Falls hat spielerisch zwar nichts mit GTA 6 gemein, erzählt aber auch eine Geschichte um Gewalt und Kriminalität. Es geht um die Geschichte zweier Familien, deren Schicksale im Jahr 1998 nach einem gescheiterten Raubüberfall und einer Geiselnahme untrennbar miteinander verknüpft werden. In As Dusk Falls steuert ihr die Spielfigur dabei nicht direkt durch eine 3D-Welt, sondern lenkt vielmehr den Handlungsverlauf eines interaktiven Dramas. Das Gameplay beschränkt sich im Wesentlichen auf zwei Mechaniken: Ihr trefft Dialog- und Gewissensentscheidungen unter Zeitdruck und absolviert Quick-Time-Events in zunehmend brenzligen Situationen. Dabei bestimmen eure Eingaben unmittelbar das Schicksal der Beteiligten und den weiteren Verlauf der Erzählung.

articles.title: Nvidia says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
articles.text:
Starting Nvidia’s quarterly earnings call on Tuesday, new board chair Harvey Jones said that when former CEO Jensen Huang resigned, “the Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”
Nvidia says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
The board said it would not take additional questions on the call about Huang’s departure.
Jones added, “We will not be addressing or taking questions on today’s call regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation and the ongoing investigation.”
Huang had publicly floated the idea of returning earlier on Tuesday. In a statement posted to X, he wrote that he “did not live up to the standards expected of everyone” at the company, that he regretted his mistakes, and that he would cooperate with the Nvidia board’s investigation into his actions. He added that he’d be willing to return to the chief executive role if offered it, though a day earlier, the Nvidia board reportedly said it was not considering bringing him back. “NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company,” Huang wrote. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
But since his November 12th resignation, Huang remains entangled in scandal. He’s reportedly had three affairs, two with subordinates at Nvidia, one with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset suspected of facilitating illicit chip sales. (Huang has pushed against restrictions on Nvidia chip sales in China.) He’s scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1st, and an internal company investigation is ongoing.
Tech industry heavyweights have still voiced their support for Huang, dubbing him “irreplaceable” and petitioning for his return. Some have cast doubt on the allegations that Alice Huang (no relation) was spying on behalf of China and painted the leaks about their relationship as a conspiracy against the former CEO. President Donald Trump, a close ally of Huang for much of the past year, has also backed him. On Monday, Trump said he “would not mind” Huang returning, adding that “I think he learned a big lesson — I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another.”
Trump’s closeness with Huang could also complicate things for Nvidia, however. The company has ramped up its lobbying in Washington, D.C., spending $5 million in 2025 and $4.7 million so far in 2026. But as Democrats prepare to take Congress, they’re planning to investigate Trump’s dealings with Big Tech and other industries, alleging potential corruption. “The election wasn’t very positive for AI, and [the news around Huang’s resignation] is only going to complicate things, especially for the company in particular but for AI as a whole going forward,” Brendan Glavin, director of insights at OpenSecrets, told The Verge in an interview last week.
Lior Prosor, managing partner at Deep33, a tech VC firm, said last week that he didn’t expect Huang’s resignation to pop the AI bubble, although Huang has had a significant hand in mobilizing funds for the AI infrastructure buildout in the U.S. Under Huang’s leadership in August, Nvidia entered into partnerships with six financial institutions for about $500 billion to fund such endeavors. “NVIDIA supplies roughly 75 percent of the AI compute hardware the industry consumes, and demand continues to dramatically outpace supply,” Deep33’s Prosor said in an interview with The Verge. “Neither its customers nor its competitors can easily replace the capabilities it provides, and the economic incentives driving the AI trade remain unchanged.”
Even so, a potential market cooling has some worried, as Anthropic’s IPO, slated to potentially be the largest of all time, is set for Thursday. The chipmaker had agreed to buy $10 billion in Anthropic shares via private placement, on top of a $10 billion funding promise Nvidia had already made last year.

articles.title: Telkom returns to growth as MTN revives takeover talks
articles.text:
Telkom, South Africa’s third-largest telecommunications company, reported stronger earnings with growing demand for mobile and fibre services, as MTN Group, Africa’s largest mobile operator, explores a potential acquisition.
The state-controlled telecommunications group reported a 2% revenue increase to R22.5 billion ($1.3 billion) for the six months ended September 30, 2026. Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) rose 5.8% to R6.4 billion ($377 million), while free cash flow increased by 37.8% to R998 million ($58.8 million).
Released on Tuesday, on the sidelines of the Africa Tech Festival in Cape Town, the results show a business improving profitability and extracting more value from its telecommunications infrastructure just as its ownership could be on the verge of a significant change.
Telkom confirmed on Monday that MTN had approached it with a proposal to acquire its issued share capital, bringing the operators together in one of South Africa’s biggest telecommunications transactions. Telkom said there is no certainty that a transaction will materialise.
A potential acquisition would combine two telecommunications businesses with complementary infrastructure, customer bases and enterprise capabilities. Telkom’s results show the financial position of the business MTN is seeking to acquire.
“These results demonstrate the benefits of the deliberate choices we have made to strengthen Telkom’s businesses. We are improving the quality of our earnings and generating greater value from our operations,” Telkom chief executive officer (CEO) Serame Taukobong said in a statement on Tuesday.
Data remains the strategy’s biggest driver. Group data revenue increased by 6.6% to R13.9 billion ($819 million), accounting for 61.8% of total revenue, compared with 59.1% a year earlier. That growth reflects the shift towards mobile connectivity and fibre broadband.
Telkom’s mobile business recorded revenue growth of 4.7% to R13.3 billion ($784 million), while mobile service revenue increased by 4% to R11.5 billion ($678 million). Prepaid data revenue grew 12%, and mobile data subscribers jumped 13.6% to 21 million.
Mobile EBITDA rose 17.1%, with its margin reaching 30.8%, supported by lower roaming costs and network efficiencies.
Its fibre business, Openserve, grew as it focused on converting existing infrastructure into paying customers. Revenue rose 4.2% to R6.6 billion ($389 million), while external revenue grew 11.9% and broadband revenue grew 10.1%.
Connected homes rose by 15.1% to 870,856, lifting Openserve’s fibre connectivity rate to 54.8%, from 52%. However, the recovery remains uneven, particularly at BCX, Telkom’s enterprise technology services provider.
BCX revenue declined by 8.2% to R5.4 billion ($318 million), reflecting weakness in converged communications and lower information technology (IT) hardware and software revenue. Cloud revenue jumped 16.2% and cybersecurity revenue by 8.7%.
Wider recovery
Telkom is repositioning BCX around a core portfolio that management estimates represents 70% of its revenue. The business is pursuing cost controls and improved commercial execution to restore profitability.
Taukobong acknowledged the uneven performance, saying in the interim statement that “traditional voice revenues continue to decline, Mobile service revenue growth has moderated, and BCX continues to strengthen the foundations of its enterprise technology business.”
The group is generating more cash while spending less on capital investment. Capital expenditure fell by 22.5% to R2.2 billion ($130 million), reflecting selective fibre investment and the modernisation and optimisation of its mobile network. Free cash flow increased from R724 million ($42.7 million) to R998 million ($58.8 million).
Telkom expects investment to increase in the second half, focusing on network modernisation, customer experience and opportunities supported by identifiable demand.
The improved performance gives Telkom a stronger financial footing as it enters a pivotal period. Its net debt-to-EBITDA ratio stood at 0.6 times, within its medium-term guidance range, while profit for the period increased by 10.8% to R1.8 billion ($106 million).
“The next phase of Telkom’s transformation is not simply about proving that our business can withstand a changing market. It is about demonstrating that we can consistently convert our customer relationships, infrastructure and capabilities into sustainable earnings, cash generation and long-term value,” Taukobong said.

articles.title: Ten Years On, Google Updates the SRE Book for the AI Era
articles.text:
Google has announced a completely rewritten second edition of their seminal book Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems, ten years after the original book was first published. The book updates thinking on site reliability engineering (SRE) to encompass modern cloud architectures, platform engineering and AI workloads, whilst keeping the original emphasis on applying good software engineering techniques to operations work.
Announced by Google's SRE programme manager Betsy Beyer and software engineer David Huska, the new edition is positioned as a response to a production environment that has changed substantially since 2016, when the first edition appeared. The authors argue that the central problem is no longer adopting cloud infrastructure, but maintaining reliability as systems become more distributed, interdependent and continuously changing.
"Modern production environments operate under constant change. System boundaries are more complex, dependencies are deep, and failure modes are more complex and damaging than ever before."
Betsy Beyer and David Huska, Google Cloud Blog
The original SRE book became influential because it gave a public account of how Google operated large-scale services. It described practices such as service level objectives (SLOs), error budgets, toil reduction, incident management and postmortems. InfoQ's 2016 review noted that the book presented SRE as the application of software engineering to an operations function, with engineers expected to automate repetitive operational work rather than simply respond to it.
The second edition does not present SRE as a fixed set of practices. Instead, it describes how those practices have changed as organisations have moved from early cloud migration and monolithic applications towards microservices, multi-cloud deployments, serverless systems and internal developer platforms.
One of the clearest changes over the years concerns SLOs and error budgets. Google says that teams once relied on basic availability metrics and manually applied error-budget policies. The revised guidance describes user-centred, multi-tiered SLOs, dynamic burn-rate alerting and automated policy enforcement. Reliability practice itself has evolved away from infrastructure uptime alone and towards measures that describe the effect of failures on users.
Observability has also evolved, and the book's new edition talks this through. The first edition's world of static dashboards, basic logs and manual alert triage has given way, in Google's account, to OpenTelemetry, distributed tracing and automated anomaly correlation. The aim is not merely to collect more telemetry, but to reduce the time between an alert and a credible explanation of what has failed.
Automation is the third major area of revision. Google describes a movement from custom scripts addressing isolated tasks towards declarative infrastructure as code, internal developer platforms and self-healing systems. This aligns with the platform-engineering model now common in larger organisations: reliability capabilities are built once into a platform and consumed by product teams, rather than being reimplemented by every team.
Reliability testing has also changed. Google contrasts scheduled game days and synthetic load tests with continuous resilience checks, automated pipeline testing and live production canary verification. The practical implication is that resilience becomes part of the delivery pipeline rather than an occasional exercise performed before a major release.
"Rather than relying solely on scheduled game days and synthetic load tests, modern engineering embeds continuous resilience checks, automated pipeline testing, and live production canary verification."
Betsy Beyer and David Huska, Google Cloud Blog
Capacity management is another area where the book has been updated. Google says that manual provisioning and static forecasting have been replaced by dynamic auto-scaling, cloud FinOps alignment and optimisation for GPU and TPU clusters. This matters because AI training and inference workloads can concentrate demand on scarce accelerated computing resources, making capacity planning, networking and cost control more operationally significant.
Generative AI inevitably appears in the second edition, in two facets. First, SRE is presented as a discipline needed to operate AI infrastructure. The book covers the reliability of large GPU and TPU clusters, network topologies, non-deterministic model outputs, latency behaviour and the pipelines used for training, fine-tuning and data processing. These are different operational problems from those posed by a conventional stateless web service.
Second, AI is presented as a tool for reliability engineers. The post welcomes generative AI support for incident triage and postmortem writing, natural-language queries over telemetry, and predictive models that identify resource bottlenecks before they cause an outage. The examples in the announcement mostly place AI in a supporting role, gathering and organising evidence for engineers, rather than claiming that AI can replace operational judgement. Recent industry activity appears to support this, with InfoQ reporting in October 2026 that Datadog had released Scout, a specialist model intended to investigate production problems inside its Bits AI SRE product. Other vendors are exploring similar territory, including Honeycomb's Canvas Agent, Splunk AI SRE and New Relic's SRE Agent. InfoQ also reported in February 2026 on Google Cloud SREs using the Gemini CLI during real outages; using AI to help engineers work through incidents, rather than as an autonomous replacement for on-call staff.
The announcement also revises the organisational side of SRE. Google describes a move beyond dedicated SRE teams attached to particular applications, towards hybrid models, platform-engineering integration and reliability champions embedded in product teams. This has come about because many organisations cannot staff a central SRE team for every service, so reliability expertise has to be distributed more widely.
Despite the technological updates, Google argues that the underlying culture has not changed. The authors restate the importance of reliability-focused culture and expand the book's coverage of the human aspects of systems engineering. David Blank-Edelman made a related point in a presentation, You Are Asking the Wrong Questions (about Reliability and SRE), delivered at InfoQ Dev Summit Boston in 2025. He argued that reliability work should start from the customer's perspective rather than the component's perspective, and described SRE as fundamentally collaborative. He also challenged the conventional focus on a single root cause, favouring an examination of the contributing factors behind a failure.
The second edition is available in physical format through Google Books and in digital format from O'Reilly. For teams already practising SRE, its value is likely to lie less in introducing familiar concepts than in showing how those concepts have been adapted for platforms, distributed systems and AI-heavy infrastructure. For organisations earlier in their reliability journey, it remains a substantial reference on how to make operations a software-engineering problem rather than a collection of manual tasks.

articles.text:
The Download: Jensen Huang’s open-source dilemma and cognitive immortality
Plus: The US is tightening controls on China’s remote access to AI chips.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
A petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO has attracted more than 115,000 signatures, including Elon Musk, but comb through the names, and you’ll notice a significant number come from a particular slice of the tech world: open-source AI.
Huang had become a sort of ringleader for open source, but his credibility as an advocate is now under threat. Revelations about Nvidia chips in China and a new rule in the US could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress
Read the full story to find out why.
—James O'Donnell
This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Monday.
Roundtables: inside the quest for cognitive immortality
The quest to overcome the human brain's limits is moving beyond science fiction. From gradual brain replacement to uploading memories to the cloud, researchers and technologists are exploring radical ways to extend human cognition. Today, MIT Technology Review examines these ideas in a live Roundtables discussion.
Join science editor Mary Beth Griggs and senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado to explore what cognitive immortality could look like, and how close we might be to achieving it.
Tune in live today, Tuesday, November 17, at 5:00 p.m. GMT / 12:00 p.m. EST / 9:00 a.m. PST.

Kenya’s Great Rift Valley is home to five geothermal power stations, which harness clouds of steam to generate about a quarter of the country’s electricity. But some of the energy escapes into the atmosphere, while even more remains underground for lack of demand. That’s what brought Octavia Carbon here.
Last year, the startup began harnessing some of that excess energy to remove CO2 from the air. The company says the method is efficient, affordable, and—crucially—scalable. But the project also faces fierce opposition.

articles.title: AI models can be tricked into identifying civilians as military targets by telling them it's a game | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Some AI models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and other leading AI labs could be easily tricked into identifying targets for military strikes — even if they include civilians or locations like schools — simply by being told they’re playing a game, according to a new research report by Vals.
Vals, a San Francisco-based AI evaluation startup, tested whether leading AI models could be manipulated into participating in autonomous warfare. Researchers used simulated scenarios and a combination of generated and real imagery from Ukraine and Iran to see if the AI models would mark targets in drone and satellite imagery.
The models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek, and other companies frequently identified potential targets in drone and satellite imagery, including civilians and surrendering soldiers. When the models refused to cooperate, researchers were able to jailbreak them by claiming the battlefield scenarios were part of a game.
The findings come amid growing fears about the immediate risks posed by AI, beyond the existential threats associated with artificial general intelligence.
Earlier this year, Anthropic became embroiled in a dispute with the Department of Defense after it told the agency it could not use Anthropic’s technology for mass surveillance of Americans or autonomous warfare. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has insisted that today’s AI systems aren’t reliable enough to make life-or-death decisions without a human in the loop. Meanwhile, the Pentagon argued it should be able to deploy the technology for any lawful military purpose.
The new research raises further questions about whether AI companies are capable of preventing their models from being used in warfare.
Ironically, AI models from Anthropic performed the worst in these simulated scenarios. But none of the models performed particularly well. None of the researchers’ requests were blocked by a safety classifier, and refusals were uncommon. Even when models did refuse, they often complied after being told they were playing a game.
Anthropic spokesperson Eduardo Maia Silva told TechCrunch the company appreciates Vals’ report, recommendations, and collaboration, and acknowledged that the outcomes were not acceptable.
“The examples in the report are very clearly against our rules and we have banned and will ban users when we see this behavior,” according to an emailed company statement sent by Silva. “Even for authorized settings, Anthropic has long been firm that today’s frontier AI systems are not reliable enough to power fully autonomous weapons.”
Anthropic told TechCrunch that its teams were already developing additional safeguards before the report was published and that those measures would be in place soon. Anthropic is also expanding its own testing and enhancing safeguards and enforcement to address any gaps it finds.
OpenAI spokesperson Nate Evans told TechCrunch the company prohibits using its public models to facilitate violence or for unapproved national security purposes, including in the scenarios Vals simulated.
“We actively detect and disrupt misuse, including by suspending accounts that violate our policies,” OpenAI said in an emailed statement. “We’re also developing additional safeguards for our public models against misuse involving drones and drone software.”
Vals notes in the report that the models were never asked to directly make strike decisions, a task the researchers said the models would typically refuse. That doesn’t mean their outputs couldn’t have dire or fatal consequences in the real world. For instance, targeting information could be used by autonomous weapons systems.
In some scenarios, the models were asked to report whether people were visible. Positive reports were followed by simulated strikes and the models would see the consequences.
The report relies on commercial models from frontier AI labs, not the models those companies might provide to the military. It’s not clear whether the additional safeguards would apply to military use, though.
Vals also noted that technical challenges, including latency and limited onboard computing capacity, make it difficult to use general-purpose AI models for live drone targeting. Those constraints make their deployment in combat less of an immediate threat.
A more immediate threat, the researchers say, is that AI models could be used to annotate battlefield footage at scale, producing training data for autonomous targeting systems.
For instance, researchers relied on real satellite imagery of an Iranian school that was bombed by the U.S. in February 2026, killing more than 150 civilians. Bloomberg later reported that an “overreliance on AI” contributed to the strike. In Vals’ testing, models frequently marked the school, which sat next to a military complex, as a strike target, with Claude Opus 5.5 selecting the school in 69% of ordinary trials and 72% of game-framed trials.
Anthropic no longer has an active Pentagon contract, but other companies, including SpaceXAI, OpenAI, and Google do. A recent Congressional Research Service report found that the Pentagon is not known to be using any frontier AI model in autonomous weapons systems directly.
TechCrunch has also reached out to Meta, Google, Thinking Machines Lab, and SpaceXAI for comment.

articles.title: The MacBook Neo is receiving a rare $50 discount ahead of Black Friday
articles.text:
If you’re looking for a new laptop or a gift for the student in your life, you can save $50 on the MacBook Neo at several retailers, in both storage sizes and all four colors. The 256GB model is currently discounted to $649 (Amazon, Best Buy, Target), while the 512GB model with Touch ID is down to $749 (Amazon, Best Buy, Target). None of the retailers currently list an end date for the discount, which is the biggest price drop we’ve seen since Apple raised the laptop’s MSRP by $100 in July in response to the ongoing RAM crisis.
The MacBook Neo is receiving a rare $50 discount ahead of Black Friday
While $50 might not feel like much, it brings the laptop closer to its original launch price.
Apple’s budget-friendly MacBook leverages the A18 Pro processor, a chip originally found in the iPhone 16 Pro, to keep costs down. Both the 256GB and 512GB models feature 8GB of memory, and my colleague Antonio G. Di Benedetto was impressed by the vivid 13-inch screen and speakers, the latter of which are better than those in many cheap (and even midrange) Windows laptops. The Neo isn’t super performant, especially in terms of storage speed and total memory, but it’s great for everyday tasks, casual use, and students.

articles.title: KI-Angriff ohne Mensch: Google deckt autonomen „exploit_agent“ auf
articles.text:
Angriff ohne Mensch: Google warnt vor vollständig autonomen KI-Attacken
Googles hauseigene IT-Security-Gruppe Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) hat nach eigenen Angaben zum ersten Mal KI-Angriffe dokumentiert, bei denen Kriminelle das Finden und Ausnutzen von Sicherheitslücken mit Sprachmodellen komplett automatisiert haben. Das beschreibt GTIG in einem neuen Bericht.
So funktioniert der „exploit_agent“
Das Framework trägt den Namen „exploit_agent“. Es vergleicht automatisch gepatchte und ungepatchte Versionen verbreiteter Internetsoftware – also Fassungen mit und ohne Sicherheitsupdate, um festzustellen, welche Lücken die Hersteller geschlossen haben. Aus den Unterschieden leitet das Programm dann ab, wo eine Lücke steckt. Findet es eine, schreibt es den passenden Angriffscode selbst und führt ihn aus. Laut GTIG geschieht das „ohne Intervention eines Menschen“. Bei den beobachteten Angriffen zogen die Angreifer Daten von den betroffenen Seiten ab.
GTIG fand außerdem mehrere Skripte, die nach einem erfolgreichen Einbruch automatisch loslaufen sollten. Dazu zählen die interne Erkundung im Netzwerk, Brute-Force-Angriffe mit massenhaftem Durchprobieren von Passwörtern, das Installieren sogenannter Webshells – simpler Hintertüren für dauerhaften Zugriff ohne viel Aufwand – sowie sogar das Löschen der Webshells konkurrierender Angreifer. Die Daten der Opfersysteme deuten laut Bericht darauf hin, dass es dem Verantwortlichen vor allem um französische Websites aus der Medien- und Unterhaltungsbranche sowie aus dem Bildungssektor ging.
Auch andere Gruppen setzen auf KI
GTIG beobachtete auch weitere Cyberkriminelle, die ihre Angriffe mit KI automatisieren wollen. Sie greifen dafür unter anderem auf frei verfügbare Pentesting-Werkzeuge zurück, also auf Software, die eigentlich für legale Sicherheitstests gedacht ist. Auch staatliche Akteure aus Nordkorea nutzen längst generative KI, um ihre Operationen auszuweiten.
Google rechnet damit, dass die Automatisierung weiter zunimmt: „Angesichts der niedrigen Eintrittsbarriere, der einfachen Integration neuer Exploits und des enormen Skalierungspotenzials halten wir es für sehr wahrscheinlich, dass Angreifer diese Frameworks weiterhin in Kampagnen einsetzen werden, die sich gegen Organisationen weltweit richten“, schreiben die Forschenden.

articles.title: Integrating QPUs into Supercomputing Centers Using Slurm HRES Plugins | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Quantum processors are being integrated into supercomputing centers worldwide. National programs in North America, Europe, and Asia are driving the installation of quantum processing units (QPUs) alongside high-performance computing (HPC) systems. Every supercomputer will eventually be a hybrid quantum-classical device, drawing on quantum processors to expand what’s possible in scientific research.
The scientists that will become the first power users of quantum-GPU supercomputing already run their simulations and workflows on HPC systems. Chemistry, weather modeling, engineering simulation, and other traditionally HPC-centric fields stand to benefit from quantum acceleration for certain workloads. For these scientists, the QPU is simply another accelerator, alongside the CPUs and GPUs that supercomputing centers already provide.
Making quantum computers readily available, easily programmable, and familiar to access, reserve, and execute at scale is imperative for scientific researchers to be able to adopt quantum processors into workflows. Until now, a key missing piece has been a workload manager. Slurm 26.11 changes that with Hierarchical Resources (HRES) plugins, which allow a site to schedule a QPU as a native, cluster-level resource through a short, portable Lua plugin.
This post covers why QPUs have not fit the previous scheduling models Slurm used for CPUs and GPUs. It then explains the solution: how HRES models a QPU, and what HRES plugins add in Slurm 26.11, including the API callbacks and capabilities that middleware teams build on. It also addresses how community-driven interfaces such as QRMI and QDMI have already built open source plugins on these APIs, as well as initial adoption by the quantum ecosystem and supercomputing centers.
Building quantum-GPU supercomputing
Integrating a QPU at a supercomputing center requires more than just its physical installation. The QPU must be networked with the existing computing infrastructure, and users must be able to request it at job submission the same way CPUs and GPUs are requested. Its usage must be tracked, monitored, and accounted for, and it must abide by site-specific policies. In other words, the scheduler, or workload manager, must manage the QPU like it would any other computing resource.
Until now, schedulers have had no native way to model a QPU, so most integrations are repeatedly custom-built for each new supercomputing site or QPU builder. The cost of that fragmentation falls on everyone involved:
- Users face a different interface at every site.
- Administrators must maintain custom code that complicates upgrades.
- QPU vendors rebuild their integration for each customer, with no portability.
- Global systems integrators (GSIs) cannot deliver a repeatable deployment.
On the QPU side, open source efforts such as QRMI and QDMI are unifying how such devices are described to, and controlled by, HPC software. What has been missing is a unified interface in the scheduler used by supercomputing centers for integrating QPUs into HPC deployments.
Why existing Slurm resource models don’t accommodate QPUs
A QPU is typically a cluster-wide accelerator, not part of a node. Slurm generic resources (GRES), the mechanism used for GPUs, belong to individual compute nodes. Modeling a QPU as a GRES binds it to one node, so only jobs on that node can use it. If that node fails, for example, the QPU stays unreachable until an administrator reconfigures the cluster.
Many integrations instead combine licenses, which represent cluster-wide resources, for scheduling, and use SPANK plugins for the user interface and node setup. This approach works, but it has several problems:
- Idle nodes: Without a license, SPANK only acts after Slurm has allocated nodes, so a job can hold compute nodes idle while it waits for the QPU.
- Two-flag requests: Nothing stops a job from passing device options without holding the license.
- Multiple QPUs: Hosting several QPUs on one cluster is difficult, because their SPANK plugins compete for the same command-line options.
- Upgrade risk: In practice, many SPANK plugins tie third-party code to Slurm internal APIs, so every Slurm upgrade risks breaking the integration.
- No device awareness: Slurm cannot tell on its own when a QPU is recalibrating or offline, so it keeps starting jobs that cannot use the device until it is back online.
How HRES plugins in Slurm 26.11 enable integration
Slurm 26.11 introduces an HRES plugin interface to address these gaps, so that the HPC and quantum communities can integrate with Slurm without changing Slurm itself. Its first implementation, hres/lua, runs a short Lua script. The plugin reports device health to the scheduler, accepts device options as part of the resource request, and runs setup and teardown code at each stage of the job.
A site describes the QPU as a cluster-level HRES in resources.yaml and points it at the plugin. The two files divide the work. resources.yaml holds site-specific details and policies, such as endpoints and which nodes can reach the device, under the system administrator’s control. The plugin holds the device logic, so the community or a QPU vendor can write it once and ship it to every site that deploys Slurm 26.11.
Modeling a QPU as a hierarchical resource
HRES was added to Slurm 25.05 as a beta feature and is the evolution of licenses. Like a license, an HRES is a count of a resource that does not belong to any single node. Unlike a license, that count is associated with a specific set of nodes: the ones allowed to use it (Figure 1). Slurm 26.11 also starts to allow more dynamic modeling of the relationship between nodes and HRES.
An HRES is defined in resources.yaml, in the same directory as slurm.conf. Each resource has one or more layers, and each layer has a name, a list of nodes, and a count. For a QPU, the simplest definition is a single layer covering the nodes that can reach the device, with a count of one. The plugin block attaches the Lua script and its site-specific settings:
- resource: qpu
  mode: MODE_1
  plugin:
	type: hres/lua
	config:
  	- name: path
    value: /etc/slurm/hres_qpu.lua
  	- name: endpoint               	# site settings, never secrets
    value: https://qpu-gateway.example.org
	maintenance_cycle: 30            	# seconds between health checks
  layers:
	- layer_name: qpu1
  	nodes: ["node[0001-0123]"]
  	count: 1
With this definition, a request is satisfied when a layer that overlaps the job’s allocated nodes has enough of the resource available. A job that requests the QPU runs only on nodes in that layer. Jobs request the resource with --resources=qpu:1.
The middleware is the boundary between HPC and QPU
In the model shown in Figure 2, neither Slurm nor the Lua plugin talks to the QPU directly. A third-party access middleware sits between the HPC system and the QPU and provides a unified interface to different quantum hardware APIs. The middleware is therefore the boundary between the HPC system and the QPU.
Slurm treats the QPU as a single schedulable unit. It decides whether the unit is available, which job holds it, for how long, and from which nodes. Importantly, Slurm does not orchestrate anything inside the unit: calibration, error correction, and device control stay within the QPU and its own software runtime. The approach therefore applies both to today’s noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices and to future error-corrected systems.
The plugin translates between the two sides. It asks the middleware for status and reservations, and reports the results to Slurm in Slurm’s terms: whether a layer is disabled, whether a job can start, and a payload for the job’s nodes.
HRES plugin APIs
The current implementation of HRES plugins runs a Lua script written by the community or a device vendor.
Lua
A Lua plugin is a plain text file that vendors can ship and update independently of Slurm’s release cycle. It does not link against libslurm, whose API changes each release, so it does not need rebuilding for every Slurm upgrade. Lua is also fast, embeds cleanly in C, and is already used by Slurm’s job submit and CLI filter plugins. The script must sit at the same path on the controller and on every node, and since most of its functions run as root or as SlurmUser, only root should be able to write to it.
Key capabilities include:
- Stackability: slurmctld creates a separate plugin context for each resource that defines a plugin. One cluster can host several QPUs, and several QPU types, without the option collisions that SPANK plugins run into.
- Site configuration: Endpoints and other settings live in the plugin’s config list, which Slurm hands to the plugin without interpreting it. The configuration, the job’s arguments, and any payload travel with the job to its nodes, where the job’s user can read them. This means that none of them may hold secrets.
- User inputs: Users append name=value arguments to the request, for example --resources='qpu:1[shot=1000]'. Slurm passes them to the plugin without interpreting them, which removes the need for a second command-line flag.
- Health checks: Every maintenance_cycle seconds, a maintenance callback asks the middleware whether the QPU is ready, and sets or clears disable_layer on each layer to stop or resume allocation from it.
- Job start and end: Once a job is scheduled, and before its nodes are allocated, a controller prerun can admit or hold it, so the job never holds idle nodes while it waits for the QPU. Because the prerun holds the controller’s job lock, slow work, such as reserving the QPU, belongs in an optional asynchronous prerun, whose payload Slurm sends to the job’s nodes. If the job does not start, a revoke callback undoes the reservation, and a controller epilog releases it when the job ends.
- Failure handling: A callback can return ESLURM_HRES_REMOTE_FAIL to report that the external service is unavailable rather than broken. A failed prerun then leaves the job pending, and a failed node prolog or epilog does not drain the node.
A plugin implements the callbacks in Table 1, in the order they run for a job.
| Callback | Runs | Example QPU use | 
|---|---|---|
| hres_create_context  | slurmctld, for each resource with a plugin, when the configuration is read. Every layer shows nothing used at this point | Check the service is reachable and set up connections or state | 
| hres_maintenance  | slurmctld, every maintenance_cycle seconds | Query the middleware for status; set or clear disable_layer on each layer | 
| hres_controller_job_prerun  | slurmctld, once the job is scheduled and before its nodes are allocated, under the job lock | Admit or hold the job, for example against a cached device status | 
| hres_controller_job_async_prerun (optional)  | slurmctld, in a separate thread while the job is configuring | Reserve the QPU on the service; return a payload for the job’s nodes | 
| hres_controller_job_revoke  | slurmctld, when the job does not start after its prerun succeeded | Undo the reservation | 
| hres_node_job_prolog  | Each node of the job, once, before the Prolog script | Start an access service or write per-job files | 
| hres_node_task_prolog  | slurmstepd, in each task as root, before it starts | Privileged per-task setup | 
| hres_node_user_task_prolog  | slurmstepd, in each task as the user, just before it starts | Per-task setup as the user | 
| hres_node_task_epilog  | slurmstepd, after each task exits | Per-task cleanup | 
| hres_node_job_epilog  | Each node of the job, once, after the Epilog script | Stop the service; remove per-job files | 
| hres_controller_job_epilog  | slurmctld, after all the job’s node epilogs, before its resources are returned | Release the reservation | 
| hres_destroy_context  | slurmctld, before the configuration is read again | Close connections and free anything the script holds | 
hres_create_context and hres_destroy_context also run on slurmctld whenever it reads its configuration
Most integrations need only a few callbacks. The following skeleton shows the shape of a plugin: a health check, an admission decision before any nodes are allocated, and a release when the job ends. The middleware_* calls stand in for the middleware’s own client library.
-- Callback names, arguments, fields, and return codes are Slurm's hres/lua API.
-- middleware_* calls are placeholders for your middleware's client library.
  -- Health: slurmctld, every maintenance_cycle seconds
function hres_maintenance(ctx, layers)
  local ready = middleware_status(ctx.config.endpoint)
  for _, layer in ipairs(layers) do layer.disable_layer = not ready end
  return slurm.SUCCESS
end
-- Admission: once the job is scheduled, before its nodes are allocated
function hres_controller_job_prerun(ctx, job, prep)
  if not middleware_can_admit(ctx, prep.plugin_args) then   -- cached, no network
	return slurm.ESLURM_HRES_REMOTE_FAIL                	-- the job stays pending
  end
  return slurm.SUCCESS
end
-- Release: after the job's node epilogs
function hres_controller_job_epilog(ctx, job, prep)
  middleware_release(ctx.config.endpoint, prep.payload)
  return slurm.SUCCESS
end
-- The remaining required callbacks return slurm.SUCCESS.
Community integration examples of HRES plugins
The teams that build QPU access middleware usually write the HRES plugins. Two of those communities, QRMI and QDMI, have released open source plugins built on the Slurm 26.11 APIs. Both admit jobs only while the QPU is available, and in both, the layer’s count sets how many jobs can use a QPU at the same time. The QRMI plugin acquires access to the QPU for each job before it runs. The QDMI plugin only admits jobs, and each job then queues its work with the provider. With either plugin, sites running Slurm 26.11 can connect their clusters to quantum computers from multiple providers.
QRMI: Acquiring the QPU for each job
Each HRES resource is named after a resource in the QRMI configuration file. Before a job runs, the plugin books access to the QPU with the user’s own credentials, in a separate thread outside the scheduler’s critical path, and releases it after the job ends. Depending on the backend, the booking is a reservation or a session. Existing applications run unchanged, because jobs see the same environment variables as with the QRMI SPANK plugin. For the complete configuration, plugin and a containerized test cluster, visit the QRMI HRES plugin repository.
QDMI: Leaving the queue to the provider
Each HRES resource is one device, named after its QDMI device ID. The plugin’s maintenance callback checks the device’s status and admits jobs only while it reports itself as idle or busy. The plugin reserves nothing: each job submits its work through QDMI, and the provider’s queue schedules it on the device. For the complete configuration and plugin, visit the MQSC Orchestrator.
Learn how more organizations in the quantum ecosystem are integrating HRES plugins:
User job submission
From the user’s side, the two integrations look and feel the same. A job script requests the QPU by its HRES resource name just as it requests nodes or GPUs, and runs in the partition that contains the HRES assigned nodes. Slurm holds the job until the plugin reports that the QPU is available and, where the middleware supports it, reserved. The template below works for either integration; only the resource name changes.
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=my-hybrid-job
#SBATCH --nodes=4
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
#SBATCH --resources=<qpu_resource>
srun ./my_hybrid_app
Get started with Slurm HRES plugins
Slurm 26.11 gives QPUs a native place in the scheduler. An HRES models the QPU as a cluster-level resource tied to the nodes that can reach it, and a Lua plugin connects that resource to the middleware that manages the device. Because the Lua plugin is designed to hold little to nothing site-specific, a vendor or community project can write it once and every Slurm site can reuse it, while administrators keep control of their own policies.
By design, this approach is valid for today’s generation of quantum computers and for future fault-tolerant systems, making it a lasting choice for supercomputing centers deploying quantum devices.
Ready to get started? Deploy the QRMI HRES plugin or the QDMI HRES example, or use them as starting points for your own integration. To learn more, check out the Slurm 26.11 release notes, and read the HRES documentation and the resources.yaml reference.
Acknowledgments
We thank the QRMI and QDMI communities for building on HRES plugins and for their contributions to this post.

articles.title: Instagram fine-tunes recommendation systems in India to curb sexually suggestive, violent content
articles.text:
Instagram fine-tunes recommendation systems in India to curb sexually suggestive, violent content
The India-specific measures apply to content recommended from accounts users do not follow and concern what Instagram's algorithms promote, rather than a blanket ban on the content itself
Meta Platforms said on Tuesday that it has fine-tuned Instagram's content recommendation systems in India to curb the visibility of sexually suggestive material and violent content, deploying more advanced artificial intelligence models to identify and filter unwanted posts before they reach users.
The India-specific measures apply to content recommended from accounts users do not follow and concern what Instagram's algorithms promote, rather than a blanket ban on the content itself, the company said.
The announcement comes against the backdrop of increased regulatory scrutiny of social media algorithms in India. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, in an October 10 advisory, asked Meta to review its ranking and recommendation systems to ensure potentially misleading, manipulated or out-of-context material is not disproportionately amplified.
Meta, however, did not say if the changes were linked to the government advisory.
The changes have helped halve the frequency with which users report recommended content compared with a year ago, Meta said in a post on its website.
The platform said it had strengthened default protections over the past year, tailoring its systems to content that users in India have said they do not want to see. The measures apply to recommendations across Reels, Explore and Feed, where Instagram surfaces content from accounts users do not already follow.
As part of the upgrades, Instagram is using more capable AI models to assess content directly against its Recommendations Guidelines, enabling its systems to detect and limit potentially objectionable material proactively rather than waiting for users to report or hide it.
"Today, our systems keep more of this content out of recommendations, including sexually suggestive content and content that depicts violence," Meta said.
The company said the improvements had enabled it to proactively reduce the amount of content in India that does not meet its recommendation standards. It did not disclose the absolute volume of content affected, the proportion of recommendations filtered or the methodology used to calculate the decline in user reports.
Instagram's recommendation standards are distinct from its Community Standards, which govern content prohibited on the platform. Material that violates Community Standards is removed, while content that may be objectionable, sensitive or low-quality but does not breach those rules can remain accessible without being recommended to a wider audience. Content unlawful in a particular country is restricted there, the company said.
Recommendations determine how users discover content beyond accounts they actively follow, giving the platform's algorithms considerable influence over what appears in their feeds and is amplified across the service.
Alongside platform-wide recommendation filters, Instagram offers users controls to customise the content they see and manage interactions on the platform.
Its Sensitive Content Control allows users to opt for less sensitive material across Search, Reels, Explore, suggested accounts and in-Feed recommendations. Instagram said its systems in India already exclude the most mature content from recommendations, with the setting allowing users to further limit exposure to other sensitive material.
Users can also choose to see less political content recommended from accounts they do not follow, flag posts through the "Not Interested" option and filter selected words, phrases and emojis from comments and message requests using the Hidden Words feature. Its blocking function prevents specific accounts from finding profiles, viewing posts or sending messages, including through new accounts they may create.
Teenagers receive additional age-appropriate protections through Instagram's Teen Accounts, introduced in India last year. These accounts automatically place younger users in a 13-plus content setting governed by the platform's age-appropriate content guidelines.
The changes come amid growing scrutiny of social media platforms over online safety, algorithm-driven content distribution and the exposure of younger users to potentially harmful material.
Meta said user feedback, including when people hide posts or select "Not Interested", also informs its recommendation systems and helps identify content audiences do not want surfaced to them.
The company said it would continue to refine its detection systems as user behaviour and technology evolve, with feedback from users in India guiding further changes.

articles.title: Can AI help build a healthier future? - Microsoft Research
articles.text:
Technical advancement is moving at such a rapid pace that it can be challenging to define the tomorrow we’re working toward. In The Shape of Things to Come, Microsoft Research leader Doug Burger and experts from across disciplines tease out the thorniest AI issues facing technologists, policymakers, business decisionmakers, and other stakeholders today. The goal: to amplify the shared understanding needed to build a future in which the AI transition is a net positive.
Microsoft Principal Research Manager Ava Amini, Microsoft Chief Scientific Officer Eric Horvitz, and physician-scientist and Microsoft AI health advisor Eric Topol (opens in new tab) of Scripps Research join Burger to tackle a question with ramifications for every individual on the planet: What might the future of medicine look like with AI, and what needs to happen first?
Drawing from experiences in machine learning, bioscience, and clinical care, the group explores AI-assisted medical diagnosis, the untapped potential of leveraging AI in medical imaging, whole-patient models, virtual cells, and the role of biological foundation models in scientific discovery. The group also examines why promising research can be slow to reach patients, how AI could guide experiments and drug discovery, and why better biological data and real-world validation remain essential.
This episode delivers a research-grounded conversation of what AI can do today in the health space, the challenges and opportunities still ahead, and the shape of things to come.
Subscribe to the Microsoft Research Podcast:
Transcript
[MUSIC]
DOUG BURGER: This is The Shape of Things to Come, a Microsoft Research Podcast. I’m your host, Doug Burger. In this series, we’re going to venture to the bleeding edge of AI capabilities, dig down into the fundamentals, really try to understand them, and think about how these capabilities are going to change the world—for better and worse.
Today, I’m bringing three experts in the fields of biomedicine working on the frontlines of AI, biology, and medicine to see where healthcare is going, where the deep understanding of biology is going, what medical advances are coming, and how will AI change the future of health. These questions are really important because they will determine the shape of things to come.
[MUSIC FADES]
In today’s podcast, I’ve invited three leading researchers in medicine, biology, and machine learning/AI.
Eric Horvitz is Microsoft’s chief scientist [chief scientific officer] and is both a PhD and an MD. How you spent all those years in school, I have no idea. I’ve known Eric for decades and his work has shaped the entire field of machine learning. He’s a legend in the machine learning community and is a good friend.
Eric Topol is our second guest. He’s the executive vice president of Scripps Research (opens in new tab), the largest nonprofit biomedical research institute in the United States. He’s published over 1,300 peer-reviewed papers. Shocking, [LAUGHTER] shockingly productive. Authored four books (opens in new tab). So just an amazingly impressive, prolific scientist and physician.
Finally, Ava Amini is a principal research manager in Microsoft Research. She’s a rising star in our organization, an expert in the intersection of AI and precision medicine, and she’s a co-lead of Project Ex Vivo, a collaborative effort between Microsoft and the Broad Institute that is focusing on defining, engineering, and targeting cell states in cancer.
So thank you all for joining today. I think we’ve got a really, really amazing set of people, myself excluded. And I’d like to start to my guests here.
It’s clear there’s a huge disruption happening at the intersection of biology and medicine and AI right now. Just, you know, we’re seeing things, breakthroughs, happening at an accelerating pace. Models are helping us to discover structures and create abstractions that are really useful for moving forward the field of medicine. I’ve seen some recent talks where scientists with cancer used AI to design drugs for themselves. I mean, just unbelievable.
And today, I’ve got some long-term questions for us to discuss, maybe a little bit provocative. But I’d like to start with what each of you see as what’s happening right now, like, on the, on the intersection of medicine and biology and AI.
I think each of you has a unique vantage point. I’ll go around the horn, and I know, Eric, there’s a, you know, you have a cover article on Science magazine (opens in new tab) that’s really exciting, and so maybe you could talk a little bit about that, as well. So I’ll start with you, and then I’ll go to Eric Topol and then Ava.
ERIC HORVITZ: Thanks, Doug.
I think healthcare and the biosciences are fortunate disciplines as in that there’s been a digitalization of content—whether it be protein structure over, over decades, electronic health records, and so on—that makes these fields amenable to being at the ready for AI inferences and innovation. And therefore, I’ve been extremely optimistic about the long-term futures as well as what we’ll see early on at the frontiers of AI when it comes to the biosciences and healthcare.
Just extraordinary to see what’s happened over just the last five to eight years in the biosciences with both discriminative and generative AI models. You know, the AlphaFold (opens in new tab) breakthrough was tip of the iceberg, and we see just a whole, in some ways, a crest and a crashing of the wave of possibilities now when it comes to experimental platforms, experimental design, data interpretation in the biosciences, hypothesis generation, I should say, as a, as an assistant and a companion to scientific reasoners and human scientists.
In healthcare, we have an extraordinary opportunity to address long-term challenges in patient safety, in getting to timely diagnoses, in accessibility of healthcare. And after a couple of years of intensive work, I and just fabulous colleagues at Microsoft worked intensively on taking healthcare challenges when it comes to applications of AI and benchmarking—medical diagnostic challenges, for example—and moved it into what I would call the realm of medical cognition, where instead of looking at a whole case that’s given to an AI system and looking at the accuracies that are reported on its ability to diagnose, for example, a form of differential diagnosis, we instead put the AI system in the, in the shoes of a clinician.
You get an initial set of symptoms, you get chief complaint, some history, a little window on what’s going on when a patient comes in in an ambulatory setting, and then it’s up to the clinician to ask the right questions and to then think about tests, balancing the information value with the cost of the tests. This is the sequential diagnosis challenge. And we applied AI to both the … formulating the hypothesis component of that as well as decision-making about the next best tests to order, questions to ask, and also when to call a diagnosis, even under uncertainty, as a concluding convergent diagnosis and getting on with things with therapy, for example. And showed just, I think, remarkable abilities of a number of frontier language models to do a fabulous job.
And, you know, and again, did some comparisons with human generalist physicians, which have to be taken at face value and with limitations in what we did with … on the comparison, but still show the promise of the methods for assisting clinicians of the future.
BURGER: Well, congratulations on the paper. It’s a really big deal.
Eric [Topol], moving on to you. You know, you’re the one person on the podcast who’s not a Microsoft employee [LAUGHTER], and so you see a very different, I think, set of things than we might see from our vantage point, although I think each of the three of us sees different things in general.
Could you just tell us what you’re seeing? Like, to somebody listening, you know, we have a broad listenership from all different segments, not just experts in AI or medicine. Like, what are you seeing that your, sort of, technical, smart, average listener would be able to take away?
ERIC TOPOL: Yeah, sure, Doug. I mean, I think first I do also want to congratulate Eric and the team at Microsoft because this was a seminal paper in Science. It was the first ever to take an agentic system and make more accurate diagnoses not just compared with physicians but a lot of the other frontier models. Markedly improved accuracy over physicians, almost doubling, but at lower cost. I mean, that’s stuff we haven’t seen. What we’ve seen is, you know, using AI to upcode and using AI to potentially raise costs. This really was the first demonstration you could have higher accuracy at lower cost. It’s kind of like eat more, weigh less, [LAUGHTER] or taste better, you know. Anyway, it’s pretty impressive work.
Now,what I’ve seen, which is striking, is that we have all attuned to the shiny object of generative AI, which is great. It’s, you know, four years in. But we’ve somehow missed using where it’s even more proven, which is in the image phase, a deep learning of medical images. Whether it be the retina, chest x-ray, electrocardiogram, all these things.
And so there’s this real paradox where, for example, we aren’t implementing all that we’ve learned from mammography—over a hundred thousand women in a randomized trial (opens in new tab)—or colonoscopy—44 randomized trials (opens in new tab)—and eking out all the embedded information that humans can’t see, but AI can interpret from every type of medical image that we know of. So we’re not harvesting that opportunity.
Now, why is that important? Well, the next phase of AI is, you know, I guess, what I’d call whole-patient models, whereby we would have, as Eric mentioned, electronic health records; we’d have all the images, raw images, and other layers of data.
