articles.title: Jensen Huang says he would be 'honored' if allowed to return as Nvidia CEO | TechCrunch
articles.text:
In the first public statement since his resignation, Nvidia founder Jensen Huang signaled his willingness to return as CEO if the board decides it is in the company’s best interest.
Huang’s statement, posted in full on X, reads as follows:
Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I’ve never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.
I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA. 
I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. 
Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO. 
Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.
Jensen
Huang resigned after reports of multiple affairs, including with a direct report and another with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who is suspected of working with Chinese intelligence services. Nvidia’s chip exports have faced intense scrutiny since the revelations, and Huang is scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1.
In Huang’s absence, Nvidia has formed a new executive committee to oversee export control compliance.
Still, many investors and employees associated with Nvidia have called for Huang to return as CEO, at least until an investigation can provide clearer evidence of guilt. An open letter circulated earlier this week attracted the signatures of more than 10,000 current and former Nvidia employees, as well as prominent tech figures like Elon Musk, Amjad Masad, and Travis Kalanick.
“We are concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process,” the letter reads. “If the Board believes his continued absence is necessary, provide a specific, evidence-based explanation of why it serves NVIDIA’s best interests.”
Still, many see such a return as unlikely. On Monday, an unnamed source on Nvidia’s board told The Washington Post there were no plans to reinstate Huang. There’s also significant resistance to the idea in Congress, where Huang still faces significant questions about his role in chip exports to China-linked firms.
Reached by Politico, one senator called Huang’s reinstatement “one of the worst ideas I’ve heard today.”

articles.title: Why general-purpose AI falls short in agriculture
articles.text:
Why general-purpose AI falls short in agriculture
GenAI knows farming. It doesn't know your field.
In July, a farmer in Chuzhou, China, turned to an AI chatbot for help. He needed a plan to control weeds and pests in his fields. The model produced what a Futurism journalist later called “a Long Island iced tea of agrochemicals.” The farmer sprayed this cocktail across 25 acres of crops. By the next day, every single sesame seedling was dead, costing him roughly 150,000 yuan, or about 18,000 euros.
When Wu asked the chatbot what went wrong, the AI admitted it made mistakes. That mix it proposed was suitable for broadleaf weeds. But sesame is widely classified as a broadleaf plant, so it was never the right option to begin with. Another error was suggesting spraying the entire field instead of using the targeted application.
As horrible as it is, that is just one example of AI missing the mark. Researchers from the U.S., the U.K., Kenya, Nigeria, and Colombia recently tested whether generative AI could replace human agricultural advisors. Apparently, it can’t.
CPO & COO at OneSoil.
According to their paper published in Nature Food, the team first asked chatbots to recommend treatment for the fall armyworm, a pest that destroys corn crops worldwide. In response, OpenAI's GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 models provided highly ambiguous pesticide advice.
Next, the researchers simulated questions from cassava farmers in Nigeria. ChatGPT recommended specific herbicides but gave the wrong application timing. Following that advice would have killed the crops, threatening food security for millions of people, since Nigeria is Africa's most important cassava producer.
More frequent mistakes
What's more disturbing is that these mistakes might become more frequent. With rising labor, land, and equipment costs, many farmers can no longer afford professional advice. On top of that, there is a severe shortage of trained agricultural extensionists. Extension workers rarely reach the world's most isolated fields, such as those in South America and Africa, while farmers in those regions cannot travel hundreds of kilometers to attend seminars to improve their knowledge.
Instead, they often rely on extension agencies based in capital cities. But those lack both the funding and the staff to update their outdated guides or track new farming trends. So farmers turn to digital assistants. According to a recent McKinsey survey, roughly 17 percent of farmers worldwide already use generative AI in day-to-day decisions. That is more than any other new technology in the sector, including robotics and electric-powered machinery, Bloomberg reported.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
To be fair, AI itself is not the issue. The problem is that many farmers turn to general-purpose AI chatbots such as ChatGPT or Claude for advice. These tools know crop types, chemical classes, standard practices, and textbook planting calendars. But they are not trained specifically for agriculture purposes. For example, they won't ask for necessary data from the user before providing advice. As a result, their answers can sound professional while being useless or even harmful.
Training AI for agronomic purposes
There is a way to fix it: train an AI model for agronomic purposes. That takes two steps. First, the model learns from real data about a particular field: satellite images, past harvests, current weather and the crop's stage of growth. Second, it learns from working agronomists, who teach it how to respond in different situations. Those lessons also set limits on what the model will say. If it knows what crop is in the ground, it won't recommend a herbicide that is banned for that crop.
To better understand how this works, imagine a farmer who needs to spray a wheat field to get rid of weeds. A standard AI chatbot might draw on general textbooks and suggest a strong chemical. But because it cannot see the actual field, it does not know two critical things: that the wheat is at a fragile stage of growth where this chemical will ruin the crop, and that tomorrow's high winds will blow the spray onto neighboring land. Following the AI's advice could destroy the harvest.
By contrast, an AI connected to real data checks satellite photos and weather reports first. It automatically spots the high winds, recognizes that the wheat is too fragile for certain chemicals, and picks a safe alternative. It also asks questions when information is unclear or missing. Then it shows the farmer exactly where to spray, using coordinates or a task map that targets only the weed patches. In the end, this saves money and protects future yields.
Collecting information
Having said all that, expecting farmers to gather all this information and enter it into a generic AI tool isn't realistic. It takes time most growers don't have, as well as technical knowledge. Plus, farmers have no time to do inputs regularly.
This is why I believe a new market will emerge: of specialized agricultural AI assistants with built-in access to dashboards and satellite imagery, allowing seamless movement between data sources and making accurate, field-specific information far easier to access and act on.
This market is already taking shape. Some assistants can revisit satellite data layers, analyze them visually, and answer questions like “What has changed in the last 48 hours?” in plain language. Some products also let farmers send voice messages describing what they have applied. The agent files those details in the right parts of the system and keeps them as context. This makes it easier to keep field records up to date, which helps the model give more useful answers.
Such tools can help farmers make sense of their own field data, spot meaningful changes, and spend less time piecing together multiple sources. With some luck, a wave of these purpose-built tools will help eliminate costly mistakes in agriculture, so more farmers worldwide can thrive instead of losing their crops, money and spirit.

articles.title: Nvidia’s Q3 earnings hit the mark, without mentioning the whole Jensen Huang thing
articles.text:
Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress announced the company’s Q3 earnings on Tuesday, without initially mentioning former CEO Jensen Huang or the details of his departure, or possible attempt at a return. On the earnings call accompanying the release, board chair Harvey Jones kicked things off by saying the board “does not intend to reinstate Huang as CEO,” and that “we will not be addressing or taking questions on today’s call regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation and the ongoing investigation,” before Kress started with her comments on the results.
Nvidia’s Q3 earnings hit the mark, without mentioning the whole Jensen Huang thing
Nvidia’s Q3 revenue has more than doubled, with income from data centers up 110 percent from last year, to $107.6 billion.
As it predicted in the last financial update, Nvidia is now on the list of companies that have pulled in over $100 billion in a single quarter, with revenues of $115.8 billion, up 103 percent from the same period last year and higher than its expectation of $108 billion. This quarter’s figures include data center revenues of $107.6 billion, which were up 110 percent, and edge computing (which includes the consumer gaming PC business and devices like the new RTX Spark laptops) revenue of $8.2 billion, up 42 percent.
The company reported $65.3 billion in profit, a new record.
“Our momentum is real. NVIDIA is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people,” said Colette Kress, interim CEO and executive vice president and chief financial officer of NVIDIA. “Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater.”
In the fourth quarter, Nvidia expects revenues of $130 billion.

articles.title: IEEE Celebrates 10 Years of Incorporating Ethics Into AI Systems
articles.text:
Policymakers, technologists, and members of the public have raised concerns about the harm AI’s rapid advancement might cause to society. Their concerns include bias, data privacy violations, the spread of misinformation, and losing control of AI agents.
Those issues are relatively new to many people, but the IEEE Standards Association has been working for the past decade on ways to prioritize the responsible development of AI systems.
In 2016 IEEE SA launched the IEEE Global Initiative for Ethical Considerations in Autonomous and Intelligent Systems (A/IS) and published the Ethically Aligned Design report. EAD’s mission is to encourage everyone involved in designing autonomous and intelligent systems to prioritize human well-being by applying ethical considerations for the benefit of humanity.
Developed by a multidisciplinary community of experts from around the world, the report outlined eight foundational principles for A/IS. They include human rights, people’s well-being, and transparency. More than 100 leading AI ethics experts provided input. EAD’s Version II report was released in 2017. Both versions solicited public input and received hundreds of pages of feedback, according to John C. Havens, who was the global initiative’s founding executive director, and is now the global director for IEEE Planet Positive 2030. And by 2019, there were more than 400 contributors and the community continues to grow.
“Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE,” Havens says. “At the time it was released, there wasn’t anything like it.”
Since its launch, a series of standards has been developed to provide practical guidelines on designing, building, and deploying technology that prioritizes human values. Several AI ethics certification programs have been introduced.
This year marks the 10th anniversary of EAD’s first draft. To celebrate, IEEE SA recently launched a website, a podcast series, and a blog that reflect on the report’s achievements and impact.
Eight guiding principles
The word ethics is often used interchangeably with morality, but that is not the case in responsible AI systems design, according to EAD’s first version. The report includes insights from classical ethics traditions and value-based design methodologies to offer actionable recommendations for engineers developing AI tools.
The report established eight foundational general principles for designing autonomous systems: respecting human rights, prioritizing increased well-being as success criteria for development, empowering individuals with data agency to have control over their identity, effectiveness, transparency, accountability, awareness of misuse, and competence for the system creators.
The principles shift applied ethics to the design stage of AI systems, compared with being a concern after they’re released, the authors wrote.
A suite of standards
The IEEE 7000 series of standards has been developed based on EAD’s framework. Currently the series consists of 29 projects, 11 of which have been published, and more are still being added. They cover topics such as ethical system design model process (IEEE 7000-2021), AI system transparency (IEEE 7001-2021), data privacy (IEEE 7002-2022), algorithmic bias considerations (IEEE 7003-2024), the impact on people’s well-being (IEEE 7010-2020), machine-readable personal privacy requirements (IEEE 7012-2025), and systems that mimic human empathy (IEEE 7014-2024).
AI ethics certifications
IEEE SA offers a suite of ethics in AI programs including IEEE CertifAIEd, which includes two certifications: one for individuals and one for products.
The professional certification provides individuals with skills to assess autonomous and intelligent systems for adherence to IEEE’s methodology and ethics criteria.
“Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE.” —John C. Havens, founding executive director of the global initiative
The product certification program assesses whether an organization’s AI tool or system conforms to the criteria in the IEEE Ontological Specifications. A CertifiAIEd assessor evaluates the product to ensure it meets the criteria. Upon completion of the assessment, the owner submits it to the IEEE Conformity Assessment Program, which can certify it and issue the certification mark.
IEEE SA also recently released its Responsible AI for Children certification program. This program certifies that AI products for children have been independently tested and verified to meet design and ethics requirements.
New industry connections group
The IEEE Artificial Intelligence Systems (AIS) for Global Flourishing Collaborative Industry Collections group was formed to provide the resources, knowledge, and tools needed to prioritize people’s well-being to developers of AI systems. It has more than 200 members.
The collaborative describes its work as a practical, systems-level framework for responsible technology design that translates flourishing into applied methods, metrics, and tools that can be used throughout the AIS lifecycle.
The group is establishing guidelines for how to design, evaluate, and govern systems that can measurably improve human well-being and ecological sustainability.
Subcommittees are focused on cognition, education, faith, planetary care, spirituality, and other issues.
“The group is building directly off the well-being chapter of Ethically Aligned Design and the IEEE 7010 standard (Recommended Practice for Assessing the Impact of Autonomous and Intelligent Systems on Human Well-Being),” Havens says. “That’s on purpose because if human and planetary flourishing aren’t addressed first in design, then human well-being and planetary sustainability are afterthoughts.”
Podcasts and blogs
To mark the 10-year anniversary, IEEE SA created the five-part “Ethically Aligned Design: 10 Years of Impact” podcast series. It launched on 21 October. New episodes are being released every two weeks.
The episodes center around the vision for EAD, the process for selecting its foundational principles, and how they were translated into the IEEE 7000 standards.
The first podcast, “Origins of Ethically Aligned Design,” explored early efforts to make ethics a practical part of AI and autonomous system design. The experts discussed challenges, debates, global collaboration, and the real-world impact that helped move responsible technology from ethical principles toward actionable standards and practices.
The second podcast, “The Chapters and Committees” focuses on the multidisciplinary groups that worked on turning broad human values into practical guidance for AI and autonomous systems.
The podcast discussions serve as material for a thought leadership program that also includes blog articles about the IEEE 7000 series and educational resources to continue to raise awareness and support of this groundbreaking work.

She has a bachelor's degree in applied communication from Rider University, in Lawrenceville, N.J., and holds a master's degree in corporate and public communication from Monmouth University, in West Long Branch, N.J.

articles.title: Wo ist Walter? Künstler will den Wimmelbuchhelden mit KI, 3 GPUs und öffentlichen Kameras finden
articles.text:
Wo ist Walter? Künstler will ihn mit KI, 3 GPUs und 450 öffentlichen Kameras finden
Eine rot-weiß-gestreifte Bommelmütze auf dem Kopf, ein ebenso gestreifter Pullover am Leib, dazu eine runde Brille auf der Nase und ein verschmitztes Grinsen im Gesicht: Das ist Waldo (oder auch Wally genannt). Im deutschsprachigen Raum besser bekannt als Walter. Es gibt unzählige Bücher mit Wimmelbildern, in denen die simple Frage „Wo ist Walter?“ das Konzept auf den Punkt bringt. Die Bücher stammen ursprünglich von dem Briten Martin Handford, das erste erschien 1987. Seitdem erfreut die Suche nach Walter nicht nur Kinder, auch Erwachsene nehmen begeistert die Fährte auf. Es gibt inzwischen auch eine TV-Serie über die Figur und einige Videospiele.
Dazu kommt jetzt auch eine Art technisches Performance-Projekt auf globaler Basis mit dem Namen „Wally Finder“. Jedoch läuft die Suche nach der Figur mit dem signifikanten Outfit anders. Ausgedacht hat sich das der Belgier Dries Depoorter. Er ist Künstler und bindet in seine Ideen oft Technologie mit ein. Für den Wally-Finder greift er auf mehr als 450 ungesicherte, öffentliche Kameras zu und hebt in den Frames Menschen hervor, die ein Walter-Outfit tragen oder dem sehr nahekommt. Dass das funktioniert, hat er nicht zuletzt auch Künstlicher Intelligenz und drei GPU-Servern zu verdanken. Wie er das Projekt umgesetzt hat, was dafür technisch nötig war und was er den Menschen durch die Wally-Sucher vermitteln will, erklärt er im Interview.
MIT Technology Review: Wie sind Sie auf die Idee für den „Wally Finder“ gekommen? Sind Sie ein großer Fan von Wally?
Dries Depoorter: Ich mochte die Wimmelbücher schon immer. Als Kind habe ich Stunden damit verbracht, die Seiten zu durchforsten. Und seit Jahren führe ich Projekte mit ungesicherten Kameras durch, wie zum Beispiel „Jaywalking“ und „The Follower“. Ich glaube, so ist die Idee entstanden. Irgendwann haben sich meine Begeisterung für die Wally-Bücher und mein Interesse für die Kameras miteinander verbunden. Tausende offener Kameras, die Straßen und Plätze auf der ganzen Welt zeigen, sind wie eine riesige, echte „Wally“-Seite. Also habe ich mich gefragt, was passieren würde, wenn ich eine KI das Spiel aus dem Buch Tag und Nacht in der realen Welt spielen lassen würde.

articles.title: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
articles.text:
AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
Using AI to make bionic vision smarter and more precise, scientists are bringing the possibility of restoring sight to people with blindness one step closer to reality.
- Date:
- November 12, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Santa Barbara
- Summary:
- Scientists have developed an AI-powered approach that makes experimental bionic vision technology more precise, helping predict the flashes and shapes of light perceived by a blind man with a brain implant. By learning how an individual's brain responds to electrical stimulation, the technology could bring researchers closer to restoring some degree of sight to people with blindness.
- Share:
Artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences. Researchers from three institutions, including UC Santa Barbara, have demonstrated that AI can improve how precisely an experimental visual prosthesis stimulates the brain and predicts what a person perceives.
The team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information. By analyzing the brain's responses, the technology gave researchers greater control over neural activity and helped them better anticipate the visual sensations produced by the implant.
Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes. These devices could eventually become more effective by learning how each person's brain responds to stimulation rather than relying on predetermined settings.
"Building a model in the abstract is one thing," said Michael Beyeler, an associate professor of computer science and psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara. "Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab."
How Bionic Vision Could Bypass Damaged Eyes
For decades, scientists have worked to develop technologies capable of restoring some vision to people who are blind, although the results have generally been limited. Some experimental devices stimulate the retina, the layer of tissue at the back of the eye that detects light. Others attempt to activate parts of the visual system farther along the pathway that carries visual information to the brain.
Visual cortical prostheses work differently. Instead of depending on the eyes or optic nerves, they deliver electrical signals directly to the visual cortex. This approach could offer a potential solution for people whose visual pathways have been damaged but whose visual cortex can still respond to stimulation. Possible candidates include individuals who lost their sight because of strokes, neurodegenerative diseases, or traumatic brain injuries.
The ability to regain even limited vision could be especially meaningful for people who remember what it was like to see.
Beyeler highlighted those "who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision," adding, "For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back."
The new findings build on earlier computational research supported by Beyeler's 2022 National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director's New Innovator Award. The five-year, $2 million grant has supported his efforts to make artificial vision systems more accurate, predictable, and effective.
Scientists Test AI With a Brain Implant in a Blind Man
An important opportunity to test the technology came in 2024, when researchers from Beyeler's Bionic Vision Lab traveled to Spain. Their goal was to determine whether their computer models could improve the performance of a brain implant already being used in an experimental study.
At Hospital IMED Elche, the team worked with a 27-year-old man who had become blind following a traumatic brain injury. He had received an implant containing 96 electrodes arranged in an array within his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain in place for six months before being removed.
When researchers activated the electrodes using electrical current, the participant experienced visual sensations known as phosphenes. These can appear as spots, flashes, or shapes of light, sometimes resembling stars or fireworks.
Producing these sensations is possible, but making them consistent and predictable is much more difficult. The same electrical stimulation does not always trigger an identical response, and activating particular electrodes does not guarantee that the person will perceive a specific visual pattern.
To address this problem, the researchers trained a deep neural network, a type of AI designed to recognize complex patterns, to predict how the visual cortex would respond to different electrical stimulation settings. The model also considered the brain's resting activity immediately before stimulation, giving it information about the participant's current neural state.
Using these predictions, the researchers identified combinations of electrical signals that were most likely to produce particular patterns of brain activity.
AI Makes Bionic Vision More Precise
When the scientists tested the stimulation patterns selected by AI, the results were encouraging. The new approach generated the intended patterns of neural activity more accurately than the comparison methods while requiring less electrical current.
Another important discovery emerged when the team examined the relationship between brain activity and the participant's visual experiences. The patterns recorded directly from his brain were better predictors of what he perceived than the stimulation settings themselves.
This distinction matters because activating the brain is not the same as knowing what a person will see. Even when researchers can produce a desired neural response, they still need to understand how the brain transforms that activity into a conscious visual experience.
"Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image," Beyeler said. "But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation."
The findings suggest that future visual prostheses may need to do more than simply deliver electrical signals. They may also need to monitor how the brain reacts and use that feedback to continually improve stimulation.
Teaching Brain Implants to Adapt to Each Person
A key advantage of the implant used in the experiment was its ability to perform two tasks. It could stimulate the visual cortex with electrical current while simultaneously recording the resulting neural activity.
This allowed researchers to train their AI model using the brain's actual responses rather than relying exclusively on information about which electrodes were activated and how much current they delivered.
The participant also provided feedback about what he experienced. He reported whether he saw a phosphene and, during certain experiments, described its appearance, including its shape, size, brightness, and color.
Comparing these reports with the recorded brain activity revealed that neural responses contained more useful information about the perceived visual sensations than the electrical stimulation parameters alone.
The AI system also used measurements of resting brain activity to account for changes in the participant's neural state before each stimulation. This could be particularly valuable because the brain's response to electrical signals can vary over time, including from one day to the next.
By adapting stimulation to these changing conditions, future prostheses might provide more consistent visual experiences without requiring users to adjust to a rigid set of signals.
"A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe," Beyeler said. "It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around."
A Collaborative Step Toward Restoring Sight
The research brought together scientists from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU). Beyeler described the effort as "a true collaboration."
The project was led by co-first authors Pehuén Moure of ETH Zurich, Jacob Granley of UC Santa Barbara, and Fabrizio Grani of MHU. The supervising researchers were Beyeler, Shih-Chii Liu of ETH Zurich, and Eduardo Fernández of MHU. Their work forms part of a larger feasibility trial taking place in Spain.
Although the technology remains experimental and the participant's visual experiences were limited to flashes and shapes of light, the results demonstrate how AI could improve communication between artificial vision devices and the brain.
Rather than treating every brain as if it responds the same way, future bionic vision systems could learn from each individual and adjust their signals accordingly. That personalized approach may prove essential to developing implants that can eventually restore useful vision to people who have lost their sight.

Materials provided by University of California - Santa Barbara. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Deep learning-based control of electrically evoked activity in human visual cortex. Neuron, 2026; DOI: 10.1016/j.neuron.2026.07.006

articles.title: AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot
articles.text:
AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot
The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways
The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years.
The reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward.
“Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” says Peter McMahon, associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade.
Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing.
Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator.Optalysys
“I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” says Logan Wright, assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in New Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.”
Optics to inference’s rescue?
Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication.
Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N. N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors.
VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION
The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once.
The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.
Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.
But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.
McMahon says this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”
It’s also important to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.
“Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”
With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.
Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.
Bridging the gap in free space
The startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the company’s tech to beat GPUs.
Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.
To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory.
Vector-matrix multiplication with free-space optics
Chris Philpot
The Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector.
Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.
The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.
“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”
Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.
Neurophos
Bowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.
Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”
The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is currently choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.
Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”
Bridging the gap on-chip
Free-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.
“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”
Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.
“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.”
Vector-matrix multiplication with integrated photonics
Chris Philpot
One way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.
In Q.ANT’s approach, the input data is encoded into the phase and amplitude of light pulses via on-chip modulators. A vector in this scheme is represented as a sequence of such pulses, each representing one vector element. The light is guided around the chip with waveguides. The basic computational element is an interferometer: A waveguide splits into two paths, and the light beam traveling down one path is subjected to a phase shift, controlled by a set voltage. When the two paths recombine, the resulting interference performs a computation. Then, photodetectors and analog-to-digital converters turn the result back into digital data. The serialized vector-matrix multiplication approach is slower than Goodman’s computer, where the whole calculation happens at once. However, the slower speed can be mitigated by using multiple wavelengths at once, effectively encoding multiple vectors into light simultaneously.
Q.ANT’s Native Processing Server is already being used in research institutions like the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Jülich, both in Germany. Earlier this year, the company announced a commercial sale to the cloud provider Ionos. Similarly, Lightelligence’s PACE2 processor is capable of multiplying 128-by-128-element matrices. In a paper released in 2025, the company described vector-matrix multiplication at a 1-gigahertz frequency and 3-nanosecond latency, claiming two orders of magnitude lower latency than with traditional GPUs.
The energy advantage is yet to be conclusively demonstrated, however, and Q.ANT’s Förtsch admits there is still a ways to go. The main issue is the energy cost of analog-to-digital conversion and back. As long as a fast, low-energy converter does not exist, Förtsch says, “we don’t see realistic chances that…a general vector-matrix multiplication machine in optics makes sense.”
Beyond matrix-vector multiplication
Not everyone in the field is focused on matrix-vector multiplication, despite it being all the rage in the AI inference world. In fact, while the optical vector-matrix multiply idea goes back to the 1970s, other computations with optics have been investigated as far back as the 1950s. For example, a Fourier transform—a common operation that decomposes a complex wave or signal into its constituent frequencies—can be done in optics with a single lens.
“A digital chip has to approximate [Fourier transforms] in many small steps, using hundreds to thousands of transistors and more compute cycles,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Models that use such nonlinear functions can reach the same or better accuracy with fewer parameters and fewer operations.”
Even though Q.ANT’s optical processor has been used for traditional vector-matrix multiplication, the company believes its greatest advantages lie in alternative AI architectures that leverage more complex functions. “Tasks such as image classification and segmentation rely heavily on operations like Fourier series, transformations, and other nonlinear functions, which photonics handles natively. We see similar potential in generative AI, especially image and video generation,” Förtsch says.
The Israel-based startup LightSolver is also targeting algorithms that are a more natural fit for its device. “If you look at propagating electromagnetic waves, essentially, they are running differential equations in their nature,” says Ruti Ben-Shlomi, CEO and cofounder of LightSolver. She says differential equations can be solved much faster and with higher energy efficiency on the company’s laser processing unit (LPU) than on a traditional computer.
LightSolver’s LPU is an interesting twist on the Goodman optical-computer design. It has input light, a programmable membrane in the form of a spatial light modulator, and output light, but the whole thing is placed in a cavity, where light bounces back and forth many times before reaching a steady state. In addition, the team places a gain medium inside the cavity. This gain medium functions much like those found inside a laser, causing the bouncing light to build up in intensity.
LightSolver, a startup based in Israel, is using free-space optics to quickly solve differential equations by harnessing the natural properties of light. LightSolver
Once a particular problem is encoded into the modulator, the gain medium is stimulated to emit random photons. They bounce back and forth, increasing in intensity when passing through the gain medium again, experiencing preprogrammed changes through the modulator and interacting with one another until they reach a steady state—the solution. Then, a simple camera takes a picture of the steady-state result. Using emulation, the LightSolver team recently showed that their LPU can solve differential equations 40 to 80,000 times as fast as a GPU, depending on the workflow. They are now working on explicitly benchmarking the energy improvements.
LightSolver’s team is currently working on AI applications for its LPU as well, using the company’s own algorithm to do image generation from text. “We’re not doing vector-matrix multiplication very fast. We are doing something different. We need to assume that the way you train the model, and you then do inference, is completely different. But if you do it differently, you’ll be able to do image generation with dramatic energy-consumption decrease and speedup,” Ben-Shlomi says. LightSolver has a working prototype of its LPU, and the team is working on a larger, rack-mountable box.
Computing in transit
Yet another way to leverage light’s particular strengths is being pursued by Optalysys, a startup based in Leeds, England. Nick New, founder and chief product officer, has a background in free-space optics, and so he understood that taking a Fourier transform is very easy to do with light.
The key idea behind Optalysys’s technology is taking that Fourier capability of optics in free space and making it work on-chip. “Rather than using a lens these days, we have our own component, which is a passive component in the plane of the silicon that does that same job,” New says. And by cleverly designing that component with multiple outputs, the team figured out how to perform different operations as well. “Because of how the Fourier transform response is generated, you can actually pull out different mathematical operations from it,” New says. “We can produce very large, high-precision digital functions at superhigh efficiencies, using our analog photonics approach.”
“We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.” —Nick New, Optalysis
Instead of redesigning an accelerator from scratch, Optalysys is targeting a piece of the AI workload that’s often already in the optical domain: networking. In the data center, racks of computers are connected to each other with fiber optics, and the optical connections are increasingly getting closer and closer to the GPUs and CPUs themselves.
Some computations already happen while the data is en route. These computations, which include combining results from multiple GPUs, are executed inside network switch cards. But the cards naturally use power to do that math. With passive optical components, these computations could be done essentially for free.
New says that in addition to communication between GPUs, Optalysys’s technology could be used to facilitate a GPU’s communication with memory, doing things like compression and format conversion on the fly. Going back to AI inference, this approach could improve the decode part of the workload. Unlike prefill, decode is memory bound: The most costly part is shuffling model data in and out of memory. “We’re more focused on the memory-bound applications, which fits very well with this principle of adding processing into the communication path,” New says. “We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.”
The likely future of optical computing
How likely are optical computers to replace GPUs in the data center? Yale’s Wright is not too optimistic. “The direction of algorithm development is not going to be a direction that is automatically favorable for optics,” he says. “In fact, it’s most likely to go in the opposite direction, because [AI model developers] want it to work better on GPUs.”
However, even if our AI queries aren’t going to be computed in light in the next few years, that investment in the technology won’t be in vain. Says Wright, “The reason that I and many other people in the field are at least somewhat optimistic is that there’s real investment from companies like Nvidia and TSMC in developing co-packaged silicon photonics—not for computing, but for circuit switching and interconnects, and that just kind of opens the door to do a little bit more in the future.”
Whether that technology ends up crunching vector-matrix multiplication, doing bespoke simulations, or performing in-network computations, the computing ecosystem seems ripe for a variety of approaches. “We see the data center of the future as heterogeneous: CPUs, GPUs and photonic NPUs [native processing units] each take on the tasks they are best suited for,” says Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Running each task on the most efficient hardware can significantly reduce energy use and operating costs.”

articles.title: Qwen4-Max : l'astuce géniale d'Alibaba pour booster son IA sans faire exploser les calculs
articles.text:
Pour enrichir son nouveau modèle d'IA sans alourdir les calculs dans les mêmes proportions, Alibaba lui adjoint une vaste table de représentations numériques. Une approche économe en calcul, mais qui demande de la place pour stocker les poids.
Qwen4-Max ne s’arrête pas aux 2 400 milliards de paramètres mis en avant par Alibaba. À ce réseau principal s’ajoute une table de 328 milliards de paramètres, dans laquelle l’IA vient puiser au fil du texte. À elle seule, cette table compte plus du double des 125 milliards de paramètres du réseau principal de Qwen3.8-Flash-Next. Avec son nouveau modèle lancé le 16 novembre, le géant chinois cherche ainsi à augmenter les capacités de son IA sans faire croître dans les mêmes proportions le travail des processeurs.
Une table dans laquelle l’IA vient chercher des représentations du texte
Pour comprendre le principe, il faut revenir aux tokens, ces fragments dans lesquels le modèle découpe le texte. Un n-gram est une suite de n tokens consécutifs. Là où un embedding classique associe une représentation numérique à un token, la table n-gram tient aussi compte des tokens qui le précèdent. Elle fournit donc au modèle des représentations de petits groupes, apprises pendant l’entraînement, pour compléter le traitement du fragment en cours.
Prenons, pour simplifier, l’expression « carte mémoire ». Si la suite de tokens correspondante possède une entrée dans la table, l’IA peut y récupérer la représentation du groupe. Elle ne consulte pas une définition rédigée à l’avance, mais un vecteur numérique qu’elle exploite dans ses calculs.
Le modèle ne consulte que les entrées dont il a besoin. La table peut ainsi contenir un grand nombre de paramètres sans alourdir beaucoup les calculs à chaque token. Alibaba avait déjà exploré cette piste avec Qwen3.8-Flash-Next et ses 51 milliards de paramètres d’embeddings n-gram. Sur ce modèle, la table peut être conservée dans la mémoire vive de la machine plutôt que de monopoliser celle du GPU. Les entrées nécessaires sont alors préchargées pendant que ce dernier poursuit ses calculs.
Moins de calcul ne veut pas dire un modèle léger
Le réseau principal de Qwen4-Max suit une autre voie pour limiter le travail à chaque étape. Grâce à son architecture à mélange d’experts, ou MoE, il ne mobilise que 71 milliards de paramètres par token, environ un quart de moins que Qwen3.8-Max. Les experts sollicités changent toutefois selon le token traité : les poids des autres ne peuvent pas être simplement oubliés puisque l’infrastructure doit pouvoir y accéder à leur tour.
C’est ce qui sépare l’économie de calcul de l’encombrement du modèle. Même en représentant chaque paramètre sur 4 bits, les seuls poids du réseau principal occuperaient théoriquement environ 1,2 To. Il faudrait encore ajouter la table n-gram, les données nécessaires à la quantification et la mémoire de travail utilisée pendant l’exécution.
À titre de comparaison, les PC RTX Spark montent à 128 Go de mémoire unifiée. Dans notre test de l’ASUS ProArt P16 RTX Spark, les 64 Go de la machine permettaient déjà de faire tourner Qwen3.8-27B quantifié en 4 bits, notamment pour synthétiser de la documentation. Un usage local bien concret, mais avec un modèle d’une tout autre taille.
Pour Qwen4-Max, ces calculs restent de toute façon théoriques. Alibaba propose l’accès par API et dans ses applications, sans avoir publié les poids. En août, le groupe avait attendu neuf jours après le lancement du service pour mettre en ligne Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B, le modèle texte sur lequel repose Qwen3.8-Max. Il promet cette fois des Qwen4 plus petits à poids ouverts. Leur arrivée permettra de voir ce que cette architecture peut apporter à nos machines, et combien de place il faudra réellement lui faire.
Source : Alibaba Cloud
Un embedding classique associe à chaque token (fragment de texte) un vecteur numérique fixe utilisé par le modèle. Une table d’embeddings n‑gram étend ce principe à des séquences courtes de tokens (par exemple 2 à 5 tokens), ce qui permet de représenter non seulement un mot, mais aussi une expression et son contexte immédiat. Le modèle peut alors lire directement une représentation vectorielle d’un groupe fréquent plutôt que de tout reconstruire uniquement via les couches du réseau. Techniquement, c’est une grande mémoire d’indexation : on récupère quelques vecteurs pertinents, au lieu de faire intervenir tous les paramètres à chaque étape. Le gain est surtout en calcul, pas en taille de stockage, puisque la table peut devenir énorme.
Dans un réseau dense, une grande part des paramètres participe à des multiplications à chaque token, ce qui coûte cher en FLOPs et en bande passante GPU. Une table n‑gram fonctionne plutôt comme un accès mémoire : on sélectionne quelques entrées (par ID) et on les injecte dans le traitement, ce qui revient à lire des vecteurs plutôt qu’à exécuter des couches supplémentaires. Le coût devient proportionnel au nombre d’entrées consultées, pas à la taille totale de la table. En contrepartie, il faut gérer une forte pression sur la mémoire (RAM/VRAM) et sur les transferts de données, car les poids doivent rester accessibles rapidement. C’est donc une optimisation “compute” qui peut déplacer le goulot d’étranglement vers le stockage et l’I/O.
MoE (mélange d’experts) découpe le modèle en sous-réseaux spécialisés (experts) et n’en active qu’une fraction pour chaque token, via un mécanisme de routage. On parle alors de paramètres actifs par token : le modèle ne calcule qu’avec les experts sélectionnés, ce qui réduit le coût de calcul à l’inférence. En revanche, les paramètres des experts non activés ne disparaissent pas : ils doivent rester stockés et prêts à être appelés pour d’autres tokens. Résultat : la facture en VRAM/RAM (ou en stockage si on stream les poids) reste élevée, même si les FLOPs par token baissent. C’est la différence classique entre économie de calcul et encombrement mémoire du modèle.

articles.title: iPhone 18 Pro, AirPods Pro 3, TV Mini LED : voici 6 produits en promo chez Carrefour qui vont faire de parfaits cadeaux pour les fêtes — Frandroid
articles.text:
En plus des remises immédiates, Carrefour permet de cagnotter de l’argent sur la carte de fidélité de l’enseigne. Ce bonus peut ensuite être utilisé afin de régler des achats ultérieurs chez Carrefour. Ou autrement dit : utilisé pour faire ses courses.
Pendant la période du Black Friday, Carrefour propose des remises immédiates et du cagnottage Club Carrefour sur de nombreux appareils high-tech. Dans certains cas, il est même possible de cumuler les deux. Voici six offres qui sont actuellement mises en avant sur le site du magasin :
- L’iPhone 18 Pro (noir) coûte 1 479 euros et permet de cagnotter 221,85 euros sur la carte Carrefour (également disponible en coloris Bordeaux) ;
- Les AirPods Pro 3 passent de 249 à 214 euros grâce à 35 euros de remise immédiate et s’accompagnent de 32,10 euros supplémentaires crédités sur la carte ;
- L’enceinte JBL Charge Essential 2 revient à 79,99 euros au lieu de 99,99 euros, une remise immédiate de 20 euros à laquelle s’ajoutent 20 euros de cagnottage ;
- La montre Samsung Galaxy Watch7 passe de 309,99 euros à 119,99 euros ;
- Le téléviseur Samsung Mini LED 4K est proposé à 349,99 euros au lieu de 449,99 euros ;
- Le PC portable Asus passe de 899,99 à 699,99 euros et permet de récupérer 70 euros sur la carte, soit 270 euros d’avantages au total.
Pour être sûr de profiter au maximum de ces bonnes affaires, assurez-vous d’avoir activé votre carte de fidélité au sein de votre espace client Carrefour.
L’iPhone 18 Pro rapporte 221,85 euros sur la carte Carrefour
Annoncé et sorti en septembre dernier, l’iPhone 18 Pro (version 256 Go, coloris noir) conserve son prix de 1 479 euros sur le catalogue de Carrefour (disponible aussi en coloris Bordeaux). Il donne droit à un avantage fidélité de 15 %, soit 221,85 euros crédités directement sur votre carte Carrefour après l’achat.
Pour son dernier iPhone, Apple a travaillé là où ça compte. À savoir de meilleures photos de nuit et moins de passages par la prise de courant. Son nouvel objectif principal capte davantage de lumière pour mieux saisir les sujets en mouvement et conserver les détails en soirée. Sa puce A20 Pro, accompagnée d’un refroidissement revu, permet de jouer plus longtemps sans voir les performances chuter.
Surtout, ce modèle de 6,3 pouces tient désormais une journée et demie en usage courant, avec une recharge à 50 % en moins de 20 minutes, comme mesuré lors du test de Frandroid.
Les AirPods Pro 3 cumulent deux types de réduction
Pour accompagner l’iPhone 18 Pro ou un autre iPhone, vous pouvez acheter les AirPods Pro 3 à bon prix chez Carrefour. Ces écouteurs sans fil bénéficient d’abord d’une remise immédiate de 35 euros qui fait passer leur prix de 249 euros à 214 euros. Carrefour ajoute ensuite 15 % de cagnottage, ce qui correspond à 32,10 euros versés sur la carte de fidélité. Au total, l’avantage atteint 67,10 euros.
Les AirPods Pro 3 sont la référence des écouteurs sans fil, avec une réduction du bruit parmi les plus efficaces du marché. Dans les transports, les grondements s’effacent pour laisser toute la place à la musique. Au bureau, ils font taire les collègues trop bruyants.
Le son est riche, précis, avec des basses profondes et des voix naturelles. Leur mode Transparence restitue les sons environnants comme si l’on ne portait rien. Cette génération gagne aussi deux heures d’autonomie, pour atteindre jusqu’à huit heures d’écoute avec la réduction du bruit activée, selon Apple.
L’enceinte JBL Charge Essential 2 revient à 79,99 euros
L’enceinte JBL bénéficie, elle aussi, d’un double avantage. Pour commencer, une remise immédiate de 20 euros ramène son prix à 79,99 euros au lieu de 99,99 euros. Ensuite, 20 euros sont également crédités sur la carte Carrefour après l’achat. Vous payez donc bien 79,99 euros, mais l’avantage total est de 40 euros.
La JBL Charge Essential 2 est une enceinte portable Bluetooth au son puissant. Ses basses généreuses accompagnent aussi bien une soirée entre amis qu’un week-end en extérieur. Étanche (IPX7), elle résiste à une immersion temporaire, et JBL annonce jusqu’à 20 heures d’autonomie. Elle peut même recharger votre téléphone : pratique quand la batterie menace de couper la playlist.
La montre connectée Samsung Galaxy Watch7 à moins de 120 euros
La Samsung Galaxy Watch7 de 44 mm bénéficie de l’une des remises immédiates les plus spectaculaires de cette opération Carrefour : elle passe de 309,99 euros à 119,99 euros, ce qui correspond à une réduction de 190 euros. En revanche, pas de cagnottage en vue ici, ce qui peut se comprendre.
La Samsung Galaxy Watch7 date de 2024, mais elle a encore de beaux arguments au poignet. Surtout à ce prix : lancée à 349 euros dans sa version Bluetooth de 44 mm, elle passe sous les 120 euros pendant le Black Friday. Pour ce tarif, on récupère une montre au design soigné, avec un bel écran AMOLED lisible en plein soleil et une interface simple à prendre en main.
Au quotidien, elle permet de payer ses courses, de répondre à un message WhatsApp ou de suivre son itinéraire sans sortir son téléphone Android de la poche. Son vrai point fort, c’est aussi son suivi cardiaque, dont le test de Frandroid a salué la précision, même lorsque l’effort s’intensifie.
Le téléviseur Samsung Mini LED 4K perd 100 euros
Enfin, le téléviseur Samsung 43M1EH passe de 449,99 à 349,99 euros grâce à une remise immédiate de 100 euros, sans avantage fidélité supplémentaire. Si vous désirez vous équiper d’un téléviseur connecté de 43 pouces, cela reste une offre attractive.
Sortie plus tôt cette année, cette smart TV Samsung associe une dalle LCD de 108 cm de diagonale à rétroéclairage Mini LED à une définition 4K avec prise en charge du HDR10+. Ce rétroéclairage Mini LED gère plus finement la luminosité et le contraste qu’un modèle LED classique. L’interface sous Tizen donne, quant à elle, accès à de nombreuses applications de divertissement, et les trois entrées HDMI permettent d’y relier des consoles de jeux et d’autres appareils.
Voir condition sur Carrefour.fr pour plus de détails sur les offres.

articles.title: Lakshmi Venu seeks formal partition of TVS Venu Srinivasan family assets
articles.text:
Lakshmi Venu seeks formal partition of TVS Venu Srinivasan family assets
In a partition notice to her father, she has called upon him, as head of the family, to discharge his fiduciary duties and give effect to a fair and lawful partition.
Lakshmi Venu, daughter of industrialist Venu Srinivasan, has formally sought partition of the joint family assets of a branch of the TVS family.
In a partition notice to her father, she has called upon him, as head of the family, to discharge his fiduciary duties and give effect to a fair and lawful partition.
Lakshmi, in her statement on Monday, asserted that, under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, as amended in 2005, she is entitled to her rightful share in the joint family property and has an independent right to seek its partition.
Her claim is also founded on the equal rights of daughters recognised under Section 6 of the Act.
Stating that the assets for which she seeks partition include the family interests held through the VS Trust and other holding vehicles and structures, she said, "These encompass the businesses and assets allotted to the Venu Srinivasan branch under the 2020 TVS family arrangement, including interests in TVS Holdings, TVS Motor Company, TVS Credit Services and Sundaram-Clayton".
Lakshmi maintained that the larger TVS family arrangement did not constitute a partition within the Venu Srinivasan family. No settlement or partition of the assets within her immediate family was ever initiated, let alone concluded.
In her view, management does not confer exclusive ownership or extinguish lawful rights of other family members.
Lakshmi contended that she is being wrongfully denied her rightful share of the joint family property and alleged that the concentration of beneficial interest in favour of her brother was to the exclusion of her own lawful rights.
She regarded these actions not only as a breach of law but also as a breach of trust."Patriarchy has no place in law or in a progressive India. The rights of daughters to joint family property cannot be overridden through unilateral decisions or corporate arrangements", she added.
Reiterating her preference for an amicable and equitable resolution, Lakshmi has called for the matter to be settled with fairness, dignity and respect for the rights of all family members.
Meanwhile, another statement from Mallika Srinivasan, MD, Tractors and Farm Equipment Limited, supporting her daughter Lakshmi Venu's legitimate right in the family assets, said, "It is unfortunate that requests for an amicable settlement have not so far progressed in a meaningful and timely way".
She further said, "As a mother, to me, a son and daughter are equal in every respect. I do believe that Lakshmi has a legitimate share of the family assets, not unequal to that of (Lakshmi's brother) Sudarshan’s. I reiterate that this is a matter to be settled, in the interests of all stakeholders, through transparent dialogue, with equity, clarity and amity. I sincerely hope that we can move forward constructively, with grace and dignity".

articles.title: Coup dur pour Audi : la très attendue berline électrique est repoussée à 2029
articles.text:
Audi en retard ? Oh, jamais de la vie ! Pour preuve, la marque avait prévu le coup en annonçant une A4 électrique il y a maintenant quatre ans, histoire de tailler des croupières à la Tesla Model 3. BMW et Mercedes avaient aussi des plans similaires dans les cartons, sans encore avancer quoi que ce soit à l’époque. Les anneaux avaient donc une belle avance. Hélas, les années sont passées sans grandes nouvelles.
Et les deux grands rivaux ont dégainé entre temps les i4, i3 et Classe C sans aucune réaction de la part d’Audi. Pire encore, il s’avère que les modèles précités sont d’indéniables réussites. Où est donc passée l’A4 électrique ? Aux oubliettes ? Non, bien heureusement, mais il faudra en revanche se montrer patient pour espérer la découvrir. D’après Autocar, la berline devrait débarquer d’ici… 2029. On voit déjà BMW et Mercedes sabrer le champagne.
Problèmes financiers et plateforme inédite : les raisons de la douche froide
Quelle est donc la raison d’un tel retard ? Audi a voulu faire les choses bien avec une plateforme inédite, la Scalable Systems, pour armer au mieux son modèle. Sauf que les problèmes financiers traversés par le groupe Volkswagen ont sérieusement contrecarré les plans de la marque. L’A4 devait être présentée en 2026, elle le sera finalement trois ans plus tard. La douche froide, en quelque sorte…
Qui dit nouvelle plateforme dit bien souvent nouveau logiciel. Et ce dernier connaît aussi d’importantes difficultés de développement. Rien d’inédit dans le groupe, car on se rappelle encore du lancement assez chaotique de l’ID.3 et de la Golf, qui avaient rencontré de gros soucis à ce sujet. Et la situation est encore plus compliquée pour Audi aujourd’hui car le nouveau logiciel est conçu étroitement avec Rivian.
Logiciel complexe avec Rivian et casse-tête technique
Des va-et-vient incessants sont donc nécessaires avec ce partenaire pour ajuster minutieusement chaque détail. Cela prend évidemment du temps. Pour optimiser le confort, Audi voulait aussi des caves à pieds plus profondes, ce qui empêche alors la création d’un plancher plat traditionnel. Les ingénieurs ont donc dû repenser la structure des batteries et des machines électriques pour satisfaire le cahier des charges.
L’auto, elle, devrait adopter une silhouette proche de l’A6 avec une ligne fuyante optimisant l’aérodynamisme, et donc l’autonomie. Nous n’avons encore aucune donnée technique, mais il est possible que le véhicule propose un rayon d’action dépassant les 700 km. Ce serait nécessaire vu que l’i3 atteint sans peine les 912 km et la Classe C touche les 760 km. Rendez-vous d’ici quelques années pour en savoir plus sur le sujet, donc !
