articles.title: NVIDIA Announces Rubin HPC: Science-Focused Server GPU to Arrive in 2028
articles.text:
Adding to a busy SC26 conference, NVIDIA has announced that they are developing a new GPU that will be targeted specifically at high-performance computing workloads. Aptly named the Rubin HPC, the future chip will be an HPC optimized version of the company’s Rubin GPU architecture. It would mark NVIDIA’s first significant HPC-class part since the Hopper generation almost 4 years ago.
This week’s announcement comes amidst a broader degree of soul searching that has been taking place over the part couple of years about the future of classic HPC workloads and the hardware that will run them. With commercial GPU server demand shifting over to AI-related tasks and low precision math over the last half-decade, server GPU designs have been favoring large arrays of tensor cores and other design choices that play better to AI needs. This has left traditional science and engineering users with fewer options than they have previously enjoyed, as the bulk of the prior decade saw server GPU designs treat HPC as a first-class citizen, if not a top customer.
Consequently, NVIDIA’s announcement of a dedicated HPC chip is a significant one. After the company all but sat out the HPC market with its Blackwell generation of parts, there was a question whether the leader of the AI revolution would even bother with the smaller HPC market. The answer to that turns out to be an unambiguous “yes,” though not until 2028 when the Rubin HPC chip is released. Nonetheless, it is a clear signal that NVIDIA does not intend to permanently secede the HPC (or supercomputer) market to rivals like AMD and Intel, who have been splitting up the market in recent years.
Rubin HPC: 50K+ CUDA Cores, Coming In 2028
With NVIDIA’s Rubin HPC chip not slated to arrive until 2028, this week’s announcement from the company (and a very visible VP of Hyperscale and HPC, Ian Buck) is in effect a teaser with more details to come. The company only had a few key details to share about the chip for this week’s announcement.
The headline news here is that NVIDIA’s future HPC chip will over more than 50,000 CUDA cores – NVIDIA’s ALU arrays for classic vector/SIMD processing. This is around twice as many CUDA cores as NVIDIA’s current flagship Rubin SoC, and it is of great importance to the HPC market as few HPC workloads can make heavy use of matrix multiplication and NVIDIA’s tensor cores. An ideal HPC processor needs to be a great vector processing machine and not (just) a tensor processing machine, so the announcement of a large number of CUDA cores underscores just what kind of GPU this will be.
Painting broader strokes about the design of the rest of the GPU at this time, NVIDIA is not sharing any more details about expected performance or the memory subsystem for the HPC chip. Instead, the company is touting a “balanced design” that emphasizes growing compute and data movement capabilities together, rather than jump ramping up compute throughput on its own.
This is (presumably) a reference to the chip’s other marquee feature, which is NVLink 7 support. NVIDIA’s current Rubin server GPU is on NVLink 6; in fact, it is the first chip to offer it. Which means that Rubin HPC’s scale-up networking technology will be a generation beyond that when it launches in 2028.
Reading between the lines a bit, the high-level specifications for Rubin HPC seem to be more closely tied to NVIDIA’s mid-generation refresh part for the Rubin lineup, Rubin Ultra. With it not set to be available for another year, there is only a paucity of information available on that chip as well, but most notably we already know that it is going to be the first chip to ship with NVLink 7 support. Which lends credit to the idea that the 2028 Rubin HPC chip following it will be closer to a Rubin Ultra derivative than it will be of the original Rubin server chip.
That 2028 timeframe also lines up with giving Rubin HPC access to newer HBM4e memory, rather than the HBM4 used on the current Rubin server chip.
Past that, NVIDIA has also included a render of the chip in their SC26 presentation as well as on their newsroom article, which showcases a chip that looks very similar to their current Rubin GPU renders. NVIDIA chip renders are often more aspirational or illustrative than technical this far out, but if it is at least physically accurate then we are looking at 8 stacks of HBM spread out across multiple dies, the same as the current Rubin server chip.
Finally, for this week’s announcement NVIDIA has very briefly touted what they are calling a “sparse data acceleration” capability to keep the GPU cores fed, though with no other details on how this might work. The company’s tensor cores have long supported sparse matrices, though this would seem to be something beyond that, especially with the emphasis on vector math and CUDA cores.
| NVIDIA HPC Accelerator Specification Comparison |  |  |  |  |  | 
|  | Rubin HPC | B200 | H200 |  |  | 
| CUDA Cores | >50000 | 18944 | 16896 |  |  | 
| Tensor Cores | Fewer? | 592 | 528 |  |  | 
| Memory Clock | HBM4E? | 8Gbps HBM3E | 6.4Gbps HBM3 |  |  | 
| Memory Bus Width | 2x 8192-bit? | 2x 4096-bit | 6144-bit |  |  | 
| Memory Bandwidth | TBD | 8TB/sec | 4.8TB/sec |  |  | 
| VRAM | TBD | 192GB | 141GB |  |  | 
| FP32 Vector | TBD | 75 TFLOPS | 67 TFLOPS |  |  | 
| FP64 Vector | A Whole Lot | 37 TFLOPS | 34 TFLOPS |  |  | 
| FP64 Tensor | TBD | 37 TFLOPS | 67 TFLOPS |  |  | 
| INT8/FP8 Tensor | TBD | 9 P(FL)OPS | 3.96 P(FL)OPS |  |  | 
| Interconnect | NVLink 7 | NVLink 5 18 Links (1800GB/sec) | NVLink 4 18 Links (900GB/sec) |  |  | 
| GPU | Rubin HPC | B200 | GH100 |  |  | 
| Transistor Count | ? | 208B (2x104B) | 80B |  |  | 
| Manufacturing Process | TSMC 3nm? | TSMC 4NP | TSMC 4N |  |  | 
| Architecture | Rubin | Blackwell | Hopper |  |  | 
In lieu of specific performance figures, NVIDIA is at least emphasizing that Rubin HPC will be applicable to a wide range of precisions, from NVFP4 all the way up to FP64. While FP64 (and to a lesser extent, FP32) are the biggest focuses for classic HPC workloads, more recent software efforts have looked at lower precision math as well, if only to account for how GPU hardware has changed over the years. While it was always extremely unlikely that NVIDIA would remove low precision math format support entirely, if only for binary compatibility reasons, the emphasis on supporting the full range of precisions implies that we should not expect to see NVIDIA too heavily compromise them, either.
Still, the top line figure to watch here is going to be FP64 performance, both for vector and tensor operations. NVIDIA has essentially plateaued at a bit under 40 TFLOPS for FP64 since Hopper (with Blackwell Ultra being especially poor here at less than 2 TFLOPS), so a fresh chip with a much larger number of CUDA cores would give NVIDIA the means to significantly ramp up their FP64 performance, depending in large part on just how many FP64 CUDA cores they bake into the architecture. And for that matter, how much die space they take away from tensor cores to free up the space for that FP64 hardware.
Final Words
Wrapping things up, the announcement of their Rubin HPC GPU means that NVIDIA is going to be firmly putting its hat back into the ring for HPC after something of an absence over the last few years. With the company so heavily focused on AI performance with the Blackwell generation, the Rubin generation marks a chance to reset their position in the market, not to mention to take advantage of the technologies they have developed for it. NVIDIA will not be without competition, however, as AMD is going to be launching their HPC-focused Instinct MI430X accelerator in 2027, and Intel is preparing their PCIe-based GPU D-Series. Which means that for NVIDIA, they will have a fight on their hands if they want to retake a large portion of the HPC market or its close cousin, the classic supercomputer market.

articles.title: Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string
articles.text:
Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string
- Date:
- November 11, 2026
- Source:
- ETH Zurich
- Summary:
- Researchers have created a quantum computer that stores information in microscopic vibrations, potentially making quantum machines smaller, more powerful, and better at preserving information. The breakthrough successfully demonstrated advanced quantum calculations and could help overcome major barriers to practical quantum computing.
- Share:
A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.
Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a new form of computer memory.
By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," says Yiwen Chu.
The breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.
Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers
The researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an important role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.
Chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.
The major difference lies in how that information is stored.
"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.
Quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are currently beyond their practical capabilities.
Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better
One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.
In the new system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.
Many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.
However, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.
Mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.
Another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.
New Quantum Computer Passes Major Tests
The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.
The achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.
To evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.
"The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.
Successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments showed that the new architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.
A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers
One of the most significant findings is that the new system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.
However, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.
Chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.
Practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising new route toward making those machines a reality.
Story Source:
Materials provided by ETH Zurich. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Yu Yang, Igor Kladarić, Martynas Skrabulis, Michael Eichenberger, Stefano Marti, Simon Storz, Jonathan Esche, Raquel García Bellés, Max-Emanuel Kern, Andraz Omahen, Arianne Brooks, Marius Bild, Matteo Fadel, Yiwen Chu. Mechanical resonator–based quantum computing. Science, 2026; 392 (6801): 972 DOI: 10.1126/science.aef4139

articles.title: Tesla tiene más competencia: Mercedes-Benz prepara un nuevo sistema de conducción asistida
articles.text:
Mercedes-Benz anunció dos funciones que ayudarán a sus vehículos a desplazarse por autopistas y rutas urbanas. La tecnología permitirá conducir con las manos fuera del volante en determinadas carreteras y asistir al conductor durante trayectos de punto a punto. La compañía planea desplegarla en Estados Unidos y Alemania entre finales de 2026 y 2027.
La automotriz alemana presentó una nueva generación de sistemas de asistencia bajo la marca MB.DRIVE. Su propuesta incluye Hands-free Assist, para circular por autopistas con las manos fuera del volante bajo ciertas condiciones, y MB.DRIVE ASSIST PRO, que apoyará al conductor a lo largo de una ruta, incluso en zonas urbanas con tráfico denso.
Mercedes busca competir con tecnologías como Full Self-Driving (FSD) de Tesla, pero sus funciones no convierten al auto en un vehículo autónomo. La empresa subraya que el conductor sigue siendo responsable de manejar, debe vigilar el tráfico y estar preparado para tomar el control en cualquier momento.
Asistencia para autopistas y recorridos urbanos
Hands-free Assist permitirá retirar las manos del volante en autopistas compatibles, cuando las condiciones de operación lo permitan. El sistema está diseñado para funcionar a velocidades de hasta 130 kilómetros por hora. También se complementará con Proactive Lane Change Assist, una función que puede iniciar cambios de carril para adelantar a un vehículo más lento o seguir la ruta indicada por la navegación.
Aunque las manos puedan separarse del volante en esos tramos, Mercedes mantiene la supervisión humana como requisito. El conductor debe prestar atención a la vía y responder si el sistema se lo pide o si surge una situación que requiera intervención. La compañía anunció que estas funciones llegarán a Alemania antes de que termine 2026; su despliegue en Estados Unidos está previsto para 2027.
La función urbana MB.DRIVE ASSIST PRO ofrecerá asistencia desde el punto de partida hasta el destino ingresado en el navegador. Puede ayudar al auto a cambiar de carril, incorporarse al carril correcto, girar en intersecciones y detenerse o avanzar ante los semáforos. También apoya al conductor cuando el recorrido sale de una autopista y continúa por calles urbanas.
Para operar, el sistema combina 27 componentes de percepción: 10 cámaras, cinco radares y 12 sensores ultrasónicos. La información se procesa en una computadora con una capacidad de hasta 254 billones de operaciones por segundo (TOPS). Mercedes indica que la plataforma MB.OS sirve de base para integrar las funciones de asistencia y actualizar el software de los vehículos.
Cuándo llegará y qué modelos podrán usarlo
La empresa prevé ofrecer MB.DRIVE ASSIST PRO en Alemania y Estados Unidos durante la primera mitad de 2027. Antes, desde diciembre de 2026, algunos clientes seleccionados en California, Stuttgart y Múnich podrán probar las funciones mediante un programa de acceso anticipado. Mercedes recopilará comentarios antes de ampliar su disponibilidad.
La compatibilidad dependerá del modelo y del mercado. La compañía adelantó que las funciones se incorporarán gradualmente a su gama de autos de pasajeros y vans, y que algunos propietarios de vehículos elegibles podrán agregarlas después mediante una actualización remota. Mercedes aún no anunció los precios ni el listado completo de modelos compatibles; señaló que informará esos detalles antes de cada lanzamiento.
La información inicial de Mezha sobre la competencia con Tesla también menciona modelos como CLA, GLC, GLE, GLS y Clase S, aunque la comunicación oficial de Mercedes no confirma que todos estén habilitados desde el comienzo.
Una apuesta por la asistencia, no por la autonomía total
El lanzamiento ocurre mientras Mercedes concentra sus esfuerzos en sistemas de nivel 2, que requieren supervisión constante del conductor. La compañía suspendió el desarrollo de Drive Pilot, su tecnología de nivel 3, que bajo ciertas condiciones permitía dejar de vigilar la carretera en algunos tramos de autopista.
Ese cambio refleja una apuesta por funciones que pueden desplegarse en más vehículos y que enfrentan menos barreras regulatorias. Para los conductores, la diferencia práctica será contar con más ayuda para tareas como mantener el recorrido, cambiar de carril o avanzar por la ciudad, sin ceder la responsabilidad de conducir.
Mercedes no es la única fabricante que desarrolla alternativas a Tesla: BMW también trabaja en sistemas de asistencia comparables. La competencia se centrará en ampliar lo que el auto puede hacer y, a la vez, mantener claro cuándo debe intervenir la persona al volante.

articles.title: Corma Receives $125 Million to Train Foundation Models for Defensive Cybersecurity
articles.text:
Cybersecurity startup Corma has raised $125 million in a Series A funding round, bringing the total raised to $185 million and its valuation to $1 billion.
Led by NEA, the investment round saw additional support from previous backers Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Coatue.
Founded in 2025 and headquartered in Tel Aviv and San Francisco, Corma emerged from stealth mode in August with a frontier foundation model specifically designed for defensive cybersecurity.
Corma says AI’s offensive capabilities have grown exponentially over the past several months, while its defensive capabilities have not, and it aims to fill that gap.
The startup trains frontier foundation models and deploys them as AI agents alongside existing security tools to audit security data and correlate signals across environments to improve defenses and help security teams respond to increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks.
“Cybersecurity is now a battle of intelligence against intelligence, and Black October made that impossible to ignore,” said Corma co-founder and CEO Alon Pluda.
“Since we came out of stealth, demand from the world’s largest organizations has been overwhelming, and one of our hardest problems has been securing capacity fast enough to keep up with the demand,” Pluda added.

articles.title: Daydream's new AI agent acts as your personal stylist — and can shop for you, too | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Can an AI agent serve as your personal stylist? That’s what e-commerce veteran Julie Bornstein’s fashion startup, Daydream, aims to find out.
On Tuesday, the company launched “Daydream Agent,” an AI agent that is described as a personal stylist that can help you plan a look, virtually try on clothes, surface relevant pieces based on your taste, and more.
The idea, the company explains, is to put a personal stylist in everyone’s pocket. This application of AI could be promising, given that early adopters of consumer AI agents like Meta’s Muse have found that online shopping is a key use case.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently noted that shopping was a top activity for Muse’s over 10 million users and that 25% of people who set up Muse now use it daily.
In Daydream’s case, the fashion startup has been focused on using AI to deliver personalized shopping results to its users. Its new AI agent builds on its earlier work with an AI chatbot that could help users find outfits and make suggestions, but not complete purchases.
Now the company says its Daydream Agent expands on that experience by remembering each shopper’s own personal style, fit preferences, and budget to refine its recommendations. Shoppers can also upload a photo to have the agent reuse that image to virtually try on any item they’ve saved. When they find something they like, the agent can complete a purchase through a one-click checkout process.
The agent can also handle other fashion-related tasks, like keeping an eye on when items go on sale or when brands have a new drop, or providing weekly updates or spotting new fashion trends.
Also, instead of leaving items in their cart, shoppers can save pieces they’re interested in to a persistent “clothing rack” so they can compare options and think about their purchases before deciding what to buy. Shoppers can also connect their own closet and their calendar to the agent, helping them to build outfits around what they already own and plan what to wear for upcoming events.
The tech works by pulling real-time pricing and availability information from its catalog of over 10,000 brands, then combines that with its fashion-focused artificial intelligence. It’s powered by a combination of OpenAI, Gemini, and Claude models, which it fine-tuned, along with its own trained models designed for particular use cases.
However, considering that fashion is more of an art than a science, the company says it’s keeping humans in the loop. To do so, this month it brought on its first stylist in residence, Francesca Salih, an international fashion stylist and the founder of StyleGrid. Salih provides the startup with styling content that helps shape how the agent pulls together outfits and offers advice. This advice is part of the company’s fashion knowledge database, which the agent experience relies on.
Bornstein, formerly Stitch Fix’s COO and the founder of The Yes (exited to Pinterest in 2022), started Daydream in 2023 as an AI search engine. The company, backed by $50 million in funding from Forerunner Ventures, Index Ventures, GV, and True Ventures, says more than 2 million shoppers have used Daydream to discover apparel and accessories since its June 2025 launch.

articles.title: „Ihr seid zu zögerlich“: Sam Altman rechnet mit der Gen Z ab
articles.text:
Die KI-Revolution sorgt schon jetzt dafür, dass die Zahl der Stellenangebote für Berufseinsteiger:innen rapide abnimmt – auch in Deutschland, wie eine Analyse des Jobportals Indeed kürzlich gezeigt hat. Vor allem Angehörige der sogenannten Gen Z, also zwischen 1997 und 2012 geborene Personen, fürchten, durch den zunehmenden Einsatz von KI-Tools ersetzt zu werden.
Sam Altman: Anhaltend enttäuscht von Gen Z
Sam Altman will solche Sorgen nicht gelten lassen. Im Sommer 2025 prognostizierte der OpenAI-Chef Uni-Absolvent:innen einen Arbeitsalltag der Zukunft, in dem dank KI „einfach alles besser“ ist – „astronomische Gehälter“ inklusive. Die Gen Z teilt Altmans Begeisterung offenbar nicht, was diesen „anhaltend enttäusche“, wie Fortune berichtet.
In einem Interview mit der Stanford Graduate School of Business erklärte Altman, dass die Studierenden lieber machten, was vor fünf Jahren cool war statt etwas Neues auszuprobieren. Dabei, so der KI-Verfechter, sei genau jetzt die richtige Zeit um neue Wege zu gehen.
KI-Revolution bietet auch Chancen
Es sei vollkommen richtig, dass KI eine große Zahl von Dingen, die heute noch Menschen erledigen, künftig besser, günstiger und schneller mache. Zudem übernehme die KI große Bereiche aktueller Tätigkeiten komplett. Aber: Der Umbruch biete auch Chancen für ambitionierte Arbeitskräfte, so Altman. Dazu müsse man aber bereit sein zu überlegen, welche neuen Geschäftsmodelle sich mithilfe von KI entwickeln ließen.
Die Ausgangslage sei so offen wie nie zuvor. Die KI öffne Unternehmer:innen ein seltenes Zeitfenster, um Bereiche aufzubauen, die noch vor wenigen Jahren schwierig oder gar unmöglich gewesen seien, so Altman. Auf Basis der Technologie, so der OpenAI-Chef, ließen sich Unternehmen entwickeln, die weitaus größer und bedeutender sein könnten als OpenAI selbst.
Karriere in Zeiten des größten Wandels
„Wenn ihr euch jetzt in die Welt hinausbegebt, um an etwas zu arbeiten – dann beginnt ihr eure Karriere vermutlich in einer Zeit des größten Wandels“, gab Altman den Stanford-Studierenden mit auf den Weg. Menschen mit großem Potenzial, Tatendrang, Ideen, einer neuen Sichtweise auf die Dinge sowie neuen Fähigkeiten kämen tendenziell besonders gut zurecht, „wenn der Boden am stärksten bebt“.

articles.title: Nike’s new air sole technology can mix soft and firm cushioning
articles.text:
In 2024, Nike announced its Air Max 1000 that were manufactured using a 3D-printing process resulting in a shoe that had a uniform silhouette but varying areas of support and flexibility throughout. The company is now doing something similar with its iconic air-filled soles using its new Tuned Air technology. While previously the level of cushioning in Nike Air shoes was uniform across the entire sole, a new manufacturing process can produce multiple air pockets with varying levels of cushioning and stability.
Nike’s new air sole technology can mix soft and firm cushioning
The first shoes with Nike’s new Tuned Air technology will be available for runners starting in late 2027.
Nike has been putting air pockets into its shoes for nearly 50 years as a way to increase comfort and cushioning while making them lighter. Its air pockets have even found their way into apparel as a way to improve insulation by trapping body heat, but Nike plans to use its new Tuned Air technology as a way to customize the cushioning experience in its shoes and tailor them to specific athletes and sports. The first shoes featuring the technology are expected to arrive in late 2027 and will be targeted at runners.
While one of Nike’s earliest successes was track shoes with a grip design inspired by a waffle iron, the company credits the “vibrant colors on magazine covers” as the inspiration for its latest shoe technology. A Tuned Air sole is manufactured using a “proprietary digital print and selective lamination process” where an ink is applied in specific patterns that define where the layers bond to each other. This process can be used to create internal pockets in an unlimited combination of shapes and sizes, and by fine-tuning how much air is in each of those pockets, some parts of the sole can feel firmer while others feel softer.
The Tuned Air technology will not only allow Nike to highly customize the fit and feel of air sole shoes for different sports, it will also help keep the benefits of the custom tuning consistent across different sizes. The new manufacturing process will also help reduce the amount of time it takes Nike to go from a concept for a new shoe to a final design ready for production. “Prototypes that once took three weeks can now be made in three days,” the company claims in a release today. That gives Nike’s designers more time to refine new shoes, and more opportunity to experiment.

articles.title: A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
articles.text:
A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
- Date:
- November 7, 2026
- Source:
- University of Regensburg
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a surprising quantum limit that prevents electrons from being tracked with unlimited precision in both space and time. The breakthrough could pave the way for manipulating chemical reactions and developing electronics hundreds of thousands of times faster than today's technology.
- Share:
Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.
But position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.
The discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.
Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds
Understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.
However, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.
At RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.
Tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with important changes taking place over just attoseconds.
To appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.
Making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.
Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling
To observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a new laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.
In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.
The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.
Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond."
This approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It showed that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.
What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.
This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.
"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.
A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay
To understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit."
Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.
At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.
For example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit."
The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.
The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.
A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time
Raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially."
In other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.
To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.
This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.
Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.
The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.
Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?
Beyond revealing a new aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.
One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.
Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.
Such extreme conditions could give scientists new ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.
"In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.
The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.
"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the currently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.
That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.
For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.

articles.title: Maintainers don't need more AI bug reports. They need fixes.
articles.text:
Maintainers don’t need more AI bug reports. They need fixes.
In the Codename MDASH pilot, GitHub and Microsoft turned thousands of raw AI findings into 99 checked, private reports with suggested fixes for six widely used open source projects. Maintainers have already fixed more than half.
AI has made finding potential vulnerabilities fast and cheap. Fixing them still takes human judgment, and in open source, that work falls to maintainers. Many are already flooded with AI-generated security findings, including duplicates and reports that aren’t vulnerabilities at all. Another raw scan doesn’t help them. Anyone pointing a new model at a project should ask its maintainers first and come with fixes, not just findings.
AI shouldn’t add to maintainers’ workload. So, with maintainers, GitHub and Microsoft ran a pilot together: could AI help maintainers ship fixes instead of handing them more findings?
GitHub and Microsoft are using Codename MDASH, Microsoft’s multi-model agentic scanning harness, to find and fix security vulnerabilities in widely used open source software, strengthening the foundation that much of the world’s code is built on.
The process
Our pilot had two goals: send only findings that matter, and never send a maintainer an unverified finding. Here’s how it worked:
Find.Codename MDASH, an AI system from Microsoft Security, scanned each project using Microsoft’s MAI Cyber model and suggested fixes for what it found.
Filter. An AI triage agent from the GitHub Security Lab, built on tailored Copilot skills, removed duplicates, checked validity, and focused on high-impact bugs, so maintainers never had to review raw scan results.
Report privately. Reports reached maintainers through GitHub private vulnerability reporting, with a proof of concept and a suggested fix.
Fix. Maintainers decided what to fix, how to fix it, and when.
Reports and fixes stayed on GitHub, where maintainers already work.
The result: Codename MDASH, using Microsoft’s MAI Cyber model, flagged thousands of possible issues across the six projects. After AI triage and hand review by seven Microsoft FORGE Lab researchers, maintainers received 99 private reports. As of November 15, they had fixed 55, and 14 of those fixes were already in a release.
What we learned
These lessons come from what the six projects fixed and what their maintainers chose to share. Six projects is a small sample, so read them as early lessons.
1. Fixes matter more than findings
Fixing is where maintainers spend their time. So every report arrived already checked, with a suggested fix to review, adapt, and merge. Maintainers started from a well-scoped patch, not a raw finding.
The first fixes shipped about a week after the initial scan. Caddy’s maintainers fixed all 22 of the reports they received in a week or less. Maintainers used the suggested fixes, some as written and some with changes.
AutoGPT’s maintainers had recently shipped a new check, and it was broken. The report landed three days later and pointed at the right line. They took the fix further than the suggested patch, wrote it within a day, and had it in production less than a week later.
Finding vulnerabilities is no longer our bottleneck. Fixing them is the hard part, and that depends on maintainers.
Netty maintainer
2. Codename MDASH, with researcher review, gave maintainers high-quality findings with fixes
Maintainers got a short list, not a flood. Express maintainers said the reports cut through the noise. Caddy maintainers said they surfaced obscure bugs and filled gaps that earlier reports had missed. For FastMCP, the scan went beyond what AI scanners had given them before. ImageMagick, maintained by a two-person team, received 22 reports.
AI did the finding, researchers did the checking, and maintainers stayed in charge.
One ImageMagick report looked like a kind of issue the maintainers had seen before. Its summary showed it wasn’t and pointed to the exact lines of code. They were able to push a fix in 15 minutes.
Normally, a security advisory would take us around 30 minutes to 1 hour on average to read, understand, and make a fix. It is a huge difference.
ImageMagick maintainer
Codename MDASH was able to find unknown, obscure security bugs in our project with succinct reports, and it filled in gaps from some prior reports that hadn’t been noticed.
Caddy maintainer
3. Open source still has gaps to close
The pilot worked because people did careful work at every step, and that work doesn’t scale yet. Seven researchers spent about two days per project checking findings by hand. Meanwhile, low-quality reports still reach maintainers every day.
For open source, fixes need to be delivered via private vulnerability reporting (PVR). Maintainers need to run CI/CD tests on private forks to verify those fixes. And to close the gap between defenders and attackers, maintainers need access to cyber-capable models to verify a proof of concept, before and after the fix.
The Codename MDASH scan provided unique insights into the security of our project above and beyond what AI scanners have provided us in the past
FastMCP maintainer
Why it matters
If you’re a maintainer, this approach changes what a security report costs you. A checked, private report that comes with a suggested fix takes less of your time. You shouldn’t have to triage a scanner’s output. That’s the sender’s job.
If you use AI to find vulnerabilities in open source, maintainers’ feedback points to this standard:
Check every finding before you send it, against what the project already knows and against its threat model and security policy.
Report it privately.
Include a suggested fix. Let maintainers set the pace.
Features are easier and easier to ship, but in the future maintaining software will probably come down to who cares enough to manage the security.
AutoGPT maintainer
Codename MDASH is very useful for cutting through the noise of vulnerability reports.
Express maintainer
What you can do today
If you maintain any open source project, turn on private vulnerability reporting so researchers can report security issues to you without making them public. If your project is on GitHub, turn on core security features in about two minutes with gh-secure.
If you build on open source, turn on Dependabot alerts so you know when a dependency you use needs a security update.
If you send AI-generated vulnerability reports to open source projects, hold them to the standard above before you send them.
Repositories using GitHub code security can use agentic autofix to help automatically remediate their alerts with Copilot
What happens next
Fixes, where maintainers already work. GitHub is bringing these lessons into private vulnerability reporting and security advisories, where GitHub Security Lab is already investing to reduce the burden of low-quality reports on maintainers.
MAI Cyber 2. Today Microsoft announced MAI Cyber 2. The Codename MDASH pilot ran on the earlier MAI Cyber model. GitHub and Microsoft will keep working together to help secure open source.
Closing the gaps, starting with the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund. We’re working with Microsoft to scale researcher review without cutting corners. GitHub will offer every alumni project AI security scans, with findings checked before they’re reported privately. Alumni also get GitHub Copilot Max. We’ll bring this support to future sessions of the Fund.
Everyone downstream benefits from this system. When a maintainer publishes a security advisory on GitHub and it’s reviewed for the GitHub Advisory Database, Dependabot can alert the repositories that depend on that package. That’s the idea behind the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund: 216 projects so far, with more than 300 maintainers fixing more than 4,000 vulnerabilities in software downloaded more than 20 billion times a month.
Thank you
To the maintainers of AutoGPT, Caddy, Express, FastMCP, ImageMagick, and Netty: thank you for your time, your trust, and your feedback. Thank you also to the Codename MDASH team at Microsoft Security, the MAI Cyber team, the researchers of Microsoft FORGE Lab, and GitHub Security Lab.
Maintainers do the fixing. Our job is to make sure they never do it alone.
Hear from maintainers about their experience with Codename MDASH. 👇
About the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund
All six projects in this pilot are alumni of the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund, which gives each project $10,000 through GitHub Sponsors, plus security training and a supportive alumni community.
The GitHub Secure Open Source Fund, powered by GitHub Sponsors, funds open source projects that underpin the digital supply chain, catalyze innovation, and are critical to the AI stack. Want your company to help secure the open source it depends on? Become a funding partner through the Fund page. Learn more about the Fund or apply.
Through the Fund, maintainers receive security training and Azure credits from Microsoft for Startups. That support sits alongside Microsoft’s European Security Program and its Secure Future Initiative, whose principle is security above all else. Most organizations are downstream in the same way. If your software depends on open source, do the same: back the maintainers you rely on.
I work on open source strategy and programs that support maintainers inside GitHub and across the ecosystem. I also serve on the Steering Committee for the TODO Group, where we help organizations use and sustain open source responsibly.
Git is releasing updates addressing six security vulnerabilities affecting clones, reference handling, merges, binary patches, and imports. Here is what users need to know.
GitHub now highlights ACCESSIBILITY.md files and helps maintainers document accessibility goals, known barriers, supported environments, contributor expectations, and reporting processes.

articles.title: Not even Sam Altman is safe from AI deepfakes on Instagram
articles.text:
Instagram is filled with people posting deepfaked content — including, as of late, from one of Meta’s most prominent executives.
Not even Sam Altman is safe from AI deepfakes on Instagram
Meta’s chief AI officer posted an AI video of a top competitor. It’s allowed under Meta’s AI policy.
Earlier in November, Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, shared a short clip to promote Muse, the company’s consumer AI agent. In the AI-generated clip, Wang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and Jolly, the anthropomorphic mascot of Muse, are on a four-way video call. When Altman joins the call he’s dressed like Jolly, wearing a furry hooded suit and face paint to look like the cutesy character. The clip is captioned “When the homies meet about openai product strategy,” a reference to the AI agent race and the recent popularity of Muse.
Just a few years ago, AI content portraying real people led to strong public statements rebuking the use of the technology to imitate humans. In some cases legal action was threatened. Now, AI content has become part of the texture of a new reality, especially on social media. Leading up to the midterm elections, for example, political groups ran millions of dollars’ worth of AI-generated ads attacking opponents.
Wang has been doing a lot of what some have described as “anti-PR” to promote Muse, tweeting hundreds of times and referring to more traditional marketers as “corposlops.” Still, a major tech executive posting an AI video of a competitor is notable, especially on a platform that’s been criticized recently over AI-generated content. After an AI-generated image of actress Mia Goth gained traction in October, the Pearl star’s representative told The Verge it was “incomprehensible” that Instagram allowed the image to spread instead of focusing on the “protection and integrity of a public figure’s likeness.” Other celebrities, including Scarlett Johansson, are regularly the subject of sexualized AI imagery; Meta has removed some accounts in the past that it found to be posing as someone else and using their likeness.
Meta requires AI-generated videos depicting people to be labeled as AI, like Wang’s post is. Static images, however, have no such requirement, meaning the AI image of Goth had no disclosure. To make matters worse, the image was shared by a fan account with a blue verification badge given by Instagram.
Reached for comment, Meta spokesperson Tracy Clayton noted that Wang’s post is labeled as AI content. Clayton also pointed out that Altman has made his likeness available for AI content generation, as when OpenAI launched its Sora app (and it was quickly flooded with fake Altman videos). OpenAI didn’t respond to requests for comment.

articles.title: TikTok moviliza y Facebook polariza hacia la extrema derecha: así describen las redes nuestro voto
articles.text:
TikTok moviliza y Facebook polariza hacia la extrema derecha: así describen las redes nuestro voto
Una nueva investigación con datos inéditos de una operadora francesa confirma que las plataformas inciden en el voto y permite observar cómo algunas plataformas etiquetan políticamente a sus usuarios
En dos municipios similares en renta, paro y edad, ¿a quién votan más sus ciudadanos si consumen más Facebook? A la extrema derecha. ¿Y si navegan sobre todo por Instagram? Se inclinan más por partidos más bien de centro y progresistas. ¿Y TikTok? En ese lugar, habrá más movilización, repartida entre todos los partidos. ¿Y si destacan por leer medios de comunicación en internet? Sobre todo, no votarán a la extrema derecha.
Estas conclusiones pertenecen a una nueva investigación realizada con datos muy difíciles de lograr para la mayoría de académicos: la navegación de 22 millones de ciudadanos franceses durante las elecciones europeas de 2019 y 2024. Además de las valoraciones sobre cada red social, el trabajo llega a otra gran conclusión que a menudo se pone en duda: las redes sociales tienen impacto en las democracias. “No encontrar ninguna correlación hubiera sido como una prueba de que las aplicaciones no afectan de ningún modo el voto”, dice Marco Fiore, del instituto de investigación Imdea Networks de Madrid. “Como hemos encontrado correlaciones, ya no es posible”, añade Fiore, coautor del trabajo con académicos de la Universidad Carlos III, la Universidad Northeastern (Boston) y la operadora Orange en Francia.
No todas las redes tienen un impacto significativo o en una sola dirección. El artículo mide 27 plataformas o servicios online en 2024, desde redes a medios de información agrupados o servicios de streaming. TikTok tiene un enorme efecto movilizador a favor de todos los partidos en 2024 (en 2019 no se midió por su papel menor), pero también lo tienen, aunque menos, YouTube, LinkedIn o Telegram. La mayoría de servicios de streaming no apuntan a nada muy notable.
Facebook, más que nadie
La red social con un impacto más notable y consistente en el voto entre 2019 y 2024 es, sin ninguna duda, Facebook. No solo los municipios con un uso relativo mayor de Facebook votan más a la extrema derecha de Marine Le Pen; también votan menos al resto de partidos, sobre todo La Francia Insumisa, de Jean-Luc Mélenchon, según el estudio.
La red X, antes Twitter, es un caso curioso. La opinión popular es que, desde la compra de Elon Musk en 2022, la plataforma se ha vuelto más conservadora. En las europeas francesas, al menos, el proceso ha sido el contrario: de vincularse a un voto más centrista en 2019 a algo más progresista ahora.
Los investigadores han querido comprobar también la utilidad de sus resultados para ayudar a predecir el voto: ¿qué pasa si añadimos el consumo digital de los ciudadanos a las variables tradicionales demográficas? Hicieron dos modelos: el primero trataba de predecir el voto solo con renta, paro y edad. El segundo añade las aplicaciones digitales. El segundo acierta más (y más aún con el paso de los años y la penetración del mundo online): un 9,6% más en 2019 y un 28% más en 2024. Esa mejora es la información sobre el voto que aporta internet y que los datos socioeconómicos no recogen.
El mismo grupo ya usó datos similares en 2022 para averiguar si el uso de internet también era capaz de predecir el estatus socioeconómico. Entonces los medios, la música por streaming, el WhatsApp y el email aumentaban la probabilidad de zona rica. Si, al contrario, se usaba más Facebook, YouTube, Snapchat, se miraba porno y se jugaba al Candy Crush, las opciones de que fuera un barrio pobre crecían.
“Después de aquel primer estudio donde vimos una señal tan clara, esperábamos que ocurriera en otras dimensiones de la vida”, dice Iñaki Úcar, profesor de la Universidad Carlos III y coautor de ambos trabajos. “Si eso funcionó, pues tiene que funcionar para más cosas como el voto. En el aspecto político se da una cosa que no se da en el socioeconómico. En las redes hay una retroalimentación que hace que tu comportamiento se vea reforzado”, añade.
Los investigadores insisten en que todo esto no significa que las redes provoquen nada. Es el célebre mantra de “correlación no implica causalidad”: que dos cosas pasen a la vez no significa que una sea causa de la otra. Es cierto que un usuario de Facebook puede radicalizarse viendo la red día tras día. Pero también es cierto que sea primero de ideología de ultraderecha y acabe luego en Facebook.
Es como si en municipios similares más gente viera un medio conservador o progresista. Es lógico que acabarán votando a los partidos que representen esas ideas. No estaba claro que con las plataformas online ocurriera algo parecido. Pero cada vez hay más pruebas.
También es innegable que el impacto de internet es total. “El mundo digital va teniendo una importancia mayor”, dice Fiore. “Si los operadores quieren ayudar a explicar el voto con datos agregados, ayudaría a explicar más allá de lo que se puede hacer ahora”, añade.

articles.title: Elastic{ON} Mumbai: Why context, not the model, is the real AI advantage
articles.text:
Elastic
View Brand Publisher
Elastic{ON} Mumbai: Why context, not the model, is the real AI advantage
At Elastic{ON} Mumbai, CEO Ash Kulkarni argued that every business already owns what AI models lack. The rest of the day showed what it takes to put that context to work.
As AI models become available to everyone, the advantage for enterprises is shifting to something no model providers can supply: the context that makes AI useful to a specific business. Elastic{ON} Mumbai took on that challenge, bringing together the people building and running AI in India’s enterprises to work out how to make their data count.
The Elastic{ON} Tour 2026/2027 stopped in Mumbai on September 30, bringing developers, SREs, IT and security leaders and practitioners to JW Marriott Mumbai Sahar under the theme ‘Forge the Future’. Across keynotes, live demos, customer and partner sessions, and a hackathon awards ceremony, one idea kept returning: context is what turns a widely available model into a lasting business advantage.
Context is your moat
Ash Kulkarni, CEO of Elastic, who grew up a short distance away in Vile Parle, opened by tying the company’s name to the city. “Mumbai has stretched, it has evolved, it has transformed. It has never broken,” he said.
That adaptability matters, he argued, because AI is moving faster than any earlier technology shift, and the models driving it share a blind spot. “None of these models have any understanding of your business. They don’t understand your data,” Kulkarni said. “The bottleneck is the context.”
Every industry now faces startups trading human capital for token capital. What they cannot copy, Kulkarni said, is a company’s accumulated learnings, experience, and data on how best to serve its customers and partners. “That context is your moat.”
The challenge is that context is scattered. Customer information alone sits across CRM, entitlement, and ticketing systems. Kulkarni’s answer is a bridge that connects it all, securely and with privacy built in, to any model. The result, he said, is “actual intelligence”: the reasoning power of the model combined with the context of the business. Delivering that has meant evolving Elastic’s core engine.
Making context affordable
Ajay Nair, GM, Elasticsearch and Platform, Elastic, picked up the thread. “The model’s only half the equation,” he said. An agent that does not know a customer has raised ten support tickets might still send them a renewal pitch, and that will not go well.
Nair said most teams make their models rebuild context from scratch every time a question is asked, an approach he called “top-down” context that burns tokens on every query. The more efficient pattern is “bottom-up”: deriving relationships, metadata, and risk factors once, keeping them fresh, and handing models a ready-made picture.
That is the idea behind the Elastic Context Engine, which Nair announced on stage and which is now in private preview.
Context at work in operations and security
The same foundation runs through Elastic’s observability and security solutions. Vinay Chandrasekhar, Director of Product Management, Observability, Elastic, demonstrated Elastic nightshift AI SRE, an AI agent that surfaces problems no alert was set up to catch, tests several root-cause hypotheses in parallel, and shows every step of its reasoning. Kulkarni noted that it gets better at investigating “within the context of your environment”, adding: “It’s not generic.” Elastic has since announced nightshift in private preview on Elastic Observability Serverless.
James Spiteri, Senior Director of Product Management, Elastic, argued that “the SIEM has never mattered more”. He previewed what has since launched as AlertZero, the agentic layer built into Elastic Security. Specialised groups of agents, called Watches, triage alerts, hunt for threats, and investigate incidents, learning from how a team already works, while analysts decide which actions need their approval. AlertZero is now available in technical preview across Elastic Cloud, self-managed, and air-gapped environments.
A day built with the community
Beyond the keynotes, customers carried much of the program. On the morning panel, moderated by Ravindra Ramnani, Head of Field Engineering at Elastic India, leaders from Axis Bank, Standard Chartered Bank, and Easebuzz debated whether enterprises can observe, audit, and explain what their AI agents do. Nykaa joined AWS to describe how its SREs now investigate incidents by querying logs conversationally with Elastic AI Assistant. Afternoon breakouts featured Network18 on AI governance, Qualys on closing the SOC loop with agentic AI, and Standard Chartered Bank on standardising observability across 40 countries, alongside community sessions from Iron Mountain, Jolera, and Sprinklr.
Partners showed how they ground AI in enterprise context. Google Cloud explained how its agent tooling and Gemini models work with Elastic retrieval to turn sensitive enterprise data into trusted context without moving it. Microsoft and Elastic walked through OverflowAI, Stack Overflow’s retrieval-first architecture, in which Elasticsearch hybrid retrieval grounds Azure OpenAI in the community’s validated answers.
The community also had its moment on the main stage, as the Forge the Future Hackathon awards recognised the top teams from the Grand Finale held in Bengaluru on September 18 and 19. Frustrated Engineers took first place, followed by Sandboxed in second and Defcon in third. Powered by Elastic and AWS, the hackathon challenged teams to build explainable, production-ready AI agents across search, observability, and security.
Models will change. Context stays.
Kulkarni closed with commitments that put a customer’s context, not any single model, at the centre. Elastic will stay model agnostic, he said, because “there is no winner yet, and there will likely never be a single winner.” It will also run wherever customers do, in the cloud or self-managed.
Models will keep getting better. The context that makes them useful belongs to the business, and Elastic{ON} Mumbai made the case that connecting the two is where the lasting advantage lies.

articles.title: Elle paie intégralement une BYD neuve pour les 60 ans de son beau-père, un homme en uniforme de la marque la vole dans la concession avant une course-poursuite d’une heure pour la récupérer
articles.text:
Elle paie intégralement une BYD neuve pour les 60 ans de son beau-père, un homme en uniforme de la marque la vole dans la concession avant une course-poursuite d’une heure pour la récupérer
Elle pensait faire plaisir en achetant une BYD neuve pour les 60 ans de son beau-père d'une valeur de 155 000 ¥, soit environ 20 900 €, payé par la famille. Sauf que voilà, un inconnu en uniforme BYD est monté à bord et a quitté la concession avec la voiture avant même la livraison.
C'est le 10 novembre 2026 que l'histoire a lieu à Changsha, dans la province du Hunan en Chine. Une femme dont le nom de famille est Xiong a parcouru plusieurs centaines de kilomètres avec son mari et des proches jusqu'à la concession BYD Jinxuanfeng. La famille a choisi une BYD Song à 149 000 ¥ et réglé 155 000 ¥ avec l'assurance, soit environ 20 900 €.
Une course-poursuite pour retrouver la BYD
Le contrat était signé et ne restait qu'à nettoyer la voiture puis poser des films sur les vitres. Vers 18 heures, la famille patiente dans le salon réservé aux clients quand un vendeur de la concession leur annonce la disparition de la BYD. La police a été alertée immédiatement.
Les employés ont suivi la voiture grâce à sa géolocalisation depuis une application mobile, puis sont partis à sa poursuite avec le beau-père et le beau-frère de Xiong. Il a fallu plus d'une heure et plus de 20 kilomètres pour intercepter la BYD, puis les policiers ont pris le conducteur en charge.
Au moment de son interpellation, l'homme portait une tenue de travail avec le logo de BYD. Mais le responsable commercial explique qu'il ne faisait pas partie des employés de la concession. Il s'agit d'un jeune homme qui a acheté cet uniforme sur Internet, d'une couleur différente de celle des salariés. Selon le personnel, il a des antécédents de vols de voitures et voulait simplement satisfaire son envie de conduire.
Le responsable commercial reconnaît des failles dans l'organisation de la livraison. Un employé a laissé la clé électronique dans la voiture pour la déplacer plus facilement, puis s'est absenté quelques minutes pour récupérer les plaques d'immatriculation temporaires. La concession donne directement sur la rue sans poste de garde et aucune caméra ne surveille la zone de livraison.
La famille a finalement été remboursée
Xiong et ses proches ont ensuite refusé de prendre livraison d'une voiture conduite par un inconnu. Le 11 novembre au matin, la concession a restitué les 155 000 ¥ et lancé le remboursement de l'assurance. La famille a aussi réclamé ses frais de déplacement, de carburant et d'hébergement.
Xiong a même invoqué la législation chinoise sur la protection des consommateurs pour demander trois fois le montant de l'achat. La concession a accepté de payer les frais de déplacement mais a refusé cette sanction prévue pour les commerçants qui trompent volontairement leurs clients. Son responsable explique que l'établissement a lui aussi subi le vol, avec une voiture déjà immatriculée qu'il sera compliqué de revendre comme neuve.
Le 15 novembre, Xiong a annoncé sur les réseaux sociaux que ses démarches ont abouti de manière satisfaisante. La police de Changsha a ouvert une enquête dès le soir du vol et le suspect était en détention au 16 novembre.

articles.title: Black Friday : moins de 700 € pour un vélo électrique pensé pour la ville
articles.text:
Le Black Friday bat son plein chez Intersport, qui multiplie les promotions sur les vélos électriques. Parmi les modèles concernés figure le CrossCity LTD, un vélo de ville signé Nakamura. Même si les beaux jours sont derrière nous, rien n’empêche de profiter d’une balade à vélo lorsque la météo le permet. Avec son autonomie annoncée de 60 km et son porte-bagages pratique pour transporter quelques courses, ce modèle se présente aussi comme un allié des trajets quotidiens, en alternative à la voiture.
Le CrossCity LTD passe ainsi à 699,99 € au lieu de 1 199,99 €, soit 500 € de moins. 
Que vaut le Nakamura CrossCity LTD ?
Le CrossCity LTD repose sur un cadre ouvert en acier, facile à enjamber, avec des roues de 26 pouces et une selle confort. Son moteur est logé dans le moyeu arrière, c’est-à-dire directement dans l’axe de la roue. Il délivre 45 Nm de couple, la force qui vous pousse au démarrage et dans les montées. L’assistance se règle sur cinq niveaux via un petit afficheur LED. Une transmission Shimano à six vitesses, commandée par une poignée tournante, permet d’adapter le pédalage quand la pente se durcit.
La batterie de 470 Wh se loge sous le porte-bagages. Intersport annonce jusqu’à 60 km d’autonomie, un chiffre obtenu dans des conditions optimales : terrain plat, météo favorable. Le relief, le froid et un niveau d’assistance élevé le feront baisser. Les pneus Kestrel de 26 x 1,75 sont prévus pour la route comme pour les chemins. Un sentier stabilisé ne devrait donc pas lui poser trop de problèmes. Sa fourche rigide en acier le réserve en revanche aux chemins praticables : ce n’est pas un VTT.
Côté équipement, l’essentiel est là : porte-bagages intégré, garde-boue en aluminium, béquille centrale et éclairage LED à l’avant comme à l’arrière. De quoi rentrer du marché avec le stock de poireaux. Deux limites sont à connaître. Le freinage confié à des V-brake, des patins qui pincent la jante, est simple à entretenir mais moins puissant sous la pluie que des freins à disque. Avec 24 kg sur la balance, le vélo se monte aussi difficilement dans un escalier.
À ce prix, le CrossCity LTD est-il une bonne affaire ?
À 699,99 €, la remise atteint plus de 40 % du prix d’origine. Pour ce montant, vous avez un vélo électrique prêt à rouler, avec éclairage, garde-boue et porte-bagages fournis. Ces accessoires sont souvent à acheter en plus sur les modèles d’entrée de gamme. Le poids, le cadre en acier et les freins à patins rappellent toutefois son positionnement. C’est un vélo pour la ville et les balades tranquilles, plus que pour les longues sorties sportives.
Reste que le Nakamura CrossCity LTD constitue une solution intéressante pour les déplacements quotidiens en ville comme pour les balades du week-end.

articles.title: GTA 6 sur PS5 : pourquoi la dernière mise à jour système est obligatoire — Frandroid
articles.text:
Vous avez posé votre jour de congé, libéré de l’espace sur votre disque dur et débranché votre téléphone pour jouer à GTA 6 en toute tranquillité demain ? Parfait, mais avant d’en profiter, il va également falloir que vous installiez la toute dernière mise à jour de votre PS5 ou PS5 Pro.
Sony vient en effet de déployer un correctif de dernière minute qu’il faut installer en urgence si vous espérez pouvoir lancer le jeu le plus attendu de la décennie dès sa sortie demain, note Eurogamer.
Comment mettre à jour sa PS5 / PS5 Pro pour se préparer à GTA 6 ?
En apparence, la version 26.07-14.23.00 ne fait que combler quelques failles dans le système d’exploitation, mais le compte X de PlayStation a bel et bien confirmé que l’installation du correctif était nécessaire pour pouvoir jouer à GTA 6. « Les joueurs et joueuses sont invités à télécharger cette mise à jour avant minuit le 19 novembre afin d’être prêts à jouer dès le jour de la sortie le 19 novembre », lit-on dans le message.
Pour mettre à jour votre console vers la dernière version du système, rien de bien sorcier.
- Rendez-vous dans le menu « Paramètres » (en haut à droite)
- Choisissez l’option « Système »
- Sélectionnez « Logiciel système »
- Cliquez sur « Paramètres et mise à jour du logiciel système »
- Si la mention « Mise à jour disponible » apparaît, cliquez sur « Mettre à jour le logiciel système »
  - Si la mention « À jour » apparaît, vous n’avez rien à faire
Vous pouvez aussi vérifier la version du micrologiciel installé sur votre PS5 en vous rendant dans Paramètres ⇒ Système ⇒ Logiciel système ⇒ Information de la console pour vous assurer que la version 26.07-14.23.00 est bien installée.
Une course sans fin
Cette mise à jour de dernière minute fait suite à un piratage de la version précédente du micrologiciel de la PS5 qui aurait pu permettre à des pirates un peu débrouillards de mettre la main sur les fichiers d’installation de GTA 6. Des données très très prisées à l’heure où les IA permettent de décompiler des jeux plus vite que la musique.
    Pour aller plus loin
GTA 6 sur PS5 : les réglages indispensables à appliquer avant jeudi pour jouer dans les meilleures conditions
            
Sony, comme Xbox, va devoir faire la course aux failles pendant encore quelque temps pour espérer garder leurs poules aux œufs d’or bien au chaud dans leur petit écosystème fermé.
